units.tr: To the Candid Reader, greeting.

units.la: QVadriennium jam, aut eo amplius est, amice Lector, cùm Londini inter libros agens, & privatas amicorum bibliothecas, varia mecum, quò animum à præsentibus miseriis fortiùs avocarem, quasi in lucem posteà product urus, agitabam. Inter ea erat de ortu sermonis tractatus, satis accuratus: cui comitem de verborum usu, ob argumenti affinitatem, diatribam, adjungere statueram. Jam eò rem perduxeram, ut utrique solâ transcriptione, ut typographo traderentur, opus esset. Ita verò contigit, ut absolutâ diatribâ (quæ minor longè) transcriptione, dum in priore illo tractatu occupatur amanuensis, uterque aliud agere, & quod in manibus erat opus omittere, coacti simus. Actum erat de utroque fortasse, (neque enim is ego sum, qui semel omissa libenter in manus resumam:) nisi bibliopola cui spes facta erat majoris operis & lucri, saltem quod erat transcriptum, nec ab altero sic pendebat, ut seorsim prodire non posset, ut id sibi traderetur institisset. Annuente me, prodiit in lucem De verborum usu Diatriba: in cujus primo aditu promissa de quatuor linguis, Hebraicâ, Græcâ, Latinâ, & Saxonicâ, cujus Χαρλύπωσιν pridem animo conceperam, commentatio. Τὸν χαρδιοσυνὴν tefor non aliter tum credidisse me, quin paucis, si semel aggrederer, septimanis expedire, totámque ultimâ manu impositâ publici juris facere facile possem. Erat tum vita in publicâ rerum ἀνωλαςασία valdè desultoria; ut non mirum sit, si animus quoque tale quid interdum passus est. Deerant tum libri, & charta decerant, quarum ad istud pensum pertexendum usus erat. ad aliud me contuli, ad quod & animus tum propensior, de cultu Dei, falso & vero, jam priorem partem absolveram, quam etiam viri quidam ab eruditione summi hic viderunt & legerunt; cum ecce novus terror, & omnia in Vrbe tumultus plena. Mea tum res sic tulerunt, ut relicto quicquid erat librariæ supellectilis, cum familiâ rus ad quinquagesimum usque ab Vrbe lapidem migrandum esset: atque ibi tandem in loco (mihi quidem) solo, & domo vacuâ sedes qualiscunque fixa est. Longè tum curæ Musicæ; & ita facilè mihi persuadebam, quæ me in has latebras TOT ἀῤῥ τῶν providentia detrusisset, eandem ab alioquovis munere & opere, præterquam curâ valetudinis & familiæ, vacationem, si non & plenam missionem, dedisse. Abiit sic annus unus & alter; ingenio, nescio quam, corpori certè peropportuni, cum valetudini ante hunc secessum valdè concussæ & afflictæ nunquam melius, quod gratus agnosco, fuerit. Accidit interim ut frequentes ad me perferrentur, hotorum, non unius; sed & ignotorum quorundam flagitationes super promissâ de quatuor linguis commentatione. De linguâ præsertim Saxonicâ quid illud esset quod allaturus haberem, non unus, ut narrabant, mirari; causamque cum nobilioribus istis conjungendi, scischitari. Sed & longa jam inertiâ tedium invaserat: & jam libros aliquos, quod nunquam in isto loco fore speraveram, partémq; chartularum nactus eram. Quia tamen obstinaveram, quod ultimum in manibus habueram, id primum resumere, & donec absolvissem, aliis omnibus antevertere; in eo animo morigeratus meo; & eâ curâ defunctus, ad promissam illam commentationem me converti, ab Hebraicâ, ut par erat, exorsus lingua. In hoc dum versor,
units.tr: For four years now, or a little more, dear reader, I have been turning over various projects in my mind while living in London and going through books and the private libraries of friends, partly to draw my spirit more firmly away from present miseries, and partly as if I were going to bring them to light afterwards. Among these was a fairly careful treatise on the origin of speech. Because of the affinity of the subject, I had decided to add to it a shorter dissertation on the use of words. I had brought the matter so far that both needed only to be copied out and handed to the printer. But it so happened that, once the dissertation (which is much shorter) was finished, the copyist was occupied with the first treatise, and we were both forced to turn to other business and leave aside the work in hand. The matter would have ended there for both, perhaps, for I am not one who willingly takes up again what he has once set aside. But a bookseller, who had hoped for a larger work and more profit, insisted that what had been copied, and which did not depend on the other so closely that it could not appear separately, be handed over to him. With my consent, the dissertation On the Use of Words came out. At its opening it carried the promised commentary on the four languages, Hebrew, Greek, Latin and Saxon, which I had long had in mind under a title of its own. I did not then believe otherwise than that, if I once took it up, I could finish it in a few weeks and easily make it public after a last revision. Life at that time, amid the public affairs in constant upheaval, was very restless, so it is no wonder that my mind sometimes suffered something of the same. Books were lacking then, and so was the paper needed to carry that task through. So I turned to another matter, to which my mind was then more inclined, on true and false worship of God. I had already finished the first part of it, which certain men eminent in learning saw and read here. Then behold a new terror, and the whole city full of tumult. My affairs then turned out so that, leaving behind whatever bookish furniture I had, I had to move with my household into the country, some fifty miles from the city. There at last a settled, if humble, abode was found, in a place (for me at least) quiet, in an empty house. Care for my studies was far off then, and so I readily persuaded myself that the providence which had thrust me into these hiding places amid such turmoil had granted me exemption from every other office and labour, except the care of my health and family, if not full discharge. So a year and then another passed, good for my mind, I know not how, and certainly very suitable for my body, which had been badly shaken and worn down before this retreat and had never been better, for which I gratefully acknowledge it. Meanwhile it happened that frequent requests came to me, not from one person only but from several, and from some who were unknown to me, about the promised commentary on the four languages. Especially about Saxon, people said, more than one wondered what I could possibly have to offer, and they asked why I had linked it with those nobler tongues. But long idleness had also brought weariness, and I had now obtained some books, which I had never hoped to find in that place, and a supply of paper. Yet because I had resolved to take up first the work I had last had in hand, and to put all else before it until I finished it, I gave way to my own resolve in this, and, having discharged that task, turned to the promised commentary, beginning, as was fitting, with the Hebrew language. While I am engaged in this,

units.la: Ad Lectorem.
units.tr: To the Reader.

units.la: versor, ab aliis curis, sed praecipuè charissimi & conjunctissimi capitis diuturnâ invaletudine & periculo saepius interpellatus, nihil propius factum, quàm ut omnia ista procul à me iis Μαγγείαν facesse juberem. Et feci‍ssem, puto, nisi de Saxonicâ lingua res haesisset animo, in eoque existimationis non parum interesse credidissem, ne verba Lectori dedisse, & futilibus eum (quod abominor) promissis, quibus nullus esset fundus, lactare voluisse videremur. Absoluta igitur primâ quadripartiti pensi parte, statim ad ultimam, linguam Saxonicam, quasi trajeci; magnâ deinceps constantiâ cum aliis molestissimis curis ac negotiis collustratus, donec ad umbilicum perduxissem. Hac igitur ratio Ϲυζυγίας istius, quam non ratio, sed casus obtulit. Quanquam si quod plerique docti volunt, ex Hebraicâ totâ fere vetus lingua Graeca fluxit; ex Graecâ autem tota fere, quod hic docemus, Anglica vetus: non plane contra rationem fuerit hac conjunctio. Et si quis id agat, haud pauca in Anglicâ linguâ reperiet, quae ab ipsis immediatè Hebraeis, an Graecis accepta sint, dubium sit. Sed haec utcunque dici possint, quia tamen non id à nobis hic spectatum agnoscimus,
units.tr: I was constantly interrupted by other cares, and above all by the long illness and frequent danger of my dearest and closest head [capitis]. Nothing more sensible occurred to me than to send all these things far away from me to the magic arts [Μαγγείαν]. And I would have done so, I think, had the matter of the Saxon language not stuck in my mind, and had I not believed that my reputation was not a little at stake, lest we seem to have deceived the reader and to have boasted of empty promises with no foundation, which I abhor. So, having finished the first part of this four-part task, I at once crossed over, as it were, to the last, the Saxon language. Then, with great steadfastness, amid other very troublesome cares and business, I worked through it until I had brought it to the midpoint. This, then, is the reason for this pairing, which was offered not by reasoning but by chance. Although, if many learned men are right that the old language of almost all of Greek flowed from Hebrew, and that the old English flowed almost entirely from Greek, as we teach here, this conjunction would not be entirely against reason. And if anyone pursues this, he will find not a few things in the English language whose origin, whether taken directly from the Hebrews themselves or from the Greeks, is doubtful. But however these things may be said, since we acknowledge that this is not what we are looking at here,

units.la: Ad Lectorem.
units.tr: To the Reader.

units.la: scimus, non eò confugiemus. Fateor ad plures ex prateritis de lingua Graca & Latina partibus fructum redire potuisse, in quibus tum alia, tum jactatissima de novis methodis controversia tota pertractatur. Sed hoc ipsum cùm plus sit, quàm quisquam nunc à nobis, qui rerum status, jure potuerit sibi promittere; candidi Lectoris erit si quam ex his utilitatem percipiet, non quod maluisset, importunius exposcere; sed quod nos potuimus & praestitimus, aequi bonique consulere. Vale.
units.tr: We know this, and we will not take refuge in it. I admit that more people might have profited from the earlier parts on the Greek and Latin languages, in which, among other matters, the much-debated controversy about new methods is treated at length. But since this is more than anyone can rightly expect from us in the present state of affairs, it will be for the candid reader to accept with fairness and goodwill whatever usefulness he perceives in these, and not to demand more troublesomely what he would have preferred, but to take kindly what we were able to supply and did supply. Farewell.

units.la: DE LINGUA HEBRAICA.
units.tr: Concerning the Hebrew Language.

units.la: ATque hîc primùm se nobis offert, ut quæ ad linguam Hebraicam non unâ ratione pertineat, celebratissima illa linguarum (ita vulgò vocant, quod sacer stylus, linguæ, labii, sermonum consusionem; de quo posteà pluribus:) confusio, quæ turris Babylonicæ conditoribus, justo manifestóque Dei judicio, sed occulto modo inflicta est. Sunt autem multa in hac historia, de de quibus inter doctos jam olim, & nunc controvertitur, non minore ferè judiciorum & dubiorum, si singula expendantur, varietate; quàm fuisse illam linguarum ex hâc consusione ortarum varietatem pleriq; sanciunt. Ego quidem certè in iis, quæ Pererius super his pridem commentatus est, libenter acquiesco; nec adhuc vidi, quanquam multi post illum aggressi sunt, qui plura aut certiora afferret.
units.tr: Here, first, there presents itself to us that most famous confusion of tongues (so they commonly call it, since the sacred style speaks of the confusion of tongue, lip and speech; I will say more on this later), which was inflicted on the builders of the Tower of Babel by a just and manifest judgment of God, yet in a hidden manner. Many questions in this history have been disputed among scholars, both long ago and now, and if each is weighed separately they show no less variety of opinions and doubts than the variety of languages arising from this confusion, which most writers hold to have occurred. For my part, I gladly rest content with what Pererius wrote on these matters some time ago. Although many have taken up the subject after him, I have not yet seen anyone who offered more or more certain things.

units.la: B ferret. Si quis tamen, Græcis & Latinis scriptoribus non contentus, Hebraicos quoque scriptores adhibere velit in consilium, accuratè nuper collegit eorum sententias vir doctissimus, istarum linguarum callentissimus, Johannes Buxtorfius Filius, in eruditâ Diatribâ. Sed studiosos linguarum non pæniteat alios quoque, nonnullos etiam fortasse mihi nec-dum visos, consuluisse: duos certè recentiores, viros doctissimos: Samuelem Bochartum, in Geographiâ Sacrâ; & Phari Vet. Test. authorem.
units.tr: If anyone, however, not content with Greek and Latin writers, wishes to consult the Hebrew writers as well, the very learned man, most skilled in those languages, Johannes Buxtorf the Younger, recently gathered their opinions with care in his learned Diatriba. But students of languages should not regret consulting others as well, some perhaps not yet seen by me: two more recent authors, learned men, namely Samuel Bochart, in his Geographia Sacra, and the author of Pharus Veteris Testamenti.

units.la: Nos quoque, ne plane simus in nobili hoc argumento asymboli, hoc primum de lectore nobis concedi postulamus; Quodcunque Sacra Scriptura in hoc de Linguis argumento ita claré ac dilucidè tradit, ut aliter accipere duri oris aut contentiosi sit hominis; de eo, quòd communi naturæ aut experientiæ minùs congruat, dubitare aut disputare, impium esse: quod verò ita ambiguè traditum est, ut nihil obstet, quin plures sententiæ proponi possint, per quas nulla vis S.Scripturæ verbis inferatur; ex pluribus, sine impietatis invidiâ cuivis licere, quæ ad naturam rerum & experientiam communè proximè accedat, eam amplecti.
units.tr: So that we too may not be altogether without a contribution to this noble subject, we first ask this of the reader: whatever Holy Scripture teaches so clearly and plainly on this subject of languages that to take it otherwise belongs only to a hard-mouthed or contentious man, it is impious to doubt or dispute because it does not agree well with common nature or experience. But where Scripture is handed down so ambiguously that nothing prevents several opinions from being proposed, by none of which any violence is done to the words of Holy Scripture, then anyone may, without the odium of impiety, choose from among several the one that comes closest to the nature of things and common experience.

units.la: Ex hominum dispersione, & in populos diversos sub diverso regimine divisione; ex diversis legibus, ritibus, & consuetudinibus ; ex eorundem inter fe populorum commerciis & per bella cladéfq; mixtione, magnam volventibus annis & seculis insecuturam per fe fuisse linguarum varietatem, ex ipsâ naturæ rerum cognitione & certiffima, quæ magistra rerum audit, experientiâ, nemini dubium esse potest. Ab orbe condito ad Diluvium per mille fexcentos & quod excurrit annos, unam eandémque ubique viguisse linguam, nescio an fatis certò ex ipso sacro Canone probari possit : ego quidem non dubito, ita rem habuisse. Utcunq; enim divina authoritas credendi necessitatem non imponeret, in tantâ tamen hominum longævitate,cùm plerique ad nongentesimum pervenirent annum;& ex hac longævitate,tam pertinace, tam recente rerum omnium à primâ origine memoriâ ; credibilius est, sermonem variari non potuisse : ut
units.tr: That, from the dispersion of men and their division into different peoples under different governments; from differing laws, rites and customs; and from the trade of these peoples with one another, and their mixing through wars and calamities, over many years and centuries there would arise a great variety of languages, can be doubted by no one, from the knowledge of nature itself and from the most certain experience, which is called the teacher of things. That from the creation of the world to the Flood, through sixteen hundred and some years, one and the same language flourished everywhere, I do not know whether this can be proved with sufficient certainty from the sacred Canon itself. For my part I do not doubt that the matter was so. For although divine authority does not impose the necessity of believing it, yet given such longevity of men, when most lived to the nine-hundredth year, and given this long and unbroken memory of all things from their first origin, it is more credible that speech could not have varied. So,

units.la: alia mittam, in quibus longè alia ratio istorum, qui tum, hominum ; ab illis, qui post Diluvium nati sunt. Sanè ne nunc quidem mirum fit, linguam unam, per unam aut alteram ætatem, quanquam multæ interim contingant rerum commutationes, puram illibatámque, ( præcipuè si ejusmodi fit populus, cui patrii cura studiúmque sit sermonis, ) confervare. Quid autem tot anni ab orbe condito ad Diluvium, in ista tanta longævitate ; quàm quod nunc nobis ætas una fit,alterâve ? Illorum autem qui post diluvium, aut saltem post turrim Babylonicam vixere cùm non alia feré ratio, quàm qui nunc sunt hominum fuerit : non aliter potuisse, ( sine miraculo :) quin ista varietas tandem aliquando contingeret rectè concludimus.
units.tr: to pass over other matters, in which the reasoning about those men of that time is quite different from that about those born after the Flood: indeed, it is not even now surprising that one language, over one or another age, although many changes of things occur in the meantime, keeps itself pure and unblemished (especially if it is a people who take care and pains over their native speech). But what were so many years from the creation of the world to the Flood, in such great longevity, but as one or two of our ages are now? Since, however, the way of life of those who lived after the Flood, or at least after the Tower of Babel, was hardly different from that of men now, we rightly conclude that they could not otherwise (short of a miracle) have avoided that variety eventually arising.

units.la: Jam testatur Sacra Scriptura, cùm una omnium quantum erat hominum ante cœptam ædificationem, lingua efset, immissam tunc linguæ, vel sermonum confusionem à Deo, quâ coacti à cœptis desistere, alii in alia terrarum loca sparsi sint. Eò autem potissimum spectasse istam structionem, ut ab imminente minente ex incremento dispersione conservarentur, aut saltem ut immortali aliquo ante dispersionem opere, famâ sui nominis apud posteros viverent ac vigerent; id est, à mortalitate, quantum in ipsis, se vindicarent, videtur ipse sacer Textus innuere. Confusio autem linguarum, sive sermonum, quæ multiplex esse potuit, qualis illa fuerit, S.Scriptura non docet: sed id tantùm, talem fuisse, ut alii alios non intelligerent. Sunt, qui putent non aliud quàm prioris linguæ oblivionem esse inductam, & prioris oblitos in novum variúmque sermonem sua sponte prorupisse: quod cùm à naturæ rationibus alienum sit, nec cum S. Scripturæ verbis (si quis ad miraculum consugiat:) satis conveniat, nullâ mihi veri similitudine niti videtur. Et aliud, opinor, oblivio; aliud confusio linguarum. Turbatâ verò mente, & confusis (ita Deo operante) rerum notionibus, ita contingere potuisse, ut, cùm omnes Hebraicè loquerentur, aut Hebraica saltèm verba proferrent, invicem tamen non intelligerent, non magis quàm si planè diversis omnes loquuti linguis effent;non est quod quisquam dubitet.
units.tr: Now Holy Scripture testifies that when all men, as many as there were before the building was begun, had one language, then a confusion of tongues or speech was sent by God, by which they were compelled to give up their undertaking and were scattered into different parts of the earth. That this construction was aimed chiefly at preventing them from being scattered by the impending dispersion, or at least, by some immortal work before the dispersion, at making their name live and flourish among posterity, that is, at securing themselves against mortality as far as lay in them, the sacred text itself seems to suggest. But the confusion of tongues, or of speech, which could have been of many kinds, Scripture does not describe, except to say only that it was such that they did not understand one another. Some think it was nothing other than the induced forgetting of the earlier language, and that those who had forgotten the earlier one broke out spontaneously into a new and varied speech. Since this is foreign to the principles of nature, and agrees ill with the words of Scripture (unless one flees to a miracle), it seems to me to rest on no probability at all. Forgetting, I think, is one thing; confusion of languages is another. That, with the mind disturbed and the notions of things confused (God so working), it could have happened that, although all spoke Hebrew, or at least uttered Hebrew words, they nevertheless did not understand one another, no more than if they had all spoken entirely different languages, there is no reason for anyone to doubt.

units.la: An id voluerint illi, qui Julio Scaligero sententiam suam probaverunt, nescio ; nec quicquam in hoc genere, de certo confusionis modo, rigidè definiendum concesserim:illorum autem sententiam, qui varias tum linguas, plenas & perfectas, ab Hebraicâ diversas, subitò emersisse contendunt, & aliter opinandi libertatem nobis non relinquunt,cur aliorum sententiis præferamus, nulla, quod sciam,tam dubiâ Sacræ Scripturæ authoritate, causa.
units.tr: Whether those men who approved Julius Scaliger's opinion meant this, I do not know; nor would I grant that anything in this matter about the precise manner of the confusion should be rigidly defined. But as for the opinion of those who maintain that various full and perfect languages, different from Hebrew, suddenly emerged at that time, and who leave us no freedom to think otherwise, I know of no reason, given such doubtful authority of Holy Scripture, why we should prefer their opinions to others.

units.la: Objiciunt tamen viri docti, hanc sententiam repugnare menti Scripturæ,quæ semper, ut ipsis visum, confusionis linguarum meminit ante dispersionem: ex quo evidenter argui volunt, confusionem linguarum in ipsâ extructione Urbis & turris contigisse. Utinam preßius & signatius, prout res ipsa merebatur, nobiscum egissent viri docti. In neutro enim nobis satisfaciunt; neque in antecedente Scripturæ testimonio, neque in ista quam inde eliciunt consequentia. Sed de posteriore ipsi viderint, si nos de Scripturâ quod quasi proferunt, aliter rem habere ostendi-mus.
units.tr: Learned men object, however, that this opinion is contrary to the sense of Scripture, which, as it seems to them, always mentions the confusion of tongues before the dispersion; from which they wish it to be clearly inferred that the confusion of tongues happened in the very building of the city and tower. Would that the learned men had dealt with us more precisely and pointedly, as the matter itself deserved. For they satisfy us on neither point: neither on the preceding testimony of Scripture, nor on the consequence they draw from it. But as to the latter, let them see to it themselves, if we have shown that the matter stands otherwise than they put it, as it were, in Scripture's name.

units.la: Confusionis linguarum (si verba ipsa spectemus) nullibi omnino, quod sciam, Sacra Scriptura meminit. Divisionem populorum & gentium secundum linguam vel linguas suas narrat illa quidem & saepius iterat, Genef. cap. X. Per ἀπολλύειν utique; ut alia ibi multa: usitatissimam, ut omnes norunt & agnoscunt, sibi figuram. Versu 5. Ab his divisae sunt insulae gentium (istae vero gentes non ante extructionem opinor:) in regionibus suis, unusquisque secundum linguam suam, & familias suas in nationibus suis. Versu 20. Hi sunt filii Cham, in cognationibus & linguis & generationibus, terrisque & gentibus suis. Postremo denique capite, versus 31. & 32. Isti sunt filii Sem, secundum cognationes, & linguas; & regiones in gentibus suis. Hae familiae Noe, juxta populos & nationes suas. Ab his divisae sunt gentes in terra post Diluvium. Nulla hic confusionis linguarum commemoratio: varietatis, pro familiarum, populorum, & nationum diversitate, crebra. Sed hanc varietatem linguarum ante dispersionem vel divisionem populorum contigisse neque dicitur
units.tr: Holy Scripture nowhere at all, so far as I know, mentions confusion of tongues (if we look at the words themselves). It does indeed tell of the division of peoples and nations according to their language or languages, and repeats this often, in Genesis chapter 10, where, by the usual figure ἀπολλύειν, as well as many other things there, it uses a figure most familiar to everyone, as all know and acknowledge. In verse 5: By these were the isles of the nations divided (but these nations, I think, were not before the building): every one in his own land, after his own tongue, and after their families, in their nations. In verse 20: These are the sons of Ham, after their families, after their tongues, in their countries, and in their nations. Finally, at the end of the same chapter, verses 31 and 32: These are the sons of Shem, after their families, after their tongues, in their lands, and in their nations. These are the families of the sons of Noah, after their generations, in their nations; and by these were the nations divided in the earth after the Flood. There is no mention here of a confusion of tongues; the variety of tongues is frequently noted, corresponding to the diversity of families, peoples and nations. But that this variety of tongues occurred before the dispersion or division of the peoples is neither stated

units.la: { } tur exertè, nec ullâ necessariâ consequentiâ colligitur. Ut si dicerem, In regno Sinensi plures esse pro linguarum numero; vel, (Scripturæ φυλαῖς) secundum linguas suas, provincias, & regiones; id volens dicere, tot diversas esse linguas, quot sunt provinciæ; tot provincias, quot sunt linguæ. Planius hoc aliquanto fateor; nemo tamen inde rectè colligat istam linguarum diversitatem ante provinciarum divisionem extitisse; cùm multò probabilius sit, linguarum diversitatem ex regionum & regiminum discrimine profluxisse. Cæterum, confusio (ubi de Scripturæ verbis agitur) longè aliud quàm divisio. Nam confusio in extructione contigit ante dispersionem, de quo nemo dubitat, unde & Babeli nomen: Divisio linguarum post, an ante, tacente Scripturâ, contigerit, est ipsum τὸ ἐρμηνευτικὸν, quod aliis argumentis probandum.
units.tr: explicitly, nor is it gathered by any necessary consequence. It would be as if I were to say that in the Chinese kingdom there are as many languages as there are provinces, or (in the words of Scripture, tribes [φυλαῖς]) provinces and regions according to their languages, meaning by this that there are as many different languages as there are provinces, and as many provinces as there are languages. I admit this is somewhat plainer; yet no one rightly infers from it that this diversity of languages existed before the division into provinces, since it is much more probable that the diversity of languages flowed from the distinction of regions and governments. Moreover, confusio (where the words of Scripture are in question) is something quite other than divisio. For confusio happened in the building, before the dispersion, as no one doubts, and hence the name Babel; whether the division of languages happened after or before, Scripture being silent, is itself the τὸ ἐρμηνευτικὸν [the interpretive question], to be proved by other arguments.

units.la: Atque hic obiter notamus, dictum esse Phaleg, Genef.X. 25. quod in diebus ejus, non, linguae; sed, terra divisa fit.
units.tr: Here we note in passing that it is said of Peleg (Gen. X. 25) that "in his days" it is not "the tongues" but "the earth" that was divided.

units.la: Mirum autem de linguis ibi, si ita verè res haberet, tacuisse Scripturam, quæ longè notabilior (ex miraculo scil.) quàm terræ, in quo nihil adeò mirum, divisio. Nam quod contendunt hîc etiam, τὸ לשן linguarum quoque divisionem, ídque ex ipsius vi verbi, comprehendere; quô id cogant, præter nudam affirmationem, nihil admodum ab illis proferri video. Verbum לשן, inquiunt, usurpat etiam David de linguarum divisione, Psal.LV.v.10. Fatemur: quanquam longè aliâ (quod diligenter animadvertí velim:) quàm de quâ quæritur hîc, notione. Per linguas enim, non tam sermonis, quàm animorum & consiliorum divisionem intelligi doctissimi consentiunt interpretes. Sed quicquid hujus sit; ut David de linguis: ita Daniel propheta de regni (quod à terra non multum abest) divisione usurpat; nec minùs, opinor, ille proprie de regno; quàm David de linguâ. De hominum autem in varias terras dispersione verbũ יפץ non לשן usurpari, cùm res ipsæ, hominum dispersio, & terrarum divisio, sint adeò diversæ, nihil mirum; (non magis,quod sciam,quàm concoctionem cibi & distributionem, quæ cognatæ quidem & subordinatæ, non tamen eædem sunt operationes; diversis
units.tr: It would be strange, if things really were so, that Scripture should have said nothing about a division of tongues there, since that is far more remarkable (namely as a miracle) than a division of the earth, in which there is nothing so wonderful. As for their claim that here too the word לשן [lashon] also covers a division of tongues, and that this follows from the very force of the word, I see that they offer little beyond bare assertion to compel this. They say David uses the word לשן of the division of tongues at Ps. LV. 10. We admit it, though in a sense quite different (which I would have you note carefully) from the one in question here. For the most learned interpreters agree that "tongues" there means not so much a division of speech as a division of minds and counsels. But whatever the case, just as David uses it of tongues, so the prophet Daniel uses it of the division of a kingdom (which is not far from land); and I think he uses it no less properly of a kingdom than David does of a tongue. That the dispersion of men into various lands is expressed by the verb יפץ and not by לשן is no wonder, since the things themselves, the dispersion of men and the division of lands, are so different; (no more, as far as I know, than the digestion of food and its distribution, which are related and subordinate but not the same operations, are expressed by different words;

units.la: B.ib.§.5§. diversis verbis exprimi :) & quid huc faciat, nisi ad glaucoma (quod absit) objiciendum, non intelligo.
units.tr: and I do not see what this has to do with the matter, except to be thrown up as a cataract over the eyes (God forbid).

units.la: Jam cap. XI. dicitur terra ante Babe‐ lis extructionem labii unius & sermo‐ num eorundem fuisse. Deum autem de‐ fcendiffe, ut confunderet ibi linguam eorum, ut non audiret unusquisque lin‐ guam proximi fui. Idcirco autem vo‐ catam esse Babel, quia ibi confusum est labium universæ terræ. Nihil hîc de linguarum (ut quidem linguas hîc in‐ telligunt :) confusione: nisi fi quis id pertendat, confusionem linguæ, seu fer‐ monis & labii; ut hîc sacer habet Tex‐ tus: & confusionem, id est, ut expli‐ cant, divisionem linguarum, (ut lingua pro dialecto, seu loquendi genere, ver‐ bis & idiotifmis ab alio diverso fumi‐ tur) pro iisdem, idque ex ipsorum vér‐ borum propriâ vi, habenda: ut si quis colloquentes aliquos audiat, & dicat eos confuso uti sermone, ut invicem intelligere non possint; de diversis id linguis necessario intelligendum fit; quod neminem puto dicturum. Ad cir‐ cumftantias & argumenta, quibus pro‐ bes, fi confugias, hoc jam aliud est;
units.tr: Now in chapter XI the land is said to have had, before the building of Babel, "one lip and one speech." God is said to have come down to "confuse their tongue there, so that no one would understand the tongue of his neighbour." The place is called Babel because there "the lip of the whole earth was confused." Nothing here speaks of a confusion of tongues (in the sense in which they understand "tongues" here), unless someone contends that "confusion of tongue," that is of speech and lip, as the sacred text has it, and "confusion," that is, as they explain it, division of tongues (since "tongue" is taken for a dialect, or manner of speaking, with words and idioms differing from another's), are to be held the same, and this from the proper force of the words themselves. If someone overheard some people conversing and said they used a confused speech so that they could not understand one another, it would necessarily have to be understood of different languages; and I do not think anyone would say that. As for the circumstances and arguments by which you prove this, if you take refuge in them, that is now another matter.

units.la: nec tutum fuerit, quod probabilibus fe putat aliquis argumentis & circumstantiis elicere, id Scripturæ simpliciter adscribere. Quod autem roget aliquis fortasse; Quorsum igitur si de ortu plurium deinceps non agitur, ista initio capitis de unicâ in toto priùs orbe lingua,observatio : respondeo; Ex istâ qualicunque (nobis ignotâ) quam memorat Scriptura confusione, dispersionem hominum ; ex hominum dispersione, divisionem linguarum (ut nos quidem opinamur)extitisse : ut de plurium linguarum ortu hoc agi capite minimè negemus; sed quæ post,an ante dispersionem sint ortæ; dubium (quantum ad Scripturæ verba) relinqui credamus.
units.tr: Nor would it be safe to ascribe simply to Scripture what someone elicits from probable arguments and circumstances. But someone may perhaps ask: why, if we are not going on to discuss the origin of several tongues, do we make this observation at the start of the chapter about the one tongue throughout the whole world? I reply: from that confusion, whatever it was (unknown to us), which Scripture mentions, came the dispersion of men; and from the dispersion of men came the division of tongues (as we indeed suppose). So we by no means deny that this chapter deals with the origin of several tongues; but whether they arose after or before the dispersion, we believe, as far as the words of Scripture go, is left in doubt.

units.la: Quod autem addunt iidem, Scripturam dicere populos dispersos esse כלשונותם secundum lin-guas suas; aliquid dicerent, si est hæc sententia. Scri-ptura dicit populos d.-spersos esse לשונם secundum linguas suas. hoc tam verè dicerent, quàm, ptura dicit populos d.ron animo fallendi, persuasum habeo. Mihi sanè in totâ Sacrâ Scripturâ nihil tale repertum. Nam si hoc volunt, ut velle credibile est, quòd Scriptura dicat, divisos esse populos כלשונותם (quanquam ne id quidem, quod sciam, Scriptura; sed איש ללשונו ללשונותם vel in quo non leve discrimen :) eò sequi, ut & dispersos dicat: vereor ne ratio eos fugerit. Longè enim aliud est (si quid ego intelligo) divisos esse populos secundum linguas suas: id est, pro eodem populo habitos, quibus communis esset lingua; pro diverso autem, qui diversis uterentur: aliud verò, difperfos esse. Dispersio (hominum scilicet) statim à confusione linguarum: divisio (populorum scilicet) aliquo certè, si non longo, post tempore, cùm jam dispersi in rempublicam propriis legibus, institutis, moribus, linguâ denique propriâ constantem & ab aliis diversam planè coaluissent. Sanè si id voluisset sacra Scriptura, quod ex illâ colligunt viri docti, mirum, cùm capite XI. de dispersione semel iterúmque meminit, de linguarum divisione vel varietate scribere. Neque puto, si difperfione & divisione idem voluisset, tam constanter observaturam fuisse discrimen verborum [?] & פרר: quorum hoc, ubi linguarum mentio fit, sæpius
units.tr: As for what the same men add, that Scripture says the peoples were "dispersed according to their tongues," they would be saying something if this were the sentence: "Scripture says the peoples were dispersed according to their tongues" [לשונם]. They would say it as truly as, I am persuaded, they say it without intent to deceive. For my part I have found nothing like it in all of Sacred Scripture. For if they mean this (as it is credible they do), that Scripture says the peoples were "divided" according to their tongues (though not even this, as far as I know, does Scripture say; it says איש ללשונו ללשונותם, and not without a noticeable difference), then it follows that it also says they were "dispersed." I fear their reasoning has escaped them. For it is quite different (if I understand anything) for peoples to be divided according to their tongues, that is, regarded as one people those who had a common tongue and as different those who used different ones; and it is another thing to be dispersed. Dispersion (of men, that is) came straight from the confusion of tongues; division (of peoples, that is) came some time later, if not a long time, when, already dispersed, they had grown into a commonwealth with its own laws, institutions and customs, and finally its own language, settled and different from others. Certainly if sacred Scripture had meant what learned men gather from it, it would be strange that, having mentioned dispersion in chapter XI once and again, it should write nothing about a division or variety of tongues. Nor do I think that, if it had meant the same by dispersion and division, it would have so consistently observed the distinction between the words [?] and פרר; of which this one, where mention is made of tongues, is used more often

units.la: adhibetur: illud autem cap. XI. bis, cum dispersio, nec aliud amplius, indicatur.
units.tr: than the other; while the other is used in chapter XI twice, where only dispersion is indicated, and nothing more.

units.la: Jam si quis roget; quid hac diffentiendi vel aliter opinandi libertate consequamur: non parum certè, ut mihi quidem videtur. Hoc primum, ut linguæ Hebraicæ jus suum asseramus, cujus hoc eximium esse credimus, quod sola, Deo Opt.Max.onomatothetâ, &, ut ita dicam, parente jactare se possit: quod verum non fuerit, si tot aliarum linguarum ad Deum ipsum authorem, nullâ interveniente naturæ vice, sit origo referenda. Secundum hoc erit, quòd Hebræam, aliarum matricem, eâdem operâ rectè tuebimur: quod aliter, nisi multa supponantur, non intellectu facile. Postremò id consequemur, ut nostra, plus quàm necesse est, fides, infidelium (quod sanè vel illorum causâ vera charitas suadet:) ludibrio non exponatur. Quanquam enim nihil vetat, eosdem effectus & omnipotentiam Dei & naturam interdum producere; ut puta, vitem vel segetem ante tempus maturescere, quæ paulò post suo tempore
units.tr: Now if someone asks what we gain by this freedom to disagree or think otherwise, it is, to my mind, not a little. First, that we assert the right of the Hebrew tongue, which we believe has this distinctive mark: that it alone can boast of having God the Best and Greatest as its namer and, so to speak, its parent. That would not be true if the origin of so many other tongues had to be referred to God himself as author, with no intervening natural cause. Second, that in the same work we will rightly defend the Hebrew, the mother of the others, which otherwise, unless many things are assumed, is not easy to understand. Last, we will ensure that our faith is not, more than necessary, exposed to the ridicule of unbelievers (which true charity indeed urges, even for their sake). For although nothing prevents God's omnipotence and nature from sometimes producing the same effects, as for instance a vine or a crop ripening before its time, which a little later, in its own season,

units.la: sola naturæ (sic autem vocamus statam & ordinariam Dei potestatem & providentiam :) ope maturanda fuerat : cum tamen audiunt, qui Sacram Scripturam deridiculo habent, variarum originem linguarum miraculo tribui; id illi ita accipiunt ut-plurimum, quasi sic miraculo tribueretur, ut, absque eo fuisset, nulla insequutura fuisset varietas, sed una eademque ubique terrarum lingua per naturæ ordinem in usu futura fuerit. Sed, an revera non sunt inter nos, qui ita sciscunt; & à mutis animalibus, ovibus, bobus, asinis, & similibus, quid homini naturale sit, argumenta petunt: imo qui provocant ad philosophos, & hujus linguarum varietatis causam penitus eis ignotam fuisse confidenter pronuntiant? Nostra autem longe alia semper fuit opinio, ut in tractatu De Sermonis Ortu pluribus à nobis disputatum est.
units.tr: would have been ripened by nature alone (by which we mean God's established and ordinary power and providence): yet when those who mock Sacred Scripture hear that the origin of the various tongues is ascribed to a miracle, they mostly take it as if it were ascribed to a miracle in such a way that, without it, no variety would have followed, but one and the same tongue would everywhere on earth have been in use by the order of nature. But are there not indeed some among us who so decide, and who seek arguments from dumb animals, sheep, oxen, asses and the like, about what is natural to man; indeed who challenge the philosophers and confidently declare that the cause of this variety of tongues was utterly unknown to them? Our own opinion has always been quite different, as we have argued at length in the treatise On the Origin of Speech.

units.la: Cæterum cum dicimus hanc linguarum inter homines varietatem naturale esse, observo viros quosdam doctos in verbo naturale mirifice (nequid dicam gravius) impingere. Utinam, quæ vel Aristoteles, vel Quintilianus, aliique veteres de verbi istius usu & multiplici notione bene monuerunt, in memoria habuissent. Non enim id quifquam (in hoc quidem de diversarum linguarum origine argumento) voluit, quod sciam ; certas linguas certis populis aut coeli plagis ita naturales esse, ut proceritatem corporis Germanis antiqui tribuebant, & omnis (opinor) aetas nigredinem Ethiopibus,& si quid aliud, quod ejusdem fit generis : sed naturam miraculo opponimus, ut quemadmodum crescere hominum genus, in varias spargi terras, in diversos coalescere populos,diversis uti moribus & legibus ; bellum esse inter populos, pacem rursus : commercia,foedera ; intercedere, violari : colonias mitti : hos ex antiquis sedibus exturbari vi ; alios in locum succedere : haec & similia non esse quod miremur, cum ita sint homines, & ita ferat natura rerum, ut ista vulgo fiant : ita & linguarum inter homines diversitatem contingere. Hoc aliquis ipsum fortasse malit dicere, quia natura certum aliquid & statum promittit ; verborum autem & linguarum sive mutatione sive duratione nihil fit incertius : quemadmodum & Horatius, ubi de verbis, Multa renascentur, quae jam cecidere, cadúntque; Quae nunc sunt in honore, vocabula, si volet usus; Quem penes arbitrium est, & vis, & norma loquendi.
units.tr: But when we say that this variety of tongues among men is natural, I observe that some learned men stumble wonderfully (not to say more harshly) over the word "natural." Would that they had kept in mind what Aristotle, Quintilian and other ancients have well remarked about the use and the many senses of that word. For no one (in this argument about the origin of different tongues, at least) meant, as far as I know, that certain tongues are so natural to certain peoples or regions of the sky, as the ancients ascribed tallness of body to the Germans, and every age, I think, blackness to the Ethiopians, and whatever else is of that kind. Rather we set nature over against miracle: just as the human race grows, spreads into various lands, coalesces into different peoples, uses different customs and laws; just as there is war between peoples and then peace again, commerce and treaties, alliances made and broken, colonies sent out, some driven by force from their ancient seats and others taking their place, we need not wonder at these and similar things, since men are what they are and the nature of things brings it about that such things commonly happen; so too the diversity of tongues among men comes about. Someone may perhaps prefer to say that this is itself the natural thing, because nature promises something certain and fixed; but nothing is more uncertain than the change or endurance of words and tongues. So Horace too, speaking of words: "Many words will be reborn that have now fallen and will fall; words now held in honour will, if usage wills, pass away; and the power, the right and the norm of speech lie with usage."

units.la: Atqui etiam iis, quae usu constant, sua natura est ; & haec ipsa, quâ à naturalibus potissimum differunt, incertitudo, à natura rerum communi est: ut non sine causa idem Horatius hunc qualemcunque usum naturæ comparet, Ut sylvæ foliis pronos mutantur in annos ; Prima cadunt : ita verborum vetus interit ætas : Et juvenum ritu florent modò nata, vigéntque.
units.tr: Yet even those things that rest on usage have a nature of their own. And this very uncertainty, which chiefly distinguishes them from natural things, is common to the nature of things. So Horace, not without reason, compares this kind of usage to nature: As the woods change their leaves year by year, the first ones fall; so the age of words passes away, and like young men, newly born words flourish and grow strong.

units.la: At longè alia notione in vetere illâ & inter Philosophos vexatissimâ controversiâ, Εἰ φύσει τὰ ὀνόματα ἢ θέσει ; Verba sint ex casu (placitóve, ut alii exprimunt :) an verò à naturâ : naturæ vox accipitur. De quo nos alibi prolixè. Ad hanc autem controversiam pertinet subtilis viri, Rabbi Levi Ben
units.tr: But in that old and most disputed controversy among the philosophers, whether names exist by nature or by convention [Εἰ φύσει τὰ ὀνόματα ἢ θέσει;], the question is quite different. The issue is whether words are from chance or convention (by a decree, as others put it), or whether they are from nature; here "nature" is the word taken in its sense. We have discussed this at length elsewhere. To this controversy belongs the subtle discussion of the learned Rabbi Levi Ben Gerson, which is by no means foolish.

units.la: Gerson, non insulsa sanè disputatio quam ad illam de linguarum varietate causam μαλ' ἀσυσσιονύσως trahunt viri doɗti.
units.tr: Gerson, a discussion that is by no means foolish, which learned men bring to the question of the variety of languages.

units.la: Hæc nostra de linguarum confusione sententia, in quam nos solâ veri fimilitudine inductos bonâ fide profiteri possumus. Nec tamen diffitemur eam tantò magis nobis placere, quantò propius ad ea, quæ super hoc argumento b. m. parens If. Cafaubonus in Adversariis suis reliquit, accedere postea animadvertimus. Quò melius judices, lector, en tibi ipsissima ejus verba;
units.tr: This is our view of the confusion of languages, which we can honestly profess to hold, led to it by probability alone. Nor do we deny that we later noticed it agrees all the more with what my late father, Isaac Casaubon, of blessed memory, left on this subject in his Adversaria. So that you may judge better, reader, here are his very words:

units.la: »» De linguarum confusione: Repetentibus aliarum linguarum originem, è fonte Hebraico, objicitur Moses: qui videtur dicere, Linguas toto genere diversas repente, extitisse in Babel. Negantur enim sese intellexisse: & inde volunt, omnes alias linguas esse ortas in totum ab Hebraica diversas. Nobis aliter videtur: non enim tam novas rerum notiones esse tùm inventas, quàm novas veteris linguæ ἱσχαίσεις ἢ παρεισαλίσεις: ita tamen, ut & plané nova quædam vocabula tunc sint excogitata. Hoc eò pro-
units.tr: "On the confusion of languages. When people trace the origin of other languages to the Hebrew source, Moses is brought up against them; he seems to say that languages wholly different in kind suddenly arose at Babel. They deny that they understood one another, and from this they infer that all other languages arose entirely different from Hebrew. To us it seems otherwise. For it was not so much that new notions of things were then invented, as that new idioms or changes of the old language arose; yet some quite new words were also then coined. We prove this because

units.la: C
units.tr: C

units.la: » probamus ; quia certum est, eos po-» pulos, qui tum sparsi sunt per varias» regiones,non in extremas Orbis par-» tes repentè transiisse, verùm in pro-» piores veteri patriæ suæ. Itaque ex» illis fine dubio Aflyrii, Syri,forte &» Græci, sunt primò nati, deinde ex» istis alii porrò populi, qui paulatim» ab ortûs primi loco dilatati sunt ad» quatuor Orbis cardines : donec pro-» gressu temporis πᾶζα ἡ ἐκουμένη in-» colis frequentaretur. Igitur fi in» Babele linguæ in totum diversæ factæ» effent, necessario Chaldæi, Aflyrii,» Syri, ἀλλοκότως illas linguas retinuif-» fent. Atqui contrarium videmus ac-» cidiffe. Est enim verifimum, Lin-» guas cæteras eò manifestiora & ma-» gis expressa originis Hebraicæ vesti-» gia fervaffe, & nunc fervare, quò» propius ab antiquâ & primâ homi» num fede abfuerint. Propinquitatem» hanc duplicem facimus, loci, ac tem-» poris : nam proximus quisque popu-» lus genti Hebraicæ, & situs & tem-» porum ratione,proximè ad illius lin-» guam accessit. Longinquitas verò,» & locorum & temporum, alienatio-» nem subinde majorem intulit. Clarum hoc ex comparatione linguarum Syriacæ, Chaldaicæ, Arabicæ, Punicæ, &c. cum Hebraicâ. Clarissimûm item, fi Græcam linquam diligenter spectes. Græci primi in Asiâ habitarunt: inde Iones, vel, ut Æschylus vocat Hebraicè, Javones in Europam trajecerunt. Nos autem observamus, in antiquissimis quibusque Græcorum scriptoribus, multa vocabula Hebraica, quæ postea vel defierunt esse in usu, vel admodum fuit mutata. Observamus etiam Asiaticos Græcos magis {βραχέως}, quàm Europæos. Hæc igitur sunt nobis demonstranda.
units.tr: it is certain that those peoples who were then scattered through various regions did not suddenly pass to the farthest parts of the world, but to places nearer their old homeland. So without doubt the Assyrians, Syrians, perhaps also the Greeks, were first born from them; then from these other peoples in turn, who gradually spread out from the place of first origin to the four corners of the world, until in the course of time the whole inhabited world [πᾶσα ἡ οἰκουμένη] was peopled. Therefore, if languages had become wholly different at Babel, the Chaldeans, Assyrians and Syrians would necessarily have kept those languages in an altered form. But we see the opposite has happened. For it is likely that the other languages have preserved, and still preserve, the traces of Hebrew origin more clearly and more plainly, the nearer they were to the ancient first seat of mankind. We make this nearness twofold, of place and of time: for each people closest to the Hebrew nation, both in situation and in time, came closest to its language. But distance, both of places and of times, brought in greater estrangement. This is clear from comparing the Syriac, Chaldee, Arabic, Punic languages and so on with Hebrew. It is equally clear if you carefully examine the Greek language. The Greeks first lived in Asia; from there the Ionians, or as Aeschylus calls them in Hebrew, the Javones, crossed into Europe. We observe, moreover, in the most ancient Greek writers, many Hebrew words which afterwards either ceased to be in use or were much changed. We also observe that the Asiatic Greeks are more [brief?] than the European. These then are the things we have to demonstrate."

units.la: Hactenus ille. Sed & hoc non pigebit addidisse. Quàm variè sacra hæc de turris Babylonicæ ædificatione & linguarum confusione historia ab Ethnicis in multiplices fabulas detorta fuerit, notatum pluribus. Ab eadem quoque, ni fallor, origine, quod de Momo suo tradiderunt; quem, cùm Jupiter hominum generi, ut terræ gratificaretur, infensus, de perdendo eo vel fulmine vel illuvionibus secum deliberà-ret, ret, narrant intercessisse, non tam ne perderetur, quàm ut aliâ potiùs viâ: Nempe, ut satis odiorum & inimicitiarum seminibus inter se committeretur, ac propriis viribus & manibus rueret. Impia sunt hæc, ut quæ maximè, & in Deum Opt. Max. cui nihil magis quàm concordia hominum (modò non ad malum) cordi est, valdè contumeliosa: sed quæ tamen ex pravâ & maligna (quàm maligni autem plerique Ethnici in suis de Deo judiciis, alibi peculiari Diatribâ ostendimus:) verborum interpretatione, quæ in hâc occurrunt historiâ, traducta esse credibile est: præcipuè etiam, cum Hebræi Doctores de rixis & cædibus inter operantes ex hac linguarum confusione ortis multa narrent: ut doctissimo Buxtorfio pluribus observatum. Non memini alium pleniùs hanc fabulam narrare, quàm facit Eustathius. Ejus igitur verba lectori hîc apponemus.
units.tr: So far he. I will add this too, since it would not be a bother. It has been noted by many how variously this sacred history of the building of the Tower of Babel and the confusion of languages was twisted by the heathen into manifold fables. From the same source, I think, comes what they handed down about their Momus: when Jupiter, angry with the human race, was deliberating with himself about destroying it with a thunderbolt or floods, to please the earth, they say Momus intervened, not so much to prevent its destruction as to have it destroyed by another way: namely, that men should be set against one another by the seeds of hatred and enmity, and fall by their own strength and hands. These fables are impious, as impious as can be, and deeply insulting to God, Best and Greatest, for whom nothing is dearer than the concord of men (provided it is not for evil). Yet it is credible that they were drawn from a perverse and malicious interpretation of the words found in this history (how malicious most heathen were in their judgements of God, we have shown elsewhere in a special Diatribe). This is especially likely since the Hebrew teachers tell many stories of quarrels and slaughters among the workmen arising from this confusion of languages, as the most learned Buxtorf has observed at length. I do not remember anyone who tells this fable more fully than Eustathius does. So I shall set his words before the reader here.

units.la: Τινὲς ἢ βυλὴν Διὸς εἶπον τὸ ἥ γῆν (ὡς ἢ ὁ Ευειπίδης ἐν Ὀρέστῃ μυθολογεῖ) κα-φίζαι βαςυμένυ τῷ τῶν λαῶν φόβῳ, χ' ἥ ἀνδρὸς ἀίλησιν· ἢ χάειν φασὶ τόνδε Θη-βαιῶν τὰ πρῶτα συνιςῶσαλο πόλεμον, ἡ μετ
units.tr: Some say it was the counsel of Zeus, and that the earth (as Euripides tells the myth in his Orestes) was shaken, weighed down by the fear of the peoples and by the will of one man; others say that this Theban first began the war, and that after him he brought the Trojans and the Greeks to destruction.

units.la: ἢ . μετ' ἐκεῖνον ἀνήγαγεν ὅπ φθορᾷ Τρῶας ἐξ Ἑλληνας. Μῶμον φασὶ συμβεβληκέναι μὴ κεχρυνοῖς ἢ κάλλους ἴσοις πάντα διαφθεῖ-ρειν, ἀλλ' ἀμεθόδως ἄλλως, ὡ ὑποθεμένη τῆς Θέτιδος Συνοσφίαν, ἀφ' ἧς ὁ Ἀχιλ-λεὺς, ἡ Συσαγῶς κάλλης γέννησιν, ἢ Ἑλένης ἀπαλλαγή, ἀλλ' ἥν τὰ χρ Τροίαν ἐγένοντο, πε-σόντων πολλῶν· ἡ δι' Ἀχιλλέα, τὰ μὲν πο-λεμῶντα· τὰ δὲ μηνίοντα.
units.tr: They say that Momus cast in his lot, not with anything crafty or beautiful, but in a random and unmethodical way, planting the seed of discord from which Achilles was born, with the beauty of Helen as the cause, and the destruction of Troy followed, with many falling; and through Achilles some fought, and others were angry.

units.la: Hæc erant quæ de linguæ, seu sermonis illâ primævi, quam narrat sacra Scriptura, confusione,& inde ortâ tandem linguarum varietate sive divisione, ut Hebraicæ suum jus, & nobis nostram in dubiis sacræ Scripturæ locis & sententiis libertatem assereremus, præmittenda duximus. Per hæc planior jam nobis ad ipsam, & quæ de ipsâ, de dignitate præcipuè (à qua orsuri sumus) nobis dicenda, via.
units.tr: These were the things we thought should be set down first, on the confusion of speech, or language, of that primeval time which Holy Scripture describes, and on the variety or division of languages that followed from it. We wanted to assert Hebrew's right, and our own freedom in the doubtful passages and sayings of Holy Scripture. Through this, the way is now clearer for us to come to the matter itself and to what must be said about it, chiefly about its dignity, with which we shall begin.

units.la: HEBRÆÆ linguæ (ut ordiamur inde) dignitatem per multa multi capita diduxere ; ut antiquitatem, foecunditatem ( ut quæ omnium aliarum parens:) aliáque: sed nihil majus,quàm quòd ab ipso sit authore Deo, qui ὁ ὠ𝔫𝔞𝔱𝔩𝔞𝔯 illam eum aliis non unius generis habitibus & dotibus infeverit ad quas post nati non nisi longo usu & diuturnâ consuetudine pervenere. Nec Ille tantùm, conditor illius ac plasma‐ tor, (ut ita dicam) Deus illis infeverit, sed quam sacro suo ore dignatus sit; sacris legibus ac sacrosanctæ doctrinæ destinaverit. Quæ quidem quò sunt ipsa per se majora, & admirationem habent majorem: tanto magis elaborandum nobis est, ut inter præruptas & præcipites utrinque tum cachinnorum, tum credulorum sententias,quod solidâ ac clarâ veritate nititur, aut ad eam saltem proximè accedit, assequamur.
units.tr: Many have spread out the dignity of the Hebrew language (to begin from there) under many headings: its antiquity, its richness (as being the parent of all others), and other things. But nothing is greater than that it has God himself as its author, who endowed it, not with habits and gifts of one kind alone, to which later-born languages attained only through long use and lasting custom. Not only did God, its founder and shaper, as I may say, endow it in this way, but he also deigned to speak it with his sacred mouth and to appoint it for sacred laws and the most holy teaching. Since these things are in themselves greater and carry greater wonder, we must all the more labour to reach what rests on solid and clear truth, or at least comes closest to it, while avoiding the steep and precipitous opinions on either side, both of mockers and of the credulous.

units.la: Deum Hebraicæ, aut ullius omninò linguæ immediatum authorem esse, non omnes agnoscunt: quorum sententiæ, quòd ab aliis expositæ sint, & argumenta fuse confutata, à nobis omittentur. Ejus inter alios sententiæ fuit & Gregorius Nyssæ Episcopus; quem quia aliis intactum reperio, operæ erit in rationes ejus,quibus præcipuè innitur, inquirere. Leviora sunt ista, οίκ είῥ λογοίῥ, θείῥ ῥί, &c. & aliud esse ϑαυμαστικὴν δύναμιν, aliud ipsa opera, ut scamnum, aratrum, &c. cum nemo nisi vaecors inde colligat, Deum authorem esse linguae Hebraicae, quia Θεὸς λέγει in Sacra Scriptura memoratur; aut vero facultatem ab effectu vel operibus (quae distinctio in Adami posteris locum habet) nequeat distinguere. At multa, inquit, in quacunque lingua ἀρχὴ καὶ ἀπρεπῆ, quorum inventorem Deum facere parum abest a blasphemia. Jam ista, Sartago, similia, lagena, & similia, tam vilia, tam vulgaria verba a Deo ipso quasi conditore profecta esse, quam Deo indignum est? Φλυακία τῶν τε ᾧ μαλαιότης Ιουδαικὴ, πεμπτὸν τῆς ἡ χειρίζων μεταλογίας ἐνπεπλωκῶς, τὸ οἱ ἑσ ἡ μὲν ἡ ὑλισμὸς, καὶ ἀλλὰ ποῦ ὄνομα τε καὶ νόημα ἁπλῶς, ἔπου ὤς τινα γεωμετρίαν τῆς τοιαύτης ἡ ὀρθρέων ἁπλ ἰδοῦ καίτα. i. e. Futilitas haec & vanitas est Judaica, a Christiana doctrina sublimitate & excellentia multum defecta & deflexa, Deum credere, Magnum illum & Excelsum; qui supra omne nomen, supra omnem animi cogitationem, talem, velut aliquem de trivio Grammatistam, verborum impositiones subtiliter excogitantem sedare, &c.
units.tr: Not all agree that God is the immediate author of Hebrew, or indeed of any language at all. Their opinions, since they have been set out by others and their arguments fully refuted, will be omitted by us. Among others, Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, held this view. Since I find him untouched by others, it will be worth inquiring into the reasons on which he chiefly relies. These are weaker: that it is not a matter of words, that God is spoken of, and that the power of wonder is one thing, the works themselves another, as a bench or a plough is; since no one but a fool would infer from this that God is the author of the Hebrew language because God is mentioned as speaking in Holy Scripture, or else cannot distinguish the faculty from its effect or works (a distinction that holds among the posterity of Adam). But, he says, many words in any language are base and unseemly, and to suppose God the inventor of them comes close to blasphemy. Now, that words such as sartago [frying pan], lagena [flask] and similar ones, so cheap and so common, should have come from God as their founder, how unworthy is that of God himself! This is Jewish futility and vanity, far fallen away from the sublimity and excellence of Christian teaching, to believe that God, the Great and Most High, who is above every name and above every thought of the mind, should devise word-impositions with subtlety, like some schoolboy from the crossroads, and so on.

units.la: De Deo Moses, initio Geneseos: Dixitque Deus, Fiat lux, &c. appellavitque Lucem, diem: & tenebras, noctem, &c. Vocavitque Deus firmamentum, &c. Iterumque, Et vocavit Deus aridam, terram, &c. Haec Eunomius, ut & ex recentioribus quidam non contemnendi interpretes, ita plane, ut scripta sunt, quasi a Deo ipso, etiam ante Adamum conditum, quasi prolata aut concepta essent ista paucula, intelligebant. Excipit autem Gregorius, "Ε αφλα καταοχολάζειν τοιάδε-τινα ῥήματα ἀπὸ Θεοῦ ἐφ' ἑαυτοῦ ραψωδεῖν, ὑπ' οὐδενὸς ἀπολυμένου διὰ τῶν τοιούτων φωνῶν σημασίας, ὡς οἶδα πῶς ἔτι μὴ καταγέλαστον ἅμα ἡμῖν βλάσφημον τὸ τοιοῦτον οἴεσθαι.
units.tr: Moses, at the beginning of Genesis: And God said, Let there be light, etc. And he called the light day, and the darkness night, etc. And God called the firmament, etc. And again: And God called the dry land earth, etc. Eunomius, and some of the more recent interpreters, who are not to be despised, understood these few words plainly as they are written, as if they had been spoken or conceived by God himself, even before Adam was created. Gregory objects: it is pointless to dwell on such utterances, to recite such sayings as coming from God on his own, when no one is released from the meaning through such words; and I know not how one could avoid thinking such a thing both laughable and blasphemous [ἐπεὶ ἄφελε καταγοχολάζειν τοιαῦτα τινα ῥήματα ἀπὸ Θεοῦ ἐφ' ἑαυτοῦ ῥαψῳδεῖν, ὑπ' οὐδενὸς ἀπολυμένου διὰ τῶν τοιούτων φωνῶν σημασίας, ὡς οἶδα πῶς ἔτι μὴ καταγέλαστον ἅμα ἡμῖν βλάσφημον τὸ τοιοῦτον οἴεσθαι].

units.la: Totâ fateor illâ Eunomii disputatione & argumentatione nihil vaesanius; qui, cum de verbis Graecis omnis esset controversia, quia Deus ipse rebus ante hominem conditum nomina indidisset, inde de verborum aeternâ quadam & immutabili naturâ mire philosophabatur, & impiis suis dogmatibus accommodabat; & si quis aliter sentiret, ut laesae divinae Majestatis reum, & divinae providentiae oppugnatorem quasi ἐπ' ἀὐλοφάσῳ deprehensum, atheis & Epicuræis, verbis quàm poterat atrocissimis accensebat. Hìc, piè ac graviter Nyssenus opponit, Dei Opt.Max. non in eo consistere Majestatem, ut verba fabricet, & nomina rebus imponat, qui tantis operibus (quæ pluribus ibi ab illo, non uno loco, commemorantur) infinitæ suæ tum sapientiæ tum potentiæ documenta ediderit. Sed rationes, quibus literalem illam verborum Mosis interpretationem Nyssenus impugnat, & totum illum personati Dei in superioribus verbis mimum & χλιαζμὸν, probare non possum, nec periculo carere censeo. Non satis perspexisse mihi videntur interdum viri graves, quantum impietati finum panderent, dum de rebus abstrusis differentes, & de Deo ex humano more & sermone loquentes, festivi & ingeniosi esse affectant. Ut altiora fidei nostræ mysteria omittam, quæ vel modestissimis (nisi fides & pietas contineat, quod & agnoscit Apostolus: ) ἀπαλὺν γὰλῶλα movere statim sunt idonea: nulla res magis Epicurum & ejus sectatores ad negandam Dei providentiam induxit, quàm quòd, quoquó se verteret homo petulans, & qui ex ingenio suo Deum metiretur, tam multa absurda & ridicula doctrinam illam contínere judicaret.Nec sanè deerant multa,quæ cum plausu (ut sunt ad risum & impietatem proni multi:) à plerisque exciperentur.
units.tr: I confess that nothing is more mad than the whole of Eunomius' disputation and argument. Although the entire controversy concerned Greek words, because God himself had given names to things before man was created, he philosophised wonderfully from this about a certain eternal and unchangeable nature of words, and adapted it to his impious dogmas. If anyone thought otherwise, Eunomius charged him, as one guilty of injuring the divine majesty and as an opponent of divine providence, caught as it were in the very act, with the most atrocious words he could find, and branded him an atheist and an Epicurean. Here the Nyssen, piously and gravely, objects that the majesty of God, best and greatest, does not consist in fashioning words and imposing names on things; he has given proofs of his infinite wisdom and power in such great works, which are recorded there in many places, not only one. But I cannot approve of the arguments by which the Nyssen attacks that literal interpretation of Moses' words, nor of his whole mime and jesting about the fictitious God in the preceding words, nor do I think it is free from danger. Serious men sometimes seem not to have seen clearly how much they open the door to impiety when, discussing abstruse matters and speaking of God in human fashion and language, they aim to be witty and clever. To leave aside the higher mysteries of our faith, which are apt to stir even the most modest minds at once, unless faith and piety restrain them (as the Apostle also recognises), nothing has led Epicurus and his followers more to deny God's providence than the fact that, whichever way a petulant man turns, and one who measures God by his own wit, judges that this doctrine contains so many absurd and ridiculous things. Nor were there lacking many such things which, as many men are prone to laughter and impiety, were received with applause by most people.

units.la: Qualia illa in Cicerone : Vos Dei Majestatem deducitis usque ad apum formicarúmque perfectionem, ut etiam inter Deos Myrmecides aliquis minutorum opusculorum fabricator, fuisse videatur. Et eodem libro, Etiámne hoc affirmare potes, Luculle, esse aliquam vim, cum prudentia & consilio scilicet, qua finxerit, vel, ut tuo verbo utar, fabricata sit hominem? qualis ista fabrica est? ubi adhibita est? quando? cur? quomodo? Et alibi ; Quibus enim oculis intueri potuit vester Plato, Fabricam illâ tanti operis, quâ construi à Deo atque ædificari mundum facit? Qua molitio? qua ferramenta? qui vectes? que machina? qui ministri tanti operis fuerunt? Et ibidem rursús : Sive enim ipse mundus Deus est, quid potest esse minùs quietum, quàm nullo puncto temporis intermisso versari circum axem cœli admirabili celeritate? Nisi quietum autem, nihil beatum est. Sive in ipso mundo Deus inest aliquis, qui regat, qui gubernet, qui cursus astrorum, mutationes temporum, rerum vicissitudines, ordinesque conservet, terras & maria contemplans, hominum commoda vitaque tueatur: na ille est implicatus molestiis negotiis & operosis.
units.tr: Such are those things in Cicero: You bring the majesty of God down even to the perfection of bees and ants, so that among the gods there seems to be some Myrmecides, a maker of tiny works. And in the same book: Can you affirm this too, Lucullus, that there is some power with prudence and counsel, by which he shaped, or, to use your word, fabricated man? What sort of fabrication is this? Where was it applied? When? Why? How? And elsewhere: For with what eyes could your Plato have looked upon that workshop of so great a work, by which he makes the world constructed and built by God? What was the operation? What tools? What levers? What machine? What servants were there for so great a work? And again in the same place: For if the world itself is God, what can be less at rest than to revolve around the axis of heaven with admirable speed, without any pause of a moment? But nothing is blessed unless it is at rest. Or if some God dwells in the world itself, who rules and governs, who preserves the courses of the stars, the changes of the seasons, the vicissitudes and orders of things, who looks over lands and seas and watches over men's conveniences and lives, then he is entangled in troublesome and laborious business.

units.la: Quasi vero Deus author alicujus linguae dici non possit, aut cogitari; quin necesse sit infelicis alicujus grammaticuli, literulis & apicibus suis assidentis, personam illi affingi? Aut tanta fatuitas in quenquam possit cadere, qui bona fide credat, dixisse Deum, Fiat lux, & facta est; & caetera, quae maxime miramur, solo verbi sui imperio condidisse? Aut, si qualiscunq; operum subtilitas indigna Deo est, major sit in verborum varietate & orationis partibus subtilitas, quam quae in auditus aut visus organis (si singula, quae ad istorum sensuum perfectionem spectant, accurate & anatomice expendantur) & naturali constructione conspicitur? Cujus tamen tantae ac tam variae subtilitatis accurata consideratio tantum abest, ut viros doctissimos à summi Opificis agnitione averterit, ut etiam Ethnicos ad prædicandam Dei Opt. Max. tum potentiam tum bonitatem excitaverit.
units.tr: As if God could not be called or thought of as the author of some language, and it were necessary to attribute to him the character of some wretched little grammarian, sitting over his letters and marks! Or could such foolishness fall upon anyone who sincerely believes that God said, Let there be light, and there was light, and that he founded the other things that we most admire by the sole command of his word? Or, if any subtlety of works is unworthy of God, is there greater subtlety in the variety of words and parts of speech than in the organs of hearing or sight (if each of the things that pertain to the perfection of those senses is carefully and anatomically weighed) and in their natural construction? Yet the careful consideration of so great and so varied a subtlety is so far from turning the most learned men away from the knowledge of the highest Maker, that it has even stirred up the heathen to proclaim the power and goodness of God, best and greatest.

units.la: Jam quòd verba parùm honesta(qualia in omnibus linguis aliqua) objicit Nyssenus; non eò jam digrediar, ut Stoicorum cum Epicuræis de verborum rerúmve turpitudine liti (super quâ doctissima Ciceronis extat epistola) me interponam. Hoc tantùm dicam, si aliqua sit in verbis vera & ipsis inhærens turpitudo; quantò magis in rebus, quarum verba nihil aliud quàm signa sunt & symbola? Quò tandem ista proceßura, nemo non videt; nec minùs, si cogitaßet, abominaturus Nyssenus ipse, sat scio, quàm quivis alius. Sed hic intempestivi, ubi de Deo agitur, risùs ut plurimum fructus est. Cæterùm facetias suas & elegantias, quibus simplicitatem nostram illudit Gregorius, ex Plutarcho eum mutuatum esse non ausim affirmare. Simillima sanè in Plutarcho, Περὶ τῆ μὴ χρᾶν, &c. ubi de conceptis oraculorum formulis disserit, non uno loco memini legere.
units.tr: Now, as to the words that are not very decent, which Nyssen objects to (some such words are found in all languages), I shall not go so far as to interpose myself in the dispute of the Stoics and Epicureans over the baseness of words and things (on which there is a most learned letter of Cicero). I will say only this: if there is any true baseness inherent in words themselves, how much more is there in things, whose words are nothing but signs and symbols? Where this will lead no one fails to see, and I am quite sure that Nyssen himself would abominate it no less than anyone else, if he had thought it through. But laughter that is out of place, when God is the subject, usually bears this fruit. However, I would not dare to affirm that Gregory borrowed from Plutarch his jokes and elegances, with which he mocks our simplicity. I do not remember reading in Plutarch, in his treatise On the Cessation of Oracles, etc., where he discusses the formulas of oracles, anything very similar in more than one place.

units.la: Sed ut ad verba Mosis redeamus; quod ait ille, Vocavit Deus, &c. non displicet Merceri sententia, per ἀνθρώπων ista dici, quòd ita postea post hominem conditum nuncupata sint. Sed quod addit Mercerus, fi Deus ipse indidiffet illa nomina, fine piaculo mutari aut alia usurpari non potuisse; non fatis assequor; nisi omnia, quæ Deus instituit, perpetui juris esse sanciantur. Quod fi est, ne ceremoniæ quidem legales, quarum Deus author, abrogandæ fuerunt: quod ad nugas illas Eunomianas, (quas merito Nyffenus exagitat) nimis accedere videtur. Nos igitur illorum sententiam amplectimur,qui docent, quæcunque Adam recèns creatus loquutus est, quæcunque rebus imposuit five verba five nomina, ad Deum authorem referenda esse,qui Adamum docuerit, aut potiùs inspiraverit. Nam per naturæ alioquin leges non alia Adami recèns creati ratio, quàm hominis, qui ab omni hominum consortio à primâ usque infantiâ feclusus fuerit: qualem mutum necefsario extiturum alibi docuimus. Quare vel eo nomine lingua Hebraica ab auctore suo, merito fanéta audit. Cæteràrum rùm cùm Adamus nomina rebus imponeret,pauca illum nova(si tamen ulla:) simplicia verba procudisse,sed vel communia levi inflexione propria fecisse, vel plura jungendo composuisse, res ipsa loquitur : quanquam hodie multorum rationem ignorari, tam multis deperditis aut ignoratis radicibus, necesse est.
units.tr: But to return to the words of Moses: when he says, God called, etc., Mercer's view, that these things are said by men [ἀνθρώπων], because names were afterwards given in this way after man was created, does not displease me. But what Mercer adds, that if God himself had imposed those names they could not be changed or others used without sin, I do not quite grasp; unless it is to be decreed that everything God has instituted is of perpetual right. If that is so, even the legal ceremonies, of which God was the author, would have had to be abolished; and this seems too close to those Eunomian trifles, which Nyssen rightly chastises. Therefore we embrace the opinion of those who teach that whatever Adam, newly created, spoke, whatever he imposed on things, whether words or names, must be referred to God as author, who taught Adam, or rather inspired him. For otherwise, by the laws of nature, Adam's newly created state was no different from that of a man who had been cut off from all human fellowship from his earliest infancy; and such a man would necessarily turn out mute, as I have shown elsewhere. Hence, for this reason too, the Hebrew language is rightly called holy by its author. Moreover, that Adam, in imposing names on things, coined few new words (if any at all), simple words, but either made common words his own by slight inflection, or composed more by joining several together, the matter itself makes plain; although today the reasoning of many must be unknown, since so many roots have been lost or are unknown.

units.la: Proxima linguæ Hebraicæ dignitas, Antiquitas, & eorum, quibus illa vernacula fuit, authoritas & reverentia. Nam si non sine ratione dixit emunctissimæ naris & judicii vir Quintilianus, verba vetusta majestatem quandam cum voluptate conjunctam afferre orationi : quanta sit illius linguæ majestas, quæ alia non agnoscit incunabula, non alios natales, quàm quos mundus ipse; imò, si Rabbinis fides, non tam mundo æqualis, quàm inter mundi causas numeranda ? Ita enim illi vulgò loqui solent, hanc esse linguam, in qua creatum sit mundus. Jam si manuscriptus codex (ut annosas quercus & exesos senio lapides, multorum quondam populorum numina, omittam:) si manuscriptus, inquam, codex, cujus fugientes literæ & cætera species multorum præferat seculorum antiquitatem : si veteres urbium templorúmq; ruinæ, quorum nobilitata veteribus historiis fata casúsve fuerint; sí alia denique paris vetustatis monumenta solent animos spectantium (multorum certè, nec de facte) proprió nescio quo jucunditatis & admirationis sensu percellere : quomodo affici illos par est, qui Hebraica loquentes, aut audientes, simul ita secum reputabunt, hos sonos, hæc vocabula, nascenti quondam mundo prælusisse ; in hos modos, in hæc verba,sua quondam ora finxisse ; his aures eorum personuisse, qui tanta seculorum serie vetustiores sunt illis, quos prisci Ethnici ob antiquitatem in numina secerunt : qui tum vivebant, cùm Mundus adhuc infans esset : quos præsentia sua, quos alloquio,quos tot miraculis Deus dignatus est : à quibus Orbi salus universo, & in omnem posteritatem transmissa virtutum exempla ?
units.tr: The next distinction of the Hebrew language is its antiquity, and the authority and reverence of those to whom it was the mother tongue. For if the man of most refined nose and judgement, Quintilian, was right in saying that archaic words bring a certain majesty to speech, joined with pleasure, how great is the majesty of that language, which acknowledges no other cradle and no other birth than the world itself; indeed, if the rabbis are to be believed, it is to be counted not so much as equal to the world as among the causes of the world? For they are accustomed to say commonly that this is the language in which the world was created. Now, if a manuscript codex (I say nothing of the ancient oaks and stones worn by age, the divinities of many peoples long ago), if a manuscript, I say, whose fading letters and other appearance show the antiquity of many centuries; if the old ruins of cities and temples, whose fates or calamities are made famous by ancient histories; if, finally, other monuments of similar age commonly strike the minds of onlookers (of many certainly, and not without cause) with some peculiar sense of delight and wonder: how ought those to be affected who, speaking or hearing Hebrew, reflect at the same time that these sounds, these words, once preluded to the newly born world; that in these tones, in these words, their mouths were once shaped; that to their ears sounded those who, by so long a series of ages, are older than those whom the ancient heathen made into gods on account of their antiquity; who lived when the world was still an infant; whom God deigned to honour with his presence, his speech, and so many miracles; from whom came salvation for the whole world, and examples of virtue handed down to all posterity?

units.la: Cæterùm de linguæ Hebraicæ à jactis mundi fundamentis antiquitate receptissima jam olim hodiéque inter omnes ferè linguarū peritos opinio est, tantis rerum ipsarum nixa fundamentis, ut de eo dubitare, non aliud merito videri possit, quàm τὰ ἀκίνητα κινοῦν. Scimus tamen non defuisse olim hodieque, qui aliter statuere & adstruere conati sunt: ut Goropii Becani insanissimum inceptum missum faciam; cujus inter feria meminisse, aut aliam rationem habere, quàm eorum, quæ ad lusum jocúmque, aut ad irritæ & infructuosæ subtilitatis admirationem apparantur, sobrii vix hominis crediderim. Quæ verò de lingua Chaldaicâ, Syriacâve, sed & Canaanitica, à non uno oppositæ sunt, quia à pluribus accuratè tractata & refutata sunt, libenter & illa prætermittimus. Hæc igitur quorsum? dicat aliquis fortasse. Planè, ut ad novam viri docti, & celebris inter recentiores Geographos Italiæ & Germaniæ accuratâ descriptione, nominis, de primævâ linguâ opinionem, de quâ silent alii, expendendam, aditum mihi faciam. Is est autem Philippus Cluverius, qui in Germaniæ Antiquæ descriptione de primævâ linguâ ita statuit, eam cum Paradiso terrestri planè intercidisse, & hodiè penitùs ignorari.
units.tr: The very ancient opinion that Hebrew is the language from the foundation of the world has long been, and still is, almost universally held by those skilled in languages. It rests on such firm foundations in the facts themselves that to doubt it would rightly seem nothing other than "moving the immovable" (τὰ ἀκίνητα κινοῦν).
