We know, however, that there have been, both formerly and today, those who have tried to hold and argue otherwise. I will pass over the utterly insane undertaking of Goropius Becanus. I can hardly believe that a sober man would think it worth mentioning among trifles, or would give it any consideration beyond what is prepared for play and jest or for the admiration of a vain and fruitless cleverness. As for what has been objected by more than one writer concerning the Chaldee, Syriac, and also Canaanite languages, these have been treated and refuted carefully by many, so I gladly set those aside too. Why this, then? someone may perhaps ask. Plainly, so that I may open for myself the way to weigh the opinion about the primeval language, which others pass over in silence, of a learned man of great name among recent geographers of Italy and Germany. That man is Philip Cluverius, who in his Germaniæ Antiquæ description holds that the primeval language perished entirely along with the earthly Paradise and is today utterly unknown.

units.la: Argumentum huic suæ sententiæ adduxit unicum ;-sed quod multorum instar, si tam verum, quàm speciosum, censeri possit. Ita enim ille contendit, verborum numerum vel ad millia posse colligi, quæ plerisque aut multis saltem linguis sint communia. Unde autem ista communitas, nisi ex communi linguâ matrice, primæva scilicet illâ, quæcunque fuerit? Ista autem tam multa, tam multis linguis communia, cùm minimè sint Hebraica, aut Hebraicæ originis; eò fieri, ut lingua Hebraica cæterarum matrix esse non possit. Agnoscimus nos huic inesse pondus argumento. Quid igitur superesset, quàm ut testes audiantur; & de mille, saltem centum, quando tanta res agitur ab hoc uno pendens argumento, proserantur? Ego certè ita expectabam. Sed tantum abest, ut id præstiterit Cluverius, quod expectabamus; ut pro centum vix decem talium verborum numerum expleat, quæ pluribus linguis sint communia: ex illis autem decem, vix unum sit aut alterum, quod originem, si quis idoneus arbiter, præ se non ferat Hebraicam.
units.tr: Cluverius rests this opinion on one argument only, but one which, if it is as true as it is specious, might be counted as the equal of many. For he contends that the number of words common to most, or at least many, languages can be gathered into the thousands. Whence this commonality, unless from a common mother language, that primeval one whatever it was? But these many words, common to so many languages, are by no means Hebrew or of Hebrew origin, and so it follows that the Hebrew language cannot be the mother of the others. We acknowledge that this argument has weight. What then remains but that witnesses be heard, and that from a thousand, or at least a hundred, examples be brought forward, since so great a matter is at stake and hangs on this one argument? That is what I certainly expected. But Cluverius fell so far short of what we expected that he scarcely reaches ten such words out of a hundred that are common to several languages. And of those ten, hardly one or two would, to any competent judge, show themselves not to be of Hebrew origin.

units.la: Sed hoc ante omnia monendum, quanquam pauca sunt, quæ nobis hîc exhibet Cluverius, tamen in his paucis nonnulla esse, quæ plane sunt ἀσφαλιότητα. Non enim sufficit, ut, quæ plùribus linguis cognatis sunt communia, proferantur: quales jam olim Græca & Latina; hodiè, Gallica, Hispanica, & Italica; quibus addunt alii Walachianam; quæ maxima ex parte ex Latino fluxerunt idiomate, & unius ejusdémque linguæ multiplex ex proprio populorum & locorum genio corruptio & depravatio potiùs, quàm diversæ simpliciter linguæ merito dici possint. Multa quoque in Germanicam ex Latina, ex longo commercio & aliâ necessitudine, illata: quod ita factum esse tantum abest ut mirari quisquam debeat, ut potiùs monstro simile credendum fuerit, si non ita contigisset. Quare nihil attinebat hîc de Oculo commemorare, quem Latini oculum, Germani auge vel oge, Sarmatæ oki nominant: non magis quàm vel Gallicum jeulx, vel Italicum occhi, vel Hispanicum ojos, vel Anglicum denique eyes: & multò minùs de Aure, quæ ut Latinis
units.tr: But this must be said before all else: although the few examples Cluverius sets before us are few, nonetheless some among these few are plainly unsound (ἀσφαλιότητα). It is not enough to bring forward words common to several cognate languages, as formerly Greek and Latin, and today French, Spanish, and Italian, to which others add Walachian. These languages flowed for the most part from the Latin idiom, and can be called rather a manifold corruption and depravation of one and the same language, arising from the particular genius of peoples and places, than truly different languages. Many words too have been carried into German from Latin through long commerce and other close contact. That this happened is so far from being a matter for wonder that it would rather have seemed monstrous if it had not. Therefore there was no point in mentioning here the eye, which the Latins call oculum, the Germans auge or oge, the Sarmatians oki; no more than the French jeulx, the Italian occhi, the Spanish ojos, or finally the English eyes; and much less about the ear, which as the Latins say auris, so the Germans say oor.

units.la: ris nis auris dicitur, ita Germanis oor. Talia, fateor, quivis nullo negotio mille, vel fortasse ad myriadas, congerat. Quanquam ne hoc quidem satis constat, aurem non esse originis Hebraicæ. Certè si verbum auris quasi ausis, ex Græco ὠς, ὠτός, ut doctis placet, repetendum sit: τὸ οὖς quin ipsissimum sit Hebraicum אזן, nemo poterit inficiari. Sed & oculus, si ex Græco, ut volunt, ὀφθαλμὸς (ὀπ. autem interdum migrare in x. vel λύκος lupus fidem faciat) manavit: τὸ ὄψ (& ὀψ,) ex quibus ὄπλω, ὀπλόμαι, quin ex Hebraico עין oriundum sit, dubitaturum puto neminem. Vox autem אדיר sæpes, quæ apud multas nationes invenitur, quâ tandem ratione in hunc censum venerit, cùm eam Hebraicæ quoque linguæ communem agnoscat Cluverius, ne suspicari quidem possum.
units.tr: Such things, I admit, anyone could collect without any trouble by the thousand, or perhaps by tens of thousands. Yet it is not even quite certain that aurem is not of Hebrew origin. Certainly, if the word auris is to be derived, as learned men like, from the Greek ὠς, ὠτός, as though it were ausis, no one can deny that τὸ οὖς is exactly the Hebrew אזן. But also oculus, if it came from the Greek ὀφθαλμός, as they wish (the ὀπ- sometimes changing into κ, as the Greek λύκος, lupus, bears witness), and from τὸ ὄψ (and ὀψ), from which ὄπλω, ὀπλόμαι; I think no one will doubt that it sprang from the Hebrew עין. As for the word אדיר, which is found among many nations, by what means it came into this count, when Cluverius acknowledges it as common also to the Hebrew language, I cannot even suspect.

units.la: Jam Græca πάλιν & μίτης, quis istarum rerum paulò intelligentior dubitet ex Hebraicis אן & דן profluxisse, cum in utroque τὸ (νῆρ) sit pura puta, qualis in Συνάτηρ, εὐδάτης, κερατήρ, ὀρφλήρ, ῥλήρ &c. terminatio: in utroque etiam eadem sit figuratio, sive formandi ex Hebraico ratio, inversis scilicet literis, & præpositâ vocali consonante, quæ in archetypis postponitur: quod quanquam in cujuscunque linguæ derivativis non insolens (ita exempli causâ ἀεγιὸς, rarus; ֹalbus, &c.) nec aliâ plerunque ratione nititur, quàm consuetudinis arbitrio: hîc tamen ad facilitatem pronuntiationis factum de industria esse probabile est, cum tenera balbutientium labra, à consonantibus, idque ex naturali causâ, verba libentiùs, quàm à vocalibus auspicentur.
units.tr: Now as for the Greek πάλιν and μίτης, who among those who understand these matters at all would doubt that they flowed from the Hebrew אן and דן? In both the ending τὸ (νῆρ) is simply the same termination as in Συνάτηρ, εὐδάτης, κερατήρ, ὀρφλήρ, ῥλήρ, and so on. In both too the formation is the same, or the same method of forming from Hebrew, namely with the letters inverted and a vowel placed in front, which in the originals comes after. Although this is not unusual in the derivatives of any language (thus, for example, ἀεγιὸς, rarus; albus, and so on), and rests for the most part on nothing other than the decision of custom, here it is probable that it was done deliberately for ease of pronunciation. Tender lips of stammering children, for natural reasons, begin words more readily with consonants than with vowels.

units.la: Ad verbum Θεὸς quod attinet, cum pleraque sacrorum vocabula Græca Hebraicæ sint originis, ut non ab uno jam prolixè ostensum & probatum est; & præterea tum compositum שׁוּר, tum simplex ר, & sono & significatione tam prope accedant; cur quisquam de origine Hebraicâ dubitet, nisi qui nondum in scirpo quærat, causam non video. Nec parùm originem hanc confirmat vox altera affinis Græca πατὴρ, quatenus patrum significat. Valde impediti sunt Græci in reddendâ ratione nominis: quare scilicet patrui, Θεῖοι, id est,(ut quidem vox vulgò sonat, à Θεὸς derivata) divini nuncupentur. Inter alios, Simplicii philosophi hæc est sententia; Tantam veteres parentibus exhibuisse reverentiam, ut non solùm divinis eos honoribus affecerint, sed etiam Deos nuncupare voluerint. (ὡς ἡ Θεὸς ἀυτὸν ὁρμῆσαι χαλέιν.) Sed reveritos tamen divinæ Majestatis præcellen- tiam (ἀλλὰ δὲ ἡ θείαν ὑπερέχω) cùm Deos non auderent & parentes communi appellare nomine: at parentum saltem fratres divinos indigitasse, ut ex illis ita nuncupatis, quid parentibus ipsis conveniret, homines conjicerent, atque ita in parentum honorem ista appellatio redundaret. Hæc mens Simplicii, quam corrupit Latinus (doctissimus alioquin) interpres, dum priora illa vertit, Ut Deos appellare eos non dubitárint. Ad rem vero quod attinet ipsam; persuadeat fortasse Simplicius illis, qui de verbis singulis, etiam vulgatissimis, à philosophis, priùs quàm imponerentur, itum in consilium credunt. Nos, qui de verborum origine longè aliter opinamur, plane pro fabula habemus, quod Simplicius comminiscitur: nec tamen facile, melius aliquid reperire, nisi ad Hebraicas origines recurramus. Ibi enim דור patrum, ex quo paulatim, primo ו in affine θ. verso, ut passim; & simplice vocali in diphthongum (quod non minus frequens) producta; & loco finalis ו assumpta pro more (ut ךלמ, λαμπας, &c.) terminatione Graeca Θ, factum θεῶ. Et ut à דור θεῶ, ita à דודה θεια amita. Nec id magis mirum, quam à דים (mamma) formari πιθω, πιτθω, πιθω, πιτθω, & tandem πιθαστω, πιθωω, πιθνω, πιθυνιος, ζηλος, & ejus generis alia, de quibus accurati Lexicographi tum veteres, tum recentiores consulendi. Neque, ego quidem, dubitaverim, ex Chaldaico ארבא (pro Hebraico אריה) lupus, Graecum λυκος, λυκοσ, & λυκων, quanquam paulo remotius accersere; cum exempla remotiorum Etymologiarum, de quibus nemo dubitat, sint in promptu non pauca.
units.tr: As for the word Θεὸς, since most of the sacred Greek words are of Hebrew origin, as more than one writer has already shown and proved at length, and since both the compound שׁוּר and the simple ר come so close in sound and meaning, I do not see why anyone should doubt its Hebrew origin, unless he is still looking for a knot in a rush. Nor does the other related Greek word πατὴρ, insofar as it means patrum ("of fathers"), confirm this origin only a little. The Greeks were much perplexed in giving an account of the name: the patrui, Θεῖοι, that is, as the word commonly sounds, derived from Θεὸς, were called divini. Among others, this is the view of the philosopher Simplicius: the ancients showed such reverence to parents that they not only honoured them with divine honours but wished to call them gods. But, reverencing the pre-eminence of the divine majesty, since they did not dare to call parents by the common name of gods, they designated at least the brothers of the parents as divini, so that from those so named people might guess what suited the parents themselves, and thus the title would redound to the parents' honour. This is Simplicius's meaning, which the Latin translator (otherwise most learned) corrupted when he rendered the earlier part as Ut Deos appellare eos non dubitárint. As to the matter itself: Simplicius perhaps persuades those who believe that words, even the most common, were devised by philosophers in council before they were imposed. We, who think quite differently about the origin of words, regard what Simplicius invents as a plain fable, nor is it easy to find something better unless we return to Hebrew origins. For there the word דור means patrum, "of fathers", from which, gradually, first the ו was changed into θ, as often happens; and the simple vowel was lengthened into a diphthong (no less frequent); and a final ו was taken on in the usual way (as ךלמ becomes λαμπας, and so on), with the Greek ending Θ, and so θεῶ was made. And as from דור came θεῶ, so from דודה came θεια, "aunt" (amita). This is no more surprising than that from דים (mamma) the forms πιθω, πιτθω, πιθω, πιτθω, and at last πιθαστω, πιθωω, πιθνω, πιθυνιος, ζηλος, and other words of that kind were formed, about which the careful lexicographers, both ancient and recent, should be consulted. Nor, I for my part, would I hesitate to derive the Greek λυκος, λυκοσ, and λυκων from the Chaldee ארבא (for the Hebrew אריה), lupus, though this is fetched from a rather remote source, since examples of more remote etymologies, about which no one doubts, are not few and are at hand.

units.la: Ad vocem λυκαλη, & quae inde profluxere, quod attinet, nihil ego temere pronuntiaverim; nec causa quicquam obfuerit, si unum aut alterum verbum tale reperiri possit, pluribus linguis usitatum, cujus usus, aut origo Hebraica, non dicam, non sit; nam hoc in tanta verborum Hebraicorum jastura, & post tantas mutationum vices, valdè temerarium est asserere: sed à nobis indicari & demonstrari non possit. Quanquam igitur, ut jam diximus, causæ ipsius nihil interfit, Lectoris tamen φιλοsοφίας nonnihil intererit sorte, quid de verbi istius origine, cum magna veri (ut ego quidem judico) similitudine dici possit, non ignorare. Omissis igitur Græcorum conjecturis, quæ nauci non sunt; maximam esse literarum ꝛ. & γ. affinitatem, omnium; qui in his aliquid unquam studiis viderunt, tralatitia est observatio. Hinc κυβερνο, guberno: κεφάλη, grabbatum: κόμμι, gummi: & alia, quæ in omnibus occurrunt linguis, aliis passim notata; ut κόλπο, golfo: κρύπτη, grotta: & similia. Jam Hebraicum ꝛj, corpus; sed & caput, ut caput pro vertice, aut quod summum est, sumitur, significat. Sunt, qui ad diversas radices referant: alii, aliter: quod perinde nobis hïc est, modò de significatione conveniat. Ut igitur à ꝛj, κορυφή ejusdem significationis: ita erit & à ꝛj, gaph, five caph, κεφαλή. Hoc video quibufdam placuisse : quod mihi quoque valdè probatur. Quia tamen nihil hîc afleveramus,& erunt fortasse, qui huic quamvis probabili conjectura non acquiescant ; quid praterea mihi venerit in mentem,lectorem non celabo. אלה Hebraeis, dux, ductor, vulgò. Non abfudit nec sono nec significatione vox χεραλὴ:nisi quòd τὸ κ.praepositum initio, quod multis verbis accidere,ut interdum vacet,interdù defit,notant veteres Grammatici. Cujus exempla consuetudinis, κλάθ, pro ἐλάθ: ἀνθάλια, ἀνθάλια: ἀνλαυία, ἀνλαυία, ab Euftathio proseruntur : ab aliis, χαύχηματ, αὐχημα : χα-πάνη, ἀπάνη : χαλινδῆσαι, ἀλινδῆσαι : χά-φ, ἀφῆ : aliâque non pauca. Mihi certè eo magis arridet haec conjectura, quòd & Anglicum Calfe ex eodem Hebraico verbo אלף, quatenus bovem significat, fluxisse penè mihi persuadeo. Nam quòd aliquis objiciat, aliud esse bovem,aliud vitulum : quàm nihil sit ista objectio, satis intelligunt, opinor, omnes qui in hac verborum de lingua in linguam migratione, confundi saepe non aetates tantùm,sed & generation animalium,saepiùs observarunt:quod in hoc ipso verbo contigisse nemo dubitat, & ex bove Græcos elephantem fecisse. Sed & ipsum vitulus, Latinum, quis dubitat, quin ex Græco fit ἴταλὸς, quod bovem vel taurum, non vitulum, significat? Quanquam hæc fortasse nimis multa, addam tamen & hoc, Syriacè ܩܪܩܦܐ, cranium, caput: Chaldaicè, ܩܪܩܦܐ, homo magni capitis: ܩܪܩܦܠ, cutis capitis: in quibus & Latini caput, & Græci κεφαλὴ, seu κόρρη, vértigia non obscura: sed à quâ primitùs origine, peritioribus discipiendum relinquo.
units.tr: As for the word λυκαλη (lykalē) and the words that have grown out of it, I will assert nothing rashly. Nor would it harm my case if one or another such word were found, used in several languages, whose use or Hebrew origin I will not say is absent. To claim this with confidence, after so great a loss of Hebrew words and so many changes, would be very rash, and it cannot be shown or demonstrated by us. Although, as I have already said, the outcome of the cause itself does not matter to me, the reader's love of learning will care a little about what can be said with considerable likelihood (as I judge) about the origin of this word. So, setting aside the Greek conjectures, which are worth nothing, it is a commonplace among all who have studied these matters that there is a very close affinity between the letters r and g. Hence kybernao (guberno, "to steer"), kephalē (grabbatum, "bed"), kommi (gummi, "gum"), and others found in all languages, noted by others here and there, such as kolpo (golfo, "gulf"), kryptē (grotta, "grotto"), and similar words. Now the Hebrew word for body, and also caput, "head," is used for the top or, what is highest, for the summit. Some refer these to different roots, others to other roots; for me this makes no difference, provided they agree about the meaning. So just as from the Hebrew word for body comes koryphē (the top) with the same meaning, so too from gaph, or caph, comes kephalē (head). I see that this pleased some people, and I myself greatly approve of it. But since I have not yet asserted anything here, and there will perhaps be those who do not accept this conjecture, however probable, I will not hide from the reader what else has occurred to me. The Hebrews have eluph (אלוף), "leader, chief," commonly. The Greek word chelaulē is not far off in sound or meaning, except that a kappa has been put at the beginning, which the ancient grammarians note happens in many words, so that it is sometimes absent, sometimes added. Examples of this practice, such as klathō for elathō, anthalia for anthalia, anlauia for anlauia, are cited by Eustathius; others give auchēma for auchēma, chapanē for apanē, chalindēsai for alindēsai, chaphē for aphē, and not a few others. This conjecture pleases me all the more because I almost persuade myself that the English calf also flowed from the same Hebrew word, eleph, insofar as it means an ox. For if someone objects that an ox is one thing and a calf another, that objection is nothing, as I think all understand who have often observed, in the migration of words from language to language, that not only ages but also kinds of animals are confused. No one doubts that this happened in this very word, and that the Greeks made an elephant out of an ox. But who doubts that the Latin vitulus itself comes from the Greek italos, which means an ox or a bull, not a calf? Though this may be too much, I will add this also: in Syriac, qrqpʾ (qarqappa), "skull, head"; in Chaldee, the same word means "a man of great head," and qrqpl means "the skin of the head." In these both the Latin caput and the Greek kephalē, or korrē, show clear traces of kinship. But from what original source this came, I leave for the more skilled to discover.

units.la: Τὰ σπεῖρα, sunt qui à בום, concúlcare; sunt qui à יבש, incedere, deducant: utrique, satis probabiliter, quanquam, si quis me quoque roget, ego malim ex בוס repetere: cùm non affinis tantùm, sed eadem omninò sit significatio; & diphthongus guttturalem egregiè suppleat: ultima autem litera ת radicalis in terminationem, ut plerunque, transfeat.
units.tr: Ta speira: some derive it from the Hebrew bum, "to trample," others from yabesh, "to walk." Both are fairly probable, although if someone asks me too, I would rather derive it from bus (בוס), since the meaning is not merely related but altogether the same, and the diphthong supplies the guttural admirably; and the final radical letter tav passes, as usual, into the termination.

units.la: Agnoscent, opinor, in his versati nihil hîc coactum aut insoleris. Idem meritò dicamus de particula negativa non: quam, si quod aliud verbum, minimè cunctacunctabimur Hebraicæ origini afferere. Quid enim aliud suadeant Hebraica NJ no, ex quo Hiphil NJJ, renuit, iritum fecit: & ipsum ɾN en, non: quod inversum ne, est ipsissimum Græcorum vi, quod in compositis remanet, vnxtls, vnxupѕ, vnxupwѕ, & aliis multis. Quàm vulgares autem sint isti modi, in monosyllabis præcipuè, transpositiones literarum, tum alia fidem faciant in mundo exempla, tum illud inter alia Arabicum, Buxtorfio observatum, ɾN pro NJ (nunc) Hebraico: ex quo Græcorum vũv (& ex Græco Latinum nunc:) geminatâ ɾ n. litera; quod & in aliis, & in sto, de quo nobis hic sermo, non contigit.
units.tr: Those versed in these matters will recognise, I think, that nothing forced or unusual is said here. I would say the same rightly of the negative particle "not." If it were any other word, I would not hesitate to assert a Hebrew origin. For what else would the Hebrew lo (לא) suggest, from which comes the Hiphil, "he refused, made void"? And also en (אין), "not," which inverted is ne, is the very same as the Greek negative particle that remains in compounds, such as ouk-, ouch-, and many others. But how common such transpositions of letters are, especially in monosyllables, both other examples in the world bear witness, and that Arabic one observed by Buxtorf, where the Arabic an is used for the Hebrew NJ (now). From this, by doubling the letter n, came the Greek nyn (and from the Greek, the Latin nunc). This did not happen in other words, nor in the one we are discussing here.

units.la: Denique de tertiæ verbi substantivi personæ ˈi, vel est, quis laboret originem, qui quidem sciat, quam vim habeat 'W apud Hebræos? Literam Hebraicam ꝏ per st, quæ longè facilior pronuntiatio, expressere. nec id sine causa. Mixtum enim aliquid ex utroque videtur istud Hebraicum ꝏ; unde est, quòd Chaldæi pro ꝏ n n passim substituunt. ut nin, nin, nin, nnin, pro Hebraicis, ꝏ, ꝏ, ꝏ, ꝏ: & hoc ipsum ꝏ, ψ, illis אית: ut in illorum sententiam libens concedam, qui Latinum asinus, ex Hebraico אתון, ob literarum affinitatem, & frequentem permutationem derivant. Ita & snnn, resina: vavhe, nausea, &c. Cæterùm, siquis Græcum ἡμῶν (ex quo Latinum manavit:) ex Chaldaeo illo אתא malit repetere, non ego repugnaverim, nec eò minùs fit Hebraicum, cùm Chaldaica sit Hebreæ dialectus. Reliqua verbi substantivi, sum, sunt, esse, de quibus aliquid hic Cluverius, quanquam ad eosdem & ista sontes cómodè referri possint, quia tamen nostra nihil hic interest, cùm paucis tantùm linguis sint communia, ne leætoribus nimis molesti simus, omittemus.
units.tr: Finally, as for the third person of the substantive verb, ˈi or "is," who would labour over its origin, given that he knows what force the Hebrew 'W has? The Hebrew letter is expressed by st, a much easier pronunciation. Nor is this without reason. For that Hebrew letter seems to be a mixture of both sounds; hence the Chaldeans often substitute for it the letter n, as in nin, nin, nin, nnin, in place of the Hebrew forms. And this same letter, ψ, has as its Chaldee equivalent ית, so that I would willingly agree with those who derive the Latin asinus from the Hebrew athon (אתון), because of the affinity of the letters and their frequent interchange. So too resina (resin) and nausea, and so on. Moreover, if someone prefers to derive the Greek hēmōn (from which the Latin came) from that Chaldee form ita (אתא), I would not object; nor is it any less Hebrew for that, since Chaldee is a dialect of Hebrew. The remaining forms of the substantive verb, sum, sunt, esse, on which Cluverius says something here, could also be conveniently referred to the same sources; but since they are of no concern to us here, being shared by only a few languages, I will omit them, so as not to be too tiresome to the reader.

units.la: Atque ista sunt, quæ ex multis, ut ait ipse, vocabulorum millibus potissimùm delegit eruditissimus Geographus, quibus Hebraicæ linguæ primigeniam antiquitatem convellere nititur: quæ ego de multis, verè dico, millibus non postrema judicassem, quibus illam matricem omnium aliarum linguarum apud æquos & idoneos judices adstruerem. Enimverò, si vel Cluverius ipse aliquam Sanctæ linguæ cognitionem habuisset, vel peritum aliquem in confilium adhibuisset, nunquam, opinor, commisisset, ut receptam per tot ætates fœliciter opinionem, tam futilibus argumentis & exemplis impeteret.
units.tr: These are the examples which the most learned geographer chose from, as he himself says, many thousands of words, and by which he tries to overturn the primordial antiquity of the Hebrew language. Out of many thousands, as I truly say, I would not have thought these the least strong, by which I would establish that language as the mother of all others before fair and competent judges. Indeed, if Cluverius himself had any knowledge of the holy tongue, or had consulted some expert as his adviser, I think he would never have attacked an opinion held happily for so many ages with such flimsy arguments and examples.

units.la: Proxima, post nobilitatem, usus & utilitatis est consideratio, quæ multiplex est. Nam ut lingua Hebraica matrix est aliarum omnium linguarum, & tanto prior tempore; in rimandis & investigandis verborum antiquorum (cujuscunque sint illa linguæ, quanquam earum præcipuè, quæ propiùs ad illam & antiquitate accedunt & affinitate) etymologiis multum ejus peritiam conducere, imò apprimè necessariam esse, & ratio postulat, & certa confirmat experientia. Sed & antiquorum populorum origines, & locorum; adde & gentilium numinum, quorum in nominibus fere ratio omnis & natura; (eruditionis philosophicæ pars non poenitenda:) ab ultimâ pleraque pendentia antiquitate, ex intimis hujus ut plurimùm linguæ penetralibus eruenda sunt. Fidem facient doctissimorum nostræ & superioris ætatis virorum
units.tr: After nobility, the next consideration is of use and utility, which is manifold. For as the Hebrew language is the mother of all other languages, and much earlier in time, both reason demands and certain experience confirms that in searching out and investigating the etymologies of ancient words (of whatever language, though especially of those that come nearer to it in age and affinity) its knowledge contributes greatly, and is indeed altogether necessary. Likewise the origins of ancient peoples and places, and also the names of the heathen deities, in whose names almost all their reason and nature lies (a part of philosophical learning not to be despised), depend for the most part on very ancient times and must be drawn out of the innermost recesses of this language for the most part. The most learned men of our own and the previous age will bear witness

units.la: rum in hoc genere lucubrationes præstantissimæ, quæ sunt in manibus omnium, quicunque meliores literas vel summis,ut aiunt, labris attigerunt. Legant saltèm, si qui hæc legunt, hórum studiorum plane ἀμύητοι, quæ Franciscus Junius vir doctissimus in hujus argumenti oratione paucis complexus est; quæ pluribus alii, quibus hoc propositum fuit, ut sigillatim persequerentur, quæ ad hujus linguæ commendationem faciunt. Nos, qui libenter hîc aliquid offerremus Lectori, quod aliis dictum non fit, omissis iis quæ aliunde peti possunt, ad id potiùs prævertemus, quod à nobis Lector jure fortasse requirat, ut paterni scilicet operis, aut incepti potiùs, rationem ei reddamus, cujus expectationem post ejus mortem non unus publicâ ejus partim mentione partim flagitatione commovit. Meminit ejus Thomas Erpenius, linguarum, dum viveret, Orientalium decus & destina,in oratione, quam de linguâ Hebraicâ anno ante scriptam edidit a.d. 1621. his verbis: Hoc tantùm dico, Clarissimum virum Isaacum Casaubonum seculi hujus infigne ornamentum, &c. & cui plurimum debent studia mea Orientalia, si vitam ei prorogâsset, qui destrat, editurum fuisse luculentum opus, de Græca lingua ex Hebraâ origine, in quo charè satis & nervosè (quantum ex iis, quæ multa jam indigesta coacervaverat, judicare ego potui) demonstraturus erat, pleraque Græcorum themata originis Hebraica esse. Viderat, opinor, Erpenius in proprio Patris, ipso adhuc superante, Musæo; ex quo etiam plura de ipsius consilio didicisse potuit. Ego quoque dudum professus sum in opusculo, quod olim penè adhuc puero paterni nominis & virtutis obtrectatores extorserant, tale quid in manus meas pervenisse: non tamen, ut ejus edendi, quod pervenerat, aliquam cuiquam spem facerem, aut certè possem, cùm id tale esset, quod potiùs operis futuri ἀρολύτως & ἰχνογραφία, quàm quod operis affecti, nedum absoluti nomen mereretur. Aliter tamen accepisse videtur vir doctissimus & humanissimus, Greg. Greg Francus, S. Theologiæ Doctor, in Lexico sancto; & ab illo credibile est ad multos alios expectationem propagatam. Ut igitur & ipsi & aliis, quiquibus illud opus adeò expetitum, quoad ejus poterit, fiat à me satis, de eo enucleatiùs hîc, non alieno loco, aliquid dicam.
units.tr: to this in their most excellent studies in this field, which are in the hands of everyone who has touched better letters, as they say, even with the tips of their lips. Let those who read this, if any, at least read the works of those who are completely uninitiated in these studies, which Francis Junius, a most learned man, has briefly summarised in his oration on this subject; and which others have treated more fully, as they set out to pursue singly the things that commend this language. We, who gladly wish to offer the reader here something not said by others, and leave aside what can be got from elsewhere, will turn instead to what the reader may fairly ask of us: namely, to give an account of my father's work, or rather of the undertaking, whose expectation after his death was stirred in many people, partly by public mention of it and partly by demands for it. Thomas Erpenius, the glory and ornament of Oriental languages while he lived, mentions it in his oration on the Hebrew language, which he published in 1621, in these words: "I say only this: that the most distinguished man, Isaac Casaubon, the outstanding ornament of this age, to whom my Oriental studies owe very much, if he had prolonged the life which he lost, would have published a splendid work on the Greek language and its Hebrew origin, in which he was going to demonstrate, sufficiently precisely and vigorously (as far as I could judge from the many things he had already heaped up unarranged), that most Greek roots are of Hebrew origin." Erpenius had seen, I think, this plan in the library of his own father, which was still standing then, and from it he could have learned more about his intention. I too have long since declared, in a little work which some detractors of my father's name and virtue extracted from me when I was almost still a boy, that something of this kind had come into my hands; yet I did not hold out any hope to anyone that I would, or indeed could, publish what had come to me, since it was of such a kind as to deserve the name of the work to come, a sketch and outline, rather than of a finished work, let alone a completed one. Yet the most learned and kindly man, Gregory Francus, Doctor of Sacred Theology, seems to have understood it otherwise, in his Holy Lexicon; and it is credible that from him the expectation spread to many others. So that both he and others, for whom that work is so eagerly desired, may have from me, as far as it can be done, enough, I will say something about it here, more fully, though not in its proper place.

units.la: De linguarum origine quæ Patris fuerit sententia, ex iis satis liquet, quæ jam De linguarum confusione ex ipsius Adversariis protulimus. Ut autem erat ille invictus operis & laboris, & in omnes de publico bené merendi occasiones semper intentus; sed & ab omnibus, quæ ad tale opus necessaria, præterquam otio, præsidiis paratissimus: futuri operis effigiem talem animo concepit, & sibi propositum, qualem ex ipsius verbis, ex iisdem Adversariis depromptis, videre est.
units.tr: Which view the Father held on the origin of languages is sufficiently clear from what we have already quoted from his opponents in De linguarum confusione. He was tireless in his work and labour, always alert to every chance of serving the public well, and he was also very well equipped with everything such a work required apart from leisure. He conceived the plan of the coming work in his mind in the form that can be seen from his own words, drawn from the same opponents.

units.la: Σὺν τῷ Θεῷ ; Totum hoc argumentum paucis capitibus potes complecti. 1. Ἱστοδιζάς, quibus innitimur. 2. De multiplici affinitate, & de affinitatis in rerum & vocum – – – – – – causis. 3. Exempla vocum, ubi nulla facta mutatio. 4. Exempla vocum, ubi litera mutata. 5. Exempla vocum, ubi est etiam μιλδῶσις. 6. Obscurior affinitas. Sic concepta methodo, proxima cura de idoneo apparatu, quo moles instituta surgeret.
units.tr: Σὺν τῷ Θεῷ [With God's help]. You can embrace this whole subject in a few chapters. 1. The historical foundations on which we rely [Ἱστοδιζάς]. 2. On the manifold affinity of languages, and on the causes of affinity in things and words. 3. Examples of words where no change has been made. 4. Examples of words where a letter has been changed. 5. Examples of words where there is also a psilosis [ψιλῶσις]. 6. A more obscure affinity. Having fixed this method, his next care was to find a suitable apparatus on which the undertaking could rise.

units.la: In eum autem finem, ne quid ipsius diligentiam fugeret, voces Hebraicas tum primigenias, tum alias, cum variis significationibus manu sua singulas describerat; accurate posteà retractaturus & expressurus singulas, & verba Graeca, quicunque ex illis orta probabilis aliqua ratio suaderet, iis appositurus. Non pauca tamen, quae inter scribendum se illi obtulerant, jam apposuerat; ad primam praecipuè secundamque Alphabeti literam: ad quarum exemplum si cetera reliquisset, aliquid esset fortasse, quod sine lectoris, vel ipsius authoris injuriâ publicari posset. Quanquam autem nihil mirum qui tam multa scripserit & ediderit, eum multa quoque inchoata reliquisse; sed & ex multis, quae fuscperat ac coeperat, pro occasionum & opportunitatum varietate alia aliis praevertisse, ne id quidem mirum sit: pensi tamen hujus aut omittendi aut intermittendi causam aliam quoque fuisse suspicor, quod ab aliis occupatu se magna ex parte deprehenderit, qui vel post prima ipsius molimina prodierunt in lucem, aut saltem ad ejus tum primum notitiam pervenerunt, hærunt. Atque hæc de Patris operę, quod instituerat. De etymologiis in genere multa dicemus, ubi de lingua tractabimus Saxonicâ.
units.tr: To that end, so that nothing would escape his diligence, he had written out by hand the Hebrew words, both primitive and others, each with its various meanings, intending to go over them carefully afterwards and to set out each one, adding to them any Greek words that some probable reason suggested had arisen from them. He had, however, already added a good number of the points that had presented themselves to him while he was writing, chiefly under the first and second letters of the alphabet. If he had left the rest in the same way, there might have been something that could be published without wronging the reader or the author himself. Yet, although it is no wonder that a man who wrote and published so much should also have left much begun, and that among the many things he had undertaken and started he should have set some before others as occasions and opportunities varied, I suspect there was another reason why he dropped or put aside this task: he found that he had been largely anticipated by others, who either published after his first efforts or at least came to know of his work only at that time. So much for the Father's undertaking. We shall say much about etymologies in general when we treat the Saxon language.

units.la: Sed præcipua hujus linguæ utilitas est, ad promovendam rem pietatis. quâ cùm chatius ac antiquius homini nato, qui suæ sibi conscius originis ad cœlestem vitam adspirat, nihil esse debeat; consequens est, ut tantò præstet hæc utilitas, quantò anima corpori, & æterna momentaneis. Verborum compendium faciam, quando ista à pluribus prolixè tractata sunt. Ut illud igitur maximè contendat aliquis, extare tales ac tam perfectas Verbi Divini versiones, ut nihil in isto genere perfectius sperari possit; (quod quanquam stultissimum sit credere, eò tamen facilius hic postulanti concedemus, quia ad id, quod nunc volumus, nihil pertinet, & postea pluribus suo loco à nobis tractabitur:) quis rerum peritus negaverit, quemadmodum Gratior est virtus veniens è corpore pulcro, ita verborum splendorem, & orationis gratiam, ad rerum ipsarum commendationem insigniter facere? Non quæro, quid fieri debeat : & illi, nescio cui, apud Aulum Gellium philosopho facilè assentior, Ad ipsa Platonis penetralia, ipsarúmque rerum pondera & dignitates pergendum esse, non ad vocularum ejus amœnitatem, nec ad verborum venustates diverfitandum esse: nec illud arripiam, quod quidam de Platone (quos inter Dionysius Halicarnassæus) majore judicii severitate quàm veritate pronunciârunt, eum, quantus quantus est, nihil nisi verba esse: hoc certè dicam, quod alii plures tum Christiani tum Ethnici agnoscunt; quòd Plato præstantissima quæque florentissimorum ab eruditione seculorum ingenia tanta sui admiratione fixerit, detinuerítque,id sermonis ipsius singulari cuidam cum sublimitate junctæ venustati potissimum tribuendum esse. Ut non sine causa, orationis ornatum causa non parum conferre pronuntiarit Quintilianus, quod qui libenter audiant (ut ipsius verbis utar:) & magis attendant, & facilius credant. Jam, ut nulla esset peculiaris linguæ Hebraicæ elegantia, quam, tamen sunt, qui eo nomine aliis omnibus anteponant: ut nulla styli sacri cri in hoc genere prærogativa, (de quo nos alibi fusè quærimus:) quis tamen tam iniquus, ut ei neget, quod omnes, quotquot aliquis ingeniorum proventus, aliquis eruditionis usus excoluit, habere linguas nemo in linguis versatus negaverit? Habere illam suas quasdam proprietates, suos idiotismos, suas formulas, suas particulas, quibus, qui aures imbutas longo usu habuerint, nihil gratius aut venustius accidere possit: qui autem non assueverint, ab iis tanquam barbaris & asperis, & agrestibus, ne dicam etiam ridiculis, plerunque refugere? Habet hoc natura aurium, ut quemadmodum oculi novitate capiuntur, ita illæ contrà omni sermonis peregrinitate offendantur, ut Varronem alicubi observare memini. Quare quod multi dicunt se verba non mórari, rerum momenta & ponder�a consectari, frustrà sunt; cùm ut plurimùm nulli magis verbis ducantur, quàm qui ita vulgò profitentur; adeóque ipsi sibi de se fortasse persuadent; cùm etiam invitis & imprudentibus vis verborum & insinuet, & maximorum ingeniorum (ut pridem Augustinus recte) ea sit indoles & fœlicitas, ut res à verbis, & verba à rebus ipsis secernere valeant. In sacrâ vero Scripturâ interpretandâ, tanto major difficultas ita vertere, ut imperitorum auribus consulas, quanto minor interpretibus libertas concessa est. Quanquam enim alias laudemus interpretem, qui verba potius appendat (quod in vertendis Græcis de se profitetur Cicero) quàm annumeret: non tamen id in sacris licitum, ubi vel minimis apicibus sua constant momenta; nec ulla verborum jactura sine aliquo, non illo quidem præcipuæ fortasse sententiæ, sed aliquo tamen rerum detrimento, possit contingere. Quare si pietatem maximè fovet augétque jugis & assidua sacræ Scripturæ lectio; lectionem autem quamcunque (si quidem ex natura pendamus ista) delectatio maximè alit accendítque; quanti ad pietatem momenti sit ejus linguæ peritia, quis non vidit, cujus usus jucundam nobis faciat sacri textûs orationem?
units.tr: But the chief use of this language lies in advancing the cause of piety. Since nothing should be more pressing or more important to a human being, who is conscious of his heavenly origin and aspires to heavenly life, it follows that this use is as much superior as the soul is to the body, and eternity to the moment. I shall make it brief, since these matters have been treated at length by many. Suppose someone should insist that there exist such perfect translations of the Word of God that nothing more perfect in that kind could be hoped for. (That is extremely foolish to believe, yet I shall concede it readily to such a claimant, since it has no bearing on what we now want, and I will deal with it at more length in its proper place.) Who, knowing the matter, would deny that, just as virtue is more pleasing when it comes from a beautiful body, so the splendour of words and the grace of style greatly add to the recommendation of the things themselves? I am not asking what ought to be done; and I readily agree with that philosopher whom Aulus Gellius mentions: one must press on to the very inner shrines of Plato, to the weight and dignity of the things themselves, and not stop at the charm of his little words or the elegances of his expression. Nor shall I take up what some have said about Plato (among them Dionysius of Halicarnassus), with more severity of judgment than truth, that Plato, great as he is, is nothing but words. I will say this, which many others, both Christian and pagan, acknowledge: that Plato held the most outstanding minds of the most flourishing ages of learning in such admiration and attachment, and that this must be attributed chiefly to a unique charm of his language joined with sublimity. Hence Quintilian rightly declared that the ornament of style contributes no little to the matter, because people (to use his words) "listen willingly, and attend more closely, and believe more easily." Now, even if the Hebrew language had no peculiar elegance, which some nonetheless prefer above all others for that reason, and even if the sacred style had no special pre-eminence in this respect (on which we inquire at length elsewhere), who would be so unfair as to deny what everyone who has been cultivated by any productivity of talent or any use of learning, and anyone versed in languages, acknowledges, that every language has its own qualities? It has its own idioms, its own turns of phrase, its own particles, which can seem most pleasing and graceful to those whose ears have been accustomed to them by long use, while those who are not accustomed to them mostly shrink from them as barbarous, harsh and rustic, not to say ridiculous. It is the nature of the ear that, just as the eyes are captivated by novelty, so the ears are offended by every foreignness of speech, as I remember Varro observing somewhere. So when many say that they do not dwell on words but pursue the weight and substance of things, they are mistaken; for in fact nobody is more led by words than those who so commonly profess this, and perhaps they persuade themselves of it. Even against their will and unknowingly, the force of words insinuates itself, and (as Augustine rightly said long ago) it is the mark and happiness of the greatest minds to be able to separate things from words and words from things. In interpreting Holy Scripture, however, the more one must take care to translate so as to consult the ears of the unlearned, the less freedom is granted to translators. For although in other cases we praise the translator who weighs his words rather than counts them (which Cicero professes of himself in rendering the Greeks), this is not permitted in sacred texts, where even the smallest marks carry their weight, and no loss of words can occur without some detriment, perhaps not to the chief sense, but still to some part of the matter. Therefore, if constant and diligent reading of Holy Scripture chiefly fosters and increases piety, and if delight chiefly nourishes and kindles any reading (if we judge these things by nature), who does not see how great a bearing on piety is the skill in that language whose use makes the discourse of the sacred text pleasant to us?

units.la: Ex pluribus autem sacri sermonis idiotismis, quorum in vertendo, non elegantiæ tantùm, sed etiam interdum & & sententiæ detrimentum subimus, libet hîc in uno genere, quod à nemine adhuc satis tractatum vidi, diutiùs immorari. Paronomasia, (Græcis παρονομασία ; quod quidam non satis attenti παρωνομασία scripsere: ) satis notum nomen, nec res naturâ suâ valde obscura; sed à veteribus plerisque nimiâ subtilitatis aut diligentiæ affectatione, dum novis figurarum nominibus & generibus inveniendis artem se putant eloquentiæ amplificare, tantis involuta tenebris, ut illos legentibus in totâ re oratoriâ nihil spinosius aut implicitius.
units.tr: Among the many idioms of sacred speech, in translating which we suffer loss not only of elegance but sometimes also of meaning, I wish to dwell here at some length on one kind, which I have not yet seen adequately treated by anyone. Paronomasia [παρονομασία] (which some less careful writers have written as παρωνομασία) is a well-known name, and the thing itself is not by nature very obscure; but among most of the ancients it has been wrapped in such darkness, through an excessive affectation of subtlety or diligence, as they thought they were enlarging the art of eloquence by inventing new names and kinds of figures, that nothing in the whole of rhetoric is more thorny or tangled for readers.

units.la: Quintilianus tum de aliis, qui ista ante ipsum tractaverant, tum nominatim de Cicerone queritur, cujus etiam in hoc argumento quædam non intelligere se ingenuè profitetur. Alii non minùs, de Quintiliano. Eustathius recentior, in hoc argumento nec ipse tam dilucidus aut accuratus, quàm verbosus: multiplicem certè confusionem illi objiciunt viri docti, qui de linguæ Græcæ vetere & germanâ pronuntiatione commentati sunt: non uno nomine illi irati.
units.tr: Quintilian complains both of others who had treated these matters before him and by name of Cicero, and he frankly confesses that he himself does not understand some things in this subject. Others likewise complain of Quintilian. Eustathius, a later writer, is in this subject no more clear or accurate than he is wordy; learned men who have written about the old and genuine pronunciation of the Greek language certainly charge him with much confusion, and are not a little angry with him on that account.

units.la: Sunt qui παρονομασίαν à παρηχήσει distinguant, ut Eustathius alicubi: qui παρ-
units.tr: Some distinguish paronomasia [παρονομασίαν] from parechesis [παρήχησις], as Eustathius does somewhere. Others

units.la: ηχνον ἠχνὴν à παρομοίῳ, ut Donatus: qui παρονομασίαν à παρονομασίᾳ, ut Quinti-lianus. Author ad Herennium traductionem aliam facit ab agnominatione: qui tamen agnominationis varias species aut potius rationes ostendit & explicat. Quidam Hermogenis definitionem maximè probant, qui παρήχησιν & παρονομασίαν pro iisdem habens, definit, κατὰ ὁμοίων ὀνομάτων ἐν διαφορᾷ γνώσει ταυτὸν ἠχέντων; alia pleraque, quorum apud Eustathium exempla sunt, ad polyptoton referant.
units.tr: distinguish parechesis [παρήχησιν, ἠχώ] from paromoion [παρόμοιον], as Donatus does, and some distinguish paronomasia from paronomasia [παρονομασίᾳ], as Quintilian does. The author of the Ad Herennium gives another term, agnominatio. Yet he also shows and explains various species, or rather kinds, of agnominatio. Some greatly approve Hermogenes' definition, who treats parechesis and paronomasia as the same and defines it as words that sound alike though they differ in meaning [κατὰ ὁμοίων ὀνομάτων ἐν διαφορᾷ γνώσει ταυτὸν ἠχέντων]. Many other cases, of which Eustathius gives examples, they refer to polyptoton.

units.la: Nos non id hîc agimus, ut has Gramaticorum lites componamus, aut accuratius expendamus. Sufficiat igitur monuisse, cum παρονομασίας nomen à quibusdam latius, ab aliis strictius accipiatur; nobis latiorem significationem hîc placere, ut omnia illa quæsita orationis ornamenta, in quibus vel idem verbum casu, aut significatione, (quod πλοκὴν aut ἀνλαυάκλασιν proprie nuncupant:) variatum: aut diversa verba, sono syllabisve ita affinia, ut aliqua similitudinis species aurem feriat, sub hoc genere & nomine comprehendamus. Ornamenta vocamus, quia non omnis verborum similitudo in hunc censum referenda, cum talia interdum (ut Eustathius recte docet) casu contingant, quæ ut ipsis scriptoribus imprudentibus exciderunt, ita diligentius animadversa, putidum potius & ineptum, quàm diligentem lectorem arguant. Peritus lector ista facile dijudicabit. Cæterùm cùm multæ sint agnominationum species, ut apud Quintilianū aliósq; videre est, nos, omissis aliis omnibus divisionibus, duas tantùm diversas illarum seu species seu classes constituamus, ut, quæ solis sunt in verbis, & orationis tantùm concinnitati serviunt, ad primam: quæ verò mutatâ significatione aliquod etiam seu pondus seu acumen sententiæ conciliant, ad secundam classem pertineant. Exemplis hæc fient illustriora. Sed priusquàm ad exempla veniamus, de re ipsa paucis præfabimur, non id nobis hîc esse consilii, ut usum talium vel doceamus, vel commendemus. Ut ingeniorum fuerunt, pro varietate sæculorum, ita & aurium, discrimina. Fuit sæculum, cum in laudibus sermonis essent, quæ postea inter vitia numerata: sed nec uno eodemque démque sæculo eadem de optimâ loquendi ratione omnes judicârunt, ut etiam illi agnoscunt, qui rectè loquendi præcepta tradiderunt. Concursum vocalium & neglectam compositionem certum est affectasse plurimos: Gellius etiam inter elegantias Homericas numerat; quæ tamen ab aliis aliter vulgò constitui, & si quid ejus generis laudatis scriptoribus accidérit, id excusandum ducere, nemo nescit. Atque ita in plerisque aliis, quæ ad sermonem pertinent, Quid autem naturæ maximè consonum (neque enim facit opinionum varietas, ut non aliquid verum sit :) longa ac difficilis disputatio. Nos suum cuique judicium liberum relinquemus, & ea tantùm, quæ sunt hujus loci, & de quibus non controvertitur, afferemus.
units.tr: We do not intend here to settle these grammarians' quarrels or to weigh them more closely. It is enough, then, to have noted that the name paronomasia is taken by some more broadly and by others more narrowly. We prefer the broader sense here, so that under this genus and name we include all those sought-after ornaments of speech in which either the same word is varied by case or by meaning (which they properly call plokē or antanaklasis), or different words are so alike in sound or syllables that some kind of resemblance strikes the ear. We call them ornaments, because not every similarity of words belongs to this class. Sometimes such things occur by chance, as Eustathius rightly teaches. When the writers themselves fall into them unintentionally, a careful examination shows them to be silly and inept rather than a mark of a diligent author, and a skilled reader will easily judge them. Since there are many species of agnominations, as can be seen in Quintilian and others, we set aside all other divisions and establish only two kinds or classes. Those that exist only in the words and serve merely the elegance of style belong to the first class. Those that, with a changed meaning, also lend some weight or sharpness to the sentence belong to the second. Examples will make this clearer. Before we come to them, however, we shall say a few words about the matter itself. It is not our purpose here to teach or to recommend the use of such things. As talents differ, so do ears, according to the variety of ages. There was a time when things were praised in speech that were later counted as faults. Yet not everyone in one and the same age judged the best way of speaking in the same way, as even those who have handed down rules of correct speech acknowledge. It is certain that very many cultivated the clash of vowels and neglect of composition. Gellius even counts these among the Homeric elegances, though others commonly settle such matters differently, and everyone knows that if anything of this kind happens in praised writers, it is to be excused. So it is in many other matters that pertain to speech. What is most in accord with nature is a long and difficult question, for variety of opinion does not prevent something from being true. We shall leave each person free to judge, and bring forward only those things that belong to this place and about which there is no dispute.

units.la: Ad primum genus pertinent ista, Greek: νὴ ... (Greek words: ὑβρίζειν, λὴν λυπεῖν, ἀναλέγειν ἀναλεύειν, &c.) quæ Latini quoque imitati, pugnam pugnare, gaudium gaudere, &c. dixere. Ad Greek: πλεονασμὸν ista ab Eustathio aliisque diserte referuntur. Hac autem figurâ veteres Atticos scriptores, primos elegantiarum magistros, valdè delectatos esse scripta illorum indicant: unde &
units.tr: To the first kind belong such expressions as hybrizein, lēn lypein, analegein analeuein, and so on [ὑβρίζειν, λύπην λυπεῖν, ἀναλέγειν ἀναλεύειν], which the Latins also imitated in "to fight a fight" (pugnam pugnare), "to rejoice a joy" (gaudium gaudere), and so on. Eustathius and others expressly refer these to pleonasm [πλεονασμόν]. By this figure the ancient Attic writers, the first masters of elegance, are shown by their works to have been greatly delighted, whence

units.la: & Attica figura, vel Atticus idiotifmus vulgò audit. Has allusiones, five potius agnominationes (morimortem, vitam vivere, &c,) Attici frequenter sectati sunt; ait Julius Scaliger, vir incomparabilis, nisi Josephum genuisset: qui etiam ex Ariftotele & Platone exempla adducit. Sed utcunque Attici fortaffe maximè excoluerint, ab Homero tamen altior & verior origo; qui sæpè utitur; qualia sunt apud illum, ἀγρεγὸν ἀγρεδίν, λόγον λέγειν βαλὴν βαλὴν (quod uno ter aut quater occurrit libro) κλέψει κλέψει, aliàque innumerà. Et hactenus saltem in confesso est apud omnes idem verbum in oratione eleganter repeti, cùm ex eo fonte manet vulgare illud eloquentiæ magistrorum præceptum, Si idem verbum in eadem sententiâ bis ponendum fit, nihil interponendum esse: ut omnia omnibus; multa multis; homo homini; & id genus; quæ passim occurrunt. cujus generis & illud, ταῦτα ταῦτα, Matth.XXI. 41.
units.tr: it is commonly called the Attic figure, or Atticism. Attic writers often pursued these allusions, or rather agnominations (mori mortem, vivere vitam, and so on). Julius Scaliger, an incomparable man, says so, were it not that he begot Josephus; he also brings examples from Aristotle and Plato. But however much the Attic writers may have cultivated it, its origin is higher and truer in Homer, who uses it often, as in his expressions agrein agrein [ἀγρεῖον ἀγρεύειν], logon legein, bolēn bolēn [βολὴν βολήν] (which occurs three or four times in a single book), kleptei kleptei [κλέψει κλέψει], and countless others. And at least this much is agreed by all: that the same word may be elegantly repeated in speech. From this source comes the common precept of teachers of eloquence: if the same word must be placed twice in the same sentence, nothing should be inserted between them, as in omnia omnibus, multa multis, homo homini, and the like, which occur everywhere. Of this kind also is that expression, "these things, these things" [ταῦτα ταῦτα], Matt. 21:41.

units.la: Veteres Latinos scriptores (eos intelligo qui Ciceronis ætate veteres audiebant) plurimùm etiam hâc figurâ delectatos esse, ex eorum, quæ extant hodieq;
units.tr: I understand that the early Latin writers (those whom the people of Cicero's age regarded as old) were also very much delighted by this figure, as can be gathered from what of their work survives even today.

units.la: Jul.Scalig. in Animadv. x. De Hist. Anim. hodiéque, reliquiis colligere est. Sed ut suspensum Lectorem, ( quem tamen non fine causâ pluribus hæc præfatos nos, spero postea judicaturum;) quàm paucissimis absolvamus ; Ex omni Latinorum scriptorum numero, de duobus istis,Plauto & Terentio, utri palma eloquentiæ tribuenda fit, magna dudum inter doctos controversia, & adhuc sub judice lis est : quin elegantiffimus uterque scriptor fit, & quos puri & elegantis sermonis amatores nocturnâ diurnáque manu versandos sibi semper proposuerint, nulla controverfia. Ut alias illorum laudes, quæ, ut pretio suo æstimentur, ingenia minimè vulgaria , sed & matura, Terentii præcipuè, judicia postulant,omittam ; nulla magis arte utrunque suam nobis elegantiam commendare, quàm frequentibus paronomasiis, aut nihil ego intelligo, aut certissimè deprehendet, quifquis animum paulò diligentiùs adverterit. De Plauto mox videbimus.
units.tr: Jul. Scalig. in Animadv. x. De Hist. Anim. Even today, the remains can be gathered from the surviving fragments. But to finish briefly, and to keep the reader in suspense (who, I hope, will judge later, and not without reason, why I have prefaced these matters at such length): among all the Latin writers, there has long been a great controversy among scholars over which of the two, Plautus or Terence, should be awarded the palm of eloquence, and the dispute is still before the judge. But that both are most elegant writers, whom lovers of pure and refined speech have always resolved to read day and night, is beyond dispute. I shall omit their other praises, which, to be valued at their true worth, require not ordinary but mature judgment, especially in Terence. I say only that neither author recommends his elegance more by any art than by frequent paronomasias. Unless I understand nothing, anyone who pays a little more careful attention will certainly perceive this. We shall look at Plautus shortly.

units.la: Hecyræ Terentianæ Prologum magnâ arte scriptum esse notant antiqui, cùm, bis jam exacta, tertiò referretur fabula. Ecce statim initio primi Pro-logi logi——hac ut est data nova, Novum intervenit vitium. & mox,——populus studio stupidus. Et aliquot inde versibus, iterum, bis in eodem versu : & qui proximè sequitur, cognoscis nosfcite. A verbo Orator, incipit secundus Prologus; cui succinit in secundo versu, vox exorator. Ibidem jure, quod proximo quoque repetitur. Haud multò post, Spe incerta certum laborem sustuli : & mox, studiose & studio, eodem versu. Paulò post, Ut in otio esset potiùs quàm in negotio. Et aliquot versibus interjectis, vox calumitatem, ex proximo repetita. Ita verba, locus, authoritas, maxime, pari ratione repetita in sequentibus. Extremo autem Prologo, (qui sanè totus non valdè longus;) Ne eum circumventum. iniquè iniqui irrideant, Meâ causâ causam hanc suscipite. Alias prætereo sciens syllabarum allusiones magis obscuras, quæ tamen ad suavitatem sermonis non parum conducunt; qualis observat haud raro vetus Interpres: cujus etiam in Andriam vera est de toto hoc genere observatio, (in ista, Nam inceptio est amentium, haud amantium:) Amabant veteres de proximo similia dicere: Et in Adelphos, ad ista, dii tibi, Demea, omnes semper omnia optata offerant: Omnes omnia: antiqua, inquit, elegantia, & figurata. Quamcunque in Terentii partem Lector conjiciat oculos, nullam inveniat, quae talia non affatim suppeditet.
units.tr: The ancients noted that the Prologue of Terence's Hecyra was written with great skill, when the play, already twice performed, was presented a third time. Look, right at the beginning of the first Prologue: "hac ut est data nova, Novum intervenit vitium" ["since it has been given in its new form, a new fault has arisen"]. And soon after: "populus studio stupidus" ["the people, stupid with eagerness"]. And a few lines later, "iterum" twice in the same line, and the line that comes next, "cognoscis nosscite." The second Prologue begins with the word "Orator," and in the second line the word "exorator" answers it. In the same place there is "jure," which is repeated in the next line too. Not long after, "Spe incerta certum laborem sustuli" ["I have borne a certain labour on an uncertain hope"], and soon, "studiose & studio," in the same line. A little later, "ut in otio esset potius quam in negotio" ["that he might be at leisure rather than at business"]. After a few intervening lines, the word "calumniam" is repeated from the nearby line. In the same way the words "locus, authoritas, maxime" are repeated in what follows. In the last Prologue, which is altogether not very long: "Ne eum circumventum. iniquè iniqui irrideant, Meâ causâ causam hanc suscipite" ["lest they mock him unjustly as the unjust, take up this cause for my sake"]. I pass over other, more obscure allusions between syllables, which I know of, but which nonetheless contribute not a little to the sweetness of the style. The old commentator often observes such things, and his remark on the Andria holds true for this whole kind (in the line "Nam inceptio est amentium, haud amantium"): "The ancients were fond of saying similar things in close succession." And in the Adelphi, on the words "dii tibi, Demea, omnes semper omnia optata offerant," he says of "omnes omnia": "ancient elegance, and figurative." Wherever the reader casts his eyes in Terence, he will find none that does not supply such things in abundance.

units.la: Plautus vero, quanto antiquior Terentio, tanto istorum amantior & feracior, ut cuivis facile ex ipsius lectione liqueat: qui non contentus duorum verborum similitudine, aut repetitione, ad tria haud raro, quasi impleturus Gratiarum numerum; imo interdum & plura excurrit. Qualia apud illum sunt: Hic me amoenitate amoena, (ubi observet obiter Lector, hoc ipsum, cujus repetitione suavitatem orationi conciliare studuit Plautus, purum putum esse Hebraicum:) amoenus onerat dies. Et in eadem Fabula, Quoa bonis benefit beneficium, Gratia ea gravida est bonis. Et in Amphitruone, Optime optimo optimam operam das, datam pulcre locas. Et, Nam juste ab justis justus sum Orator datus: Justa autem ab iniquis petere, insipientia est. Tale & illud Apostoli, ἵνα ἐν πάντὶ πάντοτε, &c.
units.tr: Plautus, however, is all the more fond of and rich in these figures the older he is than Terence, as anyone can easily see from reading him. Not content with a repetition or similarity of two words, he often runs on to three, as if he meant to fill out the number of the Graces, and sometimes even to more. Examples in him are: "Here, with pleasant pleasantness, he [loads me]" (where the reader may notice in passing that this very repetition, by which Plautus sought to lend sweetness to his style, is pure and simple Hebrew); "the pleasant days burden him." In the same play: "The benefit that benefits the good; that grace is heavy with good things." In the Amphitryon: "You do the best service to the best man, and the service you have done you place well." And: "For I have been given as a speaker, justly, by the just; but to ask just things from the unjust is folly." The saying of the Apostle is of the same kind: "that in every thing, always" [ἵνα ἐν πάντι πάντοτε], and so on.

units.la: Secundi generis, multa apud Eustathium aliósque ex Homero exempla, quæ lector inde petere poterit. Nobis hoc venustissimum visum est, quod extat in vetere Græcorum Epigrammatum collectione, quæ vulgò Ἀνθολογία, &c. nuncupatur:
units.tr: Of the second kind there are many examples from Homer in Eustathius and others, which the reader can seek out there. To us this seemed most charming, what stands in the old collection of Greek epigrams commonly called the Anthologia, etc.:

units.la: Εἰ τὸ φέεγν σε φέεῖ, φέεε ἡ φέεγ. εἰ δ' ἀ-γανακλεῖς,
units.tr: If Fortune [τύχη] bears you, bear it; if you are angry, you grieve yourself, and Fortune still bears you. [Εἰ τὸ φέεγν σε φέεῖ, φέεε ἡ φέεγ. εἰ δ' ἀ-γανακλεῖς,]

units.la: Καὶ αυτὸν λυπεῖς, ἡ τὸ φέεγν σε φέεῖ.
units.tr: [Καὶ αυτὸν λυπεῖς, ἡ τὸ φέεγν σε φέεῖ.]

units.la: Τὸ φέεγν, id est, ἡ τύχη, ut ibi vetus scholiastes. cætera satis clara. Latinum exemplum vetus poëta Ennius suppeditat, cujus apud A. Gellium tetrastichum extat, concinnum illud quidem, ut Gellius judicat; sed aliquanto obscurius, ut ad naturam ænigmatis quodammodo accedat. Est autem illud his verbis:
units.tr: The φέεγν is, that is, ἡ τύχη [Fortune], as the old scholiast there says. The rest is clear enough. The old poet Ennius supplies a Latin example, of which a tetrastich survives in Aulus Gellius. It is neat indeed, as Gellius judges, but somewhat more obscure, so that it comes close in a way to the nature of a riddle. It runs thus:

units.la: Nam qui lepidè postulat alterum frustari,
units.tr: For whoever wittily seeks to cheat another,

units.la: Quem frustratur, frustra eum dicit frustra esse:
units.tr: whom he cheats, he says that the cheater is cheated in vain;

units.la: Nam sese frustari quem frustra sentit,
units.tr: for whoever feels that he himself is cheated by the one he cheats in vain,

units.la: Qui frustatur, is frustra est: si non, ille est frustra.
units.tr: he who cheats is cheated in vain; if not, the other is cheated in vain.

units.la: Voculæ unius mutatio planiorem fortasse sententiam fecerit: quæ tamen
units.tr: A change of a single little word would perhaps have made the sense plainer, but

units.la: utcunque propiùs attendenti non adeò recondita, ut necesse sit istis immorari. Plautus huc allusit fortasse, cum pessimum hominum genus, tum ab aliis notis,tum ab hac describit: Atque sese cum frustrantur, frustari alios stolidi existumant. Similem lusum Græci nescio cujus, antiqui Comici, in voce λοιδοπεῖν memini legere; qui nunc non occurrit: eum videtur imitatus hìc Ennius: Græcos certè, à quibus ad Latinos manavit hic usus.
units.tr: however, to one attending more closely it is not so obscure that one must linger over it. Plautus perhaps alludes to this when he describes the worst kind of men, both by other marks and by this one: "And when they cheat one another, the foolish think they cheat others." I remember reading a similar play on words in some ancient Greek comic poet, I know not whom, in the word λοιδορεῖν [loidorein]; which does not come to mind now. Ennius seems to have imitated him here, or at least the Greeks, from whom this usage passed to the Latins.

units.la: Jam ad sacra veniamus, quorum gratiâ sunt ista de paronomasiâ à nobis hìc dicta omnia. Opportunè, an contrà, penes Lectorem judicium esto. Mihi quidem ita videtur, insignem hunc esse sacri Textûs idiotismum, cujus plena perceptio, qualis usu magis, quàm præceptis ullis comparatur, non solùm obscuris sacræ Scripturæ locis plurimis lucem afferre possit; sed ad capiendum suavitatis & elegantiæ fructum, qui multus in illis exuberat, sit apprimè necessaria. Atque hîç primum se offert loquendi genus apud Hebræos ufitatissimum, cum verbo cuilibet finito verbum infinitum ejusdem originis adjungitur, elegantiæ causâ: qualia, videndo vidi, &c. Scio Grammaticos Hebræos ita vulgò tradere, id fieri ad majorem certitudinem & evidentiam: quod quanquam sæpè magis argutum, quàm solidum mihi videtur; (ut fi quis id pariter asseveret, quoties dicunt Græci Latinisve, quod faciunt sæpissimè, pugnare pugnam, gaudere gaudium, servitutem servire, furere furorem, dolorem dolere, & id genus alia, de pugnis, gaudiisve, maximis & certissimis, aut aliâ aliquâ ratione notabilibus ibi sermonem fieri; quod quamvis in multis exemplis experienti non malè forte succederet, non temerè tamen persuaderet:) ut tamen illis concêdamus, at hoc illi non negabunt nobis, quòd ita Hebræi certitudinem evidentiámve repetendo verbo maluerint, quàm aliâ ratione exprimere, non aliunde profectum esse, quàm quòd eorundem verborum repetitione gauderent, & repetendorum causas libenter ampleterentur. Nec aliter judicandum de frequentibus illis nominum tum substantivorum tum adjectivorum repetitionibus, quales, gens gens facitebant; virgam virgam accipe : vir vir cum declinaverit : decimam decimam parate : corde & corde : generationi & generationi : justitia justitia: gladius gladius,&c.quarum cum plures sint species & rationes, accuratè plerasque sub Pleonasmi titulo exequitur in Grammatica sua doctissimus Buxtorfius ; quem consulat Lector, qui de iis plura cupit. Nobis id sufficiat hîc dixisse, tales esse plerasque, ut puri puti sint Pleonasmi : quorum scilicet non alia ratio, quàm genius linguæ populive. Quod autem de quibusdam dicitur, ut de adjectivis distributivis, id ideo fieri, quód iis Hebræi careant ; nos dicimus, ideo carere eos talibus. quòd ista repetendis nominibus distribuendi ratio longè videretur elegantior.
units.tr: Now let us come to sacred matters, for whose sake all these things about paronomasia have been said here by us. Whether they are apposite or not, let the reader judge. To me it seems that this is a remarkable idiom of the sacred Text, whose full perception, which is gained more by use than by any rules, can not only throw light on very many obscure passages of Holy Scripture, but is also quite necessary for grasping the fruit of sweetness and elegance which abounds in them. And here first presents itself the most common manner of speaking among the Hebrews, in which a finite verb of any kind is joined, for elegance's sake, with an infinitive verb of the same origin, such as "seeing I saw," etc. I know that Hebrew grammarians commonly teach that this is done for greater certainty and emphasis. Although this often seems to me more ingenious than solid (as if someone should likewise assert that whenever Greeks or Latins say, as they very often do, "to fight a fight, to rejoice a joy, to serve a servitude, to rage a rage, to grieve a grief," and other such things, the discourse there concerns fights or joys of the greatest and most certain kind, or notable in some other respect; which, though it might perhaps succeed well enough in many examples for one who tries it, would not persuade rashly), yet, granting them this point, they will not deny us this: that the Hebrews preferred to express certainty and emphasis by repeating the word rather than by some other means, and that this arose from nothing else than that they delighted in the repetition of the same words and gladly embraced the reasons for repeating them. Nor should we judge otherwise of those frequent repetitions of nouns, both substantives and adjectives, such as "a nation, a nation they were;" "take a rod, a rod;" "the man, the man, when he has declined;" "prepare a tenth, a tenth;" "with heart and heart;" "to generation and generation;" "justice, justice;" "a sword, a sword," etc. Since there are several kinds and reasons for these, the most learned Buxtorf treats most of them carefully under the heading of Pleonasm in his Grammar; let the reader who wants more about them consult him. For us it is enough to have said here that most of them are such that they are pure and simple pleonasms, whose only reason is the genius of the language or the people. As for what is said about certain cases, such as distributive adjectives, that this happens because the Hebrews lack them, we say rather that they lack such forms because the manner of distributing by repeating nouns seemed far more elegant.

units.la: In observandis autem & congeren-dis sacri Textûs μεγρομαιας ejusmodi, quæ elegantiæ causâ adhibentur, si exemplo veterum quorundam Grammaticorum subtiliûs ista tractare liberet, ut non solùm plures earum species constitueremus, sed literarum interdum singularem rationem haberemus : non dubito multos repertum iri, quibus magis ridicula quàm grata futura esset ista nostra diligentia : qui aures scilicet ad has ptifci ævi elegantis diuturnâ lectione & obseruatione intributas & attemperatas non habent : quas qui habent, haud dubium, quin pasim, quamcunque partem experiantur, magnâ cum voluptate deprehendant. Nos igitur, quia quid pluribus, non quid paucis probare possimus, id hic quæstiones ; ea potius proferemus, de quibus nulla dubitatio sit, quin verborum sed similitudo diuersorum, seu eorundem repetitio studio adhibita sit: Quanquam autem in tam obuia re aliena opera minimè opus nobis est, credo tamen Lectorem, quod Isaaci Cafauboni b: m. parentis nostri de his iudicium fuerit, libenter cogniturum. Ergo igitur ipsissima ejus verba, prompta ex ejus, quæ penes nos sunt, Adversariis;
units.tr: In observing and gathering together such figures of the sacred Text, which are employed for elegance's sake, if it pleased us to treat them more subtly after the example of certain ancient grammarians, so that we not only established more kinds of them but sometimes took account of the particular reason of the letters, I do not doubt that many would be found for whom this our diligence would be more ridiculous than pleasing: those who do not have their ears trained and attuned to these things by long reading and observation of the refined age. Those who do have them, there is no doubt, would find them everywhere, in whatever part they try, with great pleasure. We therefore, since we are asking what we can prove by many instances rather than by few, will set forth here rather those matters about which there is no doubt that a similarity of different words, or a deliberate repetition of the same, was intended. Although in so obvious a matter we have no need of another's labour, I nevertheless believe the reader will gladly learn the judgement of our parent Isaac Casaubon, of blessed memory, on these matters. Therefore here are his very words, taken from his Adversaria, which are in our possession:

units.la: [ Hebraica ] Amant Iudæi hanc figuram : maximè autem Isaias. vel lege cap. XXIV. ac notâ versu 16, he-bræ misit ... conflatum ex vocibus quinque, ζωὴ ... ἡ. sic enim habet Pro-pheta ; תשמאלה, ὁ ... ἡ. Talia multa & apud hunc; ...
units.tr: [Hebrew] The Jews love this figure, especially Isaiah; or read chapter 24 and note verse 16, where the Hebrew has a combination of five words, ζωὴ ... ἡ. For thus the Prophet has it: תשמאלה, ὁ ... ἡ. Many such things also occur in him; [Ζωὴ ... ἡ; ὁ ... ἡ; תשמאלה]

units.la: {y} Vide supra.
units.tr: See above.

units.la: & apud alios prophetas. Ac videndum an ab hoc fonte fit illud in historiâ Sufannæ, in vocibus σῆν-, σῆν: & χίνω, χίζη. Cui elegantiæ prope par & gemina est Isa.c.xxx.16. Quia dixistis, ait propheta, כי על סום נסום ideò תנוסון: & quia dixistis, יקלו רפיכם על־קל נוכב propterea plane ejusdem generis elegantia: vide & XXXI. 1. Sic apud Jeremiam cap. I. verss. 11, & 12. par elegantia in vocibus שקד virga amygdalina: & שקד Deus acceleransa, & c.XLVIII. v.2. in Chesbon,& חשב. Cap.V.elegantissimè: ויקו למשפט והנה משפח: expectabam judicium, & ecce scabies, (ἀνὴ iniquitas) Sequitur; לצדקה והנה צעקה justitiam (expectabam) & ecce clamorem.] Ita ille ibi. sed & in editis ad Persium Commentariis istiusmodi (quarum hæc lingua ferax) quanti faceret elegantias, obiter his verbis testatum reliquit; [Sed huic loco (ad Persii— pappare minutum poscis, &c.) longè simillimum est,quod apud vatem divinum & verè sublimem Ifaiam observabamus,capite tertio: nam sicut heic Persius, ut delicias exprimeret molliculorum juvenum, ait illos papparé minutum poscere, id est, infantium tenellorum mores imitari: sic Hebræus scriptor, ut mulierum τρυφὴν ob oculos poneret, ait inter cætera: הליך ושפוף הלבנה ad quorum verborum singularem cum pari emphasi venustatem non adspirat linguæ Latinæ egestas. Græcè dixeris ad verbum, ἐν τῷ βαδίζειν χὴ νηπιάζειν βαδίζεσθαι: hoc est, sic incedunt, quoties per vicos ingrediuntur, ut infantium parvulorum imitentur incessum. id enim significat יפה, quod pulcherrimum est verbum.] Hactenus ὁ μαργείτης.
units.tr: and in the other prophets. And one should consider whether from this source comes that in the history of Susanna, in the words σῆν-, σῆν, and χίνω, χίζη. Isaiah 30:16 is almost an equal and twin elegance to this: "Because you said," says the prophet, "כי על סום נסום, therefore you shall flee [תנוסון]; and because you said, יקלו רפיכם על־קל נוכב, therefore..." the elegance is clearly of the same kind; see also 31:1. So in Jeremiah ch. 1, vv. 11 and 12, there is a like elegance in the words שקד, almond rod, and שקד, God hastening; and in 48:2, in Heshbon and חשב. In ch. 5 most elegantly: ויקו למשפט והנה משפח: I expected judgement, and behold a scab (ἀνὴ, iniquity). It follows: לצדקה והנה צעקה, I expected righteousness, and behold a cry. Thus he there. But also in his published Commentaries on Persius, where this language is rich in such things, he left a witness in passing, in these words, of how much he valued such elegances: [But very close to this passage (on Persius, "you demand to be fed the little morsels," etc.) is what we observed in the divine and truly sublime prophet Isaiah, in chapter three. For just as Persius here, to express the delicacies of effeminate young men, says they "demand to be fed morsels," that is, imitate the manners of tender infants; so the Hebrew writer, to set before our eyes the luxury of women, says among other things: הליך ושפוף הלבנה, the beauty of which singular elegance, with equal emphasis, the poverty of the Latin tongue does not attain. In Greek you might say word for word, ἐν τῷ βαδίζειν χὴ νηπιάζειν βαδίζεσθαι: that is, they walk in such a way, whenever they go through the streets, as to imitate the gait of little infants. For יפה, which is a most beautiful word, signifies this.] Thus far the critic.

units.la: Ad hujus autem loci, quam tantopere prædicat, elegantiam non tantùm (ut imperitioribus obiter consulamus) pertinet istius verbi יפה pulchritudo: sed etiam, tum ejusdem verbi הלך mutato casu, ad indicandum operosè quasi incedentium fastidium, repetitio: tum duorum infinitivorum τὸ διωροπλάδον, ad affectatam earundem in gradiendo concinnitatem tanto melius exprimendam.
units.tr: Now the elegance of this passage, which he praises so highly, pertains not only (to consult the less experienced in passing) to the beauty expressed by the word יפה, but also to the repetition of the verb הלך with its case changed, to indicate, as it were, the laboured disdain of those who walk; and also to the two infinitives, which express more effectively the affected neatness of their gait.

units.la: F
units.tr: F

units.la: Sed pergamus: Quid illa Ecclesiastæ initio, הבל הבלים אשר קהלת הבל (הבלים הכל הבל: ) nonne paria, ab eodem fonte & pari elegantiâ repetita? Dicat tamen aliquis fortasse, non tam ad aurium voluptatem repetita hîc verba, quàm ad exaggerandam rerum mundanarum, cujus nec finis nec modus, continuato verbo vanitatem. Quid illa, כל הבא לעבד עבדת ועבדת ? משא באהל מועד nisi hic quoque mysterium aliquod (quod ego non capio) latere pertendat aliquis. At illa Psalmi CXXII. v.7. (שאלו שלום ירושלם ישליו אהביך: יהי שלום בהילך שלוה בארמנותיך) an quisquam tam Bœotica est aure, ut ista legens, tanta concinnitate non capiatur? vel istis, II. Regum XIV. 26. (אפם עצור אפם עזוב ) quæ talia sunt, ut in aliam linguam verti non possint, sine non suavissimæ tantùm concinnitatis jactura, sed etiam non sine obscuritatis offensione. Nemo enim legit Hebraica, quin statim ex tessellatâ istâ structurâ, soníque quæsitâ gratiâ, in proverbii suspicionem, (quod iterum in Deuteronomio alibique sæpius occurrit:) incidat. quo semel comperto, nihil amplius difficultatis in verbis. In versionibus autem nulla omnino proverbii vestigia vel indicia. Psalmo autem CXLVII. versus continui non pauciores quàm quinque, pulcherrimâ aliquâ allusione insignes singuli. Primus istorum; כי חזק בריחי שעריך בך בניך בקרבך in quo ταῦ בריחי prioris membri, respondet בך in secundo. Hoc primum. Secundo, secundi membri singulæ voces (quæ tres sunt) ab unâ literâ incipiunt. Cætera Lectori relinquimus, ne nimis ipsius vel industriæ diffidere, vel ingenio videamur.
