Horum autem omnium exemplorum ea ratio est (unum fortasse aut alterum si excipias) ut soli elegantiæ & concinnitati consultum fuisse verborum, vel eorundem repetitione, vel diversorum similitudine, res ipsæ fidem faciant. Huc etiam referri possunt paronomasiæ, quæ non quæsitæ, sed ex solo linguæ genio (cui tamen sua constet ratio:) fluxisse videantur: quales istæ וַיֹּאמְרוּ אִישׁ אֶל רֵעֵהוּ הָבָה נִלְבְּנָה לִבְנִים quorum לְאָבֶן וְהַחֹמֶר הָיָה לָהֶם לְחֹמֶר: elegantiam ipsa naturæ ratio commendat. Quis enim istâ verborum similitudine אבן & לבנה : אֶבֶן & חכר : in tantâ rerum ipsarum, quarum alterę alterarum vicem præstiterint, similitudine declarandâ non capiatur ?
units.tr: But let us go on. Are not those opening words of Ecclesiastes, הבל הבלים אשר קהלת הבל (הבלים הכל הבל), "Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, vanity of vanities, all is vanity" [הֶבֶל הֲבָלִים אָמַר קֹהֶלֶת הֲבֵל הֲבָלִים הַכֹּל הָבֶל], equally repetitions, drawn from the same source and with the same elegance? Someone might perhaps say that these words are repeated not so much for the pleasure of the ear as to magnify the vanity of worldly things, whose end and measure are never reached, by the continued repetition of the word. And what of כל הבא לעבד עבדת ועבדת משא באהל מועד, "every one who comes to serve the service and the burden in the tent of meeting" [Num. 4.]? Here too someone might contend that some mystery lies hidden (which I do not grasp). But who has an ear so Boeotian that, reading Psalm 122.6–7 (שאלו שלום ירושלם ישליו אהביך: יהי שלום בחילך שלוה בארמנותיך), "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: they shall prosper that love you. Peace be within your walls, and prosperity within your palaces," he is not moved by such a close-knit arrangement? Or take 2 Kings 14.26 (אפס עצור ואפס עזוב), "there was neither restrained nor left," which are of such a kind that they cannot be turned into another language without losing not only their most delightful harmony but also incurring a loss of clarity. For no one reads Hebrew without at once suspecting, from this patterned structure and the deliberate charm of sound, a proverb (which occurs again in Deuteronomy and elsewhere more often); once this is discovered, the words present no further difficulty. In the versions, however, there is no trace or sign of a proverb at all. In Psalm 147 there are no fewer than five consecutive verses, each remarkable for some very fine allusion. The first of these is כי חזק בריחי שעריך ברך בניך בקרבך [Ps. 147.13], in which the taw of בריחי in the first member corresponds to בך in the second. That is the first point. Secondly, the individual words of the second member (there are three) all begin with the same letter. I leave the rest to the reader, lest I seem to distrust either his diligence or his wit. For all these examples, with perhaps one or two exceptions, the rationale is this: that the thing itself proves that only elegance and harmony were aimed at, either by repeating words or by the similarity of different words. Paronomasias also belong here, which seem to have arisen not from deliberate art but from the very genius of the language (which nevertheless has its own logic). Such is וַיֹּאמְרוּ אִישׁ אֶל רֵעֵהוּ הָבָה נִלְבְּנָה לִבְנִים, "And they said one to another, Come, let us make bricks," and וַיִּהְיֶה לָהֶם הַלְּבֵנָה לְאָבֶן וְהַחֹמֶר הָיָה לָהֶם לְחֹמֶר, "And they had brick for stone, and bitumen had they for mortar" [Gen. 11.3]. The very nature of the thing recommends the elegance. For who would not be captivated by this similarity of words, לבנה and לבנים, אבן and חמר, in declaring a similarity of things so great that each of the pairs has stood in for the other?

units.la: Alterum genus facimus illas parohomasias (quæ proprie allusionum sibi nomen vindicant) ex quibus præter elegantiam aliquid vel acuminis vel ponderis ipsi sententiæ accedit; &, ut latissimè dicamus, quæ tales sunt, ut ab earum intelligentiâ plus minúsve pendeat loci sententia, quáisque Lectoris intelligere maximè interest. Talia non nulla jam habuimus; ut in iis, quæ ex b. m. parentis Adversariis protulimus.
units.tr: The second kind we make of those paronomasias (which properly claim for themselves the name of allusions), from which something of point or weight is added to the sentence over and above its elegance; and, to speak very broadly, those which are such that the meaning of the passage depends more or less on understanding them, and which it matters most to the reader to understand. We have already had a few of these, such as those we brought forward from the Adversaria of my late father of blessed memory.

units.la: Sed in hoc toto genere primum locum jure meritóque sibi vindicant propriorum nominum impositiones vel historicæ vel propheticæ, prout scilicet ad aliquas vel præteritarum vel futurarum rerum circumstantias respiciunt: cum vero ex impositis nominibus editæ longo post tempore prædictiones futurorum : cujus utriusque generis exemplis scatet Sacra Scriptura, ut in re tam notâ & obviâ inutili labori libenter parcam.
units.tr: But in this whole kind, the first place is rightly and deservedly claimed by the giving of proper names, whether historical or prophetic, insofar as they relate to some circumstances of past or future events; and when predictions of future things were made, long afterwards, out of the names given. Holy Scripture abounds in examples of both kinds, so I will gladly spare myself useless labour in a matter so well known and obvious.

units.la: Occultiora & rariora sunt illa, in quibus per ignominiam levi allusione mutata sunt nomina, qualia notata doctis, משחיר pro משחר : בליעל pro בעל pro כוש : pro אישבשר, pro בעל pro כיש : ענר, pro עכן : & si Scaligeri conjectura tam vera, quàm probabilis, בעל-רעם pro בעל פעור. Ab eodem fonte, quòd Idola צירים dicuntur, allusione facta ad Dei nomen צור ; quasi diceres diri, non divi ; aut tale quid.
units.tr: More hidden and rarer are those in which names have been changed by a slight allusion for the sake of disgrace, of which the following are known to scholars: משחיר for משחר; בליעל for בעל; כוש for אישבשר, for בעל (…?) ; כיש ; ענר for עכן; and, if Scaliger's conjecture is as true as it is probable, בעל־רעם for בעל פעור [Baal-peor]. From the same source comes the fact that idols are called צירים, with an allusion to the divine name צור, as though one were to say "dire" rather than "divine," or something of the kind.

units.la: Obscurioris allusionis, sed cujus observatio sententiam multùm adjuvat, exemplum esto Proverb. XVIII. 1, 2. לחאוּר יבקש נפרד בכל תושיה יתגלע : לא יחפץ כסיל בתבונה כי אם בהתגלות לבו : Quibus verbis verum ac genuinum sapientiæ candidatum sapientissimus Solomon certis notis χαρακτηρίζει, & à sciolo scientiæ ostentatore discernit. Ait igitur primò, ingenti illum cupiditate impelli. Et merito sanè hoc primum ponit, quod in omni re persequendâ præcipuum est, ut ardor adsit animi ; qui omnes difficultates vincit, omnes labores jucundos reddit. Eò pertinet observatio Aristotelis, de quâ nos alibi, ὅτι μᾶλλον ἡ ἴχνεα κείνται ἡ ὀξυ-κεῖβεσθαι, οἱ μεθ' ἡδονῆς ἐνεργεῖν. Multa quoque in eandem sententiam Plato, tum alibi, tum in Convivio, ubi multis disputat, ϟ Ἐρωτα esse philosophum. Talem suam cupiditatem egregiè describit scriptor difertissimus Ælianus, ubi inter alia, præclara illa vox, & quovis Christiano digna, Βυλοίμην ἂν μάθη-μα ἐν γῆν πεπαιδευμένον πεγενέσθαι μοι, ἢ τὰ ἀλόμενα τ πάντ' πλεόντων χρήματα ἄμα χ' χλίμαλα. Ita enim sentio (ex disertissimi viri interpretatione) ut vel unam alicujus egregiæ disciplinæ portiunculam, potius quam celeberrimas quorumvis opes atque possessiones mihi accedere optarim.
units.tr: As an example of a more obscure allusion, but one whose observation greatly helps the sense, let us take Proverbs 18.1–2: לתאוה יבקש נפרד בכל תושיה יתגלע. לא יחפץ כסיל בתבונה כי אם בהתגלות לבו, "He who separates himself seeks his own desire; he breaks out against all sound wisdom. A fool has no delight in understanding, but only in revealing his heart." In these words the most wise Solomon marks out with certain signs the true and genuine candidate for wisdom, and distinguishes him from the smatterer who makes a display of knowledge. He says first, then, that such a man is driven by a great passion. And rightly does he put this first, for in every pursuit the chief requirement is that there be ardour of mind, which overcomes all difficulties and makes all labours pleasant. To this belongs Aristotle's observation, on which I have touched elsewhere: [ὅτι μᾶλλον ... ἐνεργεῖν], that those who act with pleasure are more apt to succeed than those who strain. Plato also says much to the same effect, both elsewhere and in the Convivium, where he argues at length that Eros is a philosopher. Such a passion is well described by the most eloquent writer Aelian, where among other things there is that noble saying, worthy of any Christian: [Βουλοίμην ἂν μάθημα ἐν γῆι πεπαιδευμένον γενέσθαι μοι...]. For I take the sense (from the interpretation of that most eloquent man) to be: that I would rather wish to acquire some small portion of one excellent discipline than the most famous riches and possessions of anyone whatever.

units.la: Altera nota est, quòd, qui talis, separet se; id est, quotidianos hominum congressus morésque, in quibus hominum politicorum studium maximè versatur, vitat, & totum se, quantum potest, studiis suis asserit: quod eleganter unico verbo dicunt Græci; ἐσκαλύπτε-ς: quod etiam Plato genuinis tribuit philosophis, quos ait, οικὸν ἐν ὀρῇ τὸ τῆχῳ φιλοσόφως: quod apud posteros in proverbium abiit. Sed digna Platonis verba, quæ hîc legantur: Ἀγοῖκον ἢ ἐς ἀπαιδεύτον τὸ ἀσχολίας ἐλθῶν τὸ ... ψυχῶν τ πολίτων ἀγαθῶν γίγνεσθαι, οἶκον ἐν ὀρῇ. ἐσῃ τὸ τεχ& σεβαλλόμενον, vertunt: Itaque & hujusmodi philosophum necesse propter nullam negotiorum exercitationem non minus rusticum & imperitum esse, quam pastores: utpote, qui perinde mœnibus in urbe, ac illi caule sepio in monte, circundentur. Paulo aliter Theodoretus in Therapeuticis accepisse videtur; ut & Antoninus Imperator in soliloquiis suis, & fortasse pro σεβαλλό-μενον, verior lectio fuerit σεβαλλόμενον. Sed hæc non sunt hujus loci.
units.tr: The second mark is that such a man separates himself; that is, he avoids the daily gatherings and customs of men, in which the zeal of men of affairs is chiefly engaged, and devotes himself as much as he can to his studies. The Greeks express this elegantly in a single word, [ἐσκαλύπτε...]; and Plato also attributes it to genuine philosophers, whom he says are like a man who has taken shelter behind a wall in a storm of dust and rain, a phrase which passed into a proverb among posterity. But the words of Plato worth reading here are these: [...οἶκον ἐν ὄρει]. They translate it: And so such a philosopher, from taking no part in affairs, must necessarily be no less rustic and unskilled than shepherds, since he is surrounded by the walls of the city just as they are enclosed by a fold on the mountain. Theodoret in his Therapeutics seems to have understood it somewhat differently, as also the Emperor Antoninus in his Soliloquies; and perhaps the truer reading for the word is another. But these matters do not belong to this place.

units.la: Hunc igitur ita animatum, & ἐγκαλυμμένον, ait porro, בְּרֵאשִׁית in quamcunque veræ ac solidæ eruditionis partem curiose pervestigaturum. Scio τὸ פְּרָשִׁים verbum ambiguum esse, cujus ἐπὶ τῷ χώρῳ (qualia πολυσχισμένη Græcis, & φιλοσοφία: Latinis, curiositas, &c.) sint alibi in hoc ipso Proverbiorum libro exempla: at τὸ יִשְׁמְרֵנִי adjunctum, cujus est magna emphasis, omnem tollit ambiguitatem. Est enim illud verbum, si quod aliud, φιλοσοφικώτατος, ad indicandam rerum quarumcunque, sed verè præcipuè sapientiæ, soliditatem impositum: Neque puto ullum Sacræ Scripturæ locum, cum sa-
units.tr: So this man, thus animated and [ἐγκαλυμμένος], wrapped up, is said further to search carefully into whatever part of true and solid learning he meets, בְּרֵאשִׁית ... Here I know that the word פְּרָשִׁים is ambiguous, and in such a case the Greeks use [πολυσχισμένη] and [φιλοσοφία], and the Latins curiositas and so on; there are examples of this elsewhere in this very book of Proverbs. But the added word יִשְׁמְרֵנִי, which carries great emphasis, removes all ambiguity. For this word, if any, is the most philosophical, imposed to indicate the solidity of things of every kind, but truly above all of wisdom. Nor do I think that any passage of Holy Scripture will be found, when it occurs so often, where it is used otherwise, though not always with the same emphasis.

units.la: pius occurrat, temerè repertum iri, ubi aliter, quamvis non pari semper emphasi, usurpetur. Mihi sanè plura loca (sed Proverb.III.19,20,21. & Micæ VI. 9. præcipuè) diligentius attendenti & contendenti,cum hominibus(nam Deo quoque non uno loco:) tribuitur,talem proprie scientiam & sapientiam videtur vox חכמה significare, quæ ex feriâ operum Dei sive naturalium, quibus constat hic mundus; sive aliorum (actiones diceremus, si de hominibus esset sermo) quibus humanæ res administrantur; ex feriâ,inquam, & accuratâ istorum(quantum homini fas est)contemplatione & cognitione comparatur. Ei rei argumenta plura dicerem, quibus adducor ut ita credam, si hoc nunc ageremus. Sufficit hîc, quod antè dicebamus, verbum istud præstantiæ alicujus significationem semper habere in Sacrâ Scripturâ.
units.tr: For my own part, when I attend and reflect more carefully on several passages (especially Proverbs 3.19–21 and Micah 6.9), where the word חכמה is attributed to men (and to God too, in more than one place), I think the word properly signifies such knowledge and wisdom as is acquired from the diligent and accurate contemplation and knowledge (as far as it is lawful for man) of God's works, whether natural, by which this world consists, or of the others (we would call them actions if we were speaking of men), by which human affairs are governed. I could give several more arguments by which I am led to believe this, if I were undertaking that now. It is enough here to say what I said before: that this word always carries in Holy Scripture the sense of some excellence.

units.la: Genuino huic sapientiæ sectatori alium opponit Solomon, qui sapientiæ studio & ipse non mediocris incendi videtur, sed non alio fine, quàm ad pompam & oftentionem: ut cor suum; vel sapientia sua: (nam τὸ ἡ utrunq; significat, ficat, ut & cor Latinis:) reveletur, sive aliis innotescat: quorum scilicet (ut à Satyrico describuntur) Scire nihil est, nisi scire illos, quodcunque est, quod sciunt, sciant alteri. Hunc illi sapientiæ fructum sibi proponunt maximum, non ut sibi aliisve vera prosint.
units.tr: To this genuine seeker of wisdom Solomon sets another, who seems himself to be fired by no small zeal for wisdom, but for no other end than display and ostentation: that his heart, or his wisdom (for the Hebrew word means both, as cor does in Latin), might be revealed or made known to others. These are men who, as the satirist describes them, think it nothing to know unless whatever they know is also known to others. This is the greatest fruit they propose to themselves from wisdom, not that it should truly profit themselves or others.

units.la: Nova fortasse videbitur iis interpretatio, qui versionibus tantum assueverunt. Qui vero Hebræos interpretes, Aben-ezram aliósque legerunt, aliter judicabunt. Hebraeis autem verbis, aut ego fallor, aut hæc interpretatio longè convenientior, quàm quas hactenus videre mihi contigit. Nam Græci, & qui illos sequuntur, (viri sanè doctissimi) aut aliud legisse, aut <bl>ת</bl> יעל cum יעל (cujus promiscuæ significationis in tota Scriptura nullum alibi vestigium) confundere videntur. Ad hanc autem interpretationem non lectio Rabbinorum, quos postea consuli; sed paronomasiæ observatio me primum induxit, cùm יתו־ף prioris versiculi, תולגהה in posteriore (qualia alibi multa) respondere comperissem.
units.tr: A new interpretation will perhaps seem strange to those who are accustomed only to the versions. Those who have read the Hebrew interpreters, Aben Ezra and others, will judge otherwise. For in the Hebrew words, unless I am mistaken, this interpretation fits far better than any I have so far been able to see. The Greeks and those who follow them, very learned men indeed, seem either to have read something different or to have confused one word with another, whose double meaning appears nowhere else in the whole of Scripture. What led me to this interpretation was not the reading of the rabbis, whom I consulted afterwards, but my observation of the paronomasia: I found that the [יתוף] of the first verse corresponds to the [תולגה] in the second, as many other such pairs do.

units.la: Alterum genus est Paronomasiæ, sive Allusionis, quæ non in aliquâ literarum soníve
units.tr: The second kind of paronomasia, or allusion, consists not in any affinity of letters or sound

units.la: sonive affinitate, sed significationis, consistit, cujus exemplum erit Proverbiorum capite XXV. versu 23. דוח צפון תחולל גשם ופנים נועמים לשון סתר: Duo hic sunt, de quibus inter interpretes non convenit. sensus verbi תחולל cui alii gignendi, alii dissipandi notionem hoc loco inesse volunt: & vera fyntaxis iftorû ופנים נועצים לשון סתר: cùm alii סתר לשון accusativum esse statuant, & ת ופנים נועמים verbo (quod fubintelligitur) praeponant: alii contrà, postrema verba recta esse, & verbo praeponenda esse censeant; priora autem illa pro obliquis habeant & verbo postponant. Ventum Aquilonem nubes dissipare, & serenitatem inducere, veteribus olim, Græcis Latiníque, creditum esse, vel Poëtæ fidem faciant; ut Ovidius in primâ Metamorphosi;
units.tr: or sound, but in affinity of meaning. An example is Proverbs 25.23, [דוח צפון תחולל גשם ופנים נועמים לשון סתר], "The north wind brings forth rain, and an angry face a backbiting tongue." Two points here are disputed among the interpreters. First, the sense of the verb [תחולל]: some think it means "to bring forth", others "to scatter". Second, the true syntax of the words [ופנים נועמים לשון סתר]: some take [לשון סתר] as the accusative and place it before the verb (which is understood), while others hold the last words to be correct and to be placed before the verb, and treat the former words as oblique and place them after it. That the ancient Greeks and Latins believed the north wind scatters clouds and brings clear weather, the poets bear witness; as Ovid does in the first book of the Metamorphoses:

units.la: Nubila disjecit, nimbíque Aquilone remotis,
units.tr: The Aquilo drove away the clouds and the rain-storms,

units.la: Et cœla terras offendit, & athera terris.
units.tr: And the sky appeared to the earth, and the air to the earth.

units.la: Et jam antea eodem libro, ubi Juppiter ex omni cœlo nimbos dimissurus inducitur,
units.tr: And earlier in the same book, where Jupiter is introduced as about to send down rain-clouds from the whole sky:

units.la: Protinus Æoliis Aquilonem claudit in antris,
units.tr: Straightway he shuts the North Wind in the caves of Aeolus,

units.la: Et quacunque fugant induĉtas flamina nubes.
units.tr: And the winds that scatter the clouds which have gathered.

units.la: Unde & Aquilo ventus in Proverbio pro, Serenitas: ut in illo Propertii,
units.tr: Hence also "the north wind" is used proverbially for clear weather, as in that line of Propertius:

units.la: Et nobis Aquilo, Cynthia, ventus erit.
units.tr: And for us, Cynthia, the north wind will be the weather.

units.la: Accedit & Jobi authoritas, c.XXXVII. versu 22. Ut Rabbinorum illorum, qui Hierosolymis rem aliter habere tradunt, quod ad Occidentem mari claudatur, observatio quanti facienda sit, aliis expendendum libens relinquam.
units.tr: The authority of Job also supports this, chapter 37 verse 22. As for the observation of those rabbis who report that in Jerusalem the case is otherwise, namely that the west is closed off by the sea, I will gladly leave its value to be weighed by others.

units.la: Sunt sanè, nec indocti, (Junius, aliique) quibus gignendi significatio hujus loci propria credita est: ego de eo nunc non contendam. nostra enim, quomodocunque statuas, parum aut nihil interest. De posterioribus verbis omnis hic mihi controversia. Hoc igitur dico: paronomasiæ (ita enim liceat indigitare) rationem postulare, ut יום ... ... in ordine sententiæ præcedat, quomodo Junius & alii plures expresse; non, ut versio Anglica, & quos, viros alioquin doctissimos, illa secuta est. Hebræis Aquilo; (pars mundi Meridiei opposita:) dicitur, quasi absconditus. condirus : ex Solis absentiâ, five quòd à Sole longiùs, ut plerique censent ; an aliâ ex causâ ; non hîc quæro. יסוד proprie significare, quod absconditum vel occultum fit ( unde & יסוד thefaurus, res abscondita:) res minimè dubia : quæ etiam est סתר significatio. quasi dicat Solomon ; Ut ab occultâ plagâ veniens ventus dissipat nubes : ita occulta lingua, vultum indignabundum. Occultam autem linguam vocaverit hîc Solomon, quam alibi non semel mollem : in cujus potentiâ variis verbis (ut in aliis quibusdam ) exponendâ & inculcandâ, multus est. quod non fine causâ maximâ ab illo factum esse, tanto melius sciamus ; fi, quæ è sapientibus Ethnicis in eandem planè sententiam prudentissimè monita sunt, ( unde & demagogorum frequens in illorum historiis detestatio : ) observemus. Ab hâc igitur mente sunt illa Solomonis, hoc ipso capite, v.15. בארך אפים &c. vertit Junius, Longanimitate pellicitur ductor, & lingua mollis frangit osseum : [vel offis virum, id est, durissimum & rigidiffimum:] & illa, capite XV. v.1, Responsio mollis frangit excandescentiam : am : verbum antem molestum excitat iram. Signatiffimè autem lingua blandiloqua, lingua occulta vocatur, quòd blandientium, eorum præcipuè, qui iratos verbis demulcere student, proprium fit simulare: unde & mentiri in Sacrâ Scripturâ satis obvium, pro subjici & ad alterius voluntatem se componere. Græci quoque, cum de talibus loquuntur, verbis xdʼθε͏ι (quod Homericum est) & κρύπτειν (inde & κρύψις, pro simulatio:) utuntur. Cæterùm non absimilis apud Propertium modò laudatum, de vi verborum ad compescendam iram, à ventis & ipsa petita similitudo: Non ita Carpathia variant Aquilonibus unda, Nec dubio nubes vertitur atra Noto : Quàm facile irati verbo mutantur amantes, &c.
units.tr: There are indeed learned men (Junius and others) who have believed that the sense "to bring forth" is proper to this passage. I shall not contend about that now: our point, however you decide it, matters little or nothing. The whole controversy for me concerns the latter words. I say this: the nature of the paronomasia (for so I may call it) requires that [יום], in the order of the sentence, precede, as Junius and many others expressly hold, and not as the English version does, and those whom, though otherwise most learned, it followed. The Hebrews call the north wind (the part of the world opposed to the south) as it were "hidden", from the absence of the sun, whether because it is further from the sun, as most think, or for some other reason, which I do not seek here. [יסוד] properly means what is hidden or concealed (whence also [יסוד] means treasure, a hidden thing), a point that is by no means doubtful, and this is also the meaning of [סתר]. It is as if Solomon said: as a wind coming from a hidden quarter scatters clouds, so a hidden tongue scatters an angry countenance. He calls this tongue "hidden" here, though elsewhere more than once he calls it "soft"; and he is much concerned to set it forth and impress it with various words, as he does with certain other matters. We shall understand this all the better, that he did not do so without the greatest cause, if we observe what the wise among the Gentiles have most prudently warned in exactly the same sense, whence also the frequent detestation of demagogues in their histories. Solomon's sayings in this same chapter, verse 15, belong to this same thought: [בארך אפים] Junius renders, "By long-suffering a ruler is persuaded, and a soft tongue breaks the bone" [or, a man of bone, that is, the hardest and most rigid]; and that in chapter 15, verse 1: "A soft answer turns away wrath, but a grievous word stirs up anger." Now a smooth-speaking tongue is most aptly called a "hidden" tongue, because it is the mark of flatterers, especially of those who seek to soothe the angry with words, to feign; whence also "to lie" in Holy Scripture is a common expression for "to submit" and to conform oneself to another's will. The Greeks too, when they speak of such people, use the words [ὑποκρύπτειν] (which is Homeric) and [κρύπτειν] (whence also [κρύψις], meaning dissimulation). Moreover, a similar comparison, drawn also from the winds, concerning the power of words to restrain anger, appears in the Propertius quoted above: "The waves of Carpathus do not change so with the north winds, nor does the dark cloud turn so with the doubtful south wind, as easily as lovers are changed by a word when angry."

units.la: Jam si istos potiùs sequimur, qui תחולל gignit vertunt, tantò expeditior erit verborum illorum סיר לשין interpretatio. Ut nimirùm lingua sycophantica, & occultè detractatoria, seu delatoria intelligatur, qualem lites & rixas parere tum plurimas, tum periculosissi-mas mas solere, vulgò notum. In hanc sententiam totum versiculum vertit vir doctissimus, Ut Cacias gignit pluviam; ita vultum indignabundum lingua fimulantis. [vel, viri absconsionis.] Sed ad omnem verborum istorum elegantiam plane intelligendam pertinet forsitan & illud, observata inter פנים ה (seu פנה, ex quo Graecum φαίνω) & תר ה ἀνλίθεος. Sed haec subtiliora, & quae non omnes capiant. Absistemus igitur.
units.tr: If we now follow rather those who render [תחולל] as "brings forth", the interpretation of the words [סיר לשין] will be much more straightforward: the tongue meant is that of the sycophant, which slanders in secret, or informs, as is commonly known to produce quarrels and strife, very many and very dangerous. A very learned man has translated the whole verse in this sense: "As the north wind brings forth rain, so a tongue of a flatterer brings forth an angry face" [or, "of a man of concealment"]. But for the full understanding of all the elegance of these words, perhaps the following also matters: the relation observed between [פנים] (or [פנה], whence the Greek φαίνω) and [תר] ... [ἀνλίθεος]. But these are subtler points, which not everyone would grasp. We shall therefore refrain.

units.la: Aliud adhuc genus paronomafiae, cum allusum verbum reticetur; quod tamen in animo loquentis fuisse, fi non certa ubique fides, saltem probabilis suspicio; quale fortasse, quod II. Samuelis c.XX. v.18. דבר ידברו בראשונה לאמר שאול ישאלו באבל וכן התמר ubi sic ampliector Junii aliorumque doctorum interpretationem, qui ex Deuter.c.XX.v.10. & sequentibus, ubi leges obsidionis legitimae proponuntur, exponunt; ut ad dictum aliquod vulgare, quale, quod Solomon postea inter sacra intulit, Ecclef. c.VII.v.2. טוב ללכת אל בית אבל &c. & v.4. לב חכמים בבית אבל &c. alludi credam: ut frustra non fit, quod vetus Interpres Latinus veteris hîc exerte proverbii meminerit.
units.tr: There is yet another kind of paronomasia, where the alluded-to word is left unstated, though if not certain everywhere, at least a probable suspicion holds that it was in the mind of the speaker. Perhaps this is so in II Samuel 20.18, [דבר ידברו בראשונה לאמר שאול ישאלו באבל וכן התמר]. Here I am inclined to follow the interpretation of Junius and other learned men, who explain it from Deuteronomy 20.10 and following, where the laws of lawful siege are set forth, and take it as an allusion to some common saying. Such a saying seems to be that which Solomon later included among the sacred writings, Ecclesiastes 7.2, [טוב ללכת אל בית אבל] etc., and verse 4, [לב חכמים בבית אבל] etc. So it is no accident that the old Latin interpreter expressly mentions an "old proverb" here.

units.la: Hujus generis aliud exemplum in Tsophaniæ prophetæ verbis, capite II.4. reperire est, quod ut melius intelligatur, totum locum Lectori repræsentabo. Ait igitur propheta : כי עזה עזובה תהיה ואשקלון לשממה אשדוד בצהרים יגרשוה ועקרון תעקר: Quatuor hîc urbium excidia prædicuntur, allusis singularum, sed non unâ ratione, nominibus. עקרון תעקר & עזה עזובה (quæ sunt extrema nomina) tám clara sunt, ut nemo tam sit oscitans, ut statim non animadvertere cogatur. Et miror interpretes, (mihi saltem visos) qui de istis extremis monent, de reliquis tacere. Sunt sanè obscuriores istorum allusiones: alludi tamen & illa, quamvis ratio non pateret allusionis, ut res ipsa postulat; ita fidelis & ingenui erat interpretis, saltem monuisse. Nobis ita videtur: Allusionem vocis אשקלון in eo consistere, quod אשקלון & אשם, quod vastare, desolare significat, priores duas literas easdem habeant. Quamvis autem non hîc ponatur אשם, sed synonymum ejus (quod etiam sono valdè
units.tr: Another example of this kind may be found in the words of the prophet Zephaniah, chapter 2 verse 4, which, so that it may be better understood, I shall set before the reader in full. The prophet says: [כי עזה עזובה תהיה ואשקלון לשממה אשדוד בצהרים יגרשוה ועקרון תעקר]: "For Gaza shall be forsaken, and Ashkelon a desolation; Ashdod they shall drive out at noon, and Ekron shall be uprooted." Here the destruction of four cities is foretold, with allusion to each of their names, but not all in the same way. The names at the extremes, [עקרון תעקר] and [עזה עזובה], are so clear that no one is so careless as not to notice them at once. I wonder that the interpreters (at least those I have seen) comment on these extreme names and say nothing of the rest. Their allusions are certainly more obscure, yet it is the duty of a faithful and candid interpreter at least to point out those too, even where the basis of the allusion is not evident, as the matter itself requires. It seems to me as follows: the allusion in the word [אשקלון] consists in this, that [אשקלון] and [אשם], which means to lay waste or make desolate, have the same first two letters. Although [אשם] itself is not used here, but its synonym [שמם] (which is also very close in sound), since no substantive of this meaning is formed from the former, that gap must nevertheless be supplied by the intelligent reader, as is usually done in such allusions made in the mind.

units.la: {G} valdè vicinum est ) שמם ( quòd scilicet ab isto priore nullum formatum fit istius notionis substantivum ;) suppleri tamen ab intelligente Lectore debet iste defectus, ut in mentalibus id genus allusionibus fieri solet. Exemplis hoc non Hebræis tantùm, sed Græcis Latinísque, si opus esset, possimus confirmare. Sed longè obscurior in altero illo אשרוד allusionis ratio, cujus nulla omninò expressa in aliis verbis indicia. Ea verò ex ipso nomine petenda est. Quid enim שדד quàm vastare, devastare? quod tamen, quò magis liqueret, additum צהרים, quod ad vastationis & excidii significationem pertinere, si non aliunde, saltem ex Psalmo XCI. 6. discimus, ubi pariter ut hîc cum verbo שדד jungitur : מקטב ישוד צהרים, a peste vastante meridie. Quorsum autem meridiei hîc fiat mentio, docti interpretes consulendi. Sed & veteribus ethnicis meridianum tempus suspectum, ut à dæmonibus nescio quibus (aliis illi nominibus usi:) infestari solitum. Testes Poëtæ. Ovidius, (ut alios nunc omittam) in Fastis:
units.tr: {G} is very close to שמם, namely because no noun of that meaning is formed from the former. Yet the intelligent reader must supply this lack, as is usual in allusions of this kind. We could confirm this by examples, not only from Hebrew but from Greek and Latin if need be. But the basis of the allusion in the other word, אשרוד, is far more obscure, for there are no clear signs of it in other words. It must be sought from the name itself. For what is שדד but to lay waste, to devastate? To make this clearer, the word צהרים is added. If we learn that it pertains to the sense of devastation and destruction from nowhere else, at least we learn it from Psalm 91:6, where, as here, it is joined with the verb שדד: "the destruction that wasteth at noonday" (מקטב ישוד צהרים). Why noonday is mentioned here, learned interpreters should be consulted. The ancient pagans also regarded the midday hour with suspicion, as a time when they were commonly troubled by I know not what demons, which they called by other names. The poets are witnesses. Ovid, to pass over others for now, says in the Fasti:

units.la: Nec Dryadas, nec nos videamus labra Diane:
units.tr: Let us not see the Dryads, nor Diana's lips,

units.la: Nec Faunum, medio cum premit arva die.
units.tr: Nor Faunus, when midday presses on the fields.

units.la: Judicet jam Lector ex hoc qualicunque specimine, qui versionibus contenti sunt, quanto illis non venustatis & elegantiae modo, quae nullo fere non loco multiplex ingerit se, dispendio constet iste alieni laboris fructus; sed etiam non raro & sententiae: ut mirum non sit, si qui aurium voluptate ad percipiendas rerum bonarum doctrinas, (ut sane partim sciens, partim etiam infciens multo maxima pars hominum: quod alibi fuse probamus:) praecipue ducuntur, a sacra lectione Scripturae, si non abhorreant, certe non illibenter abstineant, & aliis potius occupentur: Sed, in animadvertendis tamen sacris hisce paronomasiis, magno judicio & subactis longo usu auribus opus est; nequis acutior quam cautior ineptias suas, & lascivientis ingenii conceptus imaginarios pro veris ac genuinis leporibus nobis obtrudat, ac ita non se tantum, sed sacram etiam scripturam, maleferiatorum male-feriatus ipse ludibriis exponat. Non enim sufficit semper sola, vel quæcunque verborum similitudo; neque omnis locus περνομασίαι opportunus: quas etiam interdum studio vitatas diligens Lector observabit. Sed hæc justum tractatum requirunt. Nec forte de Sacrâ Scripturâ, & ejus studiosis malè mereatur, qui justum tractatum istis dicaverit: saltem, ut illa complectatur, & accuratè colligat, quæ sine aliquo sententiæ ipsius detrimento non possunt ignorari. Nam cætera & infinita sunt, & parum illos juvabunt, qui Hebraica (intelligentibus autem satis obvia:) non intelligunt.
units.tr: Let the reader now judge from this sample, however slight, what those who rely on translations lose. The loss is not only of elegance and charm, which almost everywhere presses itself on the eye in many ways, but often of meaning as well. So it is no wonder that the greater part of mankind, who are drawn chiefly by the pleasure of the ear to take in teachings about good things (as we prove at length elsewhere, partly knowingly and partly unknowingly), if they do not shrink from the sacred reading of Scripture, at least gladly abstain from it and turn to other pursuits. Yet in noticing these sacred paronomasiae, one needs sound judgment and ears trained by long practice, lest a man, more keen than careful, thrust upon us his foolish trifles and the imaginary conceits of a wanton wit in place of true and genuine witticisms, and so expose not only himself but also Holy Scripture to the mockery of those who play the fool. For a mere likeness of words, or any likeness whatever, is not always enough, and not every place is suitable for a paronomasia. A diligent reader will notice that these are sometimes avoided on purpose. But these matters require a proper treatise. Nor will he deserve ill of Holy Scripture and its students who dedicates a proper treatise to them, at least one that gathers and carefully collects those things which cannot be ignored without some loss to the meaning itself. For the rest are endless, and they will do little good to those who do not understand Hebrew, which is, however, plain enough to those who do.

units.la: Cæterùm, (quod aliquis miretur,) etiam in Novo Testamento, linguâ non Hebraicâ scripto, περνομασίαι Hebraicæ non infrequentes. Tales: Rom.IX.16. ὑ ϝ θέλοντος, οὐδὲ ϝ τρέχοντος, ἀλλὰ ϝ ἐλεῶντος Θεός: רוח : רצון : רחמים. Sed & eandem sententiam his ipsis verbis conceptam in Thalmude alicubi, virum quendam Hebraicè peritissimum me præsente olim afferere memini. Tale & I. Cor. I.23. σκάνδαλον & μωρία, ut Cornelio à Lapide, viro doctissimo rectè
units.tr: Moreover (which someone may find surprising), even in the New Testament, which was written in a language other than Hebrew, Hebrew paronomasiae are not uncommon. Such is Romans 9:16, "not of him that wills, nor of him that runs, but of God that shows mercy" (οὐ τοῦ θέλοντος οὐδὲ τοῦ τρέχοντος, ἀλλὰ τοῦ ἐλεῶντος Θεοῦ), which corresponds to רוח : רצון : רחמים. I remember that I once heard a man very skilled in Hebrew, in my presence, assert that the same sentence, conceived in these very words, occurs somewhere in the Talmud. Such also is 1 Corinthians 1:23, "a stumbling-block and foolishness" (σκάνδαλον and μωρία), as has been rightly noted by Cornelius à Lapide, a very learned man.

units.la: [Hebrew and Greek words in the text are copied as far as legible; the Hebrew line "רוח : רצון : רחמים" and the Greek Rom. IX.16 line are uncertain.] recte notatum. Item II. Petr. cap. II. versu ultimo, ὑς & κλισμα, quæ Hebraicè ab unâ radice ׳ךר: & inde vulgaris apud Hebræos Proverbii ansa.
units.tr: Likewise, 2 Peter 2:22, in the last verse, "the sow that is washed" (ὗς and κύλισμα), which in Hebrew come from one root, חור, and from which comes a common proverb among the Hebrews.

units.la: Pari quoque ratione, nisi valdè sallor, I.Tim. III.15. σὰλ῾ (sive ἐλεέωμα) & ἀλήθεια; σὰλ῾ & ἀλήθεια, non ab unâ tantùm radice, sed uno eodemque (אמונה) verbo Hebraeis designentur: atque nominatim Templi Hierosolymitani στῦλοι sive columnæ, אמונים indigitatæ (II. Regum XVIII. versu 16.) reperiantur. Quod si quis in his & similibus aliis Syrum objiciat, qui vertens non observavit, certè non expressit, interpretem; studio, an casu & ἆσ͂υπξία factum ab illo fit, alii viderint: meam certè de paronomasiis illis suspicionem non minuerit, cùm videam illum Joh. I. versu 14. ubi licebat illi vocem Græcam σκηνὴν, cujus singularem hoc loco ἔμφασιν, sed ex Hebraicâ voce & usu petendam, agnoscunt etiam illi, qui Christi æternitati non usque-quaque semper favisse videri possint; cùm liceret, inquam, illi vocem Græcam retinere, nec tamen à Syriacâ dialecto (quod in aliis fortasse non æquè liberum illi fuit, ubi Hebraica differunt à Syriacis :) difcedere, maluit tamen uti voce ЛЙ, quàm voce ЛЙ : quâ tamen alibi, ubi minor necessitas, non abstinuit.
units.tr: By the same reasoning, unless I am greatly mistaken, 1 Timothy 3:15, "the pillar and ground of the truth" (στῦλος, or ἑδραίωμα, and ἀλήθεια), the στῦλος and ἀλήθεια are designated by the Hebrews not only by one root but by one and the same word, אמונה. Indeed, the pillars or columns of the Temple at Jerusalem, called אמונים (2 Kings 18:16), are found. But if anyone objects to these and similar cases that the Syriac translator, who has not observed them in translating, certainly did not express them, whether he did so by design or by chance and carelessness, let others judge. My suspicion about these paronomasiae is certainly not lessened by the fact that in John 1:14, where he could have retained the Greek word σκηνή, whose special force in this place is recognised even by those who may seem not always to have favoured the eternity of Christ, and where, I say, he was free to keep the Greek word without departing from the Syriac dialect (which may not have been equally free for him in other places where Hebrew differs from Syriac), he chose rather to use the Syriac word, though elsewhere, where there was less need, he did not refrain from using that very word.

units.la: Sed ad alia transeamus. Non parum facit ad Hebraicæ linguæ commendationem τῆς ὀνομαλογίας consideratio: quæ cùm non humani, sed divini sit instituti, credibile est, ex ipsorum verborum ratione, & attentâ consideratione, quæ ad sapientiam faciant tum moralem tum naturalem, non pauca posse erui: si quis tamen sobrie id agat, & Deo ipso sapientior esse non affectet. Non enim si etiam in verbis sapientiæ suæ vestigia quædam seu stricturas impressit Deus, id ἀσυνξυμένως egit, ut ex verbis & etymologiis sapientia peteretur; cùm non minùs scientiarum qualiumcunque, quamvis hominum sive Græcorum sive aliorum ministerio usus, (modò tamen verarum & legitimarum) sit author Deus, quàm verborum istorum, de quibus nunc agimus. Et illarum quidem non alio fine author, quàm ut ex illis sapientia humana hauriretur, tanquam ex fontibus: cujus quòd ne verba quidem, quanquam alium
units.tr: But let us pass on to other matters. The consideration of the correspondence of names to things (τῆς ὀνομαλογίας) contributes not a little to the commendation of the Hebrew language. Since this arrangement is not of human but of divine design, it is credible that not a few things which bear on wisdom, both moral and natural, can be drawn out from the very reasoning of the words and from careful consideration of them, provided that one does this soberly and does not aim to be wiser than God himself. For even if God has impressed certain traces or marks of his wisdom on words as well, he did not do so in such a way that wisdom should be sought from words and etymologies. God is no less the author of sciences of whatever kind, even though he uses the service of men, whether Greeks or others, (provided they are true and lawful sciences), than he is the author of those words which we are now discussing. Indeed, he was the author of those sciences for no other purpose than that human wisdom should be drawn from them as from springs. But that the words themselves, though he instituted them for another

units.la: alium in finem ab ipso instituta, plane expertia esse voluit, id ad majorem sapientiæ suæ revelationem factum ab illo credimus, non ut scientias (quod modo dicebamus) ex verbis peteremus. Qui ista ulterius extendunt, & de Deo, & de lingua Hebraica, ut posteà pluribus ostendemus, male merentur.
units.tr: purpose, should be wholly free of this, we believe was done by him for the greater revelation of his wisdom, and not so that we should seek the sciences from words, as we just said. Those who extend these things further, both concerning God and concerning the Hebrew language, as we shall show more fully afterwards, deserve ill of them.

units.la: Cæterùm non negamus etiam in aliis linguis, Græcâ præcipuè, talia reperiri non pauca; plura tamen, in Hebraicâ, ni fallor; saltem pro librorum verborúmve, quæ ad nos pervenere, numero. Nec de compositis hîc ago; quorum copia, & pro copiâ fœlicitas (proprietatem ex naturâ rei petitam isto verbo intelligo;) olim Germanæ cum Græcâ communis; nunc Græcæ linguæ propria videtur esse laus. Id dico, simplicia verba Hebraica, cùm pleraque plures & diversas complectantur significationes; ex pluribus autem, unam ut plurimùm propriam & genuinam, ex quâ cæterae, quanquam fortasse non minùs usitatæ & notæ, diversâ ratione fluxerint: hujus cómmunionis sive propagationis rationes in non paucis tales esse, quarum explicatio, vel ad usum vitæ, vel ad naturæ cognitionem non parum conferat. Talium exempla cùm sint in mundo plurima, ut aliis notata prætereain, vox una כשל minùs intelligentibus sufficiet hîc ad specimen.
units.tr: Moreover, we do not deny that not a few such things are found also in other languages, chiefly Greek. Yet there are more in Hebrew, unless I am mistaken, at least in proportion to the number of books and words that have come down to us. Nor am I speaking here of compounds, whose abundance, and the felicity that goes with that abundance (by felicity I mean propriety drawn from the nature of the thing), was once common to German and Greek, but now seems to be the special praise of the Greek language. I say that simple Hebrew words, since most of them embrace several and diverse meanings, of which one, usually the proper and genuine one, is the source from which the others have flowed by different routes, though perhaps no less in use and familiar. The grounds of this communion or propagation of meanings are, in many cases, such that their explanation contributes not a little either to the practice of life or to the knowledge of nature. Since examples of such things are very numerous in the world, I will pass over those already noted by others, and for those less acquainted with the subject the single word כשל will suffice here as a specimen.

units.la: תּ כשל igitur in Kal, à doctissimo Buxtorfio, Junii, ut passim, versionem secuto redditur, secundari, prosperari: quod aliis plerisque, intelligere, perspicere, diligenter & attentè considerare. Sed cùm rarius occurrat in primâ conjugatione, & ubi occurrit, alterutra significatio bene conveniat, haud ita facile, de verâ & genuinâ statuere. Cæterùm in conjugatione Hiphil, usitatissima intelligere, intelligenter agere, &c. nec minùs certa, quamvis non tam frequens, prosperari, secundari, significatio.
units.tr: The verb כשל in Kal, therefore, is rendered by the very learned Buxtorf, following Junius as he often does, as to be made prosperous, to prosper; but by most others as to understand, to perceive, to consider diligently and attentively. But since it occurs more rarely in the first conjugation, and where it does occur either meaning suits well, it is not easy to decide which is the true and genuine one. In the Hiphil conjugation, however, the meaning to understand, to act with understanding, etc., is most common, and the meaning to prosper, to make prosperous, though not so frequent, is no less certain.

units.la: Ut ex c. Prov. XVII. v. 8. אבן חן השחד בעיני בעליו אל כל אשר יפנה ישכיל quod Junius, [Velut] gemma gratissima est munus in oculis deditì ei: quocunque spectet, prosperatur. & Angl. vulg. A gift is as a precious stone in the eyes of him that hath it; whithersoever it turneth, it prospereth. Nec aliter, præstantissimi quiq; Rabbini. Græca quoq; vetus per Ἀοσῶς hîc exprimit. Μισθὸς χαείτων
units.tr: As in Prov. 17:8, "A gift is a precious stone in the eyes of him who has it: wherever it turns, it prospers" [אבן חן השחד בעיני בעליו אל כל אשר יפנה ישכיל]. Junius renders it: Velut a most pleasing gem is a gift in the eyes of its possessor: wherever he looks, he prospers. The English vulgar version has: A gift is as a precious stone in the eyes of him that hath it; whithersoever it turneth, it prospereth. The most distinguished rabbis agree, and the old Greek here renders it by [Ἀοσῶς].

units.la: χαειτων ὢ παιδεία τοῖς χρωμένοις, ἓ ἀν ὃν ἐπισρέψη, Διόσωσιόπλαυ Interdum junguntur,ut synonyma, תשלר ו צלח & ת שלר ה ut Josh. c. I. verf. 8. כי אז תצליח את דרכך ואז תשכיל quod Junius, Tunc enim prosperaberis in viis tuis, & tunc secundaberis. Anglica; For then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good successe. appositâ tamen ibi ad oram & altera verbi significatione, [or, Doe wiselp :] ut Lectori liberum esset, quam mallet ipse, amplecti. quod & alibi saepius in istâ versione observatur, ut altera in textu, altera in adversâ orâ significatio Lectori, quasi in dubiâ re, proponatur; vel fortasse, quasi in utrâque aliquid ad sententiam aut pleniorem sensum momenti esset, commendetur. Ita certè, Josuae c. I. v.7, & 8. I.Sam.XVIII. v. 5, & 14. sed & in nomine, ab eodem verbo, substantivo, Proverb. cap. III. verf. 4. & Psal. CXI. versu ultimo.
units.tr: Sometimes the two verbs are joined as synonyms, tslach and sakal, as in Josh. 1:8: "For then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success" [כי אז תצליח את דרכך ואז תשכיל]. Junius renders it: Then indeed you will prosper in your ways, and then you will be successful. The English version has: For then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good successe. Yet beside it in the margin it gives the other meaning of the verb, [or, Doe wisely], so that the reader may embrace whichever he prefers. This is seen elsewhere in that version too: one meaning is set in the text and the other in the margin, as if the reader were offered a choice in a doubtful matter, or perhaps as if each had some weight for the sense, fuller or more complete. So certainly in Josh. 1:7 and 8, 1 Sam. 18:5 and 14, and also in the noun from the same verb in Prov. 3:4 and in the last verse of Ps. 111.

units.la: Hinc autem ansa sive discendi, sive meditandi, quod non unus veterum pro magno sapientiae arcano venditavit. sua quemque fortuna (ut apud Salustium Appius) fabrum esse: vel, suos cuique mores (ut in Attici vitâ Cornelius Nepos )fingere seu conciliare fortunam. bonos,bonam : malos,malam : ut frustrà sint homines, cùm de fatorum iniquitate queruntur, qui sui potiùs ingenii pravitatem & suam ἀξιωσίαν culpare deberent. Planè,quod Sanctus vates; Retribuit mihi Deus secundùm justitiam meam, & secundùm puritatem manuum mearum in conspectu oculorum ejus. Cum sancto sanctus eris(vel,ut alii, cum misericorde misericors eris) & cum viro innocente innocens eris. Cum mundo mundus eris, & cum perverso perverse ag., ages. Quod & Græci, iisdem ferè verbis, sed contractiùs, Ἐσθλὸν γὰρ ἀνδρὶ ἐσθλὰ χρὴ ἀιδοῖ θεός. &, Ὁ νῦς γὰρ ἡμῶν ὁ θεὸς. &, Ἡ θεὸς ἀνθρώπων, ἀλλων. quæ expressit Poëta Satyricus,
units.tr: From this comes an opening for learning or for reflection, which more than one of the ancients hawked as a great secret of wisdom: each man is the smith of his own fortune (as Appius says in Sallust), or, each man shapes, or rather makes, his own fortune (as Cornelius Nepos says in the life of Atticus). Good men have good fortune, bad men bad, so that men are wrong when they complain of the unfairness of their fates, when they ought rather to blame the wickedness of their own character and their own conduct. Clearly this is what the holy prophet means: God has repaid me according to my righteousness, and according to the cleanness of my hands in his sight. With the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent. With the pure you will be pure, and with the perverse you will act perversely. (Or, as others have it: with the merciful you will be merciful.) The Greeks say much the same, in nearly the same words but more briefly: [Ἐσθλὸν γὰρ ἀνδρὶ ἐσθλὰ χρὴ ἀιδοῖ θεός]: for a good man, God must give good things in return. And [Ὁ νῦς γὰρ ἡμῶν ὁ θεὸς]: for our mind is our god. And [Ἡ θεὸς ἀνθρώπων ἀλλων]: each man's god is his own character.

units.la: Nullum numen abest, si sit prudentia.— Plura in eam sententiam apud Salustium non uno loco: ut in bello Catilinario, Non votis neque supplicis muliebribus auxilia Deorum parantur. vigilando, agendo, bene consulendo, prospere omnia cedunt. Ubi socordia tete atque ignavia tradideris, nequicquam Deos implores: irati infestique sunt. Sed eximia, præter alias, in hoc argumento præfatio Belli Jugurthini, quam adire poterunt, quibus animus. Nemo tamen vim verbi הָשְׁמַע plenius (ut ab accuratis Lexicographis exponitur) expressit, quàm fecit Plautus, his verbis;
units.tr: The satirist expressed this idea: No godhead is absent, if there is prudence. Sallust has many similar sayings in more than one place, as in the Catilinarian War: The aid of the gods is not procured by vows or by women's supplications. By watching, acting, and taking good counsel, all things turn out prosperously. Where you have given yourself over to sloth and cowardice, you implore the gods in vain: they are angry and hostile. His preface to the Jugurthine War is outstanding on this subject, apart from others, and those who are so inclined may consult it. Yet no one has expressed the force of the verb hishkil more fully (as accurate lexicographers explain it) than Plautus did, in these words:

units.la: Si quam rem accures sobriè aut frugaliter,
units.tr: If you take care of anything soberly or thriftily,

units.la: Solet illa rectè sub manus succedere:
units.tr: It is wont to go well under your hand;

units.la: Atque adepol fermè ut quisque rem accurat suam,
units.tr: And indeed, by Pollux, as each man takes care of his own affairs,

units.la: Sic ei procedit post principia denique.
units.tr: So it proceeds for him in the end, after its beginnings.

units.la: Si malus aut nequam est, malè res vertunt, quas agit:
units.tr: If he is bad or worthless, the things he does go badly;

units.la: Sin autem frugi est, eveniunt frugaliter.
units.tr: But if he is thrifty, they turn out thriftily.

units.la: Et hæc quidem ita vera sunt, ut sunt alia pleraque moralia vel civilia, quæ in actione versantur: quæ non esse catholicæ sive mathematicæ veritatis toties monet Aristoteles: sed temporibus, & locis, & personis, & aliis, ut quis rectè judicet, circumstantiis distinguenda & circumscribenda pænè innumeris. Certè omnes omnium temporum historiæ testantur, optima sæpè consilia funestos exitus habuisse; & contrà, temeritatem, perfidiam, crudelitatem, multis pro voto, non pro merito, cessisse : & hunc quidem (quod ait Satyricus) crucem pretium sceleris, alium vero diadema tulisse. Hinc Athenienfium fœlix plerunq; Συσβυλία vulgari sermone jactata, & authoris gravissimi Platonis gravis querela, Θνητῶν ἡ μηδὲνα νομοθετῶν μηδὲν, τύχας δ' ἐὶ χρέσον ἀνυνλα τὰ ἀνθρώπινα προσφυσια. Sed neq; minùs hoc divini verbi authoritate nititur, ut vix aliud quicquam testatius esse possit. Ex multis, uno aut altero loco contenti erimus. Ecclef.VII. Ista omnia vidi diebus vanitatis meæ: esse justum, qui pereat justitia sua: & esse improbum, qui prolongeat dies in malitia sua. Et ibidem paulò post: Convertens me animadvertebam sub Sole, nec velocium esse cursum, nec fortium bellum, nec sapientium panem, nec doctorum divitias, nec artificum gratiam, sed tempus casumque intervenire omnibus his. Non enim probatur illorum mihi sententia, qui Solomonem quasi ex sensu carnis hæc pronunciare volunt; cùm res ipsa luculentis aliunde Sacræ Scripturæ testimoniis confirmari possit; modò illa, יעשו ער tempus & casum, ut ἢ πνχη crebrò in veterum Ethnicorum commentationibus, pro Deo & divinâ providentiâ, quod & ratio suadet, accipiamus.
units.tr: These things are as true as are many other moral and civic matters that concern action. Aristotle often warns that such matters do not have the certainty of universal or mathematical truth, but must be distinguished and defined by times, places, persons and other circumstances, which can be almost countless, if one is to judge rightly. Certainly the histories of all ages testify that the best counsels have often had disastrous outcomes, and that rashness, treachery and cruelty have often succeeded, according to luck rather than merit; and that one man has earned the cross as the price of his crime, another the diadem. Hence the Athenians' much-repeated saying about good fortune, and the grave complaint of the weighty author Plato: Of mortal things, none of the lawgivers has anything certain, but human affairs are subject to fortune and chance [Θνητῶν ἡ μηδένα νομοθετῶν μηδὲν, τύχας δ' ἐπὶ χρέσον ἀνυλα τὰ ἀνθρώπινα προσφυσια]. Yet this rests no less on the authority of the divine word, so that nothing could be more clearly attested. From many passages we shall be content with one or two. Eccl. 7: I have seen all these things in the days of my vanity: there is a just man who perishes in his justice, and there is a wicked man who prolongs his days in his wickedness. And a little later in the same chapter: Turning myself, I observed under the sun that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the learned, nor favour to the skilful, but time and chance come to all of them. For I do not accept the opinion of those who want Solomon to be pronouncing these things from the sense of the flesh, since the matter itself can be confirmed by clear testimonies of Holy Scripture elsewhere; provided we take time and chance [עת ופגע] as fortune [ἡ τύχη], as often in the commentaries of the ancient Gentiles, and as God and divine providence, which reason also suggests.

units.la: In hanc igitur sententiam dicemus, non sine caussâ factum esse, quòd idem verbum ⊔שכ apud Hebræos & sapientem esse & prosperari significet, cùm humana (si quidem vulgi judicia perpendamus:) non aliud sit ut plurimùm sapientia,quàm bonus successus. Dion Cassius in hanc rem : Πολλὰ χὸ ἡδὴ π- νὲς ἐκ ὀρθῶς σπυχίρήσαντες λόξαν, ὅτι ὅτι- τυχεῖς αὐτῶν ἐσυονλο, δ' βιαλίας ἔχον, ἡ ἐ- λεγει δειχα πνα προγεταλόμενοι, μωείαν, ὅτι μὴ κλίτυχον αὐτῶν, ἀφελον. Quæ Plinius Secundus in quadam Epistolâ paulò latiùs ita expressit; Est omninò iniquum, sed usu receptum, quòd honesta consilia vel turpia,prout male aut prosperè cedunt, ita vel probantur,vel reprehenduntur. Inde plerunq; eadem facta modò diligentiæ, modò vanitatis ; modò libertatis, modò furoris nomen accipiunt. Tacitus in Germania de Cheruscis, populo Germaniæ, In latere Cauchorum Catterúmque, &c. Itaque,qui olim boni æquíque Cherusci, nunc inertes ac stulti vocantur. Cattis victoribus fortuna in sapientiam cessit. Hoc idem, multi alii, Græci Latinìque. Sed quia Plauti jam in superiore usi sumus observatione, etiam hîc adhibebimus. Centum (ait ille) doctùm hominum consilia hac una devincit Dea Fortuna: atque hoc verum est, perinde ut quisque eâ utitur, Ita praecellet, atque exinde sapere eum omnes dicimus. Bene ubi quod discimus consilium accidisse, hominem cautum eum Esse declaramus; stultum autem illum, cui vertit male.
units.tr: To this opinion, then, we shall say that it is not without reason that among the Hebrews the same verb [השכיל] means both to be wise and to prosper, since human judgements (if we weigh the judgements of the crowd) make wisdom for the most part nothing other than good success. Dio Cassius on this matter: many people, having acted rightly, have been thought foolish because they did not succeed, while others who acted foolishly have been thought wise because they had good luck. Pliny the Younger expressed this somewhat more fully in a certain letter: It is entirely unfair, yet customary, that honourable or shameful counsels are approved or condemned according as they turn out badly or well. Hence often the same deeds receive now the name of diligence, now of vanity; now of liberty, now of madness. Tacitus in the Germania, of the Cherusci, a people of Germany: On the flank of the Chauci and the Catti, etc. Therefore those who once were called good and just Cherusci are now called idle and foolish. For the Catti, being victorious, passed into wisdom along with their fortune. Many others, Greek and Latin, say the same. But since we have already used Plautus in the previous observation, we shall use him here too: Fortune alone, says he, overcomes the counsel of a hundred learned men; and this is true: according as each man uses her, so he excels, and then we all say he is wise. When what we learn turns out well for our counsel, we declare the man to be careful; but the man for whom it turns out badly, we call foolish.

units.la: Sed hæc tamen (ut obiter hoc interseramus:) utcunq; habeant humana sive jura, sive judicia; certum est, apud Deum unam eandémq; veri boníq; regulam esse, ad quam exigenda olim omnia facta consiliáque: ad quam etiam provocat Apostolus, I.Corinth. cap.IV. versu 5. Ut divinus Hippocrates, nunquam meâ sententiâ magis divinus, quàm cùm velut ex sacro tripode ita sancit: * ΠANTA KATA AOΓON ΠOIEONTI, MH ΓEMOMENΩN TΩN KATA AOΓON, MH METABAINEIN ΕΦ ETEPON, MENONTOΣ TOY ΔOΞANTOΣ EΞ APXHΣ. id est, Omnia secundùm RATIONEM facienti, si non succedunt omnia secundùm Rationem, minimè tamen ad alia transeundum, sed iis standum consiliis, quæ à principio placuere. Aliter quoque verti posse posteriora verba non ignoramus ; Sed eâdem tamen (ad nos quidem quod hîc attinet) manente sententiâ.
units.tr: But these things (to add them in passing) hold good, however human laws or judgements may stand. It is certain that before God there is one and the same rule of truth and goodness, by which all deeds and counsels are to be measured; to which the Apostle also appeals, 1 Cor. 4:5. So too the divine Hippocrates, never more divine in my opinion than when, as from a sacred tripod, he lays down: [ΠΑΝΤΑ ΚΑΤΑ ΛΟΓΟΝ ΠΟΙΕΟΝΤΙ, ΜΗ ΓΕΝΟΜΕΝΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΛΟΓΟΝ, ΜΗ ΜΕΤΑΒΑΙΝΕΙΝ ΕΦ' ΕΤΕΡΟΝ, ΜΕΝΟΝΤΟΣ ΤΟΥ ΔΟΞΑΝΤΟΣ ΕΞ ΑΡΧΗΣ]. That is: For one who does all things according to reason, if all things do not turn out according to reason, one must not pass over to other things, but must stand by those counsels which pleased from the beginning. We are aware that the latter words can also be translated otherwise, but the sense, as far as it concerns us here, remains the same.

units.la: τύχης ἐκ ἀπαν[λ]ᾶ κα[λ]ὰ λόγον. Sed quò ? illud referamus ? an ἔδλον vel τέχνην subaudienda? Suspicor Synesium ὦ Λήρ; (non τλὼ) scripsisse; quod verbum est poeticum, qualia apud Platonem plurima.
units.tr: ...nothing beautifully and according to reason [ἐκ ἀπαν(λ)ᾶ καλὰ λόγον]. But to what should we refer this? Should we supply "ship" or "art"? I suspect that Synesius wrote "O Leros!" (not "I endure"), which is a poetic word, of the kind found in Plato in great abundance.

units.la: Cæterum, ut in priore illâ ἄπλοῦς (ita enim vocant Græci) ex diversâ vocis Hebraicæ significatione magnum pondus ad excitandos animos ad studia prudentiæ, cui tantum & divinæ tribuunt & humanæ literæ: ita in posteriore hâc, non minùs ad deterrendam superbiam,& nimiam suî fiduciam, (fatalem ferè præstantissimorum ingeniorum labem :) cùm ita nobiscum identidem reputabimus, nullam esse tantam humanorum consiliorum firmitatem & præstantiam, quæ non subitò quasi de cœlo tangi,& inimico sidere afflari possit; nullam tantam prudentiæ & sapientiæ inter homines opinionem, multorum quamvis annorum perpetuis successibus partam, quæ non horæ momento in temeritatis (ut humana sunt judicia) & stultitiæ invidiam vertere comparata sit: quam quidem πανσύο- φεγσύνλω; vel, ut Plato nuncupat, σωφεγσύνλω, qui arcem statuunt humanarum virtutum, non malè mihi judicare videntur. Sed hoc obiter.
units.tr: Now, just as in that earlier point, the simple (for so the Greeks call it), the different meaning of the Hebrew word carries great weight in stirring minds to the pursuit of prudence, which both divine and human letters ascribe so much to. So in this later point, the lesson is no less useful for restraining pride and excessive self-confidence, which is almost a fatal fall for the most outstanding minds. When we repeatedly consider with ourselves that no human plan is so firm and excellent that it cannot suddenly be touched, as if from heaven, and breathed upon by a hostile star; and that no reputation for prudence and wisdom among men, won by the constant successes of many years, is so great that it cannot in an hour be turned, as human judgments go, into the charge of rashness and folly. Those who set up as the citadel of human virtues all-wisdom [πανσοφίαν], or, as Plato calls it, sophrosyne [σωφροσύνην], seem to me to judge rightly. But this is by the way.

units.la: Ad hoc igitur instar multa possunt expendi in linguâ Hebraicâ non inutili- ter. In hâc autem linguâ, quamvis similia suppeditent & aliæ, tantò magis, quantò major, ut jam diximus, est ἡ ὀνομαστικὴ authoritas. Et sunt ingenia, quæ talibus citiùs capiantur, in quibus aliqua inest subtilitatis species, quàm solidiore doctrinâ, quæ vel ex vetere philosophiâ, vel ipsis sacris literis peti potest. Horum quoque rationem haberi nihil vetat, modò tamen modus adhibeatur, & ad meram μαλακολογίαν & περιλογίαν res non procedat.
units.tr: With this in mind, many things can be weighed usefully in the Hebrew language. In this language, though other languages offer similar things, the authority of the onomastic [ἡ ὀνομαστικὴ] art is all the greater, as we have said, to the degree that it is greater. And there are minds that are more quickly caught by such things, in which there is some appearance of subtlety, than by more solid learning, which may be sought either from ancient philosophy or from the sacred letters themselves. Nothing forbids that these too be taken into account, provided only that a measure is kept and the matter does not descend into mere soft talk [μαλακολογίαν] and empty chatter [περιλογίαν].

units.la: Mirum quàm transversos; viros alio‑ quin etiam graves & doctos, egerit ni‑ mius amor & immodicum studium. Nam quis credat, homines non illite‑ ratos, & mentis compotes esse repertos, qui Cabalistarum, non <bl>πάγνια</bl> di‑ cam, sed mera deliria & portenta; homi‑num seu naturæ vitio, seu superstitio‑ ne fatuorum ac cæcorum inventa, pro magnis mysteriis, nec illotis manibus tractandis ostentarent? Qui omnes sci‑ entias ac disciplinas, humaniores & sa‑ cras, & quicquid tot libris, tanto stu‑ dio aliunde petitur, ex Alphabeto, si Diis placet, Hebraico; aut certè ex lin‑ guâ Hebraicâ peti posse, impensâ con‑ tendunt & aliis persuadere conantur operâ? Mihi quidem minùs mirum, id unum aliquem, doctum alioquin gra‑ vémque, sibi persuasisse, qui mentis hu‑ manæ fragilitatem, & impotentis amo‑ ris quàm mirabiles effectus interdum sint, non uno documento comperi. Sed ægrorum & male-sanorum somnia à so‑ briis & vigilantibus magni fieri, tantò major, ut mihi quidem videtur, & in‑ tolerabiliior insania est. Sed parum est, ista hominibus nàtis contigisse, nisi eâdem operâ in linguæ Sanctæ injuriam & contumeliam ista hominum deliria redundarent. Talibus enim (quæ parùm à Magicis præstigiis distant:) haud pauci merito offensi, si non in ipsam linguam culpam omnem conferunt, certè ab ejus studio, ne & ipsi tales evadant, haud illibenter abstinent.
units.tr: It is remarkable how far excessive love and immoderate zeal have driven even otherwise serious and learned men astray. For who would believe that men not uneducated, and sound of mind, have been found who display, as great mysteries that must not be handled with unwashed hands, the inventions of the Cabalists, not to say tricks [πάγνια], but pure delusions and monstrosities, things devised either through the defect of men's nature or the superstition of fools and the blind? Who, at great expense of effort, contend, and try to persuade others, that all sciences and disciplines, the more humane and the sacred, and whatever is sought elsewhere in so many books with such great zeal, can be drawn from the Hebrew alphabet, if you please, or at least from the Hebrew language. For my part, it is less surprising to me that one man, otherwise learned and serious, should have persuaded himself of this. I have found, in more than one instance, how frail the human mind is and how wonderful are the effects that an uncontrolled love can sometimes produce. But that the dreams of the sick and the mad should be held in high regard by sober and waking men is, as it seems to me, an even greater and more intolerable insanity. Yet it is a small matter that these things have happened to men, unless these delusions of men also rebound, by the same effort, to the injury and insult of the holy language. For to such things, which differ little from magical juggling, not a few are rightly offended; and if they do not lay all the blame on the language itself, they at least, lest they become such men themselves, abstain from its study not unwillingly.

units.la: Herbarum viribus quantum tribuerit medicorum Deus Hippocrates, ex ipsius, quæ extant hodieque scriptis, cuivis liquere poterit. Post illum multi hoc studium excoluerunt, &, ut fit, quædam, quæ Hippocratis ætate comperta non erant, in lucem protraxerunt, ex quibus naturæ vis, & naturæ opificis Dei sapientia cum potentia conjuncta tanto magis nosceretur. At postquam inventi sunt inter Romanos, qui herbarum vi cœlo lunam deduci; Solis & Lunæ defectus; imbres, grandines, serenitatem, tempestates induci; exercitus fugari, mortuos in vitam revocari; & nihil non illis effici tuerentur; jamque in fabulas ineptissimas, & multiplicem superstitionem versa esset utilissima scientia; extitit subitò quidam Asclepiades, Pompeii magni ætate, qui pertæsus Oratoriæ professionis, huc totum se convertit, & inducta nova medendi ratione, omnem usum herbarum, non minùs naturalem quàm magicum, penitùs sustulit & abrogavit. Super omnia, ait Plinius, adjuvere eum Magicæ vanitates, in tantum evectæ, ut abrogare herbis fidem cunctis possent. Hoc dicit Plinius, magicam illam virtutem, quam homines vani & impostores herbis falsò tribuebant, præcipuè in causâ fuisse, quòd nova Asclepiadis medicina, quæ nullum herbarum in medicinâ usum agnoscebat, tam facilè recepta sit. Id ita in multis aliis contigisse certum est, ut nimius amor, aut nimiæ laudes plus obfuerint, quàm professa potuissent odia & vituperia.
units.tr: How much God gave to the healing power of herbs through Hippocrates, the physician, may be clear to anyone from his writings, which survive to this day. After him many cultivated this study and, as happens, brought to light certain things that were not known in Hippocrates' time, from which the power of nature and the wisdom of God, the Maker of nature, joined with power, might be better known. But after there were found among the Romans men who maintained that by the power of herbs the moon could be drawn down from heaven, that eclipses of sun and moon, rains, hail, fair weather and storms could be brought on, armies put to flight, the dead recalled to life, and that nothing could not be accomplished by them; and when that most useful science had already been turned into the most absurd fables and manifold superstition, there suddenly arose, in the time of Pompey the Great, a certain Asclepiades, who, weary of the profession of oratory, turned himself wholly to this, and, introducing a new method of healing, utterly removed and abolished all use of herbs, no less natural than magical. Above all things, says Pliny, the vanities of magic helped him, having risen to such a pitch that they could take away all faith in herbs. Pliny says that the magical power, which vain men and impostors falsely attributed to herbs, was chiefly the cause why the new medicine of Asclepiades, which acknowledged no use of herbs in medicine, was so easily accepted. It is certain that this has happened in many other things, so that excessive love or excessive praise has done more harm than declared hatred and blame could have done.

units.la: Nam quod ita colligunt nonnulli, cujus Deus author ipse sit linguæ, non posse, quin magnæ sint ejus præ cæteris prærogativæ; modò prærogativas intelligant, quæ sint linguarum propriæ, haud gravatim concedemus: sin ad alia, quæ alterius sunt generis, extendant; respondemus, Deum λόγως & ἀνθρώπων authorem, etiam linguis suas metas posuisse: ut illi frustra sint, & in
units.tr: As for what some infer, that since God himself is the author of the language, it cannot be but that its prerogatives are great above others: provided they understand by prerogatives those that are proper to languages, we shall concede this without hesitation. But if they extend them to other matters, which belong to another kind, we reply that God, the author of words and of men [λόγων καὶ ἀνθρώπων], also set limits to languages, so that those who seek them there are in vain, and...

units.la: Deum ordinis authorem injurii, qui, quod linguarum non est proprium, à linguis petendum sanciunt. Fuit & terra, quam Dei populus incoluit, non uno sancta nomine: quam etiam Deus ipse suo non semel encomio nobilitare dignatus est.Scimus tamen fuisse etiam alias fertilitate non minùs celebres, & multarum rerum, quibus illa caruerit, eximiarum feraces. Quòd si noluit Deus,ut una omnia, quamvis alioquin una sanctitatis ornata titulo, & quasi privilegio, terra ferret: quæ rationis aut veri similitudo, in tanto sacræ ipsius Scripturæ silentio, & ipsâ quasi reclamante naturâ rerum, nos inducat, ut ǵredamus, Deum scientiarum & doctrinarum, quibus vel humanæ regantur actiones, vel naturæ secreta pandantur, quasi facultates & semina, verbis Hebraicis & literarum apicibus indidisse? Quòd si lingua Hebraica, aut verò Alphabeti Hebraici literæ, quòd ab uno sint immediatè Deo, ideò ad omnia debent sufficere, quantò magis ad singulos Sacræ & Θεοπνεύστε Scripturæ libros id transferamus, multum eorum dignitati detrahere, qui neget singulos, saltem quæ ad salutem nostram necessaria sunt, omnia continere? Hoc alius posteà, ad singulos fortasse, quo miraculum crescat scilicet, & cum miraculo reverentia, versiculos transferat: parùm interim solicitus, quid alii, pari libertate, de Deo judicaturi sint, qui, cùm tam pauca sufficerent, tam multa esse voluerit. Cæterùm, non in mediorum, aut paucitate, aut varietate, Dei gloria consistit: sed in eo, ut, quemadmodum ipsam vitæ usuram, ita quæcunque, quibus hæc vita sustentatur, ornatur, fovetur, accepimus; bonorum omnium Deo authori in solidum adscribamus; neque dubitamus, qui phrygionicæ artis & polymitariæ, aliarúmque id genus, Exodi capite XXXV. & agriculturæ, quæque ad agriculturam pertinent, arcanorum, Esaiæ c. XXVIII. vers. 23. & sequentibus, sibi vindicet inventionem; quin idem aliis cujuscunq; nationis aut linguæ ingenium suffecerit, quo artes & disciplinas vitæ utiles invenirent, aut inventas expolirent: ut ad linguæ Hebraicæ sanctitatem minimè opus sit recurrere, ut de Deo authore & inventore gloriemur.
units.tr: ...they wrong God, the author of order, who lay down as belonging to languages what is not proper to languages. The land which God's people inhabited was also holy by more than one name, and God himself deigned to ennoble it with his praise more than once. Yet we know there were other lands no less famous for fertility, and fruitful in many excellent things which that land lacked. But if God did not wish that one land should bear everything, although it was otherwise adorned with the single title and, as it were, privilege of holiness, what reason or likelihood, in so great a silence of Holy Scripture itself, and with nature of things seeming to protest, should lead us to believe that God placed the sciences and doctrines, by which human actions are either governed or the secrets of nature laid open, in the Hebrew words and the shapes of the letters, as faculties and seeds? But if the Hebrew language, or indeed the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, because they come immediately from the one God, must therefore suffice for everything, how much more must we transfer this to the individual books of the sacred and divinely inspired Scripture, and so diminish the dignity of those who deny that each of them, at least what is necessary for our salvation, contains everything. Let another afterwards, perhaps, draw out single verses, so that the wonder may grow, and with the wonder reverence; meanwhile caring little what others, with equal freedom, will judge about God, who, when so few things would suffice, wished so many to exist. Moreover, the glory of God does not consist in the paucity or the variety of means, but in this: that, just as we have received the very use of life, so we ascribe wholly to God, the author of all good things, whatever sustains, adorns and cherishes this life. Nor do we doubt that he who claims for himself the invention of embroidery and weaving, and the other such arts, of Exodus chapter 35, and of agriculture and the secrets pertaining to it, of Isaiah chapter 28, verse 23 and following, could also, to others of any nation or language, supply a genius by which they might find or refine the arts and disciplines useful to life. So there is no need to have recourse to the holiness of the Hebrew language in order to glory in God as author and inventor.

units.la: SOLET à multis, inter Hebrææ linguæ laudes, & Rabbinicorum librorum utilitas commemorari: ad quos, per hanc linguam, & diligentè S.Scripturæ lectionem, non admodum difficilis aut operosus est aditus; iis præcipuè præsidiis munitis, quæ tum aliorû, tum præcipuè Buxtorfiorum laudatissima nobis opera paravit. Multa sanè in hoc eruditionis genere à viris præstantissimis esse præstita, ex quibus auctior intelligentia Sacræ Scripturæ facta est, & multa feliciter illustrata, quæ densissimis obruta tenebris erant, nemo æquus rerum æstimator negaverit; de quo multorum extant commentationes, qui & argumentis & exemplis plurimis ita rem habere docent. Cùm tamen ita fateantur omnes, & res ipsa probet, vastam molem impurissimi sterquilinii vertendam esse, ut aliquæ auri micæ legantur, quæ ex aliis literis longè minore & laboris & temporis dispendio colligi possint: nisi quis ingenii proprii ductum potiùs (cujus magnam quisque in instituendis studiis rationem habere debet,) quàm rationis & judicii sequatur; aut magnis opportunitatibus invitetur, an tanti fit opera, nescio. Nam qui se totos ad hoc studium applicârunt, ut abditissima quæq; rimarentur, & viam aliis facilitarent, quin illi vel meritissimis de republicâ literariâ, & sacris speciatim literis, viris accensendi sint, nemo sanus & æquus dubitat. Nec de summis illis ingeniis, quibus, raro fœlicitatis exemplo, in pluribus excellere & aliis prodesse datum est, nobis hic sermo. Alii, qui stultâ persuasione & ambitione inducti, quasi ad fastigium eruditionis pervenissent, quicunque Rabbinica, quantum ad ostentationem sufficiât, delibârunt, hoc studium avidè arripiunt, neglectis interim (quòd in medio positi sint) aut strictim & saltuatim inspectis, ex quorum assiduâ lectione solida pendet eruditio, Græcis Latinisq; scriptoribus; horum si minor esset numerus, nostra hæc nihil, opinor, Respublica detrimenti caperet. De quo plura fortasse, ubi de linguæ Græcæ præstantiâ tractabimus. Hic interim viros doctos, & in his studiis versatos libenter conveniam, majorem aliquanto otii fui & lectorum suorum patientiæ rationem ut habeant, quàm multorum hodiè mos est. Ita enim multi quicquid Hebraicè scriptum est, sine ullo delectu aut discrimine, studiosè conquirunt, & lectoribus suis pro bona & vendibili merce obtrudunt, quasi satis hoc cuicuimodi scripto conciliaret authoritatis, quòd Hebraicè scriptum sit: cùm tamen certum sit, multa istius generis & linguæ scripta extare, quæ ab hominibus idiotis, circulatoribus, & agyrtis, nullâ vel levissimâ melioris alicujus literaturæ tinctura imbutis, profecta sunt: quorum nugæ næniaq; cur à quoquam alio loco sint habendæ, quàm quæ quotidiè in triviis ab otiosis balatronibus & pannuciis mulierculis garriuntur aut cantillantur. causam nullam video.
units.tr: It is often commemorated, among the praises of the Hebrew language, that the rabbinical books are useful. Through this language, and a diligent reading of Holy Scripture, access to them is not very difficult or laborious, especially when one is equipped with those aids which the most praiseworthy labours of others, and especially of the Buxtorfs, have prepared for us. Certainly no fair judge of things will deny that in this kind of learning many things have been accomplished by most excellent men, from which a fuller understanding of Holy Scripture has been gained, and many things have been happily illuminated which were overwhelmed by very dense darkness. Many commentaries exist on this matter, by men who teach, with many arguments and examples, that this is so. Yet since all admit this, and the thing itself proves that an immense heap of the foulest dung must be turned over so that a few specks of gold may be gathered, which could be collected from other writings with far less expense of labour and time, I do not know whether it is worth the effort, unless someone is led by the bent of his own talent (which everyone ought to take great account of in planning his studies) rather than by reason and judgment, or is invited by great opportunities. For that those who devoted themselves wholly to this study, to probe the most hidden things and make the way easier for others, should be counted among the most deserving men of the literary commonwealth, and especially of the sacred letters, no sane and fair person doubts.
