Nor is our discussion here concerned with those highest geniuses, to whom it has been granted, by a rare example of good fortune, to excel in many things and to benefit others. Others, led by foolish conviction and ambition, as if they had reached the summit of learning, whoever have tasted the rabbinical writings so far as suffices for display, eagerly seize upon this study, while neglecting, since they stand in the middle, or glancing at only superficially and in passing, the Greek and Latin writers, from whose constant reading solid learning depends. If the number of these were smaller, I think this our commonwealth would suffer no harm. Perhaps more on this when we treat of the excellence of the Greek language. For now, I would gladly address learned men, versed in these studies, that they take somewhat more account of leisure and of the patience of their readers than is the custom of many today. For many now eagerly seek out, without any selection or discrimination, whatever is written in Hebrew, and foist it on their readers as good and saleable wares, as if it were enough to win authority for any sort of writing that it is in Hebrew. Yet it is certain that there exist many writings of this kind and language which have come from ignorant men, mountebanks and quacks, imbued with no slightest tincture of better literature. Why their trifles and lullabies should be held in any other place than that where idle babblers in the streets and ragged old women chatter or sing them every day, I see no reason.

units.la: At illud majoris aliquanto momenti, eò processisse studium doctorum quorundam, ut importunâ Thalmudicorum locorum & testium citatione, clarissima quædam de Christo testimonia convellere sint aggressi. Observatum non uni, si bene memini, solitos Judæos veteres dicere, Mundum Messiæ causâ creatum esse. Hoc arripit vir sine controversiâ Maximus, & de republica literariâ inter paucos meritus, sed in Christi causâ, nescio quo fato ad Socinianos in devexâ aetate propensior; hoc ille, inquam, studiosè arripit, ut de mundo per Christum creato clarissima alioquin testimonia nobis eripiat. Ait igitur Apostolus, Christum hæredem omnium à Deo constitutum esse, Δι' ὃν τὺς αἰῶνας ἐποίησε. Vult ille, Δι' ὃν valere, Δι' ὃν; non, per quem, sed propter quem. Ideo autem, inquit ille, hæc interpretatio hoc loco maximè se probat, quia ad Hebræos scribens videtur respicere ad vetus dictum Hebræorum; propter Messiam conditum esse Mundum. Rursus idem Apostolus Psalmistæ verba, Σὺ κατ' ἀρχὰς, Κύριε, τὴν γῆν ἐθεμελίωσας, καὶ ἔργα τῶν χειρῶν σού εἰσιν οἱ οὐρανοί; (quo quid clarius aut illustrius à quoquam dici poterit, aut fingi?) Christo aptat. At hic quoque, Quia constabat, inquit, inter Hebræos, Mundum hunc Messiæ causâ conditum esse: (quid, quaeso?) ideo τὴν γῆν ἐθεμελίωσας, id est, causa fuisti, cur fundaretur: &, opus manuum tuarum; id est, propter te factum: nam לְמַעַן Hebraicè & Chaldaicè etiam Propter significat: &c. Hujus generis plura, apud eundem. Sed hæc fortasse, dicet aliquis, ex nimio potiùs erga partes illas, quibus addictiorem fuisse modò dicebamus, studio profecta esse; quàm ex ullâ tali κακοζηλία, de quâ nobis hîc sermo.
units.tr: Yet a matter of somewhat greater weight is that the zeal of certain learned men has gone so far that, by an importunate citation of Talmudic passages and witnesses, they have set out to overturn some of the clearest testimonies to Christ. It has been observed, if I remember rightly, by more than one writer, that the ancient Jews used to say that the world was created for the sake of the Messiah. A man of undoubted eminence, who has deserved well of the republic of letters, but who in the cause of Christ has, by some unlucky fate, leaned rather towards the Socinians in his declining years, seizes eagerly upon this saying, so that he may snatch from us those otherwise very clear testimonies that the world was created through Christ. The Apostle says that God appointed Christ heir of all things, Δι' ὃν τὺς αἰῶνας ἐποίησε [di' hon tous aiōnas epoiēse, through whom he made the worlds]. He wants Δι' ὃν to mean Δι' ὃν not through whom but on account of whom. The reason, he says, why this interpretation commends itself most strongly in this place is that the writer to the Hebrews seems to have in mind the old saying of the Hebrews, that the world was made on account of the Messiah. Again, the same Apostle applies to Christ the words of the Psalmist, Σὺ κατ' ἀρχὰς, Κύριε, τὴν γῆν ἐθεμελίωσας, καὶ ἔργα τῶν χειρῶν σού εἰσιν οἱ οὐρανοί [Sy kat' archas, Kyrie, tēn gēn ethemeliōsas, kai erga tōn cheirōn sou eisin hoi ouranoi, Lord, in the beginning thou didst lay the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the work of thy hands]. (What could be said or invented more clearly or more illustriously than this?) But here too, he says, since it was established among the Hebrews that this world was made for the sake of the Messiah (what, I ask, then?), therefore τὴν γῆν ἐθεμελίωσας means thou wast the cause why it was founded; and the work of thy hands means made on your account, for לְמַעַן [lemaʿan] in Hebrew and in Chaldee also means on account of. And so on; there are many more of this kind in the same author. But someone will say that these things perhaps proceed rather from an excessive zeal for that party to which, as we just said, he has leaned rather too much, and not from any such κακοζηλία [kakozēlia, perverse zeal], which is our present subject.

units.la: Ifaiæ capite I. versu 18. Venite jam, & disceptemus, dicit Dominus; Si fuerint peccata vestra, ut coccinum; quasi nix, dealbabuntur: & si fuerint rubra, quasi vermiculus, velut lana alba erunt. Quis dubitet, quin elegantissimè Propheta & ex notissimâ ratione peccatis & sceleribus in genere rubrum colorem tribuerit, cùm natura colorem illum (nisi quis ἀποφευγμένον, aut, Apostoli φεύγει, κατακληρονομίαν ? συνείδησιν, occalluerit) saucię conscientię indicium esse voluerit? cùm præterea de sanguinolentis hîc speciatim legatur (quorum manus sanguine plena, versu 16.) quibus iste color peculiari quoque ratione convenit. Jam hoc multis linguis commune est, ut intensioris tinsturæ similitudine tum vitia tum virtutes exaggerentur, unde Græcis ἁλουργὸς βαφή, & id genus alia, de quibus, tum alii, tum b. m. parens ad Persiam non uno loco. Nivei autem coloris imagine, (cum
units.tr: Isaiah 1:18: "Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as white as wool." Who could doubt that the Prophet most elegantly gave red colour to sins and crimes in general, for a well-known reason? Nature has wished that colour to be a sign of a wounded conscience, unless someone has grown callous and seared in conscience [κεκαυστηριασμένην συνείδησιν], as the Apostle puts it. Moreover, the passage speaks specifically of bloodstained people ("whose hands are full of blood," verse 15), to whom this colour belongs for a special reason. Now it is common to many languages that both vices and virtues are magnified by the likeness of a more intense dye. Hence the Greeks have "purple dye" [ἁλουργὸς βαφή] and other such expressions, on which both others and my late father have written in more than one place in his work on Persia. But the image of snowy whiteness (with which, in these passages, learned men note that woolly whiteness is to be compared) does not language use it to signify simplicity of mind and innocence of manners? Hence candour, snowy morals, and many other such expressions, commonly known and used.

units.la: s (cum quo certare, in istis locis, albedine laneum notant hîc viri doêti: ) quæ non utitur lingua ad simplicitatem animi & innocentiam morum indicandam? Hinc candor, nivei mores, & id genus alia plurima, vulgò nota & usurpata. In his igitur omnibus cùm nihil à communi usu alienum fit, sed omnia vulgari sermone tritiffima: sunt tamen viri infigniter doêti qui ad traditiones Thalmudicas, (quarum certitudo ab eorum fide tota pendet, qui tot mendaciis & fabulis passim scatent,) de particulâ nescio quâ coccineâ inter cornua hirci emissarii, &c. appendi solitâ, nos ablegant, & inde sensum verborum Ifaiæ petere jubent; quæ qui aliter, quàm ex Thalmude, interpretentur, cæcos eos (hîc quidem certè) valde ἀπλῶς pronuntiant.
units.tr: In all these matters, then, nothing is foreign to ordinary usage; all are very common in everyday speech. Yet some men of outstanding learning send us away to the Talmudic traditions, whose certainty depends wholly on the trustworthiness of those writers who everywhere abound in lies and fables, to a little scarlet thread, I know not what, usually tied between the horns of the scapegoat, and so on. They bid us seek from there the sense of Isaiah's words. And they pronounce those who interpret otherwise than from the Talmud to be blind, very plainly (at least here).

units.la: Jam Christus in ultimâ coenâ, poculo discipulis porrecto, ita eos affatur; λέγω δὲ ὑμῖν, ὅτι ἐκ μὴ πίω ἀπ' ἄρτι ἐν τῇ γεννήματος τῆς ἀμπέλου, ἕως τῆς ἡμέρας ἐκείνης, ὅταν αὐτὸ πίω μεθ' ὑμῶν καινὸν ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τοῦ πατρός. Hîc primò certum est, Christo præcipuè propositum fuisse, ut de morte suâ propinquâ suos commonefaceret, cùm multùm (ad faciendam Divinitatis suæ fidem) nihil sibi accidisse, quod non prædixisset, discipulorum suorum interesse intelligeret. Cæterùm, ut ex re natâ & præsente prædicendæ mortis; ita, ex verbis, quibus mortem prædicit, occasionem sumit consolandi discipulos, venustâ & non insolente in Sacris Scripturis ἀντλαναλάσεις, ἀπὸ τ ὀρεξλῶν, ad τα ἀόεξλα ἡ ῥοτλα, converså verborum notione. Qui igitur alibi panis; qui aquæ,pro re natâ, scaturientis usus erat similitudine, ad regni cœlestis seu præsentes seu futuras opes & delicias exprimendas: qui obedientiam alio loco, cibi quotidiani appellatione signaverat: idem nunc cœlestia illa gaudia, quibus sanctæ, vel in hâc vitâ adspergunt & sustentantur animæ; vel olim pleno hausto perfruuntur; vini cujusdam præstantioris, quod beati potaturi sint, adumbrat similitudine. Vini autem proprium esse, ut cor hominis lætificet, & humanæ testantur literæ, & divinæ. Huc etiam pertinent & ista Lucæ XXII. v. 29, 30. Κάγω διατίθεμαί υμῖν, καθὼς διέθετό μοι ὁ πατὴρ μου, βασιλείαν· ἵνα ἐσθίητε ἡ
units.tr: Now at the last supper, when the cup was handed to the disciples, Christ addressed them thus: "But I say unto you, I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father" [λέγω δὲ ὑμῖν, οὐ μὴ πίω ἀπ' ἄρτι ἐκ τούτου τοῦ γεννήματος τῆς ἀμπέλου, ἕως τῆς ἡμέρας ἐκείνης ὅταν αὐτὸ πίνω μεθ' ὑμῶν καινὸν ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τοῦ πατρός μου]. Here, first, it is certain that Christ's chief purpose was to remind his people of his approaching death, since he understood that it mattered to his disciples that, to establish faith in his divinity, nothing had happened to him which he had not foretold. But just as he took the occasion of foretelling his death from the present situation, so from the words in which he foretold it he takes occasion to comfort the disciples, by a graceful figure, not unusual in Holy Scripture, in which the meaning of words is reversed, passing from the things of earth to the things of heaven. Thus, he who elsewhere expressed by "bread" and "water", as the occasion suggested, the image of a flowing spring, to signify the present or future riches and delights of the heavenly kingdom, and who had signified obedience elsewhere by the name of daily food, now likewise shadows those heavenly joys, by which holy souls are refreshed and sustained in this life, or afterwards enjoy in full draught, by the likeness of a more excellent wine, which the blessed are to drink. Human and divine letters both testify that it is the proper nature of wine to gladden the heart. To this also belong those words of Luke 22:29-30: "And I appoint unto you a kingdom, as my Father hath appointed unto me; that ye may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom" [Κάγω διατίθεμαί υμῖν, καθὼς διέθετό μοι ὁ πατὴρ μου, βασιλείαν· ἵνα ἐσθίητε καὶ πίνητε ἐπὶ τῆς τραπέζης μου ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ μου].

units.la: {y} ἡ ὁ πίνηλε ὅπ τῆς τεχνίζης μα, ἐν τῇ βασι-λεία μα.
units.tr: ἵνα ἐσθίητε καὶ πίνητε ἐπὶ τῆς τραπέζης μου ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ μου [that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom].

units.la: Quàm verò à communi usu non abhorreat, ut cœlestia gaudia cibi potúve vario apparatu significentur, vel ex Homero discamus, qui cùm alibi ( ut Plutarchus, Porphyrius, aliíque veteres observant ) Diis suis immortalitatem eo potissimùm afferat argumento, quòd ὲ αἴτην ἐδ ὤσ', ὲ πίνως ἀλθοπα ὄιvoν: idem ta-men eosdem Deos convivia inter fe agitantes frequenter nobis exhibet. unde & Divorum epulas, apud Latinos; & Ἀμβροσίας, apud Græcos pro ἀθανασία five immortalitate poni interdum, doctiffimi viri rectè docuerunt. Hoc sufficere poterat: sed animadvertenda præterea in Christi verbis vox χαυὸν, quâ non de communi usitatóque vino agere fe satis aperte indicat: cujus vim vocis ὑπαλι-χωλάτης doctissimus Camero diligentius hîc expendit & explicat. Quid igitur opus, ad Judæorum fabulas de uvis à creatione mundi fervatis, quas qui manducaverint, vitam eos æternam possessuros traditum fit in ipsorum Onirocriticis: Quid, inquam, opus, ad istas somniantium fabulas recurrere, ut
units.tr: How far this is from ordinary usage, that heavenly joys should be signified by the varied preparation of food and drink, we may learn even from Homer, who, while elsewhere (as Plutarch, Porphyry and other ancient writers observe) he grounds the immortality of his gods chiefly on this argument, that they neither eat bread nor drink dark wine [ou gar esthiousin artov, oute pinousin aithopa oinon], nevertheless frequently shows us these same gods holding banquets among themselves. Whence learned men have rightly taught that among the Latins the feasts of the gods, and among the Greeks ambrosia, are sometimes put for immortality. This might have sufficed; but there is also to be noted in Christ's words the word οἶνον [oinon, wine], by which he sufficiently indicates that he is not speaking of common and ordinary wine; the force of this word the most learned Camerarius examines and explains more carefully here. What need, then, is there to resort to the Jewish fables of grapes preserved from the creation of the world, of which it is handed down in their Onirocritica that whoever eats them will possess eternal life? What need, I say, is there to recur to these fables of dreamers, so that we should say that Christ alluded to those grapes?

units.la: ꝰ ut ad istas uvas à Christo dicamus alusum? Mihi sanè non videtur: quod tamen quia viris quibusdam maximis aliter placuisse video, liberum per me Lectori fit, ut, quod ipse maluerit, amplectatur: cùm nec alio fine hæc à me proferantur; non nullâ sanè viris maximis contradicendi libidine; sed ut cautiores sint, qui talia legunt, nec omnia, magnis illecti nominibus, fine delectu aut judicio adhibito amplectantur. Sed & illud observatione dignissimum, quod harum literarum peritissimis monitum est, haud pauca reperiri in veterum Judæorum scriptis, quæ ex verbis & historiis Evangelicis detorta & depravata esse res ipsa fidem faciat. A primis autem illis, qui quondam ad Chriftum, sed non plenè, conversi, ad χωρισμός opiniones & superstitiones redierunt, (sic tamen, ut aliquid ex priftino Christianismo, quo suorum commenta incrustarent & auctiora facerent, retinerent;) Judæis esse profecta talia, iidem illi viri doctissimi, rectè censuerunt: quale quid cùm veteribus quoque paganis contigisse, (de quo alibi pluribus) observaverimus; non est, quod in Judæis tantò propioribus miremur. Sed de doctrinâ Thalmudicâ quid in genere censendum sit, & quibus ea cautionibus amplectenda, consulant studiosi profundæ simul erudi-tionis & judicii virum, Johannem Seldenum, in opere eximio De Jure naturali Hebræorum,&c. cujus nos judicio libenter submittimus.
units.tr: To me it certainly does not seem so; yet since I see that this has pleased some very great men otherwise, let the reader be free to embrace whichever he himself prefers. I put these things forward for no other purpose, and not without some desire to contradict very great men; but so that those who read such things may be more cautious, and not, drawn in by great names, embrace everything without selection or judgement. But this also is most worthy of notice, which those most skilled in these writings have warned us of: that not a few things are found in the writings of the ancient Jews which the very facts make it plain were twisted and corrupted from the words and histories of the Gospel. Those learned men rightly judged that such things came from the Jews, from those first men who, once converted to Christ, though not fully, returned to separatist opinions and superstitions (yet in such a way that they kept some of their former Christianity, with which they might encrust and enlarge their inventions). It is not surprising if such things happened even among the Jews, who were so much nearer to Christ, since we have observed that the same happened to the ancient pagans as well, about which I shall speak at more length elsewhere. As to what should be thought in general of Talmudic teaching, and with what cautions it should be embraced, let serious students consult Johannes Selden, a man of profound learning and judgement, in his excellent work On the Natural Law of the Hebrews, etc., to whose judgement we gladly submit ourselves.

units.la: Patrum aut avorum nostrorum memoriâ rari erant, qui literas Hebraicas attingerent, quod partim difficultas (istis temporibus) nonnullorum, qui tardiores, conatus in ipso limine desti-tueret; partim verò rei insolentia alios omnia majora, quæ ignota, suspicantes terreret,& procul arceret. Nunc verò studio isto ad summam facilitatem doctorum laboribus perducto,viáque jam vel puerorum solis tritâ, non tam necessaria videtur nova, ad capessenda, exhortatio; quàm capessentibus, ut eum verecundiâ tractent & sobrietate, præmonitio. Satis Hebraicæ linguæ consulit,quisquis illi suam antiquitatem & sanctitatem asserit;neque puto,unquam tam malè cum gente Christianâ agetur, ut non summa ejus linguæ utilitas & & dignitas inter Christianos agnoscatur, quâ potissimùm Deus sacræ suæ voluntatis arcana, quibus ad cœlos aditus hominibus pateret, consignare dignatus est. Cæterùm in tanto, quantus nunc ubique est, Hebraizantium numero, dum pro suo quisque studio nova, quibus studium hoc provehat ac commendet, argumenta excogitat, haud pauca interdum etiam à doctis asseruntur, quæ si ad obrussam veritatis exigantur; ad ostentandum potiùs ingenium excogitata merito videantur, quàm augendam apud graves & solidi judicii viros hujus linguæ æstimationem.
units.tr: In the memory of our fathers and grandfathers, few people took up Hebrew letters. For some slower learners, the difficulty of those times discouraged their efforts at the very threshold, and for others the strangeness of the subject terrified them, since they suspected that everything unknown must be greater and kept them far off. But now that this study has been brought by the labours of scholars to great ease, and the road is trodden even by boys, an exhortation to take it up no longer seems so necessary as a warning to those who take it up, that they should handle it with reverence and sobriety. Whoever asserts its antiquity and holiness does enough for the Hebrew language. Nor do I think the Christian people will ever treat it so badly that its great usefulness and dignity go unacknowledged among Christians. It was in this language that God chose above all to set down the secrets of his holy will, by which a way to heaven lies open to men. Yet in the great number of Hebraizers now found everywhere, each man devises new arguments according to his own zeal to advance and commend the study, and quite a few of these, sometimes asserted even by learned men, would, if brought to the touchstone of truth, rightly seem contrived to display wit rather than to enhance the esteem of this language among serious men of solid judgement.

units.la: Scripsit Johannes Chisletius, haud vulgaris ingenii vir, sed partibus addictissimus, Apologeticam ad linguam sanctam Paranesim, Antwerpiæ excusam Anno Domini 1642. In eâ multa de linguâ & literis Hebraicis, quæ non sunt hujus loci: sed duo præter alios Sacræ Scripturæ loci tractantur, quos dissidentes ab Hebraicis fontibus vetustissimæ quædam versiones suspectos nonnullis reddidere.
units.tr: John Chisletius, a man of no common talent but most devoted to his party, published at Antwerp in the year of the Lord 1642 his Paraenesis in defence of the holy language. In it much is said about the language and letters of Hebrew that does not belong to this place. But two passages of Holy Scripture, among others, are treated, which some very ancient versions, departing from the Hebrew sources, have made suspect to some readers.

units.la: Quod Exodi capite VI. versu 30. Est ait Moyses coram Domino, הן אנכי ערל שפתים ואין ישמע אלי פרעה quod hodie legitur apud Græcos interpretes, Ἐγὼ ὁ ἀπειτρμένος τοῖς χείλεσιν, &c. à Clemente Romano, Sancti Pauli discipulo, ita laudatur, Ἐγὼ δὲ εἰμι ἀτμὶς ἀπὸ χύτρας: Hunc enim locum haud dubiè voluit Clemens, & nugantur, qui ad Psalmum CXIX. versu 83. eum respexisse, & Mosem pro Davide errore memoriæ posuisse cōminiscuntur, cùm tam Græca, quàm Hebraica longè ab istorum verborum, de quibus quæritur hîc, absint sententiâ. Contendit Chisletius legisse Græcos, (quam etiam pro verâ ac genuinâ lectione nobis commendat) ואני עד לשפתים; totidem quidem vocibus & literis, sed aliter divisis. Ingeniosa certè conjectura, sed quam miror Chisletium cuiquam se paulò cordatiori probaturum credidisse, nisi priùs (ἔτι ἐξ ἀπὸ ἀξα) שפר vel שפתים pro χύτρα: cum verò עד pro ἀτμίς in sacrâ Scripturâ, aut saltem Rabbinis, aut ullâ linguarum, (quod hactenus mihi non observatum fateor) quæ ad Hebraicam propiùs accedit, reperiri probâsset. Præterea, propter unum Clementem, cùm nulla versionis istius Græcæ,apud ullos antiquos Patres aut alibi, extent vestigia ; confirment autem plurimæ versiones veteres Hebraicam lectionem ; cùm alii, ἀπειτμητῷ ; ἀλόξιῳ, alii ; alii, ἀκεῖζυς ; alii denique, ὁ χάραρ, verterint ; quæ omnis varietas eòdem redit : propter unum,inquam, illum Codices Hebraicos sollicitare, periculosi res exempli est, & hominis magis ingenio suo fidentis, quàm pudóri confulentis.
units.tr: The first is Exodus 6:30, where Moses says before the Lord: "Behold, I am uncircumcised in the lips, and how shall Pharaoh hear me?" [הן אנכי ערל שפתים ואין ישמע אלי פרעה]. The Greek text read today renders this "I, being uncircumcised in the lips," and so on [Ἐγὼ ὁ ἀπειτρμένος τοῖς χείλεσιν]. Clement of Rome, a disciple of St Paul, quotes it thus: "But I am a steam from a pot" [Ἐγὼ δὲ εἰμι ἀτμὶς ἀπὸ χύτρας]. Clement undoubtedly meant this passage. Those who babble that he was alluding to Psalm 119:83, and that Moses was put in place of David through a lapse of memory, talk nonsense, since neither the Greek nor the Hebrew is anywhere near the sense of the words in question here. Chisletius contends that the Greeks read (and he commends this to us as the true and genuine reading) ואני עד לשפתים: the same words and letters, indeed, but divided differently. It is an ingenious conjecture, but I am surprised that Chisletius thought it would win over anyone moderately sensible, unless he had first proved that שפר or שפתים means "pot" [χύτρα], and that עד means "steam" [ἀτμίς] in Holy Scripture, or at least among the Rabbis, or in any language closer to Hebrew. (I confess I have not observed this so far.) Moreover, the reading rests on Clement alone. No trace of this Greek version survives among any of the ancient Fathers or elsewhere, while many ancient versions confirm the Hebrew reading. Some render it "uncircumcised" [ἀπειτμήτῳ], others "stammering" [ἀλόξιῳ], others "unskilled" [ἀκεῖζυς], and others finally with an altogether different word [ὁ χάραρ]. All this variety comes to the same thing. To disturb the Hebrew codices on account of that one writer, I say, is a dangerous precedent, and the mark of a man who trusts his own wit more than he regards modesty.

units.la: Cùm autem haud pauca istius generis alia mirarum versionum & varietatum exempla apud veteres, unum plurésve, patres extantia reperiri possint ; non est, quòd adeò miremur in hanc à cæteris adeò diversam versionem unum ex antiquis, qui ad nos pervenerint, Clementem incidisse. Si conjecturæ fit locus, quid in mentem ista fcribenti venerit, Lectorem non celabo : Sciolum aliquem fortasse, nec diu in Sacrâ Scripturâ versatum, cum non intelligeret, quid ista sibi vellent, ΑΠΕ-ΠΙΤΜΗΤΟϚ ΤΟΙϚ ΧΕΙΛΕϚΙΝ, & istis verborum prodigiis (neque enim aliter judicare poterat, qui ex vulgari Helle‐nismo de illis judicaret) non parùm offenderetur, aliquid quæsivisse, quod & sententiæ non malè conveniret, & ad scripturam ipsam, quàm proximè poterat, accederet. Annon hoc tale; ΑΠΕΡ ΑΤΜΙΖ ΑΠΟ ΧΥΤΡΑΖ? Ingens, dices, in posterioribus verbis & literis discrimen. At hoc aliquid est, quod in prioribus aliquid affine: cum mutationum talium non desint exempla, ubi & sententia & scriptura consultò planè mutata. Et fortasse vetus aliquod di‐ ctum Græcum respexit author istius mutationis. Est enim ἀτμὶς proprie, vel ἀτμὸς, ἡ ἐξ ὑγρᾶ ἀνάδοσις, ut Hesy‐ chius; vel ἡ ἐκ ζεστοῦ ἀναμωμὴ, ut author Etymologici; qualis ex ollâ, igne supposito, fervente & bulliente solet ascendere. unde & verbum Anglicum, Steame, de tali vapore proprie: ex Græca haud dubiè (ut infinita alia, & propè omnia, quæ verè Anglica, ut nos alibi probamus:) origine. Sed de conjectura hâc nostrâ Lector pro suo jure & arbitrio statuet: neque de eâ quid judicii laturus sit, valdè laboro ego. Sed & Chisletio non illibenter concedse‐
units.tr: Since many other strange versions and variant readings of this kind can be found among the ancients, in one or more Fathers, we need not be so surprised that Clement, one of the ancients who have come down to us, stumbled upon this version, so very different from the rest. If there is room for conjecture about what came into his mind as he wrote, I shall not hide it from the reader. Perhaps some smatterer, not long conversant with Holy Scripture, who did not understand what the words [ΑΠΕ-ΠΙΤΜΗΤΟϚ ΤΟΙϚ ΧΕΙΛΕϚΙΝ] meant, and was not a little offended by these verbal monstrosities (for he could judge them only by ordinary Hellenism), sought something that both fitted the sense well and came as close as possible to the Scripture itself. Would it not be something like this: ΑΠΕΡ ΑΤΜΙΖ ΑΠΟ ΧΥΤΡΑΖ? You will say the difference in the latter words and letters is great. But the first words have some affinity, and examples of such changes are not lacking, where both sense and wording were deliberately altered entirely. Perhaps the author of this change had some old Greek saying in view. For ἀτμίς properly means (or ἀτμός) the exhalation from moist matter, as Hesychius says, or the vapour rising from something hot and boiling, as the author of the Etymologicum says, such as usually rises from a pot with a fire underneath it, seething and bubbling. Hence also the English word "steam," properly of such vapour, is doubtless of Greek origin, like countless other English words, and nearly all those that are truly English, as I prove elsewhere. But the reader will judge this conjecture of mine as he sees fit. As for what judgement he will pass on it, I myself am not much concerned. But I am not unwilling to grant to Chisletius

units.la: {1} Ita rim, fieri posse, ut verba Hebraica, qnemadmodum ille digerit,aliquis Hebraismi non valdè peritus legerit; & quia, quam ex illis exculperet, alia melior non suppetebat sententia, in istam versionem incidisse: facilè enim ad ἀτμίδ& & χύτεσ significationem ab audaciore, aliquo verba illa Hebraica torqueri potuerunt: eam autem veram esse & genuinam sive lectionem sive sententiam, tum alia repugnant plurima, tum loci hujus collatio cum gemino altero, cap.IV.vers,10. ut omittam, quod ex proximè sequentibus verbis peti potest argumentum, quibus magis consonum est, ut dicat se Moses, incircumcifum labiis, ἀλόγος, (facundorum enim est, persuadere:) quàm ἀτμίδα ἀπὸ χύλεσ.
units.tr: {1} that the Hebrew words, as he sets them out, may have been read by someone not very skilled in Hebrew. Since no better sense offered itself from the letters he picked out, that reader may have fallen into this version, for those Hebrew words could easily be twisted by some bolder person to the meanings "steam" and "pot." That this is the true and genuine reading or sense, however, is opposed by very many things, including the comparison of this passage with the other, at chapter 4, verse 10. I say nothing of the argument that can be drawn from the words that immediately follow, with which it agrees better that Moses says he is "uncircumcised in the lips" [ἀλόγος] (for it belongs to eloquent men to persuade) than that he is "steam from a pot" [ἀτμίδα ἀπὸ χύτρας].

units.la: Alter locus, in quo Chisletius ingenium suum experitur, sunt illa Psalmi XCVI. versu 10. יהוה מלך אף־תכון : תבל quæ Græcus, qui pervenit ad nos, interpres reddidit, Κύριος ἐβασίλευσεν, ἡ γὰρ κατάρθωσε ἡ οἰκουμένη. Latinus; Dominus regnavit: etenim correxit orbem terra. At, inquit Chisletius, constat, tum ex Justino Martyre, tum ex Augustini commentariis, olim le-ctum, ἐξασίλευσεν ἀπὸ ξύλου : Dominus regnavit à ligno. Potuit dicere, ex Tertulliano & Cyprian quoque : qui quantò Augustino anteriores, tantò ad rem magis hîc eorum testimonium. De his autem verbis, ἀπὸ ξύλου, dudum quaesivere tum alii, tum Nicolaus Fullerus Anglus, in Miscellaneis suis, integro capite ; & in tantâ similium assumentorum, integrorum etiam aliquando versiculorum, copiâ, quantam tum Fullerus, tum alii plures observârunt, poterat sufficere, quòd vir ille doctissi-mus & acutissimus super eo commentatus est. Doctissimus Junius in suis ad Tertullianum Notis conjiciebat, fieri posse, ut lippiens aliquis pro ἐξασίλευσεν, legerit ἐξ ξύλου. Ego potiùs dicerem ineptulum aliquem verbum βασιλεὺν alludere voluisse, quasi esset βασιλεύειν, aut ex eâdem, quâ ξυλεύειν seu ξυλέ-ωαι, origine. Permutari sanè interdum istas literas, ut in ἀνάξυεις pro ἀνάσυ-εις, &c. notat Eustathius alicubi : nec magnum in Scripturâ discrimen. Sed quid Chifletius? A vulgari ac tritâ versione, quam hodierna exhibent exemplaria, quámque ut receptam olim, ac vulgò notam agnoscit; ad magis occultam & Cabalisticam provocat,quam talem fuisse sibi fingit: והוה סלך אפרן הנה ... Eadem, inquies, literæ, sive הנך חבר ... sive אפרן legas: nec caret exemplo. Sed quo,quæso,exemplo Hebraica illa, ut scribit ille ... non Hebraicè, sed Græcè legenda, ἀπὸ T. & inde, ἀπὸ ξύλς? O mirificam Cabalæ vim quæ, quicquid delirant homines; quicquid sive valentes,sive ægroti; sive vigilantes, sive dormientes somniant; id omne in scientiæ secretioris arcana, in pura puta mysteria convertere poterit: ut jam nullus ferè cerebri morbus sit, qui speciosò hoc Cabalæ nomine curari aut certè tegi non possit. Hac arte nuper (ut veteres omittamus) Robertus Fludd, & Thomas Alabaster, Angli, ingentibus voluminibus editis, suam sapientiam nobis approbárunt: mira & ignota prius mysteria revelárunt; omnibus denique, solemnia desipientibus & fastidientibus; mira, inaudita per mare,per terras consectantibus, ingentes delicias & lautitias apparárunt, . At (inquit Chifletius) rei quamvis admirabilis, & tot retrò seculis inaudita, usque eò tamen jam certa exploratáque mihi videtur, ut literam ם fœlicem ac salutarem fuisse apud Hebræos, & crucis Dominicæ figuram re & formâ præstitisse, supervacuum sit hoc loco ex Ezekiele & antiquis Samaritanorum literis ostendere. Imò minimè supervacuum, quando de loco Ezekielis,qui rationibus haud levibus inducti, tum veteres, tum recentiores aliter statuant,haud pauci sint.In ipsius Prophetæ verbis nihil esse, quod nos ad istam compellat aut inducat interpretationem, modestissimi quique ex illis partibus agnoscunt. Non tamen prætereundum arbitror, ait doctissimus Sixtus Senensis, nomen Tau, tam pro extremâ litera Hebraici Alphabeti accipi, quàm pro quocunque signo, unde cùm apud Ezechielem non ipsius litera Thau sola figura ם separatim scripta sit, sed tota ipsa dictio ום, quam ferè omnes signum interpretantur; incertum sane est, an verba prophetæ vel de ipsâ litera Thau, vel de quopiam alio signo intelligenda sint. Hactenus ille. Ad Thau autem Samaritanorum quod attinet,si hodiernas eorum literas inspiciamus, quis insiciari possit,non magis illi cum figurâ crucis convenire, quàm Cani, quod in veteri verbo,cum balneo. Nullam tamen in Alphabeto Samaritano mutationem intervenisse, faciunt Origenis & Hieronymi verba, ut asseverare non audeam, Sed quando, aut quâ occasione, magnum meo judicio praestitisset Chifletjus, si nos docuisset, Scaligerum, ad quem nos docti viri rejiciunt, adibunt & consulent, quibus adeundi (quæ nobis negata nunc est,) copia.
units.tr: The other passage on which Chisletius tests his wit is Psalm 96:10: "The Lord reigns" [יהוה מלך] "... the world" [תבל], which the Greek interpreter who has come down to us rendered: "The Lord reigned; for the world was set right" [Κύριος ἐβασίλευσεν, ἡ γὰρ κατώρθωσε ἡ οἰκουμένη]. The Latin reads: "The Lord hath reigned; for the earth hath corrected the world." But, says Chisletius, it is established both from Justin Martyr and from Augustine's commentaries that the words were once read "The Lord reigned from the wood" [ἐβασίλευσεν ἀπὸ ξύλου]. He might also have cited Tertullian and Cyprian, who, being older than Augustine, bear more directly on the matter. Many have long inquired into these words "from the wood," among them others and the Englishman Nicolaus Fuller, in his Miscellanies, in a whole chapter. Given the abundance of such additions, sometimes even whole verses, which both Fuller and many others have observed, it was enough that this most learned and acute man commented on it. The learned Junius, in his notes to Tertullian, conjectured that some man with bleary eyes may have read ἐξ ξύλου for ἐβασίλευσεν. I would rather say some silly fellow meant to play on the word βασιλεύειν, as though it were derived from the same origin as ξυλεύειν or ξυλέωαι. Eustathius notes somewhere that such letters are sometimes interchanged, as in ἀνάξυεις for ἀνάσυεις, and in Scripture the difference is not great. But what does Chisletius do? Turning from the common and familiar version that present-day copies show, which he admits was once received and commonly known, he appeals to a more hidden and Cabalistic reading, which he imagines was the original: [והוה סלך אפרן הנה ...]. "The same letters," you will say, "whether you read הנך חבר or אפרן." And there is precedent for it. But by what example, I ask, are those Hebrew words, as he writes, to be read not in Hebrew but in Greek, "from T.," and then "from wood"? O wondrous power of the Cabala, which can turn whatever men rave about, whatever the strong or the sick, waking or sleeping, dream of, into the secret mysteries of a higher science. Soon there will hardly be any disease of the brain that cannot be cured, or at least covered, under this specious name of Cabala. By this art, recently (to omit the ancients), Robert Fludd and Thomas Alabaster, Englishmen, have commended their wisdom to us in huge volumes. They have revealed marvellous mysteries never known before, and, in short, for all who are foolish and disdainful of the solemn, they have prepared great delicacies and luxuries, pursuing marvels unheard of by sea and land. "But," says Chisletius, "the matter, though admirable and unheard of for so many past ages, seems to me so certain and so well established, that the letter ת was fortunate and salutary among the Hebrews, and that in fact and form it prefigured the figure of the Lord's cross, that it is superfluous to show this here from Ezekiel and from the ancient letters of the Samaritans." Not superfluous at all, indeed, since there are not a few, both ancient and recent writers, who, led by no slight reasons, judge the passage in Ezekiel otherwise. The most modest men of those parties acknowledge that there is nothing in the prophet's own words that compels or leads us to that interpretation. "I think, however, it should not be passed over," says the learned Sixtus of Siena, "that the name Tau is taken as much for the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet as for any sign whatever. Hence, since in Ezekiel not only the letter Thau written separately as ת is found, but the whole word תו, which almost everyone interprets as a sign, it is certainly uncertain whether the prophet's words are to be understood of the letter Thau itself or of some other sign." So far he. As for the Samaritan Thau, if we look at their present letters, who could deny that it agrees with the figure of the cross no more than a dog does, as the old saying about the bath has it? Nevertheless, that no change came into the Samaritan alphabet is suggested by the words of Origen and Jerome, though I do not dare to assert it. But when, or on what occasion, Chisletius would have rendered great service, in my judgement, had he taught us what Scaliger would have said, to whom learned men refer us and go to and consult, and whose access (now denied to us) is open to them.

units.la: Sed hoc ferri potest, in quo nimiâ tantum subtilitate peccatur,cujus apud multos non parva gratia, nec adeò difficilis, maturescente judicio, emendatio. Illud non ferendum, à Christi exemplo & verbis, talibus praestigiis arcesli patrocinium, quo nihil ad fidem Christianam funditus evertendam, & invehendum atheismum, dici aut cogitari possit efficacius. Christi autem verba, Matth.capite V.versu 18.& Luc. capite XVI. versu 17. in quibus unius Iota & μιᾶς κερέαιας fit mentio, quàm nihil ad rhombum, pluribus ostenderem, nisi ab aliis jam abundè praestitum effet, à quibus locutionis istius proverbialis vis & ratio dilucidè explicata. Ludovici tamen Capelli, viri doctissimi & in Thalmudicis versatissimi, hac occasione verba, quia apprimè ad rem faciant, Lectori Rabbinicæ literaturæ cum sobrietate studioso, libens commendabo: Sic autem, ait ille, loquitur Christus, non ut probet Pharisæorum, de illis corniculis & apiculis sententiam, qui putabant, sed falsò, magna in iis latere mysteria. Nam certè si verè laterent in illis grandia mysteria, si sic Christus censuisset: qui factum, ut, nec ipse, nec ullus Apostolorum nobis ullum (nec quidem minimum) illorum mysteriorum aperuerit? Unde est, quod nullum (ne obscurissimum quidem) tantæ tamq; admirabilis sapientiæ in corniculis illis delitescentis vestigium compareat in omnibus tum Evangelistarum tum Apostolorum scriptis ullis Canonicis? Cur non ista revelâsset Christus? Cur non in illis indagandis nobis aliquatenùs præivissent vimque pramonstrassent Apostoli? Nuga itaque sunt, & mera gerra, &c.
units.tr: But this may be borne, since the fault lies only in excessive subtlety, a fault that is among many not a small attraction, and not very hard to correct as judgement matures. What cannot be borne is that such tricks should be summoned to defend a practice drawn from the example and words of Christ, when nothing could be said or thought more effective for overturning the Christian faith from its foundations and introducing atheism. As for the words of Christ, Matthew chapter 5 verse 18 and Luke chapter 16 verse 17, in which mention is made of one iota and of one little horn [μιᾶς κερέαιας], how little they have to do with the diagram I would show at length, were it not already amply done by others, by whom the force and reasoning of that proverbial expression have been clearly explained. Nevertheless, on this occasion I shall gladly commend to the reader who studies Rabbinic literature with sobriety the words of Ludovicus Cappellus, a very learned man, most versed in the Talmudic writings, since they bear especially on the matter: "Christ, however," he says, "spoke in this way not to approve the opinion of the Pharisees about those little horns and tittles, who thought, but falsely, that great mysteries lay hidden in them. For surely, if great mysteries truly lay hidden in them, and Christ had judged so, how does it happen that neither he nor any of the Apostles has revealed to us any of those mysteries, not even the smallest? Whence is it that no trace of so great and so admirable a wisdom hidden in those little horns appears in any of the canonical writings of the Evangelists or the Apostles? Why would Christ not have revealed those things? Why would the Apostles not have gone before us to some extent in searching them out and shown their force? They are therefore trifles, and mere idle talk, etc."

units.la: Cæterùm si unquam vel apud ipsum Schindlerum Chifletius observâsset, aut apud alios ex illo observatum comperisset, reperta esse quaedam exemplaria Hebraica, in quibus extaret illud יהוה מלך מעלם, omissa Cabala sua, eo potius, opinor, ut est in eas partes pronus, se convertisset, ut textus Hebraici corruptionem evinceret, & exagitaret. Facilis responsio, si fecisset; Sed labori parcam, ne contra propriam umbram pugnare videar.
units.tr: But if Chifletius had ever observed, even in Schindler himself, or had learned from others who had observed it from him, that certain Hebrew copies have been found in which that phrase, YHWH is king for ever [יהוה מלך מעלם], stands, then, I think, having set aside his Cabala, he would have turned, as he is inclined that way, to prove and assail the corruption of the Hebrew text. The answer would have been easy had he done so; but I shall spare the effort, lest I seem to be fighting against my own shadow.

units.la: Haec erant, quae de linguae Hebraeae sive usu, sive abusu, non abs re videbantur, quae tirones, harum rerum studiosos, moneremus. Aliquid de necessitate quoque coronidis loco adjiciemus. A multis proponitur quaestio, & a nonnullis uberrime tractatur, An Theologo necessaria sit Hebraicae linguae peritia. Si simpliciter & absolute dicamus necessariam, objicientur tum recentiorum & sequiorum saeculorum insigniores aliqui, tum praecipue primitivae Ecclesiae Patres & Theologi veteres, & vita & scriptis meriti, ut illustria Ecclesiae lumina & columina a posteris haberentur: quibus qui recentiores Theologos ob Hebraicae linguae peritiam simpliciter & nullo discrimine praeferre
units.tr: These were the things which seemed not out of place concerning the use, or rather the misuse, of the Hebrew tongue, things which we would advise beginners, the students of these matters. We shall also add, by way of a crown, something on its necessity. Many propose the question, and some treat it at great length: whether the knowledge of Hebrew is necessary for a theologian. If we say simply and absolutely that it is necessary, there will be objected to us both some of the more distinguished men of later and more recent centuries, and especially the Fathers of the primitive Church and the ancient theologians, men deserving well in life and in their writings, so that they are held by posterity as illustrious lights and pillars of the Church. Those who prefer more recent theologians simply, and without any distinction, on account of their knowledge of Hebrew,

units.la: præferunt, in valdè angustos limites amplam & augustam S. Theologiæ prosessionem cogere & compingere mihi videntur. Non enim statim intelligunt Sanctam Scripturam, qui Hebraica intelligunt: sed ingenio opus est, & judicio, & assiduâ lectione: ut quis autem perveniat ad eum intelligentiæ gradum, qui sacræ hujus scientiæ doctori conveniat, nullum non disciplinæ genus & eruditionis est necessarium: nullum enim, quod non juvet; & in obscurissimis (quod multis alibi nos exemplis probabimus) sæpè locis, ex infimâ arte aut scriptore lux clara peti potest. Quæ quia omnia perfectè complecti, non unius est hominis, consequens tamen est, ut tantò ille ad perfectionem propius accedat, qui plura complectitur: modò tamen par sit ingenium, quod in omni re præcipuum est: & sine quo reliqua, ad ostentationem quidem non parùm fortasse, & eruditionis laudem comparandam: ad veræ autem utilitatis fructum, quo auctiores fiant res Theologicæ, nihil omninò proderunt. Hoc certum est, si qui sine Hebraicæ linguæ peritiâ præstantes fuere
units.tr: seem to me to force and cram the ample and noble profession of sacred theology into very narrow limits. For those who understand Hebrew do not at once understand Holy Scripture; there is need of talent, of judgement, and of constant reading. And for anyone to attain that degree of understanding which befits a teacher of this sacred science, every kind of discipline and learning is necessary; for there is none which does not help, and in the most obscure passages (as we shall prove by many examples elsewhere) a clear light can often be drawn even from the lowliest art or writer. Since to grasp all these things perfectly is not the work of one man, it follows nonetheless that he who embraces more comes so much the nearer to perfection, provided only that his talent is equal to it, which is the chief thing in every matter, and without which the rest will profit nothing at all for real usefulness, though perhaps not a little for display and for winning the reputation of learning, and for the fruit of true benefit, by which theological matters become richer, not at all. This is certain: if some who were outstanding theologians lacked knowledge of the Hebrew tongue,

units.la: Theologi, eos tantò praestituros fuisse, si periti fuissent; sine exceptione tum laudandi, qui nunc vel à pueris ob istum defectum multa sibi condonari postulant.
units.tr: they would have been far more outstanding had they been skilled in it; and so they are to be praised without exception, though those who now, even from boyhood, demand that much be pardoned them on account of this lack.

units.la: Sed utcunque de illis statuamus: ut nunc quidem se res habet, in tanta studii huius facilitate, & tam vulgari usu, magis necessaria Theologo sit huius linguae cognitio, an pudenda ignorantia, non facile dixerim. Saepe audivi concionatores, qui, ex singulorum verborum proprietate, & variis notionibus magna elicerent mysteria. Fateor audivisse, quibus optime cederet, ut & ipsi non vulgaris inde acuminis laudem merERENTUR, & auditores non poenitendae doctrinae fructum referrent: nempe, cum textus ita expenditur primigenius, sive Hebraicus, sive Graecus. Nam si versionis alicujus (quaecunque sit illa) verbis ista opera impenditur, res futilis & ludicra est; & aegre abstineant à risu pueri puellaeve, viri foeminaeve, si quae, ut saepe contingit, peritae adsint; quantoque aliquis in hoc genere ingeniosior, tanto ineptior fit oportet, & ad irrisionem magis expositus.
units.tr: But however we judge those men, as matters now stand, with so great an ease in this study and so common a use of it, I would not readily say whether knowledge of this language is more necessary for a theologian, or whether ignorance of it is shameful. I have often heard preachers who, from the particular force of single words and their various senses, drew out great mysteries. I confess I have heard some whom it served very well, so that they earned for themselves no ordinary praise for acuteness, and their hearers carried home the fruit of doctrine not to be regretted: namely, when the text is so weighed in its original, whether Hebrew or Greek. For if such labour is spent on the words of some version (whatever it may be), the thing is trifling and playful, and boys and girls, men and women, if there are any skilled ones present, as often happens, can hardly keep from laughter; and the more ingenious anyone is in this kind, the more foolish he must become and the more exposed to ridicule.

units.la: Sed & ad assequendam, si aliqua sit in verbis obscuritas aut ambiguitas, (qualia hodiéq; in sacrâ Scripturâ innumera: ) veram & genuinam sententiam, non parum confert linguæ primigeniæ peritia. Nam de versionibus, à doctissimis viris elaboratis & probatis pluribus, quæ instar originalium esse possint, quod à multis respondetur, quanti sit id faciendum, cùm de Græcæ linguæ scriptoribus agemus, accuratè perpendemus. Hinc igitur ad illam ne Lectorem diutiùs moremur, orationem convertamus.
units.tr: But also, for reaching the true and genuine sense, if there is any obscurity or ambiguity in the words (of which there are countless instances even today in Holy Scripture), skill in the original tongue contributes not a little. As to the versions, many elaborated and approved by most learned men, which may be held to be equal to the originals, which many reply, we shall weigh carefully how much that is to be valued when we treat of the writers in the Greek language. Let us therefore turn to that discourse, lest we delay the reader any longer here.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: FINIS.

units.la: De lingua Anglica ve- tere; sive Saxonica; ejusque cum Græca cognatione.
units.tr: On the Ancient English Language, or Saxon, and Its Kinship with Greek.

units.la: PUerum adhuc me, b.m. parentem Isaacum, de lingua Germanica perhonorificè loquentem, atque ita optantem, ut ejus aliquando mihi perito esse contingeret, non semel audire memini. Hujus autem judicii votique sui quas ille potissimum rationes haberet, sive quòd imparem tum judicaret, quem participem faceret; sive ea puerilis ætatis ac memoriæ injuria fuerit, nullas omnino possum dicere. Habeo (si quid tamen adhuc habeo) Dictionarium Gallicum, quod Majus inscribitur, in quo rogatu Patris verba Gallica quæcunque sunt originis Germanicæ, Tobias Scultetus, Germanus, vir doctissimus, manu suâ notaverat & exposuerat; qui etiam in Epistolâ ad ad patrem ibidem annexâ magnum ejus studium prædicat erga gentem linguámque Germanicam.
units.tr: I remember hearing my father, of blessed memory, Isaac, speak very highly of the German language more than once, and wish that I might one day become skilled in it. I cannot say at all what reasons he had for this judgement and wish, whether he then thought me too young to be made a sharer in it, or whether the failing lies in my childhood age and memory. I have (if I still have anything) the French dictionary entitled Majus, in which, at my father's request, Tobias Scultetus, a German and a most learned man, had marked in his own hand and explained whatever French words are of German origin. In a letter annexed to it, addressed to my father, he also praises my father's great zeal for the German nation and language.

units.la: Anno Dom. M.D.C.X. post cædem Henricı IV. Galliarum Regis, cui de factis maximis Magni cognomen obtigit; invitante Jacobo Magnæ Britt. Rege Serenissimo, cujus inter alias multas laudes tanto fastigio dignas ea erat eruditio, quæ etiam in privato homine non exiguam laudem & admirationem meruisset: eo, inquam, non unis invitante literis, Pater in Angliam cum totâ, (sed non uno tempore) familiâ migravit; ibíque post annorum quatuor, præter propter, in summâ Regis optimi gratiâ, moram, annum agens vitæ suæ sextum & quinquagesimum, diem obiit supremum. Post ejus mortem familiâ ejus variè distractâ, in Anglià me, tum pubertatis annos ingressum, morari contigit, & inter Anglos agentem, Anglico sermoni (Germanicæ linguæ inter alias traduci non ignobili) paulatim assuefacere: cui tamen addiscendo operam non ante seriam navávi, quàm de futura profesione mecum statuissem, jámque præconis Ecclesiastici munus imminere-t. Sed neque tum, neque ullo antea, cùm in eo studio versarer, tempore, aliud propositum, præter vulgarem hunc & necessarium pro susceptæ provinciæ ratione linguæ usum; quanquam non semel inter legenda Græca observata non sine aliquâ admiratione verborum Græcorum cum Anglicis assinitas & ξυγγενεια. Neque enim aliam tum eorum rationem habebam; quàm ut ad generalem συγκρισιν, cujus in omnibus linguis essent exempla, referrem.
units.tr: In the year of our Lord 1610, after the murder of Henry IV, King of the French, who earned the surname Great for his greatest deeds, and at the invitation of James, most serene King of Great Britain, whose learning, among his many other praiseworthy qualities, was worthy of such eminence and would have won no small praise and admiration even in a private man, my father moved to England with the whole family (though not all at one time). There, after about four years in the highest favour of that excellent King, he died in his fifty-sixth year of life. After his death his family was scattered in various directions, and it fell to me, then entering my adolescence, to stay in England. Living among the English, I gradually grew accustomed to the English speech (a tongue not undistinguished among the other offshoots of the German). Yet I did not take serious pains to learn it until I had decided on my future profession, and the office of an ecclesiastical herald was already looming. But neither then nor at any earlier time, while I was engaged in that study, had I any aim beyond the ordinary and necessary use of the language for the task I had undertaken. Still, more than once, while reading Greek, I observed, not without some wonder, the affinity and kinship [ξυγγένεια] of Greek words with English ones. At that time I had no other account of them than to refer them to that general comparison whose examples are found in all languages.

units.la: Aliquot post annis in numerum Præbendariorum Ecclesiæ Cathedralis & Metropolitiæ Cantuariensis adlectus, cùm pro loci & officii, quod non semel illhic obii, ratione paterent mihi Ecclesiæ illius augustissimæ archiva; dum omnia, quæ aliquam antiquitatis speciem præferrent, avidè perscrutor: (juvabat autem majorum nostrorum laudandam diligentiam & religionem perspicere, qui non loca tantùm ab omni conflagratione munitissima profpexerant; sed & pulcherrimis & amplissimis contra situm & squallorem scriniis; quæ capsulas & pixides, numero plurimas, certo ordine dispositas & mobiles; les, continerent, omnia distinxerant & describerant: dum illa igitur diligenter & studiose perscrutor, inter alia venerandæ antiquitatis monumenta, tum plurima alia Saxonicè concepta instrumenta, tum vetustissimorum Saxonicorum Regum aliorumque temporum istorum principum virorum tam Ecclesiasticorum quàm secularium chirographa, partim Latina, partim Saxonica, sese oculis meis obtulerunt. Chirographa autem voco, non quæ ipsi scripserint, (quod absurdum cogitare) quorum chirographa perhibentur; sed quæ ab aliis scripta, propria ipsi manu, vel adscripto nomine, vel certa alia nota signaverint & insignierint. Cæterum, omnium fere, Regiorum præcipuè, tam elegans erat scriptura, ut cum pulcherrimis (qualem etiam antiquissimorum, ut plurimùm, librorum scripturam esse animadverti) quos ætas nostra vidit typis sive Plantinianis sive aliis certare possent. Memini cùm sacras illas membranas tangerem, religioso quodam horrore animum meum percelli solitum, quasi præsentes intuerer, qui monumentis illis loquebantur, quique manibus ipsi suis illa quondam tractaverant, quae nunc ego meis contingebam. Quale novitio alicui, pompae curialis infrequenti insolentique, Principis alicujus de splendidioribus & superbioribus Aula, ubi quae spectantis praestinguant oculos tum alia fortasse plurima; tum vero ante omnia, praesentis ipsius Majestas Principis, & solitus ille purpuratorum Comitatus: talè mihi locus ille solebat esse; non minus facet, nec minus spectabilis. Unum deerat ad persectam voluptatem, petitio linguae Saxonicae: cujus ignaro, plerAque quae corporis oculis erant expositæ, mentis tamen (quae potissimum lumen) intelligentiae clausa erant & abdita. Miro tum coepi flagrare desiderio linguam istam propius cognoscendi: quae quidem cupiditas ab his orta principiis, multum confirmata est, postquam accuratius ista mihi perpensa & intellecta.
units.tr: Some years later I was admitted to the number of prebendaries of the Cathedral and Metropolitan Church of Canterbury. Since, by reason of the place and the office which I discharged there more than once, the archives of that most venerable church lay open to me, I eagerly searched through everything that bore any appearance of antiquity. It was a pleasure to see the praiseworthy diligence and piety of our forebears, who had provided not only places most secure against any fire, but also most beautiful and spacious chests against dust and decay, which contained, in good order and on movable shelves, very many caskets and boxes; and they had sorted and described everything. As I searched these carefully and diligently, among other monuments of venerable antiquity there presented themselves to my eyes many documents written in Saxon, as well as the charters of the most ancient Saxon kings and of the other distinguished men of those times, both churchmen and laymen, some in Latin and some in Saxon. I call them charters not because the men themselves wrote them (which would be absurd to suppose), but because they are said to be the handwriting of those who had them written, and which they marked or signed with their own hand, either with a name added or with some other sign. Indeed, the script of nearly all of them, especially the royal ones, was so elegant that it could hold its own with the finest printing, whether Plantin's or any other, which our age has seen. (I had noticed that this was also the character of the script of the most ancient books, for the most part.) I remember that when I touched those sacred parchments, I was usually struck by a certain religious awe, as if I were looking at the very persons who spoke in those records and who had once handled with their own hands what I was now touching. It was like a newcomer's experience of a court procession, rare and unfamiliar, of some prince in the more splendid and haughty halls of a palace, where many other things might dazzle the eyes of the onlooker, but above all the very majesty of the prince himself and his usual retinue of purple-clad courtiers. Such was that place to me, no less delightful and no less impressive. One thing was lacking to complete my pleasure: knowledge of the Saxon language. Without it, most of what lay open to my bodily eyes remained closed and hidden from the understanding of the mind, which is chiefly the light. Then I began to burn with a wondrous desire to know that language more closely. This desire, arising from these beginnings, grew much stronger once I had weighed and understood these things more carefully.

units.la: Primo quidem Saxonicam linguam, veram & genuinam esse, linguam Anglicam, ut quantum à Saxonica vetere praesens Anglica recesserit, tantum à nativa puritate degeneraverit: Ut si vellem (quod homini cordato & intelligenti si non necessarium, certè non potest non jucundum esse & optabile:) verborum & locutionum, quas quotidie & loquens & scribens ufurpabam, rationes ac proprietates intelligere, ad Saxonicas origines necessariò recurrendum esse.
units.tr: First, the Saxon language is true and genuine, and the English language is so much degenerated from its native purity as the present English has departed from ancient Saxon. So, if I wished (which, for a sensible and thoughtful man, if not necessary, is certainly not unpleasant but desirable) to understand the principles and peculiarities of the words and idioms that I daily used in speaking and writing, I must necessarily recur to Saxon origins.

units.la: Secundò, eam esse linguam Saxonicam, quæ per se minimè contemnenda sit; sed dignissima cujus à quocunque veritatis & antiquitatis (quæ veritatis, ut plurimùm, testis & advocata:) studioso, ratio habeatur; ídque ut alia omittam, ob summam tum antiquitatem, tum amplitudinem; quibus duobus omnes alias vulgares (nisi valde fallor) linguas longissimo anteit intervallo. Saxonicam cum dico, Germanicam, ut nunc vocant, & Teutonicam five Belgicam intelligo, cum quibus eam per omnia fere convenisse, vetustissima quæ supersunt hodieque trium istarum linguarum monimenta (de quo posteà plura) fidem faciunt: ídque etiam ex veteribus historicis apertissimè colligitur. Trium autem tam propinquæ
units.tr: Second, Saxon is a language that is by no means to be despised in itself, but is most worthy of consideration by anyone who studies truth and antiquity (of which, for the most part, it is the witness and advocate). I say this, to pass over other reasons, because of its very great antiquity and its wide extent, and in both respects, unless I am greatly mistaken, it far outstrips all other vernacular languages by a very long interval. When I say Saxon, I mean what they now call German, and Teutonic or Dutch (Belgic), with which it agreed almost entirely, as the very ancient monuments of these three languages that survive to this day (of which more later) bear witness, and as is most clearly gathered from the ancient historians. Of these three, so closely related...

units.la: {*} (Printed small marks at the foot of the page; not legible in detail.) quæ cognationis & originis cui principatus antiquitatis potissimùm tribuendus, quæque se matricis (si tamen ulla, & non altiùs ad Celticam aut Scythicam recurrendum' est) titulo merito jactare possit, non ego sanè valdè sollicitus, aut super eo magnopere contenderim, modò id mihi concedatur, quod negari nisi ab imprudentibus, aut sultè invidis non potest, tantam esse illarum conjunctionem & ἀλλήλχίαν, ut in laudem unius vix quicquam dici possit aut inveniri, quod ad cæteras non æquè pertineat. Sed hoc tamen de veteribus illis linguis dictum velim, quales erant in usu ante octingentos vel mille annos. Nam de hodiernis si quærimus, ego quidem primas honoris illi detulerim, quæcunque sit, quæ plurimum de vetustate suâ retinet, & externarum contagio minimè contaminata est.
units.tr: Which of them is the source of this kinship and origin, and to which the primacy of antiquity should chiefly be assigned, and which may rightly boast the title of mother (if indeed any is, and we need not go back further to the Celtic or Scythian), I, for my part, am not very anxious about, nor would I contend strenuously over it. Let it only be granted to me what cannot be denied except by the imprudent or those who are plainly envious: that the conjunction and interconnection [ἀλληλουχίαν] of those three is so great that scarcely anything can be said or found in praise of one that does not apply equally to the others. But I would wish this to be said of those old languages, such as were in use eight or a thousand years ago. For if we inquire about the modern ones, I would give the first place of honour to whichever of them retains most of its antiquity and is least contaminated by the contagion of foreign admixtures.

units.la: Hæc igitur lingua est, ut vetustiora (de quibus postea dicturi sumus) omittamus tempora, quâ illi loquebantur, qui Galliam, Italiam, Hispaniam suis armis subegerunt, & Romanis eripuerunt: qui Africam quoque aggressi, Asiámque, que, non modo torrentis in morem obvia quaeque prostraverunt, sed in iis quoque locis diuturnas sedes fixerunt, imperia constituerunt, legibus & institutis propriis rexerunt: variis illi quidem nominibus & tribubus (quae ex amplitudine, variorum quasi populorum nomen sortitae sunt:) distincti, sed ejusdem aut certe simillimi sermonis commercio conjuncti: Hunni, Gothi, Ostrogothi; Wisigothi, Heruli, Franci, Burgundiones, Normanni, Wandali, Alani, Swevi, Langobardi, aliique plures, quorum nominibus istorum temporum historiae refertae sunt. Quis autem non ita colligat; Qui tantum in tot Orbis terrarum disjunctissimis partibus amplissimisque potuere; qui priftina regna & imperia vertere, abolere; nova condere, quorum plurima post tot annorum & saeculorum revolutiones ad hunc usque diem, quanquam variè concussa, permixtaque, remanent: eosdem etiam linguae suae & sermonis, quo res utplurimum administrantur humanae, vestigia multis locis, & moribus & linguis impressisse: quae loca, mores, & linguae, in dubiis & obscuris
units.tr: This, then, is the language (to pass over the more ancient times, of which we shall speak later) spoken by those who subdued Gaul, Italy and Spain with their arms and wrested them from the Romans; who also attacked Africa and Asia and not only overthrew everything in their path like a torrent, but also fixed lasting seats in those lands, established empires, and governed them by their own laws and institutions. They were distinguished by various names and tribes (which took their names from the extent of what were, as it were, various peoples), but were united by the same or at least very similar speech: Huns, Goths, Ostrogoths, Visigoths, Heruli, Franks, Burgundians, Normans, Vandals, Alans, Suevi, Lombards, and many others, whose names fill the histories of those times. Who, then, would not conclude that those who could hold so much in so many most widely separated and vast parts of the world, who overturned and abolished ancient kingdoms and empires and founded new ones, many of which, after so many revolutions of years and centuries, remain to this day, though variously shaken and mixed, must also have impressed traces of their language and speech (in which human affairs are for the most part conducted) on many places, customs and tongues? These places, customs and tongues, being doubtful and obscure in many respects, as many things commonly are, can receive no little light from a perfect knowledge of that ancient language. And these things, which we have said about the common idiom of those peoples who overthrew and occupied the Roman Empire, since they belong to a more recent memory, so...

units.la: multis, (qualia passim multa) ex veteris illius linguæ perfecta cognitione non parum lucis accipere possint. Et hæc quidem, quæ de populorum istorum, qui Romanum Imperium everterunt & occuparunt, communi idiomate dicta sunt à nobis, ut recentioris sunt memoriæ, ita tam certa sunt, ut nemo possit contradicere.
units.tr: in many places (as many such things are everywhere), receive no little light from a full knowledge of that ancient language. What we have said about those peoples who overthrew and seized the Roman Empire, in their common idiom, concerns recent memory, and it is so certain that no one can contradict it.

units.la: Ad priora illa tempora si veniendum est, ex quo primùm cœpit Græcis Latinisve Germanum nomen innotescere; quanquam ob summam vetustatem non adeò liquida res est, ut tam certò affirmare audeamus; non levibus tamen adducti conjecturis doctissimi quidam viri in eâ fuere sententiâ, linguam Thracicam Phrygiámque (quæ in Asia latissimè olim patebant) non alterius fuisse originis quàm Germanicam. Quorum sententiæ accedere videtur magnum sæculi sui ornamentum Cl. Salmasius in priore de Linguâ Hellenistica (quæ sola adhuc ad manus meas pervenit) commentatione. Addit porrò de lingua quoque Persica vir summus, Persica quoque sive Parthica, quæ & ipsa authores originis habuit Scythas, infinitas finitas prefert voces, quæ eadem reperiuntur in Græca pariter Dialecto & in Teutonica. Idem quoque in præfatione ad Cebetis Tabulæ versionem Arabicam, post commemoratum Joh. Eichmanni M. D. obitum, & deploratam quam in tanti viri morte Respubl. literaria fecit jacturam, ut qui (præter alia) in Persicæ linguæ cognitione parem in Europa non habuerit, nec temerè habiturus sit, ita pergit: Quod ad hoc ævi latuit plerosque eruditorum, ex eadem origine compererat fluxisse Germanicam & Persicam linguam, ad hanc illum conjecturam ducente infinita vocum copia utrique lingua communium; sed & verbis similiter terminatis, eodem modo compositis, aliisque multis argumentis.
units.tr: If we must go back to those earlier times, when the German name first became known to the Greeks and Romans, the matter is not so clear, given its great antiquity, that we dare to affirm it with confidence. Nevertheless, some very learned men, moved by no slight conjectures, have held the view that the Thracian and Phrygian languages (which once spread very widely in Asia) were of no other origin than German. The great ornament of his age, the illustrious Salmasius, seems to agree with this opinion in his first commentary on the Hellenistic language, the only one of his works so far to come into my hands. This eminent man adds, concerning the Persian language as well: The Persian or Parthian language, which also had Scythians as its authors of origin, has countless words that are found equally in the Greek dialect and in the Teutonic. In the preface to his Arabic version of the Tablet of Cebes, after mentioning the death of Johann Eichmann, and lamenting the loss the learned republic suffered in the death of so great a man, who (among other things) had no equal in Europe in knowledge of the Persian language and was not likely to have one, he goes on: What has lain hidden from most scholars until now, he had discovered, that the German and Persian languages have flowed from the same origin, and he was led to this conjecture by the endless number of words common to both languages; and also by words similarly ending, similarly compounded, and by many other arguments.

units.la: Jam Illyriorum, Germanorum, Gallorum, Hispanorum, Britannorum unam olim eandemque fuisse linguam, (quæ utique Germanica fuerit, ut ex prisci s plurium rerum vocabulis capite VIII. evincere satagit) pluribus argumentis adstruere nititur Phil. Cluverius, Germaniæ suæ lib. primo, cap. V. & aliquot sequentibus. Gallorum certè (cujus olim nominis & gentis quanta amplitudo nobilitásque fuerit, foli nescıunt, qui in vetere Historiâ plánè sunt hospites)linguam non aliam fuisse quàm Germanicam, quanquam dialecto diversam,receptissima opinio est. Qui ita censeat ac sanciat, unum nominabo, sed qui unus instar omnium esse possit, Jos. Scaligerum, cujus hæc in Propertium poëtam castigationibus verba: Verdomarus, ad verbum ζίνιας πΘ. Nam mar apud nostros erat equus: author Pausanias. Gallorum veterum idioma sine dubio Teutonicum fuit. Huc etiam faciunt quæ de Getis & Getarum linguâ posteà dicturi sumus:quam si Gothicam fuisse (ut plerique omnes hactenus crediderunt) obtinemus, magna hinc linguæ Germanicæ veteri amplitudinis accessio fuerit, cùm Getarum natio per longissima terrarum spatia diffusa fuerit. Sed de Getis,posteà pluribus. Quid,quòd & Orbis Novi,quà ad Septentrionem situs est, linguas ex Germanicâ plerasque Vir sine controversiâ Maximus in tractatu de Origine gentium Americanarum repetit? Huic ejus sententiæ quid alii non contemnendæ nendæ & ipsi auctoritatis & eruditionis viri opposuerint, non ignoramus, quam tamen interdum sic impugnant, ut non omninò negent, dum gentium istis linguis utentium, nonnullarum saltem, originem Germanicam esse non abnuunt. Nos non ista ad nostram cenfuram revocamus. Id tantùm dicemus; quòd ad Vocabularia nos rejiciunt viri docti, in eo minimè nobis satisfacere.
units.tr: Now, that the languages of the Illyrians, Germans, Gauls, Spaniards and Britons were once one and the same (which was certainly German, as he strives to prove from the words of ancient usage for many things, chapter VIII), Philip Cluverius endeavours to establish by many arguments, in the first book of his Germania, chapter V, and several following chapters. It is a very widely accepted opinion that the language of the Gauls (of whose name and people, once so great and noble, only those are ignorant who are complete strangers to ancient history) was none other than German, though differing in dialect. To name one who holds and affirms this, I will name Joseph Scaliger, who alone may serve in place of all, in these remarks of his on the poet Propertius: Verdomarus, on the word [ζίνιας]. For mar among our people meant horse; the authority is Pausanias. The idiom of the ancient Gauls was without doubt Teutonic. What we shall say later about the Getae and the language of the Getae also bears on this. If we hold that their language was Gothic (as almost all have hitherto believed), this will be a great addition to the extent of the old German language, since the nation of the Getae was spread over very long stretches of the earth. But more on the Getae later. What of the fact that that man, beyond dispute the greatest, in his treatise on the origin of the American peoples, traces most of the languages of the New World, where it lies toward the north, to German? We are not unaware of what others, men of no small authority and learning, have set against this opinion; yet they sometimes oppose it in such a way that they do not wholly deny it, and they do not refuse to admit that the origin of some, at least, of the peoples who use those languages is German. We do not bring these matters before our own judgment. This only we shall say: that when learned men refer us to vocabularies, they do not satisfy us in that respect at all.

units.la: Quod enim de loquentibus à non uno observatum scimus, nihil obstare quin linguæ sint cognatæ, imò cognatissimæ, quamvis in verbis ultrò citròque temere jactatis nihil tale percipiant aures peregrinæ: idem nos de Vocabularia volventibus, quanquam sedulò fiat operâ, non sine caussâ affirmemus; cùm præter vulgarem istam diligentiam, propria quædam ad deprehendendas linguarum & verborum cognationes & origines ingenii sagacitas opus sit, quâ qui destituuntur, haud mirum sit, si in plenâ interdum segete multo labore nihil metant. Ipse audivi quosdam linguæ Persicæ peritissimos cùm ita profiterentur, se in omni linguâ Persicâ non ultra 10,aut 12, verba observare servare potuisse, quæ cum Germanicâ vel Anglicâ convenirent. At alios scimus non minore nec peritiâ nec ingenio fuisse, qui longè aliter reperirent, & aliis persuaderent. In linguâ certè si quis hoc experiatur Anglicâ, & ad Vocabularia, solis suis auribus fretus, se conferat, quanquam infinita adhuc superesse minimè dubito, quæ nobis hîc præterita sunt; valde tamen ego fallor, aut ille quisquis est, præter laborem & industriam aliquid hîc requiri expertus intelliget, & agnoscet.
units.tr: For what we know has been observed by more than one person about speakers, namely that nothing prevents languages from being related, indeed most closely related, although foreign ears perceive nothing of the kind in words rashly tossed back and forth: this we affirm, not without cause, about those who turn over vocabularies, even when they do so with diligence. For beyond that common care, there is needed a particular keenness of wit for detecting the relationships and origins of languages and words. Those who lack it need not be surprised if, in a full harvest, they sometimes reap nothing despite much labour. I myself have heard some who were very expert in Persian declare that in the whole Persian language they had been able to observe and keep no more than ten or twelve words that agreed with German or English. But we know of others of no less skill and wit who found far otherwise and persuaded others of it. Certainly, if anyone tries this in the English language, and betakes himself to vocabularies relying on his ears alone, I do not doubt that many things still remain here that have been passed over by us. Yet I am much mistaken if he, whoever he is, will not come to understand and acknowledge, by experience, that something beyond labour and industry is required here.

units.la: Hoc interim tertium, quod linguam Saxonicam de meliore notâ nobis commendavit, à nobis commemorabitur, quod dum in illam propiùs inquirimus, ita planè rem habere comperimus, eam vel Græcæ, sed ab ultimâ origine, propaginem fuisse; vel certè ab eâdem, qua, & Græca, origine, ut à Græcâ solâ differet dialecto, profluxisse. Sed is, quia nostræ hujus de lingua Saxonicâ commentationis præcipuus est scopus, & unica jam deinceps proposita materia, uno verbo rem tetigisse hoc loco sufficiat.
units.tr: Meanwhile, this third point, that the Saxon language has commended itself to us as of better repute, will be dealt with by us. For while we inquire into it more closely, we find the matter to be plainly this: that it was either a offshoot of Greek, though from an ultimate origin, or at least sprang from the same origin as Greek, differing from Greek only in dialect. But since this is the chief aim of our present treatise on the Saxon language, and the only subject now proposed from here on, it will suffice to touch on it in a single word here.

units.la: Atque hæc sunt præcipuè quorum feria consideratio sacro quasi nescio quo thyrso tactum ad linguae Saxonicae studium vehementer impulerunt. Non jactabo profectum meum, qui longe ab eo absum, ut inter peritos ejus linguae locum aliquem mihi postulem. Ille vero qualiscunque fuerit, me certe operae non poenitet. Nec defuit voluntas. Sed ne longe progrederer, tum alia studia, tum negotia pro loco & tempore ingruentia, ac tantum non obruentia, suerunt in caussa.
units.tr: These, above all, are the things which, having been touched as if by some sacred thyrsus, have vehemently impelled me to the study of the Saxon language, whose serious consideration... I will not boast of my progress, for I am far from claiming for myself any place among the experts in that language. Yet whatever it may be, I certainly do not regret the effort. Nor was the will lacking. But other studies, and affairs pressing in upon me according to place and time, and all but overwhelming me, were the cause of my not advancing far.

units.la: Commode interim accidit, ut Guilielmus Somnerus Cantuarien-sis, ex honesta familia natus, antiquae ipse probitatis & simplicitatis Vir, mihi innotefceret. Hujus ego genio ingenioque magnopere captus, quod & industriam ejus non vulgarem in scrutandis patriis antiquitatibus animadverterem, & in summa modestia acre & subactum judicium valde probarem, ad Saxonicae linguae, dignum ipsius industria ingenioque, studium capessendum, vehementer adhortari & impellere coepi: meam ipsi operam, si qua utilis esse posset, & qualemcunque supellectilem Saxonicam ultro offerens. Ne longum faciam, cùm ille cònsilium meum probasset, tam pertinace deinceps industriâ, parique ingenii bonitate & fœlicitate rem prosecutus est, ut intra paucos annos vel peritissimis (ut parcissimè dicam) æquari posset. Hujus autem profectus ipsius & peritiæ testes eruditæ in hoc genere, & laboriosæ lucubrationes plurimæ, quas ille dudum publici juris fecisset, multa quoque præstiturus alia, nisi funesta hæc bella, ac feralis rerum ϰλαςεφῳ, non minorem literis & ingeniis, quàm terris vastitatem inducens, intervenisset. Hactenus quidem nihil in vulgus emisit, præter Antiquitates Cantuarienses: Pium & laboriosum opus, nec istius tantùm florentissimæ quondam Civitatis studiosis, sed omnibus veteris Historiæ Anglicæ non incuriôsis perutile. Præter hunc primum ingenii sui fœtum scripsit in Leges Henrici I. à Rogero Twisden, ordinis equestris viro, sed virtutibus & eruditione, quàm titulis ornatiore, haud ita pridem editas, Notas & animadversiones uberes & doctas cum Glossario utilissimo. Item de celeberrima & antiquissima consuetudine dine Cantiana, quæ vulgò Ḃauelksnɑ nuncupatur, justum tractatum Anglicè. De Portu Iccio Disquisitionem,sive Dissertationem. Leges quoque Saxonicas à Guiliel.Lambardo viro doctissimo pridem editas, & ab eo sic versas,ut majorem Latinitatis, quàm Saxonici sermonis & idiomatis rationem haberet, denuò ille sic Latina fecit, ut Linguæ Saxonicæ studiosis versione suâ consuleret: nonnullis præterea additis Legibus,quas Lambardi codices non exhibuerant. Omitto ejus in varia Glossaria, & Saxonicorum quæ hactenus in lucem prodierunt scriptorum versiones,animadversiones & [illegible, ~4 letters] quibus instructissima habet Adversaria.
