Ex his cùm satis supérque quid in his studiis posset amicis suis probaverit, ego dudum flagitare non destiti, ut de Dictionario Saxonico adornando cogitare vellet;quo maximè opère de lingua illa optimè eum meriturum, & ingentes de studiosis ejus gratias relaturum promittebam. Sed tam iniquis temporibus quid æquus Lector sibi possit promittere, aut ego pro eo spondere, ipsi judicandum relinquo.
units.tr: Meanwhile it happened opportunely that William Somner of Canterbury, born of an honourable family and himself a man of ancient integrity and simplicity, became known to me. Greatly captivated by his disposition and talent, since I noticed his uncommon industry in searching out the antiquities of our country, and greatly approved of his keen and well-disciplined judgment combined with the utmost modesty, I began to urge and impel him strongly to take up the study of the Saxon language, worthy of his industry and talent, offering freely my own help, if it could be of any use, and whatever Saxon resources I had. To be brief: when he approved my advice, he pursued the matter with such persistent industry and equal goodness and felicity of talent that within a few years he could be matched by the most expert (to speak most sparingly). Of his progress and skill, the learned witnesses in this field, and his many laborious studies, which he had long since published, are evidence; he would have done many other things, had not these deadly wars, and the dreadful [κλαυθμῷ] of affairs, bringing a devastation of letters and talents no less than of lands, intervened. So far he has published nothing among the public except the Antiquities of Canterbury, a pious and laborious work, very useful not only to students of that once most flourishing city, but to all who are not indifferent to English ancient history. Besides this first fruit of his talent, he wrote, in the Laws of Henry I, recently edited by Roger Twysden, a man of the equestrian order, more adorned by virtues and learning than by titles, rich and learned notes and observations, with a most useful glossary. Likewise a just treatise in English on the very famous and most ancient custom of Kent, commonly called Gavelkind. A disquisition or dissertation on the port of Iccius. He also gave a new Latin rendering of the Saxon laws, long since edited by the most learned William Lambarde, who had translated them in such a way as to respect the Latin style more than the Saxon speech and idiom; this new version was made to serve students of the Saxon language, with some laws added that Lambarde's manuscripts had not contained. I omit his notes and observations on various glossaries and on the translations of Saxon writers that have so far come to light, with which he has a well-stocked collection of papers. Since he has shown his friends sufficiently and more than enough what he can do in these studies, I for my part have not ceased for a long time to beg him to consider preparing a Saxon dictionary, a work by which I promised he would deserve very well of that language and win great thanks from its students. But what a fair reader may promise himself in such unfavourable times, or what I may promise on his behalf, I leave for him to judge.

units.la: Cæterùm quod ante dicebamus, tantam esse Saxonicæ veteris cùm Teutonicâ & Germanicâ vetere affinitatem, ut qui unam noverit, omnes noverit; ejus clarissimum & luculentissimum testimonium Lectori nunc impertiam. Cùm enim aliquando in manus meas incidisset Justi Lipsii V. Cl. ad Henricum Shottum Epistola, quæ, inter alia, satis prolixam verborum quorundam veterum Germanis ante 800, aut 900 plus minus annos in usu, sylvam continet; & inter legendum non pauca statim occurrerent, quæ Saxonifmum purum putum resipere viderentur: visum est Somnerum meum experiri, & quid ille censeret, missâ illâ collectione explorare. Erat ille tum Cantuariæ; ego Londini. Intra paucos dies remissa verba cum animadversionibus, quæ cognationem Germanicorum cum Saxonicis (quod illi mihique propositum unum erat) ostenderent. Hanc igitur ipsius opellam, quam ille mihi meo regatu navavit, jam publici juris pro meo jure faciam. Quia tamen longior est, quàm ut hujus meæ Diatribæ corpori commodè possit inseri, ad calcem seorsim sub authoris ipsius exhibebitur nomine:
units.tr: Now, as I said before, the affinity between old Saxon and old Teutonic or German is so close that whoever knows one knows them all. I will now give the reader a very clear and convincing proof of this. Once a letter from the most distinguished Justus Lipsius to Henry Shotte fell into my hands. Among other things it contains a fairly long list of old German words that were in use some 800 or 900 years ago. As I read it, many words at once struck me as tasting of pure Saxon. I decided to test my friend Somner and to learn his opinion by sending him that collection. He was then at Canterbury and I was in London. Within a few days he sent the words back with comments showing the kinship between the German and Saxon words, which was the one aim both he and I had. I will now make public, on my own authority, this small work which he did for me at my request. Because it is too long to be conveniently inserted into the body of this my Diatribe, it will be given separately at the end, under the author's own name.

units.la: Sed ad intelligentiam veterum Germanicorum scriptorum quantum conducat Anglicæ sive Saxonicæ veteris peritia, tum aliunde discamus, tum ex notis Anonym. viri, sed digni qui clarissimus esset, apprimè doctis in WilIerami Abbatis geminam Paraphrasim in Canticum Canticorum, Lugd. Batavorum An. Dom. 1598. Paulo Merulâ G. F. P.N. viro doctissimo accurante, editam. Marquardus quoque Freherus, vir clar. & doctiss. quanti Saxonica nostra faceret, edito cum Oratione Dominicâ & symbolo Apostolorum, Decalogi versione vetere Saxonicâ, cum Notis eruditis, omnibus palam fecit: quanti facturus beatum hunc Saxonicorum scriptorum, quo nunc fruimur, proventum, qui in tantillo specimine, & (ut Senecæ verbo utar) oculiferio, non dicam laureolâ quæsivit; (apagel) sed operam suam & nomen, vir tam doctus & gravis, apparere non detrectavit. Enimverò vel eo nomine dignæ quæ ab omnibus magni æstimetur veræ antiquitatis amatoribus hæc lingua, quòd plura, longè plura, ni fallor, vetuftatis suæ monumenta literaria præferat & ostentet, quàm ulla earum quæ vulgares vulgò audiunt. Testor præter alia quædam minora, quæ nuper, & quæ jam diu vulgata non paûca ; Conciliorum volumen amplum; & Bedæ Hiftoriam, cum Appendicibus, non multò minorem.
units.tr: How much a knowledge of old English or Saxon helps in understanding the old German writers, we may learn from other sources, and also from the notes of an anonymous man, though one worthy to be the most distinguished, which were added to the twofold Paraphrase of Willeram, Abbot, on the Song of Songs, published at Leiden in 1598 under the editorship of the very learned Paulus Merula. Marquard Freher, a distinguished and most learned man, also made clear to everyone how highly he valued our Saxon writings. In an edition with the Lord's Prayer, the Apostles' Creed, and an old Saxon version of the Decalogue, with learned notes, he showed what he thought of the blessed harvest of Saxon writers which we now enjoy. He sought from such a small specimen, which (to use Seneca's word) is eye-catching, not to say a laurel wreath (away with that!), but a man so learned and serious did not refuse to put his effort and his name to it. Indeed, this language deserves to be valued by all lovers of true antiquity for this reason alone: that it presents and displays, I think, many more, far more, literary monuments of its age than any of those languages that are commonly heard from the mouths of ordinary people. I call as witness, besides some other minor works, both those recently published and those long since in print, a large volume of Councils and Bede's History, with its Appendices, which is by no means much smaller.

units.la: Sed hæc ab aliis pluribus fortasse differentur, quibus ista diutiùs excolere & accuratiùs pernoscere, quàm mihi datum est. Quod nobis propositum hîc esse dicebamus, & cujus unius gratiâ hæc à nobis opera suscepta est, id jam aggrediemur. Quia autem circa verborum etymologias utplurimùm versabimur, primum id erit, ut de toto hoc genere, quid & quibus argumentorum ponderibus nitentibus nobis videatur, ostendamus. Eò enim res pervenit, ut quamvis graves interdum viri in rebus gravissimis, ad etymologias scrutandas, posito supercilio, se convertant; adeóque super originibus verborum atrocissimè non raro digladientur; plurimi tamen ita censeant, nihil hoc studio levius aut futilius quicquam reperiri.
units.tr: But these matters will perhaps be deferred by others, who have more time than I have to cultivate them and study them more carefully. The subject we said we had here, and for whose sake alone this work was undertaken, we will now take up. Since we shall be dealing mostly with the etymologies of words, the first task will be to show what we think about this whole kind of inquiry and on what weighty arguments our view rests. For things have reached such a point that, although serious men sometimes, in very serious matters, put aside their pride and turn to the search for etymologies, they often fight most bitterly over the origins of words, yet most of them nevertheless think that nothing is found more trivial or futile than this study.

units.la: Nec nova haec quaestio est, sed jam multis retro saeculis, non inter Grammaticos tantum, sed & philosophos agitata, An verborum sit Etymologia; verè scilicet, & in rebus ipsis: an verò res sit ἀνυπόστατος & imaginaria, quae solo constat nomine. Res mea (dicebat olim S. Augustinus) sententia nimis curiosa, & non nimis necessaria. Et paucis de Cicerone interfertis, Quòd si omnino multum juvaret explicare originem verbi, ineptum esset aggredi, quod profiteri profectò infinitum est. Et mox, Hoc accedit, quòd ut somniorum interpretatio, ita verborum origo pro cujusque ingenio praedicatur. Talia apud alios tum veteres, tum recentiores non paucos.
units.tr: This question is not new. For many centuries it has been debated, not only among grammarians but also among philosophers: whether there is an etymology of words, that is, truly and in the things themselves; or whether the thing is unsubstantial [ἀνυπόστατος] and imaginary, existing only in its name. Saint Augustine once said: My opinion is too curious and not very necessary. And after quoting a few words of Cicero: If it really helped much to explain the origin of a word, it would be foolish to undertake it, since to profess it is surely endless. And soon after: To this is added that, as with the interpretation of dreams, the origin of words is proclaimed according to each person's talent. Many such remarks are found in other writers, both ancient and more recent.

units.la: Mihi autem hac de re saepe ac saepiò cogitanti quid venerit in mentem, non gravabor (quia nunc id agimus) exprome-re. Ut in aliis non paucis, ita in hoc quoque etymologico argumento, non aliud verborum videbatur esse factum, quàm quod ipsarum quoque rerum esse comperiretur: sive eas res spectemus, quae particulari subsistentes existentiâ materialésque, sub sensum cadunt : sive illas quæ seu naturâ suâ immortales & æternæ, seu operâ intellectus abstractæ à particularibus, nobiliore sensu dijudicantur, & ad scientias proprie pertinent: Nam si quis ita animum instituat suum, ut nihil verum in rebus esse pertendat; sed omnia illa de quibus tot extant volumina, [illegible, ~5 letters] esse [illegible, ~4 letters], (quæ de virtute morientis olim Bruti querela) prætereà nihil; nec deerunt magnæ authoritatis qui patrocinentur viri, nec argumentorum pondera; qualia apud Sextum Empiricum Pyrrhonicæ sectæ philosophum doctissimum, si non invicta, certè speciosa. Ita dico: nullam puto esse tam certam artem vel scientiam, cujus vel vanitas, vel incertitudo, si quis id agat, multis non possit verbis exagitari.
units.tr: As for me, when I have often and repeatedly thought about this matter, I shall not hesitate (since this is our present purpose) to set out what has occurred to me. As in many other cases, so in this etymological question too, it seemed that the origin of words is no different from the origin of the things themselves, whether we consider those things which exist as particular, material, and fall under the senses, or those which are either immortal and eternal by their own nature, or are abstracted from particulars by the work of the intellect and are judged by a nobler sense and belong properly to the sciences. For if someone should so direct his mind that he maintains nothing is true in things, but that all those matters about which so many volumes exist are nothing else than what is [illegible] (as the complaint of Brutus when dying about virtue goes), then there will be no lack of learned men of great authority to defend him, nor of weighty arguments, such as those which Sextus Empiricus, the most learned philosopher of the Pyrrhonist sect, brought forward, if not unconquerable, at least plausible. So I say: I think there is no art or science so certain that its vanity or uncertainty could not be attacked with many words by anyone who set out to do so.

units.la: Ut in re minimè invidiosâ, & quæ præter alias artes & scientias in natura maximè fundata videri possit, hoc aliquatenus pateat; sumatur in exemplum medendi scientia. Primum igitur, quemadmodum qui olim contra Verborum Etymologias disputabant; Quod Græci vulgares [illegible, ~6 letters], Athenienses [illegible, ~8 letters]: quorum illud habes
units.tr: To make this clear, in a matter that is not at all open to ill will, and which may seem to be founded in nature more than other arts and sciences, let us take the science of medicine as an example. First, then, let us consider how those who once argued against etymologies of words said that the common Greeks [illegible], and the Athenians [illegible]: of which you have the one [illegible].

units.la: Greek words in this line are not fully legible on the scan and are marked as illegible. habet Etymon ; istud autem (quod quidem noffent) ἀνίτυμον ; nec tamen inde minùs Athenienses in sermone, vel Atticos, vel Græcos fuisse: ita nos dicemus, multas olim, quæ medicos non haberent, Plinio, aliúque commemoratas gentes fuisse: in omni verò gente multos ubique reperiri, qui sine ullo medicinæ usu ad summam senectutem pervenerint ; aut ex summis periculis, solâ curante & operante naturâ, evaferint. Cæterùm, inter eos qui medendi artem profitentur, de medendi ratione minimè convenire: Aliam olim (ut Seneca alicubi objicit) Hippocratis sectam fuisse, aliam Asclepiadis, aliam Themifonis: nec diversâ tantùm, sed planè contrariâ viâ qui grassarentur, extitisse. Fuisse qui herbis omnia tribuerent ; & solas sufficere crederent : fuisse qui penitus abdicarent, nec minùs tamen placerent, aut minora præstare crederentur, quàm qui illis usi fuerant. Empiricos à Dogmaticis, ut præstigiatores explodi ; Dogmaticos ab Empiricis contemni non minùs ac, rideri. Ut hodierna factionum nomina taceam; Galeniftas, Chymiftas, Paracelsiftas,aliósque, quos inter ne de ipsis quidem naturalium corporum principiis convenit, & adhuc sub judice lis est: nedum ut in medendi ratione, quæ ex illis principiis præcipuè pendet, consensum quis expe̓tet.
units.tr: (The Greek in this sentence is largely illegible on the scan.) ... has an etymon; but the other (which they indeed did not know) is without etymon [ἀνίτυμον]. Nevertheless, the Athenians were no less Athenians, or Attic, or Greek, in speech for that. So we shall say that in former times there were many peoples mentioned by Pliny and others who had no physicians; and that in every nation many are found everywhere who reached extreme old age without any use of medicine, or who escaped from the greatest dangers by nature alone caring for them and acting. Moreover, among those who profess the art of healing, there is no agreement at all about the method of healing. Once, as Seneca objects somewhere, there was one sect of Hippocrates, another of Asclepiades, another of Themison; and there arose not only different but plainly opposite ways of practising. Some attributed everything to herbs and believed that these alone were enough; others utterly rejected them, and yet were no less pleasing, or were believed to achieve no less, than those who had used them. The Empirics were rejected by the Dogmatists as charlatans, and the Dogmatists were despised and mocked by the Empirics no less. I say nothing of the names of the present-day factions: Galenists, Chymists, Paracelsians, and others, among whom there is no agreement even about the first principles of natural bodies, and the dispute is still before the judge; much less can anyone expect agreement about the method of healing, which depends mainly on those principles.

units.la: Hæc igitur & similia si quis contra medicinam objiciat, non nihil ille fortasse dixisse, nec immeritò, multis videatur; cùm tamen & plura & certiora opponi possint, quibus artis illius utilitas & dignitas asseratur. Ut igitur est in rebus ipsis & naturâ, veritas, sed tot obstructa difficultatibus, ut ad ejus qualemcunque cognitionem non nisi multâ sedulitate & sagacitate perveniatur: ita & verbis haud dubium quin sua constet origo & originis ratio tam certa, quàm quod in rebus certissimum: sed cujus indagatio tot habet difficultates, tot undique ludibriis & frustrationibus obnoxia est, ut in nullâ veri investigatione majore fit opus aut industriâ, aut judicio. Quòd si quis ita pertendat, tanti rem non esse, ad quam tanto molimine perveniendum sit; per me quidem fruatur ille quisquis est judicii sui libertate. Trahit enim, ut ille olim non inscitè, sua quemque voluptas, & suum cuique pulchrum: neque ego cuiquam author sim, ut invitâ Minervâ in hoc studiorum genere operam ponat. Erunt alii quibus hæc cordi futura sunt: neque eò minùs certum est, (ut de voluptate nihil dicam:) ad explorandam ac percipiendam, quæ in rebus ipsis est, veritatem, infigniter prodesse perfectam verborum cognitionem; quæ valdè manca est, & propè nulla, ignorată origine. sed hæc alibi fufiùs. De difficultate hujus studii sermo nobis hîc est.
units.tr: If someone brings these and similar objections against medicine, perhaps he may seem to many to have said something, and not undeservedly. Yet more and more certain things can be put forward to assert the usefulness and dignity of that art. Just as in things themselves and in nature there is truth, but it is so hemmed in with difficulties that we reach any knowledge of it only through much diligence and sagacity, so there is no doubt that words too have their origin, and a principle of origin as certain as what is most certain in things. But its investigation has so many difficulties, and is so exposed on every side to mockery and frustration, that no search for truth needs more effort or judgement. But if someone maintains that the matter is not worth reaching by such a great effort, then let him, whoever he is, enjoy the freedom of his own judgement. For, as someone once rightly said, each person is drawn by his own pleasure, and each finds his own thing beautiful. Nor would I advise anyone to take up this kind of study against Minerva's will. There will be others to whom these things will be dear. And it is no less certain (to say nothing of pleasure) that a complete knowledge of words, which is very incomplete and almost nothing when its origin is unknown, is of great service in searching out and grasping the truth that is in things themselves. But this I have treated more fully elsewhere. Our discussion here concerns the difficulty of this study.

units.la: Antiquis, quò boni minùs essent Ety- mologistæ, præcipuè obstitit primævæ lingua ignorantiæ. Nam quis Aristoteli succenseat, quòd cùm verbi Αἰτ- ων, & Ἐίνχυον originem quæreret, ita scripserit: Ἐπεὶ τῶν ᾗ ὑνομάζε) Αἴχυον, ὅτι Ἐίχα ἔχειν, ὥσπερ ἂν ἔι τις εἴπει Ἐίχαι- ον, ᾗ ὁ Ἐιχάσης, Ἐιχάσης: aut vero Platoni, cui Ἐίχυον quasi Ἐαῖδν, ἡ κ Ἀὐχμίας ἴνλς (ut ipse loquitur) assumpto? An alterutri eorum potuit incidere suspicio aliqua vocis Hebraicæ ּ שׁ , aut בְּרָא ut ex illis suum illud Ἐἴκν, vel Ἐἰχιον arcesserent? Cujus ut ratio derivationis melius intelligatur, sciendum est (quanquam alias primam syllabam qualemcunq; per aphaeresin tolli, non insolens:) Hebraicum ʒ à Graecis & Latinis per simplex s saepius exprimi: ut in Sadduͣai, Sidon, aliisque plurimis: imo, hoc ipsum צדק, à Syris ܨܕܩ; & צריק, ܨܕܝܩ scribitur. Vitatur autem ʒ multis haec litera ut difficilis & ingratae pronunciationis: unde sunt & ista, siζα, à שוש; & φιάλη, à פלה: aliaque. Ab aliis contrà (pro diversis vel hominum vel locorum ingeniis) affectatur & aspiciturn. Hinc apud Graecos, φιλαξ, φιλαξ; σμικρος, μικρος; & alia non pauca promiscuè usurpata. Latini quoque in multis à Graecis acceptis, abjecere: ut in fallo, ex σφάλλω: funda, ex σφενδόνη, aliisque vulgò notis. Ut mirum fit in origine tam obviâ & certâ reperiri qui malint nova comminisci, quàm rectè inventis acquiescere. Tale etiam illud ejusdem Aristotelis μαγίζω à χαίρω derivantis, cujus origo vocis procul dubio est Hebraica: ab eâdem, ni fallor, quâ & Mercurius radice.
units.tr: Of the ancients, what chiefly prevented them from becoming good etymologists was their ignorance of the primitive language. For who could blame Aristotle, when he sought the origin of the words αἴτιον and εἴκυον and wrote: "Since they call it αἴτιον because it has ἔχειν [to have], just as if one were to say εἰκαῖον from εἰκάσης..."? Or Plato, who, taking εἴκυον as if it were ἐοικός, and assuming it from ἀρχή (as he himself puts it)? Could either of them have suspected some Hebrew word, such as שׁ or בָּרָא, from which they might have drawn their own derivations? To understand his method of derivation better, one should know that, although it is not unusual elsewhere for the first syllable to be dropped by aphaeresis, the Hebrew ṣade is often rendered by the Greeks and Latins with a simple s, as in Sadduai, Sidon, and very many others. Indeed the very word צדק is written by the Syrians as ṣdq, and צריק as ṣdyq. Many avoid this letter as difficult and unpleasant to pronounce, and so come siza from שוש, phiale from פלה, and others. Others, on the contrary, affect it and aspirate it, according to the different natures of people or places. Hence among the Greeks philax, philax; smikros, mikros; and many other words used interchangeably. The Latins too, in many words received from the Greeks, have dropped it: as in fallo from sphallo, funda from sphendonē, and other commonly known examples. So it is remarkable that, when the origin is so obvious and certain, some should prefer to invent new explanations rather than rest content with those rightly found. Such is also that other derivation of Aristotle's, deriving magizo from chairo, whose origin of the word is undoubtedly Hebrew, from the same root, unless I am mistaken, as that of Mercury.

units.la: Sed etiam in illis quorum non erat externa origo, parvam aut nullam feré analogiæ rationem aut certè cognitionem veteres habuisse certum est. Pleni Varronis (doctissimi alioquin viri) libri ineptissimarum Etymologiarum: quem eo nomine merito Quintilianus etiam reprehendit. Nihil enim plerumque insulsius. Stoicos tamen excipio, qui in hoc negotio tam putidè, tam pueriliter se gesserunt, ut Joh.Goropio ad sua deliria præivisse videri merito possint. Hodie autem postquam lingua Hebraica vulgaris esse cœpit, tanta plerosque libido invasit ad Hebraicos sontes omnia revocandi, tantámque sibi torquendi vocabula, addendo, detrahendo, mutando, transponendo sine ullo aut modo aut ratione certâ licentiam sumpsere, ut quicquid uspiam verborum non veterum tantùm, sed & recentiorum in Germania, Gallia, alibi vel remotissimorum, pari ratione Hebraicum fuerit.
units.tr: But it is certain that even for those words whose foreign origin was not evident, the ancients had little or almost no sense of analogy, or at least no knowledge of it. The books of Varro (otherwise a most learned man) are full of most foolish etymologies, and Quintilian rightly criticises him on this account, for nothing is usually more silly. I except the Stoics, however, who behaved so foolishly and so childishly in this business that they may fairly be thought to have set the pattern for the follies of Joannes Goropius. Today, since the Hebrew language has begun to be common, a great many people have been seized with such a passion to trace all things back to Hebrew sources, and have claimed such licence to twist words by adding, removing, changing and transposing them without any sure method or reason, that whatever word anywhere is found, not only of the old words but of the more recent ones in Germany, France or elsewhere, or of the most remote, can by the same method be shown to be Hebrew.

units.la: Edidit Harmoniam Etymologicam multarum linguarum vir doctissimus Steph. Guichardus, excusam Parisiis Anno Domini 1606. Istius editionis exemplar penes me nunc est, viri cujusdam dam doctissimi magníque in his literis judicii miniatulis ceris notatum, & multis obelis passim confossum: qui etiam fronti libri supra titulum, suum de opere universo judicium his verbis praescripsit: Penus μεˊλεωεʒλογίας ἀνεqυ- πνεᴦ. Quin tamen ab authore istius Harmonia multa solerter & felicitér indagata sint, multa acutè & ingeniosè, aliis antea non observata, in lucem eruta, valdè iniquus (meo judicio) fuerit, qui non agnoscat: neque aliter opinor de eo judicaturus fuerit vir ille doctus quisquis fuerit, si publicè ferenda sententia fuisset. sed extorsit illi (viro minimè inepto, ut suspicor, & otioso) tanta vis ineptissimarum conjecturarum, tum aliarum fortasse, tum earum praecipuè, quae solâ literarum transpositione (quoferè uno constat artificio liber iste) nituntur: de quo quidem genere quid nobis videatur, & quatenus admittamus, exemplis appositis, posteà fusius exponemus. Ut omittam quod linguarum quarum arcana se referare profitetur author, planè ἀμύνῃ& ex Lexicis totus pependisse, ex multis deprehenditur, ut cum יוד rubus,
units.tr: The very learned Stephanus Guichardus published an etymological Harmony of many languages, printed at Paris in the year of our Lord 1606. I now have a copy of this edition, marked in tiny wax-like notes by a certain man, very learned and of great judgement in these matters, and everywhere pierced with many obeli. This man also wrote at the head of the book, above the title, his judgement on the whole work in these words: Penus ... ἀνεqυπνεᴦ. Yet to deny that much has been skilfully and felicitously investigated by the author of this Harmony, and that much has been brought to light sharply and ingeniously, not observed by others before, would be, in my judgement, very unfair. Nor do I think that learned man, whoever he was, would judge otherwise if a public verdict had been demanded. But such a great mass of most foolish conjectures has been wrung from him (a man, I suspect, not at all foolish or idle), some perhaps of other kinds, but especially those which rest solely on the transposition of letters (on which device this book almost entirely depends). What we think of this kind, and how far we admit it, with examples set out, we shall explain more fully later. To omit that the languages whose secrets the author professes to unlock depended wholly on lexicons and were entirely unexamined, as is clear from many instances, such as when with יוד rubus,

units.la: ꝰ rubus, errore ut videtur inductus typographico, legit ꝏ fened: & inde fentis Latinum deducit, quasi non re magis, quàm voce geminum. His eò libentiùs impertiendos lectores duxi; non quòd de merito authoris quicquam detractum velim, quem & re & voluntate de publicâ re literariâ bene meritum agnosco; sed ut moniti, non omnia illius promiscuè & ἀβαωρίως ampleƈterentur, quod quosdem, aliàs non ineruditos, nimis quàm pueriliter ac putidè facere comperimus.
units.tr: ꝰ rubus, apparently led astray by a typographical error, he reads fened, and from that derives the Latin fentis, as if the two were twins not in substance but only in sound. I thought it more willing to point these things out to readers, not because I wish to detract anything from the author's merit, whom I acknowledge to have deserved well of the public republic of letters both in achievement and in intention, but so that readers, having been warned, would not embrace all his claims indiscriminately and without discrimination, which we have seen some men, otherwise not unlearned, do all too childishly and foolishly.

units.la: Quanquam autem in hoc Etymologico argumento multa jam ab aliis prudenter ac cautè tradita & constituta non nescìam; qui tamen certis limitibus ac metis infinitam istam licentiam circumscribere ac coercere conatus sit, nondum mihi repertus. Digna certè res summi alicujus ab eruditione & judicio viri curâ. Nos interim aliquid hîc pro virili nostrâ tentabimus: saltem quantum ad præsens institutum sufficiat. Ab universalibus autem quibusdam incipiemus, quibus semel positis & impetratis, cætera quæ volumus facilius impetrabimus.
units.tr: Although I am not unaware that many have already prudently and cautiously set out and established much on this etymological subject, I have not yet found anyone who has tried to restrict and curb that boundless licence within fixed limits and boundaries. It is certainly a matter worthy of the care of a man of the highest learning and judgement. Meanwhile I shall make an attempt here, as far as I can, at least so far as is enough for my present purpose. I shall begin with certain general principles, and once these are laid down and granted, the rest that we want will be granted more easily.

units.la: Hoç
units.tr: Hoc

units.la: Hoc igitur primum esto ; Linguas alias esse matrices, alias traduces : matrices autem alias ἀπλᾶς & simpliciter ; alias χρητί, & ut vulgò dicunt, respectivè.
units.tr: Let this then be the first point: some languages are mothers, others daughters; and the mother languages are some absolute and simple [ἀπλᾶς], others relative [χρητί], and, as people commonly say, relatively so.

units.la: Hoc uno postulato os illis obturatur, qui negant ulla esse verborum ex aliis verbis origines, & derivationes : omnes etymologias, pro rebus commentitiis habent & imaginariis : qualis ille nescio quis cujus meminit VanderMylius, qui Belgicum neque ex Latino nasus ortum esse adduci non poterat ut concederet. Sanè si id ille dixisset, ex sola verborum affinitate non sequi, ut alterum ex altero ductum sit, cùm talia ex casu multa contingant, & in omnibus (ut posteà videbimus) linguis aliqua reperiantur ; aliquid dixisset. Sed ille sine dubio, ut ex Mylio colligere est, fuit ex isto genere, quales aliquos jam olim fuisse diximus, qui totum hoc studium ut rem inanem & ἀνυπόστατον respuerent. Cæterum, cum sint ex illo numero, qui imperitiâ potiùs peccant, quàm certâ animi destinatione & ἀφελείας, quæ multis pro judicio est ; ita puto, qui tales, erroris sui convinci poterunt. 'Rogem saltem an Italicum naso, ex Latino nasus ortum concedat? Negat, & fortuitum pertendit? Ergo & illa fortuita, capo, capelli, crine, dente, occhi, orecchi, mano, piedi, ungie, diti, atque alia pleraque quæ sunt propria corporis vocabula: quæ qui audiet, & cum Latinis conferet, quis tam perfrictæ præfractæve frontis, ut casui tribuere sustineat? Ab Italis ad Gallos transfibimus; ab illis ad Hispanos, & in utraque lingua tantam vim verborum cum Latinis convenientium proferemus, ut quisquis non est invictæ pertinaciæ, tanquam tot clarissimorum testium copia obrutus, manus facile porrecturus sit. Quanquam ut quis rectè judicet, non illi tantum similium verborum numerus spectandus, sed non minùs rerum ipsarum verbis expressarum cognatio & propinquitas: ut si quæ linguæ in numeris à primo ad decimum usque conveniant, quanquam decem tantùm sint numero verba, stultum sit id casu tribuere, sed vel alterām ex alterā mutuatam esse; vel ambas ex una aliquā; vel etiam ex diversis, quæ tamen ex unā aliquā primitùs, primitus, credendum fit. Me certè vel ista quatuor tam cognata vocabula, Father, Mother, Brother, Daughter, Anglis Persísque communia, ad suspicandam, quae postea à folertioribus deprehensa creditur in infinitis aliis, Persicae linguae cum Germanicâ cognationem plus movissent, quàm vel centum alia, quibus nulla inter se significationis affinitas.
units.tr: By this one postulate the mouths are stopped of those who deny that words have any origins or derivations from other words, and who regard all etymologies as invented and imaginary things. This is like that man, I know not who, whom VanderMylius mentions, who could not be brought to concede that the Dutch nasus-word was not derived from the Latin nasus. Certainly if he had said that it does not follow from mere similarity of words that one is derived from the other, since many such resemblances arise by chance, and in all languages (as we shall see later) some are to be found, he would have said something. But he undoubtedly belonged, as may be gathered from Mylius, to that class of people, of whom we have said that there were some even long ago, who rejected this whole study as an empty and unreal thing. Yet since they are among those who sin rather through ignorance than through a settled purpose of mind and simplicity, which for many passes as judgement, I think such people can be convinced of their error. Let me at least ask whether he concedes that the Italian naso is derived from the Latin nasus. He denies it and insists it is accidental? Then are those also accidental: capo, capelli, crine, dente, occhi, orecchi, mano, piedi, ungie, diti, and many others which are the proper names of the body parts? Who, on hearing these and comparing them with the Latin, has a brow so hardened and so stubborn that he can bring himself to attribute them to chance? From the Italians we shall pass to the French, and from them to the Spaniards, and in each language we shall produce such a store of words agreeing with the Latin that whoever is not of unconquerable obstinacy, overwhelmed as by so many most distinguished witnesses, will readily be ready to hold up his hands. Yet to judge rightly, one must consider not only the number of similar words, but no less the kinship and closeness of the things themselves expressed by the words: for example, if certain languages agree in the numbers from one to ten, then although there are only ten words, it would be foolish to ascribe this to chance, but one must believe either that one borrowed from the other, or both from some single source, or even from different sources which nevertheless were originally one. Certainly those four such closely related words, Father, Mother, Brother, Daughter, common to the English and the Persians, would have stirred in me a suspicion of kinship between the Persian and the German tongue, which (as is later believed to have been discovered by the more skilful in countless other cases) more than a hundred other words would have done, which have no affinity of meaning among themselves.

units.la: Alia tamen eorum ratio, quae propria sunt artium vocabula: ut & ventorum, coelíque plagarum propria: quae multis linguis ex alia occasione communia esse probabile est. Pergamus igitur: Romanorum cum Germanis per multa saecula, odia, bella, foedera, & cujuscunque generis commercia, Romanae Historiae pars non minima: à Graecis quoque tum Historicis, tum Geographis narrata. Quorum omnium certissima monumenta superstunt hodieque, urbes celeberrimae, aut urbium à Romanis in Germania conditarum rudera, inscriptiones, opera, coloniae: ut solem meridie lucere pariter neget, qui de eo dubitet. Ex hac permixtione non aliter potuisse, quin multa in Germanismum verba Latina irrepserint, ac paulatim pro genuinis ac germanis obtinuerint, quotidiana (si nihil aliud) populorum hodiernorum ac linguarum historia ab invitis extorserit. Judicio esse praeterea non unum aut alterum, qualia casui possunt adscribi; sed bene multa, aut mere Latina, aut a Latinis non adeo detorta & deflexa, quin ipsa suam prae se ferant originem: qualia corporis propria (praeteristud neas,) coop,caput; ooze, auris; tant,dens; palme, palma; baert, barba; mamme, mamma; arm, armus; lippe, labium; aliaque id genus. Addo, cum Galli dicant nes; Itali, nasō; Angli, nose; Belgae, neus; Germani, nas; Latini (ut alios omittam) nasus: non est credibile tam varios populos in eandem appellationem casu incidisse: quod si non casu; quaerenda ergo origo, quam Latinam esse multiplex ratio evicerit. Ceterum cum neus illud ex Latina asserimus origine, non id ita intelligendum, quasi de immediata afferamus origine. Potest enim fieri ut Belgae, ut & infinita alia, a Gallis acceperint. Non minus enim quam Angli pessima illa & patriæ linguæ injuriosissimâ (quantum quidem ex Kyliani farragine ad calcem Lexici sui colligere licuit) adscititio- rum & exoticorum verborum <bl>ꝛɑκoζn- ʎi</bl> Belgæ laborant. Hoc tamen verbum prisci potius ævi crediderim, cum & veteres Angli <bl>nase</bl> pro naso dixerint; unde & <bl>nafthpzlo</bl>,nares,illis: ut Psalmi CXIII. v. 14. <bl>nafthpzlu bt bab-</bl> <bl>bath</bl>, <bl>and nā geftingeatb</bl>. (Nares habent, & non odorabunt.) Verbum <bl>ftincken</bl> olim medium, quod tam in bonam quàm malam partem accipiebatur, ut vir doctus in Notis ad Willeramum. At olim etiam activè seu neutraliter usurpatum fuisse, hinc videtur colligi posse.
units.tr: Their other reasons, however, concern the proper terms of the arts, and likewise the names of the winds and the quarters of the sky. It is probable that many languages shared these on some other occasion. Let us go on. The dealings of the Romans with the Germans over many centuries, including hatreds, wars, treaties and every kind of commerce, form no small part of Roman history, and Greek historians and geographers also recorded them. The most certain monuments of all this survive even today: famous cities, or the ruins of cities the Romans founded in Germany, inscriptions, public works and colonies. Anyone who doubted this would be as foolish as one who denied that the sun shines at noon. From such mixing it could not but happen that many Latin words crept into German and gradually prevailed as if they were genuine and native. The daily history of present-day peoples and languages, if nothing else, forces this even on the unwilling. Moreover, the evidence is not one or two cases that might be put down to chance, but many words that are either purely Latin, or not so twisted and bent away from Latin that they fail to show their own origin. Such are the names of body parts (to pass over the rest): kop, caput; oor, auris; tant, dens; palme, palma; baert, barba; mamme, mamma; arm, armus; lippe, labium; and others of that kind. I add that the French say nes, the Italians naso, the English nose, the Belgians neus, the Germans nas, and the Latins (to omit others) nasus. It is not credible that so many peoples happened by chance to fall upon the same name. If it was not by chance, then its origin must be sought, and many considerations have shown that it is Latin. Yet when I claim that neus derives from Latin, this should not be taken to mean that I assert an immediate origin. It is possible that the Belgians, like countless other peoples, took the word from the French. The Belgians suffer no less than the English from that wretched and most injurious habit of mixing their native tongue with adopted and foreign words, as far as one may gather from Kilian's farrago at the end of his dictionary. I would, however, rather think this word is of an older age, since the old English also said nase for naso, whence they had nosthyrl for nares, as in Psalm CXIII. v. 14: nosthyrlu hi habbath, and na gestincgeath. (They have nostrils, and they will not smell.) The verb stincan was formerly middle, taken in both a good and a bad sense, as a learned man observes in his notes on Willeram. But that it was also once used actively or intransitively, this seems to be gathered from here.

units.la: Hoc exemplo possunt aliæ quoque traduces linguæ matricibus suis facilè asseri, ut omnibus palam liqueat, alias esse matrices, alias traduces linguas. Sed præter verborum singulorum similitudinem, est aliud quoque quo id colligatur magni ponderis argumentum; quod ex Grammaticis scilicet observationibus & Analogiis: ex Idiotismis & particularum, puritati & proprietati sermonis infetvientium, consideratione ducitur.
units.tr: By this example, other languages too that are called offshoots can easily be shown to descend from their mother tongues, so that it is plain to all which are the mothers and which the daughters. Besides the similarity of single words, there is another argument of great weight by which this is established, drawn from grammatical observations and analogies, and from the consideration of idioms and of particles which serve the purity and propriety of speech.

units.la: In constituendis autem Matricibus linguis, multa consideranda veniunt; & multæ cautiones & conditiones adhibendæ, priusquam aliquid statuatur, ne res reprehensioni aut calumniæ obnoxia fit. Linguam simpliciter & absolutè Matricem ego quidem unam agnosco, Hebraicam. Ex hac aliæ omnes initium sumpserunt; sed itaáit in aliis majorem multò quàm aliis mutationem dudum passa fit. Hoc autem quomodo contigerit, ignorato (ut alibi dicebamus) confusionis linguarum modo, & in tanta temporum istorum & migrationum caligine, nostrum non est definire. In plerisque linguis hodiernis manifesta reperiri primævæ vestigia, certum est: sed ab omnia à primis illis incunabulis, an ex recentiore cum Judæis commercio nonnulla, non hic dispiciendi locus.
units.tr: In identifying mother tongues, however, many matters must be weighed, and many cautions and conditions observed before anything is settled, lest the claim lie open to objection or calumny. I myself recognise only one language as the mother tongue in the simple and absolute sense, Hebrew. All the others took their beginning from it; but in some of them far more change has long since occurred than in others. How this came about, given (as I have said elsewhere) the confusion of tongues and the great darkness of those times and migrations, it is not for us to define. That in most present-day languages clear traces of the primeval tongue can be found is certain; whether some of them came from those first beginnings or from more recent dealings with the Jews, is not a question to be examined here.

units.la: Cæterùm matrices linguæ aliæ pro aliis temporibus, quæ traduces eædem non minùs dici possint. Inter Europæ matrices linguam Græcam & Latinam constituit Jos. Scaliger: qui tamen alibi Græcam linguam veterem ferè totam ex Hebraica fluxisse, ut & Latinam ve-tergnt terem ex Græca non semel agnoscit: quod & ipsa res evincit. At ex iis linguis multas hodiernas ortas esse æquè certum est: ut ex Latina, Gallicam, Italicam, Hispanicam; & Valachicam; de quâ Stephanus Zamosius, in Analectis lapidum & antiquitatum Daciæ: ex Græcâ, hodiernam illam, quæ quamvis hodieque Græcæ (sed vulgaris) nomen retineat, non minùs à vetere Græcâ discrepat, quàm Italica à Latinâ: hanc igitur vulgarem; præter alias, quorum in quibusdam Insulis quæ quondam Græcis subditæ, usus obtinet: de quibus Edw. Brerewoodus Anglus in erudito de linguis & religione hodiernis syntagmate. Pari modo inter linguas matrices minores linguam Wallicam Scaliger enumerat: nec fine causâ, si præsentis temporis ratio habeatur, cùm tantùm ab omnibus aliis Europæ linguis differat. Eadem tamen, si vetera spectentur tempora, & verum sit quod plerique censent, easdem suisse, aut certè simillimas, veterem Gallicam & Wallicam; veterem itidem Gallicam, Germanicæ fuisse Dialectum; non matrix lingua, sed pro-
units.tr: Moreover, different languages are mothers at different times, and the same ones may equally be called offshoots. Among the mother tongues of Europe, Joseph Scaliger set up Greek and Latin. Yet elsewhere he acknowledges more than once that old Greek flowed almost entirely from Hebrew, and that old Latin was in part derived from Greek; the facts themselves prove this. But it is equally certain that many modern languages arose from those tongues: from Latin, French, Italian, Spanish and Valachian (on which Stephanus Zamosius writes in his Analecta of Dacian Stones and Antiquities); from Greek, that modern tongue which, though it still keeps the name of Greek (or rather of the vernacular), differs from old Greek no less than Italian differs from Latin. This vernacular, besides others, is used in certain islands once subject to the Greeks; Edward Brerewood, an Englishman, describes these in his learned treatise On Present-Day Languages and Religion. In the same way Scaliger counts Welsh among the lesser mother tongues, and not without reason if one considers the present state, since it differs so much from all the other European languages. Yet if one looks at older times, and it is true, as most hold, that old French and Welsh were the same or at least very similar, and that old French was a dialect of German, then it is not a mother tongue but must be regarded as an offshoot

units.la: M pago Germanicæ statuenda est.
units.tr: of German.

units.la: Secundò, alias esse legitimas & genuinas matrices ; alias ex casu & ex parte tantùm. Nullam autem esse linguam, aut vix ullam, præter Hebraicam, quæ non ex pluribus matricibus, partim legitimis, & ut ita dicam naturalibus ; partim fortuitis repetenda sit.
units.tr: Secondly, some mother tongues are legitimate and genuine, while others arise only by chance and in part. Indeed there is no language, or hardly any, except Hebrew, that does not derive from several mothers, partly legitimate and, as one might say, natural, and partly accidental.

units.la: Exemplo sit Hispanica lingua. Hispani veteres priusquam à Romanis subigerentur, propriam linguâ habebant à Latinâ (nemo dubitat) planè diuersam. Eam fuisse quæ Cantabrica hodie vocatur, & in usu remanet apud Vascones, sive Biscainos, cis & ultra Pirenæos montes latè sparsos, (inclytum ob conseruatam per tot sæcula libertatem & linguam populum). res ipsa suadet, & luculentis argumentis adstruxit vir doctissimus, Arnoldus Oihenartus Mauleofolensis ; qui etiam vim magnam verborum collegit Cantabricorum, quæ hodiéque aut integra aut paululum immutata agnoscit & usurpat lingua Hispanica. Quanquam, ut hoc obiter dicam; de Hispanico verbo aχușena, lilium, (quod in ipso limine occurrit) afsentiri illi non possum, cùm Hebraicam potiùs potius sapiat originem, nec à scapi rectitudine sic dictum sit, sed ex numero sex foliorum, quibus constat lilium. Post Romanos proximè Gothi Hispaniâ potiti sunt. Tum Saraceni, gens Arabica, Hispaniam in suam potestatem fere universam redegerunt, ac per plura & ipsi saecula ibi regnarunt. Postea iterum Gothi: sed hoc nihil ad nos hïc. Quis igitur aliter expectet, quàm ut Gothicæ sive Germanicæ; ita & Arabicæ dialecti multæ sint in lingua Hispanica? Quæ tamen fateor, non temporibus semper metienda sunt; cùm unius interdum sæculi possessio majorem longè inferat mutationem, quàm alio loco aut tempore plurium. Non enim omnium, in propriâ linguâ propagandâ, vincentium par studium: non æqua omnium in retinendâ suâ, qui victi, pertinacia: ut multas alias temporum & morum circumstantias omittamus, quæ ex historiis petenda sunt. Hebræi certè in Ægypto per trecentos plus minùs annos primò hospites, deinde servi, propriam linguam puram illibatámque (uno fortasse aut altero verbo, quo linguam suam locupletárunt; pletarunt, excepto) confervarunt. Iidem in Babylonia non totis centum annis captivi, adeo patriam linguam dedidicerunt, ut interpretibus, ( quod ex sacrâ discimus Historiâ) opus haberent, cùm Hebræa legerent. Sed ut ad Hispanicam linguam redeamus; ut Cantabrica illius; ita Gothica & Arabica sunt quì collegerunt. Joseph.Scaliger Arabica, quartam admodum partem conficere censebat: sed hoc alii negant. Sed quicquid ejus sit, matrix Hispanicæ sola Latina vulgò audit, ob longè majorem ex illa lingua numerum verborum. Ita Hispanica : & pariter res habet in aliis linguis,aut omnibus, aut certè plerisque.
units.tr: Let Spanish serve as an example. The ancient Spaniards, before they were subdued by the Romans, had a language of their own, quite different from Latin (no one doubts this). It was what is now called Cantabrian, and it remains in use among the Basques, or Biscayans, scattered widely on both sides of the Pyrenees, a people famous for keeping their liberty and language through so many centuries. The matter itself suggests this, and the very learned Arnold Oihenart of Mauléon has established it with clear arguments. He also gathered a great number of Cantabrian words, which the Spanish language still acknowledges and uses, either whole or slightly altered. Yet, to say this in passing: I cannot agree with him about the Spanish word axuchena, the lily, which occurs at the very threshold of his book. It smacks rather of Hebrew origin, and it was not named from the straightness of the stem, but from the number of six petals of which the lily consists. After the Romans, the Goths next possessed Spain. Then the Saracens, an Arabic people, brought almost the whole of Spain under their power and themselves reigned there for many centuries. Later the Goths came again, but this has nothing to do with us here. Who, then, would expect otherwise than that, just as there are Gothic or German dialects, so there should be many Arabic dialects in the Spanish language? I admit, however, that these cannot always be measured by time. The possession of a single century can sometimes bring a far greater change than the possession of several centuries in another place or age. For not all conquerors have an equal zeal for spreading their own language, nor do all the conquered have the same stubbornness in keeping theirs; to say nothing of the many other circumstances of time and custom, which must be sought in histories. The Hebrews, certainly, while in Egypt for some three hundred years, first as guests and then as slaves, kept their own language pure and unimpaired (except perhaps for one or two words with which they enriched it). Yet in Babylon, where they were captives not a full hundred years, they so unlearned their native tongue that they needed interpreters, as we learn from sacred history, when they read Hebrew. But to return to the Spanish language: as some have gathered Cantabrian words from it, so others have gathered Gothic and Arabic ones. Joseph Scaliger thought the Arabic made up about a quarter, but others deny this. Whatever the truth, the Latin alone is commonly held to be the mother of Spanish, because it supplies by far the greater number of words. So it is with Spanish, and likewise with other languages, either all or at least most.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Tertiò, in vestigandis originibus magna ratio habenda analogiæ, tum communis, tum peculiaris cujusque linguæ.
units.tr: Thirdly, in investigating origins, great weight must be given to analogy, both the general analogy common to all languages and the particular analogy of each language.

units.la: Analogiam voco quicquid in verborum formatione, vel literarum permutatione, ratione aliquâ, in natura vel consuetudine fundatâ, nititur. Hoc omnibus linguis commune est, ut in verbis aliæ sint literæ radicales, aliæ accidentales & asciticiæ. Ut terminationes, sive breviores, sive longiores, non sint de essentia verborum. Ut literæ ejusdem aut affinis potestatis facillimè permutentur inter se: nullæ autem tam dissimiles sint & alienæ, quarum vel euphoniæ causâ, vel aliunde, permutatarum exempla non reperiantur.
units.tr: I call analogy whatever in the formation of words, or in the interchange of letters, rests on some principle grounded in nature or in usage. This feature is common to all languages: in words some letters are radical and others incidental and added. Endings, whether short or long, do not belong to the essence of a word. Letters of the same or a related sound are very easily exchanged for one another, and there is hardly any letter so unlike and foreign that examples of its exchange cannot be found, whether for the sake of euphony or for some other reason.

units.la: De literarum Græcarum ( nec alia feré Græcarum ratio, quàm aliarum quarumlibet ) potestatibus, affinitatibus, & mutuis permutationibus, accuratissimè tractavit Caninius in doctissima Grammatica. Multa quoque Julius Cæsar Scaliger in eximio De lingua Latina opere. Extat & Johannis Passeratii, viri doctissimi, De literarum inter se cognatione ac permutatione liber, in quo quicquid in isto genere exemplorum lingua Latina suppeditat, accuratissimè congeritur, & ordine digeritur alphabetico. Alii passim multa, quicunque de verborum vel obiter, vel composito tractant origine. Nos alió festinamus.
units.tr: Caninius treated the sounds, affinities and mutual exchanges of the Greek letters with great exactness in his learned Grammar; the Greek system is hardly different from that of any other language. Julius Caesar Scaliger also has much on this in his admirable work On the Latin Language. There is too a book by the very learned Johannes Passeratius, On the Kinship and Interchange of Letters, in which everything that the Latin language supplies in this kind of example is gathered with great care and arranged in alphabetical order. Many others, wherever they treat the origin of words, whether briefly or at length, have much to say. We, however, are hurrying on to other matters.

units.la: Cæterùm præter communem linguis analogiam, suas habet quæque lingua proprias consuetudines & idiotismos, quorum observatio magni usus in scrutandis verborum originibus. Latinis auribus litera x vastior visa est: cujus fugâ axillam in alam contraxerunt: quam literam etiam è maxillis & taxillis & vexillo & paxillo consuetudo elegans latini sermonis (Ciceronis ùtor verbis) evellit. Huc igitur recurrendum est; & qui hoc nescîret, frustra se in verborum istorum ala, mala, velum, talus, & si quæ sunt ejusdem generis aliorum etymis inveniendis torquebit. Eandem literam quòd plane respuerent aut ignorarent veteres Britanni Latina quæ per x efferebantur, aliter ipsi scribere coacti sunt. Hinc tascia, pro taxatio, in nummis; doctissimus ut dudum Camdenus observavit. Contrà Latini cùm nullum verbum (ut nec Græci) in χ Græcum sive ch terminent, Germani autem veteres hodiernique plurima: χ illud finale Germanorum in verbis Germanicis in r suum verterunt, unde obscurata multorum proprionum nominum (ut Beat. Rhenanus aliíque rectè docuerunt) origo. Itali quoque Latinam x sæpè emolliunt in sc.ut in esco, ex exeo; sciagurato, ex exauguratus; aliisque quæ Caninius observat fervat. Interdum tamen in simplex f. vertunt; ut in efalare, efajperare; (exhalare, exasperare;) & similibus. Et nescio an inde fit, quod litera f apud illos (contrà quàm apud Græcos & Anglos veteres, apud quos initió sæpe vacat per ἐπίνθεσιν,) tum verbis tum nominibus pluribus præpositá, vim habet particulæ privativæ; ut fbarbato, imberbis; fbrigliato, ffrenato, effrenis: ffortunnato, infortunatus: ffare, fconfortare, fdentare: destruere, affligere, edentare, & aliis similibus plurimis. Ea certè vis & Latini x in multis, ut in exanguis, exuccus, exanimis, aliisque. sed undecunque illud s fit, sive ex x, sive dif, (cum dicant etiam diffare, profare, &c.) propria ea ac satis mira non assuetis, Italici sermonis videtur esse consuetudo. Syri & Chaldæi verbis exoticis à litera f cum consonante alterâ copulatâ incipientibus, præponunt N cum vocali: Chaldæi quidem cum vocali i. (quæ tamen interdum cum a etiam efferuntur:) Syri cum e: quos Galli & Hispani,(in quibusdam:) nescio an & alii imitantur; ut efchole, eftomac, efperer, eftudier: effera, efpirituat,&c. ut Cambrobritanni Chaldæos yfgoll, yftuminog, &c.
units.tr: Besides the analogy common to languages, however, each language has its own customs and idioms, and the observation of these is of great use in searching out the origins of words. To Latin ears the letter x seemed too harsh, and to avoid it they contracted axilla into ala. Elegant Latin usage (I borrow Cicero's words) removed this same letter from maxilla, taxillus, vexillum and paxillus. We must therefore keep this in mind, and whoever does not know it will waste his effort in trying to find the etymologies of ala, mala, velum, talus and any other words of that kind. Because the early Britons could not stand this same letter, or did not know it, and so pronounced Latin words written with x in another way, they were forced to write them differently: hence tascia for taxatio on coins, as the learned Camden long ago observed. On the other hand, since the Latins (like the Greeks) never end any word in the Greek χ, or ch, while the early and modern Germans do so in very many words, the Germans changed that final χ in German words into r, and from this the origin of many proper names has been obscured, as Beatus Rhenanus and others have rightly taught. The Italians too often soften the Latin x into sc, as in esco from exeo, and sciagurato from exauguratus; Caninius notes other cases of this. Sometimes, however, they change it into a simple f, as in efalare and efasperare (for exhalare and exasperare) and similar words. I wonder whether it is from this that among them the letter f, placed before many words and nouns (unlike the early Greeks and English, among whom an initial vowel was often given a prefixed letter by epenthesis), has the force of a privative particle: fbarbato for imberbis; fbrigliato and ffrenato for effrenis; ffortunnato for infortunatus; ffare, fconfortare, fdentare, meaning destroy, afflict, deprive of teeth, and many other similar words. Certainly the Latin x has this same force in many words, as in exanguis, exsuccus, exanimis and others. But wherever that s comes from, whether from x or from dis (since they also say diffare for profare, etc.), this peculiar and rather strange custom seems to belong to the Italian language, which is not familiar to others. The Syrians and Chaldeans, when foreign words begin with f joined to another consonant, put n with a vowel in front: the Chaldeans with the vowel i (though sometimes it is also pronounced with a), the Syrians with e. The French and Spanish (in some words) imitate them, and I do not know whether others do too, as in efchole, eftomac, esperer, estudier, effera, espirituat, and so on. In the same way the Welsh Britons say yfgoll and ystuminog for Chaldean words.

units.la: Solent Hispani in multis Latinis vocabulis quæ à duplici confonante, quarum posterior est litera l. incipiunt, præcedentem quoq; confonantem(præcedentem autem confonantem à sequente d'ꝑovia causâ in multis verbis affici & mutari, Arabicæ & pluribus aliis linguis commune est: qualia Italorum lotta,vetta; pro,luͤlta,vetlura,&c. imò & integram syllabam;qualia Græcorum xdμoç, pro xdlάμop, &c.) in alterum l mutare: quod duplex ll Hispanicum dicuntur Lusitani in ch vertere:ut Pluvia, Hisp.lluvia; Luf.chuva. Planus, H. llano, L. chano. Clavis, H. llave,L.chave,&c. Mira Bavarorum consuetudo, qui pro ll.sequente r. substituunt Ilb; dicentes Ilb rltel lt ein guts Ilbrentlen:quod alii Irtlopbel lt ein gut Ilrentlin: ut ex Fabiano Franco Gesnerus; ex Gesnero VánderMylius. Spinosiora hæc quibusdam & subtiliora fortasse videbuntur: quæ tamen sunt ejusmodi, sine quorum diligenti observatione stultum sit & temerarium rei sese Etymologicæ ullatenus immiscere. Anglı
units.tr: In many Latin words beginning with a double consonant, of which the second is l, the Spanish are accustomed to change the preceding consonant, and it is a custom common to the Arabic and many other languages to alter the consonant that comes before (the preceding consonant being altered by the following one for the sake of ease in many words, as with the Italians' lotta and vetta for lutta and vettura, and even a whole syllable, as with the Greek xdμoç for xdlάμop, and so on) into another l. The Portuguese are said to change the Spanish double ll into ch: Spanish lluvia, Portuguese chuva (rain); Spanish llano, Portuguese chano (plain); Spanish llave, Portuguese chave (key), and so on. The Bavarians have a strange custom, substituting Ilb for ll before a following r, saying Ilb rltel lt ein guts Ilbrentlen where others say Irtlopbel lt ein gut Ilrentlin; this is reported by Gesner from Fabian Franck, and by Vander Mylius from Gesner. These points will perhaps seem rather thorny and subtle to some, but they are of such a kind that without careful attention to them it is foolish and rash to meddle at all with etymology.

units.la: Ioan.
units.tr: John.

units.la: Angli veteres v. confonans Latinorum videntur ignorasse: in diphthongum u (quemadmodum & Græci; ʼOυαλςεἰαν©-, ʼOυεαπαδιαν©-, &c.) sive duplex u. (quod n.Germanicum à nonnullis appellatur)vertentes: ut vallum, a wall; vir, were; velle, to will; væ, woe; ventus, winde; volvo, to wal- low; vastus, waste; vibrare, (quod apud Festum vibrasse:) to warble, &c. Interdum in f: ut vadum, a foord; at vadare, ut prius, to wade. Ita & vannus a fan; at vannire,ut supra, to win- now; volare, to flie; vitiæ, fetches; vellus, a fleece; vulgus, folcks; & id genus alia. Quæ autem à Gallis posteriores Angli acceperunt, in iis Gallorum quoque pronuntiationem retinuerunt. Nec alia promptior ratio antjqua & legitima à novitiis istis & spuriis dignoscendi. Wine, antiquum: Saxonicè, win. at wiñger,(acetum)recens: quod olim ecede. Wineparð, antiquum quidem verbum; sed recens scriptura: nam olim, wineparð: apud Willeramum Abbatem, wingarden. Ita woym, antiquum; Sax. woyme: at, vermine, recens. Wirta, vel wyrta; viridia,
units.tr: The Old English writers seem to have not known the Latin consonant v. They rendered it either by the diphthong u (as the Greeks also do) or by a double u, which some call the German w: vallum, a wall; vir, were; velle, to will; væ, woe; ventus, winde; volvo, to wallow; vastus, waste; vibrare (which in Festus is vibrasse), to warble, and so on. Sometimes they rendered it as f: vadum, a foord; but vadare, as before, to wade. So too vannus, a fan; but vannire, as above, to winnow; volare, to flie; vitiæ, fetches; vellus, a fleece; vulgus, folcks; and other words of that kind. But the words that the later English took from the French they also kept with the French pronunciation. Nor is there any readier way to tell the old and legitimate words from these newcomers and counterfeits. Wine is old: in Saxon, win. But wiñger (vinegar) is recent; formerly it was ecede. Wineparð is indeed an old word, but its spelling is recent: formerly it was wineparð, and in Abbot Williram it is wingarden. Likewise woym is old, Saxon woyme; but vermine is recent. Wirta, or wyrta (green things): old.

units.la: ʼ . , viridia, herbæ ; vetus : at bert, ab eodem viridi, sed recentius, pro pabulo viridi, in Legibus quas vocant Forestìcis. Vidua, a widow, antiquum ; Sax. a wiudape : at bopde, vacuus, ex Gallico, (quod ab eodem vidua:) vuide.
units.tr: Herbs: old. But bert, from the same green root, is more recent, meaning green fodder, in the laws called the Forest Laws. Vidua, a widow, is old; Saxon a wiudape. But bopde, empty, comes from French (from which also vidua, vuide).

units.la: tini voci calidus notionem affinxere. quod autem pro calidus ipsi bott substituerunt, in eo genium linguæ suæ & propriam analogiam secuti sunt. At verbum kalt (frigidum) si ad Latinum contrariæ significationis propius accedat, id ex merâ συγχεία est; cùm longè alia sit origo, ut alibi docebimus. Quanquam ne summo viro falsò hoc crimen impingatur, valdè vereor. Certè in illo De linguâ Latinâ capite ad quod rejicimur, exprobrationis ullius, nedum falsæ, neq; vola, neq; vestigium. Id tantùm dicit, ibi quidem, Scaliger, eadem verba diversas apud diversos, interdum & contrarias habere significationes: cujus inter alia multa verbum kalt, exemplum ab illo adducitur. Sed hoc obiter. Ex Græcis autem plurima pari ratione derivata sunt; quæ suis locis in verborum collectione indicabuntur. Quanquam ex his ipsis quæ supra posita sunt, quædam fortasse, ut halme, & hempe, ex Græcis κάννα & κάλαμο immediatè sumpta sint.
units.tr: calidus. But in substituting bott for calidus they followed the genius of their own language and its proper analogy. As for the word kalt (cold), if it comes closer to a Latin word of opposite meaning, that is mere chance; its origin is quite different, as we shall show elsewhere. Yet I greatly fear that this charge is being laid falsely on so great a man. Certainly in that chapter of De lingua Latina to which we are referred there is not a trace or vestige of any reproach, let alone a false one. There Scaliger says only that the same words have different and sometimes contrary meanings among different peoples, and among many examples the word kalt is cited. But this in passing. Many Greek words have been derived in the same way; these will be pointed out in their places in the collection of words. Yet some of the words mentioned above, such as halme and hempe, may perhaps have been taken directly from the Greek [κάννα] and [κάλαμος].

units.la: Ejusmodi plurima sunt in omnibus linguis, quæ diligenter illis attendenda, qui cum judicio ista tractaturi sunt. Plurima sunt, fateor, in omnibus linguis, singularis cujusdam juris, quæ ad nullam possunt analogiam referri: plurima quoque, quæ præter & contra aliorum consuetudinem. Putidissimum sit, meâ sententiâ, ad regulas omnia velle redigere, vel exigere: sed nec minùs temerarium, consueta & obvia negligere, & in tritis & expeditis acumen ingenii experiri: Τύπτω, τίτυπται, τύπτῶ. Λείπω, λέλοιπα, λοιπὸς. Κύπτω, κέκυφα, κυφὸς. Λέγω, λέλογα, λόγ. Τίμνω, τέτμηκα, τέμνω. Quis igitur dubitat, quin pari ratione, Θάπτω, (vel ut olim τάφω) τέταφα, ταφῶ? Non ego certè, neque stuporis invidiam metuam, si negem quod vir doctus pertendit, τὸ τάφω, ex Hebraico קבר ductum. Nemo facile repudiet, inquit, nisi γόον ἀπορρῶ, & qui nescit quam sepulcra etiam veterum mire signata fuerint, aut ornata, ἐπίγραφή, lapide, statua, aliis. Mos ille, res in confesso est: sed ut ab illo more τάφω vox sumpta sit, nulla cogit necessitas: non magis certè quàm Latina sepulcrum, cùm tamen & Latinis mos ille non minùs solemnis. At ipsum Θάπτω haud dubiè est Hebraicum, idq; fecundum ἀναλογίαν: ut à ϥλγ, λυπέω; & alia passim, in quibus prima gutturalis absorbetur: ita à qυϗ quod tegere,obruere (ex quo videtur & nostrum to burie manasse) significat, est τάφω, vel θάπτω sepelio.
units.tr: There are very many such things in all languages, and those who intend to treat these matters with judgement must attend to them carefully. I admit that all languages have many peculiarities which cannot be referred to any analogy, and many which run against or contrary to the usage of others. In my view it would be the height of foolishness to try to reduce everything to rules or to insist on it, but it is no less rash to neglect what is customary and obvious and to try the sharpness of one's wit on worn and familiar material: τύπτω, τέτυπται, τυπτῶ [τύπτω, τέτυπται, τυπτῶ]; λείπω, λέλοιπα, λοιπός [λείπω, λέλοιπα, λοιπός]; κύπτω, κέκυφα, κυφός [κύπτω, κέκυφα, κυφός]; λέγω, λέλογα, λόγ [λέγω, λέλογα, λόγ]; τέμνω, τέτμηκα, τέμνω [τέμνω, τέτμηκα, τέμνω]. Who then doubts that by the same reasoning θάπτω (formerly τάφω), τέταφα, ταφῶ [θάπτω, τέταφα, ταφῶ]? I certainly do not, and I do not fear the charge of ignorance if I deny what that learned man maintains, that τὸ τάφω is derived from the Hebrew קבר. "Nobody will easily reject it," he says, "unless he is at a loss for words [γόον ἀπορρῶ], and he who does not know how wonderfully the tombs even of the ancients were marked or adorned with inscription, stone, statue and other things." That custom is admitted, but no necessity compels us to hold that the word τάφω was taken from that custom, any more than Latin sepulcrum was, although the custom was no less solemn among the Latins. But θάπτω is undoubtedly Hebrew, and by analogy: as ϥλγ gives λυπέω, and in many other places where the first guttural is absorbed. So from qbr (קבר), meaning to cover or bury over (from which our English bury seems also to have come), comes τάφω or θάπτω, to bury.

units.la: Verbum Germanicum buss pro domo, (quod Angli boufe) ex Græco οἶκος profectum multis contendit Abr. Vander-Mylius, vir doctissimus & candidissimus, in luculento De lingua Belgica syntagmate. Cum autem longius id petitum videri possit, opponit (si quis id objiciat) tum alia, tum exemplum verbi Hispanici hazer, quod ex Latino facere fluxisse cum nemo dubitet, non minus ab origine suâ recesserit. Poterat & alia facilè, ut boga, ex folium: huz, ex fascis; quæ non minus remota. Sed non est eadem ratio. Nam quamvis hazer, à facere, &c. sono quidem multum differt; certissimâ tamen nituntur hæc analogiâ. Ita enim passim Hispani Latinum f in h. convertunt. Hinc fœmina, illis hembra: fames, hambre: focus, huigo: fugere, huir: aliáque non pauca. At ut ex Græco οἶκος, Germanicum buss emergat, nulla, quod quód sciam, suadet analogia: nisi ad metathesin confugiamus, & ex οἶxΩ primo fiat χοῖΩ; ac tum demum bufs, vel bœufe. Atqui nihil opus eò confugere, cùm præsto sit Latinum casa; ex quo mutata pro more (de quo diximus) primâ consonante in aspirationem, facilè emergat buts vel bœufe. Quanquam (ne quid Lectorem celem) quoties solemne illud Romanorum fores domorum pultantium heus, heus, apud Comicos lego; subit suspicio ex hâc ipsâ pultantium formulâ domibus ipsis (qualia multa contingunt) apud Anglos veteres appellationem remansisse.
units.tr: The German word buss, meaning house (which the English call boufe), is derived by many from the Greek οἶκος, as argued by Abr. Vander-Mylius, a very learned and fair-minded man, in his brilliant treatise De lingua Belgica. Since this may seem to be sought too far afield, he answers any objector both with other examples and with the Spanish hazer, which, since no one doubts it flowed from Latin facere, has departed no less from its origin. He could easily have adduced others, such as boga from folium and huz from fascis, which are no less remote. But the case is not the same. For although hazer, from facere, and so on, differs much in sound, these forms nevertheless rest on a most certain analogy. Spaniards regularly convert Latin f into h: hence fœmina becomes hembra, fames hambre, focus huigo, fugere huir, and not a few others. But so far as I know no analogy suggests that the German buss emerges from Greek οἶκος, unless we take refuge in metathesis and first make from οἶκος the form χοῖκος; and only then bufs or bœufe. Yet there is no need to take refuge there, since the Latin casa is at hand; from it, the initial consonant being changed into an aspirate as is customary (as I have said), buts or bœufe readily emerges. Still, lest I hide anything from the reader: whenever I read in the comic poets that solemn Roman cry of those knocking at doors, heus, heus, a suspicion arises that from this very formula of knocking the name was kept among the old English for the houses themselves (as many things happen).

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Postremò, cùm non sint ultra 24. plus minùs (non enim id nunc agimus) literæ, ex quibus, sive pluribus, sive paucioribus, velut elementis omnia omnium linguarum vocabula formantur; non posse aliter fieri, quia multa in linguis diversis occurrant vocabula, quæ sono & scripturâ sint eadem, aut valdè affinia: multa quoque quæ non sono tantùm, sed & potestate sive significatione partim eadem sint, partim valdè similia: quorum nulla alia præter generalem illam quam attigimus, particularis ratio reddi potest alia, quàm pura puta ᵓʃχυεία, sive casus.
units.tr: Finally, since there are no more than twenty-four letters, more or less (for we are not treating that point now), from which, whether many or few, as if from elements, all the words of all languages are formed, it cannot be otherwise: many words occur in different languages which are identical or very closely alike in sound and spelling; many more which are partly the same in sound and also in power or meaning, and partly very similar. For none of these can be explained by any other particular reason than the general one we have touched on, namely sheer chance or accident.

units.la: Hac unâ conclusione corruunt infinitæ ob quam malè audit hoc studium etymologiæ, (aut pseudologiæ potiùs:) quæ nullâ aliâ veri similitudine nituntur, quàm aliquâ soni similitudine. Nam ad significationem quod attinet, vix est ut ulla sint tam alienæ per se significationis verba, quin aliquid subtiliter excogitari possit, quo propinquitas inducatur aliqua, quæ levibus ingeniis ad etymologiam sufficiat. Nam quid dicam de illis, quæ tamen occurrunt passim, & ex quibus grandia consurgunt volumina, quæ ex literis partim inversis, partim mutatis? sed objiciat aliquis: An igitur nullæ in verborum scrutandis originibus admittendæ metathefes? nullæ literarum mutationes? De hoc mox videremus. Istud interim quod modò dicebamus de verbis & sono & significatione χ᾽ ᵓʃχυεία iisdem, quia magni momenti est, quò magis liqueat, exemplis aliquot illustrabimus.
units.tr: This one conclusion overthrows the countless things on account of which this study of etymology (or rather pseudology) has a bad name, since they rest on no plausibility other than some similarity of sound. For as to meaning, there are hardly any words so alien in themselves that something cannot be subtly devised by which some connection can be induced, enough for etymology to light wits. What shall I say of those which nevertheless occur everywhere, and from which huge volumes arise, built partly from letters reversed and partly from letters changed? But someone may object: are no metatheses to be admitted in searching out the origins of words? No changes of letters? We shall see about that shortly. Meanwhile, since what I have just said about words identical in both sound and meaning is of great importance, I shall illustrate it with some examples, so that it may be clearer.

units.la: ᾿Αβίῳ; Græcum est, diversarum, ipso & & contrariarum significationum verbum. Nam & inopem exponunt, & divitem : tum etiam robustum, & invalidum : praeterea, brevem aevi ; & ut alii, longaevum : quorum omnium ratio cuivis in Graecis non hospiti ex diversa potestate (intensiva vel privativa) particulae α : tum vero diversitate radicis βια, vel βίΦ, manifesta est. ‏יְהוּדָה‏ Hebraicum, quo, sono & scriptura nihil potest affinius esse, pauperem & egenum, ex radice quae desiderare ( quis autem magis quàm pauper & egenus?) significat, notat. Cui autem fano, vel minima subloriatur suspicio vel Graecum ex Hebraico ; vel Hebraicum ex Graeco, quorum, ut diximus, tam manifestae rationes originis, ortum esse ? Eadem ratio sequentium : quod semel moneo, ne idem saepius repetendum sit.
units.tr: ἄβιος [ἄβιος] is a Greek word with diverse and even contrary meanings. For they explain it as poor and as rich, and again as robust and as feeble; besides, as short-lived, and, according to others, as long-lived. The reason for all of these is plain to anyone who is not a stranger to Greek: it lies in the differing force of the particle α, intensive or privative, and then in the difference of the root βια or βιο. The Hebrew word [אֶבְיוֹן], which has nothing more akin to it in sound and spelling, means poor and needy, from a root meaning to desire (and who is more in desire than the poor and needy?). But who in his right mind would suspect, even in the slightest degree, that either the Greek is from the Hebrew or the Hebrew from the Greek, when the origin of each, as we have said, has such manifest reasons? The same holds for what follows, which I note once here so that it need not be repeated often.

units.la: ‏יְהוּדָה‏ Heb. judex, moderator. Graece σωτὴρ, servator. Quid vero magis competit vero judici, quàm aequâ juris administratione, ab injuriis potentiorum minùs potentes servare ? Sed & ‏אֲדוֹן‏ dominatus, quàm bene cum μυσηεία significatione convenit, cùm omni ferè dominatui sua constat arcana, sine qui-bus
units.tr: The Hebrew יְהוּדָה means judge, ruler. The Greek σωτήρ means saviour. What indeed suits a true judge more than, by an even-handed administration of justice, to protect the lesser from the injuries of the greater? But the Hebrew אֲדוֹן, lord, also agrees well with the meaning of [μυστήρια] mysteries, since almost every lordship has its secrets, without which

units.la: Heb. ‏יְהוּדָה‏ — Hebrew glosses as printed in the body of this paragraph. bus vix ullum diuturnum imperium.
units.tr: hardly any lasting dominion [could stand].

units.la: Mensura, Latinum, opinor, à metiendo verbum: Ut & קשורה Hebraicum; quod tamen cum Latino & sono & significatione planè congruit.
units.tr: Mensura is Latin, I think from metiri, to measure. So too the Hebrew [מִשּׂוּרָה], which nevertheless agrees completely with the Latin both in sound and in meaning.

units.la: Pellex, Lat. ab eadem quâ & illex, origine. At פלגש (à quo Græcum παλλακὴ & παλλακή) ejusdem soni & significationis, Hebraicum.
units.tr: Pellex is Latin, from the same origin as illex. But פִּלֶגֶשׁ (from which the Greek παλλακή comes) is Hebrew, of the same sound and meaning.

units.la: Sufficere, & sufficientia, Latina. שפע seu ספק Chaldaicum, idem planè.
units.tr: Sufficere and sufficientia are Latin. The Chaldean שֶׁפַע or סַפֵּק is exactly the same.

units.la: Passus, à passis pedibus, quòd in gradiendo pandantur sive extendantur pedes; si non certa, certè probabilis origo. פשר & יפע Hebraeis quoque idem.
units.tr: Passus, a step, is from passis pedibus, because in walking the feet are spread or extended; if not a certain origin, at least a probable one. פשר and יפע [פשר, יפע] are the same among the Hebrews too.

units.la: Βύκερως, corniger. unde Lucretio, Buceria graecè; & bucera facla. Hebraeis בקר non bovem tantùm significat; sed & boves, armentum.
units.tr: Βύκερως means horned, [βύκερως]. Whence Lucretius has buceria from the Greek, and a form bucera was made. The Hebrew בקר means not only ox but also oxen, a herd.

units.la: ἐξ ἐνιαυτοῦ, festum dedicationis: ἐγκαινίζω, dedico, renovo. Heb. חנך dedicare; חנכה dedicatio, initiatio.
units.tr: ἐξ ἐνιαυτοῦ [ἐξ ἐνιαυτοῦ] means the feast of dedication; ἐγκαινίζω [ἐγκαινίζω] means to dedicate, to renew. Hebrew חנך means to dedicate; חנכה means dedication or initiation.

units.la: Ἀφορίζειν, separare: פרש & אפריש, idem.
units.tr: ἀφορίζειν [ἀφορίζειν] means to separate. The Hebrew פרש and אפריש mean the same.

units.la: Caldarium, Latinis, à calore foci, (ut θερμαντήριον Græcis:) ex quo Gal. chaudron. Heb. קדרה, ab atrore: נ ישן ὾ωϳy Hebr. quod onus significat, peperit fortasse Latinum onus: & Graecum ἐνΘ-. At Anglicum burden, ex Latino burdo, quamvis eadem ratio, absurdum deducere: cùm φέρειν, (ex quo, to beare:) & φορτίον propiora.
units.tr: Caldarium, in Latin, is from the heat of the hearth (as θερμαντήριον is for the Greeks), whence French chaudron. The Hebrew קדרה comes from blackness, from soot. The Hebrew word meaning burden perhaps gave birth to Latin onus. But the English burden, from Latin burdo, although the reasoning is the same, is absurd to derive that way, since φέρειν (whence English to bear) and φορτίον are closer.

units.la: Ναχελὶς, ναχελία, ναχελίζω, tarditas, imbecillitas, &c. quàm propè accedunt ad Gallicum, non chalant: ut & Latinum fœneus (quid homo fœneus olim, docet Asconius in Ciceronem:) ad faineant; ex quàm diversâ origine?
units.tr: Ναχελὶς, ναχελία, ναχελίζω [ναχελίς, ναχελία, ναχελίζω] mean slackness, feebleness, and so on. How closely they approach the French non chalant, not caring!
