And likewise Latin fœneus (what homo fœneus once meant Asconius teaches in his commentary on Cicero) approaches faineant. Yet from how different an origin!

units.la: Base, usitatissimum Anglis verbum, nominibus adjectum vilitatem & turpitudinem rei notat. Idem verbum per modum Interjectionis usurpatum; usitatissima quaedam est quasi abominandi seu exprobrandi formula. Quàm antiquum sit nescio: origo certè, Gallicè intelligentibus non obscura. Atqui eundem quoq; apud Arabes usum habet haec vocula, ut Erpenii in Alcoranum notae me docuerunt, بيس Bifa (inquit ille) vocula est quâ cum admiratione quâdam rei malitia indicatur, q.d. O quàm malum! contrarium Nihma, O quàm bonum! Ut Anglici ex Gallico idiomate: ita Arabicorum istorum verborum ex Hebraico non minus manifesta origo. Quò etiam respexit Hesychius, cùm Βάζω, ἀιχμάζω exponit: ne quis & Græcos ita locutos suspicetur. De Anglici tamen verbi (ut verum fatear) origine ampliùs cogitanti, eò propè adducor ut ampliandum putem. Movet autem me, quód Gallos suum illud bas sic usurpare (per interjectionem, vel exclamationem) nunquam memini: tum verò quod etiam Anglicum blush, pudore suffundi, manifestam prodit ex Hebraico בוש, ex quo Arabicum illud manavit, originem. Illis autem assentior qui Gallicum bas, ex Græco βάσις ortum conjiciunt.
units.tr: "Base", a word very commonly used by the English, when added to nouns, denotes the worthlessness and baseness of a thing. The same word, used as an interjection, is a very common formula of loathing or reproach. How old it is I do not know; its origin, at any rate, is not obscure to those who understand French. Yet this little word is also used among the Arabs, as the notes of Erpenius on the Koran have taught me: Bifa (he says) is a particle by which the wickedness of a thing is indicated with a certain wonder, as if to say "O how bad!", the opposite of Nihma, "O how good!" As the English derive theirs from the French idiom, so the origin of these Arabic words is no less plainly Hebrew. Hesychius also had this in view when he glosses bazo [βάζω] and aichmazo [ἀιχμάζω], lest anyone suspect that the Greeks spoke in this way too. Yet, to tell the truth, when I think more deeply about the origin of the English word, I am almost led to think it must be traced further back. What moves me is that I never remember the French using their bas in this way (as an interjection or exclamation); and also that the English "blush", to be suffused with shame, clearly reveals its origin in the Hebrew root meaning to be ashamed [בוש], from which the Arabic word came. I agree, however, with those who conjecture that the French bas is derived from the Greek base [βάσις].

units.la: רדה Hebr. dominari, castigare: Latinum, erudire: Anglicum, rod[?]: sono & significatione (quis non agnoscat?) cognatissima: originibus disjunctissima.
units.tr: Hebrew רדה [rada]: to rule, to chastise. Latin erudire, to instruct. English rod[?]. In sound and meaning (who would not recognise it?) they are very closely related, but in origin they are quite unconnected.

units.la: Talia, ne longus nimis sim, אפתם, Græc. ἀφελῶ; Lat. affatim: שרבים ἀχηρον: פרחמים, οἱ ἀφθοι[?], & alia plurima quæ quæque lingua suppeditat. Hæc γλῶσσα[?] sufficient hîc; cùm quivis paulò attentior multa ex propriâ possit observatione supplere.
units.tr: To avoid being too long, here are some such cases: Hebrew אפתם [?], Greek ἀφελῶ, Latin affatim, enough; Hebrew שרבים, Greek ἀχηρον; Hebrew פרחמים, Greek οἱ ἀφθοι[?]; and many others that each language supplies. These Greek words [γλῶσσα?] will suffice here, since any reasonably attentive reader can add many more from his own observation.

units.la: Concludimus igitur : verborum cum rebus, quæ naturâ censentur,in multis convenientiam observare est ; éstque utilis ea, jucundáque (ut mihi quidem semper visum ) speculatio. Prolem parentes, & illos proles ipsa oris & indolis similitudo sæpe prodit, ut multis aliàs ignaris, solus indicium fecerit consptus. Ita quidem olim gravissimus & facundissimus Basilius in notissimâ Epistolâ : Ἐπήγων σε ἡ ἔπισολῶ ἄσαρ ὅτι τοῦ ἡ φίλων παῖδας ἐκ τῆς ἐπαγγελμένης ἀνδρὸς ὁμοίοτητ ὡς τοῦ ἀπόσπα γνώσεται. Quo pertinet illud Poëtæ suavissimi, Sit suo similis patri Mallio, & facile insciis Nosci tetur ab omnibus.
units.tr: We conclude, then, that in many cases one may observe a correspondence between words and the things they name, which are regarded as natural. This study is useful and pleasant, at least as it has always seemed to me. Parents are often revealed by their children, and children by the likeness of face and disposition, so that to many who are otherwise unobservant the resemblance alone is evidence. So long ago the most serious and eloquent Basil, in his well-known letter, wrote: "I learn from your letter that the children of our friend will be known from the likeness of the father who is absent" [Ἐπήγνων σε ἐκ τῆς ἐπιστολῆς ὅτι τοῦ ἡμετέρου φίλου παῖδας ἐκ τῆς ἐπαγγελμένης ἀνδρὸς ὁμοιότητος ὡς τοῦ ἀπόντος γνώσεται]. To this belongs the line of that most charming poet: "Let him be like his father Mallius, and he will easily be recognised by all who do not know him."

units.la: Quæ quidem opinio apud veteres adeò obtinuit, ut ipse non veritus sit Aristoteles pronuntiare partum parenti dissimilem,monstrum quoddam esse ; nec pro legitimo naturæ fœtu habendum. si quis tamen hoc κατὰ φύσιν fisus , aliis omnibus indiciis & γνωρίσματα insuper habitis, de genuinâ prole pronunciare præsumet ; quantam, quæso, in rebus confusionem inducet? Quàm multos ille & legitimos abjudicabit ; & spurios, adulterinos, ignotos, pro veris ac genuinis adoptabit? Ut autem in rebus, non una similitudinis species : alia enim oris & vultus ; alia indolis & ingenii : ita in verbis, alia soni similitudo, alia analogiæ, quæ plerumque certius est χρῆσιμον. Ut ex.gr. verbum Hispanicum hijo, quod filium significat, si ex sono pronuntiamus, Græcum υἱός statuamus originem ; si ex analogiâ illâ Hispanicæ linguæ propriâ, de quâ suprà ubi de etymologiâ verbi hoüse, vel huis, egimus ; Latinum filius ; quam veriorem esse etymologiam & illud suadet, (quod etiam ad analogiam referri poteft) quòd lingua Hispanica fit Latinæ tradux, ut ex infinitis ejus linguæ verbis ex Latinis variè inflexis, cuivis liquere queat : Græcæ autem linguæ perpauca, si fortè aliqua, in eâ reperiantur.
units.tr: This opinion was so widely held among the ancients that Aristotle himself did not hesitate to declare that an offspring unlike its parent was a kind of monstrosity and not to be regarded as a lawful product of nature. Yet if anyone, trusting in this "according to nature" [κατὰ φύσιν], and setting aside all other indications and marks [γνωρίσματα], should presume to pronounce on true offspring, what great confusion, I ask, would he cause in things? How many lawful children would he disown, and how many spurious, adulterine, or unknown children would he adopt as true and genuine? In things, however, there is not one kind of likeness: one is of face and features, another of disposition and mind. So in words there is one kind of similarity of sound, another of analogy, and the latter is generally the more reliable criterion [χρῆσιμον]. For example, if we judge by sound the Spanish word hijo, meaning son, we shall set the Greek υἱός as its origin; but if we judge by that analogy proper to the Spanish language, which we discussed above when treating the etymology of house or huis, we shall set the Latin filius. That the latter etymology is truer is also suggested by the analogy (which may also be referred to analogy) that Spanish is a translation of Latin, as anyone can see from the countless words of that language derived from Latin words variously inflected, whereas very few, if any, Greek words are found in it.

units.la: Sed ut ad exempla illa redeamus, & quod inde nobis hîc præcipuè propositum fuit : si talia passim in omnibus linguis occurrunt ; quid illi, quæso, censendi sunt, qui verborum origines, ( ubi nulla alia ratio, quæ suadeat,) ex mera & multiplici captant literarum transfpofitione & permutatione ? Aut verò mirum fit multa hâc viâ graffantibus succedere ; cùm tam multa reperiantur ejusdem plané & soni & significationis, quæ tamen certum fit diverfæ gentis & familiæ esse ? Quæ tamen non eò dicuntur à me, quòd omnem literarum metathefin aut adeò permutationem in explorandis originibus explodendam censeam.: quibus negatis omnis ferè concidat etymologica res necesse est. Nos multa in hoc genere postea afferemus. Vel linguas ex Latinâ ortas, fi quis morofior est, infpiciat. Quàm crebræ, quàm manifestæ, permutationes ejusmodi,& metathefes occurrunt ? Eadem ratio verborum Latinorum ex Græcis ortorum; aut Græcorum ex Hebraicis. Cùm tamen ex adverso certum fit, fi ubivis admittatur ista ratio, quamlibet ex aliâ quavis linguâ derivari posse linguam, ac post multiplicia ludibria, eò tandem rem necessariò redituram, ut nihil in hoc genere certum fit: plane, aut otiosis ista relinquenda, aut præfigendi certi limites, quos intra debeant consistere, qui in istis occupantur. De quo donec alii peritiores statuunt, mihi hæc in mentem veniebant.
units.tr: But to return to those examples, and to what we have mainly proposed here: if such cases occur everywhere in all languages, what, I ask, must we think of those who seek the origins of words, where no other reason recommends them, through mere and manifold transposition and exchange of letters? Is it any wonder that many people who proceed in this way succeed, when so many words are found of exactly the same sound and meaning, yet are certainly of different peoples and families? I do not say this because I think that every metathesis or exchange of letters should be rejected in the search for origins; if that were denied, almost all etymology would necessarily fall. I shall give many examples of this kind later. Or let anyone who is too stubborn look at the languages derived from Latin: how frequent and how obvious such exchanges and metatheses are! The same holds for Latin words derived from Greek, or Greek from Hebrew. Yet on the other side it is certain that if this method is admitted everywhere, any language can be derived from any other, and after many absurdities the matter must inevitably come to this, that nothing in this field is certain. Either such things must be left to idlers, or fixed limits must be set within which those who occupy themselves with them ought to remain. Until others more skilled decide on this, these thoughts came to my mind.

units.la: Primum igitur hoc erit, ut affinitas aliqua propior linguarum ex quâ & in quam translata verba perhibentur, demonstretur.Cujus quidem demonstrationis ratio duplex est: vel ex historiâ: aut fi historia (quod potest accidere) deficit, saltem ex congerie verborum, vel tantâ,ut ipsa multitudo indicio fit; vel talium, ut res ipsa apud æquos & idoneos judices fidem faciat, casu ista accidere non potuisse.
units.tr: The first step, therefore, will be to demonstrate some closer affinity between the languages from which and into which words are said to have been transferred. The method of demonstrating this is twofold: either from history, or, if history fails (which can happen), at least from a collection of words, either so large that the very multitude is the evidence, or of such a kind that the thing itself will convince fair and competent judges that it could not have happened by chance.

units.la: Proximum erit, ut modus adhibeatur, & admissâ(fi forte)unâ aut alterâ, aut etiam pluribus,sed quibus & sonus favet, (quâ in re adhibendum est judicium aurium)& significatio vel eadem, vel certè valde propinqua, per metathefin derivatione, adblandiente subtilitate illecti nimis non evagemur & excurramus.
units.tr: The next step will be to apply a method, so that, admitting perhaps one or another, or even several, instances in which the sound also agrees (in this matter the judgement of the ear must be used), and the meaning is either the same or at least very close, we do not wander off and run beyond bounds, enticed by an excessive cleverness in deriving words by metathesis.

units.la: Exemplo fit radix Hebr. ꜣ ex qua statim λέφος & λφω, obviâ ratione, & rectâ, ut ita dicam, lineâ, emergunt. Nam de Alphonfo quod addunt, mihi non persuadent. Germani viderint, qui sibi vindicant. Jam si quis ex inversis in פלא literis, πι πηλυ quoque eliciat, quanquam non desit propriæ originis non improbabilis ratio, & alia sint verba Hebraica, ex quibus minori opere repeti possit; non ego tamen valde repugnaverim. At pergunt qui suæ licentiæ nullas metas posuere: & φύλη, inquiunt, ab hoc (imaginario, inverso:) פלא: sed & πόλλας, & πῶλ©. At cur non potius φύλη, ἀ φύω, ut φύλλον: & πόλλας non à fictitio illo, sed vero verbo פלש, ut doctissimus Junius censebat; vel certè ץלפ, ut alii? Ad τὸ πῶλ© quod attinet, facilè concesserim originem exoticam sapere: inepta enim videtur, quam Grammatici Græci asserunt. Eruditissimus Caninius ex Punico verbo (mihi, fateor, ignoto) Phala deducit. Sed hoc nihil ad imaginarium istud. Pergunt tamen. Etiam Pales, Dea rustica, ab eâdem, inquiunt, origine. At quanto probabilius alii ex Syriaco פלחא ex quo פלחרא agricola, vinitor? Pergamus: Πελὸς, Græcum, satis vulgari significatione, quod niger Latinis. Hinc πέλιοι λύκοι, πελίας ὀνῷ, πέλλης
units.tr: As an example, from the Hebrew root ꜣ [ʾ-l-p?] there at once emerge, by an obvious and straight, so to speak, line of reasoning, the Greek λέφος and λφω. For what they add about Alphonsus does not convince me; let the Germans see to it, since they claim him. Now if someone also draws πι, πηλυ, from the letters of פלא inverted, although there is no lack of a not improbable reason for its proper origin, and there are other Hebrew words from which it could be derived with less labour, I would not strongly object. But those who have set no limits to their licence go on: "φύλη," they say, "comes from this (imaginary, inverted) פלא"; but also πόλλας and πῶλος. But why not rather φύλη from ἀ φύω, as φύλλον? And why πόλλας not from that fictitious word, but from the real word פלש, as the most learned Junius thought, or certainly from ץלפ, as others think? As for πῶλος, I would readily concede that its origin smacks of the foreign: the derivation the Greek grammarians assert is absurd. The most learned Caninius derives it from a Punic word (which I confess is unknown to me), phala. But this has nothing to do with that imaginary word. Yet they go on. Pales, the goddess of the countryside, also comes, they say, from the same origin. But how much more probably others derive it from the Syriac פלחא, from which comes פלחרא, a farmer or vintner! Let us proceed. Πελός, a Greek word, with the quite common meaning "dark," which Latin speakers render as niger. Hence πέλιοι λύκοι, πελίας ὄνος, πέλλης [dark wolves, dark ass, dark].

units.la: πηλὸς βῶς: quibus color istorum animalium fuscus seu ater indicatur. Extant autem ista vix ullibi, nisi apud Grámaticos veteres; quorum testimonium ut ut verum sit, an verba tamen eorum ab omni mendâ, ut in re obscurâ & insolente, libera ad nos pervenerint, dubitari potest. Sed ut & ista recte habeant, quis tamen Etymologistam nostram, quicum nobis hîc res est, docuit πελειὰς, ἀπαθῶς, idem esse quod πελειὰς ὄνος? aut πέλλην, quod βῶν πέλλω? sed opinor quia πελειὰς, ἀπαθῶς, pro columba nigrâ: ideò & illa quoq; similiter. Quasi quis ita disputet, quia Negro absolutè sumitur pro Æthiope; cur non & Niger absolutè pro cane nigro? His igitur postulatis ac concessis, quid superest quàm ut imaginarium πελειὰς, i.e. ὄν⊖; & imaginarium πέλλη, i.e. βῶς; ab imaginario ΝΤΩ deriventur? Sed nondum finis. Nam βέπηλ⊖ quoque apud Suidam in Aristophane exponitur ὄν⊖. Unde igitur & illud πηλ⊖, nisi ex isto fœcundissimo ΝΤΩ? Certè quantum ex verbis quæ profert Suidas, datur colligere, βέπηλ⊖ non fuerit ὄν⊖, animal proprie; sed homo duri corii, quale illorum debet esse, qui sunt magni luctatores, aut qui cum bobus, & tauris audent congredi: quae Græci verbi vis est.
units.tr: Πηλὸς βοῦς: by these the dusky or black colour of those animals is indicated. These words, however, hardly occur anywhere except in the ancient grammarians; and although their testimony may be true, one may doubt whether their words have come down to us free from every corruption, as is likely in an obscure and unusual matter. But even granting that these things are right, who has taught our etymologist, with whom we have to do here, that πελειὰς, without qualification, is the same as πελειὰς ὄνος, or that πέλλην is the same as βοῦν πέλλω? But I suppose he reasons that since πελειὰς, without qualification, means a black dove, so the others too are similar. As if someone argued: because Negro is used absolutely for an Ethiopian, why should Niger not also be used absolutely for a black dog? Granted these assumptions and concessions, what remains but that the imaginary πελειὰς, that is ὄνος, and the imaginary πέλλη, that is βοῦς, should be derived from the imaginary ΝΤΩ? But the end is not yet. For βέπηλος also is explained in Suidas, in Aristophanes, as ὄνος. Whence, then, that πηλός as well, unless from that most fruitful ΝΤΩ? Certainly, as far as one can gather from the words Suidas quotes, βέπηλος was not properly an ass, an animal, but a man of tough hide, such as those must be who are great wrestlers, or who dare to contend with oxen and bulls; this is the force of the Greek word.

units.la: Unum adhuc restat, idque in hoc genere palmarium, ex quo lector intelligat, quo iflorum processerit audacia. Gallicum palfroy (ut & Anglicum palfrey) cum proprie de equis insignioribus qui ad pompam, aut honorem vectorum manu ducuntur, usurpetur, quis non iis assentiatur qui ex Gallicis verbis par le frain compositum verbum existimant? Certè, etiam in Historia Æthiopica mentio fit sex puerorum nobilium, qui vocantur Legameneos: i.e. pueri ad capistrum, quòd equitantis Neguz latus proximè stipent & ambiant. Palfhredus, vel Palefredus, vulgò equus dicitur. Germanicè, palfernter: Gall. Palefrenier: Italicè autem, palafrenero, dicitur anteambulo; ut Kylianus notat in suo Etymologico. alii fervitore di stalli exponunt. Quædam vulgata Lexica τὸ palefrenier, manducus interpretantur. Quod si aliquâ vetere nititur authoritate, & est manducus (nam à manduco longè aliud) quasi manuducus, optimè vim nominis expresserit. Non me latet aliunde quoque ab aliis arcesli verbum. Sed de inversâ illa * radice Hebraicâ, quis unquam, nisi per somnium, cogitasset? Idem tamen alibi postea in ꟾꟾꟾ ex Latino veredus (q. d. parave-redus, &c.) non multò probabilius deducit: cùm (praeter alia:) veredus, equus sit cursorius, aut venaticus, proprie; palfrsdus autem, qui ad pompam lentè ducitur, aut incedit.
units.tr: One more example remains, and it is the best of this kind, so that the reader may see how far these men's boldness went. The French palfroy (as also the English palfrey) is used properly of the finer horses that are led by hand in procession or to honour a rider. Who would not agree with those who think the word was compounded from the French par le frain, "by the bridle"? Certainly the Ethiopian History also mentions six noble boys called Legameneos, that is, pueri ad capistrum, "boys at the halter", because they stand close beside and surround the side of Neguz as he rides. Palfhredus or Palefredus is commonly said to mean a horse. In German it is palfernter; in French Palefrenier; in Italian palafrenero means a forerunner, as Kilian notes in his Etymologicon, though others explain it as fervitore di stalli, "a stable servant". Some common lexicons translate palefrenier as manducus. If that rests on some old authority, and manducus (which is quite different from manduco) stands for manuducus, "led by the hand", it expresses the force of the name very well. I am not unaware that others derive the word from elsewhere. But who would ever have thought of that inverted Hebrew root, except in a dream? Yet he later derives the same word elsewhere, in the Belgian section, from the Latin veredus (as if parave-redus, etc.), and that is not much more probable: since, among other things, veredus properly means a running or hunting horse, whereas palfredus is a horse led or ridden slowly in procession.

units.la: Ex his paucis judicet lector quid de caeteris ipsi sperandum sit; ut non mirum, si viro illi gravi ac docto bilem moverit. Quanquam non negem in quibusdam optimè illi acumen succedere. Et per me quidem plus meruerit ille gratiae pro paucis illis; quàm invidiae pro pluribus dissimilibus. Cum Varrone dicam, sed paululum mutatis verbis: De originibus verborum, qui aliqua dixerint commodè, potiùs boni consulendum; quàm qui multa nequiverint, reprehendendum. Qui rara & sublimia captant, audendum illis est. Magnorum ingeniorum ut plurimùm haec labes. Hinc tamen alii non pauci, quamvis impares ingenio, pari tamen audaciâ se gerentes, hoc exemplo se tuentur. Sunt qui Etymologiis, quas per allusionem vocant, multum delectantur. Ut qui diabolum, quasi qui duos bolos, &c. Quanquam plures, opinor, haud probant; ego tamen eâ conditione excusarem, ut qui talia sectantur, saltem inter veras Etymologias non miscerent, ne vel imperitis, cum veris temerè confundentibus, errandi, ne dicam delirandi; severioribus autem totum hoc studium deridendi ansam praebeant. Nulli certè de eo pejus merentur, quàm qui vertunt in ludibria: Et veritatem rerum (quod Etymologiæ verbum pollicetur) professi; ad alia converti, vim veritatis omnem dum ludunt, elidunt.
units.tr: From these few examples the reader may judge what we can hope for in the rest, and it is no wonder that this learned and serious man should have stirred up bile. Yet I would not deny that in some matters his cleverness succeeds very well, and for my part he deserves more thanks for those few successes than blame for the many dissimilar failures. I shall say with Varro, though with slightly changed words: "In the origins of words, we ought rather to be grateful to those who have said some things well, than to blame those who have failed in many." Those who seek rare and lofty things must be allowed to dare; this is for the most part the failing of great minds. Yet not a few others, though unequal to it in talent, but acting with equal boldness, shelter themselves behind this example. Some take great delight in etymologies which they call per allusionem, "by allusion", as those who derive diabolum ("devil") as if it were duos bolos, "two throws", and so on. Most people, I think, do not approve of these; yet I would excuse them on this condition: that those who pursue such things should at least not mix them among true etymologies, lest they cause error, not to say delirium, to the unlearned, who confuse them carelessly with the true ones, and give the more serious readers cause to mock the whole enterprise. Certainly none deserve worse of this subject than those who turn it into a joke: having professed the truth of things, which is what etymology promises, they turn to other matters, and while they play, they destroy all the force of truth.

units.la: Neminem libenter nominem, nisi ut laudem. Sed nec peccata reprehenderem, nisi ut aliis prodessem. Libenter igitur Joh. Avenarium hoc loco commemorabo: quem ego judico in hoc argumento modestissimè, & optimo judicio versatum esse. De Germanicis ejus, meum non est judicium. In Græcis autem ex Hebraicis eruendis, pauca ejus hactenus, obiter & ex re natâ tantum versanti mihi occurrerunt, in qui-bus bus sagacitatem suam non optimè probaret. Ut mirer in tanto Hebraizantium numero, qui Hebraicas origines tam studiosè consectantur, majori in pretio non esse istud opus, quo nihil in isto genere perfectius hactenus in lucem prodiisse persuasum habeo.
units.tr: I name no one gladly, except in order to praise him. Yet I would not rebuke faults, except to be of use to others. I therefore gladly mention here Johann Avenarius, whom I judge to have worked on this subject with the greatest modesty and excellent judgement. On his German studies I do not pass judgement, since that is not my business. But in drawing Greek words from Hebrew, the few instances I have come across so far, while I have been working on this only in passing and as occasion arose, show that his acuteness is not at its best. I am surprised that, among so many Hebraists who pursue Hebrew origins so eagerly, this work is not more highly valued, since I am convinced that nothing more perfect in this kind has so far appeared in print.

units.la: Hoc ultimum, quod jam suprà monuimus, nec frustra tamen hîc inculcabitur; ut ἀναλογίας semper, quantum fieri potest, ratio habeatur; neque ad remota referamus, cujus in propinquo causa est.
units.tr: This last point, which we have already mentioned above, will not be pressed here in vain: that analogy [ἀναλογίας] should always be taken into account as far as possible, and that we should not refer to distant things what has its cause nearby.

units.la: Atque hæc hactenus in genere præfati sumus; quæ quanquam per se talia, ut non abs re lectoris non unius fortasse quocunque loco futura sint: aliis autem nonnullis, qui facilè carere poterant, intempestiva videri possint: nobis tamen necessaria visa sunt, à quibus, priusquam Saxonicas Etymologias aggrederemur, inciperemus. Id jam nobis curandum scilicet, ut quæ deinceps superstructuri sumus, iis quæ præstruximus, congrua sint & consentanea; de quo lectoris erit judicium.
units.tr: So much for what we have said by way of preface in general. These things, although they are of such a kind that they may perhaps be useful to the reader wherever they occur, may seem out of place to some others who could easily have done without them. Yet they seemed necessary to us, and we had to begin with them before we undertook the Saxon etymologies. It is for us to take care that what we shall build upon these foundations agrees and harmonises with what we have laid down; the judgement on this rests with the reader.

units.la: Linguam igitur Saxonicam, sive Anglicam veterem, linguæ Græcæ traducem esse, aut magnâ cum lingua Græca cognatione conjunctam esse, persuasit inprimis vis verborum aut planè eorundem, aut solâ quasi dialecto differentium: talium inquam verborum vis, quanta sola sufficere posset ad vel averfissimos & morosissimos, modò qui sint harum rerum planè non imperiti, convincendos.
units.tr: That the old Saxon, or English, language is a descendant of Greek, or is closely related to Greek, has been shown above all by the force of words that are either identical or differ only as if by a dialect. I mean that the force of such words is so great that it alone would be enough to convince even the most hostile and obstinate, provided they are not wholly unskilled in these matters.

units.la: Quando hoc præcipuum est, non postulo ut gratis mihi credatur: res ipsa fidem faciet. Poteramus autem numerum hunc vel decuplo majorem exhibere, si Saxonica diligentius excussissemus: aut, ut dicam quod res est, melius intellexissemus. Nos verò in magnâ verborum copiâ, ea potissimùm delegimus, quæ hodieque essent in usu, quo plures possent judicare; (nam quotusquisque qui Saxonica, proh pudor! intelligat?) & fructum ex labore nostro percipere. Sciat prætereà Lector multa alia, quæ hunc numerum puto æquarent, si non superarent, nullo nos negotio potuisse congerere, verba (ut nunc quidem loquimur) Anglica, quæ Græca, aut Græcæ originis esse certissimum est: ab iis consultò abstinuisse, né ne fucum lectoribus nostris faceremus. Talia autem, verba quaedam Ecclesiastica, quae cum fide Christiana in usum sunt invecta, ut jam pridem monuit Walafridus Strabo. Quod autem hujus Walafridianae observationis sic meminerunt viri quidam docti; quasi ab ista potissimum origine repetendum esset quicquid verborum in lingua Germanica Graecorum hodie reperitur; in eo falluntur ut qui maximè: & quàm magnus est illorum error, tam facilis est ad arguendum; ut ex illis quae postea dicturi sumus liquebit. Secundò, abstinuimus à verbis illis, artium propriis, quae plurima sunt, Graecae quidem, ut omnes norunt, originis, sed pluribus jampridem linguis communia. Abstinuimus autem, quia non ab ipsis immediatè Graecis, sed à Latinis, ut Latina, ad Anglos pleraque, si non omnia, pervenere. Multa quoque à Gallis accepta, quae quanquam Graeca sint; quia tamen non à Graecis, sed ab illis accepta, nihil ad rem nostram, & ipsis relinquenda judicavimus. Quanquam autem potest fieri ut velut Angli multa ab illis; ita & vicissim nonnulla & illi ab Anglis,aut certè ab ipsis utriq; Græcis acceperint : nos tamen, ut in multâ copiâ, tam liberales fuimus, ut quæ Gallis & Anglis communia cognovimus, omnia aut certè pleraque quoad ejus potuimus prætermitteremus.
units.tr: Since this is the chief point, I do not ask that my word be taken without proof: the thing itself will carry conviction. We could have set out a number ten times larger, had we searched the Saxon more carefully or, to say the truth, understood it better. But among the great abundance of words we chose especially those which are still in use today, so that more readers could judge them, for how few, alas, understand Saxon at all? and so that they might gain some profit from our labour. Let the reader further know that we could have gathered with no trouble many other words, which would have matched this number, if not exceeded it: English words, as we now speak, which are certainly Greek or of Greek origin. We deliberately refrained from them, so as not to deceive our readers. Such are certain ecclesiastical words, which were brought into use together with the Christian faith, as Walafrid Strabo noted long ago. But some learned men who recall this observation of Walafrid's speak as if everything that is found today in the German language of Greek origin must be traced to that source above all; in this they are as mistaken as anyone, and their error is as great as it is easy to refute, as will become clear from what we shall say later. Secondly, we abstained from those words belonging to the arts, which are very many. They are, as all know, of Greek origin, but have long been common to several languages. We abstained from them because they came to the English not directly from the Greeks, but from the Latins, as Latin words; for most, if not all, passed to the English in that way. Many were also received from the French, which, although Greek, since they were received not from the Greeks but from the French, we judged to have no bearing on our purpose, and to be better left to them. Although it may be that, just as the English got many things from the French, so in turn the French got some from the English, or both alike got some from the Greeks themselves, we nevertheless, though we had plenty to choose from, were so generous that we passed over, as far as we could, all those we found to be common to French and English, all or at least most of them.

units.la: Scripsit de linguæ Gallicæ cum Græcâ cognatione Henricus Stephanus,author immortalis operis, quod Thesaurum linguæ Graecæ indigitavit. Ut autem erat ille Vir in omni literaturâ meliore consummatissimus, linguæ autem Græcæ vel ad miraculum peritus, ita hoc opere defunctus est. Ita enim omnia in utriusque linguæ consuetudine vel abditissima & minutissima diligenter rimatus est ; omnes orationis particulas, (quarum quantò in omni lingua difficilior, tanto utilior observatio : ) omnes idiotismos excussit, eruit, explicavit, similia cum similibus comparavit, ut exemplum quidem in hoc genere aliis ad imitandum reliquerit absolutissimum. sed quod pauci sint assecuturi. Nos quoque multa notaveramus olim in libris nostris locutionum & idiotismorum genera, in quibus lingua Anglica cum Græca conveniret. Sed quia quos olim legeramus & notaveramus libros, dudum iis maxi‑ mam partem privati sumus, hanc par‑ tem quæ in comparatione locutionum & idiotismorum consistit omittemus. In repræsentandis autem singulis ver‑ bis, cautiores erimus quàm fuit incom‑ parabilis ille vir, ne artium vocabula scilicet, aliáque à Latinis accepta, cum veteribus & genuinis confundamus, quæ à Græcis immediatè manasse con‑ tendimus. Talia Anatomie, antidater, (Anglicè, to antidate) apoplexie, apo‑ stat, apostre, (Angl. an apostle) apostume, (Angl. vulgò impostume) apothiquaire, archevesque, archidiacre, (Angl. archbishop, archdeacon) arithmetique, ar‑ monie, (Angl. harmonie) authentique, aliáque innumera, quæ in ipsius colle‑ ctione utramque ferè quod aiunt pa‑ ginam faciunt. Quod tamen in illo non adeo miror, quàm Vander-Mylium, qui non Stephano quidem quod sciam, quem fortassè non legerat; sed Trip‑ paulto (mihi nunquam viso, nec antea vel audito) hoc objicit; eundem tamen in suâ collectione ab illis non abstinu‑ isse, quæ certissimum esset partim à O Gallis, partim à Latinis ad Belgas transiisse. Nisi quis ista Belgica, fozme, rose, fpeloncke & similia, potius ex Græcis, μορφὴ, ῥόδον, σπηλαῖον, orta esse, quàm vel Latinis, forma, rosa, spelunca; vel Gallicis, forme, rose; possit in animum inducere ut credat: cùm tamen ex utrâque linguâ passim multa in linguâ Belgicâ esse, & quotidie multa sumi nemo possit negare.
units.tr: Henri Estienne, the immortal author of the work which he named the Thesaurus of the Greek Language, wrote on the kinship of French with Greek. But as that man was most accomplished in all good literature, and marvellously skilled in Greek, so he performed this task. He examined with great diligence everything in the usage of both languages, even the most hidden and minute; he went through, brought out and explained all the particles of speech (the more difficult such observation is in any language, the more useful it is), all the idioms; he compared like with like. So he left others a most complete model to imitate in this kind, though few will reach it. We too had once noted many kinds of expression and idiom in our books in which English agrees with Greek. But since we have for the most part lost the books we had read and noted long ago, we shall omit that part which consists in comparing expressions and idioms. In setting out individual words, we shall be more cautious than that incomparable man was, so as not to confuse the technical terms and other words received from the Latins with the old and native words which we maintain came directly from the Greeks. Such words are: Anatomie (anatomy), antidater (English "to antidate"), apoplexie (apoplexy), apostat (apostate), apostre (English "an apostle"), apostume (English commonly "impostume"), apothiquaire (apothecary), archevesque (archbishop), archidiacre (archdeacon, English "archbishop", "archdeacon"), arithmetique (arithmetic), armonie (English "harmony"), authentique (authentic), and countless others which in his collection fill nearly every page, as they say. Yet I do not wonder at this in him as much as at Vander Myle, who objects this to Trippault (whom I have never seen or even heard of before), not to Stephanus, as far as I know, whom perhaps he had not read. Yet in his own collection he did not refrain from those words which are quite certainly passed partly from the French and partly from the Latins into Dutch. Unless someone can be persuaded to believe that the Dutch words vorme, roose, spelonck and similar ones arose from the Greek morphe, rhodon, spelaion rather than from the Latin forma, rosa, spelunca, or the French forme, rose. No one can deny that many Dutch words come from both languages at random, and that many are taken up every day.

units.la: Præter numerum, ipsa verborum qualitas & propria quædam ratio, quam in multis animadverti, multùm moverunt, ut ita crederem. Jure id, an injuriâ, judicet lector.
units.tr: Apart from the number, the very quality of the words and a certain peculiar pattern, which I have noticed in many of them, moved me greatly to believe this. Whether the reader judges rightly or wrongly, let him decide.

units.la: ᾿Αγαθός, (γάθ&) Anglicè, good: idem verbum: sed hoc nihil. At βέλτιων, βέλτιστος, ex ἀγαθός, non ordinaria; & miræ olim inter Grammaticos Græcos (teste Plutarcho) de origine concertationes. Utrumque Angli, better, best, inflexis paululum, & contractis ad suam consuetudinem, verbis. Unde autem, nisi ab illis?
units.tr: ἀγαθός (gath), in English "good": the same word, but that proves nothing. But βέλτιων [better] and βέλτιστος [best], derived from ἀγαθός, are not regular forms, and there were once remarkable disputes among the Greek grammarians about their origin (as Plutarch testifies). The English use both, "better" and "best," with the words slightly inflected and shortened to suit their own habits. Whence did they get them, if not from the Greeks?

units.la: Μέγαλος, (ita olim, quod postea μέγας) Angli olim, mikell: vel mitchel: unde proprium nomen, Mitchel-grove: quasi Magnus lucus. Apud Wille-
units.tr: μέγαλος (formerly, what later became μέγας [great]): the English once said "mikell" or "mitchel," whence the proper name Mitchel-grove, as if it meant Magnus lucus. In Abbot Willeram's text it appears as "mikelon."

units.la: ramum Abbatem Ϙίκτελον. Μεΐζων, (quod etiam μέγαν) major, Anglicè, mara: ut Mat.XI. mara Johanne Fulwhitere: major Jóh.Baptistâ: & mox, ꝑ bῑth mara: eft illo major. Μέγιστος, maximus, nunc most, quod olim marstan. In mara, τὸ s folemne eft comparativi Saxonici characteristicum, idque Græcorum, ut infrà videbimus, imitatione.
units.tr: μεΐζων (also μέγαν) [greater], "major" in Latin, is in English "mara," as in Matthew 11: "mara than John Fulwhitere," that is, greater than John the Baptist. And soon after: "he is mara," that is, greater than he. μέγιστος [greatest], "maximus," is now "most," which was formerly "marstan." In "mara" the letter s is the regular mark of the Saxon comparative, and this too is an imitation of the Greeks, as we shall see below.

units.la: Μιχρός, ελάσσων, ελάχιστος. Pro μικροῦ, aliud ejusdem ferè significationis substantivum Græcum substituerunt Angli: Λάττ, little. Comparativum & superlativum idem retinuerunt: ἐλάσσων, lesse: ἐλάχιστος, lest. Videbuntur fortasse imperitis infolentiores ejusmodi contractiones verborum, ἐλάχιστος, lest. at nos posteà, quæ magis mirentur, de quibus tamen nulla potest esse controversia, proferemus.
units.tr: μικρός [small], ἐλάσσων [smaller], ἐλάχιστος [smallest]. In place of μικροῦ, the English substituted another Greek noun of nearly the same meaning: λάττ, "little." They kept the comparative and superlative forms: ἐλάσσων becomes "lesse" and ἐλάχιστος becomes "lest." Such contractions of words as ἐλάχιστος into "lest" may seem rather strange to the unlearned, but later I shall bring forward others that are more surprising, yet about which there can be no dispute.

units.la: Notissimus apud Græcos & ufitatissimus comparandi typus, ut comparativus definitur in ἐς; superlativus in τῶ: quod hodieque, quantum ad characteristicas literas attinet, retinent Angli: Long, longer, longest. Short, shorter, shortest. Atq; ita veteres Angli seni-or fer ter (συνέτὸς) prudens: fnotere vel fnotra: (συνετώτερος) prudentior: fnotereft, συνετώτατος. Rigbt wpfe, justus: rigbt wpfere, vel rigbt wpfra, justior: rigbt wpfeft, justissimus. Ealð (ἑωλός) vetus: ealðre, vel ealdra, (ἑωλότερος) veterior: ealdeft, (ἑωλότατος) veterrimus. Ut omnino Verfteganus Anglus, de Saxonibus alioquin optimè meritus, cùm superlativi veterem formam seu terminationem ftan fuisse statuit, & terminationem est recentiorem esse sancit, in errore fuerit.
units.tr: The most familiar and commonly used pattern of comparison among the Greeks is that the comparative is formed with -ες and the superlative with -τῶ. In its essential letters the English still retain this today: "long, longer, longest"; "short, shorter, shortest." So too the older English had "seni-or" for the wise (συνετός) and "fnotere" or "fnotra" for wiser (συνετώτερος), and "fnoteft" for wisest (συνετώτατος). "Rigbt wpfe" means just; "rigbt wpfere" or "rigbt wpfra" means more just; "rigbt wpfeft" means most just. "Ealð" (ἑωλός) means old; "ealðre" or "ealdra" (ἑωλότερος) means older; "ealdeft" (ἑωλότατος) means oldest. So Verstegan, an Englishman otherwise deserving well of the Saxons, was altogether mistaken when he held that the old form or ending of the superlative was "stan," and declared that "-est" was a more recent ending.

units.la: Nominum Græcorum declinandorum typus inter alios usitatissimus, τυχὴ, τυχῆς, τυχῇ. Veteres Angli an plures declinationum formas habuerint, incompertum mihi. Ista autem quàm fuerit usitata quò melius lectori constet, non pigebit ex Ælfrico, vetustissimo Grammatico (cujus usum doctissimo & amicissimo Somnero debeo,) Saxonicæ istius formæ exempla per omnes Latinarum Declinationum ordines hic apponere.
units.tr: Among the various models for declining Greek nouns, one of the most common is τυχή, τυχῆς, τυχῇ. I do not know whether the older English had several forms of declension. But so that the reader may know how common these forms were, I will not hesitate to set out here, from Ælfric, the oldest grammarian (whose use of him I owe to the learned and very kind Somner), examples of this Saxon form through all the orders of Latin declensions.

units.la: Prima Declinatio: Nominativo, hic cytharista, tbes bearpoze. Genit. cytharistæ, tbeses bearpozes. Dat. cytharistæ, tbtsam bearpoze. II. De-
units.tr: First declension. Nominative: "hic cytharista," "thes bearpoze" (this harper). Genitive, of the harpist: "theses bearpozes." Dative, to the harpist: "thisam bearpoze."

units.la: II. Decl. Nom. hic faber, thes smitth: Gen. hujus fabri, theses smithes: Dat. huic fabro, thisam smithe.
units.tr: Second declension. Nominative: "hic faber" (this smith), "thes smitth." Genitive, of this smith: "theses smithes." Dative, to this smith: "thisam smithe."

units.la: IV. Decl. Nom. hic sensus, this andgit: Gen. hujus sensus, theses andgites: Dat. sensui, thisam andgite.
units.tr: Fourth declension. Nominative: "hic sensus" (this sense), "this andgit." Genitive, of this sense: "theses andgites." Dative, to the sense: "thisam andgite."

units.la: V. Decl. hic & hæc dies, this dæg: Gen. diei, thises dæges: Dat. thisum dæge.
units.tr: Fifth declension. "Hic & hæc dies" (this day), "this dæg." Genitive, of the day: "thises dæges." Dative, to this day: "thisum dæge."

units.la: Hactenus Ælfricus. Jam Infinitivorum Græcorum terminatio inter alia, & præ aliis usitatissima, est in ων: ut πῖνειν, &c. Saxonicorum, (ut hodiéque Belgarum & Germanorum) in en vel an. ut spllen, dare. settan, ponere. sendan, mittere. secgan, exprimere. Et ut Græci Infinitivis vulgò præponunt articulum neutrum τό, ut τὸ ἐδεῖν, τὸ πίνειν; edere, bibere: ita Angli vulgò, to eate, to drinke. Τὸ ζῆν, καὶ τὸ ἐνεργεῖν: Philipp. II. v. 13. to will, and to doe. Τὸ τοῖς πολλοῖς ἀρέσκειν, τοῖς σοφοῖς ἀπαρέσκειν ἔστι, to pleafe many (vel cum articulo, the many:) is to displease the wise. tolfe. Τὸ ἀδίκεῖν ἢ ἀδίκεῖν βέλτιον, to suffer wrong is better then to doe wrong. Si hoc tam notabile omisissem, non unus fortasse oscitantium reprehendisset. Ingenuè tamen fateor subdubitare me an in ista constructione Anglicum to, sit loco articuli Græci. Sæpe enim ad exprimendum Latinorum gerundium in dum adhibetur hæc particula loco præpositionis ad: ut, And they rose to eate: & surrexerunt ad edendum, &c. Quò referas illa vetera, & longè elegantissima, to become thine rite: vel, to cpmcth thine rie: adveniat regnum tuum: in vetustis Orationis Dominicæ versionibus. Interdum etiam cum verbis eleganter coalescit ista particula; ut, And thees temple wæbzpit, wearth to sliten en midden; & velum templi scissum est medium.
units.tr: So far Ælfric. Now the Greek infinitive ending in -ων is, among others and above others, very common: as in πῖνειν, and so on. The Saxon infinitives, as the Belgians and Germans still have them today, end in -en or -an: as "spllen" (to speak), "settan" (to set), "sendan" (to send), "secgan" (to say). And just as the Greeks commonly put the neuter article τό before infinitives, as in τὸ ἐδεῖν, τὸ πίνειν (to eat, to drink), so the English commonly say "to eate," "to drinke." "Τὸ ζῆν" and "τὸ ἐνεργεῖν" [to live and to work] appear in Philippians 2:13 as "to will, and to doe." "Τὸ τοῖς πολλοῖς ἀρέσκειν, τοῖς σοφοῖς ἀπαρέσκειν ἐστί" [to please many is to displease the wise] is rendered "to pleafe many" (or with the article, "the many") "is to displease the wise." "Τὸ ἀδικεῖν ἢ ἀδικεῖσθαι βέλτιον" [to suffer wrong is better than to do wrong] is rendered "to suffer wrong is better then to doe wrong." If I had left out so notable a point, perhaps more than one careless reader would have found fault with me. Yet I frankly confess that I have some doubt whether the English "to" in this construction takes the place of the Greek article. For this particle is often used, in place of the preposition "ad," to express the Latin gerund in -dum, as in "And they rose to eate" (et surrexerunt ad edendum, and so on). To this you may refer those old and very elegant phrases in the early English versions of the Lord's Prayer: "to become thine rite" or "to cpmcth thine rie" (let your kingdom come). Sometimes this particle also combines gracefully with verbs, as in "And thees temple wæbzpit, wearth to sliten en midden" (and the veil of the temple was rent in the middle).

units.la: In his, locus articulo Græco cùm non fit, aut ita statuendum est, duplex esse illud τό, quorum illud articulo Græco respondeat; istud verò Latinæ præpositioni non tantum cùm gerundio præponitur, sed aliàs quoque; ut cum motus indicatur, <bl>to goe to the towne</bl>, ire ad urbem, &c. aut (quod non minùs probabile) fuerit idiotifsmus Anglicanus, aut Germanicus; (nam Belgicis quoq; verbis haud paucis ita præfixum video, ut coalescat:) non gerundia tantùm, sed & Infinitivus módus, aut Infinitivorum potiùs præsentia tempora, ad Gerundiorum Latinorum normam exprimere.
units.tr: Where there is no place for the Greek article in these examples, one of two things must be assumed: either that the English "to" is double, one part of which answers to the Greek article and the other to the Latin preposition (which is placed before the gerund and elsewhere too, as when motion is indicated: "to goe to the towne," to go to the town); or else, which is no less probable, it is an English or German idiom (for I see that many Belgian verbs have the same prefix, joined to them in the same way). In that case the English express not only gerunds but also the infinitive mood, or rather the present tenses of the infinitives, according to the pattern of the Latin gerunds.

units.la: Erat aliud quoque quód de articulis & aliis particulis quibusdam dici posset: sed quæ fortasse subtiliora quibusdam videbuntur. Nos igitur ad manifestiora properamus.
units.tr: There was also something else that could be said about the articles and certain other particles, but it may seem rather subtle to some. So I hasten on to matters that are more evident.

units.la: In recensione verborum cognatorum,* ab elementis incipiemus. Earth, terra: dubium ex Græco γῆ; an Hebr. אָרֶץ. Air, aër: ex Græco ἀήρ, an Latino aër. At fyer, ignis, ex Græco πῦρ (quod tamen non est origine Græcum; sed Phrygicum:) & water, aqua, indubiè ex Græco ὕδωρ: unde consequens videtur, ut & illa dua priora ab eadem sint origine. Weather, æther, αἰθήρ; potest ex utrovis duci. sed rainc, pluvia, non est dubium, quin ex Græco ὑετός. Shade umbra, non tantùm σκιά umbra) peperit; sed, ni fallor, & σκιά shite,
units.tr: In reviewing related words, I shall begin with the elements. "Earth," terra: uncertain whether from the Greek γῆ or the Hebrew אָרֶץ. "Air," aër: from the Greek ἀήρ or the Latin aër. But "fyer," fire (ignis), from the Greek πῦρ, though this word is not originally Greek but Phrygian; and "water," aqua, undoubtedly from the Greek ὕδωρ. Hence it seems to follow that the two earlier words also have the same origin. "Weather," æther, from αἰθήρ, may be derived from either. But "raine," rain (pluvia), is undoubtedly from the Greek ὑετός. "Shade," umbra, not only produced σκιά (shadow), but, unless I am mistaken, also "shite,"

units.la: * Ex fontibus Anglicis. skie, cœlum. Id enim videtur etiam Græca vox olim significasse; & inde σκιοθηρεῖν, non umbras tantùm, sed & cœlum observare; ut in Hesychii loco, ubi φρέαρ ὀρφνίᾳ, quid sit docet. Ait autem: Φρέαρ ὀρφνίᾳ, σκιοθηρεῖν: οἱ δὲ ἀπὸ τῶν μαθηματῶν εἰώθασι τὰς μετεωρίσεις, λαμβάνειν ἡ σκιοθηρεῖν ἐν τῇ φρεάτῳ. Etiam Saxonicum lyfte ambiguum, quod non cœlum tantùm, sed & nubes, quæ cœlum obumbrant (aut terram potiùs) significat. Lumbre Hispanicum quod lucem significat, ex umbra Latino, vel Gallico l'ombre factum (mira significationis inversione) videri posset. Sed salluntur, opinor, qui ita censent. Ex Latino siquidem lumen, interposito b. ut in multis aliis, verior etymologia. Moone, luna, ipsissimum μήνη: cur non & month, mensis, ex Græco potius μηνῶ, μηνὸς; quàm Latino mensis? sic father, mother: pater, mater: ex Latinis possunt, & ex Græcis provenisse: ut ab his tamen potiùs credamus, suadent ejusdem nomenclatura alia: ut υἱός, (in accusativo υἱὸν) versâ pro more (de quo posteà) in sibilam literam aspiratione, a sen; quod olim etiam sunt.
units.tr: * From English sources. "skie," the sky. For this Greek word seems also to have once meant the sky; and hence σκιοθηρεῖν means not only to observe shadows but also to observe the sky, as the passage of Hesychius shows, where he explains what φρέαρ ὀρφνίᾳ is. He says: "Φρέαρ ὀρφνίᾳ: σκιοθηρεῖν. Οἱ δὲ ἀπὸ τῶν μαθηματῶν εἰώθασι τὰς μετεωρίσεις, λαμβάνειν ἢ σκιοθηρεῖν ἐν τῷ φρεατί." Also the Saxon "lyfte" is ambiguous, meaning not only the sky but also the clouds which overshadow the sky (or rather the earth). The Spanish "lumbre," which means light, could seem to have been made from the Latin umbra, or from the French l'ombre, by a strange reversal of meaning. But those who think so, I believe, are mistaken. For the truer etymology is from the Latin lumen, with a b inserted, as in many other words. "Moone," moon, is exactly μήνη. Why should "month" (mensis) not come from the Greek μηνῶ, μηνός, rather than from the Latin mensis? Likewise "father" and "mother" (pater, mater) could have come from either Latin or Greek; yet the other names in the same family suggest that we should rather believe they come from the Greeks: for example υἱός [son] (in the accusative υἱόν), with the aspiration turned, as is customary (of which more later), into the sibilant letter, giving "a sen," which once was also "sunt."

units.la: Item Svyátηρ, daughter: & sister, ex υσέρα, nomine substantivo, quod matricem, &c. significat; ut & μήτηρ, ἀπὸ τῆς μήτρας, quod ejusdem est significationis; quae videntur primò generalia nomina fuisse, pro foemina in genere; postea usu propria facta: Ut hoc de foemina matre, seu quae mater esset; illud de foemina, quae soror, proprie dicerentur. Quid mirum, cùm foemina Latinum (ita mutant significationes, de quo postea pluribus tamen) Sax. virginem proprie; & fæmnhade virginitatem denotarit? Sed & φρήτωρ apud Græcos magis generale verbum, quàm vel frater apud Latinos; vel brother apud Anglos: quae tamen ex isto communiore verbo manasse nemo dubitat. Cæterùm, τὸ μήτηρ, ex μήτρα; an hoc ex illo derivemus, non magni interest: & fieri potest, ut Synonyma olim, (ut & mother Anglicum, quod utrumq; significat,) postea significatione distincta sint. Nam τὸ μήτηρ ab Hebraico אם immediatè fluxisse suadet affine אֵם, ab אם: ut jam antea in Hebraicis asseraruimus.
units.tr: Likewise "Svyátηρ" [sister], "daughter"; and "sister" comes from ὑστέρα, a substantive noun meaning the womb, etc., as does μήτηρ [mother], from μήτρα, which has the same meaning. These words seem at first to have been general terms for a woman in general, and only later became proper to particular uses: so that the one was properly said of a woman who was a mother, or who was a mother by being one, and the other of a woman who was a sister. Is it any wonder, since the Latin "foemina" (woman) (so meanings change, of which more below) and the Saxon "virginem" properly denoted a maiden, and "fæmnhade" denoted virginity? But also φρήτωρ among the Greeks is a more general word than "frater" among the Latins or "brother" among the English; yet no one doubts that these came from that more common word. Moreover, whether we derive τὸ μήτηρ from μήτρα or the reverse matters little; and it may happen that synonyms once existed (as the English "mother" also, which means both), and afterwards became distinct in meaning. For that τὸ μήτηρ flowed directly from the Hebrew אם [em] is suggested by the related word אֵם, from אם, as we have already argued above in the Hebrew studies.

units.la: Sed alia videamus. Ἠεῖδ, ἐνδρα. si hoc solum erat, dicerem probabile tantum, & casu ita potuisse fieri. Sed jam ἐρημία, earmnesse, (paupertas:) ἐχαλιά, scantnes : χίσσ⊙, ἡ χορεία, scantnes : Ecce quatuor ejusdem prope significationis vocabula, eadem apud Græcos (quantum dialecti varietas admittat :) & Anglos. Quis tam ferreus & bardus, ut hanc tantam affinitatem ad propiores aliquas non referat causas? Cæterum, posteriora illa duo scantnes & scarcenes hodieque notissima. At earmnes olim triftissimum, nunc apud Anglos (nam Germani adhuc habent) exolevit. Pro eo dixerunt etiam, pimtb, quasi ex ἐρημότης ; (ut φιλία, φιλότης, &c. & φαυλότης, filtb : de quo suo loco :) quod idem, sed alterius formæ verbum. Occurrit in Saxonicis Evangeliis, Sothlice thes of hpze pimthe : hæc vero de penuria suâ : de viduâ paupere scil. quæ ibi vocatur, earme wtdnwe.
units.tr: But let us look at other examples. ἠεῖδ and ἐνδρα [Greek]: if this were the only pair, I would say it is merely probable and could have happened by chance. But there are also ἐρημία [Greek], which in English is "earmnesse" (poverty); ἐχαλιά [Greek], "scantnes"; χίσσ⊙ [Greek]; and ἡ χορεία [Greek], "scantnes" again. Here are four words of nearly the same meaning, found in the same sense among the Greeks (as far as the variety of dialects allows) and among the English. Who is so iron-hearted and dull as not to refer such a great affinity to some nearer causes? Moreover, the last two, "scantnes" and "scarcenes", are still very well known today. But "earmnes", which was once very sad, has now fallen out of use among the English (though the Germans still have it). In its place they also said "pimtb", as if from ἐρημότης [Greek] (as φιλία, φιλότης, and φαυλότης [Greek], "filtb", which I will discuss in its place), which is the same thing but a word of another form. It occurs in the Saxon Gospels: "Sothlice thes of hpze pimthe", that is, "for they gave of their want", and of the poor widow, who there is called "earme wtdnwe".

units.la: Multis verbis utuntur Græci, ut verborum ῥύμεζν & ῥομεζὴν vim explicent. Poterant tot verbis Anglicè, & quidem clarissimè, to ramble,& to romble. Sed quia ῥύμεζον (ex quo ῥομεζίω) non una
units.tr: The Greeks use many words to explain the force of ῥύμεζν and ῥομεζὴν [Greek]. In English, the same could be expressed with many words, and very clearly too: "to ramble" and "to romble". But since ῥύμεζον [Greek] (from which ῥομεζίω [Greek]) does not have one

units.la: apud Græcos notio, eam nos hîc volumus, quâ ῥόμβος instrumentum significat ad strepitū excitandū: quod ideò in sacris Deæ Cybeles (quæ & Rhea, seu Dea mater nuncupata) cum tympano circumferebatur. Scholia Græca in Ἀριστοφάνης Græcorum Epigrammatum: ῥόμβῳ ἢ τυμπάνῳ φθέγγεσ ἰλάσκοντλαι. ῥόμβος δ' ὅτι προχίοσ ὃν στρέφεται ἰμάντ' τύπτουσιν, ἢ ἕπω κλύπον ἀπολλᾶσ. Etymologicum exponit, μυστικὸν σανίδιον· ὁ στρέφεται εἰς τ' ἀέρα, ἢ ἕπως ἦχον ἐμποιῶσι. Unde Hesychius, Ῥόμβος, Φόμβος, στρόφος, ἦχος, δῖνος. Addit autem Etymologicum idem instrumentum βρυτήρα etiam nuncupatum. Unde fortasse manavit & Gallicum bruit. Angli à Gallis, an Græcis acceperint, nescio: sed & illi brutte de rumore (qui linguæ sonus) usurpant.
units.tr: meaning among the Greeks, we want the one in which ῥόμβος [Greek] denotes an instrument for making a noise. This was carried around with a drum in the rites of the goddess Cybele, who is also called Rhea or the Mother of the gods. A Greek scholion on Aristophanes, in the verse of the Greek epigrams, says: they propitiate with the rhombus or the drum sounding out [Greek]. The rhombus is so called because it is a little board turned round, which they strike with a thong, or which makes a sound by swinging [Greek]. The Etymologicum explains it as a mystical little board, which is whirled through the air so that it produces a sound [Greek]. Hence Hesychius: ῥόμβος, φόμβος, στρόφος, ἦχος, δῖνος [Greek]. The Etymologicum adds that the same instrument is also called βρυτήρ [Greek]. Perhaps the French "bruit" (noise) also came from this. I do not know whether the English received it from the French or from the Greeks, but they too use "brutte" for rumour, which is the sound of the tongue.

units.la: Quis ad Græcorum verborum sonos aures habet vel tantillum imbutas, qui cùm audit quotidie solemne illud in omnium ore, good morrow, non Græcos audire se putet, χαῖρ' ἡμέραν, Gallici Bon jour) dicentes? Quòd τὸ morrow, posteà ad crastinum diem significandam translatum est; aut verius, rius, de crastino die proprie usurpari coepit,hinc factum puto. ʿHμέρα, ut notum, pro luce saepe sumitur, inde τὸ μοϱγεν, & μοϱρoτω, de luce matutina proprie; & tandem de toto die,quatenus tenebris noctis opponitur. Dicebant autem, ni fallor, μοϱρoτω, de praesenti; το μοϱρoτω de crastina diei luce. At recepto semel Latino Dæg (nunc Dap) quod jam ante mille annos in usu fuit: τὸ, μοϱρoτω, five μοϱγεν, de matutino tantum tempore, & crastina luce usurpata sunt. Nos quidem nunc distinguimus, & illud, μοϱντωg, hoc, μοϱρoτω dicimus. At in scriptis Saxonicis τὸ μοϱγεν de utroque reperias: ut & hodieque apud Belgas. Etiam Graecum ἀϱιστον (ut quidem derivant veteres Grammatici) matutinam lucem vel auroram proprie videtur fignificaffe: ἡς ἀϱιστον autem, proximi diei lucem, & inde crastinum. Usus tandem obtinuit, ut ἀϱιστον absolute quoque diceretur (ut & Anglicum μοϱρoτω:) pro ἡς ἀϱιστον. Quod si τὸ μοϱρoτω, vel μοϱγεν apud vetustissimos Anglos pro die, (nos enim sola conjectura ducimur) non occurrat, sed tantum de matutino temPore, & de crastino, quemadmodum apud, posteriores mille abhinc plus minùs annis reperimus, & hodie durat apud Belgas; tum dicemus, hæc verba, <bl>Ɵoð</bl> moꝛoтω, propriam matutini temporis salutationem fuisse, quâ sibi mutuò novam lucem gratulabantur.
units.tr: Who has ears even slightly trained in the sounds of Greek words, and hears daily that familiar greeting on everyone's lips, "good morrow", does he not think he is hearing Greeks saying χαῖρ' ἡμέραν [Greek] (the French "Bon jour")? I think "morrow" came to mean the following day because it was later transferred to that sense; or rather, it began to be used properly of tomorrow. ἡμέρα [Greek], as is well known, is often taken to mean light, whence τὸ μόρεν and μορητω [Greek] were used properly of morning light, and finally of the whole day, as opposed to the darkness of night. They used, unless I am mistaken, μορητω of the present, and τὸ μορητω of the light of tomorrow. But once the Latin "Dæg" (now "day") had been adopted, which had been in use already a thousand years ago, "morrow" or "morwen" was used only of the morning time and the light of the next day. We now distinguish them, and say "morrow" for one and "morning" for the other. But in Saxon writings you will find "morwen" used of both, as is still the case today among the Dutch. The Greek ἄριστον [Greek] (as the ancient grammarians derive it) seems properly to have meant morning light or dawn, and ἡς ἄριστον [Greek] the light of the next day, and so tomorrow. In the end custom prevailed so that ἄριστον was also used absolutely (as the English "morrow" is), in place of ἡς ἄριστον. But if "morrow" or "morwen" does not occur among the most ancient English in the sense of day (for we are led only by conjecture here), but only of morning time and of tomorrow, as we find in later writers from about a thousand years on, and as it lasts today among the Dutch, then we will say that these words, "good morrow", were the proper greeting of the morning, by which they congratulated one another on the new light.

units.la: Jam cùm dicunt, quod non minùs vulgare est, sweet beart: quid aliud quàm Græcè loquuntur, ἡδὺς χαρδία? Nam τὸ sweet, est ipsissima vox Græca, aspiratione, in literam f. ut passim, versâ: ut in, ὑς, sus; ὑπὲρ, super: ἑξ, sex: ἑπτὰ, septem: ὄλκος, sulcus: ἱδρως, sudor: & id genus aliis quàm plurimis. Sed in genere de litera f. præter ea quæ jam supra notata, sciendum est, nullam literam in omnibus linguis aut addi facilius, aut omitti. In aliis linguis obvia exempla, & offerent se nobis aliqua fortasse in sequentibus. Ita in Anglicâ, quod olim smilte & milde; nunc milde tantùm: quod smilles (in quibus etiam literæ t. in affinem D. mutationem, ut in sweet ex ἡδύς notarem, si in tam trivialibus & obviis immorandum crederem:) nunc mildnes: quod Latini nurus, illi snoze: ut hodiéque sparrow ex passer: snow, ex nix: flime, ex limus: Et contrà, tinne, ex stanno. Sed & in eisdem interdum verbis, (ut in Græcis, de quibus suprà) promiscuè scribitur vel omittitur: ut in Evangel. andtwarodun, (responderunt) quod mox andswozode: (respondit.) Obtinuit nunc usus ut semper cum f. scribatur: cum verò ut cuique libitum, andtwirde, andtwirst, &c. Hodieq; tamen, neefe, & sneefe: ut alia omittam. Ad τὸ heart (ex καρδία) quod attinet, est ea quoque pura puta Græca vox, ad idiotismum Anglicum flexa: ꝥ c. vel x. in adspirationem emollito: de quo suprà egimus, & multa deinceps alia, in collectione verborum proferentur exempla. Simile est quod etiam ex Latino, cervus, fecerunt heart. In vetere Glossario, quod Somneri mei bibliotheca suppeditavit, ita legebam: hzeod, carenam; hæfer, caper; hæferes, capri; hozutogo, cornicem; hiefn, cornix. Eiusdem generis sunt & ista: καλαυδους, halt; κλῆ, κλῆος, heard; κυ-ρυλ, corylus; hasel: (Belgis, hazeler:) aliáque aliis observata, aut à nobis deinceps observanda.
units.tr: When they say, which is no less common, "sweet heart", what else is this but Greek speech, ἡδὺς καρδία [Greek]? For "sweet" is the very Greek word, with the aspirate turned into f, as happens everywhere: as in ὑς [Greek], "sus" (sow); ὑπὲρ [Greek], "super" (over); ἕξ [Greek], "sex"; ἑπτὰ [Greek], "septem"; ὄλκος [Greek], "sulcus" (furrow); ἱδρώς [Greek], "sudor" (sweat); and many other words of this kind. In general, concerning the letter f, besides what has already been noted above, it should be known that no letter is more easily added or omitted in any language. Examples are common in other languages, and some will perhaps present themselves to us in what follows. So in English, what was once "smilte" and "milde" is now only "milde"; what was "smilles" (where I would also note the change of t into D, as in "sweet" from ἡδύς, if I thought it right to dwell on such trivial and obvious matters) is now "mildnes". Compare the Latin nurus, which the Germans call "snoze"; so also "sparrow" from "passer", "snow" from nix, "flime" from limus; and conversely "tinne" from stanno. But sometimes in the same words, as in the Greek examples above, the letter is written or omitted indiscriminately: as in the Gospels, "andtwarodun" (they answered), which soon became "andswozode" (he answered). Custom has now settled that it is always written with f, but otherwise, as each person pleases: "andtwirde", "andtwirst", and so on. Even today, however, "neefe" and "sneefe" (sneeze), to omit other examples. As for "heart" (from καρδία [Greek]), this too is a pure Greek word, bent to English idiom: the c or x softened into an aspirate, which I have discussed above, and many other examples will be given in the collection of words that follows. It is similar to what they also made into "heart" from the Latin cervus (stag). In an old glossary, which the library of my friend Somner supplied, I read as follows: "hzeod", a carena; "hæfer", a goat; "hæferes", of goats; "hozutogo", a crow; "hiefn", a raven. Of the same kind are these: καλαυδους [Greek], "halt"; κλῆ, κλῆος [Greek], "heard"; κυρυλ [Greek], "corylus"; "hasel" (in Dutch "hazeler"); and others that I have noted elsewhere, or shall note later.

units.la: Qui norunt quem usum apud Græcos verba τρίζω, & σμήχω (quorum præterita pass. τέτριμμαι, & ἔσμησμαι) habeant, super origine verborum Anglicorum trim & smugg, opinor, nòn hæsitabunt. Exponit autem Hesychius τὸ σμήχω, τρίζω, κατάιζω. A tonsorum aut fullonum artificio videtur primùm hæc significatio manasse, ut exempla Græca suadent, quamvis usus ad alia quoq; transtulit. Plutarch° de curâ circa pocula loquens,utrumq;(ut & Angli sæpè jungunt) adhibuit: Τί ἢ ἐαυτὸν ἐκλέγειςθαι ἢ δίκαιος λαχὼν, κ λαμβάνειν &c. Sed caveant tyrones Angli ne similitudine decepti σμήχω cum σμύχω confundant, quod longè aliud: sed & hoc Angli mutuati sunt: dicunt, to smutt: vel ut alii scribunt, to smutch.
units.tr: Those who know how the Greek verbs τρίζω and σμήχω [Greek] are used (whose passive perfects are τέτριμμαι and ἔσμησμαι [Greek]) will not, I think, hesitate about the origin of the English verbs "trim" and "smugg". Hesychius explains σμήχω as τρίζω, that is, to rub down or scrub [Greek]. This sense seems first to have arisen from the craft of barbers or fullers, as the Greek examples suggest, although usage later transferred it to other things too. Plutarch, speaking of care about cups, used both verbs together (as the English often join them): [Greek]. But let young English students beware of being deceived by the resemblance and confusing σμήχω with σμύχω [Greek], which is quite different. The English have borrowed this too: they say "to smutt", or, as others write it, "to smutch".

units.la: Σίδηρος Græcis ut ferrum Latinis, metonymicè, haud raro ensem significat: unde & αἰδηροφόρος. Σίδηρος, Anglis, solitâ contractione, a stwoxD; vel ut olim scribebant a stwurD. ἀμέλυς αἰδηρος, a blunt (usitatissimâ,ut infrà docebimus, apharefi) stwoxD; & fieri potest ut Dint (quod alii scribunt Dent quasi ex Latino dens) fit ex Δεινόπης. Galli dicunt, pointe de l'esprée: quem admodum & Latini aciem de ingenio quoq; dicunt. Certè τὸ Δεινὸς cum ὀξὺς haud raro jungi, ac idem, quamvis in metaphorico sensu, valere certum est. Sed quicquid hujus sit, non dubium quin τὸ blade,fit ex ὀβελὸς (quod Græci posteriores per diminutivum ὀβελίσκοι; ut ex Polluce patet, aliisque.-Ita & ξίφος, pro quo Æoles σίφος dixere, peperit Anglis, a knife.
units.tr: Σίδηρος [Greek], like ferrum for the Latins, often means a sword by metonymy: whence αἰδηροφόρος [Greek]. For the English, σίδηρος [Greek] has been contracted in the usual way to "stwoxD", or, as they once wrote it, "stwurD". ἀμβλὺς σίδηρος [Greek], a blunt sword, is "a blunt stwoxD" (by the most common aphaeresis, as I will show below). And it may be that "dint" (which others write "dent", as if from the Latin dens) comes from Δεινόπης [Greek]. The French say pointe de l'espée (the point of the sword), just as the Latins also say aciem of wit. Certainly δεινός [Greek] is often joined with ὀξύς [Greek], and it is certain that the two mean the same thing, though in a metaphorical sense. But whatever the truth of this, there is no doubt that the English "blade" comes from ὀβελός [Greek], which later Greeks made diminutive as ὀβελίσκοι [Greek], as is clear from Pollux and others. So also ξίφος [Greek], for which the Aeolians said σίφος [Greek], gave the English "a knife".

units.la: "Ῥαχὶς Græcis, spina dorsi, Anglis, the ridge of the back. ῥάχις ὑψηλὴ Græcis, porrecta montis longitudo: Eustathio, ὑψηλὴ ὄρος: Anglis similiter, a ridge of an hill. Dixit Homerus, ῥάχιν νὼς, dorsum suis: (ad cibum scil: parati; & convivis appositi:) dicunt Anglii quotidie, a rack of mutton, in eandem planè sententiam. ῥαχία Græcis, strepitus inconditus, qualis maris allu entis, & littoribus sese infundentis esse solet: (unde proverbium, ῥαχίας λαλίσεῷ:) racket Anglis in quotidiano & familiari sermone, strepitus major & inconditus: ῥαχίης, Græcis, alastor, pestis, pernicies, magnorum malorum auctor : talis Anglis quoque vulgò, a wretch, wretched; quod non passivè tantùm, sed & activè usurpatur; sed adjectis ut plurimùm ad discrimen epithetis : a poor wretch : a base wretch : a wretched villain, &c. Ecce tam multa ab unâ, ἀρχή, origine, seu radice : cùm tamen hæc scribenti alia quoque venirent in mentem ab eâdem fortasse origine : sed quia dubito, abstineo. Certè aut nihil in verbis certum, aut illa pleraque certa sunt, quæ hactenus adduximus.
units.tr: The Greeks use rhachis [ῥαχὶς] for the spine of the back, which the English call "the ridge of the back." A high rhachis [ῥάχις ὑψηλὴ] means to the Greeks a long stretch of raised mountain; Eustathius glosses it as a high mountain [ὑψηλὴ ὄρος]. The English likewise say "a ridge of an hill." Homer speaks of rhachis of swine [ῥάχιν νὼς], the back of a hog (that is, ready for food and set before the diners). The English say every day "a rack of mutton," with exactly the same meaning. The Greeks use rhachia [ῥαχία] for a confused noise, such as the sea makes when it breaks in and pours itself upon the shores (whence the proverb, rhachias lalisis [ῥαχίας λαλίσεῷ]). In everyday and familiar English speech, "racket" is a greater and disorderly noise. The Greeks use rhachiēs [ῥαχίης] for a scourge, plague, or ruin, the author of great evils; the English commonly use "wretch" and "wretched" in the same way, and not only in the passive sense but also actively, usually with epithets added to make the meaning clear: "a poor wretch," "a base wretch," "a wretched villain," and so on. See how many words come from one archē [ἀρχή], one origin or root! Yet while writing I also thought of other words that perhaps come from the same origin, but since I am unsure, I refrain. Certainly either nothing in words is certain, or most of those we have cited are certain.

units.la: Walliæ gaff, (quod hodie, <bl>bolp Ghost</bl>) quid aliud quàm ἅγιος ἅγιος? Multa alia possent hic inseri : quæ suis locis in Alphabetica (ne nimis hic prolixi simus) collectione reperiuntur. Et hæc opinor satis multa sunt, quibus propiòr hæc Anglicæ linguæ cum Græca, quàm volumus, affinitas probetur, quæ nec ad generalem aliquam linguarum omnium inter se cognationem, nec ad casum referri possit. Quid multa? Ego non dubito, si quis id agat, & utriusque linguæ bonâ fide peritus sit, quin bene longus Dialogus contexi possit verbis quæ & Græca sint & pariter Anglica. Hoc ego bona fide profiteri possum, non semel haerentem in locis obscuris Graecorum auctorum, linguam Anglicanam adhibuisse, nec parum ex ea commodi percepisse. Multis exemplis hoc possem ostendere, si libris illis fruerer, quos olim legi. Uno nunc contenti erimus.
units.tr: What else is the Welsh gaff (which today is "holy Ghost") but hagios hagios [ἅγιος ἅγιος]? Many other examples could be inserted here, but they are found in their proper places in the alphabetical collection, so as not to be too long-winded here. I think these are enough to prove that this affinity of the English language with Greek is closer than we might wish, and it cannot be ascribed to any general kinship of all languages with one another, nor to chance. Why say more? I have no doubt that anyone who sets himself to it, and who is genuinely skilled in both languages, could compose a fairly long dialogue of words that are both Greek and English at once. I can honestly declare that I have more than once, when stuck on obscure passages of Greek authors, made use of the English language, and gained no little advantage from it. I could show this by many examples if I still had those books which I read long ago. For now we shall be content with one.

units.la: Multas Libanium inter, sophistam quondam celeberrimum, avitis superstitionibus addictissimum; & Basilium Magnum, Christianae pietatis antistitem sanctissimum & eloquentissimum, epistolas ἀμοιβαῖας interceccisse, nemo ignorat, cui utriusvis eorum, Libanii, Basiliive opera unquam inspecta. Ex illis quae hodie extant, quaedam sic incipit: Πῶς μὲν ἐδιδάχθη, πεζὸν ἐμὲ ... Συγγενῶν. Erat autem sophisticus stilus, praeeminentia elegantiae (cui uni studebant) affectatione ut plurimum putidior. Quod etiam Photii est (si bene memini) de Libanio judicium. Praeter structuram orationis affectatam, vocibus etiam non vulgaribus & desitis, sed Platonicis tamen, libenter utebantur. Talis haec vox Συγχώρησις videtur fuisse, quam vix in ullo Graecorum, (sed neque χαρὰ ...
units.tr: No one who has ever looked into the works of either Libanius, once a most celebrated sophist, very devoted to his ancestral superstitions, or Basil the Great, a most holy and eloquent prelate of Christian piety, is unaware that they exchanged many letters in reply to one another. Among those that survive today, one begins thus: How indeed he was taught, me on foot ... of kinsmen [Πῶς μὲν ἐδιδάχθη, πεζὸν ἐμὲ ... Συγγενῶν]. The sophistic style, however, aimed at elegance above all else, and through affectation was mostly rather tasteless; this is also (if I remember rightly) Photius's judgement of Libanius. Besides an affected structure of sentences, they readily used words that were not common and were obsolete, yet Platonic. Such a word seems to have been synchōrēsis [Συγχώρησις], which scarcely appears in any Greek (but neither chara [χαρὰ] ...

units.la: [illegible, ~4 letters] βάσις, aut γαμίζω, aut γάμισμα :) qui nunc extant scriptorum reperias. Basilius insolentia vocis, ut ex ipso conjicere est, non parum offensus, quæsitam tandem invenit vel in Platone, vel aliquo (qualia tum multa extabant) Platonicorum verborum Lexico, sive Glossario. An hodie reperiatur in Platone, non possum dicere. Non memini certè ibi legere, nec ullum ex Platone locum ab aliis notatum reperio. Cæterùm, Basilium longè aliter accepisse, quàm Libanius voluerat, aut ejus sententia ferebat, tum verborum ipsius contextus, tum vocis ipsius vis plane persuadent.
units.tr: [illegible] basis [βάσις], or gamizō [γαμίζω], or gamisma [γάμισμα]) you could find in the writers now extant. Basil, not a little put out by the strangeness of the word, as one may gather from his own words, eventually found it sought out either in Plato or in some lexicon or glossary of Platonic words (of which many then existed). Whether it is found in Plato today I cannot say. I certainly do not remember reading it there, nor do I find any passage of Plato noted by others. Moreover, that Basil understood it quite differently from what Libanius intended, or from the sense of his letter, is plainly shown both by the context of his own words and by the force of the word itself.

units.la: An verò tam petulans & incivilis Libanius, qui tantam in cæteris omnibus epistolis erga Basilium reverentiam prodit ; ut nullo ab ipso vel male dicto vel facto provocatus, tam abruptè avaritiam, & διχοξενίαν (eò enim spectat Basilii responsio, ut id voluerit Libanius) Basilio & aliis ejusdem ordinis omnibus exprobraret ? Τεῖσμα, à veteribus Grammaticis κέρδος, seu lucrum exponitur. Hinc Συσχεδιάσμον dictum volunt, ex quo lucrum non facilè percipitur. Quanquam nulla alibi ejus significationis exempla, ego tamen & Basilii authoritate motus, qui ita exponit; & Anglicæ linguæ Hellenismo facile adducor, ut credam id quoque quondam verbum illud significasse. Angli siquidem hodiéque griping, de homine per fas & nefas lucrum sectante usurpant: & olim, hominem avarum, gifre levi transpositione, ex eâdem, ni fallor, origine, vocabant. Ita reperio in Saxonicâ N. Test. versione: Thus thing ealle the Farisei gebyjdon tha the gifre woeron and bi bine fældon: Audiebant autem omnia hæc Pharisæi qui erant avari, & deridebant eum. Luc. XVI. v. 14. Sed ut hoc concedam, non tamen eò spectasse Libanium necesse est, cùm plures ejusdem verbi notiones esse possint. Mentem Libanii in hoc verbo facilè Anglus intelliget: me certè ut intelligerem, non parum juvavit & confirmavit verbum Anglicum. Alius si roget; respondeo, me consultò supersedere, donec Libanii Basiliíque interpretes, ad quos adire in hac solitudine, in quâ hæc scribebam, non licebat, consuluerim. Vix est enim, ut locum tam insignem, & si quid ego judico, obscurum, intactum & intractatum prætermiserint: quem si ego nunc explicare conor, non tantùm fortasse, actum agere videar, quod equidem nolim: sed & plagii suspicionem incurram. Cæterùm Epistolæ illæ de quibus egimus, quia perbreves sunt, & utræque in suo genere lectu dignissimæ; utriusque exemplar, quales illas exhibet Aldina Græcarum Epistolarum ex multis collectarum editio, quæ ante annos centum & quinquaginta prodiit, hîc apponam.
units.tr: But could Libanius really have been so insolent and uncivil as to reproach Basil and all others of his order so abruptly for avarice and dichoxenia [διχοξενίαν] (for Basil's reply aims at this, as Libanius must have meant it), when he shows such reverence toward Basil in all his other letters, and was provoked by no evil word or deed from him? The ancient grammarians explain teisma [Τεῖσμα] as kerdos [κέρδος], that is, gain. Hence they say it was called syscheodiasmon [Συσχεδιάσμον], from which gain is not easily gathered. Although I find no other examples of this meaning elsewhere, I am moved both by Basil's authority, who explains it thus, and I am easily drawn by the Hellenism of the English language to believe that this word once had that meaning too. For the English even today use "griping" of a man who pursues gain by fair means or foul; and formerly they called an avaricious man a gifre, by a slight transposition, from the same origin, unless I am mistaken. So I find in the Saxon version of the New Testament: "Thus thing ealle the Farisei gebyjdon tha the gifre woeron and bi bine fældon," that is, "Now the Pharisees also, who were covetous, heard all these things, and they derided him" (Luke 16:14). But even if I grant this, it is not necessary that Libanius had this in view, since the same word may have several senses. An Englishman will easily understand Libanius's meaning in this word; for my own part, the English word helped and confirmed me in understanding it, and not a little. If someone else asks, I reply that I have deliberately held back until I have consulted the interpreters of Libanius and Basil, whom I am not allowed to consult in this solitude in which I am writing these things. For it is hardly likely that they would have passed over such a notable passage, and, as far as I can judge, an obscure one, untouched and unexplored; if I now try to explain it, I may perhaps seem to be doing what has already been done, which I would rather avoid, and I shall also incur suspicion of plagiarism. However, since the letters we have been discussing are very short, and both are most worth reading in their kind, I shall set out here a copy of each, as the Aldine edition of Greek letters collected from many sources presents them; it appeared a hundred and fifty years ago.

units.la: Αἰβάνιος Βασιλεύς.
units.tr: Aibanios the King.

units.la: Πᾶς μὲν ἀδικοῦντος, ψεῦσμα ξυσχέντ- ες σὺ ἢ ὅσῳ πως ἄλλως παρελήλυθας λογόπλις, ποσὶν ἢ φόβον μοι παρέχεις, μὴ πως ἐξαρνῷ σὺς ψεύς ἢ ἀπιστον κἀπείδη τρωλήρων ἀξομαι, χάμαχας ἀν ἢ χάρις ἀμῷ εἶπε σοφιστής, ἢ χρῄζων, ἀλλὰ τοῖς ἐνμελίοις ἐμφαλλωπίζομεν, ἢ ἡ χείας γυνῶ ἐγὼ ἢ, εἰ μὴ σὺ παρέχοιο, ὑπαιθρῷ διαχύμασω.
units.tr: Since you have been wronged, you have, through some lying tale or other, slipped past me with your words; you cause me fear that you may deny your deceit and make me look like an unbelieving fool. As the sophist said, the grace of our reply is... but I am not looking for that. We will boast in our Melian songs, or I will know the grace of the... and if you do not comply, I will be scattered in the open air.
