units.la: Βασιλεῦ
units.tr: O King [Βασιλεῦ].

units.la: Βασιλεὺς Αἰβανίω.
units.tr: The King to Aibanios.

units.la: Εἰ τὸ χερδλαινὸν, τῶτο γνῶζιν λέξεως, ᾧ πᾶσιν ἔχει τ' σημασίαν ἢ λέξις, ἣν ἐν τῇ Πλάτωνος ἀδύνων ἢ σοφιστικὴ σε ὑμῖν ἀφεγχθρήσαι, σκόπωσον, ὦ Δαυμάσι, τῆς μᾶλλον ἔξ Δυσχερήσης· ἡμεῖς οἱ ὑπὸ Δι' ἔπισολι-μαίας Δυνάμεως ἀπογαρχικὸς ἢ τὸ τῶν σοφισῶν γὰρ, οἷς τίχνη τὸ πλανῶν τῶν λέ-γεις ἔδι. τίς ἡ ἐπισκόπων τῆς λόγος ἐφορε-σίτες; τίς τῶν μαθηλόμενος μισοφόρες ἀγλεσίαν; ὑμεῖς οἱ ἀρχινίνδες τῶν λόγος ἄνια, ὥσπερ οἱ ἡ μέλλ' ἐλθᾶ τὰ με-λίττικά. Ὅρᾷς ὡς γ' ἡ γίγνονται ἀρχονικῶν ἔνδ πομπύνουσι, ἰσχείδες τῆς ἐν Θερμοπύλαις ἀξωνιζομένοις σεχλιώτης σρωλήσας χρησ-νᾶι ἀσθενέστατος ἀπαυλᾶς ἀμῆν ἐστιν. Ὀμηρον δολιχοστέες, ὡς ὁ ἱερὸς Εὐσεδὴς ἀπογεγλασάσιν ἀγλεπηγγελλώ.
units.tr: If that is your gain, then learn the meaning of the word, the one whose sense the word carries everywhere. Consider, my friend, the word which in Plato's manner you have set against us in sophistic fashion: we who are under the power of the ... are the ones who are rebuked for it. Who are the overseers of such speech? Who are the ones who hate the crowd of the learned? You, who begin the words, are like those who are about to come to the Melitic things. You see how they boast of the victories of their leaders, and how the one who fought at Thermopylae proved the weakest of all. Hesiod, Homer's rival, has announced to the holy and pious ones what has been proclaimed.

units.la: Quanquam nihil hoc ad Bafilium, ad propofitum tamen noftrum multum facit, ut Anglici verbi perfectam cum Græco in fignificationum varietate consonantiam oftendamus, atq; eādem operā Hefychium illustremus. Τρηπώ-μένα, μῶμα, exponit Hesychius, συνελκόμενα ἡ ἀπαλωδῶς συμπαθῶς ἐγλίζουσα. Eadem verba habet Etymologici Magni auctor, nisi quòd correctiùs ille ἀπαλωδῶς, pro ἀπαλωδῶς; & συνελίζουσα, pro ἐγγίζουσα. pro συνελίζουσα autem apud Etymologicum rectissimè conjicit doctissimus Sylburgius legendum συνελιασόμενα. Non enim aliud γεμπόμενα sive γεμπόμενα, hoc sensu quem indicare voluit hîc Hesychius, quàm quod Angli vulgò, gripings, de stomachi, vel intestinorum torminibus.
units.tr: Although this has nothing to do with Basilius, it nevertheless serves our purpose greatly: to show the perfect agreement of the English word with the Greek in the variety of its meanings, and at the same time to illustrate Hesychius. Hesychius explains [τρηπώμενα], "[μῶμα]", as [συνελκόμενα] or [ἀπαλωδῶς συμπαθῶς ἐγγίζουσα], drawn together or touched with gentle sympathy. The author of the Etymologicum Magnum has the same words, except that he more correctly writes [ἀπαλωδῶς] for [ἀπαλωδῶς] and [συνελίζουσα] for [ἐγγίζουσα]. For [συνελίζουσα] in the Etymologicum the most learned Sylburg rightly conjectures that we should read [συνελιασόμενα]. For [γεμπόμενα] or [γεμπόμενα], in the sense which Hesychius here intends, means nothing other than what the English commonly call gripings, the pains of the stomach or bowels.

units.la: Nec dubito, quin multa antiquorum Glossographorum fœliciter illustrari & explicari ex hâc linguarum comparatione possint. Ait Hesychius Εὐὰν apud Indos hederam significare. Est autem Εὐὰν acclamatio bacchantium: quæ sacra apud Indos primùm instituta & celebrata sunt: & inde fortasse Hesychii suspicio Indicum verbum esse. Crediderim potiùs Scythicum fuisse. Quanquam & Indoscythos ab antiquis commemorari non ignoramus. Certè pote hodiéque Anglis hedera.
units.tr: I do not doubt that many of the ancient glossographers can be happily illustrated and explained by this comparison of languages. Hesychius says that [Εὐάν] among the Indians means ivy. But [Εὐάν] is the cry of the Bacchants, the rites first instituted and celebrated among the Indians; and perhaps from this comes Hesychius' suspicion that it is an Indian word. I would rather believe it was Scythian. Yet we know that the ancients also mention the Indo-Scythians. At any rate, the English still today can have "hedera" (ivy).

units.la: Celebratissima & usitatissima in sacris illis acclamatio, εὐοῖ, (unde & εὐάζω) ἀναζῳ) quod interpretantur Bene sit illi. Pro ἰβοῖ autem Phrygas vel Thracas ἀβοῖ dixisse notant veteres Grammatici. Thracicam autem & Phrygicam linguam aut eandem fuisse, aut non multum à Germanicâ discrepasse, ex nonnullorum sententiâ prius docuimus. Certè in ἀβοὶ aliquid safe videor mihi subolere. Save be, fuerit Hosanna. Si, safe be, tunc planè idem quod ἰβοῖ, ut vulgò exponunt.
units.tr: This most celebrated and commonest acclamation in those sacred rites, euoi [εὐοῖ] (whence also euazo [εὐάζω]), is interpreted as "May it go well with him." The ancient grammarians note that the Phrygians or Thracians said aboi [ἀβοῖ] for iboi [ἰβοῖ]. Earlier, according to some opinions, I showed that the Thracian and Phrygian languages were either the same or did not differ much from German. Certainly I seem to detect something of "safe" in aboi. "Save be" would have been Hosanna. If it is "safe be," then it is plainly the same as iboi, as they commonly explain it.

units.la: ᾿Αβιε, ait idem Hesychius, ἔξαλλον, Σκυθαις. Si id vult Hesychius, τὸ ἀβιε apud Scythas veteres eâ notione usurpatum fuisse, ut ἔβαλλον, (quod velle videntur ejus verba) seu projeci significaret: optimè congrueret hoc cum Anglico sermone. Sæpius enim audivi pilâ ludentes, & manibus aut baculo strenuè percutientes, in ipso percussionis aut emissionis momento exclamantes, bante, vel beye: quod contractum puto ex Have at you. Solitos autem posteriores Græcos τὸ β. pro v. vel b. promiscuè scribere, notius opinor, quàm ut monendum sit.
units.tr: [Ἀβιε], says the same Hesychius, means [ἔξαλλον], in the Scythian language. If Hesychius means that the ancient Scythians used [τὸ ἀβιε] in the sense of [ἔβαλλον], that is, to throw or project, as his words seem to intend, then this would agree very well with English speech. For I have often heard people playing at ball, and striking vigorously with the hand or a stick, shouting at the very moment of striking or throwing, bante or beye, which I think is shortened from Have at you. I think it is better known than needs saying that the later Greeks wrote the letter β indiscriminately for v or b.

units.la: Sed nos hæc ut qui in tenebris incedunt, suspenso pede, nihil affirmantes:
units.tr: But we, like those who walk in darkness, go with a cautious step, affirming nothing:

units.la: Videbunt alii & Hellenismi & Saxonifmi peritiores. Hoc mihi certissimum,in quo alios quoque non iniquos judices accessuros puto, non pauca in optimis scriptoribus Græcis, ex Anglicis illuftrari posse.
units.tr: Others more skilled in Hellenism and Saxonism will see. This is most certain to me, and I think other fair judges will agree: that not a few things in the best Greek writers can be illustrated from English.

units.la: Superest de compositis verbis in quibus. Germanicam linguam ad Græcæ fœlicitatem proximè accedere, passiva observatio est. Agnoscit & Julius Scaliger,qui etiam more suo in causas subtiliter inquirit: sed præcipuam tamen omisit, Germanicæ cum Græcâ non in eo tantùm, sed in tam multis affinitatem, ut vel propago ipsius, aut certè consanguinea (ut ita dicam) constituenda sit. Apparet autem ista fœlicitas tum in aliis, tum in propriis nominibus, quæ omniaferè ut ex pluribus verbis mirâ facilitate, & ut ipsâ pronunciatione generosum quid spirent, coalescentibus constant; ita nullum est,cui non constet,aut olim saltem, eodem id quoque confirmante Scaligero, sua ratio constiterit. Præter illa autem quæ Græco more & exemplo composita sunt, qualia illa vetera, Æftertplin-gend, (Διάλογος) Ἀεεr-ceoʒl : (χωρ-ρς:)
units.tr: There remains the matter of compound words, in which the German language is recognised as coming closest to the felicity of Greek. This is a commonly observed point. Julius Scaliger also recognises it and, in his usual way, inquires subtly into the causes, but he has omitted the chief one: the affinity of German with Greek is not only in this, but in so many things that German must be regarded as either an offshoot of Greek or at least a close kinsman, so to speak. This felicity appears both in common words and in proper names, which nearly all consist of several words coalesced with a remarkable ease, so that by the very pronunciation they breathe something noble. And so there is no word that does not, once, or at least originally, have its own meaning clear to someone, Scaliger himself confirming this. Besides those words that are compounded in the Greek manner and after the Greek example, such as the old compounds Æftertplingend (Dialogue [Διάλογος]), Ærcæðl (...) [χωρ...], [...]

units.la: ρς:) ψ̈s : ) Æfenblptta : (συμμοςῳ, συμμί-λοχῳ :) An•twtge : (μονομαχίας: ) an• mode (σύμφυχῳ:) Boc-bo;b: (βιβλιο-θήκη:) Bzpde-bure, (quasi dicas πεςὶ θεο-νοκόλων : nam Sæλαμῳ, est Hebraicum, עלמר ארח : ) & id genus alia plurima : præter hæc inquam, quædam alia supersunt in usu hodiéque apud Anglos, quæ ex puris Græcis composita sunt : qualia, οἰκογενὴς, & cockny: a bzibegroeme, (q. d. πεςὶ θεονόμῳ, vel περιθεονόμῳ, ut nunc quidem scribimus cum litera z, at olim bzpdegnma ; constanter fine z.) a thzelbold, q. d. σωφρονόμῳ: aliáque, quæ quotquot se nobis offerent, suis locis invenientur.
units.tr: ... Æfenblptta (sharing in common [συμμορῷ], fellow-combatant [συμμίλοχῳ]), An•twtge (single combat [μονομαχίας]), an• mode (with one spirit [σύμψυχῳ]), Boc-bob (library [βιβλιοθήκη]), Bzpde-bure (as if you said "concerning the gods' guardians"; for Sæλαμῳ is Hebrew, [עלמר ארח]), and many other kinds of the same sort. Besides these, I say, there are certain others that are still in use today among the English and that are composed of pure Greek: such as oikogenes [οἰκογενὴς] and cockny; a bzibegroeme (that is, "concerning the god of law" [περὶ θεονόμῳ], or "around the god of law" [περιθεονόμῳ], as we now indeed write it with the letter z, but formerly bzpdegnma, always without z); a thzelbold, that is, "of sound mind" [σωφρονόμῳ]; and others, which, however many present themselves to us, will be found in their proper places.

units.la: Ultimum nunc superest argumentum, quod ab historiâ, & rerum gestarum memoriâ. Ego sic censeo: Si funditus periisset lingua Germanica, ut nullum ex verbis argumentū duci posfit ; ex ipsarum tamen rerum gestarum, quæ memoriæ mandatæ sunt, circumstantiis probabiliter inferri posse, linguam Germanicam de Græcâ multum traxisse, & ex illâ partim constitisse. Sed hoc ad hujus opellæ coronidem referbamus. Ad verborum Syllogen nunc properamus: quam tamen prius quam exhibemus, quia veteris dicti memores, Homine imperito nihil iniquius esse, ita animo praesagimus, multos his non assuetos repertum iri, qui solitas verborum contractiones, protractiones, inflexiones; literarum inter se non affinium tantum, sed aliarum quorumcunque permutationes, & non raro transpositiones ex insolentiâ miraturi sint, & inde nostras Etymologias si non plane respuituri, pro suspectis tamen & coactis habituri: quanquam facile erat labori parcere, & ad linguas in confesso traduces & cognatas, Gallicam, Italicam, Hispanicam, aliasque ejusdem generis, tales remittere; Et jam multa dicta sint, ex quibus minus illa mira & incredibilia videri debeant: nos tamen quò nostram de omnibus bene merendi voluntatem tanto magis probaremus, alia quoq; nonnulla praeter ea quae jam attulimus, eodem spectantia, collectioni nostrae praemittenda duximus.
units.tr: There remains now the last argument, which comes from history and the memory of events. My view is this: even if the German language had perished utterly, so that no argument could be drawn from its words, it could still be reasonably inferred from the circumstances of the events that have been committed to memory that the German language drew much from Greek and in part was constituted from it. But I was reserving this for the crown of this little work. Now we hasten to the collection of words. Yet before we set it out, since we remember the old saying, "Nothing is more unjust than an ignorant man," I anticipate in my mind that many who are not accustomed to these things will be found who, from unfamiliarity, will marvel at the usual contractions, prolongations and inflections of words, and the interchanges not only of letters that are unrelated to one another but of any letters whatever, and not infrequently transpositions; and therefore, if they do not altogether reject our etymologies, they will at least hold them suspect and forced. Although it would have been easy to spare myself the labour and to refer them to languages agreed to be kindred, such as French, Italian, Spanish and others of the same kind, and although many things have already been said from which those marvels and incredibilities ought to seem less strange, I have nevertheless thought fit to put forward, before our collection, several other things besides those already mentioned that bear on the same point, so that I may show all the more how eager I am to deserve well of everyone.

units.la: Hoc igitur primum; in omnibus linguis obscuriorum quarundam, & remotiorum originum & significationum num exempla reperiri, quibus tamen ubi probabilis ratio subest admittendis, non eo nomine rejiciendas esse, quod obscurae sint & remotae.
units.tr: This, then, is the first: in all languages there are examples of certain more obscure and remote origins and meanings, which, where a probable reason underlies them, are to be admitted, and are not to be rejected merely because they are obscure and remote.

units.la: Obscurioris originis ratio non una. Prima haec, cum multa intervenit, sed quae tamen analogia nititur, literarum mutatio. Exempla jam plura in prioribus attulimus, & omnes linguae innumera suppeditant. Quanquam quid opus exempla longe quaerere, quae ipsa loquendi ars, a qua pueri initiantur, abunde suppeditet? A τύπτω, exempli causa, per multas mutationum vices, sed notas & statas, formatur praeteritum passivum τέτυμμαι: tanta quidem soni & elementorum diversitate, ut plane aliud verbum videri possit; cum tamen sit praesentis istius vera & germana soboles. Tale comparativum ἀγ-αθον, ab ἀγγὺς nam ἀμείνων, ἀφείων, &c. quae positivo ἀγαθὸς comparativorum usum praestant, ab alia sunt quam positivus origine. Sed ἄσσον ab ἀγχύς, & si non minus alienum sono, certa tamen analogiae ratione nititur. Talia multa Grammatica suppeditat, quae vel leviter inspicientibus occurrent.
units.tr: There is more than one reason for an obscure origin. The first is this: when much has intervened, yet it rests on an analogy, the change of letters. We have already given several examples in what precedes, and all languages supply countless more. Yet why should we seek examples far off, when the very art of speaking, by which boys are initiated, supplies them abundantly? From τύπτω, for example, through many changes, yet known and fixed ones, the passive perfect τέτυμμαι is formed, with such a difference of sound and letters that it might seem a quite different verb, although it is the true and genuine offspring of that present. Such a comparative as ἀγ-αθον, from ἀγγὺς? No: ἀμείνων, ἀφείων, etc., which supply the use of comparatives to the positive ἀγαθὸς, are of a different origin from the positive. But ἄσσον from ἀγχύς, although no less alien in sound, nevertheless rests on a sure ground of analogy. Grammar supplies many such things, which will meet anyone who looks at them even lightly.

units.la: Sed & illorum verborum, alio quamvis in genere,non obscura minùs,quanquam certa in multis, origo, quibus plurium cauffarū ab ipsorum verborū significatione remotiorum connexio, & certi quidam eventus ; aut certæ denique φεσέσις & loquendi formulæ ortum dedere. Tale apud nos istud notiffimum Church: ad cujus originem ut perveniamus, primo Κυεὶς, absolutè, pro Κύει© Χειστός ; deinde κυειανὸν, vel κυειακὸς οἶκ©, pro loco in quo Κύει© ille coli solitus, explicanda: quorum certitudinem evincunt antiqui Canones & alia veterum Christianorum scripta : cùm tamen magis obvia, sed falsa, ex Latino cors, (unde cohors:) vel certè ex Græco κηρύσσω, κηρυκεῖον, (quasi locus prædicationis,) derivatio.
units.tr: But the origin of some words, though in other respects no less obscure and in many cases certain, lies in the connection of several causes more remote from the meaning of the words themselves, in certain events, or finally in certain idioms and turns of speech. Such is the very well-known English word Church. To reach its origin, we must first explain Kyriakos, used absolutely, for Kyrios Christos [Κύριος Χριστός]; then kyriakon or kyriakos oikos [κυριακὸν or κυριακὸς οἶκος], for the place where that Kyrios was usually worshipped. The certainty of this is shown by the ancient canons and other writings of the early Christians. Yet the more obvious derivation, from Latin cors (whence cohors), or certainly from Greek κηρύσσω, κηρυκεῖον [kēryssō, kērykeion] (as if it were a place of preaching), is false.

units.la: Vocem charta ( Græcè χάρτης ) ex Græco χαίρειν, quòd ejus olim præcipuus usus esset ad salutem ( seu π χαίρειν ) scribendam & mittendam, plerifquè non sine ratione creditum : nec viris summis assentiri possum, ex Arabico petentibus. Affinis vox saltem, ex salutem contracta; quòd qui nihil aliud haberent quod scriberent, hoc saltem, salvere
units.tr: The word charta (in Greek χάρτης) is commonly and not without reason believed to come from the Greek χαίρειν [chairein], because its chief use was for writing and sending greetings (or the formula χαίρειν). I cannot agree with the great men who seek its origin in Arabic. A related word, at least, is contracted from salutem: those who had nothing else to write would write at least this, salvere.

units.la: [Remaining word(s) at the foot of the page not legible.] salvere amicos jubebant; & propriam nuntiabant salutem. Haud dissimilis Gallici verbis chere; & Anglici feed, origo, de quo in ἀφιλῶς.
units.tr: [Remaining word(s) at the foot of the page not legible.] salvere they bade their friends, and announced their own salutem. Not unlike this is the French word chere, and the English feed, whose origin I discuss under ἀφιλῶς.

units.la: Mira vocis oppido pro valde origo, quam tradunt veteres Grammatici non unus. Translatio à rusticis, inquit Donatus, qui interroganti quεadmodū fruges provenissent, respondebant, Oppido : id est, quae sibi & oppido sufficere potuissent. Paulo aliter Festus, qui tamen in summâ convenit. Confirmat hanc etymologiam vox Græca ὀππία, quam ex Hebraico ּ, ejusdem cum Latino oppido significationis, ortam conjiciebat in Adversariis ὁ μακαρίτης parens meus. De verbo, seu adverbio potius Græci παντάλως origine, quid idem in Adversariis, quia hactenus alibi quod meminerim non occurrit, Lectori quoq; promere non pigebit.
units.tr: The remarkable origin of the word oppido, meaning "very," is given by more than one ancient grammarian. Donatus says: "It is a figure taken from country people, who, when asked how the crops had turned out, answered oppido, that is, that they could be enough for themselves and in plenty." Festus gives it a little differently, but agrees in substance. The Greek word ὀππία [oppia] confirms this etymology; my late father conjectured in his Adversaria that it arose from a Hebrew word of the same meaning as Latin oppido. I will not be reluctant to set out for the reader also what the same man wrote in the Adversaria about the origin of the Greek adverb παντάλως [pantalōs], since, as far as I remember, it has not occurred elsewhere up to now.

units.la: Quid est, (ita ille) cur παντάλως significat frustrà? Veteres cùm initum hominis conatum notare vellent, ἀλλὰ ἐλθῶν παῖδες ἐποίησαν dicebant. Arist. Περὶ I. I. c. 32. ὡς ἀλλὰ ἔλθεῖν παντάλως, &c. Sic & Latini loquuntur. Inde quidem adverbium παντάλως, Sic apud
units.tr: "Why," he says, "does pantalōs mean in vain? When the ancients wished to denote a man's first attempt at something, they said ἀλλὰ ἐλθὼν παῖδες ἐποίησαν [alla elthōn paides epoiēsan]." Aristotle, Περὶ ... book 1, chapter 32: "as if to go in vain," and so on. The Latins also speak in this way. Hence indeed the adverb pantalōs. Thus among

units.la: Latinos, è vestigio, oppido, extemplo, saltem, aliáque adverbia è φεγσιαν ἐκαστ nata. Haclenus ille.
units.tr: the Latins: immediately (è vestigio), oppido, extemplo, saltem, and other adverbs derived from a phrase of this kind. So far he.

units.la: Hebrǣi quidem, seu Chaldæi verbis abundant, ex ejusmodi contractionibus ortis, qualia hoc ipsum כנמא (ejusmodi: ) כביכ : aliáque istius linguæ peritis satis nota.
units.tr: The Hebrews, or the Chaldeans, indeed abound in words arising from such contractions, such as the word meaning "of such a kind" (ejusmodi) and the word for "like this," and others well known to those skilled in that language.

units.la: Hæc igitur obscuriora sunt: qualia tamen, ut jam diximus, in omnibus linguis plurima: in quibus eruendis non minore judicio, aut etiam majore, quàm sagacitate opus est, ne in Goropiana deliria & portenta res excidat; quo nihil fœdius.
units.tr: These, then, are more obscure; yet, as we have already said, there are very many such in all languages. In unravelling them one needs no less judgement, or even more, than sagacity, lest the matter collapse into the dreams and monstrosities of Goropius, than which nothing is more foul.

units.la: Sed & hoc in multis obscuritatem parit, quòd verba sæpe ex altera quidem lingua, sed in aliam significationem transferuntur: aut certè longo usu in alterutra seu matrice seu traduce lingua à primæva significatione degerant.
units.tr: But this also produces obscurity in many cases: words are often taken from one language but transferred into another meaning, or, through long use in one or the other language, whether the mother tongue or the language that passed them on, have wandered from their original sense.

units.la: Innumera sunt in lingua Syriaca, Hebrææ propagine, quæ Hebraica sunt & sono & scripturâ, sed diversæ apud Hebræos & diversæ apud illos significationis: in non paucis tam diversæ, ut cùm eadem sint verba, nulla tamen significationum cognatio vel affinitas percipi possit. Μάτηρ, Græcis, mater; aliud mamona Latinis, qui à Græcis acceperunt. Ita vox Tbetis, illis terra; his, mare. Βλάτα aliud Græcis, aliud Fissus Latinis. Κύρι⊙ itidem, aliud quicurtus. Aliud fot Gallis & Belgis, quovel Græcis, (ἀσπίδ⊙ :) vel Anglis, quamen à Gallis videntur accepisse. Ἄ-mus, calx, limus; Anglicè, arme, thalb, lime, vicina quidem, sed diversa tamen significatione. Λάμπας Græcis fax; Anglis, lucerna, a lampe: & contrà, λύχ-νο, Græcis lucerna; Anglis, a lincht, lampas. Apothecarius, aliud Latinis, aliud Gallis, & Anglis. Divinus, nomen substantivum, Latinis & Gallis, ariolus: Anglis, Theologus, a Divine.
units.tr: Countless words in Syriac, a branch of Hebrew, are Hebrew in sound and in writing, but have a different meaning among the Hebrews and among the Syrians; in not a few cases the meanings are so different that, although the words are the same, no kinship or affinity of meaning can be perceived. μήτηρ [mētēr] means mother to the Greeks; but another word, mamona, means something else to the Latins, who took it from the Greeks. So the word Tbetis means earth to the one people and sea to the other. Βλάτα [blata] means one thing to the Greeks and another to the Latins. Κύριος [kyrios] likewise means one thing in one language and something else in another. Fot means one thing to the French and Dutch, and something else to the Greeks (ἀσπίς [aspis]), or to the English, though these seem to have taken it from the French. Ammus, lime, mud: in English arme, thalb, lime, similar in form but with a different meaning. Λάμπας [lampas] means a torch to the Greeks; to the English, lamp means a lantern; and conversely λύχνος [lychnos], a lantern to the Greeks, is for the English a lamp. Apothecarius means one thing to the Latins, another to the French and the English. Divinus, used as a noun, means a soothsayer (ariolus) to the Latins and French, but to the English it means a theologian: a divine.

units.la: Improbare, quid sit Latinis, omnes norunt: to improve, Anglis, propè contrarium. Quanquam (ut hoc obiter) dubito, an ex improbare, & non potiùs ex improbus; quo sensu dixit Virgilius, labor improbus, & Plinius, improba vires; & A. Gell. improba subtilitas; & Seneca, improbum lumen; de maximis, & in suo genere, præcellentibus. An simplici probe, (quod ex proficere, vel probare; i. ἀχαθὲν: ) addita præpositio Anglica, ut in aliis non paucis: quemadmodum & tmpaire, (Gall.empirer:) ex pejorare ? Quicquid hujus sit, certè λυὴ Græcum, & lues Latinum, contrafia : ut & ⵎⵎⵎ Hebraïs, & ⵎⵎⵎ Arabibus; ut jam olim notatum doctissimo Rabbinorum Maimonidi. Tale & ἀφὸς (ut οἶς, οὗτος : ἀὴρ, οὐνὶ : ἄορυ, ἀνερπὴς, &c. inserto ꝑ v.) pravus: cujus ratio ex effectu potius, quàm ex ipsâ rei naturâ,cùm lenitas & facilitas, alios ut plurimùm, ipsa per se aliòquin laudatissima, depravent & corrumpant. Ita denique ⅰtranch. Anglis, agilis; Germanis & Belgis, ægrotus.
units.tr: What improbare means in Latin, everyone knows; to improve in English is almost the opposite. Although (to mention this in passing) I doubt whether it comes from improbare rather than from improbus, in which sense Virgil said labor improbus, Pliny improba vires, Aulus Gellius improba subtilitas, and Seneca improbum lumen, of the greatest things, excellent in their kind. Or is it simple probe (from proficere or probare; that is, ἀγαθόν [agathon]) with an added English preposition, as in many other cases; just as the French empirer comes from pejorare? Whatever the answer, the Greek λύη [lymē] and the Latin lues are opposites, as are the Hebrew and Arabic words, as the most learned rabbi Maimonides already noted long ago. Similar is ἀφαυρός [aphauros] (as with οἶς, οὗτος; ἀήρ, οὐρανός; ἄορυ, ἀνερπής, and so on, with an inserted letter), pravus: its basis lies in the effect rather than in the nature of the thing itself, since gentleness and easiness often corrupt and ruin others, though in themselves they are otherwise most praiseworthy. Finally, the English agile is tranch, and the Germans and Dutch have ægrotus.

units.la: Sed in omni hac circa voces & Etymologias ⅰⅰⅰⅰⅰⅰ nihil est in quo plùs sibi consuetudo permiserit, quàm in contrahendis ac decurtandis vocabulis: Nulla autem lingua, quæ monosyllabis variisque verborum compendiis plus delectetur, quàm Anglica. Hinc illa prænominum, quorum usus in ore vulgi creberrimus; vulgatissima contractio; ut <bl>Besse</bl>, pro Elizabeth: <bl>Batt</bl>, pro Bartholomew: <bl>Hitt</bl>, pro. <bl>Christopher</bl>: Ban, pro Barnabas, &c:
units.tr: But in all this discussion of words and etymologies, nothing is more freely permitted by custom than the shortening and clipping of words. And no language delights more in monosyllables and various verbal abbreviations than English. Hence come those forenames, very common on the lips of the people, the most widespread contractions: Besse for Elizabeth, Batt for Bartholomew, Hitt for Christopher, Ban for Barnabas, and so on.

units.la: quibus haud abfimilia, gaffer, gam- mer, pro good father, good mo- ther: buffe, pro bonfetwpfe; quæ familiariffimæ & ufitatiffimæ compellationes. Non minús autem contracta, fpittle, ex bofpitalle; oipin, ex auri pigmento; palfp, ex παρέλνυσ; parflp, ex petrofelynum; gourd, ex cucurbita. Talia Gallorum fouley, ex folifequium: & poulx, ex pediculus. Ex cujus ultimâ syllabâ (quod fateor non ordinarium, cùm terminatio non fit de essentiâ verborum) lonfe (vel ut alii lotofe) fufpicetur aliquis etiam Anglicum fluxiffe: nifi fit Latinum lues, Græcorum imitatione, quibus φθεῖρες, ἀπὸ τ φθογες. In plerisque contractis, aliqua etiam literarum tranfpofitio intervenit: quæ tanto magis obfcurat originem, ut in aridus, Dzp [?]: humidus, motst [?]: afper, sharp [?]: & fimilibus. Caterum quamvis in aliis non minús vulgaris, in propriis tamen, urbium præcipuè, locorumque quos hiftoria aut infignis aliquis eventus nobilitavit nominibus, magis obfervabilis contractio; ut Stambol, vel Sttmbotle, (quorum illud Turcis, hoc Græcis ufitatum tradunt:) ex Constantinopolis : Baldon, ex Camalodunum: Milan, ex Mediolanum : Bzenoble ex Gratianopolis : & illud quo nil contractius esse potest, & quod nullam habet dubitationem, Atr, ex Aquae Sextiae.
units.tr: Not unlike these are gaffer and gammer for good father and good mother, and buffe for ... (the most familiar and common forms of address). Equally contracted are spittle from hospital, oipin from a pigment of gold, palsy from παράλυσις [paralysis], parsley from petroselinum, and gourd from cucurbita. Similar are the French fouley from folisequium, and poulx from pediculus. From the last syllable of the latter (which I admit is not usual, since an ending is not of the essence of words) someone might suspect that even the English lonfe (or as others have it, lotofe) flowed, unless it is the Latin lues, by imitation of the Greeks, who said φθεῖρες [phtheires], from lice. In most contracted forms some transposition of letters also occurs, which obscures the origin all the more, as in aridus (Dzp [?]), humidus (motst [?]), afper (sharp [?]), and similar words. Yet although the contraction is more common in other words, it is more noticeable in proper names, especially of cities and places made famous by history or some notable event: Stambol, or Sttmbotle (the former used by the Turks, the latter, they report, by the Greeks), from Constantinopolis; Baldon from Camalodunum; Milan from Mediolanum; Bzenoble from Gratianopolis; and that which can be contracted no further, and about which there is no doubt, Atr, from Aquae Sextiae.

units.la: De literarum singularum permutatione qui consulendi, jam priùs indicavimus. De literis tamen l. & r. quod non uno monitum fimus, non pigebit hîc, (quia magnum usum habet) uno verbo tetigisse, non eas tantùm omnium aliarum literarum frequentissimâ consuetudine invicem permutabiles esse ; sed etiam utramque τῆ εὐφωνία in contrahendis aut producendis pro cujusque linguae consuetudine vocabulis ; in transponendis & coagmentandis literis ut plurimùm inservire.
units.tr: Those who wish to consult on the interchange of single letters we have already indicated earlier. Concerning the letters l and r, on which we have been warned more than once, it will not be tedious to touch on them briefly here, since they are of great use: not only are they interchanged with the most frequent custom among all other letters, but both also serve euphony (τῆ εὐφωνία [tē euphōnia]) in contracting or lengthening words according to the usage of each language, and mostly in transposing and joining letters.

units.la: Ad vocales autem quod attinet, quanquam etiam inter illas ut & inter consonantes aliae aliis & sono & potestate propinquiores sint, atque inde facilius inter se permutentur ; nulla tamen tam alienae ab altera potestatis aut soni, ut non facile confundantur, & mutuas sedes occupent. Exempla ubique in omnibus linguis obvia : & abundè ad fidem minus expertis sufficiant, quæ Caninius & Jul. Scaliger in hoc genere suppeditant. Angli multa hodie exilius proserunt, quæ olim latius & pleniùs. quod discrimen etiam in hodiernis dialectis observes. Affixum privativum, quod Anglis, lesse ; Belgis,loofe ; ut quod illi goðloofe, Angli goðleffe, &c. Ita illis oogbe, ooie, oo, quod Anglis, epes, hepie, eare, &c. Ex Latino lippus,Belgæ loope; ex piscis,Galli poiffon effinxerunt. Sed & in eodem ejusdem linguæ dialectiq; verbo eadem varietas interdum occurrit, ut foot,in singulari ; plurali, feet : ita tooth, teeth, &c.
units.tr: As for the vowels, although some are closer to others in sound and power, and so are more easily interchanged, none is so far removed from another in power or sound that they are not readily confused and take each other's place. Examples are found everywhere in all languages, and those less experienced in the matter will find enough in what Caninius and Julius Scaliger supply on this subject. The English today pronounce many sounds more thinly that formerly were broader and fuller, and you may observe this difference in present-day dialects too. The privative affix that the English write as "less," the Dutch write as "loos"; so what they write as goðloofe, the English write as goðleffe, and so on. Likewise the Dutch oogbe, ooie, oo correspond to the English epes, hepie, eare, and so on. From the Latin lippus the Dutch formed "loope," and from piscis the French formed poiffon. Sometimes the same variation also occurs within one word of the same language and dialect: "foot" in the singular, "feet" in the plural; so "tooth" and "teeth," and so on.

units.la: Eadem porrò diphthongorum quæ vocalium ratio. aliæ aliis naturâ propinquiores, sed omnes permutabiles. Sed & vocales simplices in diphthongas, & diphthongi in vocales sæpè migrant. Exempla apud Caninium,& Scaligerum quibusvis obvia. Multa quoq; Robertus Stephanus, non ille celeberrimus, de melioribus literis meritiffimus ; sed ejus opinor filius, Henrici frater,in Grammaticâ suâ Gallicâ, Latinè Gallicéque excusâ : ubi Gallicorum verborum ex Latinis derivando-rum rum rationem doctissimè docet, & accuratissimè.
units.tr: The principle for diphthongs is the same as for vowels: some are naturally closer to others, but all are interchangeable. Simple vowels often pass into diphthongs, and diphthongs often pass into simple vowels. Examples obvious to anyone can be found in Caninius and Scaliger. Robert Estienne, not the most famous of that name, who deserved very well of good letters, but (I think) the son of Henri and his brother, also supplies many in his French Grammar, printed in Latin and French. There he teaches, very learnedly and very accurately, how French words are derived from Latin ones.

units.la: Monendus præterea, Lector, in Hesychii Lex. Gr. passim reperiri verba, non alibi apud Græcos qui nunc extant reperienda, quæ vel plane sunt Anglica, aut ad Anglica tam propè accedunt, ut ejusdem merito censeantur originis & profapiæ. Quæ quidem verba, quia incertum erat, an Hesychius pro genuinis Græcis, sed jam rarioribus & obsoletis, qualia in illo plurima: an verò pro barbaris, qualibus itidem refertam esse istam farraginem, verissimè doctorum pridem non unus observarit, exhiberet: id inquam nobis quia incertum erat, neque id nobis consultum videbatur, ut de iis judicium nobis sumeremus; ut non nimis curiosè conquirenda duximus, quæ præstare Græca genuina non possemus; ita nec repudianda quæ se nobis offerrent; vel eo certè nomine, ut Hesychio, de linguâ Græcâ tam benè merito, aliquid inde lucis accenderetur. Talia autem suis locis, addito plerumque Hesychii nomine, exhibebimus.
units.tr: The reader should further be warned that all through Hesychius' Greek lexicon there are found words not found elsewhere among the Greeks who survive today, which are either plainly English or come so close to English that they may rightly be judged of the same origin and stock. Since it was uncertain whether Hesychius gives these as genuine Greek words, though now rarer and obsolete (as most of his words are), or as barbarisms (with which, as more than one learned man has long ago rightly observed, that whole hodgepodge is also stuffed), I say, since this was uncertain to us, and it did not seem advisable to us to form a judgment about them, we did not think we should search too curiously for what we could not vouch for as genuine Greek; nor should we reject what presented itself to us, if only for this reason, that some light might thereby be kindled for Hesychius, who has deserved so well of the Greek language. We will set out such words in their places, usually adding Hesychius' name.

units.la: Cæterùm, valde tempestivè hoc loco
units.tr: Moreover, the most learned observation of Marcus Varro, praised by Gellius, presents itself very opportunely here.

units.la: se nobis ingerit doctissima M.Varronis observatio, Gellio laudata. Multas scil. Romanas voces, origine Græcas esse, quarum tamen origines vulgò ignorentur, quòd verba illa Græca, ex quibus orta sunt, aliis, ut fit, in locum receptis, esse in usu desierint, & ipsis jam Græcis ignota aut certè peregrina sint. Istius esse generis hoc ipsum, Gracum, quod olim τεγινὸν apud Græcos, in usu quotidiano; & à Græcis ad Romanos primùm pervenerit: postea, altero ἴσλω in usum recepto, istud exolevisse, & apud Romanos tantùm remansisse. Item puteus, lepus; quibus addit Gellius, & τὸ fur: quæ omnia sunt originis Græcæ, sed apud Græcos, recentioribus aliis substitutis, desita, aut certè, obsoleta. Geminam huic observationem habet & Plutarchus, in De Isside & Osiride; cujus verba hîc apponam, non eo tantùm nomine, quòd ad nostra hæc opportunissima & appositissima sunt; sed eò quoque libentius, ut cum Varronianis collata facilius intelligantur: cùm ex Latinâ eorum, quæ vulgata est, versione haud temerè quisquam ad mentem Plutarchi penetret. Plutarchus igitur in isto tractatu multis passim verbis & nominibus Ægyptiacis ad Græcas origines inflexis & traductis, quorum tamen rationes à Græcæ linguæ consuetudine partim penitus alienæ, aut partim alieniores, quàm ut aliis pro talibus approbare se posse speraret: ita quodam loco se excusat: Οὐ δεῖ ϑ' Θαυμάζειν τ' ὀνομάτων τ' εἰς τὸ Ἑλληνικὸν ἀνάπλασιν· ἡ γὰρ ἄλλα μύεια τοῖς μετιοῦσιν ἐν τ' Ἑλλάδ' συνεκπεσόντα, μεχεὶ νῦν ἀφειμένη ἡ ξενιλεύσι παρ' ἑτέρους, ὧν ἔνια τῷ ποιητικῷ ἀναχαλκευμένῳ διαβάλλειν ὡς βαρβαρίζοντες οἱ γλωσσάς τὰς τοιαύτας (vel ut quidam ibi conjiciunt, τὰ τοιαῦτα) περιαφορευόντες. Plutarchi hæc sententia est: Qui ex Græcia variis temporibus & occasionibus in varias terras migrarunt, multa secum transportasse vocabula Græca, quæ in Græciâ posteà publico usu, nescio quo fato, intermissa & abdicata, apud Barbaros durent & peregrinentur: Poëtas autem qui talibus pro re natâ, ut probis & legitimis utantur, immeritò à nonnullis culpari, quasi barbaris & peregrinis (quæ γλώσσας vocabant:) utentes vocabulis. Magno igitur in Hesychianis illis, de quibus dicebamus, verbis utendum judicio, ne quis temere pro genuinis Græcis vel admittat vel rejiciat. Cæterùm, non ad ipsa tantùm verba, sed & varias verborum notiones pertinet illa observatio; quas sæpè mutasse, ut aliud alio sæculo significaret idem verbum, non minùs certum est. De quo aliquid in voce ἀλάζων. Tale etiam, vox θέναι, quæ olim, operari, facere, significabat: ut ab Helladio vetere Grammatico in Chrestomathiâ notatum fuisse legimus apud Photium Patriarcham. Hujus autem significationis vestigia apud Homerum aliósq; scriptores Græcos superesse hodiéque plurima. Hinc verbum θής, mercenarius: ut ibidem Helladius. Ab hoc θής, ductum videtur Saxonicum thegn, vel thein, (ut apud Verstegarium:) quod servum liberum significat; planè ut & illud θής, de libero, sed qui paupertate adactus operam locare cogeretur, proprie dici notant veteres. Sed & Anglicum þeg, & Germanicum (seu Belgicum) dienen, quæ ministrare significant, ab eodem, ni fallor, fonte.
units.tr: Varro observes that many Roman words are of Greek origin, yet their origins are commonly unknown, because the Greek words from which they came have gone out of use, other words having been taken in their place, and they are now unknown or at least foreign even to the Greeks themselves. Of this kind is the very word gracum (the Greek word once in daily use among the Greeks, tegînon [τεγινὸν], which came first from the Greeks to the Romans); afterwards, when another word, ishlō [ἴσλω], was received into use, that one fell out of use and remained only among the Romans. Likewise puteus and lepus; to which Gellius adds fur. All these are of Greek origin, but among the Greeks they ceased, or at least became obsolete, when other, more recent words were put in their place. Plutarch too makes a similar observation twice, in his treatise On Isis and Osiris. I will set down his words here, not only because they are most apt and pertinent to our present subject, but also because they are more readily understood when set beside Varro's, since no one could easily grasp Plutarch's meaning from the Latin version that is in common use. In that treatise Plutarch, throughout, bends and transfers many Egyptian words and names to Greek origins; but since their grounds are partly quite foreign to Greek usage, or partly too far removed for him to hope to win approval from others as genuine, he excuses himself at one point thus: "One should not be surprised at the remodelling of names into Greek; for many foreign words that went out from Greece along with those who migrated, and that have since been let go and handed over to other peoples, some of which the poets have reshaped and renewed, are wrongly blamed by some as barbarizing, since these people, who use such words, are called foreign-speakers [γλώσσας]." Plutarch's meaning is this: those who migrated from Greece to various lands at various times and for various reasons carried with them many Greek words, which, by some fate, were afterwards dropped and abandoned in Greece by public usage, yet survive and wander among the barbarians. The poets, who use such words as fit the occasion, as proper and legitimate words, are unjustly blamed by some, as if they used foreign and alien vocabulary (which they called glōssas [γλώσσας]). Great judgment must therefore be used in those Hesychian words of which we were speaking, so that no one rashly admits or rejects them as genuine Greek. Moreover, that observation concerns not only the words themselves but also their various senses; that these have often changed, so that the same word signified one thing in one age and another in another, is no less certain. Something on this point has been said under the word alazōn [ἀλάζων]. Similar is the word thēnai [θέναι], which once meant to work or to make; as we read that the old grammarian Helladius noted in his Chrestomathy, as cited by Photius the Patriarch. Traces of this meaning survive in Homer and other Greek writers in very many places. Hence thēs [θής], a hired man, as Helladius also says there. From this thēs I think the Saxon thegn or thein (as in Verstegan) is derived, which means a free servant; just as the old writers note that the word thēs is properly used of a free man who, reduced by poverty, was compelled to hire out his labour. And the English þeg and the German (or Dutch) dienen, which mean to serve, come, I suspect, from the same source.

units.la: Postremum hoc: Extat liber, & per omnium, Anglicarum antiquitatum non plane incuriosorum, Anglorum manus sub Clarissimo Cambdeniano nomine volitat, Paralipomena Anglica, inscriptus. Cambdenum authorem esse, cum nullum authoris nomen adscriptum sit, ego non praestem. Sed quisquis author fuerit, nescio qua occasione aut consilio, Graecarum originum in aliis linguis jactatores & scrutatores, maximos certe viros, Budaeum aliosque perstringens, ut ne hac quidem laude (quam tamen ille nullam esse satis faustuose pronunciat,) linguam Anglicam deficere aut aliis cedere ostendat, vocum syllabum exhibet, quas adeo cum Graecis convenire contendit, ut de uno fluxisse fonte cuivis facile liquere possit. Sunt sane talia illa, quae ab eo proponuntur: quanquam sunt ex illis quaedam ejus generis (ut γαλ-πάζω, μωκάω, μύσαχες, πολίετον, &c.) quae nos ex nostro syllabo exclusimus, quod incertae essent, a Gallis, an ipsis immediate Graecis, originis. Sed qualiacunque sunt, nos ea seorsim hic ordine digesta alphabetico lectori exhibemus. Ita enim satius visum est, quam nostris immiscere, ne aliena nobis arrogare videremur. *Αγχέας, to bang. *Αξίνη, an axe. *Ασπὶς, a starre. *Αχῶ, ache. Γεύσις, grasse. Ἐλάσων, lesse. *Εγέα, earth. Ζέω, to seeth. Θήρ, a deere. Θέρσης, rash. Θύεα, a dooze. Καχάω -----Καλέω, to call. Καλπάζων, to gallop. Κλεβῶ, a crabbe. Κλίμαξ, a climbing. Κόπτω, to cut. Κρίκω, to creake. Κυειαχὴ, a Church. Κύσαι, to kisse. Λάππω, to lappe, Λοῖδω, last. Λύχνω, a linck. Μύνη, the Spoone. Μύλη, a mill. Μύσαχες, maffacbes. Μωμάω, to mocke. Νέω, new. ᾿Οαεγι, whozith spoze. ᾿Ολκάς, a hulke. ᾿Ολω, whole. ᾿Οχαθω, an orchard. Οὔθαρ, an udder. Πάτω, a path. Ποτήειον, a pot. Πῶλω, a foale. Ραβδὸς, a rodde. Ράιφν, to raze out. Ράκω, a ragge. Ραvὶς, raine. Ραπίζω, to rappe. Ρασωνη, rest. Σκάφη, a chipp. Σκώπτω, to scoffe. Στρόφω, a roape. Στρωννυμι, to strow. Τίτθω, a tett. Φαῦλω, fonle. Χάρμη, skirmish, ᾿Ωχέα, oker.
units.tr: Lastly, there is a book, flying about in the hands of all the English, not wholly careless of English antiquities, which goes under the most famous name of Camden and is entitled Paralipomena Anglica. I will not vouch that Camden is its author, since no author's name is attached to it. But whoever the author is, for some reason or purpose, while he attacks those who boast of and search out Greek origins in other languages, very great men indeed, such as Budaeus and others, he sets out a syllabary of words to show that the English language does not fall short of, or yield to others, even in this distinction. He argues that these words agree so closely with Greek that anyone could easily see they flowed from one source. Indeed such words as he proposes are of this kind, although some of his examples are of a sort (such as gal-pazō [γαλ-πάζω], mōkaō [μωκάω], mysakhes [μύσαχες], poliēton [πολίετον], and so on) that I have excluded from our own syllabary, because their origin, whether from the French or directly from the Greeks, was uncertain. But whatever their worth, I set them out here separately, arranged in alphabetical order for the reader. For this seemed better than mixing them with our own, lest we should seem to claim for ourselves what belongs to others. aggheas [Ἀγχέας], to bang axine [Ἀξίνη], an axe aspis [Ἀσπὶς], a starre akhō [Ἀχῶ], ache geusis [Γεύσις], grasse elasōn [Ἐλάσων], lesse egea [Ἐγέα], earth zeō [Ζέω], to seeth thēr [Θήρ], a deere thersēs [Θέρσης], rash thyea [Θύεα], a dooze kakhaō [Καχάω], ----- kaleō [Καλέω], to call kalpazōn [Καλπάζων], to gallop klebō [Κλεβῶ], a crabbe klimax [Κλίμαξ], a climbing koptō [Κόπτω], to cut krikō [Κρίκω], to creake kyeiakhē [Κυειαχὴ], a Church kysai [Κύσαι], to kisse lappō [Λάππω], to lappe loidō [Λοῖδω], last lykhnō [Λύχνω], a linck mynē [Μύνη], the Spoone mylē [Μύλη], a mill mysakhes [Μύσαχες], maffacbes mōmaō [Μωμάω], to mocke neō [Νέω], new oaegi [᾿Οαεγι], whozith spoze holkas [᾿Ολκάς], a hulke holō [᾿Ολω], whole ocharthō [᾿Οχαθω], an orchard outhar [Οὔθαρ], an udder pato [Πάτω], a path potēeion [Ποτήειον], a pot pōlō [Πῶλω], a foale rhabdos [Ραβδὸς], a rodde rhaiphō [Ράιφν], to raze out rhakō [Ράκω], a ragge rhavis [Ραvὶς], raine rhapizō [Ραπίζω], to rappe rhasōnē [Ρασωνη], rest skaphē [Σκάφη], a chipp skōptō [Σκώπτω], to scoffe strophō [Στρόφω], a roape strōnnymi [Στρωννυμι], to strow titthō [Τίτθω], a tett phaulō [Φαῦλω], fonle kharmē [Χάρμη], skirmish ōkhea [᾿Ωχέα], oker

units.la: Jam ad nostra veniamus. Ab iis autem incipiemus in quibus τὸ α initiale per aphæresin Anglis usitatissimam præscin-ditur: qualia quoque ex Latinis haud
units.tr: Now let us come to our own language. We shall begin with those words in which the initial alpha is cut off by aphaeresis, a practice most common among the English.

units.la: pauca,ut apis,a bee: aper, a boare,&c. fed ex Græcis longè plura ; ut ex longâ exemplorum serie patebit. Atqui hoc ipsum ex usu & genio linguæ Græcæ ad Anglos derivatum. Talia enim illis ; ἀλάζων, λάζων : ἀσαφὶς,σαφὶς : σάχυς, ἀσάχυς : ἀμαυρόω, μαυρόω : βλήγξ, ἀ-βλήγρ : ταράλαξ, ἀταράλαξ : ταράιρω, ἀ-ταράιρω : ἀσεγτὴ, σεγτὴ : aliáque plurima. Jam Anglica, bono, ut sperus, à boni verbi aufpicio, videamus.
units.tr: few, such as apis, a bee; aper, a boare, etc., but from the Greek far more, as a long series of examples will make clear. And indeed this very habit was derived by the English from the usage and genius of the Greek language. For they have such pairs as: alazōn, lazōn [ἀλάζων, λάζων]; asaphis, saphis [ἀσαφὶς, σαφὶς]; sakhus, asakhus [σάχυς, ἀσάχυς]; amauroō, mauroō [ἀμαυρόω, μαυρόω]; blēnx, a-blēgr [βλήγξ, ἀ-βλήγρ]; taralax, ataralax [ταράλαξ, ἀταράλαξ]; tarairō, a-tarairō [ταράιρω, ἀ-ταράιρω]; asegtē, segtē [ἀσεγτὴ, σεγτὴ]; and very many others. Now let us look at English words, with good fortune, as I hope, under the auspices of a good word.

units.la: A
units.tr: A

units.la: Ἀγαθὸς, bonus, Anglicè, good, de quo videantur quæ jam suprà. Ab eodem, & τὸ Θεὸν, quòd Deum significat, fluxisse multi non improbabiliter opinantur. Deus enim cùm solus bonus, ídque perfectissimè bonus sit, merito κατ' ἐξοχὴν dicitur ὁ Ἀγαθὸς : Hoc faciunt Christi verba, Εἷς ἀγαθὸς : Saxonicè, An God is god. Sed & ipsi sapientiores Ethnici idem agnoscunt. Eximium Platonis locū proferam ut cum verbis Christi contendatur : Τνὰ ἀνδρὸς ἀγαθὸν, χαλεπὸν ἀληθῶς· οἷον τε μὲν τοι ἐπὶ χρόνου τινὰ Φυόμενον ἢ διαμένειν ἐν τούτῳ τῇ ἕξει, ἢ τὸ, ἀνδρὸς ἀγαθὸν, ὡς δς οὐ λέγεις δ' Πίστιν, ἀδύνατον ἢ ἐκ ἀν- θρώπων, ἀλλὰ Θεὸς ἂν μόνῳ τῷ τοῦ ἔχοι τὸ χεῖρας. Quem tam eximium locum mirror illos fugisse, quibus quicquid apud exteros, quod quoquo modo ad sacri hujus Evangelistæ sive verba, sive sensus trahi posset, undique colligere propositum fuit. Sed & Latinis Deus, usitatâ formulâ, Optimus, Maximus: & quidem Optimus, priusquam Maximus; quæ Ovidii Poëtæ, ut alios omittam, præclara alicubi observatio est. Merito igitur τὸ Θεὸν, ex γοὸν, sive ἁγιασμός. Interim, de Hebraicâ quid dici possit, aut Ægyptiacâ quid ab aliis dicatur origine, non me latet: quæ accuratius excutere non est hujus loci.
units.tr: Agathos [Ἀγαθὸς], bonus, in English good; on this see what has been said above. Many think, not improbably, that from the same root comes theos [τὸ Θεὸν], which signifies God. For since God alone is good, and is good in the most perfect degree, he is rightly called ho Agathos [ὁ Ἀγαθὸς] by way of eminence. Christ's words, Heis agathos [Εἷς ἀγαθὸς], "One is good," do this. In Saxon it is An God is god. But the wiser heathen also acknowledge the same thing. I shall quote a remarkable passage of Plato so that it may be set beside the words of Christ: "It is truly hard for a man to become good; for it is possible for a man, for some time, to grow and remain in this state, but for a man to be good in the sense of... it is impossible; only God could have this privilege" [Τνὰ ἀνδρὸς ἀγαθὸν, χαλεπὸν ἀληθῶς· οἷον τε μὲν τοι ἐπὶ χρόνου τινὰ Φυόμενον ἢ διαμένειν ἐν τούτῳ τῇ ἕξει, ἢ τὸ, ἀνδρὸς ἀγαθὸν, ὡς δς οὐ λέγεις δ' Πίστιν, ἀδύνατον ἢ ἐκ ἀν- θρώπων, ἀλλὰ Θεὸς ἂν μόνῳ τῷ τοῦ ἔχοι τὸ χεῖρας]. I am surprised that those who tried to gather from foreign writers everything that could in any way be drawn to the words or the sense of this sacred Evangelist have missed so remarkable a passage. The Latins too, by a customary formula, call God Best and Greatest, and indeed Best before Greatest; a fine observation of the poet Ovid, among others, somewhere. Rightly, then, theos [τὸ Θεὸν] is derived from agathos, or from hagiasmos [ἁγιασμός]. Meanwhile I am not unaware of what may be said about a Hebrew origin, or what others have said about an Egyptian one; but to examine these more carefully is not the place for it.

units.la: Ἀγάλλεσθαι, gestire, gaudere, exultare: so be glad: nisi ex ἀγάλλεσθαι, quod idem, significat, ut Hesychius exponit.
units.tr: Agallesthai [Ἀγάλλεσθαι]: to exult, rejoice, be glad: <bl>so be glad</bl>; unless it comes from agallesthai itself, which has the same meaning, as Hesychius explains.

units.la: Ἀγάζεσθαι, admirari, venerari: so gaze.
units.tr: Agazesthai [Ἀγάζεσθαι]: to wonder at, to revere: <bl>so gaze</bl>.

units.la: Ἀγασθῆς: ἀλλ' ἀγαστὸν, apud Homerum, id est, ἐπιφανὲς, terribilis species, ut Eustathius exponit. Saxonicè, gaff (hodie, gboft) spiritus. Unde & gaftly, terribilis. Nihil enim plerisque tali specie terribilius. Hinc illa discipulorum Christi consternatio, narrata Matthaeo, XIV.v.26. Hinc Apuleio, in solemni imprecatione, species mortuorum, busstorum formidamina, sepulchrorum terriculamenta.
units.tr: Agastēs [Ἀγασθῆς]; but agaston [ἀγαστὸν] in Homer means the manifest, that is, a terrible appearance, as Eustathius explains. In Saxon, <bl>gaff</bl> (today <bl>gboft</bl>), a spirit. Hence also <bl>gaftly</bl>, terrible, for nothing is more terrifying to most people than such an appearance. Hence the consternation of Christ's disciples, related in Matthew 14:26. Hence Apuleius, in a solemn curse: "the appearances of the dead, the terrors of the ghosts, the frights of the sepulchres."

units.la: ᾿Αλεγνὸς, infirmus, languidus, iners; <bl>a Dzone</bl>: nisi quis malit ex σπάναξ, sucus.
units.tr: Alegnos [Ἀλεγνὸς]: weak, languid, sluggish; <bl>a dzone</bl>; unless someone prefers to derive it from spanax [σπάναξ], juice.

units.la: ᾿Αλεπχὴς, non videns: etiam ἀφανὴς, obscurus, ut Hesychius exponit: <bl>Dark.</bl>
units.tr: Alepchēs [Ἀλεπχὴς]: not seeing; also aphanēs [ἀφανὴς], obscure, as Hesychius explains: <bl>dark</bl>.

units.la: ᾿Αβαχὴς, mutus, taciturnus: (ἀβαχέω, sileo; non habeo quid dicam:) planè ut Angli, cum dicunt, <bl>We was very</bl> <bl>blanck.</bl>
units.tr: Abachēs [Ἀβαχὴς]: mute, taciturn (abacheō [ἀβαχέω], to be silent; not to have anything to say), just as the English say, <bl>we was very</bl> <bl>blanck</bl>.

units.la: ᾿Απλοῦς, simplex, sincerus, <bl>Dull</bl>: Vide infrà, in ἁπλοῦς.
units.tr: Haplous [ἀπλοῦς]: simple, sincere; <bl>dull</bl>. See below, under haplous.

units.la: ᾿Αληθὴς, verus: ἀληθεία, veritas: true, truetb. Veteribus trtwtan, fidere; & trtwtb, fidelitas: quæ cum etymologia verbi ἀληθὴς, quæ à veteribus Grammaticis traditur, bene conveniunt: quibus ἀληθὴς, quasi ἀλήθης, impavidus. Prodendæ siquidem ut veritatis, ita & fidelitatis inter causas, præcipuus timor.
units.tr: Alēthēs [Ἀληθὴς]: true; alētheia [ἀληθεία], truth: <bl>true, truetb</bl>. Among the old writers <bl>trewtan</bl> meant to trust, and <bl>trewtb</bl> faithfulness. These agree well with the etymology of alēthēs given by the ancient grammarians, who derived alēthēs, as if alēthēs, from "fearless." For among the causes of both betraying the truth and failing in faithfulness, fear is the chief one.

units.la: ᾿Απλήρης, contumeliosus, acerbus, <bl>tart.</bl>
units.tr: Aplērēs [Ἀπλήρης]: insulting, harsh, <bl>tart</bl>.

units.la: ᾿Αλάζων, ἀλάζων: vulgò, superbus, jactator. ător. Sed interdum mendax, ut ex Suida notum, & aliis notatum. B. m. parens, in Adversariis suis ad Platonis Protagoram, inter alia: Inprimis notandum quantâ curâ Socrates mentem Simonidis eo afmate scrutatur. Deinde observandum multa Graeca aliter sonare apud alios, ut de voce χαλεπὸς pro χαχὸς apud Lesbios ibi notatum. Talis observationis exemplum clarissimum in voce ἀλάζων pro mendace apud Atticos: quod non observatum Platonis interpretes turpiter fefellit. Hactenus ille. Anglis veteribus, leas, mendax: ele man leas: omnis homo mendax. Leafe, & lea- sunge, falsa, mendacia: leafe getrît- nesse, falsum testimonium; in vetere Decalogi versione, ubi Freherus: [Leas, quod nobis los, falsus. Glossa dicta, Falsus, vel mendax, leas. Aliae Belgicae; Fraudulentus, loes: Dolus, lotheft: Dolose, lofleker.] Ejusdem significationis, sed ab aliâ, ni fallor, origine, Belgicum & Germanicum, lie- gen, mentiri: ex quo lugben & logben, mendacium, &c. quod & Saxonibus in usu fuisse videtur; unde, Cunga beoja bi lugon bím: lingua suâ mentiti sunt illi. Psal. LXXVII. v.40. Ducunt à λῆρ, (unde, λόγοι, logi; pro nugæ, fabulæ, mendacia:) nòn improbabiliter. Cæteríùm ad priora illa lees, &c. pertinet, opinor, & Gallicum illud, quod in veteribus libris occurrit crebrò, lofengier: Ital.lufinghiero: Hisp.lifoniero: pro fimulatore, vel adulatore, qui mendacium pessimum genus.
units.tr: Alazōn [ἀλάζων]: commonly, proud, boastful; but sometimes lying, as is known from Suidas and noted by others. The late father [B. m. parens] in his notes on Plato's Protagoras, among other things: "First it must be noted with what care Socrates examines the meaning of Simonides in that passage. Next, it must be observed that many Greek words sound different among different peoples; here the word chalepos [χαλεπὸς] is noted for chakos [χαχὸς] among the Lesbians. The clearest example of such an observation is the word alazōn [ἀλάζων] used for liar among the Attic writers, which Plato's interpreters, not having noticed it, shamefully missed." So far he. Among the old English, leas means lying: ele man leas, every man is a liar. Leafe and leasunge, falsehood, lies; leafe getrîtnesse, false witness, in the old version of the Decalogue, where Freher has: [Leas, which for us is los, false. A gloss says: False, or lying, leas. Other Flemish: Fraudulent, loes; deceit, lotheft; deceitfully, lofleker.] With the same meaning, but from a different origin, unless I am mistaken, are Dutch and German liegen, to lie, whence lugben and logben, a lie, and so on, which also seems to have been in use among the Saxons; whence, cunga beoja bi lugon bím: with their tongue they have lied to him, Psalm 77:40. These are derived, not improbably, from lēr [λῆρ], whence logoi [λόγοι], for trifles, tales, lies. Moreover, I think the French lofengier, which often occurs in old books, belongs with those earlier lees and so on; the Italian lufinghiero, the Spanish lifoniero, meaning a dissembler or flatterer, who is the worst kind of liar.

units.la: ᾿Αχμόφις, immotus, asper, gravis: <bl>stiff.</bl>
units.tr: Achmophis [Ἀχμόφις]: immobile, harsh, heavy; <bl>stiff</bl>.

units.la: ᾿Αχμ@, mutus, <bl>dumb.</bl> Germanicum <bl>stomme.</bl>
units.tr: Achmē [Ἀχμ@]: mute; <bl>dumb</bl>. German <bl>stomme</bl>.

units.la: ᾿Αλλήχι@, inter alia, erro: <bl>a loptet-</bl> <bl>rer.</bl>
units.tr: Allēchi [Ἀλλήχι@]: among other things, to wander; <bl>a loptet-rer</bl>.

units.la: ᾿Αμβλύς, obtufus, blunt: (de quo suprà :) ut ex Latino, ambo, both.
units.tr: Ambly's, obtusus, blunt: (on which see above:) as from the Latin ambo, both. [ἀμβλύς]

units.la: ᾿Αργός, ἀρφ@: iners: otiosus. argus, apud nonnullos mediæ ætatis scriptores, a rogue.
units.tr: Argos [Ἀργός]: idle, lazy, unemployed. Latin argus, among some writers of the middle ages, a rogue.

units.la: ᾿Αβλαςής, non germinans, infœcun-dus, <bl>blasted:</bl> βλασφοσσῆν, <bl>to blast:</bl> Vide & in Βαλλὸς.
units.tr: Ablastēs [Ἀβλαςής]: not sprouting, barren, <bl>blasted</bl>; blastophoein [βλασφοσσῆν], <bl>to blast</bl>. See also under Ballos.

units.la: ᾿Αναύλ@, imprudens, stultus, &c. ἀνόνηλ@, inutilis, &c. <bl>naughty, naughtie.</bl>
units.tr: Anaul- [Ἀναύλ@]: imprudent, foolish, etc.; anonēl- [ἀνόνηλ@]: useless, etc. <bl>naughty, naughtie</bl>.

units.la: Αἴσλη & ἀσλαῖα, splendor, lux, fulgor: ἀσλαῖς, & ἀιγλῆς, spendidus, lucidus: ἀσλαίζεσθ, lucere, splendere: <bl>to</bl> glitter. Item gold, aurum: ex fulgore, quo alludit & vulgare dictum, Ƈverp thing is not gold, that glitters: Non omne quod fulget, aurum est.
units.tr: Aisle and aislaia [Αἴσλη & ἀσλαῖα]: splendour, light, brightness; aislais and aiglēs [ἀσλαῖς, & ἀιγλῆς]: splendid, shining; aislaizesthai [ἀσλαίζεσθ]: to shine, to glitter; <bl>to glitter</bl>. Likewise <bl>gold</bl>, Latin aurum, from its shining, to which the common saying also alludes: Not everything that glitters is gold.

units.la: *Ἀρφῶ, spuma, froth.
units.tr: Arphō [*Ἀρφῶ]: foam; <bl>froth</bl>.

units.la: *Ἀσυ, urbs, a town.
units.tr: Asy [*Ἀσυ]: city; <bl>a town</bl>.

units.la: *Ἀχχυς, caligo, a cloud.
units.tr: Achnys [*Ἀχχυς]: mist, <bl>a cloud</bl>.

units.la: Aiξ (ex Hebraico, ץ) αἲξ ἡ : caper & capra: sed hoc tamen ut plurimum. Ex ejus genit. αἰγὸς (nam & ex obliquis interdum formantur nomina:) Anglis, ut videtur, a goat; quod caprum significat. At βύκη, quod ab Hesychio exponitur capra, veteribus Anglis (ut & hodie Gallis, Italis, & Germanis:) bucean, caprum significabit.: Videtur autem apud Græcos veteres ovem primitus (quod & origo suadet ex βῆ propriâ voce ovium) significasse, ut ex Galeno & Hippocrate docet Stephanus: nec multum abludit vetus Anglicum sceap (nunc sheep) si metathesis admittatur. Hinc etiam (ex ἰστο βύκη) videtur Gallicum biche manasse, quod cervam Gallis significat; Anglis autem, canem fœmininam. Ita non sexus tantum permutantur, sed & species animalium in verbis transferendis.
units.tr: Aix [Aiξ] (from the Hebrew, ץ), aix [αἲξ], he-goat and she-goat: but this mostly. From its genitive aigos [αἰγὸς] (for names are sometimes formed from the oblique cases too), the English, it seems, have a goat, which means a he-goat. But bykē [βύκη], which Hesychius explains as a she-goat, will mean for the old English bucean, a he-goat (as it still does for the French, Italians and Germans). It seems, moreover, that among the older Greeks the word for sheep originally meant ovis (as the origin itself suggests, from the proper word for sheep, bē [βῆ]), as Stephanus shows from Galen and Hippocrates; and the old English sceap (now sheep) does not differ much from it, if metathesis is allowed. Hence too, from the Greek bykē, the French biche seems to have come, which means a hind to the French, but to the English a female dog. So not only do sexes change in translated words, but also the kinds of animals.

units.la: R *Ἀπμῷ;
units.tr: R [*Ἀπμῷ]: (the word is unclear in the source).

units.la: *Ἀτομος, atomus, a moate: ut autem potius ex Graeco ducam quàm Latino, faciunt exempla priorum, in quibus eadem quasi forma servatur. Caeterùm ex Latino atomus, factum recentius verbum, an atome.
units.tr: Atomos [*Ἀτομος], atomus, a moate. But whether I should derive it from the Greek rather than the Latin, the examples of earlier words suggest, in which the same form seems to be preserved. Otherwise, the word atome is a more recent word made from the Latin atomus.

units.la: 'Ἀπασία, jejunium, inedia; <bl>faft, fa-sting.</bl>
units.tr: Apasia [Ἀπασία]: fasting, starvation; <bl>fast, fasting</bl>.

units.la: 'Ἀχὼν, cos, a bone. De mutato Ϝ κ. in aspirationem, praeter ea quae suprà, vide in litera K.
units.tr: Achōn [Ἀχὼν]: cos, <bl>a bone</bl>. On the change of the digamma into an aspiration, besides what was said above, see under the letter K.

units.la: *Ἀχυνσις, (quod etiam χυνσις) spina dorsi; proprie in quadrupedibus, a <bl>chyne.</bl>
units.tr: Achynsis [*Ἀχυνσις] (also chynsis [χυνσις]): the spine; properly in quadrupeds, <bl>a chyne</bl>.

units.la: 'Ἀθροίζω, (à quo ἀγέθλω, ἀσφθὲς, &c.) congrego: to gather. ab eâdem etiam origine, together, simul.
units.tr: Athroizō [Ἀθροίζω] (from which agethlō [ἀγέθλω], asphthes [ἀσφθὲς], etc.): to gather together; <bl>to gather</bl>. From the same origin also <bl>together</bl>, that is, at the same time.

units.la: 'Ἀμβλίσκω, activâ tantum significatio posterioribus Graecis nota: hebeto, caecutire facio. Angli, neutraliter, <bl>to</bl> <bl>blinck</bl>: Ita Ἐξλλήσαι, apud vulgares Graecos, activum; ab Alexandrinis neutraliter usurpatum fuit: ut auctor Etymologici notat: & talia passim plurima. Sed & βλάνγ, ταφλάδης, ab Hesychio exponitur. Angl. a <bl>blinckard.</bl>
units.tr: Amblίskō [Ἀμβλίσκω]: in later Greeks the active sense only is known: to make dull, to make dim-sighted. The English use it intransitively, <bl>to blink</bl>. So Exlēsai [Ἐξλλήσαι], among the common Greeks, is active; the Alexandrians used it intransitively, as the author of the Etymologicum notes, and many such cases occur everywhere. But also blagg [βλάνγ] and taphladēs [ταφλάδης] are explained by Hesychius. In English, <bl>blinckard</bl>.

units.la: 'Ἀμαυρόω, μαυρόω: hebeto, retardo: metaphoricè, extinguo, pessumdo, planè ut Angli, <bl>to marre.</bl> 'Ἀνωκάζω,
units.tr: To dull, to make sluggish: [ἀμαυρόω, μαυρόω]; figuratively, to extinguish or ruin, exactly as the English "to mar" is used. [ἀνωκάζω]

units.la: 'Αλυσκάζω, fugio, in bello : subter-fugio. verbum Homericum. to slinck; to slinck away. Forté &, to lurck.
units.tr: To flee, to escape in battle, to slip away: [ἀλυσκάζω]. A Homeric word. Compare English "to slink" and "to slink away". Perhaps also "to lurk".

units.la: 'Αταίρω, ταίζω : proprie de motu dicitur animantium, cum morte colluctantium. Homerus cum voce πίσης sæpius jungit, quia pedes ultimi ut plurimùm palpitare videntur. to spiagtle. De piscibus etiam, aliisque ex supposito igne in sartagne salientibus usurpatur. Etymologicum, ad pisces proprie pertinere, (ut & alterum ταίζω) & eorum motus; author est : to spring.
units.tr: [ἀταίρω, ταίζω]: properly said of the movement of living creatures struggling with death. Homer often joins it with the word fish [πίσης], because the hindmost feet of such creatures seem mostly to twitch. It is also used of fish and other creatures leaping in a pan over a fire placed beneath it. The Etymologicum says that it belongs properly to fish, as does the other form [ταίζω], and to their movements. The author gives the English "to spring".

units.la: 'Ανυλάω, occurrere, respondere : eventu respondere, sive convenire, congruere : qui usus verbi rarior, sed elegantissimus. Usurpant Angli hodie que suum past, de re seu verbo, quæ pro præsenti occasione optimè quadrent. Ab eâdem quoque, ni fallor, origine ejusdem propè significationis verbum, to stt; quod congruere significat : litera p.in affinem f.pro more, (ut in pes, pater, &c.) mutatâ. Erunt fortasse qui ex Latino aptus utrumque malint repetere. Ego potiùs hoc ipsum aptus (in hac conveniendi seu congruendi notione : nam ut suspensum significat, ex alia est origine:) ex hoc eodem ἀπυλᾶν.
units.tr: [ἀνυλάω]: to meet, to answer; to correspond with an outcome, or to agree, to fit. This use of the verb is rarer but very elegant. The English today use their past of a thing or word that fits the present occasion exactly. From the same origin, I think, comes the verb "to suit", which has nearly the same meaning and means "to agree", the letter p having been changed, as usual, into the related f (as in "pes", "pater", etc.). Some will perhaps prefer to derive both from the Latin aptus. I would rather derive this very aptus, in the sense of meeting or fitting (for as to its meaning of suspended it has another origin), from this same [ἀπυλᾶν].

units.la: ᾽Αλφὼν, vel ἀλφὶν: invenire, ἀλφησὶς: inventor. Hom. to find.
units.tr: [ἀλφών, or ἀλφίν]: to find; [ἀλφησίς]: an inventor. Homer. The English "to find".

units.la: ᾽Αρεὶν, ἀρεύειν: irrigare, adaquare, to drench. Etiam, to drink. πολίζειν & ἀρεύειν, affinia re, & in sermone permutabilia, ut notant viri doctissimi in Rom.cap. III. versu 6.
units.tr: [ἀρεῖν, ἀρεύειν]: to water, to irrigate, to drench. Also "to drink". [πολίζειν] and [ἀρεύειν] are related in meaning and are interchangeable in speech, as very learned men note on Romans 3:6.

units.la: ᾽Αγᾶζ, imprecari, to cure: Sed & to curse, ab eadem, ni fallor origine. Vide infrà in κᾶλαγᾶζ. Cùm autem ἀγᾶ & ἀρει̃, βλαβὴ quoque exponantur, posset & τὸ to ͅsong inde duci, nisi propior ex verbo to ͅting origo succurreret: eâdem quâ & Galli tort, extorquere, ratione.
units.tr: [ἀγᾶζ]: to invoke a curse, to cure; but also "to curse", which I think comes from the same origin. See below under [κᾶλαγᾶζ]. Since [ἀγᾶ] and [ἀρει̃] are also explained as "harm", the English "to song" might be derived from this, unless the nearer origin in the verb "to ting" suggests itself, by the same reasoning by which the French tort, to wrest, is derived.

units.la: ᾽Αγᾶρ̃ν, vel ἀγᾶρ̃ν, inter alia, convitiis impetere; ut apud Sophoclem, to rate.
units.tr: [ἀγᾶρν, or ἀγᾶρν]: among other meanings, to assail with abuse, as in Sophocles. The English "to rate".

units.la: ᾽Αφιᾶς, adverbium; profusè, liberaliter: ἀφιᾶς, ἀφιᾶς; vox ad liberaliorem compotationem, invitatoria: unde videtur Anglicum, to feed, manasse; ut ex simili, χαῖρε, Gallicum, chere, pro lautitia.
units.tr: [ἀφιᾶς]: an adverb meaning lavishly, generously; a word inviting to more generous drinking. From it the English "to feed" seems to have come, as the French chere, for good cheer, comes from the similar [χαῖρε].

units.la: In his quæ hactenus adduximus omnibus, ratio fere traductionis omnis est per aphærefin, Anglis usitatissimam, ut initio monuimus. Contractio etiam in nonnullis, & metathesis aliqua. Pergamus nunc ad alia.
units.tr: In all the words we have so far cited, the method of derivation is nearly always by aphaeresis, which the English use most often, as I noted at the start. In some there is also contraction, and some metathesis. Let us now go on to others.

units.la: *Ἀγρι@, trux, immitis: <bl>angrp.</bl> nisi tamen ab ὀργὴ, ira, per metathesin, <bl>an-</bl> <bl>ger</bl>, & inde, <bl>angrp.</bl>
units.tr: [ἀγρι-], fierce, savage: English "angry". Unless it comes from [ὀργή], anger, by metathesis: "anger", and from that "angry".

units.la: ᾿Αγκὼν, curvatura genuum, vel cubitorum. Anglis, <bl>ande</bl>, curvatura pedum, talus. <bl>ande bone</bl>, malleolus. Sed ἀγκὼν, late patens verbum, exponitur, lorum, amentum, vitium linguae, (cum adscititiis nescio quibus membranulis & vinculis impeditur:) & ἀγκύλον, hamus catenae, &c. ex quibus videntur Anglica <bl>ande, angle</bl>, (hamus, nisi quis malit ab ἀγκύλης:) imo & per metathesin, <bl>latch</bl>, fluxisse.
units.tr: [ἀγκών]: the bend of the knees or elbows. In English, "ande" is the bend of the foot, the ankle. "Ande bone" is the ankle-bone. But [ἀγκών], a broadly used word, is explained as a thong, a loop, a defect of the tongue (it is hindered by certain added little membranes and bonds, I know not which), and [ἀγκύλον] as a hook of a chain, and so on. From these the English "ande", "angle" (a hook, unless one prefers to derive it from [ἀγκύλης]) seem to have come, and even, by metathesis, "latch".

units.la: *Ἀκων@, glans ilicis: Anglice; (l. in r. ut passim, mutato, & addito ad Euphoniam n.) <bl>acorns</bl>. Magis arridebit forsan nonnullis quae vulgo affertur Etymologia, <bl>acorne</bl>, quasi <bl>okecorne</bl>; granum ilicis. Sed confirmet priorem, quod hodieque Belgae, <bl>Eeckel</bl>, dicunt: & Germani, <bl>Eyebel</bl>. Sed & ipsum <bl>Oke</bl>, quercus, (quod illi <bl>Eech</bl>, & <bl>eich</bl>; Saxones, ac, ni fallor:) ab ἀκων@ per apocopen fieri potuit, ut arbor ex frustu nominaretur.
units.tr: [ἀκορν]: an acorn. In English, with l changed to r as usual and an n added for euphony: "acorns". Perhaps the etymology commonly offered will please some more: "acorne", as if "okecorne", a grain of the oak. But the earlier derivation is confirmed by what the Dutch still call it, "eeckel", and the Germans "eyebel". Also the word "oke", oak (which they call "eech" and "eich", and the Saxons, I think, the same), could have come from [ἀκορν] by apocope, so that the tree was named from its fruit.

units.la: "Αγιος, sanctus; Saxonicè, <bl>balige</bl>: Belg. & Germ. <bl>bepligh</bl>: afpiratione in h verfa, de quo fupra diximus, & exempla pofuimus; & l. ad ιυφωνιαν pro more inferto. Angli hodierni <bl>holy</bl>, extritâ confonante radicali, cujus abfentia originem facit obfcuriorem. Sed & <bl>hallow</bl>; ab eodem. <bl>Hallowed</bl>, olim <bl>gehalged</bl>, ut in Oratione Dominica, Matth. VI.
units.tr: [ἅγιος], holy; in Saxon "balige"; Dutch and German "bepligh", with an aspirate prefixed to the h, as I said above, where I gave examples, and with l inserted for euphony as usual. The modern English "holy", with the radical consonant worn away, whose absence makes the origin more obscure. But also "hallow", from the same. "Hallowed", formerly "gehalged", as in the Lord's Prayer, Matthew 6.

units.la: Αἱλῶ (ἀολίμης) verfutus, callidus, <bl>wyle</bl>; fed abftractum Anglis ufitatius, <bl>wyles</bl>, <bl>wylines</bl>, verfutia, calliditas.
units.tr: [αἱλῶ] (cf. [ἀολίμης]): crafty, cunning; "wyle". But the abstract form is more usual in English: "wyles", "wylines", craftiness, cunning.

units.la: "Αχῶ, dolor, an ache: habuimus jam fupra, in Cambdenianis; fed id eò hic iterum, ut praeterea notem, quod non omittendum credidi, quòd quemadmodum Angli ex hoc fubftantivo verbum formént, to ake, dolere: mutato ch. in k. ita apud Graecos reperiri praeteritum ἔαχαν, ἐαχὼς, ἐαχότης, quae apud Hefychium fingula, ejufdem plane cujus eft Anglicum illud fignificationis: ut apud Hefychium videre eft. Nifi quis dicat Hefychium Anglica verba exponere voluiffe, cùm valdè affinis fit
units.tr: [ἄχω]: pain, "an ache". I have already noted this above, in the Cambden material. But I repeat it here in order to note further something I thought should not be omitted: just as the English form from this noun the verb "to ake", to grieve, with ch changed into k, so among the Greeks there are found the perfect forms [ἔαχαν, ἐαχώς, ἐαχότης], which in Hesychius, each one, have plainly the same meaning as that English word, as can be seen in Hesychius. Unless someone says that Hesychius wished to explain English words, since the pronunciation of

units.la: Anglici a pronunciatio literis illis ea : à quibus ista incipiunt. Ego tamen potius crediderim antiquum fuisse, sed dudum apud Græcos antiquatum.
units.tr: the English a is very close to the letters ea with which these words begin. I would rather believe, however, that the word was ancient but long ago obsolete among the Greeks.

units.la: Αχθ@, pondus, <bl>toetgbt.</bl>
units.tr: [ἄχθος]: a weight; "toetgbt".

units.la: Αμπρ@, (pro ανάπρ@ : ut ἀμβολή, pro ἀναβολή, & id genus alia plurima:) mutilatus, læsus. Hesychius habet, & compositio Græcum legitimum probet. Quod movet me ut Anglicum tmpas- teD, tam propinquum & sono & significatione, inde potius repetendum ducam, quàm ex ficto Latino impejorare ; ut antea conjiciebam.
units.tr: [ἄμπρ-], (for [ἀνάπρ-], as [ἀμβολή] for [ἀναβολή], and very many other things of that kind): mutilated, injured. Hesychius has it, and the compound proves that the Greek is legitimate. This leads me to derive the English "tmpas-teD", so close in sound and meaning, from this rather than from the invented Latin impejorare*, as I had previously conjectured.

units.la: Αχ@,podex. Hesychius.Anglicum est, nisi quod τὸ χ excidit in Anglico, ut in ἀράχνη, araneus, &c.
units.tr: [ἄχ-], the backside. Hesychius. It is English, except that the χ has dropped out in English, as in [ἀράχνη], araneus, etc.

units.la: Αδεκαν, πονηρὸς, malus. Hesych. Anglicè, adle. Veteres de morbis, (quæ mala corporis) usurpabant, ut Mat.IV. v. 23. Ꝑlenᴅe ælce ᴀᴅle, ᴀnᴅ ælce unᴛʀanpsse on them folce : Satans omnem languorem & omnem infirmitatem in populo : & cap.VIII. v.17. ᴜʀe ᴀᴅla : ægrotationes nostras : τὰς νόσος.
units.tr: [ἀδεκαν], wicked, evil. Hesychius. In English, adle. The ancients used this of diseases (which are the evils of the body), as in Matthew 4:23: "Plende ælce adle, and ælce unᴛʀanpsse on them folce": Satan's every languor and every infirmity in the people; and chapter 8, verse 17: "ure adla": our infirmities, [τὰς νόσος].

units.la: 'Αλίσω, similis, <bl>alикe,икe.</bl>
units.tr: [ἀλίσω], like; English "alike", "like".

units.la: 'Αλὼ, multis verbis opus est, ut vim vocis hujus Latine quis exprimat: ut. apud veteres Grammaticos, & qui illos exhibet,Stephanum videre est. Uno verbo Anglicè dicas, to aple: ut cùm tristitiam præ fe ferentem, & animi præter morem affecti seu vultu seu factis indicia prodentem(interdum etiam cum indignatione, quasi insaniam exprobrantes) ita compellamus, What apleth you? Quòd autem Plutarchus contendit etiam contrariam significationem habere, & pro gaudere apud Homerum reperiri, non puto id ex illo quem profert loco (ut apud Stephanum reperio: non enim nunc Plutarchus ad manum:) probari posse. *Η ἀ-λύῆς ὅπ Ἰεσν ἐιίχνσας ἡ ἀλήτλω; Non enim ibi ἀλύῳ lætari, simpliciter; sed impotenter & ex levi caussâ efferri; quod animi non benè compositi signum est. Anglicè optimè exprimas, What? are you wilt becanse, &c. Ita enim illi suum illud weilt, (quod tamen ab aliâ videtur origine) de impotente lætitiâ & exultatione interdum usurpant. Ut omittam quod in verbis ἀλύῃ & ἀλήτης allusio ab Homero, ut ego quidem censeo, quæsita: quales aliæ in eodem libro, *Ιφ&, & ἡεχ: *Ιςῶ, ἀιςῶ: & *Ιφῳ, *Ιερω, ωείνεlo ϑυμὸς ; aliaeque venustiffimæ.
units.tr: [ἀλώ]: many words are needed to express the force of this word in Latin; one can see it in Stephanus, who records the old grammarians and those who cite them. In one English word you could say "to aple", as when we address someone who shows sadness and displays by face or deeds signs of a mind disturbed beyond its custom (sometimes also with indignation, as if reproaching them with madness), with the words: What? What apleth you? But as to Plutarch's claim that it also has the contrary meaning, and is found in Homer for rejoicing, I do not think this can be proved from the passage he cites (as I find in Stephanus, since Plutarch is not now at hand). [ἀλύῃ ὅπ Ἰεσν ...]? There it does not simply mean to rejoice, but to be carried away immoderately and on slight cause, which is a sign of a mind not well composed. In English you may express it very well: What? are you wilt becanse, &c. For so the English use their weilt (which seems, however, to come from another origin) of an uncontrolled gladness and exultation. I pass over that in the words [ἀλύῃ] and [ἀλήτης] there is an allusion, sought by Homer, as I at least judge; as there are other such in the same book, and others most graceful.

units.la: 'Αξίδω, inter alia, peto, postulo, <bl>to</bl> afke. Litera ξ sæpe mutatur in σ. ut σκιῳ, pro ξίῳ ; σκιφία, pro ξιφίας ; ἀξίνη, ascia : ut alia omittam ex linguâ Etrusca, (sive Italicâ ;) & Hispanicâ, doctissimo Caninio notata. Germani ochs, quod Angli ose ; Belgæ, os.
units.tr: [ἀξίδω], among other things, to seek, to ask; English "to ask". The letter ξ is often changed into σ, as [σκιῳ] for [ξίῳ]; [σκιφία] for [ξιφίας]; [ἀξίνη], an axe. To omit others from the Etruscan (or Italian) tongue and the Spanish, noted by the most learned Caninius. The Germans have ochs, which the English have as "ose", and the Dutch "os".

units.la: 'Ανύω, perficere, to end.
units.tr: [ἀνύω]: to accomplish; English "to end".

units.la: *Αρνυμαι. Deest Latinis verbum, quo exprimant. Nam capio, recipio, consequor ; & similia, sunt nimis generalia. Angli optime, to earne : ut in vulgaribus illis exemplis, ἀρνυς μίσθον, to earne wages : ἀρνυς βίλον ἐκ χειρῶν, to earne his living with his hands. Ab eádem autem origine est earnest ; pro, serius, vel studiosus. Cætera enim pleraque quasi per jocum & perfunctorie : at ubi lucri res agitur, (talis præcipuè ex quo vita pendet, qui Græcis ideò βίω) tum serii, & si unquam, animis intenti plerique sumus. Sed & verbum ἀρνυς, pro studiosè aliquid prosequi, olim sine dubio vulgare, cujus apud Homerum vestigia significationis, in istis, quæ doctissimus Stephanus ex ex illo profert, 'Apvúpʎv©ἡνῖε ⸗ʎvxλω, ꝯ νόσον ἑταίρων, confequi conans,&c. ut ibi vir doctiffimus. Si liceret ex ufitato nomine, inufitatum verbum fingere, diceremus uno verbo, earnesting.
units.tr: [ἀρνυμαι]: the Latins lack a verb to express it, for capio, recipio, consequor and similar words are too general. The English have it excellently: "to earne", as in those common examples, [ἀρνυς μίσθον]: "to earne wages"; [ἀρνυς βίον ἐκ χειρῶν]: "to earne his living with his hands". From the same origin is "earnest", meaning serious or eager. For most things we do in a jesting and perfunctory way; but when the matter concerns gain, especially that on which life depends (for which reason the Greeks say [βίος]), then most of us are serious, and as intent of mind as ever. But the verb [ἀρνυς], meaning to pursue something eagerly, was without doubt once common, and traces of this meaning remain in Homer, in those passages which the most learned Stephanus cites from him, trying to pursue (as the most learned man there puts it). If it were permitted to form an unused verb from a common noun, we would say in one word "earnesting".

units.la: 'Aʌʃω, necto, connecto (unde ἀʌʃις, vel ἀʌʃις, connexio, vinculum:) to bapse.
units.tr: Aʌʃω (I tie, I bind, I connect; whence ἀʌʃις, or ἀʌʃις, connexion, bond): to bapse.
