units.la: 'Ἀλᾶζ, errare: vagari. Wallen, olim, idem.
units.tr: Ἀλᾶζ, to err, to wander, to roam. Wallen, formerly, the same.

units.la: 'Αμέζ, falire, saltare. Πηγὴ ὕδα· ἀλλομένη: fons aquæ salientis: Joh. IV. verf. 14. Veteribus Anglis, wallen, & wellen, bullire. Well, hodiéque, puteus. Vide & infrà, in βεύω.
units.tr: Ἀμέζ, to leap, to spring. Πηγὴ ὕδα· ἀλλομένη: a fountain of water springing up (John 4, v. 14). Among the old English, wallen and wellen meant to boil. Well today means a well. See also below, under βεύω.

units.la: 'Aei, semper, ap; ut foj ape, in aeternum: apegreene, ἀιέωον; ne quis ex Latino evum, natum sufpicetur.
units.tr: Aei, always, ever; as in foj ape, for ever; apegreene [ἀιέωον]. Let no one suspect that it is derived from the Latin evum.

units.la: 'Ava, pro ἀνάσῃ, furge,perge. Hortatorium, seu excitatorium verbum, Homero familiare. Angl. on: vel geminatum, on, on.
units.tr: Ava, for ἀνάστα: rise up, go on. An exhortatory or rousing word, familiar to Homer. English on, or doubled, on, on.

units.la: Αὐτὰρ, caeterum,autem,&c. vox Homero frequentissima apud quem sæpe etiam cum ἐπὶ conjuncta reperitur: αὖλαξ ἐπὶ: postea vero;vel autem. Hinc Anglicum after manasse credibile est: after, pro αὐτὰς ἐπὶ: quod non tam
units.tr: Αὐτὰρ: moreover, but, and so on. A word very frequent in Homer, where it is often found joined with ἐπί: αὖτ' ἐπί, afterwards, or however. Hence it is credible that the English after came from it: after for αὐτὰρ ἐπί. This is not so remarkable

units.la: mirum eft,quàm ex Latino magis,quòd alicubi pro fed pofitum fit, Gallicum mais(quod fed fignificat,) fluxiffe : quæ doctiffimi Caninii,aliorúmque poft illum fententia eft.
units.tr: as that the French mais (which means sed, but) flowed from the Latin magis, since somewhere it is used in place of sed. This is the opinion of the most learned Caninius and others after him.

units.la: B
units.tr: B

units.la: Βεάλεφ, βάλιτ. Angl. better,beet: de quibus fuprà.
units.tr: Βεάλεφ, βάλιτ. English <bl>better, beet</bl>: of which see above.

units.la: Βαζιν, nomen pifcis,ex illo genere pifcium, qui ob infignem fterilitatem ἀπλεγέα nuncupantur : de quo ait Aristoteles, eum (βαζίνου fcil.) neque ovum parere, neque femen ullum prolificum habere. Hinc fortaffe Anglicum barren : Nifi quis malit ex vetere unberend (cui tamen ipfi ex Græco φύφ prima origo: unde ἀρρεν, ἀρρενία, &c. & ἀρρενίδ eft, ἀρρενῶνιοι, Hefychio :) contractum effe.
units.tr: Βαζιν, the name of a fish, of that kind of fish which, on account of their notable sterility, are called ἀπλεγέα. Of it Aristotle says that it neither lays eggs nor has any fruitful seed. Hence perhaps the English <bl>barren</bl>, unless someone prefers that it was contracted from the old <bl>unberend</bl> (to which, however, the first origin is from the Greek φύφ, whence ἀρρεν, ἀρρενία, etc., and ἀρρενίδ is ἀρρενῶνιοι, in Hesychius).

units.la: Βεάβεύω, proprie, præmium do ut judex certaminis ; Angli abfolutè pro præmium dare acceperunt: & ut ᵓnw Hebr. quod munus in genere fignificat, fæpè accipitur pro munere quod ad corrumpendos judices dabant: ita Anglicè ex βεάβεύφ, fuum to bribe fecerunt ; quod etiam aliter, to gibe a reward, sacræ Scripturæ phrasi dici possit.
units.tr: Βεάβεύω, properly, I give the prize as judge of a contest. The English took it absolutely to mean to give a prize. And as the Hebrew ᵓnw, which generally means a gift, is often taken for the gift they gave to corrupt judges, so from βεάβεύφ the English made their own to bribe. This could also be put otherwise, to give a reward, in the phrase of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Βρῶσις, esca, cibus, potui solet opponi: Anglis, <bl>bread</bl>; panis qui potissimus cibus. Ita & Heb. לחם panem, & alium quemvis cibum significat. Sed & <bl>bread</bl> ab eodem fonte. Esculentis enim merito accensetur, etiam dum hauritur; & ut plurimùm, multo pane temperatur.
units.tr: Βρῶσις, food, victuals, which is usually set against drink. For the English, <bl>bread</bl>, the bread which is the chief food. Thus also the Hebrew לחם means bread and any other food. But <bl>bread</bl> too has the same source: for it is rightly counted among eatables, even while it is being swallowed; and for the most part it is taken with plenty of bread.

units.la: Βίος, arcus; apud Homerum saepè occurrit: vix alibi. a bow: & inde fuerit verbum, to bowe, flectere: potiùs quàm nomen ex verbo. ut & arcuare, ex arcus. At τὸ bough, pro ramus, etsi magna in rebus affinitas, ab alia tamen, ut puto, origine: & potiùs ad συγγενείαν referendum; quales in omnibus linguis crebræ.
units.tr: Βίος, a bow; it often occurs in Homer, but scarcely elsewhere: a bow. From this the verb to bowe, to bend, probably came, rather than the noun from the verb, as also arcuare comes from arcus. But bough, for a branch, though it has a great affinity in meaning, has a different origin, I think, and should rather be referred to συγγενείαν (kinship); such cases are frequent in all languages.

units.la: Βάλαχος, (quod & βαλάχος Hesychio) rana; <bl>a frogge</bl>. Nisi potius ex φρῦνος vel φρῦνος, rubeta, rana proprie venenosa.
units.tr: Βάλαχος (which is also βαλάχος in Hesychius), a frog: <bl>a frogge</bl>. Unless it is rather from φρῦνος or φρῦνος, a toad, properly a poisonous frog.

units.la: Βλαύς. Vide suprà in 'Αμβλίσκω. Caterum & si aliud caecutiens, aliud caecus; merito tamen & τὸ <bl>blind</bl>, ad hoc βλαύς referatur, cum ita saepe verborum notiones ad alias affines transferantur.
units.tr: Βλαύς. See above under Ἀμβλίσκω. Yet even if one word means dim-sighted and another means blind, the English <bl>blind</bl> is nonetheless rightly referred to this βλαύς, since the meanings of words are so often transferred to other, related ones.

units.la: Βασιλεύς,
units.tr: Βασιλεύς,

units.la: germino, pullulo, to budde. Efflorebit, bleiptb, Saxonicæ verfionis, Psal.CXXXII. v.19.
units.tr: to sprout, to shoot up, to bud: <bl>to budde</bl>. <bl>Efflorebit, bleiptb</bl>, of the Saxon version, Ps. 132, v. 19: "It shall flourish."

units.la: dormire, fopire. Utrumque convenit carmini illi fopitorio nutricum Anglicarum, quod alumnis fuis decumbentibus folent occinere, bp bp identidem repetendo. Hinc Βαυβάω nutrix Cereris, ab ejufmodi fine dubio cantilenâ fic dicta, quòd ἰβαυβα (ut optimè Stephanus:) id eft, baubando (ut ego interpretor) fopire foleret Cererem. At baubari Latinis aliud longè: quod non mirum. Cæterum confirmat expofitionem noftram quòd etiam vox ἀδαα fuit πωιδ̓ιχὸν ἐπίφθεσμα, ut ex Luciano docet ad Theophrafti Characteres vir doctus. Unde Latini fuum lallare; pro dormire, vel fopire finxerunt. Solent autem nutrices Anglicæ cantillantes utrumque jungere, Lalebp, &c.
units.tr: to sleep, to lull to sleep. Both agree with that lullaby of English nurses, which they are accustomed to sing to their charges as they lie down, repeating bp bp again and again. Hence the nurse of Ceres, Βαυβώ, was so called, doubtless from such a song, because she used to lull Ceres to sleep with ἰβαυβα, as Stephanus well says; that is, by barking (baubando, as I interpret it). But for the Latins baubari means something quite different, which is not surprising. Moreover, our explanation is confirmed by the fact that ἀδαα was also a childish exclamation, as a learned man shows from Lucian on Theophrastus' Characters. Whence the Latins coined their lallare for to sleep or lull to sleep. English nurses, when singing these lullabies, usually join both, Lalebp, etc.

units.la: Βοάω, clamo; to bawle.
units.tr: Βοάω, I shout: <bl>to bawle</bl>.

units.la: Βωσρίω, aliquem vociferando & manibus palpando (ψηλαφῶν, ut veteres Grammatici exponunt:) quæro. Hinc Angl. bolftroue, de tumultuante, & inconditum clamante.
units.tr: Βωσρίω: I seek by shouting at someone and feeling about with my hands (ψηλαφῶν, as the ancient grammarians explain). Hence the English <bl>bolstroue</bl>, of one who makes a tumult and shouts without order.

units.la: Βρύκω, βρυχάω, βρόχω; edo, comedo, <bl>to brooke.</bl> Devorare miserias dicunt & Latini : quod & Græci, ( de quo Longinus si bene memini.) ἀναξφοφαξεῖν.
units.tr: Βρύκω, βρυχάω, βρόχω: I eat, I devour: <bl>to brooke</bl>. The Latins also say they devour miseries; so do the Greeks, as Longinus has it, if I remember rightly: ἀναξηροφαγεῖν.

units.la: Βρύω, scateo, pullulo : de fontibus, ut plurimùm. Anglis, bourne, tum aquam ipsam scaturientem, tum fontem significat, ut Versteganus docet. Olim burna; sed & brunno, ut apud Willeramum Abbatam. Hinc quoque fuerit ᵹ brooke, ejusdem ferè significationis. Vide tamen infrà in ῥυάξ. Ita & beke, de quo idem Versteganus, ex μυή, haud dubiè.
units.tr: Βρύω: to abound, to bubble up; said of springs, for the most part. For the English, <bl>bourne</bl> means both the water itself gushing up and the spring, as Verstegan teaches. Formerly <bl>burna</bl>, but also <bl>brunno</bl>, as in Willeram the Abbot. Hence <bl>brooke</bl> too may have come, of nearly the same meaning. See, however, below under ῥυάξ. So also <bl>beke</bl>, of which the same Verstegan (derives it) from μυή, undoubtedly.

units.la: Βάλλω, jacere, ferire, vulnerare, a blow : adderem, & bowle, nisi id Gallicum quoque esset. Occurrit tamen & aliud, to fell : βεβλημένος, projectus ; (quasi ex Aorifto βληθείς:) fell. Nam alioquin Græci compositò potiùs utuntur, καταβάλλω, ex quo Gallicum, ni sallor, accabler.
units.tr: Βάλλω, to throw, to strike, to wound: a blow. I would add bowle, unless that too were French. Yet another meaning occurs, to fell: βεβλημένος, cast down (as if from the aorist βληθείς): fell. For otherwise the Greeks more often use the compound καταβάλλω, from which, unless I am mistaken, comes the French accabler.

units.la: Βελόνη, acus, transpositione literarum,& d.(ut in cinis. Gall. cendre ; cinder : vagari, wander, &c.) interpositò, a needle. Nec illud magis remotum, quàm Gallicum esguille, ex Latino, acus. Vide infrà in ςίζιν.
units.tr: Βελόνη, a needle: by transposition of letters and the insertion of a d (as in cinis, French cendre, cinder; wander, etc.), a needle. This is no more remote than the French aiguille from the Latin acus. See below under ςίζιν.

units.la: Βαθὺς, profundus ; per transpositionem, Deep. Quod ne cui minus assueto nimis audax videatur; talia sunt, μόρφη, forma: φαυνλη, pennula: κύφλω, fucus: χῦ&G, decus: χιτὼν, tunica: & alia quæ in omnibus linguis plurima. Multa Caninius, id genus, ex pluribus linguis: & Avenarius, ex sacris Scripturis, in Grammaticis suis.
units.tr: Βαθὺς, deep: by transposition, <bl>Deep</bl>. Lest this seem too bold to anyone not much accustomed to such things, there are others like it: μόρφη, form; φαυνλη, a little feather; κύφλω, a dye; χῦ, grace; χιτὼν, tunic; and very many more in all languages. Caninius gathers many of this kind from several languages, and Avenarius from Holy Scripture, in his grammars.

units.la: Βάλανος, glans; arbor ipsa glandifera. Hinc quidam deducunt a wal-nut; (sive juglans,) quæ etiam alicubi apud Belgas, oker-nutte: ut ex balæna, a walvis. Aliam tamen originem oftendit Kylianus, quem adeat & sequatur, qui volet. Cæterùm, nux avellana, (ne quis propinquitate soni decipiatur) alia res, & ex alia origine.
units.tr: Βάλανος: an acorn; also the oak tree itself which bears acorns. Hence some derive wal-nut (or juglans), which is also somewhere among the Belgians oker-nutte, just as walvis (whale) comes from balaena. Kilianus, however, shows another origin, which whoever wishes may consult and follow. Moreover, nux avellana (lest anyone be deceived by the similarity of sound) is a different thing, with a different origin.

units.la: Βαλλὸς, ἀπόλλυμι, sideratus, <bl>blighted.</bl>
units.tr: Βαλλὸς, to destroy: <bl>sideratus</bl>, <bl>blighted</bl>.

units.la: Γ
units.tr: Γ

units.la: Γαίω, glorior, gap.
units.tr: Gaio [Γαίω], to glory; gap.

units.la: Γλῶσσα, lingua, to gloze.
units.tr: Glōssa [Γλῶσσα], tongue; to gloze.

units.la: Γένυον, mentum, the chin: ut ex γένυς, gena, the cheek.
units.tr: Genyon [Γένυον], the chin, as from genys [γένυς], the cheek.

units.la: Γνῖλα, intestina, guts. Thracum propriam vocem fuisse volunt quidam. Thracicam & Gethicam unam eandemque fuisse linguam, præter Strabonis nis authoritatem, alia multa suadent. Gethicam autem non aliam quàm Gothicam, sive Germanicam fuisse, suo loco probabimus.
units.tr: Gnila [Γνῖλα], guts, entrails. Some hold that this was the proper word of the Thracians. That Thracian and Getic were one and the same language, many things besides Strabo's authority suggest. That the Getic language was none other than Gothic, or German, I shall prove in its place.

units.la: - Τυλὸς, vel ut alii, γνώΘ, pera militaris, in quâ viaticum, & alia necessaria milites circumferebant. Hinc videtur Anglicum to gull, defraudare, fluxisse; quo modo & Latinum, manticulari, pro furari, dolosè agere, ex simili ratione. Affinis vox, to begutle, ex gutle, (quod & togle; de quo suprà;, fraus, impostura :) ad quam si priorem illam malit aliquis referre, fruatur suo judicio; ego aliter censeo.
units.tr: Tylos [Τυλὸς], or as others have it, gnōth [γνώΘ], a soldier's pouch, in which soldiers carried their provisions and other necessities. From this, it seems, the English "to gull", to defraud, has come; in the same way the Latin manticulari, to steal or to act deceitfully, comes from a similar idea. The related word "to beguile", from "guile" (which is also "togle", of which above), means fraud or imposture. If anyone prefers to refer it to the former, let him enjoy his own judgment; I think otherwise.

units.la: - Τρπτιζὶν, γπτισμὰλα, vide suprà.
units.tr: Trptizein [Τρπτιζὶν], gtptisma [γπτισμὰλα]: see above.

units.la: Τωειὰω, subsanno; falsè rideo. Ita vulgò ex Plutarcho in Lycurgo docent. Ibi certè in ῥῆτρα quadam Lycurgi vetere, extremâ, reperio: ἔτως εἰσφέρειν τε ᾧ ἀρ- ισαδς γαμωλᾶν γεσὰν ἢ μὴ ᾧ κεχτ; ut praestantissima Henrici Stephani editio illa exhibet. Quae miror à Plutarcho, qui cetera istius Sciti explicat, praeterita esse. Si is est locus quem volunt, infirmo fundamento nititur ista expositio. Sed de verbo Graeco aliàs fortasse quaeremus, cùm aliae erunt Plutarchi. tarchi editiones in potestate quas confulere possimus. Ego certè tantò magis. illis crediderim,quod & Anglis to jeer, irridere, cujus synonyma, to scoffe, ex <bl>σκώπ</bl> in Cambdenianis jam habuimus; & posteà suo loco, to tatont, & to ttwitt; ex <bl>τωθάζω</bl>; (quibus addi potest & to slaunder, ex <bl>λοιδορέω</bl>, ut quibufdam placet:) habebimus. Sed & to mock, ex Græcis potiùs ipsis, ( his exemplis adductus:) ad Anglos pervenisse quis non credat, quàm Gallis? <bl>Τέρπω</bl>, pòns, a bridge. <bl>β.π.φ.</bl> literæ affines,sæpe inter se mutabiles; ut multis exemplis docet Caninius: <bl>βρέμω</bl>, fremo; <bl>βοάλίνω</bl>, safcino,&c. qui etiam observat & multis exemplis probat literam <bl>ϱ</bl>. in derivatis ut plurimùm loco moveri,sive transpositionem pati.Olim <bl>βίβρ</bl>, & <bl>βίβεχ</bl>. De litera d. insita, diximussuprà in <bl>βελόνη</bl>.
units.tr: Tōeiaō [Τωειὰω], to mock, to laugh falsely. This is commonly taught from Plutarch in his Life of Lycurgus. There, certainly, in an ancient rhetra of Lycurgus, at the very end, I find the words: "thus to bring in ... and not to ..." as the most excellent edition of Henri Estienne presents it. I am surprised that Plutarch, who explains the rest of this Scythian's sayings, omitted this one. If this is the passage they mean, the explanation rests on a weak foundation. But we will perhaps look into the Greek word elsewhere, when there are other editions of Plutarch in our hands that we can consult. For my part, I would believe them all the more readily because the English "to jeer", to mock, whose synonyms "to scoff", from skōpt [σκώπ], we already had in Camden, and afterwards in its place "to taunt" and "to twit", from tōthazō [τωθάζω], (to which may be added "to slander", from loidoreō [λοιδορέω], as some think), we shall have. But who would not believe that "to mock" reached the English from the Greeks themselves, led by these examples, rather than from the French? Terpō [Τέρπω], pons, a bridge. The letters b, p, f are related and often interchange with one another, as Caninius shows by many examples: fremo [βρέμω], fremo; bo-alinō [βοάλίνω], safcino, etc. He also observes, and proves by many examples, that the letter r in derivatives is for the most part moved about, or undergoes transposition. Formerly there were bibr [βίβρ] and bibech [βίβεχ]. I have discussed the inserted letter d above, under belonē [βελόνη].

units.la: Τεάν, ridere; to laugh.
units.tr: Teān [Τεάν], to laugh; to laugh.

units.la: Ταμὲν, de viro, uxorem ducere: de fœminâ, nubere: uno verbo, matrimonio jungi. Hinc, opinor, Angl. to game. Solent enim per paria ut pluririmùm, ut certare,ita & ludere: & est istarum rerum, ut in matrimonio, <bl>συ-</bl>
units.tr: Tamēn [Ταμὲν], said of a man, to take a wife; said of a woman, to marry; in one word, to be joined in wedlock. Hence, I think, the English "to game". For, as they are for the most part used in pairs, so contending and playing go together; and of these things, as in marriage, there is a certain yoking [syzygia, συζυγία].

units.la: s ζυγία ζυγία quædam. Pari ratione, ex μαχη, pugna, fit Angl. match: quod & pugnæ,& lusui, & matrimonio commune verbum est. At match, pro sulphurato, ut aliud longè significatione, ita & ab alia longè origine. Venit tamen in mentem verbum, mate, socius, ex quo prius illud matcb ortum esse, probabile videatur: nisi & hoc ipsum, est Græcum μαχήτης. Quod Germanorum moribus quales illos describit Tacitus, optimè conveniat. Dotem, inquit, (de Germanorum matrimoniis agens.) nox uxor marito, sed uxori maritus offert. Intersunt parentes ac propinqui, ac munera probant. munera, non ad delicias muliebres quæsita, nec quibus nova nupta comatur, sed boves, & frænatum equum, & scutum cum framea, gladioque. In hæc munera uxor accipitur, atque invicem ipsa armorum aliquid viro offert: hoc maximum vinculum, hæc arcana sacra, hos conjugales Deos (arma, scilicet) arbitrantur. Sed plura fortasse, alio loco: in μαχή, vel μάχ.
units.tr: By the same reasoning, from machē [μαχη], battle, comes the English "match", a common word for battle, for play, and for marriage. But "match", meaning a sulphur-tipped taper, differs as much in meaning as in origin. Yet the word "mate", meaning companion, comes to mind, from which the former "match" seems probably to have arisen; unless this itself is the Greek machētēs [μαχήτης]. This agrees very well with the customs of the Germans as Tacitus describes them. He says, speaking of German marriages: "Dowry is not brought by the wife to the husband, but by the husband to the wife. Parents and kinsfolk attend and approve the gifts: gifts not sought for womanly delights, nor such as a new bride is adorned with, but oxen, and a bridled horse, and a shield with spear and sword. In these gifts the wife is received, and in turn she brings to her husband something of arms. This is the greatest bond, these are the secret rites, these the marriage gods" (that is, arms, they think). But perhaps more on this elsewhere, under machē or mach-.

units.la: Τογγύζειν, murmurare, indignari, to grudge, to grotvle: si hæc, cur non & to gromble, quamvis & Galli dicunt grommeler! Τεῤῥω,
units.tr: Toggyzein [Τογγύζειν], to murmur, to be indignant, to grudge, to grumble. If these, why not also "to gromble", although the French also say grommeler! Terrō [Τεῤῥω],

units.la: Γράφω, scribo, sculpo: Nempe, quòd ut sculpebant stylo, ita & (in pugilaribus scil.) olim scribebant aut eodem, aut simillimo. Anglis, to grave; sculpere: olim (ne quis ex Gal. graver mutuatum sùspicetùr:) grafen. grafenum anliengffum beoza : sculptilibus suis, Pfal.LXXVIII. 58. Hinc etiam fortaffe & alterùm synonymum, to carve, ? ?.leviter tranfpofito, ut in χαράσσω, χάρ-ᾳ, &c. & γ. in κ. (quod non rarum) mutato. Aliam tamen originem non minùs probabilem paulò post ex verbo ἐξυκεάς excuIpturi fumus, de quâ lectoris (ut in dubiis) esto judicium.
units.tr: Graphō [Γράφω], to write, to carve. Namely, because as they carved with a stylus, so also (on wax tablets, that is) they formerly wrote with the same or a very similar instrument. The English "to grave" means to carve. Formerly (lest anyone suspect it was borrowed from the French graver): grafen, grafenum, anliengffum, beoza, with their carved images, Psal. LXXVIII. 58. Hence perhaps also the other synonym, "to carve", slightly transposed, as in charassō [χαράσσω], char-ō [χάρ-ᾳ], etc., with g changed to k (which is not rare). I shall offer another origin, no less probable, shortly, derived from the verb exykeas [ἐξυκεάς]; but as in doubtful matters, the judgment is left to the reader.

units.la: Γραφὴ, scriptura, sculptura, a grave: ut proprie de monumento pro more inscripto vel insculpto, dictum fuerit.
units.tr: Graphē [Γραφὴ], writing, carving, from "grave": as properly said of a monument inscribed or carved according to custom.

units.la: Γλύφω: Vide in Κίρχος.
units.tr: Glyphō [Γλύφω]: see under Kirchos [Κίρχος].

units.la: Δ
units.tr: D

units.la: Ἀϊς, Ἀλίμ, convivium, bailtles. Est igitur, a bailtle man: proprie, cupediarum, & scitamentorum fe-ctator, liguritor. Gallice, un friand. Est tamen alloquin etiam λίβαξ, catillo, liguritor: & λιβάς, substantivum: Item & λιβάς, ejusdem significationis ver-bum: bum : ex τίνδω, vel τίνδω, edo, rodo, arrodo, ῥύγχδω.
units.tr: Ἀϊς, Ἀλίμ: a feast; a bailtle man. It is, therefore, properly a seeker after dainties and delicacies, a glutton (in French un friand). It is also, besides, λίβαξ, a dish-licker, a glutton; and λιβάς, as a noun, and λιβάζω, as a verb of the same meaning, from the root of τίνδω or τίνδω, to eat, gnaw, nibble, and ῥύγχδω.

units.la: Αδαμα, umbrosus, tenebrosus, du-skie. ...
units.tr: Ἀδαμα: shady, dark, dusky (in Old English duskie). ...

units.la: Δρῦς, quercus, arbor quaevis, (δένδρον, sylva :) a tree. Quaevis quoque ligna δρῦς olim nuncupata esse, notat auctor Etymologici in voce Δρύφαξ. Apud Willeramum Abbat. apbelbera, quod nunc, apple-tree. Si quis tamen ex δένδρον (arbor:) malit in tree repetere, per me liceat.
units.tr: Δρῦς, oak, or any tree of any kind (δένδρον, a wood): in English, a tree. The author of the Etymologicum, under the word Δρύφαξ, notes that any wood was also formerly called δρῦς. In Willeram the Abbot it is apbelbera, which is now "apple-tree". If anyone prefers to derive it from δένδρον (tree) and repeat it as "tree", let him do so; I have no objection.

units.la: Δρᾶμα, fabula, (Anglicè, a Play, or Comedie:) ad vitam saepe transfertur: δρᾶμα ἢ βίος, fabula vitae; quod vita humana, fabulae simillima. Hinc opinor Anglicum Dreame, somnium : quod & de vitâ, si quid aliud, verissimum.
units.tr: Δρᾶμα, a play (in English, a play or comedy), is often transferred to life: δρᾶμα ἢ βίος, the play of life, because human life is very like a play. Hence, I think, the English "dream", which of life too, if anything, is most true.

units.la: Δμώη, ancilla, a maide : per metathesin.
units.tr: Δμώη, a maidservant, a maid: by metathesis.

units.la: Δοῦλος, servus. Et hinc fortasse Anglicum Dull, (tardus, hebes, stupidus,) manavit. Nota Aristotelis opinio, δοῦλοι esse à natura, qui scilicet κοινωνικὸν ἢ λόγῳ πιστεύειν, ὅσον ἀδυνατοῦσι, ἀλλὰ μὴ ἔχειν : quos etiam ad corporis minis-teria natos, à bestiis usu μηχανὴν ἀναγκάζειν sancit. Germanos autem qui ad libertatem omnia referrent; hoc quoque probro servientium conditionem notare voluisse, probabile est. Est tamen propria quaedam servorum, nequitia, calliditas, & vafrities, Graecis Latinisque comicis decantatissima. Hinc illud Comici, Hic Geta, praeterea, ut captus est fervorum, non malus. Hinc est, quod ipsum servi nomen schalck, quod olim famulum, servum, significabat; nunc astutum & vafrum, apud Germanos: & Anglicum, Knaab; nunc nebulonem, hominem nequam apud Anglos significat. Origo igitur non minus probabilis (Lector pro suo arbitrio poterit alterutrum eligere) ex Graeco ἀπλῶς, simplex, omni fraudis & doli expers: usitatissimâ illâ veteribus Anglis, (cujus tot in litera a. exempla protulimus:) aphaeresi: ἁπλῶς, πλῶς, Dull. Ita & Graecis, εὐήθης, simplex, probus, candidus: Item, stultus, fatuus. Ita & in aliis linguis exempla; nec ratio, cui noti mores, obscura cuiquam. Doll; dicunt hodieque, ni fallor, Germani.
units.tr: Δοῦλος, a slave. From this, perhaps, the English "dull" (slow, dim, stupid) came. Note Aristotle's opinion that slaves are so by nature: namely, those who cannot have reason but only share in it so far as they perceive it; and he lays down that they are born for bodily services and are compelled by nature to use the strength of beasts. It is probable that the Germans, who refer everything to liberty, wished to mark the condition of servitude with this reproach too. There is, however, a certain characteristic of slaves, namely wickedness, cunning and craftiness, which the Greek and Latin comic writers celebrate most of all. Hence that saying of the comic poet: Here is Geta, moreover, as slaves go, not a bad one. Hence the very word for slave, schalck, which formerly meant a servant or slave, now means among the Germans sly and crafty; and the English knave now means among the English a scoundrel, a worthless man. The origin is therefore no less probable (the reader may choose whichever he likes) from the Greek ἁπλῶς, simply, free of all fraud and guile, by that aphaeresis which was very common among the ancient English (of which we have brought forward so many examples under the letter A): ἁπλῶς, then πλῶς, dull. So also the Greeks have εὐήθης, simple, honest, candid; and also foolish, silly. Other languages offer similar examples, and the reasoning is not obscure to anyone who knows their customs. The Germans, I think, still say Doll today.

units.la: Δώρον, donum, dos, ut apud Homerum, πολύδωρος, id est, πολύεδνω, a Dowzie, vel Dower. Caeterum (nam hoc quoque ad rem nostram, quò originem non linguæ tantùm Germanicæ, sed & hominum ex Græcis pro re natâ asseramus :) quod modò ex Tacito in moribus Germanicis didicimus, Dotem non uxorem marito, sed maritum uxori dare solitum ; id apud veteres quoque Græcos obtinuisse ex multis colligere est. Erat autem dos, munera ; munerum verò id præcipuum, ut & ibi Tacitus, boves. Hinc virgines ἀλφεσίβοιαι dictæ Homero, quæ ob eximiam formam multos boves dotis nomine consequebantur. De quo verbo & vetere consuetudine multa erudité notat author Etymologici Græci in ἀλφεσίβοια. Est etiam Gallis dovaire in usu, sed strictiore sensu, pro dotis incremento quod post mariti mortem cedit uxori. Dos alioquin illis dost, ex Latino verbo. Διδάσκειν, docere, to teach. Δέχεσθαι, suscipere, capere, to take. Δείδω, timeo, to dread. Δαμάλιω (Δεδάμω) terrefacio, to daunt : δεδαμένος, intrepidus, undaunted. Δοκεῖν, videri, to thinke: δοκεῖ μοι, methinckes. Δύϊν.
units.tr: Δώρον, a gift, a dowry, as in Homer, πολύδωρος, that is πολύεδνος, "a dowzie" or "dower". Moreover (for this too bears on our purpose, namely to derive not only the German language but the origin of the people itself from the Greeks, as occasion arises): what we have just learned from Tacitus in his account of German customs, that the husband gave a dowry to the wife, not the wife to the husband, may be gathered from many sources to have prevailed among the ancient Greeks as well. The dowry consisted of gifts, and the chief of these gifts, as Tacitus there says, was oxen. Hence Homer called maidens ἀλφεσίβοιαι, because on account of their remarkable beauty many oxen were obtained as their dowry. On this word and the ancient custom the author of the Greek Etymologicum notes much learnedly under ἀλφεσίβοια. The French also use dovaire, though in a narrower sense, for the increase of dowry which passes to the wife after the husband's death; otherwise they have dost, from the Latin word. Διδάσκειν, to teach: "to teach". Δέχεσθαι, to receive, take: "to take". Δείδω, to fear: "to dread". Δαμάζω (Δεδάμω), to terrify or tame: δεδαμένος, fearless, "undaunted". Δοκεῖν, to seem: δοκεῖ μοι, "methinks". Δύϊν...

units.la: Αὑω, Ἰύρω, Ἰύεᾳ, mergi, occidere: proprië de fole: unde Ἰύος, occidens. Anglis to dpe, mori: item to dlde, immergere se.
units.tr: Δύω, Δύομαι, Δύεσθαι, to sink, to set, to perish; properly said of the sun, whence δύσις, the west. To the English "to die" and also "to dive", to plunge oneself under.

units.la: Αεἰϕ, madefacere, irrigare, tingere, Ἰλοπποὺς, tinctor: Angl. to dpe: fed & deto, ros, (quæ irrigatio terræ) ab eodem fonte.
units.tr: Βάπτω, to wet, to water, to dip, to dye; βαφεύς, a dyer. To the English "to dye"; but also "dew", the watering of the earth, comes from the same source.

units.la: Αείν, & Ἰέν, ligare, to tpe.
units.tr: Δέω and Δέειν, to bind, to tie: English "to tie".

units.la: Αοχεῖτη, Ἱικη, loculus, conditorium: Angl. a Dock, receptaculum navium: non portus vel statio, fed ubi subduntur & compinguntur. A Ἰοχεῖον é-tiam ducere possimus.
units.tr: Δοχεῖον, a little chest, a place for storing: English "a dock", a receptacle for ships; not a harbour or anchorage, but where they are drawn up and fastened together. We may also derive it from δοχεῖον.

units.la: Ἀάκω, mordeo, Ἰάκω, animal mórsu noxium; morsus quoque, ut docet Etymologicum: Angli canem, a dogge.
units.tr: Δάκνω, to bite; δάκος, a biting animal, harmful by its bite. The Etymologicum also teaches that the bite itself is so called. The English say "dog" for the animal.

units.la: Ἀιυότης, vis, acumen, dlnt: de quó suprà.
units.tr: Δύναμις... force, keenness, "dint": concerning which, see above.

units.la: Αύπω, aquam subeo, Ἰύπης, urinator, qui aquas subit: Angli active, to dippe; & a dipper, qui alios tingit.
units.tr: Δύπτω, to go into water; δύπτης, a diver, one who goes under the water. The English in the active sense say "to dip", and "a dipper" is one who dips others.

units.la: Ἀπυπηλίς, fructus jam adultus & maturus: jamjam (quippe ex Ἰεύς & πίπω compositum:) cafurus: Ἰπύπ & Ἰπυπηνς, idem, sed aliunde compofita, significant. Hinc credibile est Anglicum dyep, quod de maturis fructibus sæpe ufurpatur, fluxiffe. Fortaffe & Dɪoope, vergere deorfum, inclinare ; nifi potiùs ex ϐέπω,d. præpofito.
units.tr: Ὀπωρινός... fruit already grown and ripe, just ready to fall (compounded, as it seems, from a word meaning "ripe" and πίπτω, to fall); and words of the same meaning, though compounded in another way, also exist. Hence it is credible that the English "ripe" (dyep), which is often used of ripe fruit, arose from this. Perhaps also "dip", to incline downward, to slope; unless it rather comes from βέπω with a prefix.

units.la: Δεΐπω, colligo, carpo, to reape: ut ex Græco Λεΐσ𝔾ρος, Latinum ejufdem fignificationis.
units.tr: Δρέπω, to gather, to pluck, to reap: as from the Greek λειστήρ, the Latin word of the same meaning comes.

units.la: E
units.tr: E

units.la: EΙα, gramen, bap.* Eĺι, adhuc, pef.
units.tr: Eia, grass, bap.*; eti, yet, still, pef.

units.la: Ερίω, remigo. Dixerunt poftea ἐρίπω. Sed illud antiquum afferit locus Homericus Ληίσσα χρσὰν ἐμὴν. Non enim, poteft ex Λιεριάω, aoriftus Λιήισσα formari; fed ex Λιερίω : idque ex Herodiani fententiâ, quem laudat Etymologicum : Angli, to rotwe.
units.tr: Eriō, to row. They later said eripō. But the old form is attested by the Homeric passage "Lēissa chrysēn emēn". The aorist Lēisa cannot be formed from Lieriaō; it must be formed from Lieriō, according to the opinion of Herodian, whom the Etymologicum quotes. English: to rowe.

units.la: Ευδιου, domicilium, diverforium, an Inne. D.litera fæpè excidit, ut in Gallicis illis, loner, fuer, cheir, cruel, &c. ex laudare, fudare, cadere, crudelis, &c. Verfteganus ingeat etiam fcribit. De quo viderit ille. Certè ⁊o inne, vetus, Matth. XIII. 36. and com to bis inne, venit in domum.
units.tr: Eudiou, dwelling-place, lodging, an inn. The letter d often drops out, as in those French words loner, fuer, cheir, cruel, etc., from laudare, fudare, cadere, crudelis, etc. Verstegan also writes it so. Let him see to that. Certainly the old English inne, Matth. 13.36, "and came to his inne", that is, came into the house.

units.la: Ελιννύω, Pigrari, ceffare; etiam tempus terere: tardare, morari; cunctari. Tot enim tum Hefychius, tum Suidas, & & pluribus utuntur verbis, ut vim hujus verbi exprimant: Angl. <bl>to tinger.</bl>
units.tr: Elinnyō, to be idle, to cease; also to waste time, to delay, to linger, to hesitate. For both Hesychius and Suidas use so many words to express the force of this verb. English: to tinger.

units.la: Ἕτερος, alius, alter, <bl>other.</bl>
units.tr: Heteros: another, the other; English: other.

units.la: Ἕκαστος, unusquisque, <bl>each.</bl>
units.tr: Hekastos: each one; English: each.

units.la: Ἐνλέχια, folertia, calliditas: Angl. <bl>trick,</bl> & <bl>tricke,</bl> id est, sophismata: Ἐντυγχάνει, incurrit, convenit, quadrat, aptum est, <bl>to be trigg.</bl> in eam sententiam non semel audivisse mihi videor.
units.tr: Enlechia: cleverness, cunning; English: trick and tricke, that is, sophisms. Entygchanei: it falls in with, agrees, fits, suits; English: to be trigg. I seem to have heard this used in that sense more than once.

units.la: Εἱλέω, verto, volvo, εἱλεῖς circumplicari & obvolvi: Anglicè, <bl>a wheele,</bl> rota: item <bl>to wtlde,</bl> circumagere.
units.tr: Eileō, to turn, roll, twist; eileis, to be entwined and wrapped round. English: a wheele, a wheel; likewise to wield, to turn round.

units.la: Εἴλλω, prohibeo; εἵλω, frenum, vinculum; εἵλαρ, propugnaculum: Angl. <bl>to hold;</bl> ut cum dicunt, <bl>hold your hand,</bl> abstine manum: item <bl>a hold;</bl> arx, propugnaculum.
units.tr: Eillō, to prevent; eilō, a bridle, a bond; eilar, a bulwark. English: to hold, as when they say "hold your hand", that is, refrain your hand; likewise a hold, a stronghold, bulwark.

units.la: Ἔργον, opus, <bl>a worke.</bl>
units.tr: Ergon: work, deed; English: a worke.

units.la: Ἐργώδης, operosus, laboriosus, molestus, <bl>trckfome.</bl>
units.tr: Ergōdēs: laborious, toilsome, troublesome; English: troublesome.

units.la: Εὐρώς, situs, <bl>rust.</bl>
units.tr: Eurōs: squalor, filth; English: rust.

units.la: Ἐρέω, ἐρέω, ἐρείνω, interrogo, denuncio, quæro, <bl>to errand.</bl>
units.tr: Ereō, ereō, ereinō: to question, to announce, to seek; English: to errand.

units.la: Ἔπω, ἔπω, dico, <bl>to speake.</bl>
units.tr: Epō, epō: to say; English: to speake.

units.la: Ἐθέαι, proprie, ἐκ τῆς κοσμουμένας, ἢ ἐπιμελείας ἐξ ἔθους ἀξιώματος. Cæsaries, ex more culta & ornata: ut Hesychius & Etymologicum explicant. Unde ἐθίἐομψον, in genere, κοσμώμενον, ἀσαλλόμενον; ornatum, cultum ab Hesychio exponitur: Angl. to attire, & attired.
units.tr: Ethea, properly from the adorning or the care that comes from custom and dignity: caesaries, hair dressed and adorned according to custom, as Hesychius and the Etymologicum explain. Hence ethi-eompsos, in general adorned, dressed, decked out; Hesychius explains it as adorned, cultivated. English: to attire, and attired.

units.la: ᾿Εμπολάω, comparo, acquiro, lucror: ἐμπολαὶ, Hesychio, ἀραγμαλδέλαι, ἀπεύχεσθαι; negotiatur, circumit: Anglicè, to pole, & a poleur: etiam ἐμπολή, merx, φορλίον, unde fortasse, implements; nisi Latinum, implementa, (quod tamen verbum Latina lingua, quod sciam, non agnoscit) vetaret. Sed nec illud implements fortasse vetus & genuinum: Belg. tamen Im-boel, inboel, supellex, apud Kylianum.
units.tr: Empolaō: to buy, to acquire, to gain; empolai, according to Hesychius, bargains, pleas, prayers; to trade, to go about. English: to pole, and a poleur. Also empolē, merchandise, goods; perhaps hence implements, unless the Latin implementa (a word which, so far as I know, Latin does not recognise) forbids it. But perhaps implements is not an old or native word either. The Dutch, however, have inboel, inboel, household goods, in Kilian.

units.la: ᾿Εμφυλος, innatus; ἐμφυλίζω, infero: Angl. to impe, an impe, furculus.
units.tr: Emphylos: innate; emphyliazō: to graft in. English: to impe, an impe, a young shoot.

units.la: ᾿Εγγεγράφειν, inscribo, insculpo, scarifico, to graffe, or ingraffe.
units.tr: Engegraphein: to inscribe, to engrave, to scarify. English: to graffe, or ingraffe.

units.la: ᾿Εμφύναι, adhaerere, amplecti: ἐμφύναι τ χερσὶ, manibus amplecti, & firmiter tenere: Anglicè, to fang, or fong: manu prehendere. Fortasse & hinc fingers, digiti: item ἐμφύναι, φύναι, (unde participium, φύνλες, i.e. ἐμπλακέντες: ) ἐμφυέντες, amplecti, osculari: de puero collo matris inhaerente, τῷ ἡαχήλῳ τ μητρὸς ἐμφύναι. Et hinc fortasse, to be fond, & fondnesse;
units.tr: Emphynai: to cling to, to embrace; emphynai tais chersi: to embrace with the hands and hold firmly. English: to fang, or fong, to take hold with the hand. Perhaps hence fingers, digits. Also emphynai, phynai (whence the participle phynes, that is, emplakentes, entangled), emphyentes, to embrace, to kiss: said of a child clinging to its mother's neck, tō tracheilō tēs mētros emphynai. And perhaps hence to be fond, and fondnesse,

units.la: de puerorum deliciis, & nimiâ parentum erga liberos indulgentiâ. Sed & fond, stultus; fondnesse, stultitia, amentia: nempe, Quia mollis illa educatio, quam indulgentiam vocamus, nervos omnes & mentis & corporis frangit. Quintiliani sunt verba: sed Germanorum eam fuisse sententiam, ex educationis ratione liquet. Tacit: Dominum ac servum nullis educationis deliciis dignoscas. Reliqua apud ipsum leguntur.
units.tr: of children's delights and of parents' excessive indulgence towards their children. But also fond, foolish; fondnesse, folly, madness. Namely: "Because that soft upbringing, which we call indulgence, breaks all the sinews both of mind and of body." These are Quintilian's words. That this was the opinion of the Germans is clear from their manner of upbringing. Tacitus: "You could not tell master from slave by the pampered delights of their upbringing." The rest is read in him.

units.la: 'Ἐρυθρὸς, ruber, red.
units.tr: Erythros: red; English: red.

units.la: 'Ἔαρ, ἔαρος, ver. Angl. peare, (Germ. jar.) annus: quòd à vere annum multi auspicarentur.
units.tr: Ear, earos: spring. English: peare (German jar), year; because many began the year from spring.

units.la: 'Εἰμί, sum, I am.
units.tr: Eimi: I am; English: I am.

units.la: 'Ἐλπίς, spes, hope; an & to helpe, cùm spes & præsidium sint affinia?
units.tr: Elpis: hope; English: hope; and perhaps to helpe, since hope and help are related?

units.la: 'Ἑλκω, trahere, to hale.
units.tr: Helkō: to draw; English: to hale.

units.la: 'Ἐϋω, inflammare, torrere, to sindge. De aspiratione in f. vertente, vide supra.
units.tr: Euō: to set on fire, to scorch; English: to sindge. On the change of the aspiration into f, see above.

units.la: 'Ἑστιάω, convivio excipere: ἑστιάτωρ, conviva: Angl. a gueft.
units.tr: Hestiaō: to entertain at a feast; hestiatōr: a guest at table; English: a gueft.

units.la: Εἰδω, Præter. οἶδα, novi, scio: Angl. wote: ἐκ οἶδα, I wote not.
units.tr: Eidō, perfect oida: I know; English: wote; ek oida: I wote not.

units.la: Εἰδὼ, φρόνησις (Hesychio) prudentia: εἰδὼς, sciens, peritus, witt, wittie.
units.tr: Eidō, phronēsis (according to Hesychius), prudence; eidōs: knowing, skilled, experienced; English: witt, wittie.

units.la: 'Ἐγχλιώσιν, ᾿Εγχλύσῃν, ἐγχυκάζειν, (Hefychius:) indulcare, to glatt, & to clote. ..
units.tr: Enchlioein, enchlysein, enchykazein (Hesychius): to sweeten; English: to glatt, and to clote.

units.la: ᾿Εξυεγὲς, & χυεγὲς, Hefychio, (qui Æfchyli locum citat:) ἡ ὁρυφὴ χ᾽ ὁ χεαπῆς πίνακ̈ς : vel ἡ ἐν τοῖς ὀεγφώμεσι χεαφὴ : tectum domus; item pictura seu tabulæ pictæ (ut Stephanus interpretatur) quibus laquearia & tecta ædium exornari solent. Idem Hefych. ἐξυεγὲς, ὁ γεγαμμένος, pictus, interpretatur. Conjicit autem doctissimus Stephanus (& recte conjicit, ut ego sentio:) dictam esse χυεγέλα, vel ἐξυεγέλα, ὥσπερ ἡ χόρων, quæ in sese τῶν χοφῶν imagines pictas habeat; Puellarum puerorumve imaginibus exornata. Hinc igitur Anglicum, to carve, sculpere,& a carver, sculptor: ut proprie sit a carver, qui puerorum puellarúmve imagines (quibus ut plurimùm ædes exornantur:) facit aut sculpit. Notant Anglici quidam Lexicographi, cozuell, vetus verbum; quo pars anguli, nescio quæ; sed & domus frontispicium nuncupatum est: quod si verum est, (nam mihi aliàs inauditum:) hinc quoq; ductum merito censeri possit.
units.tr: Exyegēs, and chyegēs, according to Hesychius (who cites a passage of Aeschylus): the roof of a house, or a painted board, or the painted work in the carvings; also a picture or painted panels (as Stephanus explains), with which ceilings and roofs of buildings are usually adorned. The same Hesychius explains exyegēs as painted, that which has been drawn. The very learned Stephanus conjectures (and, as I think, rightly) that chyegela or exyegela was so called, like the choros, which has painted images of dancers within it; adorned with images of girls or boys. Hence the English to carve, to sculpt, and a carver, a sculptor: so that properly a carver is one who makes or carves images of boys or girls, with which houses are mostly adorned. Some English lexicographers note cozuell, an old verb, by which part of a corner, I know not what, and also the frontispiece of a house, was named. If this is true (for I have heard otherwise), it may rightly be thought to derive from here.

units.la: ᾿Ευὼν, ἑωλ, ἐχαλία, ἐνδία, (need, sed & <bl>want.</bl>) De his in superioribus,ut occasio se dabat, jam egimus.
units.tr: Euōn, eōl, echalia, endia (need, but also want). We have already dealt with these in the preceding pages, as occasion offered.

units.la: 'Ἐρεθενῶν, cavillari, scommate illudere,ludificari,nugari, to wrangle; sed & to rale; quamvis Galli quoque habeant, railler, & raillerie : ἐρεθενία, ludificatio, &c. wrangling.
units.tr: Erethenōn: to cavil, to mock with a sneer, to ridicule, to trifle; English: to wrangle; but also to rale, although the French too have railler and raillerie. Erethenia: mockery, and so on; English: wrangling.

units.la: Εὐχὴ, precatio, votum ; εὔχομαι, precor, voveo : <bl>a vow</bl>, <bl>to vow.</bl>
units.tr: Euchē: prayer, vow; euchomai: to pray, to vow; English: a vow, to vow.

units.la: 'Ἐγγυάω, proprie, in manus trado : <bl>I give</bl> : item spondeo, desponso: quod & Angli, proprie, <bl>to give.</bl>
units.tr: Engyaō: properly to hand over into the hands; English: I give. Likewise to pledge, to betroth; which the English also use, properly, as to give.

units.la: 'Εἶτα, postea, <bl>and.</bl>
units.tr: Eita: afterwards; English: and.

units.la: Z
units.tr: Z

units.la: Ζέω, ferveo, to seeth. Est in Cambdenianis: sed ideo repeto, ut ejus occasione (alieno quamvis loco, nisi quòd à ζέω non alieno :) Græcorum proverbium lectori impertiam. Dicebant enim ; Ζὰ χύτρα, ζῇ, φιλία : Fervet olla, viget amicitia: Quo nihil aptius ad mores Germanorum, quales eos describit Tacitus, fingi potest : ut ab illis ortum videri possit. Sed & hoc ipsum non factis tantum, sed & verbis illos usurpasse, docebit de re Anglicâ vetere meritissimus, & pretiosæ apud omnes bonos, ob summam probitatem, summum candorem, memoriæ, Henricus Spilmannus, in optimo Glossario, in voce Geldum. De quo plura quoque Somnerus meus, in Glossario suo, in Croco Crowellet.
units.tr: Zéō, I boil, I seethe, to seeth. It is in Camden's Britannia, but I repeat it here so that, on this occasion, I can pass on to the reader a Greek proverb. The place is not foreign to the subject, since the word is from zéō: they used to say, Zà chýtra, zē, philía [Ζὰ χύτρα, ζῇ, φιλία]: the pot boils, friendship lives. Nothing could be better suited to the customs of the Germans as Tacitus describes them, so that the proverb might seem to have come from them. That the English used this not only in deeds but also in words will be shown by Henry Spelman, a man deserving of great credit in matters of old English history and valued by all good men for his great integrity and candour, in his excellent Glossary under the word Geldum. My Somner also says more about this in his Glossary under Croco Crowellet.

units.la: Ζάξλη, vel ζάξλον: ἁρπαγον, falx. Vox Siculorum propria, ut notant veteres Grammatici. Hinc, ni fallor, vox à quibusdam Italiæ populis (ut Varro docet) usurpata, secula, pro falce. Varro quidem ipse à secando ducit. At typus ille verbi diminutivus, secula, rei non bene convenit. Nec verisimile est, vocem apud ipsos Latinos raram & ferè ignotam, ad Anglos pervenisse. Varronem autem falsum fuisse, nemo mirabitur, cùm talia apud illum passim occurrant: qui etiam vocem Pater, ex Latinâ, (quo nihil ineptius) quòd femen patefaciat, origine: & Proserpina, à proserpendo, ducere maluit; quàm ex Græcâ, tam obviâ alioquin & certâ, repetere. Multa autem ex Siculorum dialecto in Linguam Latinam translata esse, satis notum est. Vident, quibus animus, quæ de voce catasta notant docti viri in Persium. Hinc igitur fuerit
units.tr: Záxlē, or záxlon [ζάξλη, ζάξλον]: a sickle, falx. It is a word peculiar to the Sicilians, as the ancient grammarians note. Hence, unless I am mistaken, the word secula, for a sickle, which some peoples of Italy used (as Varro teaches). Varro himself derives it from secando, cutting. But that diminutive form, secula, does not fit the thing well. Nor is it likely that a word so rare and almost unknown among the Latins themselves reached the English. No one will be surprised that Varro was wrong, since such things occur throughout his work. He also preferred to derive the word Pater from Latin, which is most absurd, because it femen patefaciat (opens the seed), and Proserpina from proserpendo, rather than from Greek, which is otherwise so obvious and certain. It is well known that many words were carried from the Sicilian dialect into the Latin language. Those whose minds are inclined to such things can see what learned men note on the word catasta in Persius. So it will have come about, as I for my part think, that the English word is sickle.

units.la: ꝛ rit, ut ego quidem censeo, Anglicum, ficlle. De affini verbo {ptl}e, in postrema parte dicturi sumus.
units.tr: ...so it will have come about, as I for my part think, that the English word is sickle. We shall speak of the related verb "{ptl}e" in the last part.

units.la: H.
units.tr: H.

units.la: *Hιὸν, maxilla, the jaw. 'Ηίων, juvenis, a youth. Venient, haud dubito, lectori in mentem, young, ex juvenis, & youth, pro juventute, ex hoc ipso juventus, originem, istud quidem certissimam, hoc autem, probabilem, præferentia. Quæ mihi quoque cùm venerint in mentem, caussam tamen, cur respuenda effet origo Græca, in tanta linguarum istarum affinitate, non videbam : cùm nec illud exemplo careat, ut verba & sono & significatione penè eadem, à diversâ tamen sint origine.
units.tr: Hion [Ἡιὸν], the jaw. Hion [Ἡίων], a youth. No doubt the reader will think of "young", derived from "juvenis", and "youth", put for "juventus" and derived from that very word. The first derivation is certainly the more sure, and the second is probable. These also came to my mind, but I saw no reason why a Greek origin should be rejected, given such close affinity between these languages, since this too is not without precedent: words nearly identical in both sound and meaning may nevertheless have different origins.

units.la: Ημίεχ, ἡλὺς. De his supra.
units.tr: Hemiech [Ἡμίεχ], helys [ἡλὺς]. See above on these.

units.la: Θύγατερ, filia, a daughter. Θάνατος, mors, death; nisi ad ν νύκτ, de quo supra, pertinet: Ope, death. Vide ibi.
units.tr: Thygater [Θύγατερ], a daughter. Thanatos [Θάνατος], death, unless this belongs to the ν of nykt [νύκτ], discussed above. Ope, death. See there.

units.la: Θίδη, arca scirpea; proprie: sed latius interdum pro loculo quovis, aut repositorio, ex quacunque materia: ut ex Atheni locis patet, a tabb.
units.tr: Θίδη [Thídē], a chest of rushes, properly; but more widely, sometimes, any container or receptacle, of whatever material, as is clear from passages in Athenaeus.

units.la: Θυμέλη, locus editior, in scæna, vel alibi, in agris, unde Bacchici vel Dionysiaci τεχνῖται seu artifices, saltationibus & gesticulationibus populum oblectabant: unde & Θυμελικοί, tales dicti, saltatores, & gesticulatores publici. Sax. tambe, to Daunce: tambeD, danceD, ut Verstheganus docet. Hodie, to tumble, jactare se, cernuare, prostrare.
units.tr: Θυμέλη [Thymélē], a raised place on the stage, or elsewhere, in the fields, from which the Bacchic or Dionysiac artists (artifices) entertained the people with dances and gestures; whence also Θυμελικοί [Thymelikoí], so called, dancers and public mimes. Saxon tambe, to Daunce: tambeD, danceD, as Verstegan teaches. Today, to tumble: to toss oneself about, to pitch headlong, to prostrate oneself.

units.la: Θίασος, coetus (Bacchantium proprie, sive Bacchi sacra celebrantium:) saltantium, & tripudiantium. Unde Θιάσευ, ab Hesychio exponitur, χορεύσαι, choreas ducere, tripudiare: & Θιάσον, χόρευσον, id est, tripudiato: & Θιάσωται, χορευταί, i.e. tripudiatores. Hinc petenda, ni fallor, Gallici verbi danse à danser, circa quam multi laborant, etymologia. Sed hoc nihil ad nos. Nam Angli à Gallis, ut probabile est, acceperunt. At Anglicum est, vetus & probum, to tosse, ejusdem ferè cum praecedente, to tumble, significationis. Belgicum taffen, aliud; ex Gallico verbo, tas.
units.tr: Θίασος [Thíasos], a company (properly of Bacchants, or of those celebrating the rites of Bacchus), of dancers and revellers. Whence Θιάσευ [Thiáseu], explained by Hesychius as χορεύσαι [choreúsai], to lead dances, to dance; and Θίασον, χόρευσον [Thíason, chóreuson], that is, dance!; and Θιάσωται, χορευταί [Thiásōtai, choreutaí], that is, dancers. Hence, unless I am mistaken, is to be sought the etymology of the French word danse from danser, about which many labour. But this is nothing to us, for the English, as is probable, took the word from the French. The English to tosse is old and good, and of nearly the same meaning as the preceding to tumble. The Dutch taffen is another word, from the French tas.

units.la: Θύμεσθ, Θεμεγὸς, σεμνὸν; (ut Hesychius exponit:) id est, grave, honestum, venerabile: Θεμερὸν, σεμνὴ, βεβαία, ἀσφαλὴς; gravis, stabilis; firma. Θεμερύνεος (sic: Θεμερύνεος, ex Stephani seu exemplari, seu correctione:) σεμνύνεος, morum gravitatem & verecundiam præ se ferre. Nullibi nunc quod sciam extat hoc verbum; quod tamen genuinum esse & vetus Græcum, (ex σεμνὸς fortasse per dialectum formatum: quod & hic innuit Hesychius:) patet ex composito Θεμεγέρφων, id est, σνυέλὸς, σώφρων, apud eundem. Angli habent, demure, id est, gravis, modestus. Nam qui ex Gallicis, de bonne mœurs, ductum volunt; suo more ludunt. Demurre, affine sono, sed plane aliud & origine & significatione.
units.tr: Θέμεσθ [Thémesth], Θεμεγὸς, σεμνόν [Themegòs, semnón] (as Hesychius explains): that is, grave, honourable, venerable. Θεμερόν, σεμνή, βεβαία, ἀσφαλής [Themerón, semnḗ, bebaía, asphalḗs]: grave, stable, firm. Θεμερύνεος (so written, from Stephanus, either from his manuscript or from his correction) [Themerýneos], to show the gravity and modesty of manners. So far as I know, this word is found nowhere now. Yet that it is genuine and old Greek, perhaps formed from σεμνός [semnós] by dialect (as Hesychius also hints), appears from the compound Θεμεγέρφων [Themegérphōn], that is, σώφρων [sṓphrōn], prudent, in the same author. The English have demure, that is, grave, modest. For those who want it derived from the French de bonne mœurs are playing their usual games. Demurre is similar in sound, but clearly different both in origin and in meaning.

units.la: Θαρρεῖν, audere, to dare.
units.tr: Θαρρεῖν [Tharreîn], to dare, <bl>to dare.</bl>

units.la: Θελξεῖν, mulcere, demulcere (quod oratoris proprium:) Angl. to talke. Nisi quis malit (quod etiam probabile est): ex Θελξεῖν, Θελξεῖς (quod in usu tantum est:) differere, sermocinari; contractum esse. Unde ortum videtur & vetus Belgicum, taelen (ut apud Kilianum) loqui, & taele, sermo, oratio; (Θελ(Διάλεξις:) Anglis hodieque, a tale, fabula.
units.tr: Θελξεῖν [Thelxeîn], to soothe, to charm, which is the orator's proper work. English: <bl>to talke.</bl> Unless someone prefers (which is also probable) that it is contracted from Θελξεῖν, Θελξεῖς [Thelxeîn, Thelxeîs] (used only in this way), to differ, to converse. From this seems to derive the old Dutch taelen (as in Kilian), to speak, and taele, speech, discourse (Θελ = διάλεξις [dialexis]). The English still have tale, a story.

units.la: Θεωρέω, contemplor, to stare. Vulgo, ab astrorum seu stellarum (quæ starres) contemplatione. Ego istud verius credo.
units.tr: Θεωρέω [Theōréō], I contemplate, <bl>to stare.</bl> Commonly it is derived from the contemplation of the stars (which are called starres). I believe this derivation is the truer.

units.la: Θρέω, clamo, loquor; Σπόος, sonus, sermo. (hinc ἀλλόσποος, Homero, diverfilinguis:) Angl. I trow, id est, puto, credo. Putare & loqui, affinia natura: Unde אמר Hebraeis, utrumque: & vulgo dicimus, what say you? Lat. Quid ais? sententiam rogantes.
units.tr: Θρέω [Thréō], I cry out, I speak; Σπόος [Spóos], sound, speech (hence ἀλλόσποος [allóspoos], of a different tongue, in Homer). English: I trow, that is, I think, I believe. Thinking and speaking are akin in nature. Hence the Hebrew amar [אמר] means both; and we commonly say What say you?, in Latin Quid ais?, when asking for an opinion.

units.la: Θρύς, tumultus, clamor; Anglis, a throng, turba, tumultus, vel tumultuosa hominum congeries. Nisi tamen ex Σπρύβω, quod idem; vel, ἀσπόω, consertus.
units.tr: Θρύς [Thrýs], tumult, clamour. For the English, <bl>a throng</bl>: a crowd, a tumult, or a tumultuous gathering of people. Unless perhaps it comes from Σπρύβω [Sprýbō], which means the same, or from ἀσπόω [aspóō], to join together.

units.la: Θορέω, salio, insilio; Σπρω, impetuosus: qui cum impetu assultat: Anglis, throwes, parturientium dolores, ἀδῖνες, qui subiti & impetuosi esse solent. Sed in genere, throwtigen, pati, Saxonicum. (Matth. XVII. v. 12.)
units.tr: Θορέω [Thoréō], I leap, I leap upon; Σπρω [Sprō], impetuous: one who assaults with force. English: <bl>throwes</bl>, the pains of women in labour, ἀδῖνες [adînes], which are usually sudden and violent. But in general, <bl>throwtigen</bl>, to suffer, is Saxon. (Matth. XVII. v. 12.)

units.la: Θερμός, calidus, warme. Vide in Κεύω.
units.tr: Θερμός [Thermós], warm, <bl>warme.</bl> See under Κεύω [Keúō].

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: 'Ικτιν, milvus, a lɩtte. 'Ιμάνλωνς, lignum (ita interpretatur Hieronymus, ut aliis notatum reperio) quod ad continendos parietes in medio structurae ponitur: Angli vocant, the mantle, (vel mantletree) of a chimnie, transversum lignum quod anteriorem partem camini (ut nunc loquimur: deest enim aptius verbum; quia res ignota Romanis, ut ex Philandro in Vitruvium, aliisque notum:) sustinet & continet. Quod verbum quanquam aliis quoque fortasse Gallis, Italisve commune, non tamen praetereundum duxi, quod paucis notam originem credrem. Stultum enim est quod de mantele somniant.
units.tr: Ἴκτιν (ἴκτῖνος), a kite, a bird of prey. Ἱμάντλων, a piece of timber (so Jerome interprets it, as I find noted by others), which is set across the middle of a structure to hold the walls together. The English call it the mantle (or mantletree) of a chimney: the transverse beam that supports and holds the front part of the fireplace. (We speak of it thus because no more apt word exists; the thing was unknown to the Romans, as is clear from Philander on Vitruvius and others.) Although this word may perhaps be common to other Frenchmen and Italians as well, I thought it should not be passed over, since I believe its origin is little known. It is foolish to dream that it comes from mantele.

units.la: 'Ιαίνω, calefacio, tepefacio, proprie: & inde, liquefacio, dissolvo, solvo, perfundo. Cum animo attribuitur, perfundere laetitiâ significat. Proprium enim caloris est, aperire & solvere. Unde sparsis per totum corpus spiritibus, quaedam cum languore conjuncta voluptas sequitur. Hujus autem affectus, crebra oscitatio saepe indicium est: quam ut fluxa cujusdam & aperta securitatis, strenuo & serio homine indignæ, argumentum vitio olim datam, ex A. Gellio (IV. 20.) discimus.
units.tr: Ἰαίνω, to warm, to make tepid, properly; and from this, to melt, to dissolve, to loosen, to pour over. When it is applied to the mind, it means to fill with joy. For it is the proper effect of heat to open and loosen. Hence, when the spirits are spread through the whole body, a certain pleasure joined with languor follows. Of this feeling, frequent yawning is often the sign; and from Aulus Gellius (IV. 20.) we learn that it was once taken as a fault, a proof of a loose and open carelessness unworthy of a vigorous and serious man.

units.la: Inde & flores cùm ad calorem solis aperiuntur, oscitare dicuntur. Vis verbi Græci optimè à Plutarcho ἀεὶ ἢ ψυχρᾷ exponitur his verbis: Τὸ ἁπλῶς ... Innuit autem Plutarchus, aut innuere saltem videtur, si non verbo, certè eâ notione verbi ἰαίνεσς, ut lætitiam significaret, primum Homerum usum esse; ut hinc quoq; transire sæpè significationes ad alias res affines, discamus. Anglis, to yawne, oscitare est.
units.tr: Hence also flowers are said to yawn when they open to the heat of the sun. The force of the Greek word is best explained by Plutarch with the words "ἀεὶ ἢ ψυχρᾷ" [Τὸ ἁπλῶς ...]. Plutarch suggests, or at least seems to suggest, that Homer was the first to use the verb ἰαίνειν, if not in this word, then in the sense of signifying joy; so that we may learn how meanings often pass to other, related things. In English, to yawne means to yawn.

units.la: Ἰαλεμίζειν, lamentari, flere, lugere: ἀλαλεμῶ, lamentum, cantilena lamentabilis, & lugubris. Anglis, to howle, lugere, cum clamore lamentari.
units.tr: Ἰαλεμίζειν, to lament, to weep, to mourn; ἀλαλεμῶ, a lament, a plaintive and mournful song. In English, to howle means to mourn, to lament with a cry.

units.la: Ἰστάναι, stare; item, sistere. Ita & Anglicum, to stap, utrumque. Quod evincit, non ex Latino, sed Græco ortum esse. Hinc quoque credibile est & verbum staffe, quo corpus quasi sistitur (sæpè sine eo ruituruM) & sustentatur. Quæ & Hebraici ρψωɔ ratio: sed & Latini (ut plerisque placet) scipio. "Ιππος equus, a bobbie, de quodam equorum genere.
units.tr: Ἱστάναι, to stand; likewise, to set in place. So too the English to stap means both. This shows that it arose from the Greek, not the Latin. From this too it is likely that the word staffe comes, by which a body is, as it were, held in place (often it would otherwise fall) and supported. This is also the reasoning behind the Hebrew ρψωɔ; but also the Latin scipio (as most think). Ἵππος, horse: from bobbie, of a certain kind of horse.

units.la: K
units.tr: K

units.la: KΑρπὸς, fructus, in genere, quivis: καρπὸς ἀρούρης, fructus terræ. Interdum,ut docti viri observarunt,frumentum, proprië: καρπάω, carpo, fructus colligo. Anglicè, a croppe, annona; messis unius anni.
units.tr: Καρπός, fruit, in general, any fruit; καρπὸς ἀρούρης, the fruit of the earth. Sometimes, as learned men have observed, it means grain, properly. Καρπάω, to pluck, to gather fruit. In English, a croppe: a harvest, the produce of one year.

units.la: Καρπὸς, palmæ prima pars, junctura manus cum cubito: λαμβάνειν ἐπὶ καρπῷ, apud Homerum: Anglicè, to grapple, or grasple, conferere manus, implicari.
units.tr: Καρπός, the first part of the palm, the joint where the hand meets the arm. In Homer, λαμβάνειν ἐπὶ καρπῷ, to take hold by the wrist. In English, to grapple or grasple: to join hands, to become entangled.

units.la: Κάρφω, palea,festuca,stipula arida: κάρφω, & καρφύνω, sicco, arefacio: etiam καλαππυπλίνω, sordido, squallidum reddo: κάρφη, Hesychio, φορυλὸς, quisquiliæ aridæ. Anglis scurfe, furfures capitis, arida scabies: scurbie, scabiosus, proprië. Sed cùm ad mores transfertur, ex ἀλγεὶς ductum videri possit, quod turpem significat.
units.tr: Κάρφω, chaff, straw, dry stalk; κάρφω and καρφύνω, to dry up, to make withered; also καλαππυπλίνω, to soil, to make squalid. In Hesychius, κάρφη is φορυλός, dry rubbish. In English, scurfe means dandruff of the head, dry scabies; scurbie means scabby, properly. But when it is transferred to morals, it may seem to be derived from ἀλγεινός, since it signifies foul.

units.la: Κίρκοι, vel κείνοι, inter alia, (nam multa significant:) ab Hesychio exponuntur, ἁρπαγες, & πάνλα τὰ ὀτκίαμάτι, id est, harpagones; & in genere, quicquid aduncum est. Anglici Lexicographi creeke, vel crooke, (utroque enim modo scriptum reperio:) exponunt etiam harpagonem, sive machinam, quâ onera tollunt. Ejusmodi machina etiam κέαν@ à Græcis dicta: Anglicè, (ex Græco) a crane.
units.tr: Κίρκοι, or κείκοι (for it has many meanings), are explained by Hesychius as ἅρπαγες, and πάντα τὰ ὀγκίαμάτα (that is, grappling hooks); and in general, whatever is hooked. English lexicographers give creeke or crooke (for I find it written both ways), and explain it as a grappling hook or a machine by which loads are lifted. A machine of this kind is also called κέρανος by the Greeks: in English (from the Greek), a crane.

units.la: Κίρκ@ (vel κείκ@) circulus, annulus, ansula, quicquid aduncum. Ex hac multiplici verbi significatione manat fortasse Anglicum qwirke, pro opere subtili, vel sophismate.
units.tr: Κίρκος (or κείκος), a circle, a ring, a little loop, whatever is hooked. From this manifold meaning of the word perhaps comes the English qwirke, for a subtle work or a sophism.

units.la: Κεσνῆες, dentes genuini vel maxillares. Anglicè, to scrantch, edere; sed indecorè, lacerando dentibus, aut conterendo.
units.tr: Κεσνῆες, the genuine or grinding teeth. In English, to scrantch: to eat, but indecently, by tearing or grinding with the teeth.

units.la: Κλοῖς, collare, proprie caninum: jugum ligneum, quo ferociores canes domantur. Tale lignum vocant hodieque Angli, a clogge: & inde verbum, to clogge, impedire, implicare. Unde & τὸ clogge, ni fallor, pro trunco. Solent enim ejusmodi κλοῖς ex appenso trunco concinnare.
units.tr: Κλοῖς, a collar, properly one for dogs: a wooden yoke by which fiercer dogs are subdued. Even today the English call such a piece of wood a clogge; and from it comes the verb to clogge, to impede, to entangle. Whence also the clogge, unless I am mistaken, for a log of wood; for such collars are usually made with a log attached.

units.la: Κορυφή, vertex, summitas quævis, cacumen. Olim croppe, pro quavis ab Anglis summitate usurpatum; ut apud quosdam Lexicographos reperio.
units.tr: Κορυφή, the top, any summit, a peak. Formerly croppe was used by the English for any summit, as I find in certain lexicographers.

units.la: Κόλλυξ, corium, seu caro nescio quæ durior in sive tergis sive cervicibus bovum; item & ovium. Hinc κόλλυπες & κόλλαβοι claviculæ quædam ex isto corio confici solitæ, quibus fides intendere & remittere solebant. Alii παλάλλες, ἐξ ὧν ἐξάπτονται αἱ χορδαὶ interpretantur, & ex κωλλίδες, i.e. ex agglutinatione ita vocatos istos κολλάβυς tradunt. Haud longè abit Anglicum, clasps.
units.tr: Κόλλυξ, the hide, or some tougher flesh, on the backs or necks of oxen; likewise of sheep. Hence κόλλυβες and κόλλαβοι, small pegs made from that hide, by which they used to tighten and loosen the strings. Others interpret them as παλάλλες, from which the strings are fastened, and say that those κολλάβοι were so named from ἐκ κωλλίδες, that is, from agglutination. The English clasps is not far from this.

units.la: Κόλλαβοι vel κόλαβοι dictæ etiam sunt portiunculæ panis, nescio quæ, in certam formam ex majore quantitate concisæ ; ex κολοβόω, decurto, minuo, mutilo, Angli vocant collops, particulas porcinas, ad subitos usus ex integrâ succidiâ decisas. Imò & quælibet offulæ carneæ ita vocantur.
units.tr: Κόλλαβοι or κόλαβοι are also the name of certain small pieces of bread, cut from a larger quantity into a fixed shape. From κολοβόω, to shorten, diminish, mutilate, the English call collops little pieces of pork, cut from a whole flitch for sudden use. Indeed, any small piece of meat is called so.

units.la: Κῦμα, κύημα, partus, conceptus. Anglis, a qualme, deliquium animi quoddam, quale parturientibus usitatum. Possit etiam ex κάμνω; ut alterum faint- neffe, ex Latino, fatigo, vel fatisco. Sed illud magis probo. Hinc etiam squa- mish, qui delicato & fastidioso laborat stomacho.
units.tr: Κῦμα, κύημα, a birth, a conception. In English, a qualme: a certain faintness of the spirits, such as is common to women in labour. It might also come from κάμνω, as the other word faint-neffe (faintness) comes from the Latin fatigo or fatisco. But I prefer the former. Hence also squamish, for one who suffers from a delicate and fastidious stomach.

units.la: Κεχύμβη, brassica, fastidium parere solita, unde proverbium, Crambe bis costa: Græci dicunt; Δὶς κεχύμβη δὶς αὐτὸ. Hinc puto Anglicum, to cramme. Alioquin ex χοῖω, unde κεχορτιμένος, satiatus, ducerem. Facit tamen ad priorem rationem, quòd Bœotos κεχύμβω, pro χοῖει dixisse, notat ex Athenæo. Euftathius.
units.tr: Κεχύμβη, cabbage, which is wont to cause disgust; hence the proverb Crambe bis costa, which the Greeks say as Δὶς κεχύμβη δὶς αὐτὸ (cabbage twice, the same thing twice). Hence I think comes the English to cramme. Otherwise I would derive it from χοῖω, whence κεχορτιμένος, satisfied. It favours the former explanation, however, that the Boeotians are noted by Athenaeus as having said κεχύμβω for χοῖει. Eustathius.

units.la: Κάμπτω, curvo, inflecto. Anglis, to crumpe. Unde, crump-legg'd: crumpshouldred, &c. to crumble aliud, quod ex crumme, mica. Καμπή, flexura, curvamen. flexus artuum, articulus, nodus, suffrago. Angl. crampe, spasmus. Krimpen, Belgis, contrahere, quæ propior origo merito censeatur. Sed hoc ipsum ex Græco κάμπτειν, cùm flectendo res contrahantur: aut certè ex χείμπτω, appropinquare facio, admoveo. Sed & τὸ crtpple, mancus, claudus; ab eodem, ni fallor, κάμπτω.
units.tr: Κάμπτω, to bend, to bow. In English, to crumpe. Whence crump-legg'd, crumpshouldred, and so on. To crumble* is another word, from crumme, a crumb. Καμπή, a bending, a curvature; the bend of the limbs, a joint, a knot, the hock. English crampe, a spasm. The Dutch krimpen, to contract; this is deservedly regarded as the nearer origin. But this itself comes from the Greek κάμπτειν, since things are contracted by being bent; or certainly from χείμπτω, to bring near, to move towards. But also crtpple, maimed, lame: from the same κάμπτω, unless I am mistaken.

units.la: Κρώβυλοι, cincinni, crines intorti: puerorum proprie. Hodie, curled bapre: olim crul, ut ex Chaucero notatum quibusdam. Sed & crocks olim pro cincinnis usurpatum notant iidem.
units.tr: Κρώβυλοι, curls, twisted locks of hair, properly those of children. Today curled; formerly crul, as some have noted from Chaucer. But the same authors note that crocks was also once used for curls.

units.la: Κόβαλος, παντόρφος, χαχῶς, quasi χαχοβυγαχόβαλ, ut quidam volunt: maleficus, vafer, &c. Anglis, goblins, mormolucii nescio cujus nomen, quo infantes terrere solent: ex Græcâ haud dubiè origine. Antiquitas hujus notionis & usus, futilem eorum conjecturam arguit, qui ex Italâ Gnibellinorum factione ortum crediderunt. Joannes Meletius in Epistolâ ad Georgium Sabinum, de religione & sacrificiis veterum Borussorum: Eadem gentes (inquit) colunt spiritus quosdam visibiles, qui lingua Rutenicâ coltky, Græcâ Coboli, Germanicâ Coboldi vocantur. Hos spiritus credunt habitare in occultis ædium locis, vel in congerie lignorum: nutriúntque eos lautè omni ciborum genere, eò quòd afferre solent nutritoribus suis frumentum ex alienis horreis furto ablatum. Hactenus ille.
units.tr: Κόβαλος, παντούργος, κακῶς (mischievous), as if from κακοβυγαχόβαλ, as some hold: a malefactor, a cunning fellow, and so on. In English, goblins: the name of some bogey, with which nurses are wont to frighten infants; without doubt of Greek origin. The antiquity of this meaning and use refutes the futile conjecture of those who believed it came from the Italian faction of the Ghibellines. John Meletius, in his letter to Georg Sabinus on the religion and sacrifices of the ancient Prussians: The same peoples (he says) worship certain visible spirits, which in the Ruthenian language are called coltky, in Greek Coboli, in German Coboldi. They believe these spirits dwell in hidden places of the house, or in heaps of wood; and they feed them sumptuously with every kind of food, because they are wont to bring to their keepers grain stolen by theft from other people's granaries. So far he.

units.la: Κρότος, pulsus, plausus manuum pedúmve, proprie: applausus. συσσεῖν, coire, confspirare. συσσεισμός, coitio, confspiratio. Anglis, clutter, sonus inconditus, tumultus: a crue, societas, coitio.
units.tr: Κρότος, a beating, a clapping of hands or feet, properly; applause. Συσσεῖν, to come together, to conspire. Συσσεισμός, a coming together, a conspiracy. In English, clutter: an unruly noise, a tumult; from a crue, a company, a gathering.

units.la: Κρύος, frigus; κρυερός, frigidus: Anglis, cold, utrumque, frigus & frigidus.
units.tr: Κρύος, cold; κρυερός, chilly. In English, cold means both, cold and chilly.

units.la: Literarum l. & r. mutua inter se permutatio, tam tralatitia observatio, tam in omni sermone obvia, ut merito verear ne nostra in talibus diligentia lectori non uni putidior quàm gratior accidat. Nos tamen quia novum hoc & fortasse minus probabile videbitur etymon, aliquot exempla legentibus ob oculos hic ponemus: ἄλως, area; λείειον, lilium; χανθήλιον, cantherius; σάλπιγξ, frigilis; γαςτρεσών, gurgulio: Ululare, butler, urlare; παρέλυσις, palfie; χαρύοφυλλα, caryophylli flores, gillyflowers. Hæc in derivatis exempla. Sed in uno eodémque verbo sæpè alternant, ut שרשרת, & שלשלת. κρώμαξ, κλώμαξ: κλωμακός, κρωμακός, aliisque plurimis: ut Galenus Latinum cerebrum Græcè scripturus, κλέβεον, quasi perinde esset, cum litera l vel r. scriberetur, expresserit: & contrà, φέρλιον, pro Latino flagellum, Joh. II. 15. aliibque reperiatur. Sed dicet aliquis fortasse; Nonne ex Latino gelidus (quod & doctis viris, Helvidio, aliisque placuisse scimus) kalo vel colo, verso ut sæpè g. in c. promptior & paratior Etymologia? sanè, si sonum spectemus, quin gelidus
units.tr: The mutual interchange of the letters l and r is so commonplace an observation, and so common in all speech, that I fear my care in such matters may seem more tedious than welcome to more than one reader. Still, since this etymology will seem new and perhaps less probable, I will set out here a few examples for the reader's eye: ἄλως, threshing floor; λείριον, lily; χανθήλιον, gelding; σάλπιγξ, trumpet (frigilis); γαστρεών, gurgulio (gullet). Ululare, butler, urlare; παράλυσις, palfie; χαρύοφυλλα, carnation flowers, gillyflowers. These are examples from derivatives. But in one and the same word they often alternate, as שרשרת and שלשלת. κρώμαξ, κλώμαξ; κλωμακός, κρωμακός, and many others: as Galen, when about to write the Latin cerebrum in Greek, expressed it as κλέβεον, as if it made no difference whether the letter l or r were written; and conversely, φέρλιον for the Latin flagellum, is found in John 2:15 and elsewhere. But someone may perhaps say: is not the more ready and convenient etymology that gelidus (which we know also pleased learned men such as Helvidius) becomes kalo or colo, changing the g into c, as often happens? Certainly, if we look at the sound, I would not deny that gelidus...

units.la: [Marginal notes are not legible in the scan.] gelidus fit propior origo, non ego negaverim : si vero significationem, non fine causâ Græca præferatur. Aliud enim, quamvis affinia, gelidum ; aliud frigidum. At commendat Latinam origine vox etiam frigidus, ex quâ quis dubitet quin τὸ ψυχρὸν manaverit? ego vero dubito, & ex Græco φείκω, quod horrorem frigoris (& inde timoris : quamvis hoc usitatius :) proprie significat, potiùs duxerim. Tres gradus frigoris in febricitante Alex. Aphrodisæus (ut doctissimus hîc ex illo Stephanus) constituit : ἀπυρέτωσιν, φείκω & ψυχρὸ : ex utrovis horum posteriorum, quibus intensum frigus indicatur, φείκω vel ψυχρὸ, τὸ ψυχρὸν, duci potest : ut & Latinum frigidus. At Græcam commendat originem vox tōarme, calidus, è Græcâ θερμὸς ; quod non nobis sic visum primis. Eò autem magis aliis ita statuentibus assentimur, quòd literam illam aspiratam θ in derivatis haud raro excidere non uno exemplo didicimus: vide in αἰθέω, &c. Sed & Latinos ex hoc ipso θερμός, olim finxisse formas; notant docti viri. Cur non & Angli veteres suum tōarme ; quòd non magis, quàm illud Latinum, ab origine suâ recedit?
units.tr: Gelidus may be the nearer origin, if we look at the sound, and I would not deny it; but if we look at the meaning, the Greek is not without reason preferred. For gelidum and frigidum, though related, are different things. Yet the word frigidus also commends a Latin origin, and who would doubt that it came from τὸ ψυχρὸν? I do doubt it, and would rather derive it from the Greek φείκω, which properly means the shuddering of cold (and so of fear, though this use is more common). Alexander of Aphrodisias (as the learned Stephanus notes) lays down three degrees of cold in a feverish person: ἀπυρέτωσιν, φείκω and ψυχρὸ. From either of the last two, which mark intense cold, φείκω or ψυχρὸ, the τὸ ψυχρὸν can be derived, as can the Latin frigidus. But the Anglo-Saxon tōarme, warm, commends a Greek origin, from θερμὸς; this did not seem so to our first authors. And we agree the more with those who so hold, since we have learned from more than one example that the aspirate θ often drops out in derivatives; see under αἰθέω and so on. Learned men also note that the Latins of old formed forms from this very θερμός. Why should not the old English tōarme too be derived in the same way, since it departs no more from its origin than the Latin word does?

units.la: Κοῖλος, cavus; κοίλη νεὸς, cavum navis, venter navis, carina. Hodie, the keel, proprie carina; nec aliter sumitur. olim autem, keeles, συνεχδοχικῶς, naves. Nisi tamen ista potiùs distinguenda, & τὸ keele, ut carinam significat, sit ex κοίλη: ut autem navem, ex κέλης: quod navigii genus, ex uno remigum ordine, (non ut quidam puerili errore, quòd uno remo & non duobus ageretur :) constans, ad velocitatis & praedationis usum potissimum comparatum significat.
units.tr: Κοῖλος, hollow; κοίλη νεὸς, the hollow of a ship, the belly of a ship, the keel. Today the keel properly means the keel, and is taken in no other sense. Formerly, however, keeles was used by synecdoche for ships. Unless perhaps these should rather be distinguished, so that τὸ keele, as it means the keel, comes from κοίλη, but the word for ship comes from κέλης, a kind of vessel consisting of a single row of rowers (not, as some have childishly supposed, because it was driven by one oar and not two), which was chiefly fitted out for speed and for plunder.

units.la: Κέλης, equus desultorius; ad cursum aptus. Anglis, a colt, pullus equinus: juvenis equus, quales ad cursum aptiores. Sed olim fortasse equus simpliciter ita dictus, ut mare, olim equus in genere; nunc equa tantum.
units.tr: Κέλης, a horse for leaping, fit for running. To the English it is a colt, a foal, a young horse, such as are better suited to running. But formerly perhaps the horse was simply so called, as the English mare was once used of horses in general; now it is used of the female only.

units.la: Κάρτη, praesepe, a crib.
units.tr: Κάρτη, a manger, a crib.

units.la: Κώρυκος, pera, sacculus, proprie coriaceus; ad custodienda, & circumferenda cibaria aptus; ut ex Homero patet. Crock Anglis olla in quâ coquuntur carnes.
units.tr: Κώρυκος, a pouch or small bag, properly of leather, fit for keeping and carrying food, as is clear from Homer. To the English, crock is the pot in which meat is cooked.

units.la: Κῖκκος, gallus (Hesychio:) κίκκα, gallina : chick, & chickens : pulli gallinacei.
units.tr: Κῖκκος, a cock (Hesychius); κίκκα, a hen: chick and chickens, the young of fowls.

units.la: Κύρ, juvenis, inter puerum virumque medius : qui, ut plurimùm, ferociores & petulantiores esse solent : <bl>ceoil</bl>, olim, (nunc <bl>churle</bl> :) duri agrestisque viringenii : sed & rusticus.
units.tr: Κύρ, a youth, midway between boy and man, who are usually fiercer and more wanton. The old English ceoil (now churle) meant one of a hard and rustic temper, but also a countryman.

units.la: Κυείλιος, & ... apud Homerum, de marito & uxore, qui juvenes. Saxonicè, ceozlian, ... Matth. XXII. verf. 30. ne big ne ceozlsatb on tham arrise : neque nuptum dentur in resurrectione.
units.tr: Κυείλιος, applied in Homer to husband and wife, who are young. In Saxon, ceozlian. Matt. 22.30, in the Saxon: neither marry nor are given in marriage in the resurrection, they neither marry nor are given in marriage in the resurrection.

units.la: Κόρη, & κάρη, filia, puella ; <bl>a gyrle.</bl>
units.tr: Κόρη and κάρη, a daughter, a girl; a girl.

units.la: Κόννος, menti barba, apud Lucianum. Anglis, <bl>chin</bl>, mentum.
units.tr: Κόννος, the chin of the beard, in Lucian. To the English, chin, the chin.

units.la: Κοσμὸς, ornatus nimius, affectata corporis elegantia ; <bl>comely</bl>, nitidus, elegans.
units.tr: Κοσμὸς, excessive ornament, affected elegance of body; comely, neat, elegant.

units.la: Κυίζιν, κυίνδαν (verbum Tarentinum, de quo Scal.in Virgilii Catal.) prurire, <bl>to itch.</bl>
units.tr: Κυίζιν, κυίνδαν (a Tarentine verb, on which see Scaliger on the Virgilian Catalepton), to itch; to itch.

units.la: Κνίδη, urtica ; <bl>a nettle.</bl>
units.tr: Κνίδη, a nettle; a nettle.

units.la: Κῆδος, affinitas ex nuptiis contracta : κηδεστής, affinis, socer, gener : κηδεύω, affinitatem contraho, &c. Angl. kinred, affinitas, propinquitas. Si quis tamen malit ex γνώ, συγγενής, συγγένεια. ψ&, &c. non valdè repugnem. Hispanicum, cunnado, ex cognatus, ni fallor. Cæterùm, Anglicum kind, tum genus significat, quando substantivè sumitur; tum verò, cùm adjectivè, humanum, amicum, commodum; cui non abfimile Græcum ξεινος, quod tum propinquum, tum familiarem & commodum significat: unde etiam Anglicum verbum per usitatam aphæresin duci potest.
units.tr: Κῆδος, affinity contracted by marriage; κηδεστής, a relative by marriage, father-in-law or son-in-law; κηδεύω, I contract affinity, and so on. English kinred, affinity, kinship. If anyone prefers to derive it from γνώ, συγγενής, συγγένεια, I would not greatly object. The Spanish cunnado comes, unless I am mistaken, from cognatus. Moreover the English kind, when used as a noun, means kind or race; when used as an adjective, it means humane, friendly, kindly. Not unlike this is the Greek ξεῖνος, which means both kinsman and friend, and also kindly; so the English word may also be derived from it by the usual aphaeresis.

units.la: Κάπηλος, caupo, institor, propolá, tabernarius: καπηλεύω, cauponor, &c. Anglis, ceapman (nunc chapman:) vel ceap-man: q. d. institor homo, nundinator: þecpp, vendito: Matth.xix. verf. 21. Item to chaffer, mercari; & chaffering, mercatus, nundinatio. Fortaffe & to pickle, muriâ condire, inde ortum, cùm ad caupones & id genus hominum proprie pertineat.
units.tr: Κάπηλος, a innkeeper, a pedlar, a huckster, a tavern-keeper; καπηλεύω, I trade as an innkeeper, and so on. In English ceapman (now chapman), or ceap-man, that is, a dealer, a trader, a seller; þecpp, sell (Matt. 19.21). Also to chaffer, to trade, and chaffering, trade, bargaining. Perhaps also to pickle, to season with brine, derived from this, since it properly belongs to innkeepers and that sort of men.
