units.la: Κείζω, strido, to scritch: xerý, stridor noctuæ, a scritching; a scritch- owle. An & a cricket, obstrepērum cicadæ, vel locustæ genus.
units.tr: Κείζω, I shriek; to scritch. ξερή ([xerý]), the screech of an owl; a scritching; a scritch-owl. Perhaps also a cricket, the chirping of the cicada, or a kind of locust.

units.la: Κεφαλή, caput; veteribus Anglis, <bl>cop</bl>.
units.tr: Κεφαλή, the head; to the old English, cop.

units.la: Κρύπτω, abscondo; simulo: κρύψις, absconabfconfio, fimulatio. Anglis, craff, & craftie ; vafrities ; vafer. Item a croft, o2, underoroft, κευθμὼν, i.e. locus subterraneus, &c.
units.tr: Κρύπτω, I hide; I pretend: κρύψις, concealment, dissembling, pretence. English craft and craftie, cunning; cunning. Also croft, and undercroft, from κευθμὼν, that is, an underground place, and so on.

units.la: Κενὸς, vacuus, inanis ; κενὴ κοιλία, venter vacuus. Anglis, cleane, mundus ; aliquando vacuus; ut cùm dicunt, cleane gone ; cleane riddance ; cleane teeth: Κενεαγχία, κεναγχία, vaforum vacuitas: Hippocráti, fames, inedia. Unde poteft etiam effe, ϝ κ. in h. (de quo fuprà fufè ; & mox exempla plurima:) migrante, hunger, fames, inedia.
units.tr: Κενὸς, empty, void, vain; κενὴ κοιλία, an empty belly. English cleane, clean, pure; sometimes empty, as when they say cleane gone, cleane riddance, cleane teeth. Κενεαγχία, κεναγχία, emptiness of the vessels; in Hippocrates, hunger, fasting. Hence hunger, famine, fasting, may also have come about through the change of κ into h, on which we have spoken at length above, and many examples follow soon.

units.la: Κόπτω, fcindo, to chopp: κόπτεσθαι, vexari, plangere, to chafe.
units.tr: Κόπτω, I cut, to chop; κόπτεσθαι, to be harassed, to lament; to chafe.

units.la: Καλέχω, occupare, firmiter tenere, aut amplecti ; to catch.
units.tr: Καλέχω, to occupy, to hold firmly, or to embrace; to catch.

units.la: Καλλάζω, garrire ; to chat.
units.tr: Καλλάζω, to chatter; to chat.

units.la: Κόκκω, (vel ut alii, κόκω) Atticis pro ταχύ, celeriter. Angl. quick, & quickly. Nifi tamen id conceptui propriuin: & tum fuerit à κῶφ.
units.tr: Κόκκω (or, as others have it, κόκω), among the Attics for ταχύ, quickly. English quick and quickly. Unless, however, this is more properly referred to the sense, and then it would come from κῶφ.

units.la: Κηλέω, delinio, demulceo ; to claw; Κοεῖν, i.e. νοεῖν, διανοεῖσθαι: intelligere, sentire. Verbum vetus, fed cujus apud veteres Grammaticos frequens memoria, in tradendis diverforum verborum Etymologiis, ut κοῖ​Θ, κοάλευΘ, κλέα​λΘ; λ&, ϶υοπχό&, &c. Apud Etymologicum in κοάλεμ& profertur ex Callimacho locus, ubi ita usurpatum reperitur. Habet etiam Photius in Bibliotheca sua, in derivatione verbi μἀχοᾶν, ex Helladio Byzantino. Est etiam apud Hesychium κοθεῖ pro ἀιδάνελαι, voεῖ : i.e. sentit, intelligit. Hinc fortasse fuerit & vox ἀλλόχολ&, peregrinus, incognitus: potius quàm ex πχλ&, ut vulgò tradunt. Veteribus Anglis, cuth, notus, cognitus; uncuth, (hodiéq; vulgò) incognitus, inusitatus.
units.tr: Κηλέω, I charm, soothe, caress; to claw. Κοεῖν, that is, νοεῖν, διανοεῖσθαι: to understand, to perceive. It is an old verb, and frequently mentioned by the ancient grammarians in giving the etymologies of various words. In the Etymologicum, under κοάλεμ, a passage of Callimachus is quoted in which it is found so used. Photius in his Bibliotheca also has it, in deriving a verb from Helladius of Byzantium. In Hesychius there is also κοθεῖ for ἀιδάνελαι, νοεῖ, that is, he perceives, he understands. Hence perhaps also the word ἀλλόχολ& (a stranger, unknown) comes, rather than from πχλ&, as is commonly taught. The old English cuth, known, acquainted; uncuth (still commonly used today), unknown, unusual.

units.la: Κουνῆν, i.e. συνιέναι, ἐπίσταῖς intelligere: κουνῆσι, γινώσκει, sciunt, intelligunt; to konne; Item cunning: peritus, intelligens: & inde Koning, nunc King, Rex. Sed & to kenne, videre, perspicere: the kenne of sense, judicium sensuum.
units.tr: Κουνῆν, that is, συνιέναι, ἐπίστασθαι, to understand; κουνῆσι, γινώσκει, they know, they understand; to konne. Also cunning, skilled, intelligent; and hence Koning, now King, Rex. But also to kenne, to see, to perceive; the kenne of sense, the judgment of the senses.

units.la: Κύων, praegnans: κύων, quae peperit; olim quena, vel quinde, (ut Verstegatus) uxor, vel mulier in genere. Nunc Queene, κοιλ' ἐξοχῶ regina. Sed & queane, probrosum, pro meretrice: fortasse, ex alia origine. Verstegnanus, sterilem vaccam proprie ita nuncupatam docet. Ipsum autem Kaw, pro vaccâ ex Latino potiùs per aliquantulam inversionem, & contractionem, quàm ex Græco derivem.
units.tr: Κύων, pregnant; κύων, one who has given birth. Formerly quena or quinde (as Verstegan has it), a wife, or woman in general. Now Queene, queen, par excellence. But also queane, a term of reproach for a harlot; perhaps of another origin. Verstegan teaches that a barren cow was properly so called. I would rather derive kaw, for cow, from the Latin, through some slight inversion and contraction, than from the Greek.

units.la: Κυὼν, canis; a curre; item a kennell, canum cubile, vel agmen.
units.tr: Κυὼν, dog; from curre; also kennell, a dog's kennel or pack.

units.la: Κυνίσιον, catellus; a hound: ℞ κ. in h. verso, ut suprà in κυνὸς, κυνάξιχα: & suprà, de idiotismis, multis exemplis probatum. Hic alia nunc subnectemus, ex quibus intelligi posset, quanti momenti ad veras origines expiscandas, sit talis observatio.
units.tr: Κυνίσιον, a puppy; hound. The change of κ into h, as above in κυνὸς and κυνάξιχα; and above, concerning idioms, has been proved by many examples. Here we will now add others, from which it may be understood how much weight such an observation carries for digging out true origins.

units.la: Κλέψιν, occultare, to hide.
units.tr: Κλέψιν, to conceal; to hide.

units.la: Κόνδυλος, pugnus, a hand: κονδυλίζειν, pugnis cædere; proprie: & inde fortè, to cudgel, quod sustis, pugnorum usum in tali re, præstet: ut & τὸ πύξ (pugnus:) ex Latino fustis ortum esse non improbabile. Ita Græcis πυγμὴ tum pugnum significat; tum cæstus, seu potiùs pugilatum qui cæstibus exercebatur. At knuckle, est κόνδυλος.
units.tr: Κόνδυλος, a fist, a hand; κονδυλίζειν, to strike with the fists, properly. Hence perhaps to cudgel, since a club does for such a purpose the work of fists. It is not improbable that τὸ πύξ (the fist) also arose from the Latin fustis. So for the Greeks πυγμὴ signifies both the fist and the cestus, or rather the boxing practised with the cestus. But knuckle is κόνδυλος.

units.la: Καμπὴ, flexura artuum corporis inter incedendum: ut cum Aristoteles de quibusdam animalibus, εἰς τὸ πλάτιον ἔχειν τὰς καμπὰς, id est, obliquè incedere. Angl. the bannne, popies, poples,cujus inflexione incessus instituitur.
units.tr: Καμπὴ, the bending of the joints of the body in walking; as when Aristotle says of certain animals that they have their bends εἰς τὸ πλάτιον, that is, that they walk obliquely. English the hams and poples, the hollow of the knee, by whose bending walking is carried out.

units.la: Κοίλὸν, cavum; <bl>bollotu</bl> : κοιλόφθαλμΘ, <bl>bolloτu-epeθ</bl>.
units.tr: Koilon [κοίλον], hollow; bollotu. Koilophthalmos [κοιλόφθαλμος], bolloτu-epeθ.

units.la: Κεζα, casaries; <bl>bapze</bl>.
units.tr: Kesa [Κεζα], hair; bapze.

units.la: Κεραυνὸν, asperare : κερχωδης, qui aspera est voce. Angl. <bl>barcθ</bl>, asper.
units.tr: Keraunon [Κεραυνὸν], to make rough. Kerchōdēs [κερχωδης], rough in voice. English barcθ, rough.

units.la: Κορδύλη, Suidas πᾶν τὸ ἐξέχον ἢ συνεστραμμένον, quicquid eminet, & convolutum est: ἐσκοπαλυμμένον, intectus, involutus ; a barble : crates ex viminibus textis, parietum usum ad includendos homines, pecudesve præstantes. Item, to buoble, involvere : to booub, acervare, condere : potiùs quàm ex Gal. hardes, impedimenta. Est etiam κορδύλη, ἀπελλημμα τ κεφαλῆς, involucrum capitis ; a booo, Anglis, cucullus.
units.tr: Kordyle [κορδύλη]. Suidas: whatever sticks out or is twisted, whatever is protruding and convoluted. Eskopalymmenon [ἐσκοπαλυμμένον], covered over, wrapped up. From barble: a hurdle of woven wicker, used as a wall to enclose men or valuable livestock. Likewise, to buoble, to wrap up; to booub, to heap up and store. This is preferable to deriving it from the Gallic hardes, obstacles. There is also kordyle [κορδύλη], a covering of the head, a wrapping for the head; from booo, in English, a cowl.

units.la: Καβάλλης, ἐργάτης ἵππῳ: equus operarius; caballus, Latinè: quod vilitatis habet significationem, ut ex sexcentis authorum Latinorum, & nonnullis Græcorum locis cuivis liquere potest. Tale, olitoris caballus, apud Horatium, & id genus alia, doctis viris notata. Ut qui id negant, (quod faciunt quidam Persii interpretes) miram suam in his literis infantiam prodant. Nam quod afferunt, chevalier, apud Gal. cavaliero, Italis nomina esse honorifica: perinde faciunt, ac si dicerent, queane, aut schalck, aut knave, quia olim honesta fuerint, talia nunc esse, nec aliter usurpari posse. Næ illi verborum naturam cognitam non habent qui sic disputant. Cæterum ἱππάλης, cabalus, vox origine Græca sit, an Latina, merito dubitemus. Plutarchus aliquoties usurpat; sed ille ex posterioribus est Græcis, qui à Latinis potuit accepisse. Deinde quod de Etymologiâ verbi tradunt Grammatici Græci, ex ἱππάλλω, pro ἱππάλλω, id est onera injicere: id primum ostendere debebant, ἱπ-πάλλω eâ notione reperiri. Mea tamen sic est opinio, verbum Græcum esse, & ita proprie vocatum, equum caducum & sternacem, quem Angli vulgo, a stumbling jade huncupant: vel equum vectigalem, quem ad publicos pro re natâ usus, oneribus ferendis aptum, alere cogerentur. Utramvis, usitatæ verbi καλαβάλλῳ significatione optimè conveniat. Talia autem multa sunt vetustissimis Græcis ufitata, quæ posteà exolevere: ut in superioribus ex Varrone & Plutarcho observavimus. Aliquid etiam in verbo ζάςχανς. Anglis, to bobble subsultare est: quod equi fuccuffarii, id est caballi proprium. Lucil. Succuffator tetri tardique caballi. Hobbt genus quoddam equi,ut volunt,Hybernici. Hobblers, hobbellarii, in jure Anglico municipali vocati, qui lege prædii fui equum cursorium ad publicos usus alere tenerentur.
units.tr: Kaballēs [καβάλλης], a working horse, from ergatēs hippō [ἐργάτης ἵππῳ]: a workhorse. Caballus in Latin has a sense of cheapness, as anyone can see from six hundred Latin authors and some Greek passages. Such is olitoris caballus in Horace, and other expressions of that kind noted by learned men. Those who deny this (as some commentators on Persius do) reveal their own remarkable childishness in these matters. As for their claim that chevalier, which in cavaliero is an Italian word, is an honorific: they are doing the same as if they said that queane, or schalck, or knave, once being honourable, are now such things and cannot be used otherwise. Those who argue like this do not understand the nature of words. But whether the word hippalēs [ἱππάλης], caballus, is of Greek or Latin origin, we may rightly doubt. Plutarch uses it several times, but he is one of the later Greeks, who could have received it from the Latins. Next, as to the etymology the Greek grammarians give, from hippallō [ἱππάλλω], for hippallō, that is, to lay on burdens: they should first have shown that hippallō is found in that sense. My own opinion, however, is that the word is Greek and properly so called: a horse that falls and stumbles, which the English commonly call a stumbling jade; or a tax horse, which men were forced to keep for public use as the need arose, fit for carrying loads. Either sense agrees well with the usual meaning of the word kalabállō [καλαβάλλῳ]. Many such words were in ordinary use among the most ancient Greeks and afterwards fell out of use, as we observed above from Varro and Plutarch. Something similar also holds for the word zaschanes [ζάςχανς]. In English, to bobble is to jolt, which is the proper motion of a jolting horse (succussarii equi, that is, of a caballus). Lucilius: "a jolting, slow hack." The hobby is, as they say, a certain kind of Irish horse. Hobblers, called hobbellarii in English municipal law, were bound by the law of their holding to keep a running horse for public use.

units.la: Kōμη, puella, filia; Anglis olim bore, (nunc toboze) meretrix. Plane ut Gallis, garce, vel garse tam puellam, quàm meretricem significat. Sed & Anglis, verùm fecundum aliam analogiam, ex hoc,
units.tr: Korē [Κōμη], girl, daughter; formerly in English bore, now toboze, a harlot. Just as in French garce or garse means both a girl and a whore. But in English also, by another analogy, from this,

units.la: Kōμη, puella, mutato, ut in multis, c.in g. factum est Angl. gitle, puella.
units.tr: Korē [Κōμη], girl, with the change of c to g, as happens in many words, English gitle, a girl.

units.la: Kαλά, contra; gainst, against.
units.tr: Kata [Καλά], against; gainst, against.

units.la: Κύκλω, circulus, orbis, rota; a wheel,
units.tr: Kyklō [Κύκλω], circle, orbit, wheel; a wheel.

units.la: Vide tamen in ειλέω supra. Καλῶς, bene ; well.
units.tr: See, however, eileō above under eilō [ειλέω]. Kalōs [Καλῶς], well; well.

units.la: Κείρω, tondeo ; to sheare.
units.tr: Keirō [Κείρω], to shear; to sheare.

units.la: Κοιλὸν, & κοίτη, lustrum ferarum, cubile, &c. a cote, (nunc cottage) tugurium.
units.tr: Koilon [Κοιλὸν] and koitē [κοίτη], a den or lair of wild beasts, a bed, etc. From cote (now cottage), a hut.

units.la: Κλάδω, neo ; κλῶθες, Parcæ, ob assiduam in nendo operam ; clotb, pannus.
units.tr: Klaō [Κλάδω], to spin; Klōthes [κλῶθες], the Fates, from their constant work at spinning; clotb, cloth.

units.la: Κιγγλίζω, crebrò movere, & agitare: κιγγλισμὸς, crebra agitatio & motio. Angl. to jangle, & jangling.
units.tr: Kigglizō [Κιγγλίζω], to move and shake often; kigglismos [κιγγλισμὸς], frequent shaking and motion. English to jangle, and jangling.

units.la: Κρέω, pulso : κρεμβάλοις κρότῳ, crembala pulsare : ἡ κιθάρα κρότῳ, citharam pulsare: κρότος, sonus qui editur cum organorum musicorum pulsatione. Item, (ut quidam interpretantur) carmina,odæ ; a crouD. Notissimum & usitatissimum instrumentum musicum, ad quod cantare & saltare solent.
units.tr: Krelō [Κρέω], to strike: krembalois krotō [κρεμβάλοις κρότῳ], to strike cymbals; hē kithara krotō [ἡ κιθάρα κρότῳ], to strike the lyre; krotos [κρότος], the sound made by striking musical instruments. Likewise (as some interpret) songs, odes; English crowd. It is a very well-known and common musical instrument, to which people are accustomed to sing and dance.

units.la: Κύσω, opprobrium : κυσὰζω, convitiari ; to chide, increpare : quod plerumque non sine opprobriis.
units.tr: Kyso [Κύσω], reproach; kysazō [κυσὰζω], to rail at; English to chide, to scold; which is usually not without reproaches.

units.la: Καλαράζω, imprecari, maledicere : solet τὸ χ in compositione contrahi, ut καλίβαλε, κάββαλε, (inde καββαλικὸς, & Lat. caballus:) καλακείτην, καλακείτην, &c: sed & coalescere, ut χ κορυφῶ, καχκορυφῶ : χ πεδίον, καπεδίον : χ μέσον, κλμέσον, &c. to curse; quasi ex καρρᾶζ, ut ex κλαπίζειν demulcere, Galli sunum carasser effinxisse memini alicubi legere. Vulgò tamen (sed non ita probabiliter) ex χαρίζεσθαι, quod aliud est.
units.tr: Kalarazō [Καλαράζω], to curse, to speak evil; in composition the chi is usually contracted, as kalibale, kabbale (whence kabbalikos, and Latin caballus), kalakeiten, kalakeiten, and so on; but it also coalesces, as chi koryphō becomes kachkoryphō, chi pedion becomes kapedion, chi meson becomes klmeson, etc. English to curse; as if from karraz, as from kalapizein [κλαπίζειν], to soothe. I remember reading somewhere that the French formed the word carasser. Commonly, however (though less probably), it is derived from charizesthai [χαρίζεσθαι], which is a different word.

units.la: Κιχάω, κιχάνω, & κίχημι, Homero usitatissima: proprie, cursu & pedum pernicitate aliquem assequor, & comprehendo: corripio. Anglis, to kick, pede ferire: Ferire, pro adsequi, vel tangere etiam Latinis usurpatum. Horatius, Sublimi feriam sidera vertice.
units.tr: Kichaō, kichanō, and kikhēmi [Κιχάω, κιχάνω, κίχημι], very common in Homer; properly, to overtake and seize someone by speed of foot and swiftness; to catch hold of. English to kick, to strike with the foot. Ferire, in the sense of to reach or to touch, is also used by the Latins. Horace: "I shall strike the stars with my lofty head."

units.la: Κυΐλ, culex, a gnatt: quod non tam remotum quàm est pavo, ex ταώς; sphinx, ex σφίγξ; & similia, quæ doctissimis viris placuerunt, & arcaniore quadam analogiâ se tuentur.
units.tr: Kylis [Κυΐλ], gnat, a gnatt; not as far removed as pavo is from taōs [ταώς], or sphinx from sphinx [σφίγξ], and similar words, which have pleased very learned men and are defended by a certain rather hidden analogy.

units.la: Καρδία, καρδίων, κυνίδες, &c. Vide suprà, ubi de Idiotismis, &c.
units.tr: Kardia, kardiōn, kynides [Καρδία, καρδίων, κυνίδες], etc. See above, where I dealt with idiomatic expressions, etc.

units.la: A
units.tr: A

units.la: Ἐλάσσω, (unde λέκτος, lectus: ἀλέκτωρ: & κλαλαξίων. &c.) jacere, cubare, to lie: Item, λέγω, cubare, vel jacere facio, (apud Homerum, ut & prius:) <bl>to</bl> <bl>late.</bl>
units.tr: Lecho [λέχω] (whence lectus, a bed; alector, a cock; and klalaxion, etc.): to lie, to recline. Also lego [λέγω], to make to lie down or to lay down (in Homer, and as above): English to lie.

units.la: Λάκω, lingo; <bl>to lick.</bl>
units.tr: Lakō [λάκω], to lick; English to lick.

units.la: Λάγνης, vel λάγνος, (quasi λάγνος) libidinósus, salax; <bl>lecherous.</bl>
units.tr: Lagnēs, or lagnos [λάγνης, λάγνος] (as if from lagnos), lustful, lascivious; English lecherous.

units.la: Λαγών,
units.tr: Lagōn,

units.la: Λαγὼν, λαγόνες, ilia, lumbi; <bl>the</bl> loynes.
units.tr: Lagōn, lagones [λαγών, λαγόνες]: the flanks, the loins; English the loins.

units.la: Λαγὼν, angiportus ; a lane.
units.tr: Lagōn: a narrow lane, an alley; English a lane.

units.la: Λέγνον, fimbria ; & in genere, (ut Hesychius explicat) τὸ ἔσχατον, quod extremum est ; a ledge.
units.tr: Lenogn [λέγνον]: a fringe, a border; and generally (as Hesychius explains) that which is extreme, the outermost edge; English a ledge.

units.la: Λόχμη, densa sylva ; & metaphoricè, crines densi. Angl. locks ; cincinni : sed & λοξὸς, obliquus, non rectus : quod & cincinnis, sive intortis crinibus non male quadrat.
units.tr: Lochmē [λόχμη]: a thick wood; and metaphorically, thick hair, locks, curls; English locks, curls. But also loxos [λοξός], slanting, not straight; which fits the curled or twisted hair not badly.

units.la: Λαxαρὸς, laxus, vacuus, non distentus : Angl. <bl>lanck</bl>.
units.tr: Laxaros [λαξαρός]: loose, empty, not stretched; English slack.

units.la: Λίχνος, qui cupediis est deditus, liguritor, cupes, catillo ; <bl>lickerish</bl>.
units.tr: Lichnos [λίχνος]: one given to dainties, a glutton, a licker of dishes, a dish-licker; English lickerish.

units.la: Λόφος, inter alia, tumulus, collis, locus editus, <bl>a loft</bl>, & <bl>aloft</bl>.
units.tr: Lophos [λόφος]: among other senses, a hillock, a hill, a raised place; English a loft, and aloft.

units.la: Λάβρος, avidus, vorax, impetuosus ; nimius : λάβρον στόμα, os procax. Angl. <bl>lavish</bl>, <bl>a lavish tongue</bl>.
units.tr: Labros [λάβρος]: eager, greedy, violent, headlong; excessive: labron stoma [λάβρον στόμα], a bold mouth. English lavish, a lavish tongue.

units.la: Λάξ, cum calcibus ; vel ut quidam apud Homerum (λὰξ ποσὶ κυνήσας, & similibus ) interpretantur, molli pede : ἀκρῳ τῷ ποδὶ, pede extremo. Anglis <bl>lagg</bl>, tardus, postremus ; quod tamen etiam ex λήγω, cesso, desino, duci possit.
units.tr: Lax [λάξ]: with the heels; or as some interpret it in Homer (lax posi kynēsas, and similar phrases), with a soft foot; akrō tō podi [ἀκρῳ τῷ ποδί], with the extreme foot. English lagg, slow, last; though this may also be derived from lēgō [λήγω], to delay, to cease.

units.la: Λίαν, attritus, seu detritus usu.
units.tr: Lian [λίαν]: worn, or worn away by use.

units.la: Λίαπ γλῶσσα, quo sensu Athenienfibus à lepidissimo Comico objecta, cónsulendi ejus interpretes & scholiastæ. Hadrianus Junius,vir doctissimus, lubricâ ac suaviter balbutientem linguam interpretatur. Angl.igitur,a lisping tongue; λίσπη φθογγή. Et enim tongue, Græcum quoq;ut idem vir eruditissimus pridem monuit, & nos suo loco docebimus.
units.tr: Lias glōssa [λίας γλῶσσα]: in which sense the most witty comic poet reproached the Athenians; its interpreters and scholiasts should be consulted. Hadrianus Junius, a most learned man, interprets it as a slippery and sweetly stammering tongue. English, therefore, a lisping tongue; lispē phthongē [λίσπη φθογγή]. For tongue is also Greek, as that most learned man long ago observed, and we shall show in its place.

units.la: Λαγχάνω, fortior, fortitò obtineo: τὸ λαχὸν, quod forte obtigit: λαχμὸς, fors, luck & luckie: quanquam dubito utrum ex eâdem sint origine: & non potiùs luckie, fit ex λευκὸς, candidus, albus; dicunt enim Græci, λευκὴ ἡμέρα, fœlix & faufta dies: Angli, a luckie day.
units.tr: Lanchanō [λαγχάνω], to obtain by lot, to attain by chance: to lachon [τὸ λαχόν], that which fell by lot; lachmos [λαχμός], chance, fortune; English luck and lucky. Though I doubt whether these have the same origin, and whether lucky rather comes from leukos [λευκός], white, bright; for the Greeks say leukē hēmera [λευκὴ ἡμέρα], a happy and fortunate day; the English say a lucky day.

units.la: Λεύσσω, video, aspicio; to looke: quod minùs remotum, quàm βλέπω; ex quo tamen prius illud doctissimi Grammatici deducunt.
units.tr: Leussō [λεύσσω], to see, to look at; English to look: which is less remote than blepō [βλέπω]; yet from this the learned grammarians derive the former.

units.la: Λύω, λύσαι, folvere; to loose: Λυσιμάχιον, herbæ nomen; Angl. loose-strife: quasi dicas, λυσιπόλιον. Vide infrà in σεφὴ. Idem λύσαι, dissolvere, refcindere, abfcindere, evertere (ut apud Homerum, λύειν πόλιν, evertere, perdere urbem, &c.) to lose, id est, perdere, amittere; losse, damnum, jactura.
units.tr: Luō [λύω], lusai [λῦσαι], to loosen; English to loose. Lysimachion [λυσιμάχιον], the name of a herb; English loosestrife, as if you said lysipolion. See below under sephē [σεφή]. The same lusai also means to dissolve, to rescind, to cut off, to overthrow (as in Homer, luein polin [λύειν πόλιν], to overthrow or destroy a city, etc.); English to lose, that is, to destroy, to let go; loss, damage, forfeit.

units.la: Λείπω,
units.tr: Leipō [λείπω],

units.la: Λείπειν, relinquere, linquere, to leave. Λαὸς, turba, populus: Anglicè, letoo, improbus, flagitiosus: quales è turba plerique. Obvia philosophorum in eam rem testimonia.
units.tr: Leipein [λείπειν], to leave behind, to leave; English to leave. Laos [λαός], a crowd, the people; in English lewd, wicked, disgraceful: such as most of the crowd are. The testimonies of the philosophers on this matter are ready to hand.

units.la: Λᾶ, λᾶς, λᾶ, (pro Σέλω, Σέλας, Σέλα; apud Callimachum, Theocritum, aliósque:) volo, cupio, &c. 3 lift. Hinc autem, aut ex λεληθὸς, quod exponitur Σέλᾳ, ὁρμᾷ σπεύδειν, est, to lust: & nomen substantivum, lust: nisi quis malit ex λοίδωρ, (quod ab Hesychio exponitur ἀκρατὴς περὶ τὰ ἀφροδίσια, circa res venereas incontinens, salax) deducere. Quæ quanquam sunt valde probabilia, non tamen omittendum, λύσσα, vel λύσσα, quod apud Græcos de caninâ rabie proprium est, ad alios quoque, majores & impotentiores, (ut amoris iræve,) qualescunque affectus non raro transferri. Unde & Anglicum verbum manasse, nonnullis forte magis arridebit.
units.tr: La, las, la [λᾶ, λᾶς, λᾶ] (for selō, selas, sela; in Callimachus, Theocritus and others): to wish, to desire, etc.; 3 lift. Hence, either from lelēthos [λεληθός], which is explained as selā, hormā, speudein [σελᾳ, ὁρμᾷ, σπεύδειν], comes to lust; and the noun lust; unless one prefers to derive it from loidōros [λοίδωρος], which Hesychius explains as akratēs peri ta aphrodisia [ἀκρατὴς περὶ τὰ ἀφροδίσια], incontinent in venereal matters, lustful. Although these are very probable, we must not omit that lyssa [λύσσα], or lyssa, which among the Greeks is properly used of canine rabies, is often transferred also to other, greater and more violent passions, such as love or anger, or any affections whatever. Whence the English verb may perhaps have sprung; this will please some more.

units.la: M
units.tr: M

units.la: Μύρον, unguentum; to bcsmeere: ungere: τὸ μύρω præponitur, ut in aliis multis. Simplex igitur fuerit, to fmeere. Sed & mpze lutum ex eodem fonte ; cum τὸ μύεγμα, ex quo μύεγν ortum, flere, fluere, fundere, in genere significet, & ista vulgò confundantur. Αλείφὶν, ungere, & illinere: ἀλοιφὴ, unguentum, & tectorium, quo parietes illinantur. Ita & Latina, venenum, inficere, in utramque partem usurpantur ; & alia plurima.
units.tr: Myron [μύρον], ointment; English to besmear, to anoint: the prefix mu- is placed before it, as in many other words. The simple form would therefore be to smear. But also mire, mud, comes from the same source; since myema [μύεγμα], from which myein [μύειν] arose, generally means to weep, to flow, to pour out, and these are commonly confused. Aleiphein [ἀλείφειν], to anoint and to smear over; aloiphē [ἀλοιφή], ointment, and plaster, with which walls are smeared. So too the Latin venenum (poison) and inficere (to infect, to stain) are used in both senses; and many others.

units.la: Μυσάω, nimio humore & uligine vitior; præ nimio humore seu madore putresco : μύσηοις, vitium quod ex nimio humore & madore contrahitur ; mud, muft ; mudd̃p, mustp.
units.tr: Mysaō [μυσάω], to be spoiled by excessive moisture and damp; to rot from excessive wetness: mysēsis [μύσησις], a defect contracted from excessive wetness and damp; English mud, must; mudd, musty.

units.la: Μέλδω, liquefacio : Item macero, consumo, &c. to melt : Item, to moul-der.
units.tr: Meldō [μέλδω], to melt; also to steep, to waste away, etc.; English to melt; also to moulder.

units.la: Μιγνύεγμαι, lamentor ; to mourne.
units.tr: Mignyesthai [μιγνύεσθαι], to lament; English to mourn.

units.la: Μῶλ@-, πόλεμ@-, μάχη, σύρυβ@-, μόλ@-, bellum, pugna, turba, labor ; Angl. to mople : vulgò jungunt, cum tolle, (to motle and toile) de quo vide in ἔταλ@-.
units.tr: Mōl-, polem-, machē, syrybo-, mol- [μῶλ-, πόλεμ-, μάχη, σύρυβ-, μόλ-]: war, battle, crowd, toil; English to mople. They commonly join it with tolle (to motle and toile), on which see under etalō [ἔταλ-].

units.la: Μιγνύω, miscere ; to mingle : μίγμα, mixtio ; a mixmalh.
units.tr: Mignyō [μιγνύω], to mix; English to mingle; migma [μίγμα], a mixture; English a mixmash.

units.la: Μαεγίνω, tabefacio ; μαεγνης, vel μαεγμός, tabes ; moraine, vel morrein : lues, tabifica lues: inter pecora proprie.
units.tr: Maraino [μαραίνω], to waste away; marasmos [μαρασμός] or marasmēs, wasting disease; English moraine or morrein: a plague, a wasting plague, properly among cattle.

units.la: Μαΐνσδ,
units.tr: Mainomai [μαίνομαι],

units.la: Μαίνεσθαι, infanire ; μανία, infania ; tobe mad, madnesse : de d inferto, vide supra. Hebraeis recentioribus מלנא, μεταξυ, μανία.
units.tr: Mainesthai [μαίνεσθαι], to be insane; mania [μανία], insanity; English to be mad, madness: concerning the added d, see above. Among the later Hebrews, מלנא [malna], from the Greek mania, madness.

units.la: Μισύλλω, in minutas partes seco, in parva fruftra concido ; to mince.
units.tr: Misyllō [μισύλλω], to cut into small pieces, to chop into little bits; English to mince.

units.la: Μαλίχιος, vel μελίχιος, fuavis, manfuetus, affabilis ; metlo.
units.tr: Malichios or melichios [μαλίχιος, μελίχιος], sweet, gentle, affable; English mild.

units.la: Μαΐα, obstetrix ; a mid-wife.
units.tr: Maia [μαῖα], a midwife; English a midwife.

units.la: Μέγιστος, maximus ; greatest : de mag-ftan, & moft, in superioribus.
units.tr: Megistos [μέγιστος], greatest; English greatest: from magstan and most, in the earlier discussion.

units.la: Μηχανᾶν, excogitare; moliri, struere; to make.
units.tr: Mēchanān [μηχανᾶν], to devise, to contrive, to construct; English to make.

units.la: Μυελὸς, medulla ; marrow.
units.tr: Myelos [μυελός], marrow; English marrow.

units.la: Μόλυβδος, plumbum ; lead : Vide exempla contractorum, de quibus in superioribus egimus : & infra, in μαστροπὸς, & μαστύλλη. Item & πολύς.
units.tr: Molybdos [μόλυβδος], lead; English lead. See examples of contracted words, of which we treated above, and below under mastrōpos [μαστροπός] and mastyllē [μαστύλλη]. Likewise under polys [πολύς].

units.la: Μαντνὸν, pro magno, seu ingenti, vox (authore Plutarcho) Phrygiaca. Potuit alioquin (ut jam olim Erasmo aliisque notatum :) & Graeca merito censeri, cum etiam a Lat. infanum, pro magno usurpetur. Caeterum linguam Phrygicam ejusdem fuisse cum Graeca origine, ut quae ex illa sunt, etiam Graecae, sed quae antiquissimis temporibus obtinuit, adscribi possint, ex quorundam sententia sententiâ priùs notavimus: Anglis, maine, ingens. Utuntur & substantivè, cùm dicunt, <bl>wttb mtgbt</bl> and maine.
units.tr: Mannon [μάννον], as a word for great or huge, is Phrygian (according to Plutarch). Otherwise it could rightly be counted as Greek too (as was noticed long ago by Erasmus and others), since the Latin infanum is also used for great. Moreover, that the Phrygian language was of the same origin as Greek, so that what belongs to it may be ascribed also to Greek, but to that form which prevailed in the most ancient times, we noted earlier according to the opinion of some. English: mane, huge. They also use it as a noun, when they say with might and mane.

units.la: Μάνης, s ἁλ, servus. Aristophanes, (ut alios omittam) bis utitur; ubi Scholiastes, ὀικέτης, domesticos, exponit: ut doctiss. Stephano notatum. Græcam tamen non redolet originem: de quo alii pluribus. Anglis man, homo, vulgò pro famulo, sed ἀγλαχρηςιάνως, ut Latinis puer; & Græcis παῖς. Quidam ex Latino mas repetunt, ut Lipsius; alii ex homo. Ego ἐπίχω. Movet me tamen, quod affine, two-man ex Latino fœmina fluxisse credibile est. Quanquam magis probarem Verstegani sententiam, woman, quasi womb-man, ἐνμολογίαν, si constaret τὸ wombe, mulieris uterum proprie, non ventrem in genere apud antiquos denotasse. Regeret tamen aliquis fortasse, utcunque nomen illud tam viris quàm mulieribus commune, nihil obstare tamen, quin mulieribus ab illâ potissimum parte nomen ductum fit, in quâ præcipuum à viris discrimen, & quâ illæ maximè notabiles. Enimverò, & γαςὴρ commune utrique sexui; ad ea tamen quæ mulierum propria, sæpe transfertur : ut cum ἐν γαμεῖ ἔχῳ[?],&c. dicuntur. Cæterùm, ut nunc woman, ita wife olim,commune sexus nomen erat : quod nunc usus conjugibus addixit. Hodie, enim wife, uxor; houfe-wife, mater familias.
units.tr: Manēs [μάνης], a slave, a servant (Greek δοῦλος, which is not the same as Hebrew). Aristophanes, to omit others, uses it twice; where the Scholiast explains it as oiketēs [οἰκέτης], a household servant, as the most learned Stephanus has noted. It does not, however, smell of Greek origin; others have said more about this. English man, a human being, commonly used for a servant, but in the way the Latins use puer, and the Greeks pais [παῖς], a boy. Some derive it from the Latin mas, male, as Lipsius does; others from homo. I hold my judgment. Yet it moves me that two-man seems credibly to have flowed from the Latin femina. Though I would prefer the opinion of Verstegan, that woman is as if womb-man, an etymology from the common idea, if it were established that wombe properly denoted the womb of a woman, and not the belly in general among the ancients. Someone might perhaps reply that, however that name is common to both men and women, nothing prevents the name of women from being taken chiefly from that part in which the chief difference from men lies, and in which they are most remarkable. Indeed gastēr [γαστήρ] is common to both sexes, yet is often transferred to those things which belong to women; as when they say en gamei echō [ἐν γάμει ἔχω], etc. Moreover, as now woman is, so wife once was, a common name of the sex; which usage has now restricted to married women. Today wife means a spouse, and housewife means the mother of a family.

units.la: Μάννος, vel μάνος ( quod & μανιάκης ) κόσμος ἀπὸ Σαχάνιος, ut Theocrit Scholiastes ; genus ornamenti collaris, vel collo apti: χρυσοῦν ἕλλιον φορέσα ἐπὶ τὰς χεῖρας ἢ πεάχνλον οἱ Ταλὰ[?] : ait Polyb. ut ex illo docet hic doctissimus Stephanus. Angli hodiéque, a mane, vel maine jubam vocant equinam: quæ equi præcipuum, præcipuè si cultus accedat, ornamentum. Plinius de Leonibus : Leoni præcipua generositas, tunc cùm colla,armósque vestiunt juba. Idenim ætate contingit, è leone conceptis. Quos verò pardi generavere, semper insigni hoc carent.
units.tr: Mannos or manos [μάννος, μάνος] (which is also maniakēs [μανιάκης]), an ornament from Sachanios, as the scholiast on Theocritus says; a kind of collar, or an ornament fitted to the neck: chrysoun hellion phoresa epi tas cheiras ē peaschnlon [χρυσοῦν ἕλλιον φορέσα ἐπὶ τὰς χεῖρας ἢ πεάχνλον] (as Polybius says, and as this most learned Stephanus teaches from him). The English still call a horse's mane mane or maine, which is the chief ornament of a horse, especially if decoration is added. Pliny on lions: The lion has its chief nobility when mane and shoulders are clothed with a mane. This comes with age, in those born of a lion. Those which leopards have begotten always lack this distinguishing mark.

units.la: Mela, (præpositio:) cum : Saxonicè, mid. Eadem præpositio, quando cum accusativo construitur, sæpè (apud Homerum præcipuè :) motum significat ad locum, ponitúrque pro, πρὸς vel εἰς : ut Ζεὺς ᾧ ἐπὶ ἀκαλὴν μετ' ἀμύμονας Αἰ-θιοπᾶς (Σοφοκλῆς ζῶν [?] (id est) Jupiter enim in Oceanum ad inculpatos Æthiopas Hesternus ivit. Et, Ἀλλ' ἴσι νῦν μὴ λαὸν, proficiscere ad populum. Et, Βῆ δ' ἰμεναι μὴ ᾿Ωκ. Pervenit ad sues. Ex hac praepositione fecerunt Angli (ut Graeci ipsi ex ἀντὶ praepositione, verbum ἀντιάω, seu ἀντιάω: & similia:) verbum to meet: convenire. Unde & substantivum meet, id est, aptum, conveniens. Ita & Graecis ἀπαντᾶν, quadrare, convenire: de quo supra suo loco. Eadem praepositio genitivum regens, conjunctionis aut participationis habet significationem, Latinae cum, vel una cum respondens: μετ' ἡμῶν, nobiscum; μετ' ὑμῶν, vobiscum: vel conjunctis viribus. μετὰ Δικαιοσύνης, cum justitia; vel justitia comite, &c. Unde & compositum, μετοχὴ participatio; & verbum μετέχω, interfuim: (κατελθόντες με-τέχειν, inter juniores convertari, &c.) & interdum, μέτα (accentu retracto:) pro μέτεστι, praesens est; interest. Hinc, aut ego fallor, mate, socius, sodalis. Imitantur etiam Graecos Angli in usu hujus praepositionis, suo aster: pro
units.tr: Mela (the preposition) "with." In Saxon, mid. When this preposition takes the accusative, it often (especially in Homer) signifies motion toward a place and stands for πρὸς or εἰς, as in Zeus's journey to the blameless Ethiopians (Sophocles: "Zeus went yesterday to Ocean, to the blameless Ethiopians"), and "Go now to the people," and "He came to the swine." From this preposition the English made the verb to meet, to come together (just as the Greeks themselves formed the verb ἀντιάω from the preposition ἀντί). From it also comes the adjective meet, meaning fitting or suitable. So too the Greek ἀπαντᾶν, to fit, to agree, which I discussed above in its proper place. The same preposition with the genitive has the sense of conjunction or sharing, corresponding to the Latin cum or una cum: μετ' ἡμῶν, with us; μετ' ὑμῶν, with you; or with united strength; μετὰ Δικαιοσύνης, with justice, or with justice as companion, and so on. Hence also the compound μετοχὴ, participation, and the verb μετέχω, I take part (as in κατελθόντες μετέχειν, to mix with the younger men, and so on), and sometimes μέτα (with the accent drawn back) for μέτεστι, it is present, it is of concern. From this, unless I am mistaken, come mate, companion, and sodalis. The English also imitate the Greeks in their use of this preposition, with their aster, in place of:

units.la: Sid Ꞓiɑ: ut cùm dicunt, Ṽe is gone aster such a thing. μετ' δαῖτα, aster a dinner, i.e. to get a dinner. χρυσέον μετ' χώας, aster the golden fleece. Latini non possunt ista verbatim reddere: verbatim simul & eleganter Angli possunt. Sed hoc ad idiotismos pertinet: de quibus nos alias; (infinita enim sunt in hoc genere digna quae observentur:) aut alii, quod malo, peritiores.
units.tr: Sid: as when they say, "He is gone after such a thing," μετ' δαῖτα, after a dinner, that is, to get a dinner; χρυσέον μετ' χώας, after the golden fleece. Latin cannot render such things word for word; the English can do so both literally and elegantly. But this belongs to idioms, about which we shall speak elsewhere, since there are endless such expressions worth observing, or else to others more expert, which I prefer.

units.la: Μύθος, verbum, dictum, oratio, fabula. Hinc, ni fallor, Anglorum, mouth: Os sanè pro oratio non raro ponitur. Sed Germanorum mut, animus, ex σύμper inversionem, facit ut dubitem. Os enim pro animo saepe ponitur, ut ab eadem origine possit & Anglicum verbum esse.
units.tr: Μύθος: word, saying, speech, fable. Hence, unless I am mistaken, the English mouth, since Os is indeed often used for oratio. But the German mut, mind or spirit, derived from σύμ by inversion, makes me hesitate. For Os is often used for animo, so the English word could come from the same origin.

units.la: Μύω, claudo oculos, (subaudiendo ὀφθαλμὸς, vel ὄμματα:) claudo, seu obstruo os, (subaudiendo στόμα:) μύσις, occlusio, compressio, obstructio. Angl. to muzle.
units.tr: Μύω, I close the eyes (understanding ὀφθαλμὸς or ὄμματα); I close or stop the mouth (understanding στόμα); μύσις, a closing, compression, obstruction. English: to muzzle.

units.la: Μάσσω, pinso, subigo: misceo, φυράω (μᾶζα, ἀλφίτα πεφυρμένα ὕδατι ἢ ἐλαίῳ:) μάσμα, materiae cujusvis expressae, vel agitatae massa, vel recrementum; a mash. Μαςίνη, vel μαςίνα, lautitiæ, delicatior cibus; meat.
units.tr: Μάσσω, I knead, work up; I mix, φυράω (of barley meal, μᾶζα, mixed with water or oil); μάσμα, the mass of any material pressed or stirred, or its dregs; from mash. Μαςίνη or μαςίνα, a delicacy, a more refined food; meat.

units.la: Μασεγτὸς, ὁ ὑ ἡ, leno, vel lena; a strumpet.
units.tr: Μασεγτὸς, a pimp or procurer, male or female; a strumpet.

units.la: Μαξύλλη, lena; μαξυλλεῖον, ἰ.πορνεῖον, lupanar; a trull.
units.tr: Μαξύλλη, a procuress; μαξυλλεῖον, a brothel; a trull.

units.la: Μέλγα, ὄλον τὴ διὰ γάλακτ῾ο· ; edulium ex lacte constans. Extat apud Galenum & posteriores aliquos Græcos; sed ut Romanum verbum, non Græcum. Meursius non aliud fuisse censet, quàm quod veteres Græci ὀξύγαλα: q. d. lac acidum nuncuparunt. Mirum apud Latinos; ut hìc observat Stephanus, non reperiri. Credibile est eos istum lactis usum, quicunque fuerit, à Germanis didicisse; & inde nomen Germanum retinuisse. Quis tamen non dicat originem Germanici melcb, vel ut Angli milck, esse Græcam; ab ἀμέλγω, mulgeo? Quid enim lac aliud, quàm quod mulgendo ex animalibus exprimitur? Cæterùm monendus femel est lector, alia quoque non pauca, ut γῦνα, a gowne: ὤόιον, a bole: μέθυ meade, &c. in Meursii, viri doctissimi, Glossario Græco-barbaro reperiri, quæ Anglica quoque sunt,& ab Anglis, aut Germanis
units.tr: Μέλγα, a dish made of milk, a food consisting of milk. It occurs in Galen and some later Greeks, but as a Roman word rather than a Greek one. Meursius thinks it was nothing other than what the ancient Greeks called ὀξύγαλα, that is, lac acidum, sour milk. It is remarkable, as Stephanus observes here, that it is not found among the Latins. It is credible that they learned this use of milk, whatever it was, from the Germans, and so kept the German name. Yet who would not say that the origin of the German melch, or English milk, is Greek, from ἀμέλγω, to milk? For what is milk other than what is squeezed from animals by milking? Moreover, the reader should be warned once for all that many other words, such as γῦνα, a gown; ὤόιον, a bowl; μέθυ, mead, and so on, are found in the Glossarium Graeco-barbarum of Meursius, that most learned man. These are English as well, and came from the English or the Germans to those more recent Greeks.

units.la: ℓ Germanis ad illos recentiores Graecos pervenere. Et hactenus quidem nihil ad nos. At inter illa, si quis accuratius excutiat, nonnulla fortasse, quae utcunque posterioribus Graecis ignota, Graecae tamen originis reperiuntur. Sed istis diutius immorari, alterius & otii, & operae est, quàm quae nostra nunc est.
units.tr: They came from the Germans to those more recent Greeks. So far, indeed, this has nothing to do with us. But among those words, if someone examines them more carefully, some may be found which, however unknown to later Greeks, are nevertheless of Greek origin. But to linger over these longer belongs to a different kind of leisure and effort than the task we have now.

units.la: Mavdxus, Hefych. ὀλιγάχυς, ὀραγίως, ἐ- πυχνὰ, id est, parcè, raró: vel etiam, spissè, densè. Non dubito fore, qui Hefychium depravatum contendent, & pro ἡ πυχνὰ corrigendum esse, μὴ πυχνὰ: non spissè, vel densè. Facilis lapsus sator, & conjectura non improbabilis. Quanquam & illud dicendum, non deesse exempla vocabulorum, in omnibus fortasse linguis aliquorum, sed in Graeca non paucorum, quae contrarias res aut actiones significet: ad vulgatam autem lectionem Hefychii afferendam & illustrandam insigniter facere linguam Anglicam, quae eodem ferè & ipsa verbo mante, & meane, (quorum illud multitudinem, copiam, abundantiam; hoc, exile, tenue, rarum fignificat:) res dissimillimas exprimit. Istud autem meane, quanquam Latinum mi- nutum. nutum, & Gallicum menu, non longè abeunt: cur aliundè quis malit, quàm ex Græco μανὸς, quod rarum, non densum significat, arcessere, causam non video: μανόκαρπος, rarum ferens fructum: μανόφυλλος, non habens folia: Angli dicunt, meanlp ftozeb, vel meanlp tarnifbeb: in eandem planè sententiam.
units.tr: Mavdxus, in Hesychius: ὀλιγάχυς, ὀραγίως, ἐπυχνὰ, that is, sparingly, rarely; or also thickly, densely. I do not doubt there will be those who contend that Hesychius is corrupt, and that ἐπυχνὰ should be corrected to μὴ πυχνὰ, not thickly or densely. It is an easy slip of the pen and not an improbable conjecture. Yet one should also say that examples are not lacking of words, in perhaps all languages but in Greek a good number, which signify contrary things or actions. For bringing forward and illustrating the common reading of Hesychius, the English language does remarkably well. It has, in almost the same way, both mante and meane (of which the former means multitude, plenty, abundance, and the latter slight, thin, rare), and these express very dissimilar things. Now that meane, though it does not differ far from the Latin minutum or nutum, nor from the French menu, why one would rather derive it from elsewhere than from the Greek μανὸς, which means rare, not dense, I do not see. Compare μανόκαρπος, bearing sparse fruit, and μανόφυλλος, not having leaves. The English say meanly stored or meanly furnished, in exactly the same sense.

units.la: Μαλεσὶν, ἀλφὸν, σιάφ: (Hesych:) farina, pasta; meale.
units.tr: Μαλεσὶν [μαλεσίν], ἀλφὸν, σιάφ (Hesychius): meal, flour, paste; meale.

units.la: Μανεγω; vide suprà, ἀμανεγω.
units.tr: Μανεγω [μανεγώ]; see above, under ἀμανεγω.

units.la: Μάχη; vide suprà in γάμος.
units.tr: Μάχη [μάχη]; see above, under γάμος.

units.la: N
units.tr: N

units.la: NEω, νήθω, neo, acervo, glomero. Sunt qui νέω, neo; & νέω, glomero, diversa themata constituant, & τὸ νήθω ad prius referant. Sed aliter Hesychius, qui νήθων νλω, σιφδίων νλω exponit. Anglicè, to knitt, texere, contexere, connectere. Interdum proprie de texturæ genere, quæ duabus, aut etiam pluribus, pro operis ratione, prælongis acubus peragitur. Hoc genus an veteribus in usu fuerit, incertum est. de quo plura b. m. parens in Exercitationibus editis. Cæterum, de litera x. pro arbitrio
units.tr: Neo, nētho [νήθω]: to heap up, to wind into a ball, to spin. Some take νέω (to spin) and νέω (to heap up) as two different roots and refer τὸ νήθω to the former. But Hesychius explains it differently, as νήθων (spinning) and σιφδίων (?) . In English, "to knit"; to weave, to interweave, to connect. Sometimes it is used properly of a kind of weaving carried out with two or even more very long needles, according to the nature of the work. Whether this kind was in use among the ancients is uncertain. My late father discussed it at length in his published Exercitationes. Otherwise, concerning the letter x, prefixed or omitted at will, we have said more in our De lingua Hebraica.

units.la: trio trió præpositâ, vel omissâ, plura nos in De linguâ Hebraicâ.
units.tr: (The continuation of the note on the letter x, prefixed or omitted at will, is found in De lingua Hebraica.)

units.la: Z
units.tr: Z

units.la: Ξιφος οξιφος ; a Knife. Vide supra.
units.tr: Xiphos [ξίφος], oxiphos [ὀξίφος]: a knife. See above.

units.la: Ο
units.tr: O

units.la: Ὄρνις, avis, in genere, quævis. Interdum speciali͏ùs, de gallinaceo genere, a heme, Anglis, avis ardea : hen, gallina.
units.tr: Ornis [ὄρνις], a bird, in general, any bird. Sometimes more specifically, of the kind of fowl: in English "heme", a heron (avis ardea); "hen", a hen (gallina).

units.la: Οἶκος, vel ... ; tectum, culmen ; a roofe.
units.tr: Oikos [οἶκος], or ...: a roof, a ridge; in English, a roof.

units.la: Ὀλολυγμα, & ὀλολυγμὸς, lamentatio, ploratus, planctus ; a dirge : scio vulgò ex solemni in his (ut aiunt) sacris verbo dirige originem repeti. Quàm probabiliter id dicatur, melius judicarem, si ante oculos illæ formulæ: Nam quòd ad Deum dirigantur istæ preces, nimis id dilutum est, cùm non illæ magis, quod sciam, quàm quævis aliæ: Præterea movet me, quòd in nullâ aliâ linguâ his sacris inditum ab hoc dirige nomen reperiam.
units.tr: Ololygma [ὀλολυγμα] and ololygmos [ὀλολυγμὸς]: lamentation, wailing, lament; in English, a dirge. I know it is commonly said that the word is traced to the solemn word dirige ("direct"), used in these rites, as they say. I would judge better how probable that claim is if those formulas were before my eyes. For that these prayers are directed to God is far too diluted, since, so far as I know, they are no more so than any other prayers. Moreover, it strikes me that I cannot find this name dirige given to these rites in any other language.

units.la: Ὀρθρος, diluculum, tempus antelucanum, proprie ; rath, rathest.
units.tr: Orthros [ὄρθρος], daybreak, the time before dawn, properly; in English, "rath", "rathest".

units.la: Ὀνχὴ, [?]
units.tr: Onchē [ὀγχή], [?]

units.la: ὄγκὸς, pondus, vis; a bulcke : de quo vide infrà, in ῥάμψ.
units.tr: Ongkos [ὄγκος], weight, force; in English, "bulk". On this see below, under rhamps (ῥάμψ).

units.la: ὄφρὺς, supercilium : τὰς ὀφρῦς συνά-γῃ, supercilia contrahere. Angli uno verbo,to frowne : sed & brow, frons, supercilium, ab eâdem origine, cùm & de monte quoque dicant Angli, the brow of a hill : ut Græci, ὀφρὺν Ϝ ὄφρυς.
units.tr: Ophrys [ὀφρῦς], eyebrow: "to contract the eyebrows" (τὰς ὀφρῦς συνάγειν). The English say "to frown" in one word. But also "brow", forehead, eyebrow, from the same origin, since the English also speak of the brow of a hill, just as the Greeks say ὀφρὺν (the brow) for ὄφρυς.

units.la: Οἰκοφυὴς, domi natus; & educatus; verna, vernaculus. Πάντυ σφόδρα οἰκοφυὴς, apud Platonem, genuinus Atheniensis, sermone ( de sermone enim quæstio ibi proposita ) & natalibus : peregrino & externo oppositus. Ita & vernaculus apud Latinos, non eum tantùm qui domi natus est significat, sed qui urbanam vitam totus colit, ruris & peregrinationis expers. Apud Senecam vagus atque erro, vernaculis opponitur : De Benef. VI.c.XI. Idem Epist. LI. vernam & urbanam conjungit, & montanis opponit. Anglis, a cockney ; qui in urbe natus, raro aut nunquam foras extra natalitia pomœria pedem extulit, rerum omnium, præterquam urbanarum, plane expers, & ex merâ insolentiâ stultus & incredulus admirator. Ut autem verna, (unde vernilitas) & vernaculus
units.tr: Oikophyēs [οἰκοφυής], home-born, and brought up at home; native, homebred. "Pantu sphodra oikophyēs" in Plato means a genuine Athenian, in speech (for the question there concerns speech) and by birth, opposed to foreign and outlandish. So also in Latin vernaculus means not only one born at home, but one who lives wholly the city life, without experience of the countryside and of travel. In Seneca, wandering and straying (vagus atque erro) is set against the homebred: De Beneficiis VI, c. XI. In Epistle LI he joins verna and urbana and sets them against the mountain folk. In English, a "cockney": one born in a city who has seldom or never stepped outside the boundaries of his birth, wholly ignorant of everything except city matters, and through sheer inexperience a foolish and credulous admirer. But as verna (whence vernilitas) and vernaculus

units.la: apud Latinos pro ἀρέσκω sæpè sumitur (ut ad Antoninum dicebamus) qui verborum blanditiis & quæstioribus, sed & putidioribus officiis gratiam hominum captat; ita & Græcum οἰκονόμος usurpatum olim videtur; quamvis hujus usus & notionis, nisi apud Antoninum Imperatorem, nulla nunc quod sciam, superstunt exempla. Apud illum enim Primo De seipso, ἐαυτὸν & οἰκονομίας in eam sententiam conjuncta: quanquam nos aliter quoque, quòd ejus usus deerant exempla, interpretari ibi conabamur. Sed jam puto me in Anglica lingua reperisse. Illis enim, to cogge, est adulari, blandè & verniliter alloqui: a cogger, ἀρέσκος, adulator: quæ quidem ex fonte Græco manasse nullus dubitò.
units.tr: among the Latins is often used for ἀρέσκω [areskō, to please] (as we said in the note on Antoninus), of one who courts men's favour with flattering words and more artful, though also more contemptible, services; so the Greek oikonomos seems once to have been used in the same way, though no examples of this use and meaning survive now, so far as I know, except in the Emperor Antoninus. For in his first book To Himself (De seipso), heauton [ἐαυτὸν] and oikonomias are joined to this sense; although I also tried there to interpret them otherwise, since examples of that usage were lacking. But now I think I have found it in the English language. For they have "to cogge", which means to flatter, to address someone with blandishment and servile fawning; "a cogger", areskos [ἀρέσκος], a flatterer. No one doubts that this word flowed from a Greek source.

units.la: Ὀπτάζω, inspicio, inspecto: ὀπτατής, visor, speculator; to peep.
units.tr: Optazō [ὀπτάζω]: I look at, I examine; optatēs [ὀπτατής], a watcher, a spy; in English, "to peep".

units.la: Ὀπίζω, porrigo, extendo: τὰς χεῖρας ὀπίζειν: manus porrigere, tendere. Item ὀπίζω, porrigo, alio sensu, pro præbeo; seu porrectâ & tensâ manu præbeo. Angli, levi soni discrimine, sed ut idem verbum agnoscas, prius, to streach: posterius, to reach, dicunt. Sed & Græci in quibufdam literas σ, præponunt; ut ἐρύβ&, ρεύβ&, &c.
units.tr: Opizō [ὀπίζω]: I stretch out, I extend; tas cheiras opizein [τὰς χεῖρας ὀπίζειν]: to stretch out the hands. Also opizō, in another sense, I offer, or I give with an outstretched and extended hand. The English say, with a slight difference of sound but so that you recognise the same word, "to stretch" for the former and "to reach" for the latter. The Greeks, too, put a sigma before some letters, as in ereubō and reubō and so on.

units.la: Οὐνάω, vulnero; <bl>to wound.</bl>
units.tr: Ounaō [οὐνάω]: I wound; in English, "to wound".

units.la: 'Οἰχάζω, fimplex; ex quo compositum ἐνοχάζω, quod exponit Hefychius, τὰ παιδία ἢ χερσὶν ἀνασείειν, infantes manibus certo ritu agitare, vel quatere: de quo ritu plura viri docti ad Perfii, Tunc manibus quatit, &c. to rock, cunas agitare.
units.tr: Oichazō [οἰχάζω], the simple form, from which the compound enoichazō [ἐνοχάζω] is made, which Hesychius explains as "to shake infants with the hands" (τὰ παιδία ἢ χερσὶν ἀνασείειν), that is, to rock babies with the hands in a set manner; learned men have said more about this custom in their notes on Persius' Tunc manibus quatit, and so on. In English, "to rock", to rock a cradle.

units.la: 'Οὔλω, folum, pavimentum, terra. Anglis, threshold, eft limen domus: quod compositum reor, ex Ἰσθ, (Anglice, ex Græco, θύρα:) & ἔδαφος: q.d. pavimentum januæ. Eft enim pars inferior januæ, folo proxima; fuperliminari oppofita.
units.tr: Oulō [οὖλω], floor, pavement, ground. In English, "threshold" is the sill of a house. I think this is a compound of isth- (from the Greek thyra, door) and edaphos [ἔδαφος], floor; that is, the pavement of the door. For it is the lower part of the doorway, nearest the ground, opposed to the lintel above.

units.la: Οὔρῳ, (vox Homero familiaris; pro quâ pofteriores φυλάσσω maluerunt:) cuftos: ἀρέω (ex alia tamen hoc origine:) curare, cuftodire. Anglis, ward, warden; cuftos, quod etiam, ward, &c. Olim waren, cuftodire, de quo Notæ ad Williramum, p.11. Item hodiernum warie, cautus, fedulus, follicitus. Item, to beware, cavere, præcavere.
units.tr: Ouro [οὔρῳ] (a word familiar to Homer, for which later writers preferred phylassō): a guardian; aireō [ἀρέω] (though from a different origin): to care for, to guard. In English, "ward", "warden"; a guardian, which in English also is "ward", and so on. Formerly "waren", to guard, on which see the notes to Williram, p. 11. Also the present-day "wary", cautious, diligent, anxious; also "to beware", to take heed, to guard beforehand.

units.la: Οἴρῳ, ftimulus, &c. (unde compofita, sita, διςεχμανὴς, διςεχμαλὴξ, &c.) fo stirre: incitare, irritare.
units.tr: Oirō [οἴρῳ], a goad, and so on (whence the compounds diskhemanēs, diskhemalēx and so on): in English, "to stir": to incite, to provoke.

units.la: Οἰεν, putare ; fo tweene : olim, tweenan : οἴνος pro sοχνσσοφία, a tweening, vel ever-tweenting.
units.tr: Oien [οἴεν], to think; in English, "to tween": formerly tweenan. Oinos [οἶνος] for sophia...: "a tweening", or "ever-tweenting".

units.la: Ὀλλω vel ἀλέω, ἀλέσαι: perdere, amittere : ἀλέσαι ϯ λαὸν, perdere vel pessundare populum : ἀλέσαι ϯ πατέρα, amittere patrem : id est, desiderare. Angli pariter : fo loose, perdere, & amittere. Vide suprà in Ἀνὼ.
units.tr: Ollō or aleō, aleasai: to destroy, to lose; aleasai laon [ἀλέσαι λαὸν]: to destroy or ruin the people; aleasai patera [ἀλέσαι πατέρα]: to lose a father, that is, to miss him. The English likewise: "to loose", to destroy, and to lose. See above under Anō.

units.la: Ὁμιλία, colloquium, commercium, confabulatio. Veteribus Angl. mallus, colloquium, parliamentum, conventus. Sed & hodiernum meale, hinc quoque fortasse procedit, quòd ad capiendum statis horis cibum plures simul convenirent: unde & Græcum κοινὴ, cœna.
units.tr: Homilia [ὁμιλία]: conversation, intercourse, talk. To the old English, mallus meant conversation, parliament, assembly. The present-day "meale" perhaps also comes from this, because several people gathered together at fixed hours to take food; whence also the Greek koinē, supper.

units.la: Ὀβελὸς, ex quo diminutivum ὀβελίσκος, quod à Polluce exponitur lamina ensis, (Galli vulgò, lame d'espee: est autem lamina quoque verbum Græcum, ἔλασμα, vel ἐλαμίνη, ut docti norunt) & ita apud Polybium reperiri tradunt: Angli, a blade.
units.tr: Obelos [ὀβελὸς], whence the diminutive obeliskos [ὀβελίσκος], which Pollux explains as the blade of a sword (the French commonly say lame d'épée; lamina is also a Greek word, elasma or elamine, as learned men know). They say it occurs thus in Polybius. In English, "a blade".

units.la: Ὀαῤῥ, (& ὄος) uxor : ὄαρες, γυναῖκες ; uxores, mulieres : Item confabulationes, colloquia, consilia : [?]αείζω, confabulor, colloquor. Unde verbale [?]αμιστὴς, confabulator: [?]αειμὸς & [?]αειςὶς, confabulatio, colloquium : [?]πολέμα [?]αειςὶς, apud Homerum, conversatio & commercium cum bello ; id est, lex belli. & [?]αειςάν, apud Hesych. [?]μάχη, pugna, exponitur. Ex his puto patet origo Anglici warre, pro bello. Quanquam enim dubium sit hoc Hesychii postremum, & fortasse mendosum sit : notum tamen est, uxores & mulieres præcipuam belli occasionem fuisse. quod & Homerus tum alibi toto suo poemate, tum his inter alia verbis paucis docet, Ἀν-[?]δ̓ρῶν μαχομένοις [?]ολέων ἕνεκα σφετέρων. Rapi quoque uxores olim solitæ, nec aliæ faustiores, quàm quæ sic comparcarentur, creditæ. Ut monomachias & singularia certamina omittam, uxorum & mulierum causâ, nullo non sæculo, frequentissima. Quid quod etiam enses [?]ξίφες exponuntur ab Hesychio ? Certè [?]τὸ ξίφος, vel ut alii [?]ξιφος, neutrum, ensem apud Homerum sæpè significare, nemo dubitat, & obvii loci, qui probent, plures. Cæterùm, etiam ab [?]ἄρης, Mars, bellum, ferrum, ? warre, non improbabilis origo: sed nos quod maximè probaremus, indicavimus.
units.tr: Oar [ὄαρ] and oos [ὄος], wife; oares [ὄαρες], women, wives; also talks, conversations, counsels; oaizō [ὀαίζω], I converse, I talk. Whence the verbal noun oaristēs [ὀαριστής], a talker; oarismos and oarisis, conversation, talk. In Homer, oaristys [ὀαριστύς] is conversation and commerce with war, that is, the law of war. And oaizein in Hesychius is explained as battle [μάχη]. From these, I think, the origin of the English "warre", for war, is clear. Although the last of Hesychius' glosses is doubtful and may perhaps be corrupt, it is well known that wives and women were the chief occasion of war. Homer teaches this both elsewhere throughout his whole poem and in these few words among others: "Of men fighting for the sake of their own cities" (Andrōn machomenōn poleōn heneka sphetearōn). It was also customary of old to carry off wives, and it was believed that no other women were more fortunate than those so won. To omit single combats and duels, they have been most frequent for the sake of wives and women in nearly every age. Why, Hesychius even explains xiphē [ξίφες] as swords! Certainly nobody doubts that xiphos, or as others say xiphos, neuter, often means a sword in Homer, and there are several passages that prove it. Moreover, a not improbable origin of "warre" is also Arēs [ἄρης], Mars, war, iron; but what we would most favour we have indicated.

units.la: Οὐδὲν, nullum, nihil; ουηθ.
units.tr: Oudēn [οὐδὲν], none, nothing; [ουηθ].

units.la: ᾽Οφις, serpens; a feend, Anglicè, (vel fiend) tum inimicus, in genere; tum speciatim, dæmon, diabolus. Harum autem duarum significationum quæ primaria, & verbi propria, non facilè dixerim. Utrumvis certè ad ὄφιν optimâ ratione referatur. De diabolo, nullus opinor Christianus monendus, cui lapsi seductíque primi parentis historia nota. At illa non nota gentilibus. Dicemus igitur ita tum nuncupatum diabolum, cum primùm diaboli natura ex sacrâ historiâ illis innotuit. Posteà, ad quosvis inimicos per exaggerationem tractatum verbum. Aut si primùm ita dicti quivis in genere inimici, quòd serpentis conspectum horrent naturâ plerique, (unde & proverbium Latinum, angue pejus odisse:) tum potest compertam ab antiquis illis Anglis diaboli naturam, & erga genus humanum malitiam; probabile fuerit, ad illum κατ' ἐξοχὴν indigitandum tractatum commune verbum, quòd nullum facilè occurreret, quod naturam ipsius meliùs
units.tr: Ophis [ὄφις], serpent; in English, "a feend" (or "fiend"), both an enemy in general and specifically a demon, the devil. Which of these two meanings is the primary one and the proper sense of the word I could hardly say. Either certainly refers best to ophis. About the devil, I think no Christian needs warning, since he knows the history of the fall and seduction of our first parents. But that history was not known to the gentiles. We shall say, therefore, that the devil was so named only once the devil's nature first became known to them from sacred history. Afterwards the word was applied by exaggeration to any enemies. Or if any enemy in general was first so called, because most people naturally shudder at the sight of a serpent (whence the Latin proverb, angue pejus odisse, "to hate worse than a snake"), then it is probable that the ancient English, having learned the devil's nature and his malice towards the human race, took up as the name to designate him above all others a common word, since none readily occurred that would express his nature better.

units.la: — (the page ends mid-sentence) meliùs exprimeret: unde & Satan Hebraeis, tum inimicum in genere quemlibet & adversarium,tum proprie diabolum comprehendit.
units.tr: ...more fully expresses it. Whence also the Hebrews' Satan covers both any enemy or adversary in general and, properly, the devil.

units.la: 'Οργὴ, ira: vide suprà in ἀγγ@.
units.tr: Orgē, anger [ὀργή]: see above under ang-.

units.la: 'Ολ@, totus, <bl>whole</bl>: ut suprà in Cambdenianis. τὸ ὅλον, interdum, (philosophis praecipuè, aut, τὰ ὅλα:) mundus: unde conjicio Anglicum <bl>woild</bl> manasse.
units.tr: Holos, whole [ὅλος]: as above under the Cambdenian words. The Greek to holon, sometimes (especially among the philosophers) or ta hola, means the world; whence I conjecture that the English "woild" arose.

units.la: 'Οτλ@, (οτλημα) labor,calamitas: οτλῶ & οτλέω, laboro; miser, aerumnosus sum. Angli, <bl>toyle</bl>; to <bl>toyle</bl>. Vide suprà in μῶλ@. Est etiam πόλη callus, qualis ex multo labore solet provenire: unde π᾽ <bl>toyle</bl> possit aliquibus arridere, sed illud verius.
units.tr: Otlos, from otlēma, labour, calamity [οὖλος, ὄτλημα]: otleō and otleō, I labour; I am wretched and troubled. The English have "toyle" and "to toyle". See above under mōl-. There is also pōlē, a callus such as commonly comes from much labour, so that "toyle" might please some; but the former is more likely.

units.la: 'Οργαλ@, pomarium, an orchard. Habuimus in Camdenianis. Sunt sanè ὀργ@ & ὀργαλ@ Homerica verba, unde tanto probabilius ad Anglos transiisse. Dubito tamen an illa vera origo. Dubitandi causa, quòd Belgae, oeft- gaerd, & ooft-gaerd; ut & boom- gaerd: & Germani, baum-gart: obf- gart: (luff-garte: paradisus:) dicunt. Unde probabile est, etiam Anglis esse verbum compositum: orch-yard, vel orch- oyeb-pard: (ut bine-pard, & wiin-gard, de quo supra :) ut τὸ οοft, & οζ, sint ejusdem, ex Graeco ὀπώρα, originis: cujus τὸ ꝛ apud Belgas, in f. emollitum, remanserit; τὸ ρ apud Anglos, q. d. ὀπωφυλάκιον, vel ὀπωρέειον. Vide in ὑρ, supra.
units.tr: Orgalos, an orchard [ὀργαλός], "an orchard". We had it in the Cambdenian notes. Indeed orgas and orgalos are Homeric words, so it is all the more probable that they passed over to the English. I doubt, however, that this is the true origin. My doubt rests on this: the Dutch say oftgaerd, ooftgaerd, and likewise boomgaerd; and the Germans baumgart, obfgart (luffgarte: paradise). So it is probable that the English word too is a compound, orchyard or orchoyebpard (as in binepard and wiingard, discussed above), so that the Greek ōpōra lies behind both the oft and the oz. Among the Dutch the r softened into f and remained; among the English the r remained, as if it were ōpōphylakion or ōpōreion. See under ὑρ above.

units.la: Π
units.tr: P

units.la: Πολὴν, πολίσαι, i.e. ἀρόσαι, arare; plow: πέλω, terra aratro versa, terra proscissa: plowed-ground.
units.tr: Polēn, polisai, that is, arasai, to plough [πολῆν, πολίσαι, ἀρόσαι]; plow. Pelō: earth turned by the plough, ploughed land; plowed-ground.

units.la: πόλω, capitis vertex, cranium, calvaria: τὸ σύμπαν, integrum caput, the pole.
units.tr: Pōlos, the crown of the head, skull, calvaria [πόλος]; to sympan, the whole head [τὸ σύμπαν]: the pole.

units.la: Πιθανὸς, disertus, gratus, jucundus, aptus ad persuadendum, (à πείθω nempe, id est, persuadeo:) pitby.
units.tr: Pithanos, eloquent, pleasing, agreeable, apt for persuading (from peithō, I persuade) [πιθανός]: pitby.

units.la: Ποικίλος, varius, discolor, maculis distinctus; speckled: ποικίλμα, a speck. Hinc quoque ni fallor, & morbi illius maculosi nomen, pocks, quo modo & Latini, sed posteriores, variolae, (Galli varioles:) ex macularum varietate indigitarunt.
units.tr: Poikilos, varied, of many colours, marked with spots [ποικίλος]; speckled; poikilma, a speck [ποίκιλμα]. Hence, I think, also the name of that spotted disease, pocks, just as the Latins, though only later writers, named it variolae from the variety of the spots (the French varioles).

units.la: πίτυλον, splenium, vel panniculus illitus: ut doctissimus Steph. ex Celso docet, quamvis apud Graecos qui nunc extant, vix eo fensu reperias. Anglis, a patch.
units.tr: Pitylon, a rag or plaster spread on [πίτυλον], as the most learned Stephanus teaches from Celsus, though among the Greeks now extant you would hardly find it in that sense. For the English, a patch.

units.la: Πίλ⊕, vel πίλ⊕, niger, fufcus; <bl>black.</bl> Idem πίλ⊕, fubniger quoque, fybfufcus, lividus, exponitur. Unde feu Gallicum, feu Anglicum <bl>blue</bl> fluxit. Angli interdum conjungunt, ut cùm de fuggillato dicunt, <bl>black and blue.</bl>
units.tr: Pilos or pilos, black, dusky [πελός, πέλος]; black. The same word is also explained as somewhat black, dusky, livid. Whence either the French or the English blue derived. The English sometimes join the two, as when of one who is bruised they say black and blue.

units.la: Πελιδνὸς vel πελίδνὸς, fanguine fuggillatus, lividus, ὑρᾳμ⊕. Angl. <bl>blood,</bl> fanguis; <bl>bloody</bl>, fanguinolentus.
units.tr: Pelidnos or pelidnos, bruised with blood, livid [πελιδνός]. English blood; bloody, full of blood.

units.la: Πλαδὸν, vel πλαδ⊕, humor fuperfluus: nimia humiditas: πλαδώδης & πλαδαρὸς, uliginofus, udus; <bl>a plash,</bl> <bl>plafhe.</bl>
units.tr: Pladon or pladōn, superfluous moisture, excessive wetness [πλαδὸν, πλαδῶν]; pladōdēs and pladaros, muddy, wet [πλαδώδης, πλαδαρός]: a plash, plashe.

units.la: Παῖς, puer, <bl>a bop.</bl>
units.tr: Pais, a child, a boy [παῖς]: a bop.

units.la: Πὲς, ποδὸς, pes, <bl>a foof.</bl>
units.tr: Pous, podos, a foot [πούς, ποδός]: a foot.

units.la: Πέδον, vel πεδίον, (quod nescio quàm bene Aristoteles alicubi ducit ex πὲς:) folum, campus, planicies, <bl>a field.</bl>
units.tr: Pedon or pedion, ground, plain, level [πέδον, πεδίον] (which Aristotle somewhere, I know not how well, derives from pous): a field.

units.la: Πέλλα, proprie, mulctra, feu vas in quod lac emulgebant. Interdum de aliis, ut catino, poculo, &c. Angl. <bl>a paile, a milk-paile.</bl>
units.tr: Pella, properly a milk-pail, the vessel into which they milked [πέλλα]; sometimes applied to other things, such as a dish, a cup, and so on. English: a paile, a milk-paile.

units.la: Παρθένος, (quod etiam παρθὲν⊕) virgo, (Παρθένος, devirgino,) a bzide. Germanicè, bzaut. bztoegrome : Germanicè, bzauttgam ; q. d. παρθενο- sάμ.
units.tr: Parthenos, also parthenon, a virgin [παρθένος, παρθένον]; of a virgin, a bride. In German, Braut; Bräutigam, as it were parthenogamos [παρθενογάμος].

units.la: Πεεισὸς vel ἀεινὸς, propriè, qui ultra cæteros aliquid habet in suo genere : eximius, præstans, insignis. pzettp, insignis ; sed de parvo proprie, aut in parvis rebus : in magnis, p;ouo, superbus : Item spzuce, elegans, insignis: Item pert, acer, vegetus: malapert, superbus, procax, confidens, protervus ; μάλα ἀεινὸς vel ἀεινὸς : (malapertnesse, procacitas, protervia :) quod etiam apud Græcos in sequiorem partem haud raro positum reperire est. Frequentissimi inter Græcos usus vocabulum istud fuit, & latæ notionis ; ut ex libris constat, qui supersunt : apud Atticos præcipuè : ut non mirum sit tam numerosa sobole apud Anglos pullulasse.
units.tr: Peeisos or aeinos, properly one who has something beyond the rest of his kind: distinguished, excellent, outstanding [πεεισός, ἀεινός]. English pretty, distinguished, but said properly of something small, or in small matters; with great things, proud, haughty. Also spruce, elegant, smart; also pert, keen, lively; malapert, bold, saucy, insolent, confident, headstrong (malapertnesse: boldness, saucy insolence, petulance). Malista aeinos or aeinos [μάλα ἀεινός]. This too is found among the Greeks not rarely used in a worse sense. The Greeks used this word very frequently and in a broad sense, as the surviving books show, especially the Attic writers; so it is no wonder that it sprouted with so numerous an offspring among the English.

units.la: Πυθμὴν, ἐν Θ-, fundus, imum. Angli totidem ferè literis (neque enim literæ affines b. & p. Item t. & th. in hoc argumento pro diversis habendæ:) a bottom. Scribitur vulgò, bottome : sed ε. illud finale otiosum est.
units.tr: Pythmēn, in Th-, the bottom, the lowest part [πυθμήν]. The English, with almost the same letters (for b and p, and t and th, are not to be regarded as different in this matter): a bottom. It is commonly written bottome, but the final e is superfluous.

units.la: Πύελος,
units.tr: Pyelos [πύελος].

units.la: πνέλῳ, labrum balneatorium: vas quodvis majus, sed ligneum, proprie; Idem πνέλῳ vel πνελὶς, σφυδόνη: pala annuli. Anglis, (ita reperio:) nescio unde, nisi hinc, a beztll.
units.tr: Pnelō, a bathing-tub [πνελῷ]: any larger vessel, but properly of wood; the same pnelō or pnelis, sphydonē: the plate of a ring [σφυδόνη]. For the English (so I find) a bezel, I know not whence, unless from this.

units.la: Πηλὸς, lutum, coenum; pudble.
units.tr: Pēlos, mud, dirt [πηλός]; puddle.

units.la: Πυσαείζιν, Hesych. exponit, μὴ ἀνέ-χεσθαί τῆν, ἀλλ' ἀπωσπάζειν: χαλεπαίνειν: id est, ex impatientia & indignatione refilire, molestè ferre. Angli de tumultuante dicunt, to keep a pudder. Affinis vox χολυδυνλίζω, quam Hesychius exponit, θυμῶδες: irasci, indignari, to grunt.
units.tr: Pysaeizin, which Hesychius explains as not to endure it but to thrust it away: to be angry; that is, to flare up from impatience and indignation, to take it ill [πυσαείζειν]. The English say of one who makes a commotion, to keep a pudder. A related word is cholydynlizō, which Hesychius explains as full of wrath: to be angry, to be indignant; to grunt.

units.la: Πεδάζω, vel πεδάω, impedire, ligare; to bînde: πέδη, pedica, vinculum, a bond.
units.tr: Pedazō or pedaō, to impede, to bind [πεδάζω, πεδάω]; pedē, a fetter, a bond [πέδη]: to bind, a bond.

units.la: Πλάσσω, formo; creo, compono, fingo, effingo; to plott.
units.tr: Plassō, to form; to create, compose, feign, mould [πλάσσω]: to plott.

units.la: Παίζω, ludo; to play.
units.tr: Paizō, to play [παίζω]: to play.

units.la: Παίω, Graecus Aristophanis Scholia-stes: τὸ παίζειν λέγεται, τὸ παῖν ἐπῶν συμβόλων παίειν, id est, τὸ παίζειν, proprie, quidvis expedite facere. Angli similiter, to plg. Suspicetur aliquis fortasse ex Latino, applicare. Sed longè alia syntaxis: Dicunt enim Latini, „applicare animum ad aliquid: Angli, to applp the mind. At hoc aliter, to plp bis booke: ut Græci, πα[?]ίφ Ꞩεωείαν; to plp bis meat: quemadmodum illi, πα[?]ίφ ἡ μάζαν,&c. Πα[?]ίφ Græcis, speciatim quoque, ferire, cædere, malè multare; certè & Angli, to pap, similiter. Quòd si proprium eit, non dubium quin hinc fit. Si metaphoricum, alia ratio. Cæterùm in verbis Scholiastæ, pro σωλόμως, rectum fortasse, σωλόνως: quod vim verbi Anglici, fortasse & Græci, melius exprimat.
units.tr: Paiō: the Greek scholiast on Aristophanes says: "paizein is said of ...", that is, paizein properly means to do anything quickly [παίω]. The English likewise say to ply. Someone might perhaps suspect the Latin applicare, but the syntax is quite different. The Latins say applicare animum ad aliquid; the English say to apply the mind. But they say otherwise to ply his booke, as the Greeks say paiō tēn biblon; to ply his meat, as those others say paiō tēn mazan, and so on. Paiō in Greek also means, specifically, to strike, to beat, to punish severely; and the English to ply likewise. If that is the proper sense, there is no doubt that the English word comes from this. If it is metaphorical, the explanation is different. Moreover, in the scholiast's words, for sōlomōs, perhaps sōlonōs is the correct reading, which better expresses the force of the English word, and perhaps of the Greek too.

units.la: Πάλλω, vibro, quatio, agito: παλλὸς, vibratus: παλλὸν, jaculum, telum, tragula: ἀμφιπαλλὴς, qui utrinque vibratur. to pelt. Sed & πέλλη, ab Hesychio exponitur, λίθος, lapis. Dicunt autem Angli, to pelt wtth stones; lapidibus densis impetere.
units.tr: Pallō, to vibrate, shake, brandish [πάλλω]; pallos, brandished; pallon, a dart, a missile, a javelin [παλλόν]; amphipallēs, brandished on both sides [ἀμφιπαλλής]: to pelt. But also pellē, which Hesychius explains as a stone [πέλλη, λίθος]. The English say to pelt with stones: to assail with thick-falling stones.

units.la: Πήγνυμι, πηγύω, πήσω, vel πήγω: compingo: figo, defigo, depango: πηκτὸς, fixus, defixus. a pegg: paxillus. An & to pitch, defigere? nisi potiùs ex πήττω, jacio, projicio.
units.tr: Pēgnymi, pēgyō, pēsō, or pēgō: to fasten together, to fix, drive in, plant [πήγνυμι, πηγύω, πήσω, πήγω]; pēktos, fixed, driven in [πηκτός]. A pegg: a stake, a peg. Is to pitch, to fix in the ground, also from this? Unless it rather comes from pēttō, to throw, cast forth [πήττω].

units.la: Πέσσω, πέψω, (Attice & Æolicè, pro πέπτω) coquo, concoquo: πέψαι ἢ ὀργὴν, concoquere iram. Cæterùm πέψιν ἢ ὀργὴν aut πέψις ἀνύσις, (ut ex pluribus Homeri locis, quas doctissimus Steph. adducit, quale illud, ʼΑλλ' αἰὲι γυνάϰω, ᾧ κήδεα μυρία πάσχω:) dicuntur Græcis, non tantum qui iram vel dolorem planè vincunt & profligant; sed & illi, qui intra se cohibentes, hactenus cohibent, ut foras non erumpat: qui non evomunt, sed ipsi secum, quicquid iræ aut doloris est, intus taciti versant & vorant. Unde est quòd Euftachius τὸ πιέζειν, vel πιέζειν, pro κρύπτειν, vel πιέζειν, occultare, vel comprimere positum censet. Angli hoc dicunt; to pett, & pettifb.
units.tr: Pessō, pepsō (Attic and Aeolic for peptō), to cook, to digest [πέσσω, πέψω]: pepsai ēn orgēn, to digest anger [πέψαι ἢ ὀργήν]. Moreover, to digest anger or to make digestion of it [πέψιν ἢ ὀργήν, πέψις ἀνύσις], as in many places of Homer which the most learned Stephanus cites, such as, "But always endure, you to whom sorrows are countless" [ἀλλ' αἰεὶ τέτλαθι], are said by the Greeks not only of those who utterly overcome and crush anger or grief, but also of those who, holding it within themselves, restrain it so that it does not break out: who do not vomit it forth, but in silence turn over and swallow inwardly whatever anger or grief they have. Hence Eustathius thinks that piezein, or piezein, is used for kryptein, or piezein, to conceal or compress [πιέζειν, κρύπτειν]. The English say this: to pett, and pettish.

units.la: πιέζω, premo, crucio, ango: πιέζειν φθόνῳ, premere, onerare invidiâ: proprie de oneribus, aut luctatoribus dicitur, ut Stephanus docet: to pelfter.
units.tr: Piezō, to press, to torment, to distress [πιέζω]; piezein phthonō, to press down, to burden with envy [πιέζειν φθόνῳ]. Properly said of burdens or of wrestlers, as Stephanus teaches: to pelter.

units.la: Πεσιλης, verbum Homericum, pro mendico: ut, "Ως τις ξαφαλὴς ᾧ ἀναιδὴς ἐσὶ, πεσιλης: i. e. Quam audax & impudens es mendicus? Unde Ulysses πεσιλης, cognominatus. Ex quo in Meridionalibus his Angliæ partibus agere me contigit, non semel miratus sum, cum identidem janua pultaretur, respondisse famulos, aliósve indigenas, proftorem vel proftores esse (pjooters) qui pultarent. Ad hoc enim, proflorem, pro procuratore usurpatum audivetam; nunquam pro mendicb: quod hîc familiare est. Frustra labofavi ùt cauffam hujus appellationis intelligerem, donec ad Græcas originés me contuli. Placuit fateor conjectura, & parum abfuit, quin solemne illud Δρνξ, Δρνξ, præ nimio gaudio mihimet acclamare. Ne tamen Διοχία meæ nimiùm confidam facit diversa Somneri mei fagaciffimi conjectura; Habebant, inquiebat ille, olim Ptòchotrophiâ (quæ vulgò Hospitalia; q: d. ξένοδοχεία) in Angliâ suos Procuratores, per quos tum reditus, tum eleemosynas folebant colligere. Hinc factum, ut & mendici quicunque procuratores vulgi sermone nuncupati sint: Haud improbabiliter sanè, fi procuratores isti oftiatim mendicorum more domos obibant. Cogitet Lector.
units.tr: Pesilēs, a Homeric word for a beggar [πεσιλής], as in "How shameless and impudent you are, pesilēs!" [ὡς τις ξαφαλὴς ... πεσιλής]; hence Ulysses was surnamed Pesilēs. In these southern parts of England, where I happened to live, I was more than once amazed that when the door was knocked on, the servants or other natives replied that it was the proctor or proctors (proctors) who were knocking. For I had heard proctor used for procurator, but never for a beggar, which is common here. I laboured in vain to understand the cause of this name, until I turned to Greek origins. I confess the conjecture pleased me, and I came close to shouting out for joy my customary "Eureka, Eureka" [Εὕρηκα]. Yet the very sagacious conjecture of my Somner, which differs from mine, makes me less confident of it. He said that formerly in England the ptōchotrophia (commonly hospitals; that is, xenodocheia) had their procurators, through whom they used to collect both revenues and alms. Hence it came about that any beggars too were called procurators in popular speech. Quite plausibly, indeed, if those procurators used to visit the houses door to door in the manner of beggars. Let the reader consider.

units.la: Πεξένος, hospes publicus, amicus; & qui alicujus seu boni seu mali author est alicui :. προξενητής, proxeneta, pararius, qui est veluti conciliator, interpres & internuntius ad pacifcendum; seu stipulandum; a priori: fi tamen
units.tr: Pexenos [Πεξένος]: a public host, a friend; and one who is the author of some good or evil for another. Proxeneta [προξενητής]: a broker or agent, a go-between and intermediary who arranges a peace or a bargain. It is derived a priori: if, however,

units.la: Υ tamen antiquum est, & non recentioris ætatis verbum, quod aliis à veteribus libris & memoriis instructioribus indagandum relinquo. Ab eodem certè, quo pioter, cum pro procuratore accipitur, fonte fluxisse non puto.
units.tr: the word is old, and not of a more recent age, which I leave to others to trace from older books and fuller records. I certainly do not think it flowed from the same source as the word that is taken to mean "procurator."

units.la: - Πνεγ, lignorum strues, five accensa, five non accensa, sed ad usum rogi proprie. Veteres Angli peer videntur vocasse struem lignorum & lapidum mari oppositam: Unde Dover peer, aliáque. Struem lignorum vocant hodiéque a pile of wood: & ligna struere, seu componere in acervos, to pile up; an ex isto πνεγ, mutato r.in l. ut in sexcentis aliis: an ex πλέω, seu πλέω, denso, (quod quidem de lanâ coactâ proprie dicitur; ad alia tamen interdum transfertur:) condenso: judicet Lector. Piræum, nobilem illum & famigeratissimum portum Athenarum consultò hîc prætereo, quòd alienam huic loco commemorationem ejus crederem. Longè enim aliam appellationis ejus rationem reddunt veteres Grammatici. Possit tamen aliquis suspicari ex tam nobili portu ad alios quoque qualescunque ab Anglis veteribus appellationem traductam fuisse. Sed nos non tam fumus audaces.
units.tr: Pneg [Πνεγ]: a pile of logs, whether lit or unlit, but properly one for use as a funeral pyre. The old English seem to have called a pile of logs or stones "peer," as opposed to the sea, whence "Dover peer" and others. A pile of logs is still called a pile of wood today, and to stack logs into heaps is to pile up.
