Whether this comes from that Greek word, with r changed to l as in countless other words, or from pleo [πλέω], meaning dense (properly said of compacted wool, though sometimes transferred to other things), "to condense," let the reader judge. I deliberately pass over the noble and famous harbour of Athens, the Piraeus, since I think mentioning it here would be out of place. The ancient grammarians give a quite different reason for its name. Still, someone might suspect that the old English carried the name over from so noble a port to other harbours of whatever kind. But we are not so bold.

units.la: Περάλω, cujus praeter. act. πάρακα i medium, παράσα, &c.) inter alia, tracto, administro, paratii seu proxenetae munere fungor: transigo pro aliquo: ut παρέλην χάριν: παρέλην φιλίαν, &c. Anglis, a broker, proxeneta, parasitus. Est & παρέλω (pro παρῶ, vel παρόχων) ex quo praeterita, παραχά; vendidi: παραχέναι, vendidisse, &c. quomodo & Anglicum broker etiam pro institore seu propola sumitur.
units.tr: Peralo [Περάλω], from which the aorist (the middle form in the Attic manner, and so on) means, among other things: I handle, I manage, I perform the office of a go-between or broker, I carry out a matter on someone's behalf, as in "to win favour," "to win friendship," and so on. In English, a broker means go-between, agent, parasite. There is also paraslo (for paro or parochōn), from which comes the perfect "I sold" [παραχά]; "to have sold" [παραχέναι], and so on, in the same way as English "broker" is also taken to mean a dealer or retailer.

units.la: Περάλω, agere: unde Angli, ni sallor, to prate, pro nugari, fabulari, garrire. In omnibus enim linguis ista confunduntur: facta cum verbis & sermone. Ut Lat. res, ex Græco ρήσις, &c. Sed nec ἔπω, operor, ago; & ἔπω, dico, aliter quidem solo differunt spiritu.
units.tr: Peralo [Περάλω], to act. Hence the English, unless I am mistaken, "to prate": to chatter, talk idly, babble. In all languages these are confused: deeds with words and speech. As the Latin res comes from the Greek rhēsis, and so on. But epō, to work or do, and epō, to say, differ only in breathing.

units.la: Πρᾶξις, actio, factum. Angl. praxis, action, facinus; & Ietwo praxis, malum facinus. Hinc quoque ἐκ πράξεως, ut ego conjicio, quod omnis, ut vulgo dicitur, virtutis laus in actione consistat. Certe, ut plurimum, sua aut aliorum facta narrant, qui se aut alios laudant: Possimus aliquin ex Φαίνω, admonere, nere, exhortari : (laudare autem & admonere quàm sint affinia, docet vulgatum illud distichum, Qui monet ut facias, quod jam facis, &c.) vel ἀλλοτριόω, adulari, parasitare : sed illud tamen ego magis probo, quod prius.
units.tr: Praxis [Πρᾶξις]: action, deed. English praxis, action, wicked deed; and Dutch praxis, a bad deed. Hence also, as I conjecture, "from action" [ἐκ πράξεως], because all praise of virtue, as is commonly said, consists in action. Certainly, for the most part, those who praise themselves or others recount their own or others' deeds. We could also derive it from Phainō [Φαίνω], to admonish or exhort (how closely praise and admonition are related is taught by the familiar couplet, He who advises you to do what you already do, and so on), or from allotrioō [ἀλλοτριόω], to flatter, play the parasite. But I approve the former more.

units.la: Πεῖνα, fames ; πεινάω, esurio, careo, desidero, indigeo ; to ppne. Apud Aristotel. dicitur quidam, πεινᾶν ὅτι μὴ πυρέττει. Anglicè, to ppne aster a Kingdome.
units.tr: Peina [Πεῖνα]: hunger; peinaō [πεινάω]: to be hungry, to lack, to desire, to need; to pine. In Aristotle someone is said to be hungry for anything except a fever [πεινᾶν ὅτι μὴ πυρέττει]. In English, to pine after a kingdom.

units.la: Παρα-βάλλομαι, audaciâ praecipiti projectàque periculum adeo ; periclitor : παράβολος, audax, temerarius; παράβολον ἔργον, audax facinus. Hinc parabolani, in historia Ecclesiastica, alibíque, de quibus tum Scaliger alicubi, si bene meminí ; tum b. m. parens fusè. Angli, contractè, bold, audax ; boldly, audaciter. Veniebat in mentem & τὸ parleße ; nec dubitarem si veram illam scripturam constaret, ac non peerleße potiùs scribendum effet.
units.tr: Parabállomai [Παραβάλλομαι]: to expose oneself to danger by rash, headlong daring; to risk oneself. Parabolos [παράβολος]: bold, reckless; parabolon ergon [παράβολον ἔργον], a reckless deed. Hence the parabolani in Church history and elsewhere, about whom Scaliger somewhere (if I remember rightly), and my late father at length, have written. In English, in contracted form, bold; boldly, daringly. The word "parleße" also came to mind, and I would not hesitate if that reading were established and it were not rather to be written "peerleße" [peerless].

units.la: Πλύνω, lavare, eluere ; <bl>to plunge</bl>.
units.tr: Plynō [Πλύνω]: to wash, to cleanse; to plunge.

units.la: Πίω, πίομαι, πῶσις : gustare, vesci, saturari. (Hinc ἄπαστος, jejunus : ἀπασία, inedia : de quibus supra, suo loco.) to feed & fodder. Nec oblitus sum tamen quid in ἀφιλῶς dictum fit. Sed varia (cùm se offerunt) proponendo, id ago, ut alii amplius cogitent, & quod solidissimum judicabunt, ampleƈtantur. Cæterùm, ex hoc πέω, est nomen πῶϋ, grex ; πῶϋ & πώεα οἰων, apud Homerum: & hinc fortasse, inferto (de quo jam suprà non semel) /. a flock.
units.tr: Pio [Πίω], piomai [πίομαι], pōsis [πῶσις]: to taste, to eat, to be sated. (Hence apastos [ἄπαστος], fasting; apasia [ἀπασία], starvation; of which above, in its place.) To feed and fodder. Nor have I forgotten what was said about aphilōs [ἀφιλῶς]. But when various things present themselves, I set them out so that others may think further, and may embrace whatever they judge most solid. Moreover, from this pleo [πέω] comes the noun pōy [πῶϋ], a flock; pōy and pōea oiōn [πώεα οἰῶν] in Homer; and hence perhaps, with an l inserted (as above, more than once), a flock.

units.la: πέρδω, pedere: to f.
units.tr: Perdō [πέρδω], pedere: to f.

units.la: Παρασιτίζω, (ut & simplex σιτίζω) decipere ; fraudulenter & dolosè agere; to purloyne. Quòd si de laniis, ut afferunt quidam, id proprie dicatur, tunc alia ratio. Sed fortasse mera tantùm conjectura fuerit ista illorum assertio.
units.tr: Parasitizō [Παρασιτίζω] (like the simple sitizō [σιτίζω]): to deceive; to act fraudulently and deceitfully; to purloin. If this word is properly used of butchers, as some assert, then the explanation is another one. But perhaps their assertion is mere conjecture.

units.la: Πεταλὶς, πετηλὶς, πεύχιδος, Hesychio: qui promptò aut præcipiti est ingenio ; qui promptè aut præcipitanter aliquid agit, aut aggreditur. Hinc fortasse to pole, & a pholeur, potiùs quàm ex ἐμπολέω.
units.tr: Petalis, petēlis, peuchidos [Πεταλὶς, πετηλὶς, πεύχιδος], in Hesychius: one of a ready or headlong disposition; one who promptly or rashly does or undertakes something. Hence perhaps to pole and a pholeur, rather than from empoleō [ἐμπολέω].

units.la: πτέρυξ, (quasi πτέρυξ, ut docet Etymologicum:) ala, penna, pluma ; a feather: Item, πτέρυξ, volucris, apud Homerum, a bird, Eliditur πτέρ. ut in πτέρυξ, perna, &c.
units.tr: Pteryx [πτέρυξ] (as if from pteryx, as the Etymologicum teaches): a wing, a feather, a plume; a feather. Also pteryx [πτέρυξ], a bird, in Homer; a bird. The syllable is elided, as in pterna [perna] and so on.

units.la: P
units.tr: P

units.la: PHγνυσζ, ῥηγνύμι, ῥήσσειν : rumpere, la- cerare ; to rend.
units.tr: P ῥήγνυμι, ῥήσσειν [ῥήγνυμι, ῥήσσειν]: to break, to tear, to lacerate; to rend.

units.la: ῥάσ@-, pannus tinctus : lodix : vestis stragula : Homero. a rugge.
units.tr: ῥάκος [ῥάκος]: dyed cloth; a coverlet or rug; a bedspread, in Homer; a rug.

units.la: Pῶ↓, virgultum, plurali (quod magis usitatum :) ῥᾶτες, virgulta ; ἱμαντὰ ᾿Ιώδη φυλὰ ; ait Eustathius ; plantæ ex quibus lora confici solita. Sæpius hoc inculcat Eustathius, quia apud Homerum ( præter quem vix alius habet ) eâ plerumque notione verbum occurrit, ut vel funem, vel materiam funis denotet. Adscribam unum de multis locum', cum Eustathii explicatione, ut tanto magis, quod fatis inculcari non potest, appareat, quàm Homero multum debeat Anglica lingua ; sed & Homerus veteribus Anglis, qui tot ejus vocabula apud Græcos ipsos antiquata, sua faciendo conservaverint. Homerus igitur Odyff. x, five X. ubi inducit Ulyffem de cervo ingentis magnitudinis à fe transfixo & occiso narrantem, inter alia de fune ab eo contexto, quo cervum ligatum gestare posset, hæc habet verba :
units.tr: ῥᾶτες [ῥᾶτες], a thing of twigs (the plural, which is more in use): ῥᾶτες, twigs; "thongs of Iodes' stock," says Eustathius; plants from which thongs were usually made. Eustathius often presses this point, because in Homer (beside whom hardly any other author has the word) it usually occurs in this sense, denoting either a rope or the material of a rope. I will quote one passage of many, with Eustathius's explanation, so that it may appear all the more clearly, and as it cannot be stressed enough, how much the English language owes to Homer. Homer also preserved for the old English many of his words, which the Greeks themselves had let fall out of use, by making them their own. So in Odyssey 10 (or book X), where Ulysses is introduced telling of a deer of huge size that he had pierced and killed, he tells, among other things, of the rope he twisted, with which he could carry the bound deer. His words are these:

units.la: ἀνλδς ἀὐλὰρ ἐγὼ ασασάμλω ρᾶπὰς τε λύσες τε
units.tr: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ ἀπέταμον ῥᾶπάς τε λύγους τε

units.la: - Πῆσμα δ᾽ ὅσον τ᾽ ὄρξυαν ἐϋτρεφὲς ἀμ- φολέρῳδεν
units.tr: πεῖσμα δ' ὅσον τ' ὄργυιαν ἐϋστρεφὲς ἀμφοτέρωθεν

units.la: Πλεξέμυῷ, σωϊέλησω. πάδας ἀεινοῖο πελώρε.
units.tr: πλέξας σύνδησα πόδας ἀεικέος πελώρου.

units.la: id est, Caterum ego avulsi virgultáque viminaque, Funéque ad ulnæ longitudinem bene torto undique complicato colligavi pedes ingentis monstri: ubi Eustathius, (cujus verba Stephanus etiam super hoc verbo citat) ῥῶσις inquit, φυλὰ ἱμαντλάδη, ἡ ἔτως ἀντίσιζ, ὡς ἡ πεῖσμα (ὃ δὴ ἀγοιτὶο) ἐξ ἀὐλῶν σρίφεδς ἥσι καὶ ἀσδ: id est, ῥῶσις, plantæ, vel frutices instar lori tam flexibiles & sequaces (seu vitiles) ut etiam πεῖσμα (quod proprie funem majorem seu nauticum significat:) ex illis torqueri seu neri possit. Hactenus ille. Angli sine ulla mutatione hodiéque ropes, funes, vocant. De voce σχοινος, ex qua Anglicum verbum quibusdam placuit arcessere, vide suo loco, in σχοινος.
units.tr: That is: "Moreover, I tore off twigs and withies, and with a rope well twisted to the length of an arm, bound together on every side the feet of the monstrous beast." Here Eustathius (whose words Stephanus also cites under this word) says: "ῥῶσις," he says, "plants or shrubs like a thong, so flexible and pliant (or pliable) that even a πεῖσμα (which properly means a larger or nautical rope) can be twisted or spun from them." So far he. The English, without any change even today, call such things ropes, that is, cords. About the word σχοῖνος, from which some have thought the English word should be derived, see in its place, under σχοῖνος.

units.la: Ποινὸς, curvus, inflexus, retortus: βίς, idem. Anglis, awry, incurvum, inflexum. Dubito tamen, propter Belgicum aber-recht; vel ober-recht; contrarius recto, præpositerus, sinister. Angli scriberent ouer-rtght. Sed non videntur eadem esse verba.
units.tr: Ποινὸς [ποινὸς]: curved, bent, twisted; βίς, the same. The English have awry, crooked, bent. I doubt it, however, because of the Dutch aber-recht or ober-recht, meaning contrary to straight, perverse, sinister. The English would write "ouer-right." But these do not seem to be the same words.

units.la: ʿPassλαῖος, præceps, impetuosus: ῥάςσλω, abrupte, præcipitanter; rash, rashly.
units.tr: ῥᾳσσαῖος [ῥᾳσσαῖος]: headlong, impetuous; ῥάσσλω [ῥάσσλω]: abruptly, headlong; rash, rashly.

units.la: ʿPuλῆς (& ῥυλά plur. à ῥύω, traho:) habena, lorum frœni, frœnū. Angl. clavus, seu gubernaculum navis, quòd navi habenæ usum præbet, a rudder. Jam pro ῥυλῆς, Æoles dixere βευλῆς, (quod in aliis quoque illis solemne; sed de hoc peculiariter à Grammaticis notatum:) unde Anglicum, a <bl>bridle</bl>, frænum. De verbis <bl>rhæda</bl> (quod Germanicum, seu Gallicum fuisse notum est) & hodierno, to ride, ab hac, an secùs, origine, aliàs quæremus.
units.tr: ῥυλῆς (and ῥυλά in the plural, from ῥύω, to draw): a rein, the strap of a bridle, a bridle. English clavus, or the steering-gear of a ship, a rudder, because it gives a ship the use of a rein. Now for ῥυλῆς the Aeolians said βευλῆς (which was usual with them in other words too; but this has been noted in particular by the grammarians), whence the English a bridle, a bit. We shall inquire elsewhere whether the words rhaeda (which is known to have been German or French) and the modern to ride derive from this origin or not.

units.la: ʿPυμα, tractus, intervallum loci, distantia: ῥύμη, vicus; seu liberum illud inter ædificia spatium ad ultro citróq; commeantium usum, quod vulgò Strata dicimus: ῥυμολομέω, per vicos partior, aut seco. Anglicè, roome, spatium loci liberum: loca in ædificiis distincta.
units.tr: ῥῦμα [ῥῦμα], a drawing, an interval of space, a distance; ῥύμη [ῥύμη], a lane or street; or that free space between buildings for the use of people going to and fro, which we commonly call a street; ῥυμολογέω [ῥυμολογέω], I divide or cut through by lanes. In English, room: free space of a place; places distinguished among buildings.

units.la: ʿPύαξ, Æolicè, βεύαξ, rivus; a <bl>brook</bl>. Vide suprà in βεύω.
units.tr: ῥύαξ [ῥύαξ], Aeolic βεύαξ [βεύαξ], a stream; a brook. See above under βεύω.

units.la: ʿPάxω, Æolicè βεάxω, lacera vestis, ftis,&c. fimili ratione, ex ῥήγνυμι, ῥῆξαι, ῥῆγμα, ῥῆξις, ῥαγάς; rumpi, rumpere, ruptura, fiffura, &c. fecerunt Angli, to break, a break, &c.
units.tr: ῥάγος [ῥάγος], Aeolic βεάγος, a torn garment, a rent, etc. By a similar process, from ῥήγνυμι, ῥῆξαι, ῥῆγμα, ῥῆξις, ῥαγάς, to rend, rent, a rupture, a fissure, etc., the English made to break, a break, and so on.

units.la: Ῥάμνος, rhamnus, fpinofus frutex. Spina alba, quibufdam :. rubus, fecundum alios. Anglis, præpofito ut in fuperioribus, b.a bramble. Ita & ῥεδίον, ῥεόδον, ῥείζη, pro ῥάδιον, ῥόδον, ῥίζα, & alia plurima, quæ à Grammaticis notata. Inde & ἄλκή, pondus, vis, a bulk : & Gall.blanck, ex ἀλβός, albus.
units.tr: Ῥάμνος [ῥάμνος], buckthorn, a thorny shrub. For some it is white thorn; for others, bramble. The English, with a prefix as in the words above, have a bramble. So also ῥεδίον, ῥεόδον, ῥείζη for ῥάδιον, ῥόδον, ῥίζα, and very many others noted by the grammarians. Hence also ἀλκή, weight, strength, a bulk; and the French blanc, from ἀλβός, white.

units.la: Ῥήμα, dictum, sententia, oraculum : ῥῆσις, de quo certis verbis convenit : certâ verborum formulâ comprehensus : præfinitus, conftitutus, certus: μισθῷ ῥήματι, pactâ, conftitutâ mercede : ῥήμασι, certis conditionibus : ῥήματοι νόμοι, scriptæ leges: apud Philo Judæum, ut ibi interpres. Philonis verba : Εἰσὶ γὰρ τινες οἱ τὸν ῥήτον νόμως συμβόλα νοοῦντες ὑπαξιμάτων ἀναλαμβανόμενοι, &c. Interpres Sunt enim quidam, qui dum putant scriptas leges esse figuras intelligibilium, &c. Hinc igitur Angl. to write, scribere. Porrò, etsi aliud per se scribere, aliud dicere; quàm vulgò tamen ista in diversis idiomatibus confundantur, fidem faciunt, λέγω, (dico:) Græcum; ex quo Latinum lego; alio sensu: lesen, Germ.legere; liften, Anglicum, auscultare: reden, Belgicum, loqui: read, Anglicum, legere: & id genus alia.
units.tr: Ῥῆμα [ῥῆμα], a saying, a statement, an oracle; ῥῆσις [ῥῆσις], about which people agree in set words, comprised in a fixed form of words; fixed, established, certain. μισθῷ ῥήματι [μισθῷ ῥήματι], by an agreed, established wage; ῥήμασι [ῥήμασι], on certain conditions; ῥήματοι νόμοι [ῥήτοι νόμοι], written laws, as the translator there notes in Philo the Jew. Philo's words: "For there are some who, thinking that written laws are symbols of intelligible things, take them up..." etc. The translator renders: "For there are some who, supposing that the written laws are figures of intelligible things," etc. Hence comes the English to write, scribere. Further, although to write is one thing and to say another, yet these are commonly confused in different idioms. The Greek λέγω (I say), from which Latin lego, bears witness to this in another sense; likewise German lesen (Latin legere), English listen, to listen; Dutch reden, to speak; English read, to read; and other things of that kind.

units.la: ᾿Pέῳ, membrum, quævis pars corporis. Sed peculiariter, & ῥῆ᾽ ὑξοχὴν, τὸ ὄψωπον, facies, vultus. Et hinc credibile est Anglicum wrath: (nam τὸ w. sæpe vacat initio: ut nunc whore, quod olim bore; nunc whole, quod olim bole, &c.) pro ira, manasse: ut & Hebraïs אף & plurali, אפים, tum vultum (ὄψωπον) tum iram significant. Rationem docent Hebraï Lexicographi, nec cuiquam valdè difficilis ad divinandum.
units.tr: Ῥέῳ [ῥέῳ], a limb, any part of the body. But especially, and by eminence, the countenance, face, visage. Hence it is credible that the English wrath (for the w is often idle at the start, as now whore was once bore; now whole was once bole, and so on) came to mean anger, just as the Hebrew אף [af] and its plural אפים [appayim] signify both the countenance (ὄψωπον) and anger. The Hebrew lexicographers explain the reason, and it is not at all hard for anyone to guess.

units.la: ᾿Pάσσω, (pro ἐξάρεω) illidere, collidere; to wrack: unde whip wrack; allisio navis, naufragium. Ut & ab ἐξάρεω, seu ἐξέλεω, pro convitiis impetere, to rate: de quo suo loco.
units.tr: Ῥάσσω [ῥάσσω] (for ἐξάρεω [ἐξαρέω]), to strike against, to dash together; to wrack: whence whip wrack, the dashing of a ship, a shipwreck. Also from ἐξάρεω, or ἐξέλεω, to assail with abuse, to rate; of which in its place.

units.la: ᾿Pέω, ῥέω, currere: de aquæ cursu proprie. Unde & ῥέω, ῥοὴ, ῥόω, fluxus, flumen, fluentum: to run, currere; rep, olim, flumen: unde southrep, &c.
units.tr: Ῥέω [ῥέω], to run, properly of the course of water. Hence also ῥέω, ῥοή, ῥόος, a flow, a stream, a flood: to run, to run; rep, formerly river; whence southrep, and so on.

units.la: ᾿Pυδς, pellis, cutis, corium. Anglis, rine, cortex. Est enim cortex, arboribus ; quod corium, animalibus,
units.tr: Ῥυδὸς [ῥυδός], skin, hide, leather. In English, rine, bark. For bark belongs to trees, as hide does to animals.

units.la: ᾿Ρίπτω, vergo, inclino. De maturis frugibus & segetibus proprie, quorum maturitatis indicium est cum vergunt & propendent. Hinc Anglicum, ripe, maturus. Vide supra in Ϛρυπλὶς.
units.tr: Ῥίπτω [ῥίπτω], to incline, to lean over. Properly of ripe grain and crops, whose sign of ripeness is when they bend over and droop. Hence the English ripe, mature. See above under the word noted there.

units.la: ᾿Ρίμβειν, & ῥύμβω : de his supra.
units.tr: Ῥίμβειν [ῥίμβειν] and ῥύμβω [ῥύμβω]: of these, see above.

units.la: ᾿Ραχὶς, ῥαχία, ῥαχίτης : de his etiam supra.
units.tr: Ῥαχὶς [ῥαχίς], ῥαχία [ῥαχία], ῥαχίτης [ῥαχίτης]: of these also, see above.

units.la: Σ
units.tr: Sigma [Σ]

units.la: Σ᾿Τεῖφω, funiculus, è loro aut cannabe aliáve materiâ tortus, seu plexus. Ita Stephanus. Hesych. σωσεσχμένω λᾶϱω, ἢ χοινίον. ut non sine causa suspicatus fit vir ille doctus, quem Cambdenum plerique suspicantur, in collectione verborum, quam huic nostrae praemisimus, Anglicum, rope, ex Graeco fluxisse. Nam literarum σ. initio labilium, aut ascititiarum exempla prius habuimus : quale ῥόμβω, σεμβω : aliáque. π. & φ. sunt cognatae literae, nec usu tantum, sed proprio quodam jure & lege naturae suae permutabiles. Nobis tamen ex ῥῶπος origo probabilior visa est, ubi nulla omnino literarum
units.tr: Steiphō [Σ᾿Τεῖφω]: a small rope, twisted or plaited from thread, hemp or other material. So Stephanus. Hesychius: a stone... or a basket [χοινίον]. Hence that learned man, whom most suspect to be Camden, was not without reason led to suspect, in the collection of words that we have prefixed to this work, that the English "rope" came from the Greek. For we have earlier examples of an initial sigma that is slipped in or added, such as ῥόμβω, σεμβω, and others. The letters π and φ are cognate, and are interchangeable not only by usage but by a certain peculiar right and by the law of their nature. Yet the origin from ῥῶπος seemed more probable to us, where no change of letters at all intervenes

units.la: Ut ... (marginal reference not legible) terarum mutatio intervenit, & significatio optimè conveniat, cùm in omnibus linguis sit receptissimum, ut opera qualiacunque ex suâ materiâ nominentur. Simillimum hoc, quod in mentem nunc venit. Οἴσ῾Θ, Græcis salix: φυλὸν ἱμαντλῶδες, ait Eustathius, (cujus verba etiam apud Etymologicum :) ἡ ἀπαλὸν, &c. planè ut antea in βάπτις. Hinc οἶσι, vel οἰσοί, γένθ χοινὶς (genus funis:) & οἶσ, funes nautici, retinaculæ. Judicet lector, & quod maluerit, amplectatur.
units.tr: ...and the meaning agrees best, since it is most generally accepted in all languages that works of whatever kind are named from their material. Very similar is what now comes to mind: osier [Οἴσ῾Θ], which the Greeks call a willow; a strap-like plant [φυλὸν ἱμαντλῶδες], says Eustathius (whose words are also in the Etymologicum); the soft one [ἡ ἀπαλὸν], etc., just as before in βάπτις. Hence οἶσι or οἰσοί, a kind of cord (a sort of rope), and οἶσ, nautical ropes, hawsers. Let the reader judge, and embrace whichever he prefers.

units.la: Σφόριον, σεγγύλον ζωνάειον, rotunda, seu teres Zona. sumitur etiam pro fasciis quibusdam tum capitalibus, tum pectoralibus. Hinc ducerem russe, pro colli qualicunque ornamento, quod ipsum cingat. Certè fasciis collùm cingere, non nautis tantùm, sed populis multis Hodiéque solemne. Sed de antiquitate verbi dubito ; quod si recens est, illis assentior, ex Belgico rupffelen (à quo non multum abit Anglicum ruffle :) rugare, corrugare, repetentibus.
units.tr: A round girdle [Σφόριον, σεγγύλον ζωνάειον], a rounded or smooth belt. It is also used for certain bands, both for the head and for the breast. From this I would derive the Russian ruff, for any kind of ornament that encircles the neck. Certainly, binding the neck with bands is customary today not only among sailors but among many peoples. But I doubt the antiquity of the word; if it is recent, I agree with those who derive it from the Dutch rupffelen (not far from the English ruffle), to wrinkle, to crease, by repeated action.

units.la: Σφνὴς, asper, acutus : σφνὲς βοάν, vel φωνάζω, asperè clamare. σφνὲς βρέμειν, μεν, immaniter, vel immani sono refonare: ϛεηνόφωνοι, qui asperâ voce. Apud Etymologicum τὸ ϛρηνὸν, exponitur τὸ ὀξὺ κ) ἀναllaμμένον, (ut Stephanus recte corrigit, pro ἀναπεπταμένον; quod apud Hefych. ἀναλέλαsμένον :) acutum & contentum : seu nimiâ contentione peccans. Anglis, a straineꝺ voice, & to straine bis voice; vox contenta; & vocem contendere. Ex nimia autem contentione, accidit τῇ sαχὺ κ) ϙεiCarἰες τῇ ἀxoῇ, asperitas illa vocis aures offendens, five auribus odiosa; ut apud Etymologicum. A voce, ad alia apud Anglos, verbum transiit, ad indicandum seu animi vitium, seu corporis contentionem. At τὸ straine, quòd percolare significat, ab aliâ dubio procul origine. ex Gallico scil. e﻿straindre, vel estraigner: quæ ex Latino, stringere: quibus quamvis infit aliqua contentionis, seu nixus significatio; in alio tamen illa contentio genere, & ab illâ longè diversa, quæ voci proprie competit.
units.tr: Sharp, harsh [Σφνὴς, asper, acutus]: to shout harshly [σφνὲς βοάν, or φωνάζω]. To roar fiercely, to resound with a huge sound [σφνὲς βρέμειν]; those with a harsh voice [ϛεηνόφωνοι]. In the Etymologicum, the harsh [τὸ ϛρηνὸν] is explained as the sharp and strained [τὸ ὀξὺ καὶ ἀναλελαμμένον] (as Stephanus rightly corrects it to ἀναπεπταμένον, which in Hesychius is ἀναλέλασμένον): sharp and stretched, or faulty through excessive straining. The English say a strained voice and to strain one's voice: a voice stretched, and to strain the voice. From excessive straining comes that harshness of voice which offends the ears, or is hateful to them, as in the Etymologicum. From the voice the word passed among the English to other things, to indicate either a fault of mind or a strain of body. But to strain, meaning to filter, has undoubtedly another origin, from the French estraindre or estraigner, which come from the Latin stringere. Although these carry some sense of effort or exertion, it is in a different kind of straining, far removed from that which properly belongs to the word.

units.la: ϛλίφω, adstringo, (de cibis ut plurimùm Græci:) Item spisso, condenso. Angl. to stste, adstringere ad suffocationem. Item to stuffe, densare, conftipare.
units.tr: I squeeze tight [ϛλίφω], to bind fast (said mostly by the Greeks of foods). Also, to thicken, to condense. English to stifle, to squeeze tight to suffocation. Also to stuff, to pack densely, to cram.

units.la: Σλυρεὸς. Σὶυφελὰς, durus, asper ; <bl>tuff.</bl>
units.tr: Σλυρεὸς. Hard, rough [Σὶυφελὰς]; tuff.

units.la: Σιυφελίζω, duriter, asperéque tractato, &c. Item υβείζω, maledictis, aut convitiis incesso: ονείδεσι συφελίζειν: συφελισμὸς, contumelia, υβεις. Anglis to flowt, subsannare, deridere: a flowt, farcasmus, convitium: de quo plura in φαῦλο. Iisdem to scuffle, rixari, verbis contendere. Idem συφελίζω, dispello, discutio, disjicio: deturbo, depello: συφελισμὸς, cùm quis injuriosè loco suo deturbatur: to shuffle, loco movere, mifcere, deturbare : Chuffling, verbale.
units.tr: To treat roughly and harshly [Σιυφελίζω], etc. Also to assail with abuse or insults [υβείζω]: to pelt with taunts [ονείδεσι συφελίζειν]; a pelting with taunts [συφελισμὸς], insult [υβεις]. In English, to flout, to jeer at, to mock; a flout, a sneer, an insult; more on this under φαῦλο. By the same words, to scuffle, to quarrel, to contend in words. The same συφελίζω means to scatter, dispel, shake apart, throw about: to thrust down, drive off. συφελισμὸς is used when someone is wrongfully thrust out of his place: to shuffle, to move from place, to mix up, to dislodge; shuffling, a verbal noun.

units.la: Σλίβω, calco : terram fcil. vel viam, eundo, & ambulando : σελβειν ὁδὸν dicitur, qui graditur,& viam pedibus calcat, feu terit : σεληὸς & σηλὸς, calcatus, tritus : ἀσηβὴς, non calcatus, ἀβαλὼ : ἐυσηβὴς, bene calcatus, tritus. Σλίβω; via, callis, veftigium, fignum pedis. to ftep, incedere : a ftep, veftigium pedis; fynonymum, to tread, ex Latino, terere, calcare.
units.tr: I tread [Σλίβω]: the ground or road, namely by walking and going on foot. σελβειν ὁδὸν is said of one who walks and treads or wears the road with his feet. Trodden, worn [σεληὸς & σηλὸς]; untrodden [ἀσηβὴς], unbeaten [ἀβαλὼ]; well trodden, well worn [ἐυσηβὴς]. Σλίβω also means a way, a path, a track, a footprint, a sign of a foot. English to step, to advance; a step, a footprint; its synonym to tread, from the Latin terere, calcare.

units.la: Σλάχω, eo, incedo ; proprie, ut quidam volunt, ordine quasi militari procedo ; <bl>to ftalke</bl>.
units.tr: I go, I advance [Σλάχω]; properly, as some want, I proceed in a kind of military order. To stalk.

units.la: Σκεδάω, σκεδάζω, (quod etiam κεδάω, κεδάζω) σκεδάννυμι, diffipo, difpergo.
units.tr: I scatter, I disperse [Σκεδάω, σκεδάζω, (which is also κεδάω, κεδάζω), σκεδάννυμι].

units.la: De hominibus (sparsis, dispersis, difpalatis) ut plurimùm usurpatur: to scatter. Sed & to shed, effundere, ni fallor.
units.tr: It is used mostly of people: scattered, dispersed, spread apart: to scatter. But also to shed, to pour out, unless I am mistaken.

units.la: Σκω̃ς, st. to scoyne.
units.tr: Σκω̃ς: to scoyne.

units.la: Σκηλὸν, idem. to - - -
units.tr: Σκηλὸν, the same. to - - -

units.la: Σφαδάζω, de eo proprie dicitur, qui quacunque de caussâ, seu laetâ, sive tristi, stare nescíens præ nimiâ impatientiâ, terram pulsat & ferit pedibus. De equis ut plurimùm usurpatur: sed & de hominibus cum morte colluctantibus, & jamjam expiraturis. Anglis, to sade, marcescere, occidere: de floribus, ut plurimùm: sed & ad alia quoque satis familiari translatione. De equis autem foundered cùm dicunt, vitium pedum intelligunt, quo qui laborant equi, præ ungularum teneritudine, sive mollitie, si per aspera & dura incedunt, frequenter impingunt.
units.tr: Σφαδάζω is properly said of one who, for whatever cause, whether glad or sad, cannot keep still from excessive impatience, and beats and strikes the ground with his feet. It is used mostly of horses, but also of men struggling with death and about to expire. In English, to sade, to wither, to die: mostly of flowers, but also in other rather familiar transferred senses. When they say horses are foundered, they mean a fault of the feet, to which horses that walk over rough and hard ground are prone, because of the tenderness or softness of their hooves, and often stumble.

units.la: Σφεργάω, turgeo; item vegetus sum, & corpore bene habito, ut qui in flore sunt aetatis: σφαισ̃ας ἡ ἡλικίας, florente & gestiente aetate. Anglicè, to be lusty, (quod etiam lusty:) quod etsi Gallicum quoque sit, non tamen omittendum putavi, partim quòd non constaret an ab illis acceptum sit; partim, quòd quod cum σφαδάζω conjunctum, alterum alterius confirmet originem.
units.tr: I swell [Σφεργάω]; also I am vigorous and in good bodily condition, like those in the flower of their age: in flourishing and eager age [σφαισ̃ας ἡ ἡλικίας]. In English, to be lusty (also lusty). Although this is also French, I did not think it should be omitted, partly because it is not certain that it was borrowed from them, and partly because, since it is joined with σφαδάζω, each confirms the origin of the other.

units.la: Σλέκχ{&}; truncus, caudex. Anglicè stalke, caulis,scapus,thyrsus. Caulis & caudex,si naturam speãtes, eadem res; & una à Theophrasto definitione comprehenduntur; τὸ ὑπὲρ γῆς πεφυκὸς ὑφ' ἓν: (de caule loquitur:) ὁ δὴ ἡ ὑ ἐνδρῶν ἡλιϑ.. σάλεχ. Quod ex radice supra terram eminet in uno continuo & singulari corpore: (ita ego illud ὑφ' ἓν interpretor. Sed inspicient Theophrastum quibus licet,& vacat; nos enim ex Stephano ista transcribimus:) quod in arboribus vocatur σάλεχ.
units.tr: Σλέκχ; trunk, stalk [truncus, caudex]. In English stalke: stalk, stem, shaft, thyrsus. If we look at nature, caulis and caudex are the same thing, and Theophrastus comprehends both in one definition: what grows above the ground as one [τὸ ὑπὲρ γῆς πεφυκὸς ὑφ' ἓν]; he speaks of the stem. What rises above the ground from the root in one continuous and single body (so I interpret that ὑφ' ἓν; but let those who are free and have the leisure consult Theophrastus, for I am transcribing these things from Stephanus). It is called σάλεχ in trees.

units.la: Σῆμα, stamen. Sed & de plantâ dicitur, ἡ δὲ φυλὴ, πόσοι, ait Hefychius. sed quo sensu, divinare oportet, cùm nulla quod sciam ullibi quæ doceant exempla. Succurrat Anglica lingua, quæ stemme, caulem hodiéque vulgò nuncupat.
units.tr: Σῆμα, the stamen. But it is also said of a plant, the tribe, how many [ἡ δὲ φυλὴ, πόσοι], says Hesychius; but in what sense one must guess, since, as far as I know, no examples anywhere teach it. The English language may help here, which even today commonly calls the stalk a stemme.

units.la: - Σπαθάν, texere. Angl. to spin, nere: quæ quamvis diversa, sunt tamen assinia, & muliebris utrumque muneris & artificii. Confundi interdum vel illud doceat, quòd aranea Latinis texere dicitur: unde & aranex tela; Anglis, so spin.
units.tr: To weave [Σπαθάν]. English to spin, to spin thread. These are different, yet related, and both are women's work and craft. That they are sometimes confused is shown by the fact that the Latins say the spider texere (to weave), whence also aranea tela, the spider's web; the English say so spin.

units.la: Bl. The lines of this page are often fragmentary; see notes. fpin ; unde & a fpinner, aranea. Præterea, cùm alia similia artificiorum vocabula, to weave, to knit, cloath, &c. sint Græca; probabile hoc quoque ejusdem esse prosapiæ. Sed & σπόνδυλος (seu σφόνδυλος) pars fusi, quam verticillum quidam nominant; Græcis: & Anglis, spindel, fusus.
units.tr: The lines of this page are often fragmentary; see notes. spin; whence also a spinner, aranea. Moreover, since other similar words for crafts, to weave, to knit, to cloth, etc., are Greek, this is probably of the same stock too. But also σπόνδυλος (or σφόνδυλος), the part of the spindle that some call the whorl, in Greek; and in English spindel, spindle.

units.la: Σπαδάω, & σπαλαλάω, inter alia σχοπίζειν, dissipare: unde to spatter, ductum videri possit: sed ego potius ex σπαλίλη, quod ὑγρὸν διαχώρημα, liquidum excrementum, exponitur: & ὃπ τῆς διαρροΐας à medicis usurpari notatur, ortum crediderim.
units.tr: σπαδάω and σπαλαλάω mean, among other things, σχοπίζειν, to scatter. From this, to spatter may seem to be derived; but I would rather believe it arose from σπαλίλη, which is explained as liquid excrement [ὑγρὸν διαχώρημα], and which doctors note is used from diarrhoea [ὃπ τῆς διαρροΐας].

units.la: Σπάθη, rudes; rudicula: spatha, spathula: instrumentum pharmacopolæ, &c. Hinc forte, spoone, cochleare; non idem plane, sed valde affine instrumentum.
units.tr: σπάθη: a rudder? a small scraper; spatha, spathula: an apothecary's instrument, etc. Hence perhaps spoone, a spoon; not quite the same instrument, but a very closely related one.

units.la: Σπαθμὴ, dodrans, spithama: a span. Non dubito multis, ut propiorem; atrisutam Gallicam originem, ut span, sit ab espan; & espan, ab espandre, expandere. Sed aut ego valde fallor, aut longe antiquior apud Germanos Anglosve, vox span (hodiernis Belgis, spanne: Germanis, ut apud Kylianum reperio, (pan)quàm est Gal. illud efpan-dre, à Latino, pandere, vel expandere. Jam ϟ ϡ in medio absorpti, vel inserti, ( ne quis imprudens hîc offendat ) exempla satis obvia: ut καθέδρα, ( cathedra) une chaire. ἔσλα, Dorice, ἔσλα. ἕδρα, Ital. sfma. μαλακὸς, μαλθακὸς, &c. Et quantum quæso th. diftat à d. quod Galli in innumeris ferè Latinis abjiciunt, ut fier, loner, &c. fidere, laudare, &c. Sed & inserunt in quibusdam, ut generare, gener, tener, &c. engendrer, gendre, tendre, &c.
units.tr: σπαθμὴ: half a foot (dodrans), a span (spithama): a span. I do not doubt that many prefer what they think is the nearer French origin, that span comes from espan, and espan from espandre, to expand. But either I am much mistaken, or the word span is far older among the Germans and English (among the Dutch today spanne, among the Germans, as I find in Kilian, pan) than the French espandre, from the Latin pandere or expandere. Now, as for a letter absorbed or inserted in the middle (lest anyone be offended by this), there are examples enough at hand: καθέδρα (cathedra), une chaire; ἔσλα, in Doric ἔσλα; ἕδρα, Italian sedia; μαλακὸς, μαλθακὸς, etc. And how far, I ask, is th from d, which the French drop in countless Latin words, as in fier, louer, etc., from fidere, laudare, etc.? But they also insert it in some, as in generare, gener, tener, etc.: engendrer, gendre, tendre, etc.

units.la: ϟλίζω, σίξω, pungere, figere, fignare, notare; to stick. Eupolis apud Pollucem, Ἐγὼ σίξω σε βελόναις τρισί: I will stick thee with three needles.
units.tr: στίζω (misprinted here as σίξω): to prick, pierce, mark, brand, note; to stick. Eupolis in Pollux: "I will stick you with three needles" [Ἐγὼ στίξω σε βελόναις τρισί].

units.la: ϟλίσμα, nota, quâ aliquis est compunctus, vel inustus, &c. Et ϟσμαλίζω, notas inuro, compungo. Angl. a sting, stimulus, spiculum: to sting, pungere. De apibus, ut plurimùm.
units.tr: sizma: a mark by which someone is pricked or branded, and so on. Also smalizō: I brand marks on, I prick. English a sting, a goad, a spike; to sting, to prick. Said mostly of bees.

units.la: ϟπεύδω, festino, propero; to speed, (ot, make haste) & speed: celeritas, festinatio.
units.tr: speudō, I hasten, I hurry; to speed (to hurry, make haste), and speed: swiftness, haste.

units.la: ϟπεύδω, ( pro quo olim σπεύδω dicebant, unde remansit futurũ σπεύσω, &c. quomodo autem pro σπεύδω primitivo factum sit ἀπίνδω, fuse docet Etymologicum in ἀρφ-ῥ & ἀναλ-ῶ:) libo, sacrifico. Hinc Anglicum, ni falsor, tô sœeꝺ, pro prosperari,éventu bono uti: quod veteres illi Græci,nihil ferè quod alicujus effet momenti aggredérentur, quin Deos, ut felicitér eveniret, aliquo priùs sacrificio placassent. Ex simili ratione, litare, Latinis ; & auspicari, aliâque apud alios haud pauca. Sed & tó speñꝺ, expendere, impendere, ex sacrificiorum consuetudine processit. Tunc enim tempus sumptuum,(& raro aliàs : quod etiam ex divinâ scripturâ, non uno loco, discimus:) cùm rem divinâm facerent. Hinc illud Comici, Festo die si quid prodégeris, professo egere liceat, nisi peperceris. Item, Quos in divinis rebus sumas sumptus, sapienti lucro est. Hinc étiam ex ἴσϑʼ, quod est epulari, convivio excipere, Latinum Festum, & festus dies, pro die facto : & contrà, Anglicum, (vel Gallicum potiùs) feast. & feasting, pro convivio, ex Latino,festum, pro die sacro. Similí ratione, quia nulla feré apud veteres illos sœdera, aut pacta, sine alicujus oblationis aut libationis solemnitate, hinc factum ut ipsum αὐτόω, quod proprie libare significat, pro pacisci & fœdus percutere non minus raro usurparetur. Unde & Latinum spondeo. Sed & delibare Latinum, pro minuere (quod ab Anglici verbi significatione non procul abit: ) ex sacrificiorum consuetudine. Ex quibus & infinita alia, ut Eximius, egregius, &c. paulò attentioribus obvia. Hæc eò pluribus, ob viciniam Latini pendo, expendo, impendo: (unde & Italicum spendere:) ex quibus si quis malit Anglicum verbum repetere, ego non vehementius oblutabor. Mihi aliter videbatur: & quod olim de se magnus Hippocrates; Οἱ᾿ δὲ λόγοι ἐμαυτὸν ἔπαισα, τὸ ποτὲ ἀκούοντας ἡ τὸ ἀκούειν πεισθῆναι πεζόμενοι: ita nos; quibus rationibus inducti sumus ut aliter crederemus, eas lectori candidè imperdiendas censuimus.
units.tr: spendō, I offer a libation, I sacrifice. (The Greeks once said speudō for this, whence the future speusō remains. How apindō came to be formed from the primitive speudō is explained at length in the Etymologicum under arphrh and analō.) Hence, unless I am mistaken, the English to speed, meaning to prosper, to have a good outcome. Those ancient Greeks, before undertaking almost anything of importance, first appeased the gods with some sacrifice so that it would turn out well. By a similar reasoning the Latins have litare and auspicari, and many others occur among other peoples. But also spendō, to spend or expend, arose from the custom of sacrifices. For the time of expenses (which we learn from divine Scripture in more than one place, and rarely otherwise) was when they performed the sacred rite. Hence that saying of the comic poet: "If on a feast day you squander something, you may be reduced to begging, unless you spare." Likewise: "Whatever expense you incur in divine matters is gain to the wise." Hence also from isthō, to feast, to entertain with a banquet, come Latin festum and festus dies for a day kept as a holiday; and conversely the English (or rather French) feast and feasting for a banquet, from Latin festum, a holy day. By a similar reasoning, since among those ancients almost no covenants or pacts were made without some solemnity of offering or libation, aspondō, which properly means to pour a libation, was no less often used for to make a pact and strike a covenant. Whence also the Latin spondeo. And the Latin delibare, to diminish (which is not far from the sense of the English verb), comes from the custom of sacrifices. From these and countless other words, such as eximius, egregius, and so on, which are obvious to a rather attentive reader, I have given so many examples because of the closeness of the Latin pendo, expendo, impendo (whence also Italian spendere). If anyone prefers to trace the English word back to these, I will not object too strongly. I thought otherwise, and, as the great Hippocrates once said of himself, arguments moved him to believe what he had heard. So we: the reasons that led us to think otherwise we have thought fit to submit candidly to the reader's judgement.

units.la: Σλίβας, (quod etiam σοίβας) torus, culcitra, &c. etiam ramus ex arbore excisus, ut Marci XI. 8. a stubb: stipes, truncus, &c. olim stpbbe. Ex Latino stipes malint aliqui fortasse. Sed cur non tam hoc ex Græco (ex quo & Latinum verbum:) quàm proximum
units.tr: sklibas (also soibas): a couch, a mattress, and so on; also a branch cut from a tree, as in Mark 11:8, stubb: a stump, a trunk, and so on; formerly stubbe. Some would perhaps prefer the Latin stipes. But why not derive it rather from the Greek (from which the Latin word also comes) than from the nearer stump?

units.la: <bl>stump</bl>: aut quod paulò suprà, <bl>stalke</bl>; & <bl>stemme</bl>?
units.tr: <bl>stump</bl>; or, as mentioned a little above, <bl>stalke</bl>; and <bl>stemme</bl>?

units.la: Σλύμῳ, σλεχῳ, κορμὸς, Hesychio, i,e.truncus; a stump.
units.tr: slumō, slechō, kormos: in Hesychius, that is, a trunk; <bl>a stump</bl>.

units.la: Σμώπω, (vel σμύσω: de utroque confulendus author Etymologici, in σμώλίξ: nam in Stephano non reperio:) πλάσσω, verbero, caedo; to smigbt.
units.tr: smōpō (or smusō; on either, consult the author of the Etymologicum under smōlix, for I do not find it in Stephanus): I strike, I beat, I hit; <bl>to smite</bl>.

units.la: Σλύω, tentigine laboro: unde & σύμα, σύλινος, & ἐσύλω, quae à b,m. parente in Animadverf.in Athenaeum explicantur: nam frustra alibi quaeres. Anglis, stewes, lupanar: quod quidam ex stew, vel stove, quod thermas significat,deducunt: quod aliàs quamvis non improbabile, eò magis mihi suspectum est, quòd in nulla linguarum, quibus levi discrimine, posterius hoc in usu, (estuve,stufa,estnfa, stub, stove,) prioris illius significationis vestigium ullum reperiam. Quòd autem stewes pro thermis, ex σαθάω, foveo, calefacio, tanquam verbo Graeco repetunt; cum nullibi nisi apud Hesychium reperiatur, probabilius est ex Anglico natum,quàm Anglicum ex illo; nec ab Hesychio ut genuinum Graecum afferri,sed ut verbum peregrinum explicari.
units.tr: slyō: I suffer from lust (tentigo). Hence also suma, sulinos, and esulō, which are explained by the late Meursius (of blessed memory) in his Animadversions on Athenaeus; for you will look for them in vain elsewhere. To the English, stewes means a brothel. Some derive it from stew or stove, which means a hot bath. Though this is not improbable, I suspect it the more because in none of the languages, which differ slightly in the later usage (estuve, stufa, estufa, stub, stove), do I find any trace of that earlier meaning. As for their deriving stewes in the sense of baths from the Greek sathaō, to foment, to warm, as if it were a Greek word, since it is found nowhere except in Hesychius, it is more probable that the word arose from the English rather than the English from it. It is cited from Hesychius not as genuine Greek but as a foreign word to be explained.

units.la: Est autem st̄ stetū, Anglis, carnem inter duas patinas lento igne elixare. Tanto magis id dicamus, si Hefychium ipsum adeamus, cujus hæc verba : Σἰα- Θεὸσαι, τὸ τῷ πνεῖ, ἡσυχῇ χλιένα ψέας, ἡ τὸ σπῖνσαι. Σλαθάλὸς, πεφλογμένῳ ψέψα. Quis non dicat Hefychium Anglica (ta steto, & steteped meat) in animo habuisse cum ista scriberet? Potest tamen aliter res habere, ut genuinum Græcum fuerit istud stlæ, sed dudum antiquatum apud Græcos, quod apud Anglos cum plurimis aliis (ut Plutarchus in simili re loquitur,) exulaverit. Hoc addam, si analogia spestetur, probabilius esse stetes, ex stasas (absorpto, ut in pluribus aliis, de quibus supra, medio θ.) per contractionem; quàm sταδ̄ν ex stetes ortum esse.
units.tr: Stew is, for the English, to boil meat slowly between two dishes over a gentle fire. All the more should we say this if we consult Hesychius himself, whose words are: Stheisai: to be warmed gently, to be heated slowly, or to simmer. Sthalathalos: meat cooked over a flame. Who would not say that Hesychius had the English words stew and stewed meat in mind when he wrote this? Yet the matter may stand otherwise: this stlæ may be genuine Greek but long obsolete among the Greeks, and among the English, as Plutarch says in a similar case, it has gone into exile along with many other words. I will add this: if analogy is considered, stewes is more probably formed from stasas (with the th dropped in the middle, as in many other cases mentioned above) by contraction, than stadōn arose from stewes.

units.la: Σͅυς,& ρευσς (quod usitatius) passer. Etiam struthio (aliàs ρχαδιοκμων ἀ- dictus) avis omnium maxima, & procerissima. Hinc Græcis ρχωπυς, pedes habens amplos, & longos; ut vulgò interpretantur. Sed & illi fastase sic dicti, qui incessu struthionem quasi imitantur. Hoc certum est, quæ majora solitis essent, ρψθ nuncupata; ta: unde ςρέθδα μῆλα, id est, majora. Anglis, to stowt out; inflari, turgere. Et de illis ut plurimum usurpant, qui affectato cultu & incessu longos, ut Horatius ipse de se alicubi, id est, opulentiores, & beatiores, supra fortunæ suæ conditionisque modulum, libenter imitantur.
units.tr: strouthos (more commonly rhouthos, "sparrow"). Also the ostrich, otherwise called strouthokamēlos, the largest and tallest of birds. Hence the Greeks called strouthōpous one who has large, long feet, as it is commonly translated. Also those called fastasai are so named because they seem to imitate the ostrich's gait. It is certain that things larger than usual were called strouthoi, and so strouthaia mēla, that is, larger apples. In English, to stowt out: to swell, to be puffed up. And people usually use it of those who, by affected dress and gait, willingly imitate the longos (long-striders) as Horace himself says of himself somewhere; that is, the wealthier and more fortunate, going beyond the measure of their own fortune and condition.

units.la: Στοαὶ, porticus; & de variis locis usurpabatur: στοαὶ dicebantur etiam loca, in quibus frumentum recondebatur: τὰ ταμεῖα ἐν οἷς ὁ σιτος, inquit Aristophanis, Stephano laudatus, Scholiastes: id est, horrea. Anglis veteribus, stow, locus: stowage, collocatio, dispositio, in loco: ut Verfteganus observat. Hodie, to be-stow, collocare, (ut cum de collocatione liberorum, <bl>He hath bestowed her on him</bl>, &c. aut proprii temporis & otii collocatione, <bl>how to bestow</bl>, &c.) Item, largiri, q.d. de proprio penu, & peculio: to bestow upon one, &c.) Stoudge, pabulum reconditum proprie: sed ad alia sæpe, quæ recondita servantur, transfertur. Steward, fortasse, quasi stoward, dispensator, custos, vel (ut alicubi Plautus) procurator peni, promus condus, ταμίεχος. τμιῦχ@· Ϭtoje, vel ut alii, stoare, quamvis affinia; ab alia tamen origine. ΣΤεφὶω, privo,&c.to starbe. Sed & to steale, furari; r. in l. mutato, de quo suprà.
units.tr: stoai, porticoes; and the word was used of various places. Stoai were also the places where grain was stored: ta tameia en hois ho sitos, as the scholiast on Aristophanes, cited by Stephanus, says; that is, granaries. In old English, <bl>stow</bl>, a place; <bl>stowage</bl>, a placing, arrangement in a place, as Verstegan observes. Today, <bl>to bestow</bl>, to place (as when speaking of placing a daughter in marriage, <bl>He hath bestowed her on him</bl>, and so on, or of the disposal of one's time and leisure, <bl>how to bestow</bl>, and so on). Also to give freely, as from one's own store and savings: <bl>to bestow upon one</bl>, and so on. <bl>Stoudge</bl>, properly stored fodder, but often transferred to other things that are kept in store. <bl>Steward</bl>, perhaps as if <bl>stoward</bl>, a dispenser, keeper, or (as Plautus somewhere has it) a procurator of the store-room, a steward of the pantry; Greek tamias. <bl>Stoje</bl>, or as others have it, <bl>stoare</bl>, though related, has a different origin. Stepheō, I deprive, and so on: <bl>to starve</bl>. But also <bl>to steale</bl>, to steal; r for l, changed, as mentioned above.

units.la: ΣΤλίκλω, comprimo; fo still.
units.tr: stilbō, I press down, compress; <bl>to still</bl>.

units.la: ΣΤηεἰζω, statuo firmiter,figo: sηεἰζομαι, fulciop,stabilior,&c. Angl.starbe, rigidus, immotus: ut, starbe-deno. Strong, fortis, robustus, firmus, bene stabilitus & fultus: ἰσηεὶ μιν ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ, (ii.Pet.i.) strong in the faith. Si quis malit τὸ strong. ex ςηρρὸς, firmus, validus, &c. repetere, non valde reputabo: quanquam illud verius putem.
units.tr: stēreizō, I establish firmly, I fix: stēreizomai, I prop up, make firm, and so on. English <bl>starke</bl>, stiff, motionless, as in <bl>stark-dead</bl>. <bl>Strong</bl>: strong, robust, firm, well established and supported: estērikto in the faith, 2 Pet. 1, strong in the faith. If anyone prefers to derive <bl>strong</bl> from sthrōs, firm, valid, and so on, I will not contend much, though I think the latter more correct.

units.la: ΣΤιφ̣ρ̣ς, firmus,validus,rigidus. Hinc stiff; nisi ex ἀσφαλής, de quo suprà.
units.tr: stiphros: firm, strong, stiff. Hence <bl>stiff</bl>, unless it comes from asphalēs, mentioned above.

units.la: ΣΤιβαρὲς, gravis,firmus,robustus,validus: ςιβαρὴ βαρυχίος, & ἀνυχλὼ ςιβαρὲς apud Homerum. stubborne, contumax. storbp, robustus.
units.tr: stibaros: heavy, firm, robust, strong; stibara barychios and anychō stibaros in Homer. <bl>Stubborne</bl>, obstinate. <bl>Storbp</bl>, robust.

units.la: ΣΤορχή, naturalis amor,qualis parentum erga filios, aut filiorum erga parentes. a stoict, ciconia. Græcis, πίλαφ̣-ῶ, (unde ἀνλιπλαφ̣ὴν :) & Hebræis, דכח à חנם misericordia, ob eandem rationem: ut jam multis observatum.
units.tr: storgē, natural affection, such as that of parents toward children, or children toward parents. <bl>A stork</bl>, ciconia. Among the Greeks pelargos (whence antipelargēn); and among the Hebrews chesed [חסד], mercy, for the same reason, as many have already observed.

units.la: ΣΤνίβαλον, Σκύβαλον, stercus; ut apud Apostolum Philip. II. veteres & recentiores interpretes. Nec male. Sæpè enim ita usurpatur, ut τὸ διὰ τῶν ἐντέρων ἐκδιδόμενον, quod ex ventre excernitur, qualecunque fit, significet: ut & author Etymologici explicat. Est alioquin σκύβαλον non enim abs re Christiani lectoris, aut à professione meâ alienum, verbi Apostolici quod se nobis obtulit, & ab aliis satis jejunè tractatum reperio, explicationi aliquamdiu immorari: ) omne in genere rejectamentum, retrimentum, purgamentum: omne (ut apud Plutarchum, qui lanam, ungues, capillos, inter σκύβαλα enumerat) ἀπόψημα. Unde apud Etymologicum τὰ ἀποβέσματα (furfures tritici: vulgò bran: ídque ex Græco, βέσμα, ἀπόβεσμα: sed ad Anglos, à Gallis an Græcis; vetus id est, an novum, non scio:) σκύβαλα τῆς πυρῆς exponuntur. Cæterum, si verbi etymologia spectetur, quicquid ob vilitatem canibus objicitur, aut canibus proprie competit, id est proprie σκύβαλον, quasi κυσὶ βαλλόμενον, ut ab eodem docemur Etymologici Magni authore: Hinc micæ, & alia quaecunque epularum rejectanea quae seu à canibus, seu ab aliis quibuscunque colliguntur, σκύβαλα quoque dicuntur. In collectione Graecorum Epigrammatum(quae vulgò Ανθολογία,&c.) duo lepidissima sunt & venustissima, non eodem tantùm capite, sed & ordine proxima sibi, & cohaerentia Epigrammata, in quibus vox ista eo sensu occurrit. In priore praeparcus quidam alloquitur mures,quos jubet ex aedibus suis facessere, ut nihil quo tueri se possint inventuros. Se enim ἀυλάξεσθαι à parentibus doctum, frugi hominem esse, &c.
units.tr: skybalon [σκύβαλον], refuse, dung; as in the Apostle, Philip. II., both older and newer translators render it. Not unfairly, for it is often used to signify to dia tōn enterōn ekdidomenon, whatever is discharged from the bowels, of whatever kind, as the author of the Etymologicum also explains. It is otherwise skybalon. I find that this word of the Apostle, which presented itself to us, has been treated rather meagrely by others, and it is not out of place for a Christian reader, or foreign to my profession, to linger on its explanation for a while. Any refuse, leftover, or rubbish, anything (as Plutarch, who counts wool, nails, and hair among skybala) that is scraped off, is apopsēma. Hence in the Etymologicum, ta apobesmata (wheat bran, commonly bran, from the Greek besma, apobesma; but whether this is from the French or the Greek when it reached the English, whether old or new, I do not know) are explained as skybala tēs purēs. Moreover, if the etymology of the word is considered, whatever is thrown to dogs because of its worthlessness, or properly belongs to dogs, is properly skybalon, as if kysi ballomenon, thrown to dogs, as the author of the Etymologicum Magnum teaches us. Hence crumbs and other leftovers of food, which are gathered up either by dogs or by anyone else, are also called skybala. In the collection of Greek epigrams (commonly called the Anthology, and so on) there are two very witty and charming epigrams, not only under the same heading but also placed next to each other and connected in order, in which this word occurs in this sense. In the first, a certain thrifty fellow addresses mice and orders them to leave his house, since they will find nothing there by which they can support themselves. For he says he was taught by his parents to be a thrifty man, and so on.

units.la: Τῷ π μελλανδίς τύπον μυχὸν, ὦ φιλοξένε,
units.tr: Do not make your den in the letters of the page, O friend of strangers [Τῷ πυρὶ μελλανδὶς τύπον μυχὸν, ὦ φιλοξένε]

units.la: Οὐδ' ἀποδιπτεύς γλυπτῷ σκυβάλου.
units.tr: Nor gnaw the carved scraps of refuse [Οὐδ' ἀποδιπτεύς γλυπτῷ σκυβάλου]

units.la: Proximum, ejusdem cujus prius argumenti ; nisi quod de libris non arrodendis, ut qui etiam muribus devorati, ne dum hominibus lecti, nauseam movere possint, lepida cautio additur, Sed vox σκύβαλον in istis :
units.tr: This is next to the previous one in subject, except that it adds a witty caution about not gnawing books: even when devoured by mice, let alone read by men, they can cause nausea. But the word σκύβαλον occurs in these lines as well.

units.la: Οὐ γὰρ ποτὲ τοῦ ἀποδεξάσθε γ' ἄλλων Ιφιδάμα, ἢ δὲ τίμησον συγχρὸν ἀπὸ σκυ- (βάλων.
units.tr: For never ... of others, Iphidamas, nor do you honour [them] with the refuse [σκυβάλων].

units.la: Phocylides, poëta difertissimus & purissimus: Μηδ' ἐλλυ ἀλλ' ἀλλὰ ξένοις ἀνθρώπων ἁπαξ idest, Neque ex aliena mensa micas velut canis asserte-ris. Ex hoc usu verbi σκύβαλον non dubito quin to scamble ( quod alioquin etiam ex σκύμνος catulus, cujusecunque sit animalis, duci posset:) & scramblingly; quod de canibus proprie dicitur objectas offas avidè & cum mutuo conflictu diripientibus. Sed & squamble squamble quoque id dicunt. In accuratissimo & laudatissimo Gallico-Anglico Lexico, quod Cotgravii nomen praefert, ita reperio: [Dzlffe graffe. Dp booke or by croake: squamble squamble: scramblingly: catch that catch may.] Hinc quoque fortasse & to squable, rixari, contendere cum clamore; quod esse causa pauperes inter & egenos saepe contingit.
units.tr: Phocylides, a most eloquent and pure poet: Neither from a stranger's table pick up crumbs like a dog. From this use of the word skybalon I have no doubt that "to scamble" is derived (it could also come from skymnos, a whelp, of whatever animal), and "scramblingly", which is said properly of dogs greedily tearing at scraps thrown to them and fighting each other for them. But they also say "squamble squamble". In the very accurate and praised French-English dictionary that bears the name of Cotgrave I find this: [Dzlffe graffe. Dp booke or by croake: squamble squamble: scramblingly: catch that catch may.] Hence perhaps also "to squable", to wrangle and contend with noise, which often happens among the poor and needy for this very reason.

units.la: Σβδίομαι, quasi σεγγδίομαι, id est, (proprie) paulatim & veluti χ᾽ σεγγα, id est, guttatim deficio: tabesco, consumor: to struggle. Homerus, IX. o'.
units.tr: Σβδίομαι, as if from σεγγδίομαι, that is (properly) I fail little by little and, as it were, drop by drop, I waste away, I am consumed: to struggle. Homer, Iliad 9.

units.la: Βίλλεσιν ἠ ἀπαλὰς ἐνα χειρὶ, ἢ βίον ἀνὰ, ᾿Η ἀλλὰ σκιδίσας ἐν αὐλῇ πωλεῖτε. id est, Molins aut perire uno tempore (at once ; vel once fo; all) aut vivere, (victores scilicet, si ita contingat, extra metum, & periculum:) Quàm diu Instari, (& paulatim consumi) in gravi pugnâ.Hoc Angli dicerent, to struggle long. Hinc etiam to strive, niti, eniti, proprie : & inde, contendere.
units.tr: Either to perish at once, or to live (conquerors, of course, if it so happens, free from fear and danger) as long as they are being worn down, and gradually consumed, in a grievous battle. The English would say "to struggle" long. Hence also "to strive", properly to strain, to exert oneself, and from that, to contend.

units.la: Σλλάω, σλλάομαι : promitto, firmo, præ me fero, jacto. Ita vulgatiora Lexica : nam apud Stephanum (quod mirum:) neque in Indice, nec alibi reperio. Est autem verbum Homero usitatissimum. Inter alios, locus hic notabilis :
units.tr: Σλλάω, σλλάομαι: to promise, to assure, to show forth, to boast. So the more common lexicons give it; for in Stephanus (which is surprising) I find it neither in the index nor elsewhere. It is, however, a word very commonly used by Homer. Among others, this passage is notable:

units.la: Ἰχθὺς Ἀρφεοι, μὴ βάλλε ἢ ξεῳ Ἀχαιῶν : Σλεῦ ξὲρ τι ἕπος ἐρέῳ κοεψάλιος Ἐλλαδος.
units.tr: Fool Paris, do not boast to the Achaeans ... for I will speak one word, which the Achaeans will hear.

units.la: sunt Agamemnonis de Hectore Paridis ad Græcos mandata ferente, verba. Longâ opus est periphrasi, ut vis verbi σλῶ exprimatur. Id enim vult, Hectorem præ se ferre speciem locuturi. Sed inest præterea huic verbo ἀπαγγέλλω, (ita vocant Græci quandam præfidentis animi orisque pro re natâ præsentiam & audaciam : ex eodem quo σλύομαι illud fonte:) & confidentiæ significatio ; ut si uno verbo utendum sit,non aliud Latinum melius respondeat huic loco, quàm minatur: ( quomodo Horatius, Atqui vultus erat, pulchra & praclara minantis ; alibíque: unde & Gallicum mine pro vultu & exteriore fpecie:) Hector minatur, (id eft, ipsâ praefidentis oris fpecie promittit) fe aliquid locuturum. In aliis locis Homericis ubi idem verbum occurrit, non eadem difficultas, quòd manifeftior in illis jactantiae & confidentiae indicatio: ut cum de eodem Hectore ait,
units.tr: These are the words of Agamemnon about Hector, who carried Paris' message to the Greeks. A long periphrasis is needed to express the force of the verb σλῶ. For it means that Hector showed in his face the look of one about to speak. But there is also in this verb a sense of ἀπαγγέλλω (the Greeks use this word for a certain presence and boldness of spirit and countenance, as the occasion requires, from the same source as σλύομαι) and of confidence; so that if one word must be used, no Latin word answers this passage better than minatur (as Horace has it: "Yet his face was beautiful and splendid when he threatened"; and elsewhere; whence also the French mine for face and outward appearance). So: Hector threatens (that is, by the very look of his face he promises) that he will say something.

units.la: Σλεῦ͂ ϛ γὰρ ὑπνῶν ἀπονώϊ̈ν ἀχρα κόρυμβα
units.tr: For he was threatening to ... the ships with ... fire.

units.la: ᾿Αυλὰς δ᾽ ἐμαρπήσϊν μαλερῷ πυρὶ ἐός, &c.
units.tr: ... and to seize the ships with raging fire, etc.

units.la: Et Ια.β᾽. Σλεῦτο γὰρ δ᾽ χόμψῳ νικησῖμψ, εἴ ῳ ἂν ἀνλαί
units.tr: And in Iliad 11: for he thought he would conquer, if ...

units.la: Μεῖσι δείσοιεν χεῖρες Διὸς ἀγγίχοιο.
units.tr: ... the hands of Zeus would fear the mighty spear.

units.la: Et Ιλ.φ᾽. Σλεῦτο δ᾽ οὐ ἀμφολίρων ἀπονα- λίψ ῥα χαλκῷ.
units.tr: And in Iliad 15: he threatened with bronze ... (the spear, to strike the Achaeans).

units.la: In his & similibus, de apertâ jactatione, & infolentiore gloriatione verbum ufurpatur. Hinc Angli finxerunt suum <bl>stout</bl>, quo hominem audacem & praesidentem indicant.
units.tr: In these and similar passages the word is used of open boasting and rather insolent vaunting. Hence the English coined their "stout", by which they indicate a bold and confident man.

units.la: Σβόμβῳ, turbo, trochus: Etiam ἀνεσφῇ ἀνέμων, vertex, turbo, procella, (aliter, ῥεβίλῳ) a Cozme.
units.tr: Σβόμβῳ: a whirl, a top; also the whirl of the winds, an eddy, a storm (otherwise ῥεβίλῳ), from Cosmas.

units.la: Σχισῆς,
units.tr: Σχισῆς: a split, a cleft.

units.la: Ξυσὸς, inter alia, genus vestis interioris: χιλὰν ξυσὸς, & ξυσὸς χιλωνικὸν: & simpliciter, ξυσαί, interula, ex scissura vel incisura sic dicta: a shirt.
units.tr: Xysos: among other things, a kind of inner garment: chiton xysos and xysos chitonikon; and simply xysai, an undershirt, so called from its slit or cut: a shirt.

units.la: Ξάγαεις vel σίγγαεις, gladius Persicus, secutis: σίγαεις λυσφλεβὶς, scalprum chirurgicum (ut Celsus appellat:) quo venæ aperiuntur. Vox origine Scythica, sed Græcis satis familiaris. Cujus vestigia in Saxon. verbo {bl}fearen{/bl}; de quo verbo plura dicemus in postremâ parte.
units.tr: Xagaeis or syngaeis: a Persian sword, and in the same way a surgical lancet (as Celsus calls it) with which veins are opened. The word is of Scythian origin, but quite familiar to the Greeks. Traces of it survive in the Saxon verb "fearen", about which we will say more in the last part.

units.la: Ξλίχω, columna, cui ædificium aliudve innititur; a stoole.
units.tr: Xlichos: a column on which a building or something else rests; a stool.

units.la: Ξληεα, sterilis, βῶς ςιῆα, apud Homerum, vacca. Anglis, a steere, juvencus: ob castrationem sterilis scil. & tauro oppositus.
units.tr: Xleea: barren; bous stieia in Homer, a cow. For the English: a steer, a young bullock, so called because it is barren, that is castrated, and opposed to the bull.

units.la: Ξτίρχα, σπέρχω, urgeo, festino, &c. σπερχυὸς, festinans, pernix, studiosus, studiosè incumbens alicui rei. Nescio an hinc sparth, de infignioris agilitatis & alacritatis puero; an potius metaphora sit à sparth, scintilla. Sed est præterea σπερχυὸς, ξίΘ (ut Hesychius) ξεγκ, genus accipitris. Angl. a sparhawke, vel sparrowhawke: ex Græco fine dubio; nisi hoc ipsum verbum Anglicum ( nullibi enim quod sciam alibi:) voluit Hefychius exponere, & in ἀπερχνὸς ita contraxit ; aut contractum ab aliis exhibuit. Sed & Galli dicunt effarvier: unde fortasse fluxit Anglicum.
units.tr: Ξτίρχα, from σπέρχω: I urge, I hasten, etc. Sperchyos: hastening, swift, eager, zealously devoted to some matter. I do not know whether "sparth" (of a boy of notable agility and eagerness) comes from this, or whether it is rather a metaphor from "sparth", a spark. But there is also sperchyos, a kind of hawk (as Hesychius has it). The English say "a sparhawke" or "sparrowhawke": doubtless from the Greek; unless Hesychius meant to explain this English word itself (which, as far as I know, occurs nowhere else) and contracted it into the Greek form, or else gave it as contracted by others. But the French also say effarvier, from which the English word perhaps came.

units.la: σκῆνος, tabernaculum, &c. item corpus humanum, non apud Platonem tantùm, & Pythagoreos, (ut in II.Cor. V. v.1. doctis notatum:) sed apud medicos quoque aliósque, Τηκεδὼν φθορὰ, corporis tabes, apud Aretium medicum. Atque ita in Democriti sententiis à doctiff. Holftenio editis, bis unà fi bene memini paginâ : neq; enim nunc liber ad manum. Sed & in Fragmentis ejus, à Stephano editis, sæpius. Etiam apud Longinum ἐξ ὑλῆς, ἀνθρώπου σῶμα, humanum corpus. Hodiernis Anglis, (lin, pellis : Est autem pellis quoddam quasi corporis tabernaculum, quod omnibus ejus undique partibus ut tegmen & munimen obtenditur : quomodo & ipsum corpus animæ σκῆνος etiam & ἔνυλος ab eâdem aut simili ratione nuncupatum. Id enim reliquo corpori pellis, quòd corpus animæ. Sed nec insolens metonymia, ut pellis, pro toto quod amhbit corpore sumatur. Possit tamen & τὸ σκῆνος ab δορὸς duci: δορὸς βοὸς apud Homerum, pellis ovina: δορὸς Μαρσύας apud Herodot. pellis Marsyæ, i.e. exuviæ, ut Camerar. interpretatur.
units.tr: Skēnos: a tent, etc.; also the human body, not only in Plato and the Pythagoreans (as learned men have noted on 2 Corinthians 5:1), but among physicians and others: tēkedōn phthora, the wasting of the body, in the physician Aretaeus. And so in the Sayings of Democritus edited by the learned Holstenius, twice on one page, if I remember rightly, for the book is not at hand now. Also often in his Fragments edited by Stephanus. Even in Longinus, ex hylēs, anthrōpou sōma, the human body. For modern English, "skin" (which is a kind of tent of the body, stretched over it on every side as a covering and defence; just as the body itself is called the tent (skēnos) of the soul and enylos, from the same or a similar reason. For the skin is to the rest of the body what the body is to the soul.) But it is not an unusual metonymy that the skin be taken for the whole body it surrounds. Yet skēnos might also be derived from doros: in Homer, doros boos is a sheepskin; in Herodotus, doros Marsyas is the skin of Marsyas, that is, his hide, as Camerarius interprets it.

units.la: Σῶμα, corpus: & ut anima (ψυχὴ Græcis) per synecdochen omnibus fere linguis usitatam; ita & corpus (σῶμα) pro integro homine interdum ponitur. Anglis utrumque familiare: no soule: no bodie: pro nemo. Sed posterius tamen usitatius. Non enim dicunt some soule, ut some bodie, pro aliquis. Suspicatus sum sæpe Anglicum illud some, (quod interdum absolute, ut some are of opinion, &c. aliquando cum bodie jungitur; ut in prioribus exemplis:) ex Græco σῶμα fluxisse. Ridebunt, credo, imperiti; at non illi fortasse, qui quem usum habeant Hebraica בשר & גוף non in doctorum tantum libris, sed in ipsa quoque sacra Scriptura non ignorant. Latinum persona, factum est, ut doctis placet, ex πρὸς σῶμα: & Chaldaicum גוף (quod & Græco σῶμα fortasse dedit originem: nam ὁρώμενον pro σώματα interdum poni satis constat.) stat:) proprie,nomen; vulgò,pro aliquis usurpatur. Sed & priscos Latinosfum pro eum dixisse, ex Festo discimus: quod an hùc aliquid faciat,nescio. Sed nihil æquè auget suspicionem mèam ac doɑti viri de origine impersonalis, seu impersonalibus verbis servientis apud Gallos on particulæ origine observatio: Ita autem illé in Grámaticâ suâ Gallicâ, quæ Latinè, & Gallicè seorsim An. Dom. 1569: typis Stephanicis excusa est. Majores,inquit ille,nostri frequenter scripserunt hom in significatione impersonali passiva: veluti ut Gallicè verterent Curritur, scribebant, hom court, vel l'hom court: tanquam si Latinè dicéretur, Homo currit: unde factum est nostrum, On dit : on fuit : pro Latino; Dicitur, Fit : h.ablato, & m.verso in n. Hactenus ille: Objiciat aliquis fortasse, quòd huic Anglico some, additur interdum bodle; vel men : ut some bodle : some men;&c. Sed hoc nihil est. Prius enim illud some, quamvis (ut nos quidem suspicamur) originè idem, postquam tamen usu (ut & Gallicum illud on:) nunc aliud est; & in pronominis naturam transiit, nihil vetat, quin nominibus
units.tr: Sōma: body; and, as psychē (soul) is used by the Greeks for the whole man, a figure of speech (synecdoche) nearly common in almost all languages, so the body (sōma) is sometimes put for the whole man. Both are familiar in English: "no soule", "no bodie", for nobody; but the latter is more usual. For they do not say "some soule", as they say "some bodie", for "someone". I have often suspected that the English "some" (which sometimes stands alone, as in "some are of opinion", and sometimes is joined with "bodie", as in the earlier examples) came from the Greek sōma. The untrained will laugh, I suppose; but perhaps not those who know what use the Hebrew basar and guf have, not only in learned books but in Holy Scripture itself. The Latin persona, as learned men like to think, arose from prosōpon; and the Chaldee guf (which perhaps also gave rise to the Greek sōma, for it is quite clear that ōrōmenon is sometimes put for sōmata) properly means a name, and is commonly used for "someone". But from Festus we learn that the early Latins also said fum for eum; whether this bears on the question, I do not know. Yet nothing increases my suspicion so much as the observation of learned men on the origin of the particle on, which among the French serves impersonal verbs. The man who wrote this in his French grammar, printed in Latin and French separately in the year of our Lord 1569 and issued by the Stephanus press, says: "Our elders often wrote hom in the impersonal passive sense: so, to translate Curritur (it is run), they wrote hom court or l'hom court, as if one said in Latin Homo currit; whence came our On dit: on fuit, for Latin Dicitur, Fit, the h dropped and the m changed into n." So far he. Someone may perhaps object that to this English "some" the word "bodie" or "men" is sometimes added: some bodie, some men, etc. But this is nothing. For the former "some", although (as we indeed suspect) originally the same, after it has been used (like the French on) is now something different and has passed into the nature of a pronoun; and nothing prevents it from being joined to nouns

units.la: A a minibus ejusdem cujus & ipsum (si originem spectes) significationis, recte jungi possit. Talia multa memini observare, quae legentibus fortasse, mihi certe nunc ista scribenti in mentem non veniebant. Non omnino dissimilia, ἑνάλιος (quod ex ἔννεα & νύλες compositum:) νύλες; & ποδόνιπτρα ποδῶν; & βοῶν ἁπβέκολον ἀνὴρ; & ὑνοχοῶν ὕνον, & id genus alia quae apud Poëtam incomparabilem observarunt veteres Grammatici: in quibus cum ejusdem verbi manifesta sit repetitio, a tautologia tamen facile excusantur.
units.tr: They may rightly be joined to a noun of the same meaning as the thing itself, if one looks to the origin. I remember observing many such cases, which readers perhaps, and certainly I myself while writing this, did not think of. Not entirely unlike these are ἑνάλιος (compounded of ἔννεα and νύλες) [enalios], νύλες [nyles], ποδόνιπτρα ποδῶν [podonipra podon], βοῶν ἁπβέκολον ἀνὴρ [boōn apbekolon anēr], and ὑνοχοῶν ὕνον [hynochoōn hynon], and the other kinds that the ancient grammarians noted in the incomparable Poet. In these there is a plain repetition of the same word, but they are easily excused from the charge of tautology.

units.la: Σείω, praeter σείσω, σεισμός, quatere, concutere; to shake.
units.tr: Σείω [seiō], besides σείσω [seisō] and σεισμός [seismos], means to shake, to agitate; to shake.

units.la: Σεύω, cieo, agito, concito: Item persequor, incesso, fugo: ἀπο-σεύω, impello; to thrust. Fortasse & to shun, vitare.
units.tr: Σεύω [seuō] means to drive, to rouse, to urge on; also to pursue, to assail, to put to flight. ἀπο-σεύω [apo-seuō] means to drive off, to thrust; to thrust. Perhaps also to shun, to avoid.

units.la: Σήθω, cribro, as; excutio cribro, agito; to sist.
units.tr: Σήθω [sēthō] means to sift, to sieve; to shake out in a sieve, to stir; to sift.

units.la: Σχῆμα, habitus, cultus. Item habitus oris & gestus: dignitas, decus: ἀσχημοσύνη, immodeste se gerere: inverecundum aliquid & homine pudico indignum patrare. Etiam latius, moribus & vita turpi coinquinari. Εὔσχημον, decorus, modestus: ἀσχήμων, indecorus, immodestus. Quæ cum certa sint & obvia, nollem virum doctiss. in nupero opere afferere non tam corporis figuram, quàm habitum & vestis decus hoc verbo signari: & negare, Shematio, mediæ ætatis verbum hinc esse. Verè ille quidem poterat dicere, Shematio, ex Anglico to shame; vel Germanico Shamen immediatè factum: at illa, quæso, unde? Est & διχημοσυνη verbum, pro, modestè & honestè loquor; & διχημοσυνη nomen, modestia: constans animi status, nullis aut doloris aut gaudii perturbationibus infracti; aut obnoxii: quo omnes alias virtutes interdum referunt philosophi. Interpretes Græci Bibliorum verenda corporis, quæ Hebræi pudicè ערוה vel ערוה (αιδοιον proprie) nuncupant, verbo non minus pudico αιδημοσυνη solent exprimere. Idem verbum ערוה (unde Græc. τσεσω, & vetus Latinum, de quo multa Scaliger Catalecta Virgilii, puta: sed & Italicum potta; ex quo, puttana, putta, putaine, recentiora; pro, meretrix: fortasse & Latinum, pudor, &c.) Efdr. 16. αἰσχύνη verterunt: ערוה ערוה ערוה κύκλῳ αἰδημοσύνη τὰ αἰσχύνη (alii, αἰσχύνω)
units.tr: Σχῆμα [schēma] means bearing, dress; also the expression of the face and gesture; dignity, decorum. ἀσχημοσύνη [aschēmosynē] means behaving indecently, doing something shameless and unworthy of a modest man; more broadly, being defiled by base morals and life. Εὔσχημον [euschēmon] means becoming, modest; ἀσχήμων [aschēmōn] means unbecoming, immodest. Since these things are certain and obvious, I would not wish a learned man, in a recent work, to assert that this word signifies not so much the shape of the body as bearing and the dignity of dress, and to deny that shematio is a medieval word derived from it. He could truly say that shematio comes from the English to shame, or was formed directly from the German Shamen; but whence, I ask, do those come? There is also the verb διχημοσυνη [dichēmosynē], meaning to speak modestly and honourably, and the noun διχημοσυνη, modesty: a steady state of mind, not broken or subject to disturbances of grief or joy; to which the philosophers sometimes refer all the other virtues. The Greek translators of the Bible usually render by the no less modest word αἰδημοσύνη [aidēmosynē] the parts of the body which the Hebrews modestly call ערוה [ervah] or ערוה [ervah] (properly αἰδοῖον [aidoion]). The same word ערוה [ervah] (whence the Greek τσεσω [tsesō] and the old Latin puta, on which Scaliger has much to say in his Catalecta Virgilii; but also the Italian potta, whence the more recent puttana, putta, putaine, meaning harlot; perhaps also the Latin pudor, etc.) they rendered in Ezekiel 16 by αἰσχύνη [aischynē]: ערוה ערוה ערוה [ervah ervah ervah] ... κύκλῳ αἰδημοσύνη τὰ αἰσχύνη [kyklō aidēmosynē ta aischynē] (others, αἰσχύνω [aischynō]).

units.la: - Σίσλαι, ενώπα: inaures. Hesychius: qui etiam σίχλαι scribit, & similiter exponit. Σισλοφόρων, φάος (ut idem Hesychius) ἀνύχων τὰς χλαλαῦδας ἡ ενοῦλίων, σίσλας φάσιν· οἱ δ, ἀνὰ τὰ ενώπα: id est, ut ego interpretor, quia alibi non reperio: Σισλοφόρων, officium vel munus ad Eunuchos pertinens. Aiunt enim σίγλας scrinia monilium esse: alii, monilia ipsa interpretantur. Anglis olim, sigle, monile. Et ab illis, mediæ ætatis (ut probabile est) scriptores, sigle: de quo in aliqua Somnerianarum lucubrationum plura legere memini. Potuerunt autem à Græcis (ut alia multa Græcis usitata, etsi non Græca genuina,) habuisse Germani, seu Saxones, * quamvis Hebraicam potiùs sapiat originem, quàm Græcam. Sed videamus tamen, numquid & Græca origo, possit inveniri non incommoda. Σίσλαλός Homero verbum familiare, quod adjunctum nominibus substantivis summum earum seu pretium, seu artificium notat : tale utique,quod fpeGantes admiratione & filentio (unde & verbo fecundum quofdam origo :) figere fit idoneum. Ita Ix. ε'. Αλλ' ἀλλ' νῦν μάσησα ἡ ἴνια σαλόεντα Δίξαι. & iterum eodem libro — ἀυλὰρ ὃν' ἥρως Ὤν ἵππων ὃπηλας ἴλαβ' ἴνια σαλόεντα. Idem Οδ. ο'. Χίτωνα σαλόεντα, de Telemachi tunicâ : & alibi pariter non femel. Confulent Euftathium, quibus ejus adeundi copia. Apud auctorem Etymologici, (quem poft Euftathium commendatiffimum omnibus linguæ Græcæ ftudiofis cupiò:) fic reperio. Σιλαόεντα, σημάνει τὰ πεπονιλαμένα : ἀφὰ τὸ σίζω, σιλαόεντα, ἡ σαλόεντα: Diverfa hæc origo à priore : fed Græca tamen. At Hefychius ; Σισ-λοῖν, ποιαλόν τῇ γέαφῃ, λαμφῶν. σαλάωμα δοῖ Σνῴ ἀλυ λέγουσι, &c. cætera à libris & otio meliùs paratis relinquam. Sed ille facit Scythicam vocem. Nos autem Scytharum illorum linguam, qui Græcis notiores, & quibufcum frequentia illis ob vicinitatem commercia, non aliam remur fuiffe, quàm Germanicam. Fuerit igitur (fecundum Hefychium) vox pura puta Germanica, vel Saxonica ; & ab illis, à Græcis accepta. Sed hæc longiorem difquisitionem deriderant: nobis alio festinandum.
units.tr: Σίσλαι [sislai] and ενώπα [enōpa]: earrings. Hesychius, who also writes σίχλαι [sichlai] and explains it similarly. Σισλοφόρων [sislophorōn], as the same Hesychius has it: since I find it nowhere else, I interpret it as an office or duty pertaining to eunuchs. For they say that σίγλας [siglas] are cases for necklaces; others interpret them as the necklaces themselves. Formerly the English had *sigle*, a necklace; and from them medieval writers (as is likely) *sigle*; I remember reading more about this in one of Somner's studies. The Germans or Saxons may have had it from the Greeks, as many other things used by the Greeks, though not genuinely Greek. Yet it savours of a Hebrew origin rather than a Greek one. But let us see whether a Greek origin, not unsuitable, can be found. Σίσλαλός [sisalos]... Homer's familiar word σαλόεις [saloeis], which, joined to substantives, denotes either their chief value or their workmanship: such a thing, in short, as is fit to fix the gaze of onlookers in admiration and silence (whence, according to some, the origin of the verb). So in Iliad 9: Ἀλλ' ἀλλ' νῦν μάσησα ἡ ἴνια σαλόεντα Δίξαι [Ἀλλά νυ μάσσησα ἠδ' ἵνια σαλόεντα δῖξαι] ... and again in the same book: ἀυλὰρ ὃν' ἥρως Ὤν ἵππων ὃπηλας ἴλαβ' ἴνια σαλόεντα [aular hon' hēros ...]. The same Homer, Odyssey: Χίτωνα σαλόεντα [chitōna saloenta], of Telemachus' tunic; and elsewhere likewise, more than once. Let them consult Eustathius, whose works they may easily get. In the author of the Etymologicum (whom after Eustathius I most strongly commend to all students of the Greek language) I find this: Σαλόεντα [saloenta] signifies things that have been shaken; from σίζω [sizō], *saloenta* or *saloenta*. This origin is different from the former, but still Greek. But Hesychius: Σισ-λοῖν [sis-loin], ..., σαλάωμα [salaōma]... ἄλυ λέγουσι [aly legousi], etc. I leave the rest to those who have books and leisure better prepared. But he makes it a Scythian word. As for us, we think the language of those Scythians, better known to the Greeks and with whom they had frequent trade because of their proximity, was none other than German. So it will have been (according to Hesychius) a pure word, purely German or Saxon, and taken from them by the Greeks. But these matters would mock a longer inquiry; I must hasten elsewhere.

units.la: Σπιλὸς, macula, labes, &c. a spet, ⁊ in tʒmigrat; ut ςοὰλ, ᾳαʒολὴ, &c.
units.tr: Σπιλὸς [spilos]: stain, blemish, spot, etc., from σπέω? [speō]; the letters being transposed, as in ςοὰλ, ᾳαʒολὴ, etc.

units.la: Σωλ͂ᾳωμ, & ἀχύζομαι, irafcor, &c. to shewe: succensere, increpare: nifi potius ex ϭωλὸς, opprobrium, maledictum, de quo supra.
units.tr: Σωλ͂ᾳωμ [sōlōm] and ἀχύζομαι [achyzomai]: to be angry, to rebuke, etc.; to be indignant; to scold; unless rather from ϭωλὸς [sōlos], reproach, curse, of which above.

units.la: Σικυ̃ς, à Suidâ exponitur, ἀὑοψεὶ, ἀσινὴς, & (idque Plutarchi loco adducto:) νοσωδὴς: cibi fastidiofus, infirmus, æger; sick.
units.tr: Σικυ̃ς [sikys], as Suidas explains it: ἀὑοψεὶ [auopsei], harmless and unhurt; and (citing a passage of Plutarch) νοσωδὴς [nosōdēs], unhealthy: fastidious about food, feeble, ill, sick.

units.la: Σξοφὴ, fraudulentum effugium, callida tergiversatio: ἀντιλογία, Hefych: contentiones, contradictiones, strife, contentio. De strife, supra in ςπεῖψις: nifi & illud ipsum, ex ςπάθη.
units.tr: Σξοφὴ [skophē]: a fraudulent escape, a crafty evasion. ἀντιλογία [antilogia], in Hesychius: contentions, contradictions; strife, contention. On strife, see above under ςπεῖψις [speipsis]; unless that very word comes from σπάθη [spathē].

units.la: Σεῦνας, fatuus: stultus. puto me lefiffe vel audivisse apud Anglos saunte, pro fatuo.
units.tr: Σεῦνας [seunas]: fatuous, foolish. I think I have read or heard among the English saunte for a fool.
