units.la: Σίνω, noceo, ledo: ἀνίλης, & ἀνίλωρ, nocuus, noxius, ἀνκῆς: to sin, peccare: a sinner, peccator: Germanicè, sund, sunder.
units.tr: Σίνω [sinō]: I harm, injure. ἀνίλης [anilēs] and ἀνίλωρ [anilōr]: harmful, hurtful, noxious. to sin, to offend; a sinner, an offender; in German sund, sunder.

units.la: Σκία, umbra, &c. de quo supra: ςκιὰς, ςκιάδης, ςκιάδιον, &c. unde shade, & shadow, umbra.
units.tr: Σκία [skia]: shade, etc., of which above. σκιάς [skias], σκιάδης [skiadēs], σκιάδιον [skiadion], etc.; whence shade and shadow, umbra.

units.la: Σμύχω: Σμήχω, vide supra.
units.tr: Σμύχω [smychō]: Σμήχω [smēchō], see above.

units.la: Σίδηρος. Σιδηρος, & σιδηροφορεῖν. vide suprà. Σφεντὸς, flexilis, &c. σφενδὰ, armillæ, monilia, torques: funiculi, fibulæ, ut quidam apud Homerum exponunt; strap.
units.tr: Σίδηρος [sidēros], and σιδηροφορεῖν [sidērophorein]: see above. Σφεντὸς [sphentos], flexible, etc. σφενδὰ [sphenda]: armlets, necklaces, torques; cords, clasps, as some explain it in Homer; <bl>strap.</bl>

units.la: Σκαιὸς, lævus, sinister; ineptus, perversus, σκόλιος. Anglis, a squint, & a- skew, limus, obliquus.
units.tr: Σκαιὸς [skaios]: left, sinister; clumsy, perverse. σκόλιος [skolios]. For the English, <bl>a squint</bl> and <bl>askew</bl>: crooked, oblique.

units.la: Σχεδὸς, ἀχλὺς, ἀισχαλὸς: (Hesych.) i. portus, littus; a shore.
units.tr: Σχεδὸς [schedos], ἀχλὺς [achlys], ἀισχαλὸς [aischalos] (Hesychius): that is, a harbour, a shore; <bl>a shore.</bl>

units.la: Σβυρὸς, acerbus, austerus; de saporibus, proprie: & metaphoricè de homi-nibus; <bl>rugge:</bl> ut vulgò pronuntiatur. Sed scribitur <bl>rough.</bl>
units.tr: Σβυρὸς [sbyros]: harsh, austere; properly said of flavours, and metaphorically of men; <bl>rugge,</bl> as it is commonly pronounced, but it is written <bl>rough.</bl>

units.la: Σλαῖος, carina. Anglis, <bl>to steere,</bl> clavo assidere, navim gubernare; <bl>sterne,</bl> gubernaculum.
units.tr: Σλαῖος [slaios]: a keel. For the English, <bl>to steer</bl>: to sit at the helm, to govern a ship; <bl>stern</bl>: the rudder.

units.la: Σεμίλακες, simila, simila-go: unde simnel ducunt vulgata quædam Lexica. nam alioquin ex Latino quoque fieri potuit. ut & cracknell, & κολλύρα, collyra.
units.tr: Σεμίλακες [semilakes], simila, semolina: from which some common lexicons derive <bl>simnel</bl>; for otherwise it could also have come from the Latin, as could <bl>cracknell</bl> and κολλύρα [kollyra], collyra.

units.la: T
units.tr: T

units.la: Τρίχω, cursus: Item locus in quo currítur: Σχὸς, rota. Angl. <bl>a track,</bl> semita; vestigia. <bl>to track; oz trace,</bl> ve-stigare.
units.tr: Trichō [Τρίχω], a course; also the place where one runs. Schos [Σχὸς], a wheel. English: a track, a path, traces; to track, that is, to trace out.

units.la: Τευχοπίλη, sufflamen (quo impetus rotæ in declivibus locis sustinetur & impeditur:) a trigger.
units.tr: Teuchopilē [Τευχοπίλη], a drag-shoe (by which the force of a wheel is checked and held back on steep ground): a trigger.

units.la: Τήκω, liquefacio ; τηκομαι, liquefio, liquefco : to fath.
units.tr: Tēkō [Τήκω], to melt; tēkomai [τηκομαι], to be melted, to melt: to fath.

units.la: Τυλθὸς, parvus, parvulus, pusillus, infans: τυλθὺν βρέφος. tit. de infantibus & puerulis, in quotidiano sermone puto me non semel audivisse. tittmoufe, aliàs mitten : parus, parvula avis. Quasi equo proprie competeret, in accuratissimo Lexico Anglico-Gallico : Tit ; godal, roee, roffe, baridelle. Est etiam τιλθὸς, τιλλιτὸς, qui ab uberibus adhuc pendet, & lacte nutricis alitur: unde etiam, quando de infante & lactente usurpatur, verbum manare possit.
units.tr: Tylthos [Τυλθὸς], small, little, tiny, an infant; tylthun brephos [τυλθὺν βρέφος], a tiny baby. I think I have heard this word more than once in everyday speech, as a term for infants and little children. "Tittmouse," otherwise "mitten": a small bird, a little bird. As if it properly belonged to a horse, in the most accurate English–French dictionary: Tit; godal, roee, roffe, baridelle. There is also tilthos or tillitos [τιλθὸς, τιλλιτὸς], one still hanging at the breast and fed on the nurse's milk; whence, when it is used of an infant at the breast, the verb "to manare" (to flow) could also be applied.

units.la: Τεῖνα, lusus puerilis genus, quod Stephanus describit ; cui non absimilis, quem trap vocant Anglici pueri.
units.tr: Teina [Τεῖνα], a kind of children's game, which Stephanus describes. Not unlike it is the game English boys call "trap."

units.la: Τύπτω, verbero ; to thump.
units.tr: Typtō [Τύπτω], to beat, to strike: to thump.

units.la: Τολύνη, glomus, lanæ proprie ; sed de aliis quoque rebus dicitur : etiam de mazâ; (μαζὴ) ex quo massa Latinum ; a lamp. Ejusmodi, integrarum etiam initio syllabarum apharefes, etsi passim multæ : simillimum tamen in mentem nunc veniebat, μάζλ, recentioris Græciæ vocabulum, ex tumultu Latino factum : de quo doctissimus Meurfius in Glossario : μυλλέσιοι, tumultuarii, seditiosi. Vide & suprà in μύλυβδ@.
units.tr: Tolynē [Τολύνη], a ball or clew, properly of wool, but said also of other things, and of maza [μαζὴ], a barley cake; from which the Latin massa. Such aphaereses of whole initial syllables are common, though many are found everywhere. Yet a very similar word now came to mind: mazl [μάζλ], a word of more recent Greek, made from the Latin tumultu. On it the most learned Meursius, in his Glossary: mylleisioi [μυλλέσιοι], rioters, seditious persons. See also above under mylybd [μύλυβδ].

units.la: Τρυξ, Τυγὸς, fæx : bzeqs.
units.tr: Trygx [Τρυξ], genitive Tryges [Τυγὸς], dregs, lees: bzeqs.

units.la: Τρυσηλὸς, vindemiæ tempus, quando omnes occupatissimi : unde puto fluxisse, to bzaDge : nisi quis malit ex Τύχω, attero, vexo : Τύχομαι, atteror, conficior, &c. repetere.
units.tr: Trysēlos [Τρυσηλὸς], the time of the vintage, when everyone is very busy. I think from this came "to bzaDge," unless one prefers to derive it from Tychō [Τύχω], to wear down, to vex; Tychomai [Τύχομαι], to be worn down, to be exhausted, and so on.

units.la: Τείρω, infesto, molestiâ afficio, conficio, &c. <bl>to tpze</bl>.
units.tr: Teirō [Τείρω], to harass, to trouble, to wear out, and so on: to tpze.

units.la: Τέλλω, ἐντέλλω, mando, faciendum injungo : to tell. אמר Hebraicum, dicere, & mandare, seu præcipere.
units.tr: Tellō [Τέλλω], entellō [ἐντέλλω], to command, to enjoin something to be done: to tell. The Hebrew אמר means to say, and also to command or to order.

units.la: Τέλ@, vectigal ; (unde τέλῶ censeor, &c.) <bl>tole, tole-monte.</bl>
units.tr: Telos [Τέλ@], a tax, a tribute (whence telōō [τελῶ], to be assessed, and so on): tole, tole-monte.

units.la: Τελέω, pendo, penfito. ἀρξύριον τελὴν, & τελέσαι, sæpe occurrit apud Græcos scriptores : to tell, id est, numerare, pendere. τελῶ, attribuor, contribuor. : ἐπεὶθμέσαι, ἐπλείνομαι, ut ἀρξάμην τελέιν, cœpi numerari : εἰς Ἑλλήνας τελέιν, Græcus censeri, &c. proprie (ut Grammatici loquuntur, ad Etymologiam spectantes) dicerent Angli, 3 began to be told : &, to be told a Grecian : atque ita veteres etiam Angli suo tellan, usi : ufi:ut, And be as bim fo bearn felth: i. e. & ille nos pro liberis habuit: vel, in liberorum loco. Sed confuetudo nunc obtinuit, ut loco tell, aliud fynonymum ejus in his locutionibus ufurpetur. Dicunt enim, to be reckoneb,&c.
units.tr: Teleō [Τελέω], to pay, to weigh out. The phrases argyrion telein [ἀρξύριον τελὴν] and telesai [τελέσαι] often occur in Greek writers. In English: to tell, that is, to count out, to pay. Telō [τελῶ], to be assessed, to be contributed; epeithmesai and epleinomai (as in archomai telein [ἀρξάμην τελέιν], I began to be counted; eis Hellēnas telein [εἰς Ἑλλήνας τελέιν], to be enrolled as a Greek, and so on). Speaking as grammarians do, looking to the etymology, the English would say "I began to be told," and "to be told a Grecian." So also the old English used their tellan [tellan]: as in "And be as him so bearn felth," that is, "and he held us as children," or in the place of children. But custom has now prevailed, so that in these expressions another synonym of "tell" is used instead. For they say "to be reckoned," and so on.

units.la: Τελῶ, fum fub ditione : fum fub imperio. Hinc, ni fallor, <bl>to dwell</bl>, habitare, agere.
units.tr: Telō [Τελῶ], to be under another's sway, under command. Hence, unless I am mistaken, "to dwell": to live, to act.

units.la: Τωσάζω, dicteriis inceffo, irrideo, mordeo opprobriis,&c.<bl>to taunt</bl>. Item <bl>to twit</bl>.
units.tr: Tōsazō [Τωσάζω], to assail with taunts, to mock, to bite with reproaches, and so on: to taunt. Also to twit.

units.la: Τυΐλάζω, τυΐλαζι, id eft, (ut Hefychius exponit) ἀυλὸ ἡ ἀυλὸ λίσῃ, blatero; to twattle.
units.tr: Tyilazō [Τυΐλάζω], tyilazi, that is (as Hesychius explains) to chatter idly, to babble: to twattle.

units.la: Τάγγη, rancor : ταγγὸς, rancidus. de oleo proprie. In quibufdam Angliae partibus, (ut Cantio, ni fallor) de rancidis, aut aliter vitiatis liquidis, dicunt, It bath a tang.
units.tr: Tangē [Τάγγη], rancour; tanggos [ταγγὸς], rancid, said properly of oil. In some parts of England (as Kent, I think) they say of rancid or otherwise spoiled liquids: "It hath a tang."

units.la: Τηλίκῳ, tantus : de corporea, proprie, magnitudine ; <bl>tall</bl>, procerus.
units.tr: Tēlikos [Τηλίκῳ], so great, so large; said properly of bodily size: tall, of great stature.

units.la: Τεύπευον, veterator, vafer ; <bl>trapente</bl>, non femel audivi, vel, <bl>an old trapente</bl>, de vafro & tenace. Obviae sunt & aliae rationes, scio : sed quae mihi magis arrideat, aut tam probabilis videatur, nulla.
units.tr: Teupeuon [Τεύπευον], a sly old fellow, a crafty one: "trapente," as I have heard more than once, or "an old trapente," of a sly and tenacious man. I know of other explanations, but none pleases me more or seems so probable.

units.la: Τεχμηζα,
units.tr: Techmēza [Τεχμηζα],

units.la: Τραπέζα, mensa, pegma : a trap.decipulum : id est, ut Had. Junius in doctissimo Nomenclatore pluribus explicat, Laqueus quidam aut machina irretiendis aviculis, aut capiendis bestiis comparata.
units.tr: Trapeza [Τραπέζα], a table, a board: a trap, that is, as Hadrianus Junius explains at length in his learned Nomenclator, a snare or contrivance prepared for catching little birds or taking wild beasts.

units.la: Τρώξλης, comestor, (à τρώγω scilicet, arrodo, rodo, comedo :) vorator. Ita dicitur & Homero (ut viri doctiss. Camerarius & Steph. in suis uterque Thesauris:) qui ut habeat quod voret, quavis arte lucrum facit. Atque hæc est Eustathii & Hesychii, quorum verba Stephanus adduxit, expositio. Est autem verbum Homericum. Homeri verba quæ ab illis afferuntur, sunt hæc : ex Odyss. ζ. ἉΛΛ' ὅτε δὴ ἔσσυτο μοι ἐπιπλόμενον ἔτος ἦλθε, Αὐ τότε φοῖνιξ ἦλθεν ἀνὴρ ἀπάλιντα ἐιδός, Τρώξλης.
units.tr: Trōxlēs [Τρώξλης], a gnawer, a nibbler (from trōgō [τρώγω], to gnaw, to nibble, to eat); a devourer. The word is applied in the same way to Homer, as the learned Camerarius and Stephanus both say in their Thesauri: one who, in order to have something to eat, makes gain by any means. This is the explanation of Eustathius and Hesychius, whose words Stephanus cites. It is a Homeric word. The lines of Homer which they quote are these, from Odyssey 14 [ζ]: "But when the eighth year came round for me, then a Phoenician man came, a deceiver of false tales, a Trōxlēs [Τρώξλης]..."

units.la: id est, Sed cum octavus mihi rediens annus venit, jam tunc Phœnix vir fallacius sciens, Τρώξλης, &c.
units.tr: That is: "But when the eighth year came back to me, then a Phoenician man, skilled in deceit, a Trōxlēs, and so on."

units.la: Item ex sequente libro, Ἐν δὲ ᾗ φοίνικες ναυσὶν ἁλνὸν ἥλυθον ἀνδρες Τρῶξ, Τρῶχ), μυεῖ ἀσονλες ἀδύρμαλα ναὶ μελαίνη.
units.tr: Likewise from the following book: "There the Phoenicians, famous men of ships, came, bringing countless playthings in a black ship."

units.la: id est, Illuc autem Phœnices navibus inclyti venerunt viri, Τρῶχ), infinitas ducentes res ludicras (Gyphanianæ editionis hæc versio est) nave nigrâ. Mihi longè aliter videtur de hoc verbo, quàm vel Euftathio, vel Hefychio, aut qui ipsos sequuti sunt. Nec puto ullos eorum aliter de vero sensu quàm ego sentio, judicaturos fuisse, si linguam Anglicam intellexissent. Anglis hodié que verbum notissimum & usitatissimum, to truck, pro mercari, vel merces alias pro aliis mutare. Unde secundum analogiam, quamvis non fit in usu, trucker, (Ϛωκλης) fuerit, mercator, nundinator, negotiator. Nec mihi dubium, quin Dzuggs, & Dzugger (vel Dzuggiter) ab eâdem sint origine. Ϛωκλᾶ enim Græcis (quod & Ϛωκλια:) edulia, vesca quæcunque: sed proprie, quæ cruda (ut doctis placet) comedi solent, & secundis mensis apponi, ut raphani, pyra, poma, nuces, amygdalæ, & similia. Plura recenseuntur à Polluce: μυρλίδες, μάσπιλα, κόκκοι, ῥόα, κάρυα Πίστ-ακια, &c. quæ pleraque ex transmarinis locis locis navibus advehi solita. Talia autem pleraque quibus officinas suas instruere solent Pharmacopolæ: ut mirum non sit consuetudinem obtinuisse, ut ɒɪnggs, de Pharmacis; & ɒɪngstcr, de Pharmacopolâ proprie diceretur. Porrò, Phœnices ex Canaanitis oriundos, constans doctorum sententia est: & veteres quoque apud Procopium in eam rem inscriptiones, tum aliis, tum summo viro in De Diis Syris opere commemoratæ. Cananæi autem in Sacrâ ut omnes norunt historiâ (ut & Phœnices apud Ethnicos) à mercatura tam noti & nobiles, ut ipsum nomen Canaah, (Hebraicè, כנען) in commune mercatoris nomen transierit. כנען mercator, negotiator. כנענים, merx. Judicet jam lector, quàm appositá sit verbis Homer. hæc expositio: ut Phœnices scil. (notissimo illo & vulgatissimo apud omnes nationes Epitheto) mercatores nuncupentur; & mercatores sive negotiatores, à fraudibus & fallaciis, quibus ferè constat ista vita, perstringantur. Vulgata autem illa explicatio, quàm coacta sit & longè petita, quis non videt? Dicerem potius Φοίνικες ϛωλλῶ (si quidem ϛώϛω vera origo, & non est verbum peregrinum, quod magis probabile est;) cum primo qui ventri commeatum ex peregrinis locis adveheret, esse nuncupatum: posteà, qui res alias quascunque; ἀδύρματα praecipuè: id est, curiosorum vel delicatorum oblectamenta, quæ graviores & sapientiores pro meris ἀδύρματα (talia autem sunt quæ ex peregrinis locis à multis magno studio conquiruntur:) ludicris & ludibriis habentur. Suspectam fuisse vulgatam illam doctis viris interpretationem, indicii est, quòd prior te illo Homeri loco, in Gyphaniana editione, ϛάλλης vertitur veterator: in secundo, ingeniosus. Ego verto, ϛωλλῶ; a truckster: i e. Cananaeum, vel Cananitam: negotiatorem, &c. Literæ, s. in d. (in Dzugster, vel Dzugster, pro truckster:) mutationis, quanquam ut in literis affinibus nihil proclivius, exemplum tamen quod ultro se suggerit, dabo; Græciæ recentioris illud ϛεγγ̄ ; Ital. drogueman; Gall. truchement; (id est, interpres:) ex Chaldaico, ut notum, ⲧⲁⲏ. Τάφ, vel πίζω; præt. πέπιχα: Ἀοὴ ἰ; Parti 3. Part. ( quod apud Homerum & Apollon.)Poëtic.τελαγὼν. Exponunt quidam τείναο : alii, ππνάξας : alii denique λαβὼν, accipiens, prehendens : quos Stephanus sequitur : cujus sententiam non parum confirmat Angl. to take : capere, prehendere. Certè τῇ Imperat. ex τάω ( de quo tum alii, tum auctor Etymologici in ἀπὸ alibíque:) omnes exponunt λάβε : cape, accipe. Quanquam nec illa inepta Anglici verbi etymologia, quam supra in Ἀχελῷος attulimus.
units.tr: That is: "There the Phoenicians, renowned for their ships, came, bringing countless playthings in a black ship." (This is the version of the Gyphanius edition.) To me the sense of this word seems quite different from what Eustathius or Hesychius gives, or those who followed them. Nor do I think any of them would have judged the true sense otherwise than I do, had they understood the English language. Today the English have a very familiar and common word, "to truck," meaning to trade, or to exchange one kind of goods for another. Whence, by analogy, though it is not in use, there would be a "trucker" (Trōkles [Τρώκλης]), a merchant, a dealer, a trafficker. Nor do I doubt that "Dzuggs" and "Dzugger" (or "Dzuggiter") have the same origin. For the Greeks trōgalia [Τρώγλια], also trōgia, are edibles, any sort of food; properly those things which are commonly eaten raw (as learned men hold) and set out at dessert, such as radishes, pears, apples, nuts, almonds and the like. Pollux lists more of them. Most of these come from overseas and are brought by ship, and most are the very things apothecaries stock their shops with. So it is no wonder that the custom grew up of calling drugs "dzuggs" and the druggist properly a "dzuggster." Further, that the Phoenicians sprang from the Canaanites is the settled opinion of scholars; the ancient inscriptions to that effect, cited by Procopius and by others, and by a great man in his work On the Syrian Gods, confirm it. The Canaanites, as everyone knows from sacred history, were as well known and as famous for trade (as the Phoenicians were among the heathen) as their very name Canaan (in Hebrew כנען) passed into a common name for a merchant. כנען means merchant, trader; כנענים means merchandise. Let the reader now judge how well this explanation suits Homer's words: that the Phoenicians (by that most famous and common epithet among all nations) are called merchants, and that merchants or traders are censured for the frauds and deceits on which that way of life almost wholly rests. But how forced and far-fetched the common explanation is, who does not see? I would rather say that Phoinikes [Φοίνικες] comes from trōxō [τρώξω] (if indeed trōxō is the true origin, and it is not a foreign word, which is more probable): first, the man who brought provisions for the belly from foreign places was so named; afterwards, anyone who brought in any other things at all, especially delicacies. That is, pleasures for the curious or the dainty, which graver and wiser men regard as mere toys and trifles (such are the things which many seek out with great eagerness from distant places). That the common interpretation was suspect to learned men is shown by the fact that in the Gyphanius edition the first Homeric passage renders trōxlēs as "a cheat" (veterator), and the second as "ingenious." I render trōxlēs as "truckster," that is, a Canaanite or Canaanitish merchant, a trader, and so on. As for the change of letters, s for d (in "Dzugster" or "Dzugster" for "truckster"), though nothing is more common among related letters, I will give an example that offers itself: the modern Greek word for the same thing; Italian drogueman, French truchement (that is, an interpreter), from the Chaldee, as is well known. Tapho [Τάφ] or pissō [πίζω]; the perfect is pepicha [πέπιχα]; the aorist participle (which is used in Homer and Apollonius, the poets) is telagōn [τελαγὼν]. Some explain it as teinao [τείναο], others as pnyxas [πνάξας], others finally as labōn [λαβὼν], taking, seizing; and Stephanus follows them. The English "to take," meaning to seize or grasp, does not a little support his view. Certainly the imperative of tao [τάω], which everyone explains as labe [λάβε], take, receive (as the author of the Etymologicum says under apo and elsewhere), is the same. Yet that English etymology which we brought up above under Achelōos is not foolish either.

units.la: Υ
units.tr: Upsilon

units.la: Υόλος, nugae : υθλέω, nugor ; tole ; to be tole.
units.tr: Ὑόλος [hyolos], trifles: ὑθλέω [hythleō], to trifle; tole; to be tole.

units.la: Τλωρ, aqua ; water : de quo supra.
units.tr: Ὕλωρ [hylōr], water: of which see above.

units.la: Τδρη, serpens, aquaticus proprie, an adder : si antiquum, ut puto. nam alioquo ex hydra Latino, non minus.
units.tr: Ὕδρη [hydrē], a serpent, properly a water snake, an adder: if the word is old, as I think. For otherwise it is no less from the Latin hydra.

units.la: Τδεία, vas aquaticum, situla, &c. An ewer, si antiquum. Nam & Latinum alioquin hydria. De d.medio absorpto, vel excidente, saepius jam monuimus: Fortasse tamen ex neutro ; & ewer, ex υδρὶς ; (Graece ὑδρὶα:) ex cujus animalis cornibus pocula à Germanis olim fieri solita, ex Cæsaris commentariis, Plinio; notum, aliisque. Verum Hercyniæ sylvæ proprium animal fuisse tradunt illi veteres: unde & à Germanis sive Græcos, sive Romanos nomen accepisse; suadet ratio. Origo tamen erit Græca, si ab ὄρεσι (montibus) nomen illis inditum.
units.tr: Ὑδρεῖα [hydreia], a water vessel, a situla, etc.: an ewer, if the word is old. For the Latin is otherwise hydria. We have often already noted that a medial d is absorbed or drops out. Perhaps, however, it comes from the neuter; and ewer from ὑδρίς [hydris] (in Greek ὑδρία [hydria]), from whose animal's horns cups were once commonly made by the Germans, as is known from Caesar's commentaries, Pliny and others. But those ancient writers report that the animal was native to the Hercynian forest, whence the Germans, or the Greeks or Romans, are also thought to have received the name; reason supports this. The origin, however, will be Greek, if the name was given to them from ὄρεσι [oresi] (mountains).

units.la: ὕλη, super; ober: ὑπερφέρω, to overtake.
units.tr: Ὕπερ [hyper], over; ober: ὑπερφέρω [hyperphero], to surpass, to overtake.

units.la: ὑφή, textura, textus: ὑφάω, textile, tapetum, rete: ὑφάω, & ὑφόω, texo: Anglis, a webb; & to weave.
units.tr: Ὑφή [hyphē], a texture, a web: ὑφάω [hyphaō], textile, tapestry, a net: ὑφάω and ὑφόω [hyphoō], I weave: in English, a web; and to weave.

units.la: Φ
units.tr: Phi

units.la: Φλάω, ἀπάλλω, decipio. Notum satis & usitatum verbum: An hinc φιλήτης, fur, latro, &c. fit, ob diversam scripturam dubium est. Nam à φιλάω, φιλήτης potius scribendum fuerit: ut & φιλῶ, impostor. Seneca docet apud Ægyptios vulgare verbum fuisse, qui tamen ad Græcam originem, quasi à φιλέω (ex quo φιλητής, sed alio sensu) non à φιλάω, alludit. Verba ejus sunt: Voluptatis
units.tr: Φλάω [phlaō], ἀπάλλω [apallō], I deceive. This is a well known and common verb. Whether φιλήτης [philētēs], thief, robber, etc., is formed from it is doubtful, because of the different spelling. For from φιλάω [philaō] it would rather have been written φιλήτης; as also φιλῶ [philō], impostor. Seneca teaches that among the Egyptians there was a common word, which nevertheless hints at a Greek origin, as if from φιλέω [phileō] (whence φιλητής, though in another sense), not from φιλάω. His words are: Of pleasures

units.la: Voluptates praecipuè exturba, & invifissimas habe: Latronum more, quos philetas Ægyptii vocant, in hoc nos amplectentes, ut strangulent. Atqui Hesiodus etiam, aliíque Græci scriptores habent. Ab illis igitur (quis dubitet?) Angli, to filch, (vel ut alii propiùs ad originem scribunt, to filtch) & a fil- cher.
units.tr: Drive out pleasures especially, and hold them in the greatest hatred, like robbers, whom the Egyptians call philetae, embracing us in this, that they strangle us. Yet Hesiod too and other Greek writers have the word. From them, therefore (who can doubt it?), the English got to filch (or, as others write more closely to the origin, to filtch) and a filcher.

units.la: Σῆρες [?], fauni, (de quibus inter alios μαγαίρης parens in De Satyr. Poësi:) satyri; Anglis satyres, nymphæ: larvæ, lemures.
units.tr: Σῆρες [?], fauns (on which, among others, the author of De Satyra Poesi): satyrs; in English satyres; nymphs; larvae, lemures.

units.la: Φόρμος, teges, storea. quæ pluribus olim, (de quo aliquid ad Theophrasti Characteres :) hodiéque vice scamni, aut cubilis. Hinc Anglis, a foutme, scamnum: sedile.
units.tr: Φόρμος [phormos], a mat, a rush mat, which many formerly used (on which see something in the Characters of Theophrastus), and even today in place of a bench or bed. Hence in English, a foutme, a footstool; a seat.

units.la: Φλάω, contundo, &c. φλάσμα, pro Φλάσμα, Hippocrati, &c. contusio; a flaw: ruptura.
units.tr: Φλάω [phlaō], I crush, etc.: φλάσμα [phlasma], for Φλάσμα, in Hippocrates, etc., a bruise; a flaw: a rupture.

units.la: Φλάζω, παφλάζω, férveo, æstuo; to flaw. nisi ex φλύζω, unde φλύσις, puftula. οἰνόφλυξ, quasi vino bulliens: ebrius. De vino quoque Angli.
units.tr: Φλάζω [phlazō], παφλάζω [paphlazō], I boil, I seethe; to flaw. Unless it comes from φλύζω [phlyzō], whence φλύσις [phlysis], a blister. οἰνόφλυξ [oinophlyx], as if boiling with wine: a drunkard. The English also use it of wine.

units.la: Φλάξ, γος, flamma; a flaw.
units.tr: Φλάξ [phlax], flame; a flaw.

units.la: Φείδω, habere, agere; to faire: ut εἴχεσθαι χαλῶς; to faire well: to faire ill.
units.tr: Φείδω [pheidō], to have, to behave; to fare, as in εἴχεσθαι καλῶς [eikhesthai kalōs]: to fare well; to fare ill.

units.la: Φεῖλω, φρυάσσω, fremo, frendeo; to frett. Nisi potiùs, ex βοῤῥ, cibus: & βοῤῥ, vorax. Est enim vetus frettan, edere, proprie. Transferunt autem etiam Graeci ad animum: ut in Θυμοβορεῖν, & Θυμοβόρῳ μελεδῶνες, &c.
units.tr: Φρυάσσω [phryassō], I snort, I gnash: to fret. Unless it rather comes from βορρᾶς? (food) and βορρός? (voracious). For there is the old frettan, properly to eat. The Greeks also transfer it to the mind, as in θυμοβορεῖν [thymoboreīn] and θυμοβόρῳ μελεδῶνες [thymoboros meledōnes], etc.

units.la: Φλοιὸς, cortex; φλοίω, decortico; to flea. Item, to flaw.
units.tr: Φλοιός [phloios], bark; φλοΐω [phloiō], I strip bark: to flea. Likewise, to flaw.

units.la: Φάτνη, praesepe. Anglis, fatt pinguis. ΔΙΝ Hebraeis, faginare: ΔΙΝ praesepe.
units.tr: Φάτνη [phatnē], a manger. In English, fatt, fat. In Hebrew, faginare, to fatten: the manger.

units.la: Φεμλῆς, filices; flints.
units.tr: Φελλῆς [phellēs], ferns (filices); flints.

units.la: Φάσκωλον, φασκώλιον, & φασκώλιον: marsupium: arca, pera, cista. Anglis, a flasket: sporta, calathus, canistrum majus.
units.tr: Φάσκωλον [phaskolon], φασκώλιον [phaskolion]: a wallet, a purse; a chest, a bag, a pouch. In English, a flasket: a basket, a hamper, a larger canister.

units.la: Φυφὴν, φύφην, miscere: φύγμα, mistura. Anglis, a frap, pugna: ut Gallis meslée, ex miscendo.
units.tr: Φύρω [phyrō], to mix: φύγμα [phygma], a mixture. In English, a frap, a fight; as the French say mêlée, from mixing.

units.la: Φέγυς, optimus; excellentissimus: first, primus, princeps.
units.tr: Φέριστος [pheristos], best; most excellent: first, chief, prince.

units.la: Φρύν, φρύνη, φρύν, rubeta, rana venenosa; a frogge, rana: nisi ex βάτραχος, de quo supra.
units.tr: Φρύνη [phrynē], a toad, a poisonous frog (rubeta): a frogge, a frog; unless it comes from βάτραχος [batrachos], of which above.

units.la: Φείδομαι, parco, do veniam, misereor: Hinc ergo possit esse fond, &c. de quibus supra in Ἐμφύναι.
units.tr: Φείδομαι [pheidomai], I spare, I pardon, I have mercy. Hence the word fond may come, etc., of which above under Ἐμφύναι.

units.la: Φόγγος, vox, sonus: φθέγγομαι, loquor: ἀφθόγγος, elinguis, mutus. Angl. tongue, lingua. φώλος, ϐόρτιον, onus; sed proprie, navis. Quæ navibus apportantur, ait Camerarius. φορλάζω, onero. Anglis, fraught, onus navis: to fraught a ship, navem onerare. Scribitur etiam fralte, vel fratght; quod ad Gallicum verbum propius accedit; & est fortasse ab alia origine.
units.tr: Φθόγγος [phthongos], voice, sound: φθέγγομαι [phthengomai], I speak; ἄφθογγος [aphthongos], speechless, mute. English tongue, Latin lingua. φόρτιον [phortion], a burden; but properly a ship's cargo. "Things carried by ships," says Camerarius. φορτίζω [phortizō], I load. In English, fraught, a ship's cargo: to fraught a ship, to load a ship. It is also written fralte or fratght, which comes closer to the French word, and is perhaps of a different origin.

units.la: Φαῦλος, (quod jam supra in Cambdenianis habuimus, sed hic repetitum, quia plura super eo addenda :) vilis, facilis: nullius pretii, aut negotii. Item, malus, improbus. Hæ vulgares & usitatæ significationes. Sed Dio: Laertius in vita Platonis alias commemorat, non ut Platonis proprias, sed tamen præter quam Platoni paucis usitatas aut notas. Inter eas hæc est, ut φαῦλος pro simplice & minimè fucato ponatur: quomodo etiam Euripidem usurpasse probat Laertius adducto ipsius in hanc sententiam loco. Ut minimè dubium videatur quin φαῦλ fuole, inde manaverit. Quanquam aliam quoq; notionis istius rationem possimus reddere ex sententiâ philosophorum principis, & hominum, quibus sola ratio prævivit ad sapientiam, unius omnium post homines fatos sapientissimi; qui toties id incul-cat. eat,& non minùs solidè probat, ἀδῆνα- λον φεῤῥιμὸν τὸ μὴ ὄνλα ἀδαθὸν: i.Fieri non posse, ut qui non est bonus, idem sit sapiens. Sed à Græcis ad Anglos(quod hîc quærimus:) immediatè pervenisse hoc verbum non præstem,cùm in veteribus libris hactenus mihi non occurrerit, sed ejus loco, untvlse, dpfing, &c. At si non hoc; certè non dubium quin ze foule, vel ut alii ad discrimen (est enim foule, etiam volucris) scribunt, fowle, pro turpi & impuro, hinc profectum sit. Sunt enim vilia,ex contemptu,sæpe sordida & squallida: & quæ mala & prava, eadem & naturâ suâ impura sunt, & ita quoq; vulgò nuncupantur. Ἀκάθαρτον πνεῦμα, a fowle spirit, i.e.impium, malum. In veteribus rythmicis ante 600. plus minùs annos Orationis Dominicæ versionibus, quod in uno exemplari, Let us not in fonding fall, Dac fro evill tha fplo us all: in altero, eóque antiquiore, Pe let us fall into no foundinig, Ac ghield ous fro the foule thing. Φαυλόπης, φαῦλος vilipendo, subsanno, (unde & φαῦλον apud Hesych. φλαγίλας exponitur; & φαυλίσεια, subsannatrix) fo flowt. Φεγγὰν, Φεγνῶν, sapere, sentire: & φεγνῶν, φαλά φεγνῶν, φιλοφεγνῶν; & interdum absolutè, φεγνῶν τὰ, &c. pro, favere alicui, benevolo esse animo, &c. Anglis, absolutè, a frend, quasi & φεγνῶν, amicus. quemadmodum & Latini absolutè, velle alicui, cupere alicui, pro, bene velle; bene cupere.
units.tr: Φαῦλος [phaulos] (which we already had above among the Cambden words, but repeat here because more can be added about it): cheap, easy: of no worth or importance. Also bad, wicked. These are the common and usual meanings. But Diogenes Laertius in the life of Plato mentions others, not as Plato's own, yet used or known by Plato to few. Among them is this: that φαῦλος is used for what is simple and not at all adulterated. Laertius shows that Euripides also used it in this sense, citing his passage to that effect. So there seems little doubt that the English foul may have come from this. We could also give another reason for this meaning, from the view of the prince of philosophers, and of men to whom reason alone led the way to wisdom, the one wisest of all men since the fall; who inculcates it so often and proves it no less solidly: ἀδύνατον τὸ μὴ ὄντα ἀγαθὸν εἶναι καὶ σοφὸν εἶναι [adynaton to mē onta agathon einai kai sophon einai]: that it is impossible for one who is not good to be wise too. But I will not assert that this word came directly from the Greeks to the English (which is what we are seeking here), since I have not so far found it in old books; instead of it there are untwise, despising, etc. But if not this, there is certainly no doubt that the English foule, or, as others write it to distinguish it (for foule is also a bird), fowle, for the impure and filthy, has come from this. For things that are cheap, through contempt, are often sordid and squalid; and things that are bad and depraved are likewise impure by their nature, and are commonly so called. ἀκάθαρτον πνεῦμα [akatharton pneuma], a foul spirit, that is, an impious, evil one. In the old rhyming versions of the Lord's Prayer, made some 600 years ago or so, in one copy: Let us not in fonding fall, / Dac fro evill tha fplo us all; in another, older: Pe let us fall / into no foundinig, Ac ghield ous fro the foule thing. φαυλίζω [phaulizō], to despise, to scoff at (whence also φαῦλον in Hesychius is explained as φλαγίλας; and φαυλίσεια [phauliseia], a scoffer): to flout. φρονεῖν [phronein], to be wise, to perceive: and φρονεῖν τινί [phronein tini], and φιλοφρονεῖν [philophronein]; and sometimes absolutely φρονεῖν τά, etc., for to favour someone, to be kindly disposed, etc. In English, absolutely, a friend, as if from φρονῶν [phronōn], a friend, just as the Latins also say absolutely velle alicui, cupere alicui, for to wish well, to desire well.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: ΧΗΑΝ, forceps, seu forfex, quales cancrorum proprie. De avium quoque unguibus dicitur, ut apud Sophoclem, a clatw. Sed & clatches.
units.tr: ΧΗΑΝ: forceps or tongs, such as crabs properly have. It is also said of the talons of birds, as in Sophocles, from κλάω. But also κλάτχες [clatches].

units.la: Χύτλον, proprie, oleum aquâ mixtum, quo perfundi & in ungi balneantium corpora solebant. Hinc χύτλον, etiam pro ἀγγεῖον ἐλαιοδόχον, ἐν ᾧ ἔιχον οἱ παλαιοὶ τὸ ἔλαιον, ᾧ μὴ τὸ λίβας ἔχει-ον: i.e. vase, quod oleum continebat, quo post lavationem corpora veteres inungebant. Hanc interpretationem doctissimus Stephanus habet sufpectam, quod exemplorum quae proseruntur incerta lectio fit: non habiturus opinor, si scivisset in Anglica lingua hodieque vocari a kettle, haud dissimile vas, ad continenda & calefacienda liquida quæcunque comparatum. Quod tamen alioquin etiam ex χύψ@ vel χύψα, olla, cacabus, (mutato pro more r. in l.) duci possit; cùm in ejusmodi vase carnes quoque vulgò coquere soleant.
units.tr: Χύτλον, properly oil mixed with water, with which the bodies of bathers were customarily poured over and anointed. Hence χύτλον is also used for a vessel holding oil, in which the ancients kept the oil they used after bathing [ἀγγεῖον ἐλαιοδόχον, ἐν ᾧ ἔιχον οἱ παλαιοὶ τὸ ἔλαιον]: that is, a vase which held oil, with which the ancients anointed their bodies after washing. The most learned Stephanus regards this interpretation as suspect, because the examples cited have an uncertain reading. I do not think he would have held it, I believe, had he known that in the English language to this day a kettle is called a vessel not unlike this, made to hold and heat any liquids whatever. This could, however, also be derived from χύτρα or χύτρα, a pot, cauldron (with r changed to l, as is customary), since meat too is usually cooked in such a vessel.

units.la: nisi ex ἀγρός. Sed & countrep, pro regione, provincia, hinc fuerit, nisi ex conterraneus, (quod satis antiquum) barbara vox conterra, sequioribus saxculis emersit, unde istud fluxerit. Quæ quidem vox quamvis apud nullos fortasse istorum temporum scriptores reperiatur, nec in usum recepta sit; potuit tamen ex ejus quasi idea vox ista formari; qualia in lingua Gallica innumera fere observat doctissimus author Grammaticæ Gallicæ, cujus jam aliquoties mentionem fecimus. Haud parum etymologiam priorem confirmat, quòd ut Graci dicunt, χωρεῖν, ἐγχωρεῖν, ἀνχωρεῖν; pro, cedere, recedere, &c. ita Angli, to give ground q. d. χώρων διδόναι.
units.tr: Unless from ἀγρός. But also "countrep", for region or province, hence it may have come from "conterraneus" (which is quite old), unless the barbarous word "conterra" emerged in later centuries, from which that word flowed. Although perhaps no writers of those times use this word, nor has it been received into use, it could nonetheless have been formed from a sort of idea of it. The most learned author of the French Grammar, whose mention we have made several times, observes that countless such formations are nearly typical of the French language. The former etymology is no little confirmed by the fact that, as the Greeks say χωρεῖν, ἐγχωρεῖν, ἀνχωρεῖν, meaning to yield or withdraw, so the English say "to give ground", as if to say χώρων διδόναι.

units.la: χωρεῖν, ἐγχωρεῖν, ςυγχωρεῖν, cedere, concedere, &c. to grant. Est & χωρεῖν, impressionem facere hostili modo; vel in hostes. Et hinc fuerit, fo crond: violenter trudere. Hoc malo quàm ex χρέω, pulso, quod aliis placuit.
units.tr: χωρεῖν, ἐγχωρεῖν, συγχωρεῖν: to yield, to concede, and so on, "to grant". There is also χωρεῖν, to make an attack in the manner of an enemy, or against enemies. And hence perhaps "fo crond", to thrust violently. I prefer this to deriving it from χρέω, to push, as others have preferred.

units.la: xlω, χηνὸς, anser: veteribus Germanis, Plinio teste, ganze: hodiernis Anglis, a goose: Item, a gander. Plinii verba, lib. X. c. 22. de anseribus, Candidi ibi, (in Germania) verùm minores, ganza vocantur.
units.tr: χήν, χηνός, a goose: among the ancient Germans, according to Pliny, "ganze"; among the modern English, "a goose"; likewise "a gander". Pliny's words, book X, chapter 22, on geese: "There (in Germany) they are white, but smaller, and are called ganza."

units.la: Χολὴ, bilis; gall.
units.tr: Χολή, bile; gall.

units.la: χδεγξ, vitis fulcrum, &c. a crutch.
units.tr: Χηλός [χδεγξ], a prop for a vine; a crutch.

units.la: Χαλιζὶν, ἀναχαλιζὶν; de equo proprie dicitur indomito, vel aliàs effræni, & sternace. Angli pariter de equo, fkittish: qualem quia Galli vocant ombrageux; suspicetur aliquis fortasse ex οκία potiùs manasse. Sed ego illud magis probo.
units.tr: Χαλιζὶν, ἀναχαλιζὶν: said properly of an unbroken horse, or otherwise unbridled and rearing. The English likewise use "skittish" of a horse, which, since the French call it "ombrageux", someone might perhaps suspect came rather from [οκία]. But I prefer the other derivation.

units.la: χεῖλος, labium: veteribus Anglis, <bl>wzleras. Dizghten welerum mine</bl> <bl>thu untpn</bl>, &c. Domine labia mea aperies, &c. Psal. LI. v. 15.
units.tr: χεῖλος, a lip: to the old English, "wzleras". "Dizghten welerum mine thu untpn", that is, "Lord, thou shalt open my lips", etc.: Psalm 51, verse 15.

units.la: Χεῖνος, diuturnus; longo durans tempore. Χεῖνότης, & χεῖνία, diuturnitas, vetustas. Χεῖνιαῖος, vetus. Anglis, crone, proprie vetula ovis, ut docet Verstegan us.
units.tr: Χεῖνος, long-lasting; enduring over a long time. Χεῖνότης and χεῖνία, lastingness, age. Χεῖνιαῖος, old. In English "crone", properly an old ewe, as Verstegan teaches.

units.la: χῶρος, χώρα, locus sterilis, incultus; cultus : folitudo ; de quo fupra, Xαλάζα, grando ; baile.
units.tr: χῶρος, χώρα: a barren, uncultivated place, as opposed to cultivated; a wilderness; of which above. "Χαλάζα", hail; "baile".

units.la: Χαλάω, remito, laxo, relaxo : de fu-nibus, & id genus, proprie : fed ad mo-res paffim transfertur : unde χαλί-φρών, & χαλιφέρτω, &c. to flack : Item, flaggtfh.
units.tr: Χαλάω, to slacken, loosen, relax: properly said of ropes and the like, but commonly transferred to manners; whence χαλίφρων and χαλιφέρτω, and so on. In English "to slack"; likewise "flaggtfh".

units.la: Χαλέω, (vel χαλάω) fculpo, in-fculpo, imprimo : χάλυψα, nota in-fculpta, vel imprefla ; to cratch, vel fcratch.
units.tr: Χαλέω (or χαλάω): to carve, to engrave, to imprint. Χάλυψα: a carved or impressed mark; "to cratch", or "scratch".

units.la: Νέω, (fed frequentius, νέομαι) emo, mercor ; comparo mihi, im-petro, obtineo. ὠνέω, pretium. ὠνὴ ὠνή, ἵνα λάβῃ τι ; quod quis dat ut aliquid quod vcenale eft, aufe-rat ; vel fuum faciat. Hinc, τὸ ὠνεῖσθαι, proprius : & to obtine, ut proprium fibi vindicare, ac pro fuo agnofcere.
units.tr: Νέω (but more frequently νέομαι): to buy, to purchase; to procure for oneself, to obtain, to gain. ὠνέω: a price. ὠνή: that by which someone gives something in order to take away something saleable, or to make it his own [ἵνα λάβῃ τι]. Hence τὸ ὠνεῖσθαι properly; and "to obtain", as in claiming something for oneself as one's own and acknowledging it as one's property.

units.la: Ὠνέω, ficut, velut ; ὠνέω.
units.tr: Ὠνέω, just as, like; ὠνέω.

units.la: HÆC funt, amice Lector, quibus no-ftram quam expofuimus, de linguæ Saxonicæ cum Græcâ affinitate & pro-piore cognatione fententiam potiffimum niti agnofcimus. Quibus lectis diligenter ac perpenfis fi tu tamen ali-ter
units.tr: These are the grounds, kind reader, on which our opinion rests, mainly, as we recognise, the opinion we have set out concerning the affinity and closer kinship of the Saxon language with Greek. Having read and carefully weighed these, if you nevertheless think otherwise,

units.la: ter censes, & abnuis: Hoc primò,(mo‑ do tamen conatus nostros candidè in‑ terpreteris) me solabor, Non eadem (quod Poëta nescio quis) sentire bonis de rebus iisdem, Incolumi semper amicitiâ licuisse. Proximo loco, ut cando‑ re tecum certem, lestionis hujus ut desinas, & aliud agas, amicè consulo. Quem enim proposita verba & exem‑ pla non moverunt, eum ullis aliis quæ à me speret argumentis; motum non iri planè prædico.
units.tr: and reject it: first, I will console myself with the saying of some poet, provided you interpret our efforts fairly: "It has always been permitted, while friendship remains unharmed, to hold different opinions about the same things." Second, to contend with you candidly, I kindly advise you to give up this reading and turn to something else. For whoever is not moved by the words and examples set before him, I predict plainly that he will not be moved by any other arguments that I might hope for.

units.la: Sed ut ad alios nos convertamus, quos non minore numero fore confi‑ dimus; sciant illi quicunque sint, in hac adornandâ collectione non ambitiosè versatos esse, ut omnia undique conge‑reremus; sed eorum quæ se nobis of‑ ferebant delectum habuisse; magisque ut judicium nostrum lectoribus, quàm diligentiam probaremus, studuisse. sí‑que non unâ de caussâ. Ac primò qui‑ dem, quia quid operis suscepti ratio postularet, quid ad assertionem no‑stram firmandam copiæ sufficeret, pro‑ positum nobis erat; non Etymologi‑ cum Anglicum conficere. Quamvis i‑ gitur plurima se nobis offerrent, de
units.tr: But to turn to others, whom we trust are no less numerous: let them know, whoever they are, that in putting together this collection we did not busily engage in gathering everything from everywhere; rather we made a selection from what presented itself to us, and we aimed to show our judgement to readers rather than our diligence. And this for more than one reason. First, because our purpose was what the nature of the undertaking required, and what abundance would suffice to confirm our assertion; we did not propose to compile an English etymologicon. Although, therefore, very many things presented themselves to us, about the origin of which we have no less doubt than about those we have so far set out,

units.la: quorum, nos quidem, non magis dubitamus origine, quàm de his quæ hactenus exhibuimus: quia tamen obscurior erat origo, & quæ minùs in his versatis suspectior fuisset, infignioribus & illustrioribus contenti fuimus:quod spero Lectorem,qui aliorum in hoc genere conatus ac labores publici juris factos cum nostris hisce contulerit, facilè percepturum. Ut dicam liberè, quod sentio : Pauca puto verè & genuinè Anglica, five Saxonica, id est, vetera reperiri, quæ ( iis exceptis quæ Latinæ sunt originis,) fi ritè & diligenter expendantur, non possint ad Græcos fontes revocari. Sed ut quis dignè & solidè hoc opere defungatur, multis opus est, quæ non in uno aliquo facilè reperias. Nam primò, linguæ Græcæ, non vulgaris hæc, quâ multi passim fe jactant ; sed accurata pro linguæ Græcæ magnitudine.(qualem alibi suo loco describimus:) peritia requiritur ; à quâ nos longissimè abesse profitemur. Non enim sufficit ut Lexica quis, quod sibi quidam persuaserunt, diligenter evolvat ; sed omne Græcorum scriptorum, Poëtarum, Historicorum, imò & Philofophorum genus evolvendi ; cùm inter legendum, quod sæpè experti sumus, multa in mentem veniant, quæ nulla Lexicorum quamvis accuratissima lectio suppeditet. Jam Dialectorum, Deus bone ! quanta apud Græcos varietas ! quanta verborum aut eorundem, sed adeò per has dialectos immutatorum & distortorum, ut vix pro iisdem agnoscas: aut plane aliorum & singulis Dialectis propriorum varietas, ex quorum accuratâ cognitione infinitæ pendent origines. Ex una ferè Æolicâ Dialecto; totus penè fluxit, ut Quintilianus aliíque observant, Latinus sermo. Hæc observatio quanti momenti fit in Latinis originibus indagandis, norunt omnes ejus linguæ non vulgariter periti. Jam veteris linguæ Anglicæ cùm pars tantùm ad nos pervenerit, supplendus hic defectus ex cognatarum linguarum, Danicæ, Suecicæ, Belgicæ, Germanicæ, (ut nunc loquimur) exacta cognitione; neque omnino potest, ut in hoc studio quisquam feliciter versetur, aut aliquid dignum doctorum præstet approbatione, qui non fit omnium istarum linguarum callentissimus.
units.tr: nevertheless, because the origin was more obscure, and because it would have been less suspect to those versed in these matters, we were content with the more notable and illustrious examples. I hope the reader who compares our work with the efforts and labours of others in this field, published in public, will readily perceive this. To speak freely, as I think: I hold that few words are truly and genuinely English, or Saxon, that is, ancient, and that, apart from those of Latin origin, if they are weighed properly and carefully they cannot be traced back to Greek sources. But whoever is to discharge this work worthily and soundly needs many things which cannot easily be found in any one place. For first, one needs a knowledge of the Greek language, not the common kind which many boast of everywhere, but an accurate knowledge proportioned to the greatness of the Greek language (which we describe elsewhere in its place); and we openly confess that we are very far from such knowledge. For it is not enough to pore diligently over the lexicons, as some have persuaded themselves; one must read through the whole range of Greek writers, poets, historians, and even philosophers. For in reading, as we have often found, many things come to mind which no reading of the lexicons, however accurate, supplies. And then the dialects, good God, what a variety there is among the Greeks! What a number of words, or of the same words, but so changed and distorted through these dialects that you can scarcely recognise them as the same; or a plain variety of others peculiar to each dialect, from whose accurate knowledge infinite origins depend. The Latin language, as Quintilian and others observe, came almost wholly from the Aeolic dialect alone. All who are not commonly unskilled in that language know how much this observation matters for investigating Latin origins. Now, since only part of the old English language has come down to us, this deficiency must be supplied by an exact knowledge of the cognate languages, Danish, Swedish, Flemish, German (as we now speak). Nor can anyone at all succeed in this study, or produce anything worthy of the approval of scholars, unless he is thoroughly skilled in all these languages.

units.la: Quod mihi quidem, (tantam videor, ex mediocri usu in comparandis illis, affinitatem deprehendisse) non adeo difficile aut operosum videtur; modo qui fit Anglicismi tum veteris,quantum ex libris hauriri potest; tum praefentis accurate peritus. Ad hoc autem multum proderit tum Scoticae linguae, quae Anglicâ hodiernâ purior, exacta cognitio; tum variorum verborum veterum, quae pro locorum ac regionum in Angliâ varietate cuiq; ferè regioni ac loco propria multa reperiuntur, diligens observatio. Ego certè, ex quo ad Meridionales has oras,(quae vulgò Suffexia nuncupantur) diu jaßatum publica me tempestas appulit, multas observavi voces antea penitùs inauditas, quas veteres esse verisimile est: alias autem non inauditas quidem, sed alia longè notione, quàm quâ mihi priùs auditae fuerant. Ego quidem quantum potui id operam dedi,ut nullum verbum ex linguâ Graecâ peterem cujus veriorem aut verifimiliorem originem cognatarum linguarum, Belgicae puta, aut Germanicae, aliqua suggereret. Quod qui non observant sedulò,
units.tr: This, indeed, seems to me, who have by moderate practice in comparing these languages detected so great an affinity, not so very difficult or laborious, provided one is accurately skilled in English, both the older as far as it can be drawn from books, and the present. To this end, a careful observation of the Scottish language, which is purer than present-day English, and an exact knowledge of it, will be of great help, as well as careful attention to the many old words which are found peculiar to almost every region and place according to the variety of localities and districts in England. For my part, since the storm of public affairs has driven me, tossed about for a long time, to these southern shores (commonly called Sussex), I have observed many words previously entirely unheard of, which it is likely are old; and others not unheard of indeed, but in a very different sense from that in which I had heard them before. I have, as far as I could, taken care not to derive any word from Greek when the cognate languages, Flemish or German for instance, suggested a truer or more probable origin. Those who do not observe this carefully

units.la: & quicquid in linguâ Græcâ aut Hebraicâ assonat, arripiunt; non aliud quàm in arenâ multo molimine ædificant; aut quod Græci dicunt, τὰς νεφέλας ἐλαύνει. Quæ causa fuit altera, quòd à multis congerendis, imperitiæ nostræ nobis conscii, libenter abftinuerimus; & hæc ipsa (fi singularia verba spectentur; nam universæ collectionis, quantum ad præcipuum hujus operis scopum, alia ratio:) timidè proponere mus. Jam ut aliquis ab his omnibus quæ nobis desunt, fit instructissimus; nisi tamen propria quædam vis & ἀγνότης ingenii pari librata judicio accesserit, non amplius confequutus fuerit, quàm pusio aliquis, aut effœtus viri bus, armis Achillæis indutus, cum robusto pugile congressurus.
units.tr: And whatever sounds alike in Greek or Hebrew, they seize upon. They build nothing but a house on sand with great effort, or, as the Greeks say, they "drive away the clouds" [τὰς νεφέλας ἐλαύνει]. This was the second reason: aware of our own inexperience, we willingly refrained from gathering many such words, and even these we put forward timidly (I mean the individual words; for the collection as a whole, as far as the main purpose of this work is concerned, is a different matter). Even if someone is thoroughly equipped with all the things we lack, unless his own peculiar power and purity of mind [ἀγνότης], balanced by sound judgement, is added, he will achieve no more than a boy, or a man worn out by age, clad in Achilles' armour and about to meet a strong boxer.

units.la: Sed hæc obiter, & nihil ad nos, nisi quatenus hæc nostra collectio Etymo logici operis aliquod esse specimen videri possit. Ad nostra igitur ut redeamus: Quanquam literas Alphabeti singulas ordine suo exhibuimus, non tamen in verbis quæ sub unaquaque literâ disponendis ordinem literarum observavimus : nec sanè observandum credidimus; quòd multa erant, quæ collata & apposita mutuam sibi lucem fœnerarentur. Non negamus tamen melius multa disponi potuisse, si hoc nobis tanti visum esset; aut verò otium nobis tantum, ut etiam tam minutæ rei vacare potuissemus. In Latinâ Græcorum expositione cùm consultum nobis, ne suspectiores essent nostræ interpretationes, videretur, aliorum potiùs uti verbis, quàm nostris; non diu cunctandum fuit quem potissimum sequeremur; ex quo & alios hausisse, & suos, plerosque, rivulos derivasse non dubitamus. Meâ tamen usûs libertate, in quibusdam dissentire, sed reddità ratione, ausus sum: in non paucis ab Hesychio & Etymologici auctore adjutus sum, ubi deficiebat Stephanus: alios quoque, nec sine fructu, credo, libenter consulturus, si copia eorum hæc scribenti fuisset.
units.tr: But these points are incidental and have nothing to do with us, except insofar as this collection of ours may seem to be a specimen of an etymological work. Let us return, then, to our own subject. Although we have set out the letters of the alphabet in their proper order, we have not observed the order of letters in arranging the words under each letter; nor did we think this ought to be observed, since there were many words which, when compared and placed side by side, would lend each other mutual light. We do not deny that many things could have been arranged better, had we thought this worth the effort, or had we had enough leisure to give even so small a matter our attention. In the Latin explanation of the Greek words, since it seemed wise to us, so that our interpretations would be less open to suspicion, to use the words of others rather than our own, we did not hesitate long over whom we should chiefly follow; and we do not doubt that from them we have drawn some streams, and that most of our own have flowed from them. Yet in the exercise of my own freedom I have ventured, in certain points, to dissent, but with reasons given. In not a few cases I was helped by Hesychius and the author of the Etymologicum, where Stephanus failed; and I would gladly have consulted others too, not without profit I believe, had their abundance been available to me as I wrote this.

units.la: ULTIMA jam pensi nostri pars nobis restat, historia: non illa quidem planè necessaria, ac potiùs auc- tarium, quàm pars, cùm itam quam volumus
units.tr: Now that the last part of my undertaking remains, history. This is not strictly necessary, and is more an appendix than a part, but since it confirms what we want

units.la: volumus affinitatem linguarum, quamvis nulla super effent historiarum monumenta, quæ suaderent, tam numerosa(ut omnes agnoscent harum rerum periti) verborum cognatio & fimilitudo fatis evincat. Videamus tamen ecquid hinc quoque, quod tanto magis opinionem nostram confirmet, erui possit.
units.tr: to show: even if no historical records survived, the close kinship and resemblance of words, so numerous that all experts in these matters will recognise it, is proof enough of the affinity of the languages. Let us nonetheless see whether anything further can be drawn from this that would confirm our view all the more.

units.la: Gallorum veterum cum Græcis commercia, & mutuas five per victorias, five per colonias immigrationes; quæ de Galatis, de Gallo-Græcia, de Maffilienfi colonia, & id genus quæ multis observata sunt, commemorare non est hîc animus. Quæ quanquam fi vera est,quæ doctissimis probatur sententia, Gallos Germanorum progeniem fuiffe, & eandem fuisse veteribus illis Gallis & Germanis linguam, non ἀσφ(- ϐόνυα cuiquam merito videantur,cùm ipsos etiam Saxones, ex illo Gallorum genere qui in Asia sedes variis temporibus fixerunt, ac variis locis ac temporibus varias (ut solet) nomenclatu- ras sortiti sunt, & in novas quasi gentes coaluerunt, aut degenerarunt; suspicari(cùm talia passim contingant) non fine caussâ quis possit: quia tamen partim longiùs petita, partim solâ nituntur conjeƈturâ, jámque à multis inculcata sunt, nos eò non consugiemus. Græci se in Galliam immiserunt, in Græciam Galli, ait Seneca.
units.tr: There were ancient dealings between the Gauls and the Greeks, and mutual migrations, some by conquest and some by colonies. I do not intend to recall what has been noted by many writers about the Galatians, Gallo-Greece, the colony of Massilia, and the like. Although, if the opinion approved by the most learned scholars is true, that the Gauls were a branch of the Germans, and that the ancient Gauls and Germans spoke the same language, this should not seem absurd to anyone. For the Saxons themselves, who belonged to that Gallic stock that settled in Asia at various times and, as usual, took on various names in various places and times, and merged into new peoples or degenerated, one might reasonably suspect (since such things happen everywhere) that the same is true. But since these views rest partly on remote derivations and partly on mere conjecture, and have already been pressed by many, I shall not have recourse to them. The Greeks thrust themselves into Gaul, and the Gauls into Greece, says Seneca.

units.la: Ad antiquissima si recurramus tempora, Scythas totâ ferè Asiâ potitos, ac ibi sedes fixisse, in Herodoto & vetustissimis historiis legere est; ex quo Scythas cum Græcis permixtos communes in multis locis sedes habuisse cuivis in promptu colligere est. Hinc Scytho-Græci de quibus Herodot. l. IV.
units.tr: If we go back to the most ancient times, we may read in Herodotus and the oldest histories that the Scythians possessed almost all of Asia and fixed their seats there. From this anyone may readily conclude that the Scythians, mixed with the Greeks, had common settlements in many places. Hence the Scytho-Greeks, of whom Herodotus writes in book IV.

units.la: Quanquam autem Scytharum nomen apud antiquissimos scriptores valdè generale nomen est, quod omnes septentrionales populos tam Asiaticos quàm Europæos complectitur: Europæos tamen sive Celto-Scythas qui & Germani postea dicti, ab Herodoto aliisq; Scythicorum bellorum scriptoribus intelligi certissimis argumentis viri docti plures adstruxerunt. Sed & ipsum nomen Scytha Germanicam præ se fert, ut omnes ferè consentiunt, originem. Illos autem nominatim Scythas, qui alio nomine Getæ quoque nominati, per oram Ponticam latè sparfos, Græcis notissimos, Germanicæ fuisse prosapiæ; constans eruditissimorum virorum, antiquitatum Germanicarum illustratorum & indagatorum folertissimorum, est opinio. In eâdem autem orâ Græcorum coloniæ non minus frequentes ac celebres: de quibus Strabo aliíque sigillatim, & fusè. Seneca paucis: Scythia & totus ille ferarum indomitarúmq; gentium tractus, civitates Achaiæ Ponticis impositas litoribus ostentat. Inter has Tomos urbs, tum propriis cladibus non unis; tum Ovidii Nasonis, Poëtæ celeberrimi, exilio & morte (si quidem Eusebium sequimur: aliter enim quidam recentiores de morte & sepulchro ejus in superiore Pannoniâ reperto:) nobilis.
units.tr: Although the name Scythians among the oldest writers is a very general term, embracing all the northern peoples, both Asiatic and European, learned men have shown by several very certain arguments that the European Scythians, or Celto-Scythians, who were later also called Germans, are meant by Herodotus and the other writers of the Scythian wars. Moreover, it is the common view of nearly all that the very name Scytha bears a German origin. That the Scythians specifically, who were also called Getae, were widely scattered along the Pontic shore, very well known to the Greeks, and of German descent, is the settled opinion of the most learned men, illustrators and most diligent investigators of German antiquities. Along the same shore the Greek colonies were no less numerous and famous; Strabo and others discuss them individually and at length. Seneca briefly says: Scythia and that whole tract of savage and untamed peoples shows cities of Achaea set on the Pontic shores. Among these is the city of Tomis, noted both for its own disasters, not just one, and for the exile and death of the very famous poet Ovid (if we follow Eusebius; for some more recent writers place his death and tomb elsewhere, in Upper Pannonia).

units.la: Ita quidem docti plerique Germanicarum rerum scriptores omnes; uno tamen non contemnendæ authoritatis viro dissentiente, qui Getas & Gothos pro diversis habet. Ratio quâ præcipuè nititur ipsius sententia hæc est; quòd nulli, ut ait ipse, veteres, Getas Germanis accensuerint. Quod mihi non adeò mirum videtur, quàm mi-rum
units.tr: So indeed most learned writers of German history, all of them; yet one man of no contemptible authority dissents, who holds the Getae and Goths to be different. The chief reason on which his opinion rests is this: that, as he says, no ancient writers counted the Getae among the Germans. This seems to me not so much surprising as strange,

units.la: Cc rum tam multos veteres ( ut recentiores omittam ) rerum antiquarum tam diligentes & studiosos, in hanc de Getis opinionem tam unanimiter consensisse, nisi vel antiquorum monumentis, quæ fortasse, ut alia infinita, exciderunt; aut pertinaci majorum traditione, quæ pro monumentis esse debeat, in eam inducti effent; nec hactenus repertum quenquam, unum fi excipiamus Cluverium, qui contradiceret. Multa autem potuerunt accidere, cur Getæ à Germanis oriundi, aut ejusdem cum Germanis originis, alii tamen posterioribus temporibus crederentur ; quos tanta nimirum locorum intercapedo ; mores in multis immutati ; lingua quoque, ut probabile, non parum adulterata, & cum aliis confusa ; nova denique nomenclatura à notis & vulgatis Germanis difcriminarent. Credibile est Germanos aut Germanorum parentes & ϑεϱρόνες illas omnes olim oras insedisse, quas postea ut Orientalium numerus augebatur, supervenientes ( & ipsæ quoque quondam & linguâ & ortu eædem:) aliæ nationes, Græci aut Græcorum progenitores, aliive cognati populi, ad magis Septentrionales partes paulatim protuderint. Nec tamen omnes loco cessisse, qui remanserint veteres incolæ, cum suis eos advenis in unam gentem coaluisse, in quibusdam locis, mutatam gentem; linguam, eandem remansisse: in aliis, mutatam linguam, non gentem, sed mixtam tamen: ex hac mixtura & rerum vicissitudine, nova nomina orta; veteribus, novas notiones accessisse; unde insecutæ in historiis consusiones multiplices. Huc facit & Plinii in Naturali Historiâ de Scythico nomine querela. Jam linguas, essentialiter quamvis, ut ita dicam, & originitus easdem, ubi tamen multiplex ex confusione variarum accidit interpolatio & diversa pronunciatio, quis nisi peritissimus, easdem agnoverit? Imò vel affines; nisi qui utramque, aut alteram saltem probè calluerit; & in scriptis potiùs, quàm sermone (ubi longè difficilior observatio) comparationem instituat?
units.tr: That so many ancient writers (not to mention more recent ones), so diligent and studious of antiquity, should have agreed so unanimously in this opinion about the Getae does not seem to me as strange as it might. Either they were led into it by the records of the ancients, which perhaps, like countless others, have perished, or they were persuaded by the stubborn tradition of their forefathers, which ought to count as a record. And so far I have found no one, except Cluverius, who contradicts it. Yet many things could have happened to make people in later times believe that the Getae were descended from the Germans, or were of the same origin as the Germans. Such a long distance of places, customs changed in many respects, and a language, probably not a little corrupted and mixed with others, would have led them to distinguish the two peoples by new names unknown to the common Germans. It is likely that the Germans, or the parents of the Germans, and all those [ϑεϱρόνες] once inhabited those shores which later, as the number of the Orientals grew, were gradually pushed further north by newcomers, the Greeks or the ancestors of the Greeks, or other kindred peoples, who were themselves once the same in language and origin. Yet not all who remained behind, the old inhabitants, gave up their place. In some places they merged with their newcomers into one people; the people changed, but the language remained the same. In others the language changed, not the people, but the result was still a mixture. From this mixture and the changing of circumstances, new names arose, and new meanings were attached to old words, whence the many confusions in the histories that followed. Pliny's complaint in his Natural History about the Scythian name also bears on this. Now, who but the most expert would recognise languages that are essentially, so to speak, and in their origin the same, when many interpolations and different pronunciations have arisen from the confusion of various tongues? Indeed, who would even recognise languages that are merely related, unless he had a good command of both, or at least of one, and made the comparison from writings rather than speech, where the observation is far more difficult?

units.la: Nam quòd Geta Thracum progenies (ut à Cluverio objicitur) ab antiquis nonnullis constituitur, parum hoc
units.tr: For that the Geta is a descendant of the Thracians (as Cluverius objects), is asserted by some ancient writers. This moves me little, since I know how easily proximity of neighbourhood could have misled them.

units.la: me movet, qui sciam quàm facilè vicinitas illis imponere potuerit: sed & ipsos Thracas, Scythicam progeniem, ut & Germanos, à pluribus constitui, non ignorem. Cluverium autem miror, qui linguam non Gallis tantùm, Britannisque Germanis; sed & Illyriis Hispanísque communem fuisse,contra difertissima, ni valdè fallor, antiquorum plurium testimonia, statuit: eundem silentium eorum tanti facere, ut contra tantum non contemnendorum testium (Hieronymum, Spartianum, Claudianum, Aufonium, aliósque ab ipso nominatos:) consensum,Getas & Gothos pro iisdem habentium, ipse diversos statuat,quòd nulli veteres, (ex vetustioribus illis scil.) Getas Germanos fuisse testentur.
units.tr: Yet I am not unaware that the Thracians themselves are held by many to be a Scythian offspring, as are the Germans. I am surprised at Cluverius, who holds that a language common not only to the Gauls and Britons but also to the Germans, and to the Illyrians and Spaniards as well, was spoken, contrary, unless I am much mistaken, to the very clear testimony of many ancient writers. He sets so little store by their silence that, against the agreement of such witnesses, not to be despised (Jerome, Spartianus, Claudian, Ausonius, and others he names), who held the Getae and the Goths to be the same people, he himself declares them different, on the ground that no ancient writers (I mean the older ones) testify that the Getae were Germans.

units.la: Id igitur si obtinemus, quod praeter Cluverium nemo negat, Getas non aliis quàm qui posteà Gothi fuisse; quos omnes Germanicae fatentur originis; Gethicam quoque linguam, non aliam quàm Germanicam agnoscentes: Gethicam linguam Graecâ permixtam suisse locuples testis Ovidius. Nec verisimile est, quanquam id ipse alicubi negat Ovidius, nisi potior pars linguæ Geticæ, Græca fuisset, affinitatem illam tam facile animadversurum fuisse Ovidium, cùm tantum posset (inter loquendum præcipuè) dialectorum varietas, ut vir Anglus in Belga, nisi attentior & sagacior, sermonis Anglici vestigia; nec magis Belga in Anglo loquente Belgici deprehendat; cùm tamen τὰ ἐναλλάξ utriusque linguæ propiùs insipicienti sint propè eadem. Quid quòd Ovidius de se prædicat, librum se Getico sermone in laudes Augusti scripsisse? Quod si verum est, magna fuerit Getici cum Græco sermonis affinitas oportet, quem tam paucis annis tam grandis Ovidius addiscere potuerit.
units.tr: If, then, we maintain what no one except Cluverius denies, that the Getae were the same as those who were later called Goths, whom all acknowledge to be of German origin, and who recognise the Getic language as none other than German, then the Getic language was mixed with Greek, as the eloquent witness Ovid says. Nor is it likely (although Ovid himself somewhere denies it) that, unless the greater part of the Getic language had been Greek, Ovid would have noticed that affinity so readily, since the variety of dialects, especially in speech, can be so great that an Englishman in Flanders, unless more attentive and sharper, would not detect traces of English speech, nor a Fleming in England detect Flemish; yet the inverted features [τὰ ἐναλλάξ] of each language, to one who looks more closely, are nearly the same. What of the fact that Ovid claims of himself that he wrote a book in praise of Augustus in the Getic tongue? If this is true, the affinity of the Getic with the Greek language must have been great, since Ovid, so great a man, could learn it in so few years.

units.la: Ultra Tomos in superiori parte Ponticî litoris situm erat Borysthenes oppidum, fluvio celebratissimo cognomine, Græcorum vetustissima colonia: ab Herodoto descripta. Statum ejus Dionis Chrysostomi (qui sub Domitiano & Trajano Imperatoribus vixit) ætate, describit ipse ὑξ ἀνλοφίας. Narrat autem undique cinctos ac permixtos Barbaris (quos Scythas etiam sæpè appellat) pellat)quanquam ad eorum mores habitúmque alias compositos, Græcè tamen utcunque intellexisse, Homeri Poëtæ inprimis studiosos. Adeò quidem, ut studio illorum adductus, orationem apud illos, quæ Boryfthenitica ex loco nuncupata, Dio habuerit. Quis autem dubitet, quin ut homines, ita & linguæ, Græca Scythicáque, in istis locis permixtæ confuseque: & quanto Græci ibi patrii sermonis studiosores & tenaciores, quàm qui Tomis, ubi Ovidius exulabat; tanto plus ejus in vulgarem Scythicam transfusum? Tefatur ibi Dio Tauricam quoque Cherfonesum, Mæotide palude celebrem, à Scythis & Græcis promiscuè habitatam fuisse. Ibi autem hodiéq; sermonem Germanicum, & quidem (quantum ex verbis à Busbequio prolatis colligere est) qui ad Anglicum proximè accedat, in usu esse vulgò notum est. Non ignoro Gothos posterioriбus quoque sæculis istas terras occupasse: nihil tamen obstat, quin & ex prioribus illis multi, recentioribus illis permixti, sint superstites. Cæterùm de Boryfthenienfium studio philosophiæ quod
units.tr: Beyond Tomis, on the upper part of the Pontic shore, lay the town of Borysthenes, with a very famous river of the same name, the oldest Greek colony, described by Herodotus. Dio Chrysostom (who lived under the emperors Domitian and Trajan) describes its condition in his own time [ὑξ ἀνλοφίας]. He relates that it was surrounded on all sides and mixed with barbarians (whom he also often calls Scythians), who, though otherwise different in their customs and way of life, nevertheless understood Greek in some fashion, and were especially keen on the poet Homer. So much so that, drawn by their enthusiasm, Dio delivered a speech among them, called the Borysthenitic speech after the place. Who would doubt that, just as the peoples, so too the languages, Greek and Scythian, were mixed and confused in those places; and that the more the Greeks there were eager and tenacious of their native speech than those at Tomis, where Ovid was in exile, so much more of it passed into the common Scythian tongue? Dio also testifies that the Tauric Chersonese, famous for the Lake Maeotis, was inhabited promiscuously by Scythians and Greeks. And there, even today, it is commonly known that the German language is in use, and indeed (as far as can be gathered from the words quoted by Busbecq) one that comes closest to English. I am not unaware that the Goths also occupied those lands in later centuries; nothing prevents many of the earlier inhabitants, mixed with the later ones, from surviving. But as for the Borysthenites' devotion to philosophy, which Dio relates,

units.la: . quod narrat Dio, non id abhorret ab ingenio caeterorum incolarum, quos eo nomine commendant aliqui veteres; Herodotus, ni fallor, & Aristoteles alicubi. Unde sunt qui verba Apostoli Coloff. III. v. 2. βάςβαςῶ & αυνῦης; non per ἀυξηση (ut ibi Grotius aliique) sed per ἀλλίσκον accipienda contendant.
units.tr: This is no less in keeping with the character of the other inhabitants, whom some ancient writers commend for that quality: Herodotus, unless I am mistaken, and Aristotle somewhere. Hence some argue that the words of the Apostle in Colossians 3:2, βάςβαςῶ [barbarian] and αυνῦης [Scythian], are to be understood not as ἀυξηση (as Grotius and others there take them) but as ἀλλίσκον.

units.la: Jam quae hactenus disseruimus cum ad Germanos in genere pertineant; an & ad Saxones speciatim, & illos Ponticorum istorum Scytharum partem sive progeniem fuisse, non improbabiliter colligi possit, porro nobis videndum est.
units.tr: Up to this point we have argued the matter as it concerns the Germans in general. We must now consider whether it can reasonably be inferred that the Saxons in particular were also, and were a part or offspring of those Pontic Scythians.

units.la: De Saxonum origine inter doctos ambigitur, & multa à multis afferuntur, quae contemnere facilius, quam certiora, quaeq; alii probaturi sint, substituere. Caterum, de Saxonum origine aut sedibus, postquam illo nomine Romanis innotescere coeperunt, nulla quod sciam controversia. Ptolemaeus, qui primus aut inter primos illos memorat, in Cimbrica Cherfonesfo, (quae nunc Dania) & Balthici maris oris constituit. Inde eos traiecto Rheno Australiores oras ac terras infestasse & occupasse, satis certum est. Sed cùm nomen tam recens sit, quo nomine priùs noti, & unde, si non indigenæ, eò delati, non tam facile est expedire. Consentiens hodie omnium fere eruditorum est opinio (inquit eruditissimus Cisnerus) Saxones à Sagis, vel Sacis originem ducere; de quibus Herodotus, &c. Hos autem Sacas sub Scytharum (Asiaticorum sci.) genere ac nomine comprehendunt antiqui plures. ad Cappadoces autem Ponticos usque victoriis suis & incursionibus processisse Strabo author est. Eosdem ad Persas quoque progressos esse, alii tradunt: unde à Persis omnes universim Scythæ Sacæ nuncupati, ut qui ex omnibus illis notissimi. Οἱ ἡ Πέρσαι πάντες τῶν Σκυθῶν καλέσαι Σάκας: quo loco etiam habitum Sacarum describit talem, qui ScythoGermanis optimè conveniat.
units.tr: Scholars dispute the origin of the Saxons, and many have advanced many views, which it is easier to dismiss than to replace with more certain ones that others would accept. However, as far as I know, there is no controversy about the origin or dwelling-place of the Saxons once that name began to be known to the Romans. Ptolemy, who is the first or among the first to mention them, placed them in the Cimbric Chersonese (now Denmark) and on the shores of the Baltic Sea. It is fairly certain that from there they crossed the Rhine and attacked and occupied the more southern shores and lands. But since the name is so recent, it is not so easy to determine by what name they were earlier known, and whence they came, if they were not natives. Today the opinion of almost all scholars agrees, says the very learned Cisnerus, that the Saxons derive their origin from the Sagae or Sacae; of whom Herodotus speaks, etc. Many of the ancients include these Sacae under the race and name of the Scythians (the Asiatic ones, that is). Strabo reports that they advanced in their victories and raids as far as the Pontic Cappadocians. Others relate that they also advanced into Persia, whence the Persians called all Scythians collectively Sacae, as the best known of them all. Οἱ ἡ Πέρσαι πάντες τῶν Σκυθῶν καλέσαι Σάκας [The Persians call all the Scythians Sacae]. In the same passage he describes the dress of the Sacae in a way that fits the Scythian-Germans very well.

units.la: Non defuerunt qui Saxones, Axones dictos asserrerent, ex Ponto Axeno qui postea Euxenus. Sed merito hæc conjectura exploditur, quum certum sit non tam antiquum esse istud, (sive Axenos legas, sive Saxones) indigitamentum. Alii ex Cimbris originè repetunt, tunt,quos cum Cimmeriis nescio quàm rectè,(inter quos & veteres multi)confundunt: quorum opinionem multis exagitat Cluverius. Cimmerios certè extrema Ponti, sive Mæoticam paludem & vicina loca ( sive ut indigenas, ut nonnulli : sive ut advenas, ut alii :) diu insedisse, unde & Bosphorus Cimmerius, qui aliis Mæoticus, satis constat.
units.tr: There were those who asserted that the Saxons were so called from the Axeni, from the Pontus Axenus, later called Euxinus. But this conjecture is rightly rejected, since it is certain that this designation, whether one reads Axenos or Saxones, is not so ancient. Others trace their origin to the Cimbri, whom they confuse, I know not how correctly, with the Cimmerians (as did many of the ancients). Cluverius attacks this opinion at length. It is certain that the Cimmerians long inhabited the extremities of the Pontus, or the Maeotic marsh and neighbouring places (whether as natives, as some hold, or as settlers, as others hold), and hence the Cimmerian Bosporus, which others call the Maeotic, is well attested.

units.la: In hac tantâ & rerum ipsarum obscuritate, & opinionum varietate, non meum, neque fortasse cujusquam vel diligentissimi, quicquam certò statuere. Ut autem maximè verisimile sit, Saxones ex Ponticis oris & pontica Chersonesō, ubi promiscuè Græcos & Scythas habitasse prius ostendimus, in Cimbricam Cherfonesum & Germanici maris oras illas Septentrionales profectos esse; hæc inducunt me ut credam. Primò quidem, disertum Ptolemæi testimonium, qui non illos tantùm, de quibus egimus, Sacas in Asiâ constituit; sed & Safones nominat, Scythiæ populum, à Sacis oriundum. Cùm autem idem Ptolemæus Saxones in Europâ eodem tempore constituat, probabile est,tam Asiaticos illos,quàm Europæos hos ex uno aliquo loco prosectos, in diversas orbis partes expeditiones suscepisse ; &, vel antiquum nomen, quamvis eo nomine ante Ptolemæi ætatem, aut paulò ante, Græcis Geographis non innotuerint, retinuiffe: vel hoc novum, ab armis, & fusceptæ profectionis consilio ipsos sibi indidiffe. Eum autem locum, ex quo profecti sunt, cùm ex Ponticis oris & Pontica Cherfonefo variis temporibus in varias terras ingens sese colluvies effuderit, Pontum fuisse, aut Ponto vicina loca, valdè probabile est. Sed ut ita credamus, præcipuè suadet propior ista quam docuimus affinitas linguarum.
units.tr: Given such great obscurity of the facts themselves and such variety of opinions, it is not for me, nor perhaps for anyone however diligent, to establish anything with certainty. But that it is most probable that the Saxons set out from the Pontic shores and the Pontic Chersonese, where, as we have shown earlier, Greeks and Scythians lived together, to the Cimbric Chersonese and those northern shores of the German sea: this is what persuades me. First, the explicit testimony of Ptolemy, who places not only those Sacae of whom we have spoken in Asia, but also names the Safones, a people of Scythia descended from the Sacae. Since the same Ptolemy places the Saxons in Europe at the same time, it is probable that both those Asiatics and these Europeans set out from some one place and undertook expeditions into different parts of the world; and that either they retained the old name, although it was not known to the Greek geographers under that name before Ptolemy's time or shortly before, or else they gave themselves this new name from their arms and the purpose of the expedition they had undertaken. Moreover, it is very probable that the place from which they set out was the Pontus or places near the Pontus, since from the Pontic shores and the Pontic Chersonese a vast swarm poured out at various times into various lands. But what chiefly persuades us to believe this is the closer affinity of the languages, which we have shown.

units.la: Secundò, quòd mari assueti, & maritima loca consectati, ut plurimùm Saxones : quod Pontici litoris accolis, & nunc ἀπιξοις, optimè conveniat.
units.tr: Second, the Saxons, for the most part, were accustomed to the sea and pursued maritime regions, which suits well the dwellers on the Pontic shore and those now called ἀπιξοις [Apixi?].

units.la: Tertiò, quòd in moribus Getarum, ut ab Ovidio,oculato teste, defcribuntur, haud pauca, quæ cum Saxonum moribus & institutis optimè convenient. Saxones, ut notum, cæsariem alebant & ad humeros ufq; demittebant.
units.tr: Third, the customs of the Getae, as described by Ovid, an eyewitness, include not a few that agree very well with the customs and institutions of the Saxons. As is well known, the Saxons wore their hair long and let it fall to their shoulders.

units.la: Getæ pariter. Vox fera, trux vultus, (truces & cærulei oculi, de Germanis Tacitus:) verissima mortis imago: Non coma, non ullâ barba refecta manu. Et Eleg.X. Quos ut non timeas, possis odisse videndo, Pellibus, ( de Germanis idem Tacitus,Gerunt & ferarum pelles, &c.) & longâ corpora tecta comâ.
units.tr: So did the Getae. A wild voice, a fierce face (Tacitus, on the Germans, speaks of fierce and blue eyes): a most true image of death. Neither hair nor beard trimmed by hand. And in Elegy 10: Whom you could not fear, you could hate on sight, with skins (Tacitus again, on the Germans: they wear the skins of wild beasts, etc.) and bodies covered with long hair.
