units.la: Saxones cultro accincti esse solebant,quem Seaxe, indigitabant, eóque ministro ad cædes prompti. Nota historia stragis Salisburienfis(in Anglia) ad quam nota illa verborum formula, velut tessera militaris, aut classicum, præivit, Seam eour fearcs.(vel ut fcribi debere monebat Somnerus meus, nymaib eolwer fcares:) stringite gladios. Simile eorum factum narrat (ut & aliis observatum) Wittikindus Monachus, atque à majoribus illis cultris, quos ipse factos indigitatos tradit, quibus cædem illam Thuringorum perpetrarunt, Saxonibus nomen inditum contendit: quam nominis rationem probat & Butherus in suis ad Taciti Germaniam commentationibus. De quo mox plura. De Getis autem Ovidius, Dextera non segnis ftrifto dare vulnera ferro ;
units.tr: The Saxons were used to girding themselves with a knife, which they called seax, and they were ready to use that weapon for slaughter. There is the well-known story of the massacre at Salisbury (in England), which was preceded by that familiar verbal formula, as a military watchword or trumpet-call, Seam eour fearcs (or, as my Somner advised it should be written, nymaib eolwer fcares): draw your swords. Wittikind the monk tells a similar story (as others have also noted), and he claims that the Saxons were named from those larger knives, which he says were made and called by that name, with which they carried out that slaughter of the Thuringians. Butherus, in his commentaries on Tacitus' Germania, also supports this derivation. More on this shortly. As for the Getae, Ovid says: A right hand not slow to deal wounds with drawn steel;

units.la: Quem vinctum lateri, * Barbarus omnis habet.
units.tr: Which, hung at the side, every barbarian has.

units.la: Plura alius inveniet fortasse,cui omnia colligere,quæ de Getis sparsim passimque Poëta,vacaverit. Cæterum de Etymologia verbi Saxones, quamvis Cisnero aliisque concedamus, falli Wittikindum, qui ab illâ Thuringorum cæde repetit, quod multo antiquius esse certum est : nihil obstat tamen, quin ita jam olim, cùm primùm Cimbricas oras appulerunt, vel etiam ante, appellati fuerint. Ut & Scythæ, à sagittando: & Longobardi, Germanorum & ipsi Cimbrorumque progenies, ex longis, non barbis, sed hastis. Nec minùs probabile est illud Etymum, quàm quod ex Sacis Cisnero aliisque probatur. Huc etiam facit fortasse quæ doctissimo Camerario de voce σκύθη in Thesauro suo observata. Docet enim ex Paufania & Theognide, σκύθην vocatum proprie ferrum, quo caput tonderetur: unde manaverit vox ἀπεσκυθίσαι: quod tamen aliter ab aliis exponi non nescimus. Sed sive Græca vox est σκώϑη primitùs, five Scythica, quin altera ab alterâ (vel fcaʃ, à σκώϑη ; vel σκώϑη, ex fear:) profluxerit,ego vix dubito : cùm π θ in medio verbi sæpe deperdi in σκιϑικμ aliísque observaverimus ; sed & hodiéque ferrum messorium five falcem vocent Angli a spthe.. Ne quis autem miretur armorum nomen ad rûsticam supelleċtilem translatum ; haud dissimili ratione vomerem aratri vocant hódie Angli cultrum, a coulter. De litera c.vel x.pereunte,aliquid in Hebraicis.
units.tr: Perhaps someone else, with leisure to gather everything the poet scattered here and there about the Getae, will find more. Moreover, concerning the etymology of the word Saxones: although we grant Cisnerus and others, it is wrong of Wittikind to derive it from that slaughter of the Thuringians, since that name is certainly much older. Nevertheless, there is no reason why they could not have been called so long before, when they first reached the Cimbric shores, or even earlier. Just as the Scythians were named from shooting arrows, and the Lombards, also a race of Germans and of the Cimbri, from their long spears rather than their beards. That etymology is no less probable than the one from the Sacae which Cisnerus and others favour. Perhaps what the most learned Camerarius observed in his Thesaurus about the word σκύθη also bears on this. For he shows, from Pausanias and Theognis, that σκύθη was properly the name of an iron tool with which the head was shaved, whence the verb ἀπεσκυθίσαι [to shave the head] arose; though we are aware that others explain it otherwise. But whether the word was originally Greek, σκώϑη, or Scythian, and whether one derived from the other (either scaʃ from σκώϑη, or σκώϑη from scear), I scarcely doubt; since we have observed that the π θ in the middle of a word is often lost, as in σκιϑικμ and others. Even today the English call a reaping-hook or sickle a sythe. Lest anyone wonder that the name of a weapon was transferred to rustic equipment, the English today call the share of a plough a coulter by a not dissimilar reasoning. On the loss of the letter c or x, something will be said in the Hebrew matters.

units.la: Jam quod Dio testatur apud GræcoScythas illos Borysthenicos tantâ in veneratione Homerum Poëtam fuisse, ut propè pro Deo haberent, ac solum ex omnibus Poëtis agnoscerent ; magnum hinc argumentum, Saxonicam linguam illic olim viguisse. Plurima certè Anglici sermonis in Homero ; aut Homeri potiùs in Anglico sermone tum in verbis singularibus, tum phrasibus & idiotismis animadvertimus olim vestigia, quorum collectionem, si relegendi aliquando nunquam satis lećti aut laudati poëmatis illius otium & opportunitas suppetat, libenter promiserim; quanquam libentius ab alio tum Anglici tum Græci peritiore sermonis expectaturus. Hujus generis est vox Anglica tpote de homine cui supra molem corporis robur aut ingenium superat: ex Homerico scilicet illo Tydeo, de quo Poëta;
units.tr: As for what Dio testifies, that among those Borysthenite Greek-Scythians Homer the poet was held in such reverence that they almost regarded him as a god, and acknowledged him alone among all the poets: this is a great argument that the Saxon language once flourished there. There are certainly very many traces of English in Homer, or rather of Homer in English, which we have observed both in individual words and in phrases and idioms; I would willingly promise a collection of them, if I ever have the leisure and opportunity to re-read that poem, which is never read or praised enough. Yet I would more gladly expect it from another, more skilled in both English and Greek. Of this kind is the English word tpote, said of a man whose strength or ability exceeds the bulk of his body, namely from that Homeric Tydeus, of whom the poet says:

units.la: Τυδέϊς τοι μικρὸς μὲν εἶν ἰδὲ μέγας, ἀλλὰ μαχητής.
units.tr: Tydeus, indeed, was small in body but a great fighter. [Τυδέϊς τοι μικρὸς μὲν εἶν ἰδὲ μέγας, ἀλλὰ μαχητής.]

units.la: Hujus generis alia non pauca notavimus in verborum collectione: ut in ξῶντες, & ἀφεῖλης, & βάλης; aliisque, in quibus Homerus laudatus: interdum & illustratus. Jam Dionis, quia insignis est locus, verba hic apponam, & desinam.
units.tr: We have noted not a few other examples of this kind in our collection of words, such as ξῶντες, ἀφεῖλης and βάλης, and others in which Homer is praised and sometimes illustrated. Now, since the passage is notable, I will set out Dio's words here and end.

units.la: Dio Chrysost. Orat. XXXVI. de studio Borysthenitarum erga Homerum.
units.tr: Dio Chrysostom, Oration 36, on the zeal of the Borysthenites for Homer.

units.la: Ἡ Χαλκὸν δ' ἡ πάντες οἱ Βοςυσθενῖται ... μηκοὶ ἐπὶ ... ἀχιλλέως εὐνοίαν τὴν ... ἀχιλλέως κεκαλυμμένην ... Ὁμήρου.
units.tr: Now all the Borysthenites ... with goodwill toward Achilles ... concealed ... of Homer. [Ἡ Χαλκὸν δ' ἡ πάντες οἱ Βοςυσθενῖται ... μηκοὶ ἐπὶ ... ἀχιλλέως εὐνοίαν τὴν ... ἀχιλλέως κεκαλυμμένην ... Ὁμήρου.]

units.la: μίσες. κ) τᾶλλα ἐκεῖ σαφῶς ἑλληνίζονλες, διὰ τὸ ἐν μέσοις οἰκεῖν τοῖς βαρβάροις. ὅμως τῳ γε Ἰταλίδα ὀλίγοι πόλεις ἱσαν ἀπὸ ςόμαλο.
units.tr: ... speaking Greek clearly in all other respects, because they dwell among barbarians. Yet, at least, few cities of Italy ... [μίσες. κ) τᾶλλα ἐκεῖ σαφῶς ἑλληνίζονλες, διὰ τὸ ἐν μέσοις οἰκεῖν τοῖς βαρβάροις. ὅμως τῳ γε Ἰταλίδα ὀλίγοι πόλεις ἱσαν ἀπὸ ςόμαλο.]

units.la: Corollarium.
units.tr: Corollary.

units.la: LIceret jam nobis per æquum lectorem fortasse desinere; non eo tantum sensu, quo Cicero alicubi de Æsopo histrione; sed ut jam perfunctis & fide præstitâ. Corollarii tamen loco, quando de linguâ Anglicâ tota hæc dissertatio fuit, erit brevis disquisitio, An illi bene de linguâ patriâ mereantur, qui verbis exoticis undique corrasis illam locupletare (ita enim obtendunt multi) satagunt. Passim enim occurrunt doctorum querelæ, corrumpi linguas hac loquendi farragine, non ornari. Quare quid nobis videatur, paucis hic indicabimus. Ac primum illud statuimus, copiam verborum multum ad eloquentiam conferre, quantóque quæque lingua amplior & locupletior est, tantò uberiores iistius generis fructus sperari posse. Nihil sutilius Grammatici nescio cujus in Æneidem primâ observatione, copulam, &, &, apud Latinos diversas res semper copulare, cum ad exaggerandam orationem (quæ pars eloquentiæ potissima) sæpius adhibeatur. Quanquam etiam sine copula (quæ oratio vocatur ἀσύνδετον) plura ejusdem significationis verba eleganter conjungantur; quale illud Terentii, Abiit, evasit, erupit : &, Vetus, vietus, veternosus, senex : & in Cicerone, Gellio observata, vastare, exinanire, spoliare ; & decepit, fefellit, induxit : de quibus & similibus recte idem judicat, unam eandemque rem pluribus verbis vehementer atque atrociter dici: — quæ quanquam eadem fere sint, & ex una sententia oriantur, plura tamen esse existimantur, quoniam aures & animum sæpius feriunt. Sed legat lector quæ toto illo capite a doctissimo viro doctissimè disputantur, & allatis ex Homero aliisque exemplis pluribus, illustrantur. Hoc magis miremur. Est quoddam genus dicendi concisum, ac vibrantibus & contortis sententiis, quasi spiculis, inclusum : qualis Senecæ Philosophi oratio, ut plurimum. Ab hoc genere cum copiam verborum brevitas sententiarum videatur exclu-
units.tr: We might now, with the indulgence of the fair reader, perhaps bring this to an end: not only in the sense in which Cicero somewhere speaks of the actor Aesop, but because we have already gone through our task and kept our promise. Yet in place of a corollary, since this whole dissertation has concerned the English tongue, there will be a brief inquiry into whether those deserve well of their native language who labour to enrich it (as many put it) by gathering foreign words from every side. Learned men everywhere complain that languages are corrupted by this medley of words, not adorned. So we shall briefly state here what seems to us. And first we lay down this: abundance of words contributes greatly to eloquence, and the richer and fuller any language is, the more abundant the fruits of this kind that may be hoped for from it. Nothing is more subtle than the observation of a certain grammarian on the first line of the Aeneid, that the conjunction "and, and" among the Latins always joins different things, since it is often used to amplify the style, which is the chief part of eloquence. Yet even without a conjunction, which is called asyndeton [ἀσύνδετον], several words of the same meaning are elegantly joined together, like that line of Terence: He went away, he slipped off, he burst out; and old, worn out, decrepit, aged; and in Cicero and Gellius the observed pairs to lay waste, to empty, to plunder; and deceived, misled, led astray. Concerning these and similar cases the same author rightly judges that one and the same thing is said with many words, vehemently and fiercely; these, although they are nearly the same and arise from one idea, are nevertheless thought to be several, because they strike the ears and the mind more often. But let the reader go through what that most learned man argues at length in that whole chapter, and what he illustrates with many examples from Homer and others. We should marvel at this all the more. There is a certain concise style of speaking, enclosed in darting and twisted sentences, as it were in little spears, such as the style of the philosopher Seneca, for the most part. Although brevity of sentences may seem to exclude abundance of words from this style,

units.la: dere, nullum tamen genus, si propius introspicias, in quo verba magis luxuriant: ut bona pars eorum quæ in Senecâ maximè vulgò placent, perierit, si quæ per diversa verba sæpius repetuntur, ab illo dempseris. Sed hæc alii pluribus, neque nos id nunc agimus.
units.tr: yet, if you look more closely, there is no style in which words luxuriate more. A good part of what most pleases the common reader in Seneca would have vanished if you removed from him those things that are repeated often in different words. But others have treated this at greater length, and we are not concerned with it now.

units.la: Ad versiones librorum aliâ linguâ scriptorum quàm necessaria sit verborum Synonymorũ copia, fidem faciant sacræ Testamenti utriusque literæ, ubi tam frequens eorum usus, ut vix interdum Latinæ linguæ sufficiant opes; & Anglicæ bonam copiam sine dedecore liceat ejurare. Sed hæc vulgaria. Illud haud adeò protritum fortasse, ad consummatissimam sive in Oratoribus sive Poëtis eloquentiæ laudem copiam verborum multum conferre; non quatenus est copia per se (quod alterius est laudis, de quâ jam diximus:) sed quatenus in copiâ delectus, quem cum arte (ubi opus est) adhibere, ut verba cum naturâ rerum congruant, pauci quidem qui norunt, sed qui norunt, laudem summorum ac divinorum ingeniorum merito consequantur. Hac præcipuè laude excelluit & tantâ apud omnes, qui-
units.tr: That a copious stock of synonyms is needed for translating books written in another language, the sacred letters of both Testaments bear witness, where their use is so frequent that sometimes the resources of the Latin tongue scarcely suffice, and one may, without disgrace, be allowed to pass over a good store of English. But these are commonplace points. Perhaps less worn is this point: that a great abundance of words contributes much to the most accomplished praise of eloquence, both in orators and in poets; not insofar as abundance is abundance in itself (which belongs to another kind of praise, of which we have already spoken), but insofar as there is selection within the abundance, which few know how to apply with skill, where it is needed, so that words agree with the nature of things; yet those who know it deservedly win the praise of the greatest and most divine geniuses. This praise above all excelled, and in such high regard among all, who-

units.la: Dd
units.tr: Dd

units.la: quibus de meliore luto præcordia, in admiratione fuit Homerus: quem ideo dicebat Aristoteles μόνον ϰυνέμένα ποιεῖν τὰ ὀνόμαλα, vitam verbis infundere, ut qui illum legerent, non scripta legere, sed res ipsas spectare crederent. De mirifico hoc verborum cum rebus consensu plura nobis alibi dicta. Quia autem pauci sunt, qui ista vel capiant, vel iis capiantur, quòd quantò ars est exquisitior, tanto peritiorem requirit judicem; exemplo uno aut altero rem illustrare non gravabor.
units.tr: Homer was admired by all those whose hearts were made of better clay; Aristotle said of him that he alone makes words live [μόνον ϰυνέμένα ποιεῖν τὰ ὀνόμαλα], that he infuses life into words, so that those who read him believe they are not reading writings but looking at the things themselves. We have said more elsewhere about this wonderful agreement of words with things. But since few are able either to grasp these matters or be moved by them, because the finer the art, the more skilled the judge it requires, I will not hesitate to illustrate the point with one or two examples.

units.la: Multa sunt hujus generis quæ veteres Grammatici Rhetorésque in Homero observarunt, ac miris laudibus extulerunt: qui sanè unus plura in hoc genere suppeditat, quàm omnia omnium mortalium scripta qualiacunque. Post Homerum, secunda Virgilio laus merito tribuatur. Sed nos illis omissis, ex sacri Codicis Versionibus exemplum sumemus. Sublimis & exquisitæ in suo genere orationis, Psalmus CVII. quo divina providentia à divino vate, exemplis ex quotidianâ petitis experientiâ, sed summo artificio asseritur. Ejus Psalmi versus 26. in vetere (ita vulgò vocant, cant, quamvis sit hujus saeculi) Anglicâ versione ita habet: They are carried up to the heaven, and downe againe to the deep, &c. recentior autem, They mount up to the heaven; they goe downe againe to the depths, &c. Pauci fortasse discrimen observant, neq; ipsos qui mutarunt hoc spectasse praestare ausim: caeterum si quis Aristotelicâ aure legat, mirum quantum discrimen ex unâ illâ peregrinâ & ascititiâ voculâ mount, quae huic loco ad ἐνάρξιν, & rem ipsam de qua agitur ob oculos ponendam appositissima est, & ut ita dicam, φανταζόμενον. Non solùm enim vasti illi saevientis Oceani fluctus cum montibus jucundissimè comparantur (quod nec omisit Virgilius in tempestatis descriptione, qui istâ comparatione bis ibi, terve utitur; montes volvuntur aquarum, &c.) sed & in ipsa verbi mount compositione & pronuntiatione nescio quid arduum & praeruptum, quod pronuntiantibus speciem nitentium quandam ac laborantium ingerit. Sed & hoc Virgiliana fuit artis, ut in hac re versum monosyllabo terminaret, praeruptus aquâ mons. Tanti erat hoc verbum bum civitate Anglicâ donare, ut hîc legeretur: quanquâm ut hunc usum præstaret, multum contulit pronuntiatio, quæ illi ex genio sermonis Anglici accessit. )
units.tr: There are many things of this kind which the ancient grammarians and rhetoricians observed in Homer and praised with wonderful commendations; he alone supplies more of this kind than all the writings of all mortals put together. After Homer, second praise should rightly be given to Virgil. But setting these aside, I shall take an example from the versions of the sacred Scripture. Psalm 107 is a sublime passage of an exquisite kind of speech, in which divine providence is asserted by the divine poet, with examples drawn from everyday experience and with the highest art. In the old English version (as they commonly call it, the old, though it belongs to this age), verse 26 of that Psalm reads: "They are carried up to the heaven, and downe againe to the deep," etc. The more recent version reads: "They mount up to the heaven; they goe downe againe to the depths," etc. Perhaps few notice the difference, and I should not dare to claim that those who changed it had this in view. But if anyone reads with an Aristotelian ear, the difference that arises from that one foreign and borrowed little word mount is remarkable. It is most fitting for this passage, for the beginning and for setting the very thing under discussion before the eyes, and, so to speak, for a vivid image. For not only are the vast waves of the raging ocean most pleasantly compared with mountains (which Virgil did not omit in describing the storm, where he uses this comparison twice or three times: the mountains of waters rolled, etc.), but in the very composition and pronunciation of the word mount there is something lofty and steep, which gives those who pronounce it the appearance of strained and labouring men. Virgil too had this art, in that he ended the line on a monosyllable in this matter: a mountain steep with water. It was worth so much to grant this word the freedom of the English city, that it should be read here; though pronunciation, which came to it from the genius of the English language, contributed much to its being used in this way.

units.la: Sed unde proprias possit opes Anglica lingua jactare aliud ibi specimen.
units.tr: But where the English tongue may display its proper resources, there is another example.

units.la: Ut igitur balatus ovium proprius, & hinnitus equorum, & æris tinnitus, & tubarum clangor; ita & vox stridor, ut catenarum propria à Sancto Augustino commemoratur. Quod autem proprie ac naturaliter catenæ dicantur stridére, inde est opinor, ex sono illo caninæ literæ asperiore & horridiore cum sibilâ conjuncto. Confert aliquid & stridula vocalis i, ut in tinnitu; quod æris proprium. Talis vox mihi videtur & Latina ferrum, in quâ geminuss r rigorem illum ferri proprium pulchrè imitatur: unde & Græcis σιδηρον,quod nos durum, & rigidum vocamus. Laudatur illud Lucretii, —ferra stridentis acerbum Horrorem:
units.tr: So, as the bleating of sheep is proper to them, and the neighing of horses, and the ringing of bronze, and the blare of trumpets, so too the word stridor (a grating or shrieking sound) is recorded by Saint Augustine as proper to chains. That chains are naturally and properly said to stridere (to grate), I suppose, comes from that harsher and more bristling sound of the letter r joined with a hiss. The shrill vowel i also contributes, as in tinnitus, which is proper to bronze. Such a word seems to me also the Latin ferrum, in which the double r well imitates that stiffness proper to iron; whence the Greeks also call it sideron, which we call hard and rigid. That line of Lucretius is praised, on the bitter horror of the grating iron. How much more so is that other passage of the same version, on the broken brazen gates and the iron bars torn apart, in verse 16 of the same Psalm...

units.la: quantò magis illud ejusdem versionis, de confractis æneis portis, & vestibus seu repagulis ferreis disruptis, ejusdem Psalmi versu 16. For he hath broken the gates of brasse, and cut the barres of iron in sunder: quibus tum confringentis ac summo quasi robore nitentis ac prævalentis actio; tum ferri ipsius quasi obluctantis & ἀντιλυπτικῶν [?] durities, ex singularum ferè literarum propriâ potestate, & appositâ collocatione ὡς ἐναργέστατα [?] (ut mihi quidem videtur) ob oculos ponitur.
units.tr: Those who read these and similar things are moved by no less pleasure (if their palate is not dull) than those who look at the works of some Apelles or Polyclitus with care and judgement. For what pleases in those works, the imitation of nature, is no less remarkable here; and perhaps all the more...

units.la: Hæc & ejusmodi alia legentibus, non minore (fi non insipidum palatum) voluptate afficitur animus, quàm opera Apellis alicujus, aut Polycleti curiosè ac cum judicio spectantibus. Quod enim in illis placet, imitatio naturæ, non minùs hîc insigne est; & tantò fortasse major admiratio, quantò voces ad animum penetrare, quàm colores & figuræ naturâ suâ sunt idoneæ.
units.tr: Readers of these and similar passages are moved by no less pleasure (if their palate is not dull) than people feel when they look closely and with discernment at the works of some Apelles or Polyclitus. For what pleases in those works, the imitation of nature, is no less remarkable here. Perhaps the admiration is even greater, to the extent that voices, by their nature, are better suited to reach the mind than colours and shapes.

units.la: Hos igitur in usus fi quis ampliando & locupletando sermoni studeat, haud ille malè de eo mereri, meâ sententiâ, censendus fit: hac tamen conditione, ut dum aliena mutuatur, propria non negligat aut fastidiat; & id sedulò caveatur, ne novorum introductio, vetesům fit abòlitiò. Quòd côntrà fit à plerisque, qui nôn ut lòtuplèrènt linguàm, pêregrina mutuantur; sed quòd nôtà & comminùnia fàstidiant; pessimâ & ineptissimâ plèriq; pèrsuàsione, quàsi sapere eòs sùpra vùlgùs necesse essèt, qui vulgari sermône contènti non sùnt.
units.tr: So if anyone labours to enrich and expand our language for these purposes, in my judgement he deserves well of it, on one condition: that while borrowing from abroad he does not neglect or scorn what is his own, and that care is taken that the introduction of new words does not become the abolition of old ones. Most people do the reverse. They borrow foreign words not to enrich the tongue, but because they scorn what is familiar and common. They are moved by the worst and most foolish belief, as if one had to rise above the common people in order to be among those who are not content with ordinary speech.

units.la: Quàntum ingènio valèrent Ànglì, ut àlia omittàm, fidèm faciànt scriptà, quæ funestissimis hisce tèmpòribus ùtrinque in lucèm prodiêrùnt. Sèd ità sunt à nàturâ plèrîquè còmpàrati, ut quæ in mèdio pòsità sunt, insùpèr hà̂bèant, & àlienà tàm in sermône, quàm môribus & cultù cònsèctèntur: quì si ingènii sui vîm, quò pollènt, & indùstríàm, ad pàtriæ lingùæ thesàurôs ertǔ-èndôs pòtiùs cònferrènt, quàm ad lè-gèndôs àlièni sòli flôsculôs; in mâjorè apud èxtèrôs honòrè. Prìdem fuisset Anglicà lingùa, & nôbis hùjùs Differèntionis òccàsiò dudum prærêpta èsset. Gaudèbò certè, si àlii nôstrò èxèmplò incitàti, quòd nôs inchoavimus, mèliôribùs ipsi aùspiciis, & nècessàriis ad tantùm òpùs prœsidiis ìnstructiòrès pérfecerint.
units.tr: How much the English have achieved in talent, to say nothing of others, is shown by the writings that have appeared on both sides in these most deadly times. But most men are so constituted by nature that they despise what lies at hand and pursue what is foreign, in speech, in manners and in culture. If they would rather devote the strength of their talent and their industry, in which they excel, to enriching the treasures of their native tongue than to gathering the flowers of another soil, they would stand in higher honour among foreigners. The English language would long ago have been treated in this way, and the occasion for this Dissertation would have been forestalled for us long since. I shall certainly rejoice if others, spurred on by our example, complete what we have begun, under better auspices and better equipped with the resources needed for so great a work.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.

units.la: Addenda, & suis locis inferenda.
units.tr: Addenda, to be inserted in their proper places.

units.la: PAg.3.lin.14. post,potest. Hinc illa Johannis Philoponi de Græcarum dialectorum ortu : Διαστατικῶν γὰρ τέ- λων, inquit ille, εἰς πλείονας τόπος, ἡ τῷ ἀνῶ φωνῶ ἐκ ἓν φυλαξαντων, ἀλλὰ τῆ τ. τέτων μεταβολῇ ἅμα ἡ τῷ φωνῷ μεταβαλλόντων, σωέβη διαλεκτος λέξεως. Ita editum : sed puto legendum, γενικῆς : & verto ; In varia autem terrarum loca dispersis illis, (Hellenis posteris scil.) & eundem sermonem non amplius servantibus, sed pro locorum varietate sermonem quoque variantibus, ita extiterunt quæ vocantur dialecti. Ab Orbe condito, &c.
units.tr: Page 3, line 14, after "potest". Hence that statement of John Philoponus on the origin of the Greek dialects: "For when the Greeks, as he says, had been scattered into many places, and no longer kept the same speech [ἀνῶ φωνῶ ἐκ ἓν φυλαξάντων], but as their places changed, their speech changed too [τῆ τούτων μεταβολῇ ἅμα τῇ φωνῇ μεταβαλλόντων], there came to be the dialects of the language [συνέβη διάλεκτος γένεσις]." This is how it was printed, but I think we should read γενικῆς, and I translate: "In various regions of the earth, those Hellenes who came after being dispersed, no longer keeping the same speech but varying their speech according to the variety of places, there arose what are called the dialects." From the founding of the world, etc.

units.la: Pag. 9. l. 17. adde ibi ad oram adversam, Dan.II.41.
units.tr: Page 9, line 17: add in the facing margin there, Dan. II.41.

units.la: Pag.44.l.6. post, impeteret. Quanquam autem satis cavisse me puto, ne viro docto, vitâ pridem functo, in sententiâ ejus vel aliter accipiendâ vel referendâ ulla à me (quod vulgò fieri solet) fieret injuria; quia tamen magna res ṡes agitur, & tantæ molis liber non est cuivis obvius aut parabilis, rem gratam Lectori non uni facturum me censui, si totum illum, contra quem pugnamus locum, bonâ fide hic repræsentaremus.
units.tr: Page 44, line 6, after "impeteret". Although I think I have taken care enough that I do no injury, as is so often done, to the learned man, long since deceased, either in understanding or in reporting his opinion in any way, nevertheless, since a great matter is at stake here, and a book of such bulk is not easy for everyone to come by, I judged that I would be doing a welcome service to the reader, and not only to one reader, if I presented here, in good faith, that whole passage against which we are contending.

units.la: Cluver. Germ. Ant. lib. I. c.8. edit. Lugdun. Batav. Elzevirianæ. a.d.1616. pag. 73, & 74. Sed nec eorum judicium probandum, qui, ubi aliquod vocabulum in linguâ nostrâ Celticâ occurrit, quod vel Græco, vel Latino, vel Hebraico, vel Persico, vel alius cuiuspiam gentis vocabulo sit par atque simile; protinus, id nos inde habere, exclamant. Unus quum fuerit initio rerum in terris sermo, quo omnes pariter inter se, ante Babylonis fundamenta, usi sunt mortales; quémque postea ad urbis Babylonicæ ædificationem Deus, rerum omnium conditor ac moderator, non omnino è medio sustulit, novis exinde linguis creatis, sed tantum in varia ἰδιώματα, ut supra dictum, variásque διαλέκτους, confudit, seu potius dissipavit: quid mirum, si diversissima longéque inter se remotissima per universum terræ orbem gentes multa communia habeant etiamnum rerum vocabula? Exempla eorum pauca quædam dam ob oculos posuisse, haud alienum suerit. Ægyptii & Arabes, Germanique & Hispani ac Galli, supremum illud verúmque numen, omnium rerum principium, suâ quiq; lingua dixêre Theuth, Graci etiam Θεὸς, Δεὺς & Ζεὺς, & Latini Deus :Graci item alia dialecto, unà cum Germanis nostris Dan ; ut certissimis documentis infrà suo loco ostendetur. Gracis summa pars hominis dicitur κεφαλὴ, Sinis, Indica genti, Koppalab; Germanis Kopf, & alia dialecto Kop ; Latinis caput. Latinis negandi particula est non ; Germanis, variis dialectis, netn, neen, nee, nep. & na ; quorum hoc commune cum prædictis Sinis habent : Hispanis, Italis, & Anglis no ; Sarmatis, sive Slavis, ne, & nie. Adsirmandi particula Germanis, & Sinis est ja. Qua particula Latinis est apud, Danis dicitur boo, & eodem Gracis nonnumquam vocabulo ὡς. Quod Gracis est ὅτι, Latinis dicitur uti, vel ut ; Danis at. Latinis qui est oculus, Germanis vocatur auge, & oge ; Sarmatis oko. Latinis qua auris ; Germanis est ooi. Qui Gracis πούς, Latinis est pes ; Germanis suas,quasi pfuas,& aliis dialectis suat, foot ; ut Gracorum Latinorumq; pater, Germanis fater. Quæ Græcis est μήτηρ, Latinis dicitur mater ; Persis mader ; Germanis mutter, moter, mouder, & moder : Anglis mother ; Sarmatis máterz, mácz, & máti ; Ægyptiis muth. Quæ Latinis est sepes, Pœnis atque Hebræis dicitur gadir, seu gader ; nobis Germanis gadder, & aliâ dialecto gitter. Quod Lat. dicitur est, Græcis sonat ἐστί, Sarmatis jest, vel gest, Germanis ist, is, & es : neque tamen huius vocis vel indicativus, vel infinitivus modus in omnibus prædicatarum gentium linguis idem vel similis est. pluralis nihilo minus indicativi apud Latinos est sunt, apud Germanos sein, seind, & sind, apud Sarmatas Polonos, sa ; quod pene idem sonat quod son. Germanis prima indicativi huius verbi est ich bin : hunc modum Angli non agnoscunt : interim tamen imperativum & subjunctivum habent be, & infinitivum to be ; quæ Germanice scripseris bie, sive bp. Sarmatæ item indicativi præteritum habent byt, & suturum bede, quasi benden ; & imperativum badz, quasi bontsch ; cum reliquis personis, ac numero : infinitivum quoque quoq; bycz, & participium bedac, quasi bendontz. Latinis idem infinitivus est esse; Germanis sein, sin, & syn; Græcis ἦ. Iisdem his ab eo indicativus est εἰμὶ, cui eadem ratione simile est Latinorum sum, ut illi ἐστὶ, Germanorum sein. sed longè propius ad εἰμὶ accedit Anglorum am. Iam verò Latinorum sum, Sarmatis est gsem, & jestem: illorum es, his sy, & jestes. Substantivus Latinorum sim, sis, sit, Germanis est sete, seten, sete. Horum atque talium, quæ innumerâ universo orbe, non modo in hanc nostram insulam, quam Europa, Asia, Africaque nominibus distinguimus, sed in Americam etiam sunt sparsa, quum nostri illi homines, qui de linguis differunt, rationem reddere omnino nequeant, quando & quomodo à gentibus ad gentes, quam longissimè inter se dissitas, sibique invicem maximè ignotas, pervenerint, casu id accidisse, tandem statuunt. Egregium sanè judicium, in re tam serià, ac gravi! De uno atque altero verbo, vel etiam tertio, ac quarto, imo de centesimo, si ita lubeat, ego concesserim. at de mille, vel etiam millibus, quis sanæ mentis homo credat? Oportet sanè, ad recurramus, quò ante dixi. nempe hæc omnia ex primævâ illâ linguâ in variis dialectis atque idiomatibus, quæ inde apud Babylonem nata sunt, perpetuò in posterum manssisse. Quamquam non negaverim, etiam postmodò quosdam vocabula à nationibus in nationes transsisse, nempe ea, quorum res ipsas antè non habuerunt, exempli gratiâ; quis non credat verbum schreiben, sive schriven nos habuisse à Romanorum scribere? quando rem ipsam ab eâdem gente primum accepimus. Sic exoticarum avium, ferarum, piscium, plantarum, aromatum, & aliarum rerum vocabula, denique artium & actionum innumeræ adpellationes in nostram invectæ fuerunt posteriovibus temporibus linguam. At earum rerum, & actionum, quæ jam inde à gentis primordio fuerunt in gente, quis temerè crediderit, vocabula Germanos non habuisse, donec ea ab exteris populis acceperint; aut, quum habuerint, postea externis permutasse? Neque enim novarum rerum tam avidi fuerunt prisci illi Germani, quàm nunc sumus, in linguis pariter ac moribus. quod cuivis, Latinos simul Græcosque rerum scriptores res res legenti, dispicere facillimum est.
units.tr: Nor, however, can the judgement of those be approved who, whenever some word in our Celtic language resembles or matches a word in Greek, Latin, Hebrew, Persian, or any other people's language, at once cry out that we have it from them. There was at the beginning one speech on earth, which all mortals used alike before the foundations of Babylon. When God, the Creator and ruler of all things, afterwards brought about the building of the city of Babylon, he did not entirely remove that speech from the earth or create new languages, but only confused, or rather scattered, it into various idioms, as said above, and various dialects. What wonder, then, if nations most diverse and most remote from one another across the whole orb of the earth still have many words in common? It would not be out of place to set before the eyes a few examples of these. The Egyptians and Arabs, the Germans, Spaniards and French, each in their own tongue, have called that supreme and true divinity, the origin of all things, Theuth; the Greeks also Theos, Deus and Zeus, and the Latins Deus. The Greeks likewise, in another dialect, together with our Germans, Dan; as will be shown by most certain documents in its proper place. The Greeks call the chief part of a man kephalē, the Chinese and the Indian nation Koppalab; the Germans Kopf, and in another dialect Kop; the Latins caput. The negative particle in Latin is non; the Germans, in various dialects, netn, neen, nee, nep, and na; this they share in common with the aforesaid Chinese: the Spanish, Italians and English no; the Sarmatians, or Slavs, ne and nie. The particle of affirmation for the Germans and the Chinese is ja. The particle which in Latin is apud is called among the Danes boo, and sometimes in Greek by the same word, hōs. What in Greek is hoti is called in Latin uti or ut; among the Danes at. What is oculus in Latin is called auge and oge by the Germans; among the Sarmatians oko. What in Latin is auris is among the Germans ooi. What in Greek is pous, in Latin is pes; among the Germans suas, as if pfuas, and in other dialects suat, foot; as the father of the Greeks and Latins is the Germans' fater. What in Greek is mētēr is called in Latin mater; among the Persians mader; among the Germans mutter, moter, mouder and moder; among the English mother; among the Sarmatians materz, macz and mati; among the Egyptians muth. What in Latin is sepes, among the Carthaginians and Hebrews is called gadir or gader; for us Germans gadder, and in another dialect gitter. What in Latin is est sounds in Greek like estí, among the Sarmatians jest or gest, among the Germans ist, is, and es. Yet the indicative or infinitive mood of this verb is not the same or similar in the languages of all the aforesaid nations. Nevertheless, the plural of the indicative among the Latins is sunt, among the Germans sein, seind and sind, among the Sarmatian Poles sa, which sounds almost the same as son. For the Germans the first person of the indicative of this verb is ich bin; the English do not recognise this mood; yet they have the imperative and subjunctive be, and the infinitive to be, which if written in German would be bie or bp. The Sarmatians likewise have the past indicative byt, and the future bede, as if benden, and the imperative badz, as if bontsch, with the remaining persons and numbers; the infinitive also is bycz, and the participle bedac, as if bendontz. For the Latins the infinitive is esse; for the Germans sein, sin and syn; for the Greeks ē. From these same forms the indicative is eimi, to which by the same reasoning the Latin sum is similar, as estí is to ... the Germans' sein. But the English am comes much closer to eimi. Now the Latin sum, in Sarmatian is gsem, and jestem; the Latin es is theirs es, and in these languages sy and jestes. The Latin subjunctive sim, sis, sit is for the Germans sete, seten, sete. Of these and such like, which are scattered in countless numbers over the whole world, not only in this our island, which we distinguish from Europe, Asia and Africa by name, but also in America, when those men of ours who dispute about languages cannot give any account at all of when and how they passed from nation to nation, most widely separated from one another and most unknown to each other, at last they decide that it happened by chance. A remarkable judgement indeed, in so serious and weighty a matter! I would concede this for one or another word, or even a third or fourth, indeed for a hundredth, if you like. But who of sound mind would believe it of a thousand, or even of thousands? It is certainly necessary to return, as I said before, to the view that all these things have remained constant from that primeval language, in its various dialects and idioms, which afterwards arose at Babylon. Yet I would not deny that afterwards also certain words passed from nation to nation, namely those whose things they did not previously have; for example, who would not believe that we got the word schreiben or schriven from the Romans' scribere, since we first received the thing itself from that same people? So too the names of exotic birds, wild beasts, fishes, plants, spices and other things, and finally the countless names of arts and actions, were brought into our language in later times. But of those things and actions which have existed among the people from its earliest beginnings, who would rashly believe that the Germans did not have words for them until they received them from foreign peoples, or, having had them, afterwards exchanged them for foreign ones? For those ancient Germans were not so eager for new things, in language or in customs, as we are now. This is easy for anyone to see who reads the Latin and Greek writers of history.

units.la: Caeterum, de primaeva illa lingua ut pauca quaedam etiam heic dicam; minimè eorum proba mihi videtur sententia, qui Hebraicam hanc fuisse statuunt: à quâ illi, non modò omneis alias per totum terrarum orbem linguas, sed nostram quoque Germanicam, id est, Celticam, derivatam arbitrantur. Hoc si verum; certè plurima pars Hebraicae linguae jam multis abhinc saeculis interiit. quippe cùm illa, quae modò retuli, tùm innumerabilia alia linguarum peritis colligere licet vocabula, quae in diversarum longissiméque remotarum gentium sermone eamdem vim, eumdémque ferè sonum habent; nullo tamen pacto ad Hebraicam originem, vel etymologiam redigi possunt. Sententia suae maximum omnium illis est argumentum, quòd hominum, qui ante terrarum inundationem, linguaeque primaevae confusionem vixerunt, propria nomina Hebraicam habeant etymologiam. Ad hoc duplici modo iis responderi potest. aut ea quoque nomina ex antiquâ illâ ac primaevâ linguâ Hebraeis mansisse; aut, quod potiùs crediderim, Hebraeos, post gentium disperfionem, ita ea sua lingua, fou dialecto nuper exorta, interpretatos esse; quum alia ac longe diversa fuerint in lingua primæva. Nam idem usu venisse in reliquis gentium linguis, quis negaverit? Equidem ego, qui alioquin in rebus divinis temere nugari, nefas duxerim, ita mecum ipse statuo; primam illam mortalium linguam nullibi adparere, nec umquam adparituram, donec, fecundum ipsius filii Dei Iesu Christi verba, qua divus Joannes in Evangelio, c.X, v.16. refert, μία fuerit omnium Dei electorum ποίμνη, εἷς ποιμήν, hoc est, unus grex, unus pastor: id est, in vita illa futura, beata, atque æterna.
units.tr: Otherwise, let me say a few things here about that primeval language. The opinion of those who hold that it was Hebrew does not seem at all right to me, the view that from it they derive not only all other languages throughout the whole world, but also our German, that is, Celtic. If this is true, then certainly the greater part of the Hebrew language perished many centuries ago. For from the words I have just mentioned, and from countless other words which those skilled in languages can gather, which have the same force and nearly the same sound in the speech of very different and far-distant peoples, yet can in no way be traced back to a Hebrew origin or etymology. Their greatest argument for their view is that the proper names of men who lived before the flood of the lands and the confusion of the primeval language have Hebrew etymologies. To this one can reply in two ways: either those names too remained to the Hebrews from that ancient and primeval language; or, what I would rather believe, after the dispersion of the nations the Hebrews interpreted those names in their own language, or in a dialect recently arisen, since in the primeval language they were quite different and of another kind. For who would deny that the same happened in the languages of the other nations? I myself, who think it wrong to trifle rashly in divine matters, hold this view: that the primeval language of mortals appears nowhere, and never will appear, until, according to the very words of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, which the divine John reports in his Gospel, chapter 10, verse 16, there is one flock of all God's elect and one shepherd [μία ποίμνη, εἷς ποιμήν]; that is, in that future life, blessed and eternal.

units.la: Pag. 202. l. 23. post tofbulbe. Talia sunt & σκώπτειν, to scoffe: (ut τὸ γελᾶν, to laugh, omittamus:) μωκᾶσθαι, to mocke: χλευάζειν, to jeere: τωθάζειν, to twit, & to taunt: σφενιλίζειν, vel φαυλίζειν, to flout: Item ἐξεσχελάειν, to raile: ἐξευτίζειν, to rate; &c. quæ qui collectionem à nobis exhibitam cum curâ legent, facile per fe observabunt. Multa enim studiosi Lectoris industriæ reliquimus.
units.tr: Page 202, line 23, after "tofbulbe": Such are also σκώπτειν, "to scoff" (to say nothing of τὸ γελᾶν, "to laugh"); μωκᾶσθαι, "to mock"; χλευάζειν, "to jeer"; τωθάζειν, "to twit" and "to taunt"; σφενιλίζειν or φαυλίζειν, "to flout"; likewise ἐξεσχελάειν, "to rail"; ἐξευτίζειν, "to rate"; and so on. Those who read our collection carefully will easily notice these for themselves. For we have left much to the diligence of the studious reader.

units.la: Pag. 208. l. 17. post, rtoge of an bill. De literâ d, inferta, vide in verbo βλέ- λὴν. κόγη ; & exempla passim in collectione, ut in λέγνον, χρῆμα, πηλὸς, &c. Plurima addi possent, ut sella, a saddle, &c. sed hoc semel dictum sit, nullam in toto Alphabeto literam aliam esse, quâ magis in formandis & transferendis ex aliâ linguâ verbis delectentur Angli. Hinc etiam in terminationibus verborum crebra, ut sonus, a sound, &c. Excidit tamen interdum, de quo plura in Ἐνδίον.
units.tr: Page 208, line 17, after "rtoge of an bill": On the letter d being inserted, see under the word βλέ- λὴν κόγη, and the examples scattered through the collection, such as λέγνον, χρῆμα, πηλὸς, etc. Many more could be added, such as "sella, a saddle", etc., but let it be said once for all that there is no other letter in the whole alphabet by which the English take more pleasure in forming and adapting words from another language. Hence also the frequent endings of words, such as "sound", etc. Yet it sometimes drops out, and more on this under Ἐνδίον.

units.la: Pag.225.l.16.post ægrotus. De verbis autem in eâdem lingua à primævâ significatione quasi defcifcentibus, & aliud alio tempore significantibus, incidi nuper in Choerobosci, Græci nescio cujus ætatis Grammatici, super eo observationem, quâ multa congeruntur istius generis verba Græca ; non indignam meo judicio, quæ hîc apponatur. Eos alloquitur τοὺς ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ τοῖς ῥήμασι καιρόνας ζητῆσαι ὡς ὁμοίωσιν ζητῆσαι: Ait autem inter alia: Εὔεσι γὰρ ἂν τις σκοπῶν λέξις πλείστας, αἳς ἄλλως ἐπ' οἱ πάλαι ἐχρῶντο ἀνθρώποι, ἄλλος δ' οἱ νῦν. Καὶ αἱ τῶν πάλαι ἔσαι ἂν χρήσει, περιεχόμεναι, ᾗ ἀπρέπειαν ἔχει ἐν ὕστερον. Ἰδὲ γὰρ τὸ τύπον βασιλικὸν ἐν ὀνόματι σεσημείωται, βλασφημεῖ νῦν. Καὶ τὸ χυδαῖοι, χυδαῖοι, οἱ πεπληθυσμένοι ἀπὸ τ χύδλω λεγόμενον, νῦν δὴ ὀνομάσιομ λαμβάνεϑ· ϰ̓ τὸ πανϑῤϛ̓ ὅτι φερνίμων λαμβανόμενον ἐπετευόν, βλασφημεῖ̓ ϑ̓ νῦν· ϰ̓ τὸ ἐξαίσιον, ϰ̓ ἐκδικικὸν τὸ ἑξῶ τ αἰσία ϰ̓ δικαίας ἐλέξελο, νῦν δ̓ ὅτι ναλλᾶ λαμβάνεϑ· ϰ̓ τὸ ἀνόσιὀ, πάλαι μ̓ τ ἄτοφον ἐδήλε, νῦν δ̓ τ ἀσεβῆ· ϰ̓ τὸ γαδυσωμένὠ, πάλαι μ̓ τ ὅσον ἐδήλε, νῦν δ̓ τ ἀφιεχωμένον· ϰ̓ τὸ γάδαρμα ἀπὸ τ χαδαίζω, ϰ̓ τὸ ἀῖσ̓, ϰ̓ τὸ ἐναγὴς ἀπὸ ἄζω τὸ σέβομαι γνώμψα, πάλαι μ̓ δὴ ἐπαινῶ ἐ-λαμβάνονλο, νῦν δ̓ ἐπ̓ λόξ· τὸ δ̓ πανα-γὴς δὴ ἐπαινῶ μόνον ἀπὸ τ αὐτὸ ἀπαγύ-μψον· ϰ̓ μυεία ἐπερα εὐεσι τῆς ἀν τοιαῦτα ἐξελάζων, ἃ χρὴ χ̓ τ ϑεσπήκονϊα λόγον ἐκάσῳ ἀνάγειν ὡς εἰς λιμένα τινὰ εἰς τοῦ ϑεσπήκονϊας ἐν τ πεσάρων τ ὀρθογραφίας κ̓-νόνων· ἀναλογίαν, φημὶ, διάλεξιον, ἐνυμο-λογίαν, ϰ̓ ἰσοείων.
units.tr: Page 225, line 16, after ægrotus. On words in the same language that gradually drift away from their original meaning and mean different things at different times: I recently came upon an observation on this point by Choeroboscus, a Greek grammarian of I know not what date, in which he gathers together many Greek words of this kind. In my judgment it is not unworthy of being set down here. He addresses those who seek the occasions of words as one seeks likenesses. He says, among other things: "For anyone examining very many words that men of old used in one sense, and men now in another, will find that the uses of the ancients, though preserved, have become unseemly later on. For instance, the word τύραννος, once a royal title, now means an insult. And vulgar [χυδαῖοι], meaning those multiplied from the adverb χύδην, is now taken as a term of reproach. And πανοῦργος, which once meant the prudent, is now the name of a vice. And ἐξαίσιον and ἔκδικον, which once signified what lies outside the right and the just, are now taken in praise. And ἀνόσιον, which once meant the unburied, now means the impious. And καθωσιωμένον, which once meant the holy, now means a consecrated person. And κάθαρμα, from καθαίρω; and ἀσ..., and ἐναγής, from ἄζω, to revere: these once were words of praise, now of reproach. Only παναγής, a word of the same origin, is still taken in the good sense. Anyone who examines a little further will find six hundred such cases, each of which, according to its nature, must be brought back to one of the four canons of correct speech, as to some safe harbour: I mean analogy, dialect, etymology, and history."

units.la: Quanquam nihil in verbis obscurum, in eorum tamen qui Græca non intelligunt, gratiam, non pigebit Latinè vertere. Porrò, si quis id sibi proponat, multas ille voces reperiet, quibus aliter usi sint veteres, quàm qui nunc sunt homines: ut eas omittam, quæ cum olim essent in usu, postea contempta penitùs exoleverunt. Ecce vox τύφανν, regium quondam nomen, nunc contumelia
units.tr: Although nothing in these words is obscure, nevertheless, for the sake of those who do not understand Greek, I will not hesitate to render it into Latin. Moreover, anyone who sets this before himself will find many words which the ancients used in a different way from how people use them now, not to mention those which, once in use, later fell wholly into contempt and disappeared. Behold the word tyrant [τύραννος], once a royal title, now an insult

units.la: De his quatuor redi fermonis canonibus plura Grammatici veteres, auctor Etymologici, aliique. contumelia verbum. Ita & το χυδαῖοι, proprie multiplicati, ex adverbio χυδλω: nunc opprobriosum: quomodo & vox πανὑρʃ⊙, prudentem olim significans, nunc vitii nomen. Ut contrà το ἰξαίσιον, & το ἐκδικον, proprie quod extra jus & fas innuentia; nunc in laude sunt. Vox ἀνό- σι⊙ quæ olim insepultum proprie significabat, nunc impium. Vox καθοσιωμένο, olim justum & sanctum; nunc antistitem. Κάθαρμα, ex verbo καθαίρω; & vox ἀσ⊙, & ἐναγὴς, ex verbo ἀζω, veneror, orta: quondam laudis, nunc improperii vocabula. Solum nunc παναγὴς ejusdem originis verbum, quod in bonam partem accipitur. Talia sexcenta qui paulo diligentius ista scrutabitur, inveniet; quæ pro cujusque natura ratione ad unum aliquem qui proprie illi competit quatuor illorum recti sermonis canonum, tanquam ad tutum aliquem portum oportet singula perducere: analogiam dico; dialectum, etymologiam, & historiam.
units.tr: Concerning these four canons of correct speech, the ancient grammarians, the author of the Etymologicum, and others say more. The word is an insult. So too vulgar [χυδαῖοι], properly "multiplied", from the adverb χύδην, is now a term of reproach; just as the word πανοῦργος [πανοῦργος], once meaning "prudent", is now the name of a vice. Conversely, ἐξαίσιον and ἔκδικον, properly meaning what lies outside law and right, are now in praise. The word ἀνόσιος, which once properly meant "unburied", now means impious. The word καθωσιωμένος, once "just and holy", now means a high priest. Κάθαρμα, from καθαίρω; and the words ἀσ... and ἐναγής, arising from ἄζω, to revere: once words of praise, now of reproach. Only παναγής, a word of the same origin, is still taken in a good sense. Anyone who examines such things a little more carefully will find six hundred such cases, each of which, according to its nature, must be brought back by reason to one of the four canons of correct speech, as to some safe harbour: I mean analogy, dialect, etymology, and history.

units.la: Pag. 232. l. 26. lege, quæ facere, operari, minist.
units.tr: Page 232, line 26: read "to do, to work, to minister".

units.la: Pag. 287. l. 18. post, to chat. Item ἀωλίνλην, sολίως ἀπαλῶν, κολακεύην, adulari, decipere; Hesychio: & κώπλ⊙, παν̃ρʃ⊙. ⲡⲁⲁⲥ̈ⲱ̈ⲥ̈ⲁⲗ, πολλαὶ, ἀλλὰ, &c. versutus, vafer, dolosus, impostor; to cheat, & a cheater. Sciat autem Lector hac additione non id agere nos, ut nostra collectio crescat, cum legenti plurima quotidie fe offerant, quæ prudens prætereo: sed quòd illa præcipuè verba sint ad id quod volumus & hoc opere suscepimus observatione ante alia digniffima, in quibus πολυσημία verbi Anglici, πολυσημία Græci respondet. Tale verbum χειμάζω, & χείμασμα; de quo pag. 211. &c. & 215. In collectione autem, multa. Vide in Λύω, & Λύω in λέγω; λύω; & ὅλλυμι; & in μανιάχης; ὀρίζω, &c. Dicam liberè, quod sentio. Vix ulla lingua, Italica, Hispanicâve, suæ traductionis indicia majora aut manifestiora suppeditat. Jam ubi de declinationibus & casuum Saxonicorum terminatione agimus, etiam de Accusativo Saxonico debuimus addere, quæ more Græco in n ut plurimùm desinere certum est. Exempla satis obvia; nec nobis nunc immorari vacat.
units.tr: Page 287, line 18, after "to chat": Likewise [ἀωλίνλην], to flatter and to deceive, in Hesychius; and [κώπλος], the rascal; "crafty", "sly", "deceitful", "impostor"; "to cheat", and "a cheater". The reader should know that by this addition we do not aim to make our collection grow, since many such words present themselves to the reader every day, which I prudently pass over. Rather, these are especially the words that serve the purpose we have set for this work, and they are the most noteworthy of all the observations, in which the many meanings of an English word correspond to the πολυσημία of the Greek. Such a word is χειμάζω and χείμασμα, on which see pages 211 and following and 215. In the collection there are many more. See under Λύω, and Λύω in λέγω; λύω; and ὅλλυμι; and under μανιάχης; ὀρίζω, etc. I will speak freely what I think: scarcely any language, Italian or Spanish, offers greater or clearer signs of its own translation. Now, when we treat of declensions and the endings of the Saxon cases, we ought also to have added something about the Saxon accusative, which, in the Greek manner, certainly mostly ends in n. Examples are obvious enough, and I have no leisure to dwell on them now.

units.la: In eorum gratiam qui Saxonicorum Lectioni non assueverunt, Alphabetum Saxonicum hic præmittendum duximus. A b c d Є є ꝼ ȝ þ ι r l ᚹ n A b c d E e f g h i k l M n o p q ꝓ δ ɼ ʋ u p x ẏ s st x o p q r S f t u w x y Æ a a Ð ð þ ꝥ ꝸ ɂ Th th th and that .
units.tr: For the benefit of those who are not accustomed to reading Saxon, we have thought it right to set out the Saxon alphabet here. Its letters, in their Saxon forms, are rendered as follows: A b c d E e f g h i k l M n; o p q r S f t u w x y Æ a a; and the sounds Th th th and that.

units.la: GUILIELMI SOMNERI, Cantuariensis, ad verba vete- ra Germanica, à V.Cl. Justo Lipsio, Epist.Cent.III. ad Belgas, Epist. XLIV. collecta: *Notæ.
units.tr: Notes by William Somner of Canterbury on the old German words, collected from the most learned Justus Lipsius, Epist. Cent. III, to the Belgians, Epist. XLIV.

units.la: Nomina.
units.tr: Nouns.

units.la: <bl>Balgi</bl>, Ira. vide <bl>Balgon</bl>] Saxonum Æbyl izny rre, aliàs Æbilhðe, quod ab eorum Æbilgian. i. exasperare, irritare, fluens, irritationem, indignationem, notat.
units.tr: Balgi, wrath. See Balgon. Saxon Æbylizny rre, otherwise Æbilhðe, which, flowing from their Æbilgian (to exasperate, to irritate), denotes irritation or indignation.

units.la: Abirthu, Postea] Sax, Æpterpham. Aratin, Curis. ut Galli Rufes.
units.tr: Abirthu, afterwards. Saxon Æpterpham. Aratin, cares, as the French say Rufes.

units.la: Adzo, Diluculo] Hodie nobis Rath.
units.tr: Adzo, early in the morning. Today we have Rath.

units.la: After, Secundùm] Quâ acceptione vox ista nobis Anglis vel hodie nota. Saxonibus Æfteɼ.
units.tr: After, according to. In this sense the word is known to us English even today. Saxon Æfteɼ.

units.la: After allo, Ufquequaque] Videtur esse after all.
units.tr: After allo, everywhere. It seems to be the English "after all".

units.la: Abtugo, Numerum.
units.tr: Abtugo, number.

units.la: Alendt, Insulæ] Rectiùs forte Alendt, cui vicinum Saxonum ealono, quasi waterlanD; voce conflata ex ea, Sax. aqua,& lono,(nobis hodie land) terra. Terra scil. aqua circumsepta, alio nomine ɩʒope, (unde forte nostratium eigbt, eo sensu) ut & ɩʒlanD,unde nostrum Iland, g. extrito.
units.tr: Alendt, islands. More correctly perhaps Alendt, near which is the Saxon ealono, as if "waterland", a word compounded of it: Saxon aqua (water) and lono (for us now "land"), land. That is, land surrounded by water; by another name ɩʒope (whence perhaps our "eight" in that sense), and ɩʒlanD, whence our "Iland", with the g dropped.

units.la: Aleiven, Reliquiæ] Eopse sensu Saxonibus lapa, Vidua etiam hinc eis dicta lap, quasi quondam viri sui Relicta. Hinc porro nostratium to leave, pro relinquere.
units.tr: Aleiven, remains. In this sense the Saxons have lapa. A widow was also called lap by them, as if she were the relict of her husband. Hence too our "to leave", meaning to relinquish.

units.la: Ambacptman, Ministri: quod Cæsar & Festus Clientem Gallis significare notant] Sax. embebywman, ab eorum embeaɧtian, ministrare.
units.tr: Ambacptman, ministers; which Caesar and Festus note means "client" in Gaulish. Saxon embebywman, from their embeaɧtian, to minister.

units.la: Anagen, Principium : & Annagent, Initio] Hoc Sax. anzynp, cui vicinum Teutonicorum angeben: sic nos dicimus (inquit Martinius in Etymol.) angeben pro inchoare. Nobis hoc Be- gi nning.
units.tr: Anagen, beginning; and Annagent, at the start. This is Saxon anzynp, near which is the Teutonic angeben: "so we say" (says Martinius in his Etymology) angeben for to begin. For us this is "beginning".

units.la: Anbarpon, Ascia] Vide Martinii Etymologicum in voce Martiqbarbnlus.
units.tr: Anbarpon, adze. See Martinius's Etymologicum under the word Martiqbarbnlus.

units.la: <bl>Anfrefon</bl>, Interritus] Vide <bl>Fret-</bl> <bl>son</bl>.
units.tr: Anfrefon, fearless. See Fretson.

units.la: Ando, Zelus. Vide Andopa,verbum] Sax.anoa, ab eorum anoian, zelare. Anliton, vultus] Saxon. anoplıτε, quandoque plıτε, quod etiam eis decorem significabat.
units.tr: Ando, zeal. See Andopa, the verb. Saxon anoa, from their anoian, to be zealous. Anliton, face; Saxon anoplıτε, sometimes plıτε, which also signified beauty to them.

units.la: Anlocce, Facie. Vide Anloccon, verbum] Vultum alicujus nos dicimus looke, ut Speculum, a Looking-glasse, à Saxon.locian, videre, aspicere: Vultu sic dicto, quasi parte corporis visui magis obvia: unde forte Facies Saxonibus alias dicta anrine, à ʒerːeon, videre.
units.tr: Anlocce, face. See Anloccon, the verb. We call a person's countenance "look", as a mirror is a "looking-glass", from the Saxon locian, to see, to look at: the face is so called as the part of the body most open to sight. Whence perhaps the Saxons otherwise called the face anrine, from ʒerːeon, to see.

units.la: Anfomi, Fraenum: nunc Loom] Ab eâdem forsan origine nostrum Lame, i. e. mansuetus; Saxonibus & prisicis & modernis ᴛam,uti & Belgis, Germanis autem (Z. pro T. amantibus) Zam. Quæ omnia, unà cum Belg. Lammen, i.e. mansuefacere, ni fallor, veniunt à Latinorum Domo: quòd Fræno dometur, saltem cohibeatur, equus. Atque inde fortean aggerem fluminibus objectum, cum Belgis Dam vocamus.
units.tr: Anfomi, bridle: now loom. From the same origin, perhaps, is our "lame", i.e. tame; for the Saxons, both old and modern, have ᴛam, as do the Belgians, and the Germans (who love Z for T) have Zam. All of these, together with the Belgian lammen, i.e. to tame, unless I am mistaken, come from the Latin domo: because the horse is tamed, or at least restrained, by the bridle. And hence perhaps the embankment thrown up against rivers we call dam, as the Belgians do.

units.la: Anst, Gratia: alibi, Enst.
units.tr: Anst, grace: elsewhere Enst.

units.la: Angust, Angustia] Sax.anzny̆r, & anzrumnerre. Teutonicis modernis Angst.
units.tr: Angust, anguish. Saxon anzny̆r and anzrumnerre. For modern Teutonic Angst.

units.la: Anbarnunst, Intelleƈtu.
units.tr: Anbarnunst, understanding.

units.la: At, Escas. Vide Atona, verbum] Edere, dere, manducare, Sax. /Ætan; al.eᵹan, unde nostrum to eate, illo sensu: Teutonicis aet & aes. Edax Saxonibus /Ætulman [?].
units.tr: At, food. See Atona, the verb. To eat, devour, chew: Saxon /Ætan; also ᵹan, whence our "to eat" in that sense; Teutonic aet and aes. A glutton among the Saxons is /Ætulman [?].

units.la: <bl>Asca</bl>, Cinis] Saxonibus <bl>/Æxe</bl>; pluraliter <bl>/Æxan</bl>, <bl>aɥran</bl> [?]. Hoc Belgis modernis <bl>Asche</bl>; nobis hodie <bl>Ashes</bl>. Unde de Cineralia, <bl>Ashwednesday</bl> dicimus; Belg. <bl>Aschenwoensdach</bl>.
units.tr: Asca, ashes. Saxon /Æxe; plural /Æxan, aɥran [?]. This is Asche to the modern Belgians; for us today it is "ashes". Whence we call Ash Wednesday the day of ashes; Belgian Aschenwoensdach.

units.la: Andzan, vel Andarn, In vanum: nonne Italorum est Indarno?
units.tr: Andzan, or Andarn, in vain: is this not the Italian indarno?

units.la: <bl>Asgetalt</bl>, Oblivioni] Vocabulum (ut videtur) ejusdem prosapiæ ac Sax. <bl>ofenzÿtolnerre</bl>, quod eádem venit acceptione; nobis hodie, <bl>forgetful-</bl> <bl>nesse</bl>. Belg. <bl>vergbetentisse</bl>. Germ. <bl>vergessenheit</bl>.
units.tr: Asgetalt, to oblivion. A word (as it seems) of the same stock as the Saxon ofenzÿtolnerre, which has the same meaning; for us today "forgetfulness". Belgian vergbetentisse. German vergessenheit.

units.la: <bl>Ana</bl>, Extra vel Præter] Huic affine Sax. & nostrum <bl>Un</bl>, uti & Teutonicor. <bl>Dn</bl>, de quo vide Kilian. Etymolog. in <bl>Dn</bl>.
units.tr: Ana, outside or beyond. Akin to this is the Saxon and our "Un", as also the Teutonic Dn, on which see Kilian's Etymologicon under Dn.

units.la: <bl>Arug</bl>, Perversa: nos <bl>Arg</bl>] Hac de voce vide doctiss. Spelmanni Glossar. in <bl>Arga</bl>.
units.tr: Arug, perverse: we say "arg". On this word see the most learned Spelman's Glossary under Arga.

units.la: <bl>Amanendelken</bl>, Intolerabilem.
units.tr: Amanendelken, intolerable.

units.la: Verba.
units.tr: Verbs.

units.la: <bl>Afterthunsan</bl>, Detrahebant. <bl>Aftret-thunsandt</bl>,
units.tr: Afterthunsan, they detracted. Aftret-thunsandt,

units.la: thonsanbt, Detrahentes] Forte à Sax. /Ἐρτεψ,retro, & τεον, trahere; quibus etiam ορτεον pro detrahere.
units.tr: thonsanbt, detracting. Perhaps from the Saxon /Ἐρτεψ, back, and τεον, to draw [ἐρτεψ, τεον]; with which also ορτεον, to detract [ορτεον].

units.la: Abtidon, Perfecuti sunt] Ejusdem originis vox ista ac Saxonum εħτan, perfequi.
units.tr: Abtidon, they pursued. This word is of the same origin as the Saxon εħτan, to pursue.

units.la: Alβutt, Illumina] Aflonat Saxon. onlihte, quod ab eorum onlihtan fluens,illuminare fignat: unde noftrum to lighten, alias enlighten: quemadmodum etiam à Saxonum leohte, (quod Belgis light, Germanis lucht) Lux, noftratium light. Lightning autem, i.e. Fulmen,ab eorum lez.
units.tr: Alβutt, illuminate. Aflonat, Saxon onlihte, which, flowing from their onlihtan, means to illuminate: whence our "to lighten", otherwise "enlighten". Just so, from the Saxon leohte (which the Belgians call light, the Germans lucht), comes our "light". "Lightning", i.e. thunderbolt, is from their lez.

units.la: Anaftanbant, Infurgunt. Anaftan- danban,Infurgentibus] Huic affine noftrum gainstand,quod opponere sonat, compositum à Sax. onzen, azen, vel onzean, nobis against, adversus, & rtanbian,stare. Saxonibus autem, insurgere, onapiran, quod Latino propius; cum on hic, ut in istis vocibus ana, valeat in, i.e. adversus, & apiran, (unde noftratium arise) surgere.
units.tr: Anaftanbant, they rise up against. Anaftandanban, rising up against. Akin to this is our "gainstand", meaning to oppose, compounded from the Saxon onzen, azen, or onzean (now "against" for us), and tanbian, to stand. But for the Saxons, to rise up is onapiran, which is closer to the Latin; since on here, as in these words ana, means "in", i.e. against, and apiran (whence our "arise") means to rise.

units.la: Anartepon, Irruerunt]-Scribendum forte anartefon. Intellige onartfan, de quo jam dictum.
units.tr: Anartepon, they rushed in. Perhaps it should be written anartefon. Understand onartfan, of which already spoken.

units.la: Andzeott, Timet] Ab eadem origi-
units.tr: Andzeott, he fears. From the same origin

units.la: ne hoc, cum tribus vocibus proximè sequentibus, viz. Andzedandt, Andza- danDozo, Andzadondt, ac Saxonum onopæoian, timere. Hinc autem nostrum Dzead, (nomen) Timor; to Dzead, (verbum) timere, & similia. Inter cætera Dzead, & Dzad, regibus nostris in partem tituli attributum, veluti ob sacram ipsorum majestatem tremendis. Hinc etiam forte sylvæ illius Cantianis & Suffexianis communis, Ethelwerdo immanis dictæ, nomen apud Sax. Andzed, alias Andzefwald, q. d. Sylva terribilis; wald enim, sylva.
units.tr: ...this, together with the three words immediately following, viz. Andzedandt, Andzadandozo, Andzadondt, and the Saxon onopæoian, to fear. Hence our "Dzead" (noun), fear; "to Dzead" (verb), to fear, and similar forms. Among other things, Dzead and Dzad were attributed to our kings as part of their title, as those to be dreaded because of their sacred majesty. Hence perhaps also that forest, common to the Kentish and Sussex people, called "immanis" by Ethelwerd, whose name among the Saxons is Andzed, otherwise Andzefwald, that is, a terrible forest; for wald means forest.

units.la: <bl>Anlocon</bl>, Aperuerunt: ficut <bl>Belu-con</bl>, Concluserunt] Priori affine nostrum <bl>to unlocke</bl>, referare: posterius autem Teutonicis priscis (ut videtur) cum Saxonibus commune; quibus concludere, belucan, Verstegano noftro belokeη; seratum autem, & firmè claufum, belocuo, unde noftrum <bl>lock-</bl> <bl>ed</bl>. Vox hîc subsequens, <bl>Antloc</bl>, Revela, ab eâdem, ni fallor, est origine, ac <bl>Anlucon</bl>, hic.
units.tr: Anlocon, they opened: as Belucon, they shut up. The former is akin to our "to unlock", to unbar; the latter (as it seems) was common to the early Teutons with the Saxons, for whom to shut up is belucan (Verstegan, our belokeη). A thing barred and firmly closed is belocuo, whence our "locked". The word that follows here, Antloc, reveal, is from the same origin, I think, as Anlucon here.

units.la: <bl>Antbeban</bl>, Prohibebo. <bl>Antbatta</bl>, Prohibui.
units.tr: Antbeban, I shall forbid. Antbatta, I forbade.

units.la: B
units.tr: B

units.la: <bl>Balon</bl>, Cicatrices] Huic affine, & nostrum, & Teutonic. vet. <bl>Blowe</bl>, i.e. Alapa, ictus.
units.tr: <bl>Balon</bl>, scars. Akin to this are both our own word and the old Teutonic <bl>blowe</bl>, that is, a slap or blow.

units.la: <bl>Baldo</bl>, & alibi <bl>Bolatico</bl>, Fiducialiter] Audax, Saxon. balo, audaciter, balolic, unde nostratium <bl>bold</bl>, & <bl>bold-</bl> <bl>lp</bl>. Hoc Teutonicis modernis <bl>boude</bl>, priscis autem, uti Sax. bald. Kilian.
units.tr: <bl>Baldo</bl>, and elsewhere <bl>bolatico</bl>, boldly. Saxon <bl>balo</bl>, boldly; <bl>balolic</bl>, bold, whence our English <bl>bold</bl> and <bl>bold-</bl>. Modern Germans have <bl>boude</bl> for this, but earlier, as in Saxon, <bl>bald</bl>. Kilian.

units.la: <bl>Begtbte</bl>, Confessione: nos <bl>bichte</bl>. Vide <bl>begigan</bl> verbum, & <bl>Bief</bl>.
units.tr: <bl>Begtbte</bl>, confession: we say <bl>bichte</bl>. See the verb <bl>begigan</bl> and <bl>Bief</bl>.

units.la: <bl>Bebatuo</bl>, Retrorsum.
units.tr: <bl>Bebatuo</bl>, backwards.

units.la: <bl>Befuicbetce</bl>, Scandalum] Æjpic, al. zerpic, & Æppicunge, Saxonibus scandalum, offendiculum: berpic autem eis pro fraude.
units.tr: <bl>Befuicbetce</bl>, scandal. Saxon <bl>æjpic</bl>, others <bl>zerpic</bl> and <bl>æppicunge</bl>, meaning scandal or a stumbling block; <bl>berpic</bl>, however, meant fraud to them.

units.la: <bl>Betbin</bl>, alias <bl>bitbin</bl>, Propterea.
units.tr: <bl>Betbin</bl>, otherwise <bl>bitbin</bl>, therefore.

units.la: <bl>Billibires</bl>, Figuli: & <bl>Bebillte</bl>, Imagine] Saxon. Imago bilipe, Belgis <bl>beeld</bl>, Teuton. <bl>bilot</bl>. Saxon. modernis {*}similiter. Hinc autem forte nostrum <bl>tlp</bl>, & <bl>bill</bl>, E. G. <bl>to knotw one</bl> <bl>bp bis blp</bl>, <bl>o} bill</bl>, i.e. ex vultus fui forma aliquem cognoscere.
units.tr: <bl>Billibires</bl>, potters; and <bl>Bebillte</bl>, image. Saxon <bl>bilipe</bl>, image; Dutch <bl>beeld</bl>, Teutonic <bl>bilot</bl>. Modern Saxon is similar. Hence perhaps our <bl>bill</bl>, and the phrase <bl>to know one</bl> by the form of his face, that is, to recognise someone from the look of his countenance.

units.la: <bl>Bitute</bl>, Quare?] Hoc Saxon. <bl>topry</bl>, uti & <bl>popbpy</bl>. Posterius integrè quidam nostratium hodieque retinent; alii autem, brevitatis gratiâ posteriorem tantum syllabam, literis paululum inverfis, pro Sax. þpý, scribentes tobp.
units.tr: <bl>Bitute</bl>, why? This is Saxon <bl>topry</bl>, and also <bl>popbpy</bl>. Some of our people still keep the latter word whole; others, for brevity, keep only its last syllable, with the letters slightly reversed, writing it <bl>tobp</bl> for Saxon <bl>þpý</bl>.

units.la: Blsmer, Opprobrium] Vocem ufurparunt Saxones, præcipuè verò, (ut nos Blaspbemp) pro contumeliâ in Deum, rpnæc addito: calumniam tamen & contumeliam generatim signat.
units.tr: Blsmer, reproach. The Saxons borrowed this word, and especially (as we have blaspheme) used it for insult against God, with rpnæc added; yet it generally signifies slander and insult.

units.la: Btsa, Turba: ut Gall. Vent de Bize] Vide Kilian. verb. bpse, & bpsen. Turbatus Sax. abyrʒóƀ.
units.tr: Btsa, a crowd, as the French say vent de bise. See Kilian under bpse and bpsen. Saxon abyrʒóƀ, troubled.

units.la: Btspilla, & alibi Spella, Parabola] Eâpse notione Sax. bizrpelle. Posterior hujus compositi syllaba (vox enim est composita) Historiam, Narrationem, imprimis notans, in pluribus aliis eorum vocibus reperitur, cujusmodi sunt Lanrpelle, i.e. doctrina, à læpan, docere, (non lepnen, ut Minshæus noster, pro more suo perperam:) yoelrpelle, i. e. vana colloquia, ab yoel, vanus: zoorpelle, i.e. Evangelium.
units.tr: Btspilla, and elsewhere Spella, parable. With the same meaning, Saxon bizrpelle. The last syllable of this compound word, which signifies history or narrative in particular, is found in many other of their words: Lanrpelle, that is, doctrine, from læpan, to teach (not lepnen, as our Minshaeus wrongly has it in his usual way); yoelrpelle, that is, vain conversations, from yoel, vain; zoorpelle, that is, the Gospel.

units.la: Blafma, Flamma] Nos blaʒe eodem sensu, forte à Belg. blaefen, i. e. flare, fufflare, quòd fufflatione venti flamma fovetur. Saxon. Funale, blara; Incendiarius, blýrʒepe.
units.tr: Blafma, flame. We use blaze in the same sense, perhaps from Dutch blaefen, that is, to blow or puff, because the flame is fed by the puffing of the wind. Saxon for torch is blara; for incendiary, blyrʒepe.

units.la: Buokestaf, Literatura; vel potiùs ipsa Litera] ῥταϝ & bocρταϝ eodem sensu usi Saxones, uti boecftaf, & boec- ftabe, Teutonici. Vocis derivationem vide, si placet, in Wormii Literatura Runica, c. 1. Psalmorum Anglicorum, cantandi gratiâ, in metrum, ut vulgò vocant, translatorum sectiones sive partitiones, Italis stanza, Gallis stanze, hodie vocamus stabes: & ῥταχεποχτο in Bedæ Historiâ Saxon. artem signat metricam, (al. Grammaticam.)
units.tr: Buokestaf, literature, or rather the letter itself. The Saxons used ῥταϝ and bocρταϝ in the same sense, as did the Teutonic peoples with boecstaf and boecstabe. If you like, see the derivation of the word in Wormius's Literatura Runica, ch. 1. The divisions or partitions of the English Psalms translated into what are commonly called metrum, for singing, the Italians call stanza, the French stanze; today we call them stabes. And the Saxon word ῥταχεποχτο in Bede's History denotes the metrical art (others read grammar).

units.la: <bl>Barg</bl>tt, Sepulchrum: quasi tegmen hominum & operculum] Huic affine Saxonum bÿῤʒen, eodem sensu: hinc autem sic dictum, quòd aggesto in collem cespite, olim tumulabant mortuos, ut per agros hodie cernimus. Nam Colles illi, quibusdam <bl>barrowes</bl> dicti, antiquorum plerumque sunt tumuli cum nondum bÿῤʒenῥτοpa, i.e. cæmeteria in usu essent.
units.tr: <bl>Barg tt</bl>, sepulchre: as if the covering and lid of men. Akin to this is the Saxon <bl>bÿῤʒen</bl>, with the same meaning. It is so called because, with turf heaped up into a hill, the dead were formerly buried, as we see today across the fields. For those hills, which some call <bl>barrowes</bl>, are mostly ancient burial mounds, from the time when <bl>bÿῤʒenῥτοpa</bl>, that is, cemeteries, were not yet in use.

units.la: <bl>Barthon</bl>, Oneribus] Saxonum bÿῤben, & bÿῤbÿn, unde nostrum <bl>burden</bl>, & <bl>burthen</bl>, pro onere. Belgis hoc <bl>boj-</bl> <bl>dene</bl>, Teuton. <bl>burd</bl>. Kilian.
units.tr: <bl>Barthon</bl>, burdens. Saxon <bl>bÿῤben</bl> and <bl>bÿῤbÿn</bl>, whence our <bl>burden</bl> and <bl>burthen</bl> for a load. Among the Dutch this is <bl>bordene</bl>, and Teutonic <bl>burd</bl>. Kilian.

units.la: <bl>Baterie</bl>, Uter: & <bl>butrice</bl>, Utrem] Hoc Sax. bÿτπε, & bιτπε, unde forte noftratium, & <bl>bottle</bl>, & <bl>butt</bl>: posterius rius vini, potúsque menfura cœnopolis familiaris.
units.tr: <bl>Baterie</bl>, a leather bottle; and <bl>butrice</bl>, a small bottle. Saxon <bl>bÿτπε</bl> and <bl>bιτπε</bl>, whence perhaps among our people both <bl>bottle</bl> and <bl>butt</bl>; the latter being a common cellar measure of wine and drink.

units.la: Verba.
units.tr: Verbs.

units.la: <bl>Bartha</bl>, Germinans] Parere, Sax. bæpan ; unde pertumbæpeno, fructifer : cpeop pærtimbæpu, Ligna fructifera : unbæpeno, sterilis. Hinc Anglis aquilonaribus & Scotis, <bl>harne</bl>, pro sobole, quod Saxon. bæpne, Parere, vel hodie nobis <bl>to beare</bl>.
units.tr: <bl>Bartha</bl>, bearing. To bear, Saxon <bl>bæpan</bl>; whence <bl>pertumbæpeno</bl>, fruitful; <bl>cpeop pærtimbæpu</bl>, fruit-bearing trees; <bl>unbæpeno</bl>, barren. Hence the northern English and Scots say <bl>harne</bl> for offspring, which is from Saxon <bl>bæpne</bl>, to bear; today we have <bl>to beare</bl>.

units.la: <bl>Befillict</bl>, Profterneret] Sax. apil-lan, præcipitare, unde noftrum <bl>to fall</bl>, i. e. cadere ; item <bl>to fell</bl> ; dejicere, de quâ voce plura infrà in <bl>felloⁿ fal</bl>.
units.tr: <bl>Befillict</bl>, would throw down. Saxon <bl>apil-lan</bl>, to cast headlong, whence our <bl>to fall</bl>, that is, to drop; likewise <bl>to fell</bl>, to bring down. More on this word below under <bl>felloⁿ fal</bl>.

units.la: <bl>Beko</bl>, Proba: alibi <bl>bekunno</bl>, Tentâ] Probare, Saxon. acunnian. Atque hinc forsan noftrum <bl>conting of a</bl> <bl>letton</bl>, <bl>or part</bl>, quando scil. quis id quod dicturus est, sibi recenset, experiundi gratiâ utrum id memoriter didicit, necne.
units.tr: <bl>Beko</bl>, prove; elsewhere <bl>bekunno</bl>, tempted or tested. To prove, Saxon <bl>acunnian</bl>. And hence perhaps our phrase <bl>conting of a letton</bl>, or <bl>or part</bl>, when someone recites to himself what he is about to say, to test whether he has learned it by heart or not.

units.la: <bl>Begegunsta</bl>, Cœpi] Hoc Saxonibus, Verstegano teste, onzan: longè autem propiùs noftrum <bl>began</bl>. Utriusque origo à Sax. onzinnan, Belg. <bl>beginnen</bl>, incipere.
units.tr: <bl>Begegunsta</bl>, I began. The Saxons had this, as Verstegan testifies, as <bl>onzan</bl>; but our <bl>began</bl> is much closer. Both derive from Saxon <bl>onzinnan</bl>, Dutch <bl>beginnen</bl>, to begin.

units.la: <bl>Begtan</bl>, & <bl>befan</bl>, Confiteri.
units.tr: <bl>Begtan</bl> and <bl>befan</bl>, to confess.

units.la: <bl>Behofcodon</bl>, Subfannaverunt : vide <bl>Pofce</bl>.
units.tr: <bl>Behofcodon</bl>, they mocked. See <bl>Pofce</bl>.

units.la: <bl>Belgiftruthi</bl>,
units.tr: <bl>Belgiftruthi</bl>,

units.la: <bl>Belgiautbt</bl>, Irafcēre] Quod ad hoc & duo proximè præcedentia verba,(belgon,& belgon sal) vide <bl>Abalgt</bl>, supra.
units.tr: <bl>Belgiautbt</bl>, to be angry. For this word and the two immediately preceding it (<bl>belgon</bl> and <bl>belgon sal</bl>), see <bl>Abalgt</bl> above.

units.la: <bl>Befcedltolt</bl>, Obscurabitur: quasi à <bl>schadatoe</bl>, Umbra]. Ab eādem origine nostrum <bl>thadatw</bl>, Saxonibus rcaoupe? Teutonicis hodie <bl>befchaedatwen</bl>, obumbrare, Sax. rceaopian?
units.tr: <bl>Befcedltolt</bl>, will be darkened, as if from <bl>schadatoe</bl>, shade. From the same origin comes our <bl>thadatw</bl>; the Saxons had <bl>rcaoupe</bl>, and the Teutonic peoples today have <bl>befchaedatwen</bl>, to overshadow, Saxon <bl>rceaopian</bl>.

units.la: <bl>Befcurgt</bl>, Præcipita: & <bl>befco?gin-</bl> <bl>gun</bl>, Præcipitationis. vide <bl>Discurgtdt</bl>.
units.tr: <bl>Befcurgt</bl>, cast down headlong; and <bl>befco?gingun</bl>, of headlong throwing. See <bl>Discurgtdt</bl>.

units.la: <bl>Befuebet</bl>, Soporatus] Somnus, sopor, somnium, Saxon. rpepn, & rpe-pene?
units.tr: <bl>Befuebet</bl>, lulled to sleep. Sleep, drowsiness, and dream: Saxon <bl>rpepn</bl>, and <bl>rpe-pene?</bl>.

units.la: <bl>Befulck</bl>, supplanta. Suprà, <bl>befbf-</bl> <bl>cbetde</bl>, Scandalum] Saxonico convenit berpican, supplantare.
units.tr: <bl>Befulck</bl>, supplanted. Above, <bl>befbf-cbetde</bl>, scandal: the Saxon <bl>berpican</bl>, to supplant, agrees with it.

units.la: .<bl>Bethadon</bl>, Absconderunt, alibi <bl>be-baton</bl>, idem] Saxonico respondet hyoan, behyoan, Belg. <bl>boeden</bl>, abscondere,tegere; unde nostrum hodiernum <bl>bide</bl>, sive <bl>to bide</bl>, illo sensu.
units.tr: <bl>Bethadon</bl>, they hid; elsewhere <bl>bebaton</bl>, the same. The Saxon <bl>hyoan</bl>, and <bl>behyoan</bl>, corresponds, Dutch <bl>boeden</bl>, to hide, to cover; whence our modern <bl>bide</bl>, or <bl>to bide</bl>, in that sense.

units.la: <bl>Bethumendero</bl>, Deprimentium.
units.tr: <bl>Bethumendero</bl>, of depressors.

units.la: <bl>Bitpollon</bl>, Infecta: <bl>bitpollona</bl>, Inquinatæ: <bl>bitpellan</bl>, Prophanabo] Quasi à <bl>tupl</bl>, Teutonicis, turpis, forȷdidus, immundus, quod nobis hodie <bl>fotole</bl>,Sax. pul? Inquinatum quid dicimus <bl>befolwillen</bl>. pedem notans, <bl>Cripple</bl> ; qui repere potiùs quàm ire videtur. Repere autem Saxonibus modernis ( ut mihi author est Martinius in Etymologico) <bl>krupen.</bl>
units.tr: <bl>Bitpollon</bl>, polluted; <bl>bitpollona</bl>, defiled; <bl>bitpellan</bl>, I shall profane. As if from <bl>tupl</bl>, Teutonic turpis, foul, filthy, unclean, which we today call <bl>fotole</bl>; Saxon <bl>pul</bl>? We say a thing is defiled by <bl>befolwillen</bl>. Denoting a foot, <bl>Cripple</bl>, one who seems to crawl rather than walk. Modern Saxons, as Martinius in his Etymologicon tells me, say <bl>krupen</bl> for to creep.

units.la: <bl>Bannea</bl>, & <bl>kunnt</bl>, Generatio] Vide supra, <bl>kunnt.</bl>
units.tr: <bl>Bannea</bl> and <bl>kunnt</bl>, generation. See <bl>kunnt</bl> above.

units.la: <bl>Buofmeer</bl>, Butyrum] Compositum exiftimo à <bl>kuo</bl>, Saxonibus prifcis cu, modernis <bl>koe</bl>, Germanis <bl>kub</bl>, nobis <bl>cotu</bl>; & <bl>fmeer</bl>, Sax. <bl>ymype</bl>, & <bl>ymeppe</bl>; unguen, ab ungo fluente. Ungere autem nobis hodie <bl>to fpieao</bl>; & <bl>fmeare</bl>; Teuton. <bl>fmeeten</bl>, ut butyrum, praesertim inter edendum, solet. Unde mangonizantes in Caseo & Butyro, Sax. <bl>ymepemanzeptpe</bl> dicti. <bl>Buofmeer</bl>, itaque est quasi unguen vaccinum, sive quod à vacca venit. Butyrum autem Saxon. <bl>butepa</bl> dictum.
units.tr: <bl>Buofmeer</bl>, butter. I think it is compounded of <bl>kuo</bl>, which was <bl>cu</bl> for the ancient Saxons, <bl>koe</bl> for the moderns, <bl>kub</bl> for the Germans, and <bl>cotu</bl> for us; and <bl>smeer</bl>, Saxon <bl>ymype</bl> and <bl>ymeppe</bl>, an unguent, from <bl>ungo</bl>, flowing. To anoint, we today say <bl>to spieao</bl>, and <bl>smeare</bl>; Teutonic <bl>smeeten</bl>, as butter is usually spread, especially while eating. Whence those who deal in cheese and butter were called in Saxon <bl>ymepemanzeptpe</bl>. <bl>Buofmeer</bl>, then, is as it were cow's unguent, or that which comes from the cow. Butter was called <bl>butepa</bl> in Saxon.

units.la: Verba.
units.tr: Words.

units.la: <bl>Beftegoda</bl>, Anxit : an à castigando? <bl>Cozodos</bl>, Probasti.
units.tr: Beftegoda, anxious (perhaps from castigating?). Cozodos, thou hast proved.

units.la: <bl>Criedon</bl>, Cognoverunt.
units.tr: Criedon, they knew.

units.la: <bl>Bfaunt</bl>, Diabolus : quasi de <bl>bpandt</bl>.
units.tr: Bfaunt, the devil, as if from bpandt.

units.la: Anglis <bl>the Feind</bl>. De quo Versteg.
units.tr: In English, the Feind. On which see Verstegan.

units.la: Dzohttin, & Dzathttin, & Dzuttin, Dominus. Dzuttene, Domino] Saxon. ὀρηθ, & ὀρῠθεν, vox (ut Verstegano monitum) non omni Domino communis; sed Domino Dominorum, Deo scil. propria & peculiaris, de cujus etymo pluribus Martinius in Etymolog. verbo Deus.
units.tr: Dzohttin, Dzathttin and Dzuttin, Lord. Dzuttene, to the Lord: Saxon orth and orthen.
